items.title: RSA: integer primitives, CRT correctness and encoding schemes
items.text: Algorithm : RSA (RSA 公钥密码). RSA begins with paired modular-exponentiation operations on integers. Encryption and signatures need different encodings, parameters and validation rules on top. This article covers algorithm--rsa, restricted to two-prime RSA, then explains its use by OAEP and PSS. It does not complete the RFC 8017 catalog entry or provide a deployable cryptographic service. Octet strings and integer representatives Let modBits be n's bit length and k=ceil(modBits/8) its octet length. RSAEP accepts m and returns c in 0…n−1; RSADP inverts ciphertext representatives in that range. Zero and representatives sharing a factor with n are not excluded. An out-of-range value is an error: silently reducing it would alias distinct supplied inputs. The user message M is an octet string. OS2IP interprets it as a nonnegative big-endian integer. I2OSP(x, len) returns exactly len big-endian octets, including leading zeroes, and fails if x≥256^len. These are representation conversions, not confidentiality, padding or authentication. Both 00 41 and 41 represent 65, so a separate length convention matters. RSAES ciphertexts and RSASSA signatures use k octets; internal encoded-message lengths depend on the scheme. Conditions on a two-prime key Take distinct odd primes p, q, set n=pq, φ(n)=(p−1)(q−1) and λ(n)=lcm(p−1, q−1). RFC 8017 requires 3≤e<n and gcd(e,λ(n))=1; its own wording is integer between 3 and n - 1 satisfying GCD(e,\lambda(n)) = 1 (retained text rfc8017.txt:457-458), with private exponent 0<d<n satisfying ed≡1 modulo λ(n). This inverse is modular, not the fraction 1/e. Inversion modulo φ(n) also supplies a correct exponent because λ(n) divides φ(n), but the moduli should not be conflated. These arithmetic and representation conditions are not a complete secure key-generation procedure. Distinctness, primality and exponent coprimality need checking; real generation also involves randomness, prime testing, parameter constraints and key lifecycle. Neither historical size suggestions nor successful round trips establish secure deployment parameters. Correctness includes non-coprime representatives Write ed=1+t λ(n). For r=p or q, split the argument. If r divides m, both m^ed and m are zero modulo r. Otherwise Fermat's theorem gives m^(r−1)≡1; since r−1 divides λ(n), m^ed≡m modulo r. Coprimality of p, q lets CRT give a unique corresponding integer in 0…n−1, hence (m^e)^d modn=m. This never assumes every message is invertible. Applying Euler's theorem indiscriminately would miss multiples of a prime factor. The program exhausts all 3233 representatives, including 113 non-coprime ones counting zero. This checks the finite example, not the general theorem. Direct exponentiation and CRT Repeated squaring evaluates modular powers while reducing intermediate values, without constructing the full unreduced power. A private representation can store dP=d mod(p−1), dQ=d mod(q−1), qInv=q^(−1) modp. Compute m1=c^dP modp, m2=c^dQ modq, then h=((m1−m2)qInv) modp and m=m2+qh. With h in 0…p−1, m is in 0…pq−1 and has the required residues. Here qInv is q's inverse modulo p; another CRT convention must be transformed before these equations are used. Smaller moduli can accelerate operations, but no fixed fourfold speedup is universally guaranteed. Anyone knowing(n, e) can compute the public-direction power, while correct private material enables inversion. Knowing p, q yields λ(n) and an appropriate d, so the factors must remain secret. This implication does not prove that every RSA inversion algorithm is equivalent to factoring. The latter must not be presented as a general established theorem. An integer permutation, encryption scheme, signature scheme, certificate and protocol solve different problems. OAEP encodes before encryption; PSS builds a checkable signature representative. Binding an identity to a key needs authentication and protocol context. Raw RSA correctness therefore yields neither modern confidentiality nor an unforgeability guarantee. In RFC 8017's convention choose Hash with hLen-octet output, an MGF and label L. Require mLen≤k−2hLen−2. Form lHash=Hash(L) and DB=lHash PS 01 M, with zero padding PS. Generate an hLen-octet random seed; mask DB using MGF(seed, k−hLen−1), then seed using MGF(maskedDB, hLen). Set EM=00 maskedSeed maskedDB, convert it to m, compute c=m^e modn, and output C=I2OSP(c, k). MGF1 hashes its input followed by four-octet big-endian counters 0,1,…, concatenates outputs and truncates. It is deterministic, not an RNG; the OAEP seed supplies randomness. L is a separately agreed, hash-checked parameter rather than extra message content. The ciphertext has k octets but the message loses capacity to encoding overhead; arbitrary files are not single RSA messages. PSS is a signature scheme: it is not OAEP, and it is not plaintext being encrypted with the private key. Set emBits=modBits−1 and emLen=ceil(emBits/8). Hash M to mHash, use an sLen-octet salt and compute H=Hash(eight zero octets mHash salt). Form DB=PS 01 salt, mask with MGF(H, emLen−hLen−1), clear the excess high bits, and set EM=maskedDB H bc. Require emLen≥hLen+sLen+2. The private primitive maps OS2IP(EM) to s, serialized as k-octet S. Verification needs M as well as S. The public power recovers an encoded representative, not the original message from the signature. Signature length/range, trailer, high bits, padding, delimiter, salt length and recomputed H all matter. Merely checking a trailing digest or ignoring parameters is not PSS verification. Original PSS security arguments assume RSA inversion hardness and idealized hashes; standardized encoding differs from the original. A proof name is no unconditional guarantee for arbitrary implementations. TLS 1.3's specification checked on 2026-10-24, RFC 9846, excludes static RSA key transport while retaining RSA-PSS authentication. The corresponding PSS schemes constrain the digest, MGF1 digest and salt length. Thus no RSA key exchange does not mean no RSA . Certificate paths, host identity, negotiated parameters and handshake context need their own protocol checks; a valid RSA signature alone does not bind a name to a key. Raw RSA is deterministic for a fixed key. For a small set of candidate messages, anyone can encrypt each publicly and compare. Also E(m1)E(m2) modn=E(m1m2 modn). The example changes a ciphertext of 65 into one of 130 without the private key. This is malleability, not a general free-decryption algorithm. With OAEP, the equation cannot simply be interpreted as multiplication of user messages. Repeated or invalid prime factors, invalid exponent conditions, key exposure, poor randomness and incorrect encoding checks can break a system. A small public exponent applied directly to a small unprocessed message can expose an ordinary integer power before modular wraparound. No exponent name alone is a security switch; hard factoring cannot repair scheme or implementation mistakes. OAEP decoding checks length, range, leading octet, label hash and DB structure. Distinguishable responses or timing for different failures can provide chosen-ciphertext information. PKCS 1 v1.5 encryption and PSS signatures are different schemes despite their common PKCS 1 label. Shoup distinguishes general trapdoor-permutation OAEP from RSA-OAEP's special algebraic case: a gap in an early general proof is not proof of RSA-OAEP insecurity. Kocher's timing research shows secret-related leakage from some private-operation implementations. A variable-time teaching BigInt loop is not private-key implementation code. Blinding and secret-independent execution paths need dedicated design; neither implies that all physical leakage disappears. CRT also adds a fault boundary. An output correct modulo one prime and wrong modulo the other can reveal a factor through a public algebraic relation. Boneh, DeMillo and Lipton studied this for certain CRT-RSA implementations. Output checking and fault resistance are implementation duties; a normal-operation correctness proof does not secure incorrect calculations. This batch processes only public toy numbers and public fixtures, without key-custody, constant-time or fault-resistant service claims. Rivest, Shamir and Adleman's original paper, A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-Key Cryptosystems, appeared in Communications of the ACM in 1978. It presents modular exponentiation, key relations and a signature proposal. Its discussion of forgery, parameters and computing resources belongs to its research era and cannot simply become present-day guarantees. OAEP, PSS and later protocol encodings require separate specifications. Bellare and Rogaway's 1996 PSS paper studies exact signature security. Shoup's revised 2001 analysis illustrates the importance of a proof's assumptions and construction. RFC 8017 republished PKCS 1 v2.2 in 2016 and obsoleted RFC 3447. It is Informational; an RFC label does not automatically mean Internet Standard. This review rechecked TLS status: RFC 9846 appeared in July 2026 and explicitly obsoletes RFC 8446. It is used here for RSA's TLS 1.3 role, with the checking date retained. Protocol-document status, algorithm validity and availability in a particular product remain separate matters. - Wikipedia search entry for RSA 公钥密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=RSA%20%E5%85%AC%E9%92%A5%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: ARIA: a 12/14/16-round SPN block cipher
items.text: Algorithm : ARIA (ARIA 韩国分组密码). ARIA is a 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys; the three key sizes use 12, 14 or 16 rounds. It is an SPN (substitution-permutation network): odd rounds use FO, even rounds use FE, and the final round performs only SL2 and two key XORs. For a 128-bit key (12 rounds), encryption is: text P1 = FO(P, ek1) P2 = FE(P1, ek2) P3 = FO(P2, ek3) P4 = FE(P3, ek4) P5 = FO(P4, ek5) P6 = FE(P5, ek6) P7 = FO(P6, ek7) P8 = FE(P7, ek8) P9 = FO(P8, ek9) P10 = FE(P9, ek10) P11 = FO(P10, ek11) C = SL2(P11 XOR ek12) XOR ek13 A 192-bit key uses 14 rounds: rounds 1 to 13 alternate FO/FE, and the final round is C = SL2(P13 XOR ek14) XOR ek15 . A 256-bit key uses 16 rounds: rounds 1 to 15 alternate FO/FE, and the final round is C = SL2(P15 XOR ek16) XOR ek17 . Decryption uses the same process with the encryption round keys ek replaced by the decryption round keys dk. The two round functions are: text FO(D, RK) = A(SL1(D XOR RK)) FE(D, RK) = A(SL2(D XOR RK)) SL1 applies SB1, SB2, SB3 and SB4 cyclically to the sixteen bytes; SL2 applies SB3, SB4, SB1 and SB2: text SL1: y0=SB1(x0) y1=SB2(x1) y2=SB3(x2) y3=SB4(x3) ... y15=SB4(x15) SL2: y0=SB3(x0) y1=SB4(x1) y2=SB1(x2) y3=SB2(x3) ... y15=SB2(x15) SB1, SB2, SB3 and SB4 are four 8-bit S-boxes with 256 entries each. SB3 and SB4 are the inverses of SB1 and SB2, so SL2 is the inverse of SL1. The specification's examples are SB1(0x23)=0x26 and SB4(0xEF)=0xD3 . The diffusion layer A applies fixed XOR combinations to the sixteen bytes: text y0 = x3 ^ x4 ^ x6 ^ x8 ^ x9 ^ x13 ^ x14 y1 = x2 ^ x5 ^ x7 ^ x8 ^ x9 ^ x12 ^ x15 y2 = x1 ^ x4 ^ x6 ^ x10 ^ x11 ^ x12 ^ x15 y3 = x0 ^ x5 ^ x7 ^ x10 ^ x11 ^ x13 ^ x14 y4 = x0 ^ x2 ^ x5 ^ x8 ^ x11 ^ x14 ^ x15 y5 = x1 ^ x3 ^ x4 ^ x9 ^ x10 ^ x14 ^ x15 y6 = x0 ^ x2 ^ x7 ^ x9 ^ x10 ^ x12 ^ x13 y7 = x1 ^ x3 ^ x6 ^ x8 ^ x11 ^ x12 ^ x13 y8 = x0 ^ x1 ^ x4 ^ x7 ^ x10 ^ x13 ^ x15 y9 = x0 ^ x1 ^ x5 ^ x6 ^ x11 ^ x12 ^ x14 y10 = x2 ^ x3 ^ x5 ^ x6 ^ x8 ^ x13 ^ x15 y11 = x2 ^ x3 ^ x4 ^ x7 ^ x9 ^ x12 ^ x14 y12 = x1 ^ x2 ^ x6 ^ x7 ^ x9 ^ x11 ^ x12 y13 = x0 ^ x3 ^ x6 ^ x7 ^ x8 ^ x10 ^ x13 y14 = x0 ^ x3 ^ x4 ^ x5 ^ x9 ^ x11 ^ x14 y15 = x1 ^ x2 ^ x4 ^ x5 ^ x8 ^ x10 ^ x15 A is an involution, so A(A(x))=x . For example, A maps 000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F to 03020100050407060A0B08090C0D0E0F . The key schedule writes the master key K as KL KR : KL is the leftmost 128 bits, and KR is the remaining bits right-padded with zeros to 128 bits. For a 128-bit key KR is zero; for a 192-bit key the low 64 bits of KR are zero; for a 256-bit key KR is the full right 128 bits. It then defines four 128-bit intermediates: text W0 = KL W1 = FO(W0, CK1) XOR KR W2 = FE(W1, CK2) XOR W0 W3 = FO(W2, CK3) XOR W1 CK1, CK2 and CK3 are selected from three constants according to key size: text C1 = 517CC1B727220A94FE13ABE8FA9A6EE0 C2 = 6DB14ACC9E21C820FF28B1D5EF5DE2B0 C3 = DB92371D2126E9700324977504E8C90E 128-bit: CK1=C1, CK2=C2, CK3=C3 192-bit: CK1=C2, CK2=C3, CK3=C1 256-bit: CK1=C3, CK2=C1, CK3=C2 The encryption round keys ek1..ek17 are built from 128-bit left and right rotations of W0..W3 combined by XOR: text ek1 = W0 ^ (W1 19) ek2 = W1 ^ (W2 19) ek3 = W2 ^ (W3 19) ek4 = (W0 19) ^ W3 ek5 = W0 ^ (W1 31) ek6 = W1 ^ (W2 31) ek7 = W2 ^ (W3 31) ek8 = (W0 31) ^ W3 ek9 = W0 ^ (W1 <<< 61) ek10 = W1 ^ (W2 <<< 61) ek11 = W2 ^ (W3 <<< 61) ek12 = (W0 <<< 61) ^ W3 ek13 = W0 ^ (W1 <<< 31) ek14 = W1 ^ (W2 <<< 31) ek15 = W2 ^ (W3 <<< 31) ek16 = (W0 <<< 31) ^ W3 ek17 = W0 ^ (W1 <<< 19) The 12-, 14- and 16-round variants need 13, 15 and 17 round keys because the final round adds an extra key XOR. The decryption round keys are derived by reversing ek and applying A to the middle values: text dk1 = ek(n+1) dk2 = A(ek n) dk3 = A(ek n-1) ... dk n = A(ek2) dk(n+1) = ek1 RFC 5794 says ARIA is a general-purpose block cipher developed by Korean cryptographers in 2003, suitable for most software and hardware implementations on 32-bit and 8-bit processors; it became the Korean standard block cipher (KS X 1213:2004) in 2004, is widely used in Korea especially for government-to-public services, and was included in PKCS 11 in 2007. The Korean e-Government Standard Framework developer guide's standardization-trends section also states that ARIA was designated a national standard in 2004 under the national standards framework act, with standard number KS X 1213:2004. This agrees with RFC 5794's account. RFC 5794 Section 3 says ARIA is designed to resist "all known attacks on block ciphers" and that analysis by the COSIC group at K.U.Leuven, Belgium found no security flaw. This is a 2010 RFC assessment, not a formal proof against every attack model. TLS: RFC 6209 (April 2011, Informational) defines ARIA cipher suites for TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246), including CBC/SHA-2, GCM, elliptic-curve and PSK suites; it explicitly excludes SHA-1 suites. RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) Appendix B.4 defines only five AEAD-based cipher suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, AES-128-CCM and AES-128-CCM-8), with no ARIA suite; this article does not claim ARIA support in TLS 1.3. OIDs: RFC 5794 Appendix B gives an ASN.1 OID module for ARIA, including id-sea and mode identifiers for ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR, CMAC, OCB2, GCM, CCM and key wrap with 128/192/256-bit keys. These identifiers show that ARIA is not only a paper algorithm but also has citable mode-level object identifiers. Test vectors: RFC 5794 Appendix A gives three vectors, all with plaintext 00112233445566778899AABBCCDDEEFF : text 128-bit key = 000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F ciphertext = D718FBD6AB644C739DA95F3BE6451778 192-bit key = 000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F1011121314151617 ciphertext = 26449C1805DBE7AA25A468CE263A9E79 256-bit key = 000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F101112131415161718191A1B1C1D1E1F ciphertext = F92BD7C79FB72E2F2B8F80C1972D24FC For the 128-bit key, Appendix A.1 also lists W0..W3, ek1..ek13 and P1..P11, so it checks the key schedule and round functions rather than only the final ciphertext. The implementation checks these intermediates entry by entry: for example W0= 000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F , W1= 2AFBEA741E1746DD55C63BA1AFCEA0A5 , ek1= D415A75C794B85C5E0D2A0B3CB793BF6 , P1= 7FC7F12BEFD0A0791DE87FA96B469F52 and P11= E7E0D2457ED73D23D481424095AFDCA0 . RFC 5794's "resistant to all known attacks on block ciphers" and "no security flaw has been found" are designer assessments in a 2010 document, not formal proofs against every attack model, and they do not guarantee that no better analysis will appear. This article does not expand them into an absolute security claim, and it does not cite unverified attack papers to claim that ARIA has been broken. ARIA's deployment position needs to be stated carefully: it is a Korean national standard with a clear record of use in Korean government-to-public services and was included in PKCS 11 in 2007; RFC 6209 defines ARIA suites for TLS 1.2, but that RFC is Informational and TLS 1.3 has no ARIA suite. That is a national standard and one inclusion in PKCS 11 in 2007, not availability by default in every latest protocol. At the implementation level, this article's teaching code performs byte-indexed lookups in SB1..SB4 and sixteen-byte XORs and is not constant-time; caches and timing may leak key-dependent access patterns. It does not generate keys and implements no mode of operation, IV management, padding, integrity protection or side-channel defence, so it must not be used to protect real data. ARIA defines only a block cipher; the protocol layer must handle those matters. ARIA was developed by Korean cryptographers in 2003, became the Korean standard block cipher KS X 1213:2004 in 2004, and is widely used in Korea especially for government-to-public services; it was included in PKCS 11 in 2007. RFC 5794 was published in March 2010 with Informational category as an Independent Submission by J. Lee, J. Lee, J. Kim, D. Kwon and C. Kim (NSRI). RFC 6209 added ARIA suites for TLS 1.2 in April 2011 with Informational category, including CBC/SHA-2, GCM, elliptic-curve and PSK families; RFC 8446 defined TLS 1.3 in 2018 with only five AEAD suites and no ARIA. This article's ARIA entity is the 128-bit block cipher only; AES, Camellia and SEED are separate entities, TLS and PKCS 11 are protocols or interfaces that use ARIA, and RFC 5794 is an algorithm specification rather than the whole protocol stack. - Wikipedia search entry for ARIA 韩国分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ARIA%20%E9%9F%A9%E5%9B%BD%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: Blowfish: a 64-bit Feistel block cipher with pi-derived subkeys
items.text: Algorithm : Blowfish (Blowfish 分组密码). Blowfish is a 64-bit block cipher proposed by Bruce Schneier in 1993. It uses a 16-round Feistel network with keys up to 448 bits; its subkeys are an 18-entry (P1–P18) 32-bit P-array and four 256-entry 32-bit S-boxes. The F function splits its 32-bit input into four 8-bit bytes a, b, c and d: text F(x) = ((S1[a] + S2[b] mod 2^32) XOR S3[c]) + S4[d] mod 2^32 Encryption splits the 64-bit block into xL and xR. Each of the 16 rounds does: text xL = xL XOR Pi xR = xR XOR F(xL) swap xL and xR After 16 rounds, the last swap is undone and the block is whitened: text xR = xR XOR P17 xL = xL XOR P18 Decryption is the same as encryption but uses P18..P1 in reverse order. The P-array and the four S-boxes are initialized with "the hexadecimal digits of pi (less the initial 3"). For example P1=243f6a88, P2=85a308d3, P3=13198a2e and P4=03707344; the complete P/S table has 1042 32-bit words, or 4168 bytes. Key expansion first XORs the cyclically repeated key words into the P-array, then repeatedly encrypts the all-zero block with the current algorithm to replace P1..P18 and all four S-boxes; 521 iterations are required. The paper also notes that testing one key requires 522 encryptions, effectively adding about 2^9 steps to a brute-force attack. Blowfish keys range from 32 to 448 bits. The key is cycled, so a short key has "at least one equivalent longer key": if A is a 64-bit key, then AA, AAA and so on produce the same subkeys. Blowfish was designed to be fast, free, unpatented and simple, with variable-length keys (32–448 bits) and key-dependent S-boxes to resist differential and linear cryptanalysis; the paper also calls for a flat keyspace and no weak keys. Instead of DES-style bit permutations, it uses XOR, addition and table lookups on 32-bit words, which suits 32-bit processors. Data encryption is fast, but key expansion is heavy: every new key requires 521 encryptions. The paper positions Blowfish as a public, unpatented candidate rather than a published standard; in this article's analysis, applications that rekey frequently must weigh this setup cost. Blowfish still has a 64-bit block. Its birthday-collision bound is about 2^32 blocks, which limits safe data volume in large deployments. In this article's assessment it is best treated as a historical and teaching case, not as a default for new designs; new designs usually need a larger block and AEAD. The paper says Blowfish is only suitable "where the key does not change often", such as "a communications link or an automatic file encryptor"; on 32-bit processors with large data caches, such as the Pentium and PowerPC, it is significantly faster than DES, but it does not meet all new-standard requirements. The Internet-Draft's §4 lists 34 ECB vectors with 8-byte keys. The zero-key, zero-plaintext vector is: text K = 0000000000000000 P = 0000000000000000 C = 4ef997456198dd78 The third vector is: text K = 3000000000000000 P = 1000000000000001 C = 7d856f9a613063f2 The 34 vectors are encryption checks; this article encrypts each one and verifies that decryption returns the original plaintext. Because the key is cycled, a short key and its repeated form are equivalent: text K = 01234567 K = 0123456701234567 P = 1111111111111111 C = ea55f49044fe2b24 Blowfish has only a 64-bit block. HAC's birthday analysis notes that an n-bit block reaches a matching pair after about 2^(n/2) blocks; for 64 bits this is about 2^32 blocks. In this article's analysis, this limits safe use in large data volumes. A 521-encryption key schedule makes rekeying expensive. The paper treats it as an extra cost for brute-force search; in this article's analysis, it is also a practical burden in systems with high key turnover, and the 4168-byte subkey table should be protected as key material, not treated as public data. Key-dependent S-boxes make differential and linear analysis harder, but an implementation still indexes four tables by input bytes; in this article's analysis, cache, timing or fault injection may leak key-dependent access patterns. This article's teaching implementation is not constant-time and does not measure side channels. Blowfish defines only a block cipher and provides no integrity or authentication. Flipping ciphertext changes the corresponding plaintext, but Blowfish cannot detect it; this article recommends AEAD or encrypt-then-MAC when authentication is needed. This article's teaching implementation demonstrates fixed vectors only; the batch verification script runs 34 ECB vectors, 4/8/16/24/32/56-byte key round trips, a pi-table check and one-bit diffusion. It does not generate keys, run in constant time, implement a mode of operation, protocol, key management or side-channel defenses, and must not be used in production. Blowfish was proposed in the 1993 FSE paper, published by Springer in 1994, and released in the public domain with a Dr. Dobb's Journal article in 1994. The paper treats DES as "nearing the end of its useful life" and aims at a free, unpatented candidate for a new standard that runs quickly on 32-bit processors. Twofish is a separate algorithm, not Blowfish; Twofish, DES, AES and Blowfish are separate entities. - Wikipedia search entry for Blowfish 分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Blowfish%20%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: Camellia: an 18/24-round Feistel block cipher
items.text: Algorithm : Camellia (Camellia 加密算法). Camellia is a 128-bit block cipher developed jointly by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric in 2000. It takes 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys and has the same interface as AES: a fixed 128-bit block and three key lengths. It uses a Feistel structure: 128-bit keys run 18 rounds and 192/256-bit keys run 24 rounds, with an FL/FL^-1 layer after every six rounds and 128-bit whitening "before the first round and after the last round". For a 128-bit key the data path is: text M = L0 R0 L0 R0 = M XOR (kw1 kw2) for r = 1..18, except r = 6, 12: Lr = R(r-1) XOR F(L(r-1), kr) Rr = L(r-1) for r = 6, 12: Lr' = R(r-1) XOR F(L(r-1), kr) Rr' = L(r-1) Lr = FL(Lr', ke(2r/6 - 1)) Rr = FL^-1(Rr', ke(2r/6)) C = (R18 L18) XOR (kw3 kw4) A 192/256-bit key replaces the 18 rounds with 24 and inserts an FL/FL^-1 layer after rounds 6, 12 and 18 (ke1..ke6), ending with C = (R24 L24) XOR (kw3 kw4) . Decryption uses the same data path with the subkeys reversed: kw1 with kw3, kw2 with kw4, k1 with kn, k2 with k(n-1), and the remaining round and FL-layer subkeys in reverse order. The F function is F(X, k) = P(S(X XOR k)) . S maps the eight input bytes through s1, s2, s3, s4, s2, s3, s4 and s1 in that order; P applies fixed linear combinations to the eight bytes: text z'1 = z1 XOR z3 XOR z4 XOR z6 XOR z7 XOR z8 z'2 = z1 XOR z2 XOR z4 XOR z5 XOR z7 XOR z8 z'3 = z1 XOR z2 XOR z3 XOR z5 XOR z6 XOR z8 z'4 = z2 XOR z3 XOR z4 XOR z5 XOR z6 XOR z7 z'5 = z1 XOR z2 XOR z6 XOR z7 XOR z8 z'6 = z2 XOR z3 XOR z5 XOR z7 XOR z8 z'7 = z3 XOR z4 XOR z5 XOR z6 XOR z8 z'8 = z1 XOR z4 XOR z5 XOR z6 XOR z7 FL and FL^-1 operate on 32-bit halves. Let the input be XL XR and the subkey be klL klR : text FL: YR = ((XL & klL) <<< 1) XOR XR YL = (YR klR) XOR XL FL^-1: XL = (YR klR) XOR YL XR = ((XL & klL) <<< 1) XOR YR Here <<< is a 32-bit left rotation and & , and XOR are bitwise AND, OR and exclusive-or. FL and FL^-1 are inverses; they mix a key-dependent one-bit rotation and OR into the data and form the key-dependent layer inserted every six rounds. There are four S-boxes: s1 is a 256-byte table, s2(x)=s1(x) rotated left by 1, s3(x)=s1(x) rotated left by 7 (equivalent to a right rotation by 1), and s4(x)=s1(x rotated left by 1); all rotations are within 8 bits. The specification also gives the algebraic form s1(x)=h(g(f(0xC5 XOR x))) XOR 0x6E , where f and h are affine maps and g is inversion in GF(2^8) with 1/0 defined as 0, over the field defined by beta^8+beta^6+beta^5+beta^3+1=0 . Tables 4 to 7 of the specification list all 256 entries of the four S-boxes. The key schedule writes the key as KL and KR and derives KA, KB and the subkeys. The three key lengths differ: - 128-bit: KL=K, KR=0. - 192-bit: KL is the leftmost 128 bits; KR is the rightmost 64 bits concatenated with their bitwise complement, KR = (K[128..191] ~K[128..191]) . - 256-bit: KL is the leftmost 128 bits and KR is the rightmost 128 bits. KA and KB are derived with F and six 64-bit constants Sigma1..Sigma6: text D1 D2 = KL XOR KR D2 = D2 XOR F(D1, Sigma1) D1 = D1 XOR F(D2, Sigma2) D1 = D1 XOR high64(KL) D2 = D2 XOR low64(KL) D2 = D2 XOR F(D1, Sigma3) D1 = D1 XOR F(D2, Sigma4) KA = D1 D2 D1 D2 = KA XOR KR D2 = D2 XOR F(D1, Sigma5) D1 = D1 XOR F(D2, Sigma6) KB = D1 D2 The six constants are: text Sigma1 = A09E667F3BCC908B Sigma2 = B67AE8584CAA73B2 Sigma3 = C6EF372FE94F82BE Sigma4 = 54FF53A5F1D36F1C Sigma5 = 10E527FADE682D1D Sigma6 = B05688C2B3E6C1FD The specification defines them as the 16 consecutive hexadecimal digits starting at the second hexadecimal place after the point in "the hexadecimal representation of the square root of the" first through sixth primes. The subkeys are the left or right halves of 128-bit rotations of KL, KR, KA and KB. A 128-bit key produces four whitening subkeys kw1..kw4, eighteen round subkeys k1..k18 and four FL-layer subkeys ke1..ke4; 192/256-bit keys produce four kw, twenty-four k and six ke. Tables 2 and 3 of the specification list the rotation amount and half selection for every subkey; for example, with a 128-bit key kw1 = high64(KL<<<0) , kw2 = low64(KL<<<0) , k1 = high64(KA<<<0) and k2 = low64(KA<<<0) , k10 is only the right half of KL<<<60 , and kw3/kw4 are the two halves of KA<<<111 . For 192/256-bit keys kw3/kw4 come from KB<<<111 instead of the 128-bit KA<<<111 , while k23/k24 come from KL<<<111 just like the 128-bit k17/k18 . The right half of KR for a 192-bit key is the bitwise complement of the rightmost 64 bits. This is a specified key construction, not an optional implementation step; treating KR as an ordinary right 128-bit half produces incorrect subkeys for all 24 rounds. RFC 3713 states the design goals as follows: Camellia is suitable "for both software and hardware implementations", including 32-bit processors, 8-bit processors, smart cards, cryptographic hardware and embedded systems; its key setup time is excellent and its key agility is superior to AES. The RFC also notes that Camellia has the same 128-bit "block and 128/192/256-bit" key interface as AES, but is a different algorithm. Camellia received explicit recognition in standardization evaluations: the NESSIE project selected it as a recommended cryptographic primitive, and Japan's CRYPTREC included it "in the list of cryptographic techniques for" e-Government systems. ISO/IEC 18033-3:2010 lists it with AES and SEED among 128-bit block ciphers, and that edition was still confirmed as current in 2025. RFC 3713 Section 4 says the designers evaluated Camellia with "state-of-the-art cryptanalytic techniques" and confirmed that no differential or linear characteristic holds with probability greater than 2^-128, so differential and linear attacks are extremely unlikely to succeed against the full 18-round Camellia; it also says the design addresses higher-order differential, interpolation, related-key and truncated differential attacks. This article treats those statements as the designers' and RFC's assessment, not as a proof against every attack. Compared with AES, Camellia is suitable for 8-bit and 32-bit implementations and has excellent key setup time. This article treats Camellia as a separate algorithm alongside AES, not a replacement standard; the two are not interchangeable because their algorithm identifiers and test vectors differ, although both support 128/192/256-bit keys. CMS: RFC 3657 (January 2004, Standards Track) specifies Camellia for CMS content encryption and key wrapping. The content-encryption OIDs are id-camellia128-cbc , id-camellia192-cbc and id-camellia256-cbc , using CBC with a 16-byte IV; the AlgorithmIdentifier parameters MUST contain the IV. The key-wrap OIDs are id-camellia128-wrap , id-camellia192-wrap and id-camellia256-wrap , whose parameters MUST be absent; wrapping is identical to RFC 3394 AES key wrap with AES replaced by Camellia. The OID gives the KEK length but does not constrain the wrapped CEK length; implementations MUST support equal KEK and CEK lengths, and if different lengths are supported the KEK MUST be at least as long as the CEK. OpenPGP: RFC 5581 (June 2009, Informational, Updates RFC 4880) introduced Camellia into OpenPGP, assigned symmetric-algorithm numbers 11 (128-bit), 12 (192-bit) and 13 (256-bit), and specified that implementations MAY implement Camellia. RFC 9580 (July 2024, Standards Track) obsoletes RFC 4880, RFC 5581 and RFC 6637 but keeps Camellia numbers 11, 12 and 13 in the Section 9.3 symmetric-algorithm table; it requires AES-128, recommends AES-256, prohibits encryption with IDEA, TripleDES or CAST5, and permits any other algorithm. Camellia is therefore an optional current OpenPGP algorithm, not a prohibited legacy one. TLS: RFC 5932 (June 2010, Standards Track, obsoletes RFC 4132) defines 24 Camellia CBC cipher suites, 12 each for 128-bit and 256-bit keys, using a 128-bit IV. The 12 _SHA suites use HMAC-SHA1 and may be used with TLS 1.1 and earlier; the 12 _SHA256 suites use HMAC-SHA-256 and MUST NOT be negotiated by TLS 1.1 or earlier, i.e., they require TLS 1.2 or later. RFC 6367 (September 2011, Informational) adds 42 Camellia suites, covering CBC and GCM and key exchanges including RSA, DHE, ECDHE and PSK. RFC 8996 (March 2021, BCP 195) deprecates TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and lists RFC 6367 among the documents it updates. RFC 6367's GCM suites target TLS 1.2, so the current recommended version for these Camellia suites is TLS 1.2, while the _SHA CBC suites' use with TLS 1.1 and earlier is deprecated by BCP 195. RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) Appendix B.4 defines only five AEAD-based suites (AES-128-GCM, AES-256-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, AES-128-CCM and AES-128-CCM-8), with no Camellia suite; this article does not claim Camellia support in TLS 1.3. Test vectors: Appendix B of the official specification gives three single-block vectors, all with plaintext 0123456789abcdeffedcba9876543210 : text 128-bit key = 0123456789abcdeffedcba9876543210 ciphertext = 67673138549669730857065648eabe43 192-bit key = 0123456789abcdeffedcba98765432100011223344556677 ciphertext = b4993401b3e996f84ee5cee7d79b09b9 256-bit key = 0123456789abcdeffedcba987654321000112233445566778899aabbccddeeff ciphertext = 9acc237dff16d76c20ef7c919e3a7509 The teaching implementation reproduces all three vectors and verifies that decryption returns the original plaintext; the 128-bit key exercises 18 rounds and two FL layers, while the 192/256-bit keys exercise 24 rounds and three FL layers. The security statement in RFC 3713 is the designers' assessment: it says Camellia has no differential or linear characteristic with probability above 2^-128 and that the design addresses higher-order differential, interpolation, related-key and truncated differential attacks. This is a 2004 RFC assessment, not a formal proof against every attack model, and it does not guarantee that no better analysis will appear. This article does not expand RFC 3713's differential/linear assessment into an absolute security claim for every attack model, and it does not cite unverified attack papers to claim that Camellia has been broken. The right half of KR for a 192-bit key is the bitwise complement of the rightmost 64 bits. This is a specified key construction, not an optional step; it means that 192-bit key material cannot be treated as the right 128 bits of an ordinary 256-bit key, and an implementation that omits the complement produces incorrect subkeys. The 192-bit official vector verifies this detail. Camellia's current protocol position needs to be stated carefully: OpenPGP keeps Camellia numbers but treats it as optional; the CMS Camellia OIDs remain part of a Standards Track specification; the TLS Camellia CBC suites split into _SHA (usable with TLS 1.1 and earlier) and _SHA256 (requiring TLS 1.2 or later) groups, TLS 1.0/1.1 are deprecated by BCP 195, and TLS 1.3 has no Camellia suite. That Camellia was once standardized does not make it available by default in the latest protocol. At the implementation level, this article's teaching code performs byte-indexed S-box lookups and is not constant-time; caches and timing may leak key-dependent access patterns. It does not generate keys and implements no mode of operation, IV management, padding, integrity protection or side-channel defence, so it must not be used to protect real data. Camellia defines only a block cipher; the protocol layer must handle those matters. Camellia was developed jointly by NTT and Mitsubishi Electric. The official "Specification of Camellia -- a 128-bit Block Cipher" is attributed to K. Aoki, T. Ichikawa, M. Kanda, M. Matsui, S. Moriai, J. Nakajima and T. Tokita and dated 12 July 2000. It describes the 128-bit block, 128/192/256-bit keys, the 18/24-round Feistel structure, FL/FL^-1 layers, four S-boxes, the key schedule and the Appendix B test data. RFC 3713 was published by M. Matsui, J. Nakajima and S. Moriai in April 2004 with Informational category; it describes Camellia as a 128-bit block cipher with 128/192/256-bit keys and presents key scheduling and data randomizing separately. RFC 3657 specified CMS usage as Standards Track in January 2004; RFC 4132 once defined Camellia suites for TLS and was obsoleted and extended by RFC 5932 in 2010; RFC 5581 introduced Camellia into OpenPGP in 2009 and was obsoleted by RFC 9580 in 2024, which nevertheless keeps the algorithm numbers; RFC 6367 added 42 Camellia suites (CBC and GCM) in 2011. ISO/IEC 18033-3:2010 Edition 2 lists Camellia as a 128-bit block cipher alongside AES and SEED, and its 64-bit block-cipher part lists TDEA, MISTY1, CAST-128 and HIGHT; the ISO page shows that the edition was confirmed as current in September 2025. This article's Camellia entity is the block cipher only; AES, SEED, MISTY1 and CAST-128 are separate entities, CMS, OpenPGP and TLS are protocols that use Camellia, and ISO/IEC 18033-3 is a standardization document rather than the algorithm. - Wikipedia search entry for Camellia 加密算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Camellia%20%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Camellia-128 示例：密钥 0123456789abcdeffedcba9876543210 ，明文同值，密文 67673138549669730857065648eabe43 。18 轮 Feistel，含 FL/FL^-1 变换。

items.title: CAST-128: a 64-bit Feistel block cipher with three round functions
items.text: Algorithm : CAST-128 (CAST-128 分组密码). CAST-128 (also known as CAST5) is the 64-bit Feistel block cipher described by Carlisle Adams in RFC 2144 (1997). It splits a 64-bit plaintext into 32-bit halves L0 and R0, uses a 40- to 128-bit key in 8-bit steps, and runs either 12 or 16 rounds: 12 rounds for keys "up to and including 80 bits", and 16 rounds for longer keys. RFC 2144 places CAST-128 in the class of Feistel ciphers and says its overall operation is similar to DES; the RFC's introduction also calls it a DES-like SPN, but the Section 2 Li/Ri round structure is Feistel, and this article follows the Section 2 structure in calling it a Feistel cipher. text Li = R(i-1) Ri = L(i-1) XOR f(R(i-1), Kmi, Kri) After the last round (16 or 12) the final halves are swapped, and the ciphertext is R(rounds) L(rounds) : R16 L16 for 16 rounds and R12 L12 for 12 rounds. Decryption uses the same structure with the round subkeys in reverse order. CAST-128 derives 32 32-bit subkeys K1..K32 from 128 bits of key material and pairs them into 16 round keys: round i uses the masking subkey Kmi = Ki and the rotation subkey Kri = K(16+i) ; only the low 5 bits of Kri are used. The round function has three types: text Type 1: I = ((Kmi + D) <<< Kri); f = ((S1[Ia] ^ S2[Ib]) - S3[Ic]) + S4[Id] Type 2: I = ((Kmi ^ D) <<< Kri); f = ((S1[Ia] - S2[Ib]) + S3[Ic]) ^ S4[Id] Type 3: I = ((Kmi - D) <<< Kri); f = ((S1[Ia] + S2[Ib]) ^ S3[Ic]) - S4[Id] Here Ia..Id are the most significant through least significant bytes of I, + and - are addition and subtraction modulo 2^32, and <<< is a circular left shift. Rounds 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 and 16 use Type 1; rounds 2, 5, 8, 11 and 14 use Type 2; rounds 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15 use Type 3. CAST-128 uses eight S-boxes: S1, S2, S3 and S4 in the round function, and S5, S6, S7 and S8 in the key schedule; each S-box has 256 32-bit words. The eight boxes need 8 KB of storage, but after key expansion encryption and decryption need only the 4 KB used by the round function. The key schedule writes the 16-byte key as x0..xF, computes intermediate bytes z0..zF, and then derives K1..K32. The first group of formulas in RFC Section 2.4 is: text z0z1z2z3 = x0x1x2x3 ^ S5[xD] ^ S6[xF] ^ S7[xC] ^ S8[xE] ^ S7[x8] K1 = S5[z8] ^ S6[z9] ^ S7[z7] ^ S8[z6] ^ S5[z2] K2 = S5[zA] ^ S6[zB] ^ S7[z5] ^ S8[z4] ^ S6[z6] K3 = S5[zC] ^ S6[zD] ^ S7[z3] ^ S8[z2] ^ S7[z9] K4 = S5[zE] ^ S6[zF] ^ S7[z1] ^ S8[z0] ^ S8[zC] The remaining z, x and K5..K32 formulas are in RFC 2144 Section 2.4. This article's teaching implementation computes them directly and checks the result against the RFC Appendix B vectors. Keys can be 40 to 128 bits in 8-bit steps. For keys shorter than 128 bits, the key-schedule input is zero-padded on the right to 16 bytes; the round count is nevertheless determined by the declared key length, not by the padded byte count. A 10-byte (80-bit) key is padded internally to 16 bytes but still runs only 12 rounds; a caller that directly supplies a 16-byte key ending in zeros has supplied a 128-bit key that runs 16 rounds. RFC 2144 also makes CAST-128 and CAST5 synonyms, so a key size may be appended as in CAST5-40 or CAST5-128. RFC 2144 starts from the Internet community's need "for an unencumbered encryption algorithm with a range of key sizes" and adequate performance. The RFC says CAST-128 appears to resist differential, linear and related-key cryptanalysis, and lists avalanche, the Strict Avalanche Criterion (SAC), the Bit Independence Criterion (BIC), no complementation property, and the "absence of weak and semi-weak keys". RFC Section 2.7 also says the circular rotations "provide intrinsic immunity to linear and differential attacks", while the mixture of XOR, addition and subtraction and the three round-function types make analysis harder; it gives a minimum S-box "nonlinearity of 74 and a maximum" difference-distribution-table entry of 2. HAC's notes add the design-method perspective: CAST is a design procedure for a family of DES-like ciphers with fixed m×n S-boxes based on bent functions, variable key sizes and variable round counts; Adams and Tavares studied how to construct large S-boxes resistant to differential cryptanalysis and gave a partial example of a CAST cipher with a 64-bit block and eight 32-bit S-boxes. CAST-128 is the concrete instance of that design family specified in RFC 2144, not the design procedure as a whole. RFC Section 2.7 also claims that CAST-128 reaches 3.3 MB/s on a 150 MHz Pentium and that its strength is in line with its 128-bit key. This article treats those figures as the RFC's implementation claims, not as an independent benchmark or a security proof. RFC 2984 is a Standards Track document that specifies CAST-128 for CMS/S/MIME: it defines the content-encryption OID cast5CBC and the key-wrap OID cast5CMSkeywrap , recommends CBC for content encryption, and allows key lengths from 40 to 128 bits; the cast5CBC parameter's IV may default to all zeros, and its length follows the 64-bit block size, namely 8 bytes. Key wrapping is referenced to the CMS procedure in RFC 2630, and only 128-bit CAST-128 keys may be used as key-encryption keys ( cast5CMSkeywrapParameter set to 128). This shows CAST-128 being standardized for messaging infrastructure rather than remaining a paper design. RFC 4880 (OpenPGP, 2007) is a historical document that RFC 9580 obsoleted in 2024; it listed CAST5 as symmetric algorithm number 3, noted its 128-bit key and cited RFC 2144, and said implementations SHOULD implement AES-128 and CAST5. RFC 9580 now states that implementations MUST NOT encrypt data with IDEA, TripleDES or CAST5; implementations MAY decrypt CAST5 to read "older messages or new messages from implementations predating support for" RFC 2440, and SHOULD generate a deprecation warning. CAST-128's current OpenPGP role is therefore legacy decryption, not new encryption; this also shows that it has a historical deployment record in privacy tools. RFC 2144 Appendix B.1 gives three single-block vectors: text 128-bit key = 01 23 45 67 12 34 56 78 23 45 67 89 34 56 78 9A plaintext = 01 23 45 67 89 AB CD EF ciphertext = 23 8B 4F E5 84 7E 44 B2 80-bit key = 01 23 45 67 12 34 56 78 23 45 (padded internally to 16 bytes) plaintext = 01 23 45 67 89 AB CD EF ciphertext = EB 6A 71 1A 2C 02 27 1B 40-bit key = 01 23 45 67 12 (padded internally to 16 bytes) plaintext = 01 23 45 67 89 AB CD EF ciphertext = 7A C8 16 D1 6E 9B 30 2E The 128-bit key uses 16 rounds; the 80-bit and 40-bit keys use 12. This article encrypts all three vectors and decrypts each ciphertext back to its plaintext. Appendix B.2 also defines a maintenance test: starting from a=b=0123456712345678234567893456789a, repeat 1,000,000 times, each time encrypting the two halves of a under b and then the two halves of b under the updated a; the final values should be: text a = EE A9 D0 A2 49 FD 3B A6 B3 43 6F B8 9D 6D CA 92 b = B2 C9 5E B0 0C 31 AD 71 80 AC 05 B8 E8 3D 69 6E This article's verification script runs all 1,000,000 iterations, not a sample. The test covers the key schedule, the three round functions, the final swap and a large number of different subkeys. RFC 2144's security statement is that CAST-128 "appears" to resist differential, linear and related-key cryptanalysis, together with the avalanche and weak-key design properties; those are design and RFC assessments, not a proof against every attack. RFC 4880 (a historical document) warns in its Security Considerations that CAST5 is presently considered strong but has been analyzed less than TripleDES. Taken together, this article treats CAST-128 as a cipher with a long public record, but not as absolutely secure or as free of practical full-round attacks under every model. RFC 2984 Section 4 also warns that short keys such as 40, 56 or 64 bits may be unacceptably weak for some environments, and always recommends 128-bit keys (where laws permit). This article therefore treats the RFC 2144 40-bit test vector as an algorithm check, not as a recommended deployment configuration. HAC's notes mention that Rijmen and Preneel gave a cryptanalytic technique applicable to Feistel ciphers with non-surjective round functions, with LOKI'91 and an example CAST cipher as examples, and noted "cases where 6 to 8 rounds" are insufficient. That note concerns an example in the CAST design family, not a complete attack on 16-round CAST-128; this article treats it as a historical warning about the design family, not as a claim that CAST-128 has been broken. CAST-128 has only a 64-bit block. HAC Note 7.8 explains that with a small block length n a matching pair becomes likely after about 2^(n/2) blocks; for n=64 the birthday scale is about 2^32 blocks. This article therefore treats the safe data volume under one key as limited, but this is a generic birthday analysis, not a theorem specific to CAST-128. At the implementation level, the CAST-128 round function indexes four S-boxes by bytes, and the key schedule indexes four more; ordinary software implementations are not constant-time; cache or timing may leak key-dependent access patterns, while fault injection may cause incorrect outputs or key recovery. CAST-128 defines only a block cipher, not integrity, IV management or padding; those must come from the mode and protocol. This article's teaching implementation is not constant-time, does not generate keys, and does not implement a mode, protocol, key management or side-channel defenses. HAC's notes describe CAST as a design procedure for a family of DES-like ciphers with fixed m×n S-boxes, variable key lengths and variable round counts, with S-box design linked to bent functions and differential analysis; the Adams and Tavares paper cited by HAC studies large S-boxes resistant to differential cryptanalysis and gives a partial example of a CAST cipher. CAST-128 is the concrete algorithm of that family specified in RFC 2144 in 1997. RFC 2144 was published by Carlisle Adams (Entrust Technologies) in May 1997 with Informational category; it describes an existing algorithm rather than proposing a new standard. The RFC treats CAST-128 and CAST5 as synonyms and gives the 40- to 128-bit variable key, the 12/16 rounds, the eight S-boxes and the test vectors. Section 3 states that CAST-128 "is available worldwide on a royalty-free basis for commercial and non-commercial uses". In October 2000, RFC 2984 specified CAST-128 for CMS/S/MIME as a Standards Track document, including OIDs, CBC use and key wrapping; in 2007 RFC 4880 listed CAST5 in OpenPGP's symmetric-algorithm table, and in 2024 RFC 9580 obsoleted RFC 4880 and prohibited new CAST5 encryption. The CAST-128 entity in this article is this one 64-bit Feistel block cipher; CAST5 is its synonym, CMS and OpenPGP are protocols that use it, and the CAST design procedure is the family it belongs to. DES is the structural analogy used by RFC 2144 ("DES-like"), not a component of CAST-128, so this article does not treat DES as a mandatory prerequisite. - Wikipedia search entry for CAST-128 分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CAST-128%20%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: CFB mode: turning a block cipher into a self-synchronizing stream
items.text: Algorithm : Cipher Feedback (CFB 密文反馈模式). CFB (Cipher Feedback) turns a block cipher into a segment-oriented stream generator. It has a segment parameter s with 1 <= s <= b, where b is the block size. Plaintext and ciphertext are processed in s-bit segments. Encryption is: text I_1 = IV I_j = LSB_(b-s)(I_(j-1)) C_(j-1) (j = 2) O_j = E_K(I_j) C_j = P_j xor MSB_s(O_j) I_j is the j-th input block, O_j is the block-cipher output and C_j is the j-th ciphertext segment. CFB uses only the forward E_K and needs no D_K. Decryption builds the same input blocks: text P_j = C_j xor MSB_s(O_j) The first input block is the IV. Each later input block is formed by shifting the previous input block left by s bits and placing the previous ciphertext segment in the lowest s bits. Encryption must therefore be serial because the next input block depends on the previous ciphertext segment; after the input blocks are constructed, decryption can compute E_K in parallel. The CFB IV need not be secret but must be unpredictable. This is the same requirement as CBC, not the uniqueness-only requirement of CTR/OFB. A predictable IV lets an attacker test whether two messages share an initial segment or mount a chosen-plaintext distinction. CFB works in s-bit segments, and ciphertext segments have the same length as plaintext segments. With s=8, any byte string can be processed without padding to the block size; with s equal to the block size, the input length must be a multiple of the block size unless the protocol defines a final-segment rule. CFB does not change the underlying block size or key length. CFB shows a ciphertext-feedback stream construction: the block cipher still processes one block at a time, but only the first s bits of its output are XORed with plaintext, and the ciphertext is fed back into the next input block. With s=8 it processes byte streams directly; with s=b it resembles CBC chaining but has a different decryption structure. With s=8, CFB needs no block padding and only the forward cipher direction. Its costs are an unpredictable IV, serial encryption and error propagation along the feedback chain. Understanding CFB also separates a stream-like appearance from a stateless design: CFB looks like a stream cipher, but its keystream depends on the previous ciphertext segment, so it is not the independently addressable keystream of CTR. CFB is a general confidentiality mode for segment-oriented processing where block padding is unwanted. SP 800-38A addresses protection of sensitive information by federal agencies and non-government organizations, and CFB is one of its defined modes. With s=8, CFB processes data byte by byte, suitable for byte or character streams; with s=b, it feeds back complete blocks, suitable for block-structured data. The choice of s must be explicit in the protocol because it determines segment boundaries, error propagation and interoperability. CFB provides no integrity. When authentication is needed, use AEAD or add a MAC; the ciphertext looking stream-like does not make it tamper-resistant. The CFB IV need not be secret but must be unpredictable. A predictable IV lets an attacker construct plaintext so that the first encrypted segment equals a target, testing that target's first segment. This chosen-plaintext distinction targets IV generation, not AES itself. Reusing an IV under the same key repeats the first segment's keystream and leaks the XOR of the two messages' first segments; later segments usually differ because they feed back different ciphertext, but the first-segment leak already breaks confidentiality. Flipping one bit in a CFB ciphertext segment flips the same bit in the corresponding plaintext segment; the changed segment also enters the next input block, changing later output blocks. With s=b, the error usually affects the current and next block and then resynchronizes; with s<b, it spans more segments. CFB provides confidentiality only, not integrity. An attacker can modify ciphertext segments and affect plaintext, and CFB cannot detect it; when integrity is needed, use AEAD or a MAC. s is an explicit CFB parameter. Sender and receiver must use the same s, or segment boundaries and feedback differ and the ciphertext cannot be decrypted correctly. Treating CFB as a single mode without a parameter is a common protocol design error. This article's teaching implementation demonstrates only AES-128-CFB128 and CFB8 official vectors, bit flipping and IV reuse on fixed data. It does not implement secure IV generation, constant-time processing, key management, protocol state machines or side-channel defenses, and it must not be used in production. In 1980, FIPS 81 defined CFB for DES, letting a block cipher process data in segments shorter than a block. In 2001, SP 800-38A generalized CFB to block ciphers and supplied test vectors for different s values. CFB's long use shows that looking stream-like does not mean being stateless. CFB obtains self-synchronizing behavior by feeding ciphertext back, but that also makes the IV and error propagation protocol boundaries. CTR and AEAD later addressed the tension between stream processing and integrity in different ways. This history shows that CFB is a basic mode with a clear boundary: choose s correctly, generate the IV correctly and accept error propagation, and it can provide confidentiality; omit those preconditions and the mode's properties become an attack surface. - Wikipedia search entry for CFB 密文反馈模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CFB%20%E5%AF%86%E6%96%87%E5%8F%8D%E9%A6%88%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: CLEFIA: a 4-branch generalized Feistel lightweight block cipher
items.text: Algorithm : CLEFIA (CLEFIA 轻量级分组密码). CLEFIA is a 128-bit block cipher with 128-, 192- or 256-bit keys using 18, 22 or 26 rounds. It uses a 4-branch generalized Feistel network (GFN4) and is compatible with the AES interface: a fixed 128-bit block and three key lengths. The data randomizing part splits the 128-bit plaintext into four 32-bit words P0..P3. Encryption whitens P1 and P3 with WK0 and WK1, runs GFN4, and whitens the output with WK2 and WK3: text T0 = P0 T1 = P1 XOR WK0 T2 = P2 T3 = P3 XOR WK1 Y = GFN4(RK0..RK(2r-1), T) C0 = Y0 C1 = Y1 XOR WK2 C2 = Y2 C3 = Y3 XOR WK3 Each round of GFN4,r is: text T1 = T1 XOR F0(RK(2i), T0) T3 = T3 XOR F1(RK(2i+1), T2) (T0, T1, T2, T3) = (T1, T2, T3, T0) After r rounds the output is T3 T0 T1 T2 . Decryption uses GFNINV4,r with the round keys in reverse order and a right word rotation after each round, then removes whitening with WK0 and WK1. F0 and F1 are the two 32-bit round functions. F0 computes T = RK XOR x , sends the four bytes of T through S0, S1, S0 and S1, and multiplies by M0; F1 sends them through S1, S0, S1 and S0 and multiplies by M1: text F0: T = RK XOR x; T0=S0(T0), T1=S1(T1), T2=S0(T2), T3=S1(T3); y = M0(T) F1: T = RK XOR x; T0=S1(T0), T1=S0(T1), T2=S1(T2), T3=S0(T3); y = M1(T) S0 and S1 are two 8-bit S-boxes with 256 entries each. S0 is based on four 4-bit S-boxes, and S1 is based on inversion over GF(2^8); the specification's example is S0(0xAB)=0x7E . M0 and M1 are 4x4 diffusion matrices: text M0: y0 = T0 ^ 02 T1 ^ 04 T2 ^ 06 T3 y1 = 02 T0 ^ T1 ^ 06 T2 ^ 04 T3 y2 = 04 T0 ^ 06 T1 ^ T2 ^ 02 T3 y3 = 06 T0 ^ 04 T1 ^ 02 T2 ^ T3 M1: y0 = T0 ^ 08 T1 ^ 02 T2 ^ 0A T3 y1 = 08 T0 ^ T1 ^ 0A T2 ^ 02 T3 y2 = 02 T0 ^ 0A T1 ^ T2 ^ 08 T3 y3 = 0A T0 ^ 02 T1 ^ 08 T2 ^ T3 Multiplication is in GF(2^8) with polynomial z^8 + z^4 + z^3 + z^2 + 1 (low eight bits 0x1D). The key schedule has three variants. A 128-bit key first uses GFN4,12 with 24 CON constants to generate the 128-bit intermediate L, then produces WK and 36 RK values: text L = GFN4,12(CON_128[0..23], K0..K3) WK0..WK3 = K0..K3 for i = 0..8: T = L XOR (CON_128[24+4i] CON_128[25+4i] CON_128[26+4i] CON_128[27+4i]) L = Sigma(L) if i is odd: T = T XOR K RK[4i..4i+3] = T Sigma is the 128-bit DoubleSwap bit permutation: text Y = Sigma(X) = X[7..63] X[121..127] X[0..6] X[64..120] Bit 0 is the most significant bit. For 192- and 256-bit keys, KL and KR are formed first: for 192 bits KR = K4 K5 ~K0 ~K1 , and for 256 bits KR = K4 K5 K6 K7 . GFN8,10 with 40 CON constants then generates LL and LR: text LL LR = GFN8,10(CON_k[0..39], KL0..KL3, KR0..KR3) WK = KL XOR KR for i = 0..10 (192) or 0..12 (256): if i mod 4 = 0 or 1: T = LL XOR CON_k[40+4i..43+4i]; LL = Sigma(LL); if i is odd: T = T XOR KR else: T = LR XOR CON_k[40+4i..43+4i]; LR = Sigma(LR); if i is odd: T = T XOR KL RK[4i..4i+3] = T GFN8,r runs r rounds over eight 32-bit words, updating T1, T3, T5 and T7 with F0, F1, F0 and F1 and rotating the eight words left by one position each round. It is used only in the 192/256-bit key schedule, not in the data randomizing part. The CON_k constants are generated from P=0xB7E1 and Q=0x243F: text CON_k[2i] = (T_i XOR P) (~T_i <<< 1) CON_k[2i+1] = (~T_i XOR Q) (T_i <<< 8) T_(i+1) = T_i (0x0002^-1) Multiplication is in GF(2^16) with polynomial z^16+z^15+z^13+z^11+z^5+z^4+1 . The 128/192/256-bit schedules need 60/84/92 constants, with T_0 initialized to 0x428A, 0x7137 and 0xB5C0. RFC 6114 says CLEFIA is a lightweight 128-bit block cipher designed in 2007 with state-of-the-art techniques. It can be implemented within 3 Kgates using a 0.13-micron standard CMOS ASIC library while offering 128/192/256-bit security and high software and hardware performance; many lightweight algorithms sacrifice security or speed, and CLEFIA aims at a balance. It is proposed for ISO/IEC 29192-2 and the CRYPTREC revision of Japan's e-Government recommended ciphers. RFC 6114 Section 7 says no security weakness has been found for full-round CLEFIA in public scrutiny, neither by the designers nor by independent cryptographers. This is a 2011 RFC assessment, not a formal proof against every attack model. CLEFIA's standardization position is ISO/IEC 29192-2. Edition 2 (2019) lists CLEFIA with PRESENT and LEA as block ciphers suitable for lightweight cryptographic implementations: PRESENT has a 64-bit block and 80/128-bit keys; CLEFIA has a 128-bit block and 128/192/256-bit keys; LEA also has a 128-bit block and 128/192/256-bit keys. The ISO page shows that the edition was confirmed as current in March 2025. RFC 6114 Appendix A gives three vectors, all with plaintext 000102030405060708090A0B0C0D0E0F : text 128-bit key = FFEEDDCCBBAA99887766554433221100 ciphertext = DE2BF2FD9B74AACDF1298555459494FD 192-bit key = FFEEDDCCBBAA99887766554433221100F0E0D0C0B0A09080 ciphertext = E2482F649F028DC480DDA184FDE181AD 256-bit key = FFEEDDCCBBAA99887766554433221100F0E0D0C0B0A090807060504030201000 ciphertext = A1397814289DE80C10DA46D1FA48B38A Appendix B also gives the full 128-bit intermediates: L=8F89A61B9DB9D0F393E65627DA0D027E , WK0..3=FFEEDDCC BBAA9988 77665544 33221100 , and all 36 32-bit RK0..35 values. It also lists the whitened state and each round's F-function key-add, S and M values. The implementation reproduces these values, so it checks the key schedule and round functions rather than only the final ciphertext. RFC 6114's "no security weaknesses have been found for full-round CLEFIA to date" is a summary of public scrutiny in a 2011 document, not a formal proof against every attack model, and it does not guarantee that no better analysis will appear. This article does not expand it into an absolute security claim, and it does not cite unverified attack papers to claim that CLEFIA has been broken. CLEFIA's deployment position needs to be stated carefully: it is a lightweight algorithm designed by Sony, published in 2007, and proposed for ISO/IEC 29192-2 and the CRYPTREC revision of Japan's e-Government recommended ciphers; ISO/IEC 29192-2:2019 formally lists it with PRESENT and LEA as lightweight block ciphers. This article does not present it as a default algorithm for general protocols; being standardized does not mean it is available by default in every protocol. At the implementation level, this article's teaching code performs byte-indexed lookups in S0/S1 and 32-bit XORs and GF(2^8) multiplications and is not constant-time; caches and timing may leak key-dependent access patterns. It does not generate keys and implements no mode of operation, IV management, padding, integrity protection or side-channel defence, so it must not be used to protect real data. CLEFIA defines only a block cipher; the protocol layer must handle those matters. The CLEFIA algorithm was published in 2007 and designed by Sony for lightweight cryptography on resource-constrained devices. RFC 6114 was published by M. Katagi and S. Moriai (Sony Corporation) in March 2011 with Informational category as an Independent Submission; it provides the algorithm, components, key schedule, test vectors and intermediate values. RFC 6114 says CLEFIA has been publicly scrutinized since publication with no reported security weaknesses, and was proposed for ISO/IEC 29192-2 and the CRYPTREC revision of Japan's e-Government recommended ciphers. ISO/IEC 29192-2:2019 Edition 2 lists CLEFIA with PRESENT and LEA as three block ciphers suitable for lightweight implementations, and that edition was confirmed as current in March 2025. This article's CLEFIA entity is the 128-bit block cipher only; PRESENT, LEA, AES and Camellia are separate entities, and ISO/IEC 29192-2 is the standardization document that lists CLEFIA with PRESENT and LEA, not the algorithm itself. - Wikipedia search entry for CLEFIA 轻量级分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CLEFIA%20%E8%BD%BB%E9%87%8F%E7%BA%A7%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: ECB mode: the most direct block transformation and its cost
items.text: Algorithm : Electronic Codebook (ECB 电子密码本模式). ECB (Electronic Codebook) is the simplest mode of operation. It splits plaintext into fixed-length blocks and applies the forward block-cipher function to each block independently: text C_j = E_K(P_j) Decryption is equally independent: text P_j = D_K(C_j) ECB uses no IV and has no chaining between blocks. Encrypting or decrypting a block depends only on the key and that block, so blocks can be processed in parallel and accessed individually. ECB requires a complete sequence of blocks. SP 800-38A specifies that the ECB plaintext length must be a multiple of the block size; how to pad a shorter input is an application or protocol choice. This article's teaching implementation uses CMS PKCS 7 padding: append 1 to block-size bytes, each with value equal to the number of bytes added. ECB does not change the underlying block size or key length. It simply applies the same E_K or D_K independently to every block. ECB is the baseline for understanding other modes. It shows the most primitive use of a block cipher: one block in, one block out, no IV, no chaining, no state. Most other modes exist to solve the problems ECB exposes. ECB's problem is equally basic: under one key, identical plaintext blocks always produce identical ciphertext blocks. For images, database records, repeated fields or any structured data, an attacker can see repetition directly. SP 800-38A states explicitly that if this property is undesirable in an application, ECB should not be used. ECB is therefore a teaching starting point and a reference for single-block transformation, not a general-purpose mode for multi-block data in new systems. Understanding ECB's cost matters more than memorizing that ECB is insecure. ECB was the first mode FIPS 81 defined for DES in 1980, and later one of the five modes SP 800-38A generalized to block ciphers. Its historical role comes from applying a block cipher directly to data, not from protecting multi-block structure. In a single-block setting with no repetition, or when the format itself is not sensitive, ECB's determinism may not leak extra structure. Real data often contains repetition and structure, so a safe single-block example does not generalize to safe multi-block use. Modern systems that need multi-block confidentiality usually choose a mode with an IV or an AEAD; whether ECB is still acceptable must be decided from the protocol and data shape, not from the underlying cipher being AES. ECB produces identical ciphertext blocks for identical plaintext blocks. Without the key, an attacker can see which blocks are equal, which repeat and whether the data has fixed structure. For images this preserves outlines; for databases it leaks repeated fields; for protocol records it leaks repeated headers or fixed fields. ECB has no IV, so it has no predictable-IV or IV-reuse problem; but it also provides no positional confusion. Block order and boundaries remain visible, and deleting, reordering or duplicating ciphertext blocks maps directly to plaintext blocks. ECB provides confidentiality only, not integrity. Modifying a ciphertext block modifies the corresponding plaintext block, and an attacker can make controlled substitutions; ECB cannot detect them. When integrity is needed, use AEAD or add a MAC. ECB does not change the underlying block size. With a 64-bit block cipher, large block counts remain subject to the birthday bound; a 128-bit block pushes that boundary farther away. ECB's determinism problem is independent of block size; switching to AES does not remove repeated-block leakage. ECB requires complete blocks; the padding rule and padding-error handling belong to the protocol layer. Padding provides no integrity and does not stop identical plaintext blocks from producing identical ciphertext blocks. This article's teaching implementation demonstrates only the AES-128-ECB formula, official vectors, repeated blocks and independent-block properties on fixed data. It does not implement secure padding checks, key management, protocol state machines or side-channel defenses, and it must not be used in production. In 1980, FIPS 81 defined ECB for DES. It was one of the earliest standardized ways to use a block cipher on more than one block. In 2001, SP 800-38A generalized ECB to block ciphers and supplied AES test vectors. ECB's long use also made it the classic counterexample: a correct algorithm with the wrong mode still leaks data structure. CBC, CFB, OFB, CTR and AEAD each respond in different ways to ECB's determinism. This history shows that ECB is not a wrong algorithm but a mode with a very narrow boundary: it suits settings that do not need to hide block relationships; using it for structured multi-block data turns a mode property into a system security failure. - Wikipedia search entry for ECB 电子密码本模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ECB%20%E7%94%B5%E5%AD%90%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E6%9C%AC%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: GMAC: the authenticate-only specialization of GCM
items.text: Algorithm : GMAC (GMAC 认证模式). GMAC is a specialization of GCM: it sets the plaintext length to zero and keeps only the authentication path. It takes a key K, an IV and additional authenticated data A (AAD), and outputs an authentication tag T with no ciphertext. GMAC reuses GCM's components. It first computes the hash subkey H = E_K(0^128), then builds the pre-counter block J0 from the IV length: text if len(IV) = 96 bits: J0 = IV 0^31 1 otherwise: J0 = GHASH_H(IV 0^(s+64) [len(IV)]_64) Authentication evaluates GHASH over AAD with zero ciphertext length: text S = GHASH_H(A 0^v [len(A)]_64 [0]_64) T = MSB_t(GCTR_K(J0, S)) Here v is the number of zero bits needed to pad AAD to a multiple of 128, and t is the tag length. GMAC may use the same tag lengths as GCM: 128, 120, 112, 104 or 96 bits; 64-bit and 32-bit tags are limited to constrained applications. GMAC produces no ciphertext and therefore provides no confidentiality; it only answers whether the AAD was authenticated by a party holding the key. Typical AAD is message headers, addresses, sequence numbers, versions or routing information. GMAC uses only forward E_K. It shares GCM's nonce uniqueness requirement and data limits: AAD at most 2^64-1 bits and IV length from 1 to 2^64-1 bits; unless only deterministic 96-bit IVs are used, total invocations under one key must not exceed 2^32. Many protocols need to authenticate data without encrypting it: headers, routing information, control fields, versions or public metadata. Encrypting such data adds no benefit and complicates format and key management. GMAC provides a standard authenticate-only construction. GMAC is also a good decomposition of AEAD: GCM = CTR encryption + GHASH authentication, and GMAC = drop CTR encryption and keep GHASH authentication. Both share H, J0, AAD encoding and nonce discipline, so GCM's nonce-reuse risk applies equally to GMAC. But GMAC is not a general hash and not a digital signature. It is a symmetric-key MAC; the verifier must hold the same key, and it provides no non-repudiation and cannot replace public-key signatures. GMAC suits public data that only needs authentication: protocol headers, routing fields, versions, sequence numbers or other unencrypted metadata. SP 800-38D addresses protection of sensitive information by federal agencies and non-government organizations, and GMAC is GCM's authentication specialization. In protocol design, GMAC can be used separately from encryption: the encrypted part protects confidentiality and GMAC protects unencrypted metadata; the two must use distinct keys or explicit key separation rather than casual reuse of one key. GMAC provides no confidentiality. Using GMAC as encryption reveals the entire input; using its tag as a signature wrongly assumes non-repudiation. GMAC shares GCM's IV uniqueness requirement. Repeating an IV under the same key breaks GHASH authentication: an attacker may determine the hash subkey H and construct tags that verify, essentially losing authentication assurance. GMAC verification must check the tag first and fail on mismatch. Treating GMAC as a checksum or ignoring the tag means no authentication at all. GMAC forgery probability depends on the AAD block count and tag length. The standard's appendix notes a targeted forgery probability of about n/2^t, where n is the total number of AAD and ciphertext blocks; GMAC has no ciphertext, so n is dominated by AAD. Short tags are unsuitable for long AAD or high-value settings. GMAC does not hide AAD content. Anything placed in AAD is public; data that needs secrecy must be encrypted separately, not treated as confidential because it is authenticated. GMAC's AAD limit is 2^64-1 bits, and its IV length and invocation limits match GCM. Protocols must enforce these limits over the key lifetime; authenticating only does not mean that there is no resource boundary. This article's teaching implementation demonstrates only AES-128-GMAC official vectors, AAD mismatch and tag truncation. It does not implement nonce allocation, cross-message state, constant-time tag comparison, key management, protocol state machines or side-channel defenses, and it must not be used in production. In 2007, NIST SP 800-38D standardized GCM and GMAC. GMAC was defined as the authentication specialization of GCM: when the input contains only AAD and no plaintext to encrypt, GCM reduces to GMAC. Since then GMAC has appeared mainly as an authenticate-only building block in protocols and formats that protect public metadata. It also reminds developers that AEAD's authentication part can be used alone, but nonce uniqueness and tag verification do not disappear because encryption was removed. This history shows that GMAC is not an alias of GCM but the same authentication mechanism specialized to empty plaintext. Understanding the shared parts and the difference is the precondition for using GMAC correctly. - Wikipedia search entry for GMAC 认证模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=GMAC%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation.
