items.title: BLAKE3: tree-parallel, 7-round modern hash
items.text: Algorithm : BLAKE3 (BLAKE3 散列). BLAKE3 is a single-algorithm hash function: its default output is 256 bits, it supports any output length 0 ≤ d < 2^64, and it provides hash, keyed_hash and derive_key modes. It splits input into 1024-byte chunks; chunks are leaves of a binary tree, left subtrees are full and at least as large as their siblings, and parent nodes combine the two child chaining values. Input is compressed in 64-byte blocks. The compression state v0…v15 consists of eight chaining words, four IV words, the 64-bit counter t0/t1, the block byte count b and the domain flags d; IV0…IV7 are the same constants as in BLAKE2s. It uses BLAKE2s's 32-bit mixing logic but only 7 rounds instead of BLAKE2s's 10. Each round applies G to the four columns and then to the four diagonals of the 4×4 state; G uses 16-, 12-, 8- and 7-bit right rotations. After each round except the last, the message words are permuted by the fixed permutation 2,6,3,10,7,0,4,13,1,11,12,5,9,14,15,8. The domain flags are bit masks: CHUNK_START=1, CHUNK_END=2, PARENT=4, ROOT=8, KEYED_HASH=16, DERIVE_KEY_CONTEXT=32 and DERIVE_KEY_MATERIAL=64. Inside a chunk, every block's counter is the chunk index; the block length is the actual input byte count (only the last block of the last chunk may be short); the first block sets CHUNK_START and the last sets CHUNK_END. A parent node uses one compression: the message words are the left child's 8-word chaining value followed by the right child's, with counter 0, block length 64 and the PARENT flag. Ordinary nodes truncate the compression output to its first 8 words as a 32-byte chaining value; the root uses the full 16-word (64-byte) output, encoded little-endian. The XOF repeats the root compression: the first root compression uses counter 0, and each additional 64 bytes increments the counter by 1; outputs are concatenated little-endian. In keyed_hash mode, the 256-bit key is parsed little-endian into eight words as the initial chaining value, and every compression sets the KEYED_HASH flag. derive_key has two stages: first hash the context string with the DERIVE_KEY_CONTEXT flag to get eight key words, then hash the key material with the DERIVE_KEY_MATERIAL flag. BLAKE3 is an evolution of BLAKE2: it keeps BLAKE2s's 32-bit mixing logic but reduces the round count from 10 to 7, and it gains parallelism from a tree structure rather than offering multiple platform-specific variants as BLAKE2 does. BLAKE2 was announced in 2012; RFC 7693 of November 2015 specifies BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s, and the BLAKE3 specification version used in this batch is 20211102173700. BLAKE3 targets 128-bit security with a 256-bit default output. The 7-round choice is based on existing BLAKE/BLAKE2 cryptanalysis; section 4 of the specification sets out the 128-bit security goals, compression-function analysis and mode argument. The tree structure provides unbounded parallelism and supports verified streaming and incremental updates; these are BLAKE3's main new capabilities relative to BLAKE2. The specification's performance figures: on Intel Cascade Lake-SP, peak single-threaded throughput is about 4× BLAKE2b, 8× SHA-512 and 12× SHA-256; on a 32-bit ARM1176 it is about 1.3× SHA-256. BLAKE3's unified API covers ordinary hashing, keyed hashing, key derivation and arbitrary-length output; one algorithm serves BLAKE2's use cases without choosing different variants. keyed_hash can be used as a keyed PRF/MAC; the key must be secret and 256 bits, and an ordinary hash must not be used directly as a MAC. XOF suits settings that need extendable output; the tree structure supports verified streaming and incremental updates: a single chunk can be verified along the parent path from the root, and editing anywhere requires re-hashing only the modified chunks and their ancestor parent nodes, not everything to their right. BLAKE3 also provides 35 official test vectors covering input lengths from 0 to 102400 bytes and 131-byte outputs. BLAKE3 security rests on the specification's 128-bit security goals, compression-function analysis and mode argument, together with existing BLAKE/BLAKE2 analysis. Implementation mistakes (such as chunk/tree boundaries or flag combinations) produce wrong results, not almost correct results. XOF output length : BLAKE3 does not domain-separate different output lengths: a shorter output is a prefix of a longer one; output length is therefore not an independent domain label. When different domains are needed, use keyed_hash or derive_key rather than changing the output length. Keyed mode : keyed_hash security depends on a secret, uniformly random key; the key must be 256 bits, and in practice an unkeyed hash should not be used directly as a MAC. derive_key separates uses through its context and material stages; the context should be hardcoded, globally unique and application-specific, and must not contain variable data such as salts, IDs or the current time. Tree implementation : the root chunk's last block must be recompressed with the chaining value before the last block; parent nodes always use block length 64; the XOF increments the root counter per 64 bytes; flags must be combined exactly as specified. These are correctness requirements, not optional optimizations. - 2012 : BLAKE2 is announced; the BLAKE3 specification describes BLAKE2 as its evolutionary source. - November 2015 : RFC 7693 is published, specifying BLAKE2b and BLAKE2s. - 9 January 2020 : the first published version of the BLAKE3 specification is committed. - 2 November 2021 : the BLAKE3 specification is updated to version 20211102173700, the version used in this batch. - Wikipedia search entry for BLAKE3 散列. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=BLAKE3%20%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. items.title: FIPS 202: the SHA-3 and SHAKE standard
items.text: Standard : SHA-3 Standard (SHA-3 标准). FIPS 202 is a U.S. federal information processing standard that specifies the SHA-3 family and the KECCAK-p permutation family. The SHA-3 family consists of four fixed-length hash functions (SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512) and two extendable-output functions (SHAKE128 and SHAKE256); all six are sponge modes of KECCAK-p[1600,24]. The sponge construction treats the input as a bit string, absorbs it into a 1600-bit state in rate-sized blocks, and keeps a capacity c = 1600 - r that is not directly exposed; after absorption it squeezes r bits at a time until the requested length is reached. SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512 use rates of 1152, 1088, 832 and 576 bits, capacities of 448, 512, 768 and 1024 bits, and digest lengths of 224, 256, 384 and 512 bits. SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 use rates of 1344 and 1088 bits and capacities of 256 and 512 bits; the caller chooses the output length d. The six functions use suffixes for domain separation: SHA-3 hashes append 01 to the message, SHAKE appends 1111 , and RawSHAKE128/256 use 11 , with the equivalent definition SHAKE128(M,d) = RawSHAKE128(M 11,d). For byte-aligned messages, q ≥ 2 SHA-3 padding starts with 0x06 and SHAKE with 0x1F and ends with 0x80; for q = 1 these bytes merge into 0x86/0x9F. Table 6 gives the q = 1, q = 2 and q 2 forms 0x86 / 0x0680 / 0x06 00...80 and 0x9F / 0x1F80 / 0x1F 00...80 . Messages are processed as bit strings; Appendix B defines the h2b/b2h conversions between hexadecimal strings and bit strings. The state is a 5x5x64-bit array, and KECCAK-p[1600,24] runs 24 rounds, each applying the five steps theta, rho, pi, chi and iota. The HMAC input block size B for the SHA-3 hashes is the rate in bytes: 144 for SHA3-224, 136 for SHA3-256, 104 for SHA3-384 and 72 for SHA3-512. Appendix A, Table 4, lists the collision, preimage and second-preimage security strengths of the SHA-3 members. FIPS 202 standardizes the winner of the SHA-3 competition as a second hash standard alongside SHA-1 and SHA-2. The standard explains that the four SHA-3 hashes complement SHA-1/SHA-2 in FIPS 180-4: they use different design principles, providing design diversity against future advances in hash analysis, together with "some complementary implementation and performance characteristics". SHAKE128 and SHAKE256 are the first extendable-output functions standardized by NIST; applications choose the number of output bits they need. The standard also parameterizes KECCAK-p[b,nr] so future modes can be built on the same permutation family. It provides a CAVP validation route: the SHA-3 functions, KECCAK-p[1600,24] and the six modes can be tested for conformance under CAVP. FIPS 202 applies to federal departments and agencies protecting sensitive unclassified information not subject to 10 USC 2315 and "not within a national security system": federal applications requiring a secure hash algorithm implement FIPS 202 or FIPS 180. SHA3-224/256/384/512 are "approved cryptographic hash functions" and can be used in HMAC and other approved uses; the HMAC input block sizes in Table 3 are 144, 136, 104 and 72 bytes. SHAKE128/256 are approved extendable-output functions, and their specific approved uses are specified in NIST Special Publications; FIPS 202 does not approve SHAKE as a hash function. Implementations may be software, firmware or hardware, but only implementations validated by CAVP are considered compliant; the standard allows mathematically equivalent replacement steps; OIDs are published separately by NIST. FIPS 202's user-facing functions are these six, plus KECCAK-p and intermediate functions; it does not specify derived functions such as cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash or ParallelHash, which are specified in SP 800-185. Conformance is not implementation security : conforming to FIPS 202 only means matching the algorithm's outputs; the standard explicitly says that conformance "does not assure that a particular implementation is secure", so side channels, key management, protocols and deployment still need separate assessment. Related XOF outputs : output length does not participate in domain separation, and a shorter output is a prefix of a longer one; different output lengths for the same message produce related results. Do not treat output length as a domain label; in key derivation, incorporate the length and type into the input or use a dedicated domain separation. SHAKE's approval boundary : SHAKE is an approved extendable-output function, not an approved hash function; collision and preimage security decrease with small d. Use SHA3-224/256/384/512 when a fixed-length hash is required, not SHAKE as a hash function. Standard scope : FIPS 202 does not specify cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash or ParallelHash; these derived functions are defined in SP 800-185. FIPS 202 is also not a general KDF or protocol specification; HMAC is specified in FIPS 198-1. Bit strings and interoperability : the standard is defined on bit strings, with byte alignment as a common special case; a conforming implementation may restrict the supported message or output lengths, creating interoperability differences. The standard body refers detailed security analysis to the Keccak and sponge literature rather than restating the full analysis. - 2007-2012 : NIST runs the SHA-3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm Competition. - 2 October 2012 : NIST announces Keccak as the SHA-3 competition winner. - August 2015 : FIPS 202 is published, and the standard is effective immediately. - December 2016 : SP 800-185 is published, specifying cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash and ParallelHash. The SHA-3 functions differ slightly from the competition's Keccak: SHA-3 hashes append a two-bit suffix to the message to distinguish hashes from XOFs and to leave room for future domain variants. - Wikipedia search entry for SHA-3 标准. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SHA-3%20%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 202: SHA-3 Standard. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/202/final - Published standard/RFC for SHA-3 标准. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/202/final Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. items.title: RIPEMD-160: the two-line 160-bit hash
items.text: Algorithm : RIPEMD-160 (RIPEMD-160 散列). RIPEMD-160 is an iterative hash function with a 160-bit digest; it processes 32-bit words in 512-bit message blocks and keeps a five-word state h0…h4. The initial value is h0=67452301, h1=efcdab89, h2=98badcfe, h3=10325476 and h4=c3d2e1f0. Padding is identical to MD4: append 0x80, zero-pad until the length is congruent to 448 modulo 512, and append the 64-bit little-endian message length. For "abc", the padded block is 61 62 63 80 followed by 52 00 bytes and the 8-byte length 18 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ; read little-endian, X[0]=0x80636261, X[14]=0x00000018 and X[15]=0. Each message block goes through two parallel 80-step lines; each line has five 16-step rounds with different Boolean functions and constants. The five rounds use: - f1 = x xor y xor z - f2 = (x and y) or (not x and z) - f3 = (x or not y) xor z - f4 = (x and z) or (y and not z) - f5 = x xor (y or not z) The left-line constants are 00000000, 5a827999, 6ed9eba1, 8f1bbcdc and a953fd4e; the right-line constants are 50a28be6, 5c4dd124, 6d703ef3, 7a6d76e9 and 00000000. The two lines use different message-word orders r and r' and different left-rotation amounts s and s'; this is the main structural difference from the single-line MD4/SHA-1 design. Each step computes T = ROTL(A + f(B,C,D) + X[r(j)] + K(j), s(j)) + E , then A←E, E←D, D←ROTL10(C), C←B and B←T; the right line runs the same shape with f(79−j), r', s' and K'. Every line's register update includes D←ROTL10(C): C is rotated left by 10 to become the new D. After 80 steps the two lines' registers are cross-added to the incoming chaining value: h0←h1+C+D', h1←h2+D+E', h2←h3+E+A', h3←h4+A+B' and h4←h0+B+C'. The final digest is the 160-bit little-endian byte string of h0…h4. RIPEMD was developed in the EU RIPE (RACE Integrity Primitives Evaluation) project; RIPEMD-160 is the strengthened version proposed in 1996. The paper proposes both the 160-bit RIPEMD-160 and a 128-bit RIPEMD-128 plug-in substitute for RIPEMD; the 160-bit design aims to transfer the confidence built up with RIPEMD to the new algorithm. The two lines use the same five functions in opposite order (the right line uses f(79−j)), with different constants, message orders and rotation amounts; an attacker must control both lines to build a collision, raising the difficulty of differential attacks. The design goal is to make the two lines as different as possible, not to run them independently. A 160-bit digest gives an ideal collision cost of about 2^80 and preimage/second-preimage costs of about 2^160; the paper presents the 160-bit result as the security strengthening over 128-bit RIPEMD. The paper's 90 MHz Pentium measurements show RIPEMD-160 is about 15% slower than SHA-1, about half RIPEMD's speed and about a quarter of MD4's; the security increase costs about a factor of two in performance. The paper aims to increase the security margin but gives no mathematical security proof; the authors invite further security analysis of RIPEMD-160 in the conclusion. The paper lists digital fingerprinting, message authentication, key derivation and password protection as uses; these rely on preimage, second-preimage or collision resistance. Message authentication (MAC) is one of them, but the hash itself is not a MAC, which requires a keyed construction; key derivation and password protection rely on output unpredictability and preimage resistance. RIPEMD-160 is a 160-bit hash; the paper positions it as the strengthened RIPEMD and also offers 128-bit RIPEMD-128 as the original RIPEMD's replacement. Whether a protocol adopts it depends on that protocol's own specification. RIPEMD-160 uses Merkle-Damgård iteration: the chaining value after each block is the next block's input, and the final output is the chaining value; given H(M) and the length of M, one can length-extend to H(M pad(M) X), which is not a collision. This batch demonstrates it: given the digest of RIPEMD-160(abc) and the 64-byte padded length, it computes RIPEMD-160( abc pad extra ) = 1f35150185a2c3cfc80d435934579261c99da3e0 without the original message. The birthday collision bound for a 160-bit digest is about 2^80; this is a generic-attack bound, not a specific cryptanalytic result against RIPEMD-160. The 2004 Wang, Feng, Lai and Yu ePrint 2004/199 lists MD4, MD5, HAVAL-128 and RIPEMD in its title; the title says RIPEMD, not RIPEMD-160. The two are not the same algorithm, and the original RIPEMD results cannot be carried over directly to RIPEMD-160. The two-line structure also has a performance cost: RIPEMD-160 is about 15% slower than SHA-1 and about half RIPEMD's speed; if an application already uses RIPEMD and needs a 128-bit digest, RIPEMD-128 is the paper's 128-bit substitute. Algorithm choice should weigh the protocol requirement, output length and security margin. - Before 1996 : RIPEMD is developed in the EU RIPE project as an MD4-style hash function. - 1996 : Dobbertin, Bosselaers and Preneel publish RIPEMD-160 and RIPEMD-128 at FSE 1996 (LNCS 1039, pp. 71-82). - 2004 : Wang, Feng, Lai and Yu's ePrint 2004/199 lists MD4, MD5, HAVAL-128 and RIPEMD in its title; the title says RIPEMD, not RIPEMD-160. - Wikipedia search entry for RIPEMD-160 散列. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=RIPEMD-160%20%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. items.title: SHA-1: the FIPS 180-4 160-bit hash and its collision break
items.text: Algorithm : SHA-1 (SHA-1 散列). SHA-1 is one of the secure hash algorithms specified by FIPS 180-4: it takes a message shorter than 2^64 bits and outputs a fixed 160-bit (20-byte) message digest. It processes 512-bit (sixteen 32-bit word) blocks, and its internal state is five 32-bit words H0…H4. RFC 3174 (September 2001, Informational) makes the same algorithm, its C reference code and its test driver conveniently available to the Internet community, and states that it does not specify an Internet standard; this article follows FIPS 180-4 for the algorithm description and RFC 3174 for the test vectors. The padding rule is: append a single 1 bit (an 0x80 byte in implementations), then the smallest number of 0 bits that makes the bit length congruent to 448 modulo 512, and finally a 64-bit representation of the message length before padding (most significant byte first, i.e. big-endian). Padding is applied even when the length is already congruent. For "abc" (24 bits), the padded block is 64 bytes: 61 62 63 80 , then 52 00 bytes, then the 8-byte length 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 18 . Read as 32-bit words, X[0] = 0x61626380, X[15] = 0x00000018, and the rest are zero. The padded message is parsed into N 512-bit blocks, each block being sixteen 32-bit words M(0)…M(15). SHA-1's initial hash value is: H0 = 67452301 H1 = efcdab89 H2 = 98badcfe H3 = 10325476 H4 = c3d2e1f0 The first sixteen schedule words are the block words; for 16 ≤ t ≤ 79 the expansion is W(t) = ROTL1(W(t−3) xor W(t−8) xor W(t−14) xor W(t−16)) where ROTL1 is a 32-bit left rotation by one position. The 80 steps use three logical functions: steps 0–19 use the conditional select Ch(x,y,z) = (x and y) xor (not x and z) ; steps 20–39 and 60–79 use the parity function x xor y xor z ; steps 40–59 use the majority function Maj(x,y,z) = (x and y) xor (x and z) xor (y and z) . The four stage constants are 0x5a827999 (0–19), 0x6ed9eba1 (20–39), 0x8f1bbcdc (40–59) and 0xca62c1d6 (60–79). Each step computes T = ROTL5(a) + f(t,b,c,d) + e + K(t) + W(t) e ← d d ← c c ← ROTL30(b) b ← a a ← T All additions are 32-bit additions modulo 2^32, and ROTL5 and ROTL30 are left rotations by 5 and 30 positions. After the 80 steps of a block, the working variables are added back to the incoming hash value: H0←H0+a, H1←H1+b, H2←H2+c, H3←H3+d, H4←H4+e. After all blocks are processed, the 160-bit digest is the concatenation H0 H1 H2 H3 H4. SHA-1 has 80 steps divided into four 20-step stages by function and constant. SHA-1's lineage goes back to MD4: RFC 3174 says SHA-1 is based on principles similar to those used by Ronald L. Rivest in designing MD4, and is modelled after MD4. Its predecessor SHA-0 was first published in 1993 and SHA-1 in 1996; SHA-0 is SHA-1's predecessor and the two differ only by a single rotation in the message-expansion function, and NIST withdrew SHA-0 in 1996. RFC 6194 therefore says "it is not prudent to use either" SHA-0 or SHA-1 when collision resistance is required, and that any use of SHA-0 is strongly discouraged. A 160-bit digest has a birthday bound of 2^80: on an ideal hash function, finding "any two messages with the same digest" costs about 2^80 operations, while a 128-bit digest gives 2^64. SHA-1's 80 steps, four 20-step stages and per-step message-schedule word spread a local change over more rounds. RFC 3174 also notes that signing the "digest rather than the message often improves" efficiency because the digest is much smaller, and that the verifier must use the same hash algorithm as the signer. The standard does not give a security proof. RFC 3174 says SHA-1 is called secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a message for a given digest or two messages with the same digest - the security assumption of its time, not a mathematical theorem or a permanent guarantee of collision resistance. The later attacks broke exactly at the edge of that assumption. SHA-1's typical use is digital signatures: compute a message digest, then feed the digest to a signature algorithm for signature generation or verification; FIPS 180-4 also includes SHA-1 in the Secure Hash Standard. Even in 2017 it was still widely used for document signatures and TLS certificate signatures, and in software such as Git for integrity and backup. The SHAttered paper lists the Git version-control system as one of the software examples where SHA-1 was still widely used in 2017. HMAC-SHA-1 is a different use: HMAC uses SHA-1 as a keyed message authentication code rather than as a collision-resistant hash. RFC 6194 section 3.3 says that as of 2011 there is no indication that attacks on SHA-1 can be extended to HMAC-SHA-1. RFC 2202 section 3 provides seven HMAC-SHA-1 conformance test cases; case 2 uses key "Jefe" and message "what do ya want for nothing?", with digest effcdf6ae5eb2fa2d27416d5f184df9c259a7c79 . NIST's current policy separates the uses carefully: Table 8 of SP 800-131A Rev. 2 marks SHA-1 digital signature generation as "disallowed" except where "specifically allowed by NIST protocol-specific guidance", digital signature verification as "legacy use", and non-digital-signature applications as "acceptable"; the notes after the table repeat these three points. RFC 6194 concludes that SHA-1 provides less collision resistance than expected, and that protocol designers should strongly consider supporting a stronger hash; SHA-256 was the most commonly specified alternative at the time. To be explicit: "acceptable" here covers only uses "that do not require collision resistance"; no new design that requires collision resistance should use SHA-1. The SHAttered paper also records that after the 2015 freestart-collision cost estimates, the CA/Browser Forum withdrew its ballot to extend SHA-1 HTTPS certificate issuance, and the IETF TLS 1.3 specification deprecated SHA-1 digital signatures. A collision is a pair of distinct messages x and y with H(x)=H(y). For a 160-bit digest the generic birthday attack costs about 2^80; SHA-1's collision resistance was pushed below that bound step by step after 2005. RFC 6194 section 3.1 records that the first SHA-1 attack in early 2005 targeted a version "reduced to 53 rounds. The very next month" Wang, Yin and Yu "showed collisions in the full 80 rounds in" about 2^69 operations; as of 2011 no published result improved on that result. RFC 6194 also states that SHA-1's "collision security strength is significantly less than" the ideal hash function's 2^80. In 2013 Stevens presented the then-best collision attack on full SHA-1, with an estimated cost of about 2^61 compression-function calls. In 2017 Stevens, Bursztein, Karpman, Albertini and Markov provided the first known collision instance for full SHA-1: two PDF documents with the same SHA-1 hash but different visual contents. The collision cost was equivalent to about 2^63.1 SHA-1 compressions and took approximately 6,500 CPU years and 100 GPU years; the authors say this is still more than 100,000 times faster than a brute-force search. That result moved SHA-1 collisions from a theoretical possibility to an actual computation. In 2020 Leurent and Peyrin reported the first practical implementation of a SHA-1 chosen-prefix collision: the attacker can make two colliding messages begin with two arbitrary distinct prefixes, which is more dangerous than a plain (identical-prefix) collision. The chosen-prefix collision has complexity about 2^63.4 (about 2^61.2 for a plain collision); the actual computation used 900 Nvidia GTX 1060 GPUs for two months, and the authors estimate a cost of about US$45,000 (about US$11,000 for a plain collision). In the PGP demonstration, the attacker creates two keys with different identities and colliding SHA-1 certificates, so that a third party's certification signature on Bob's key transfers to Alice's forged key, yielding impersonation. The authors conclude that SHA-1 should not be used in any security protocol where some kind of collision resistance is expected; continued use of SHA-1 for certificates or for authentication of handshake messages in TLS or SSH is dangerous, and they strongly advise removing SHA-1 support. What was broken is collision resistance, not every property: - Pre-image and second pre-image : RFC 6194 section 3.2 says "There are no known pre-image or second pre-image attacks" specific to full-round SHA-1; however, a general result for narrow-pipe Merkle-Damgård hashes finds a second pre-image for a 60-byte message in about 2^106 computations. The best reduced-round pre-image attack is on 48 of 80 rounds with complexity 2^159; the RFC cautions that reduced-round results indicate a security margin, not an attack on the full algorithm. - HMAC-SHA-1 : RFC 6194 section 3.3 says that as of 2011 there is no indication that attacks on SHA-1 can be extended to HMAC-SHA-1. This is consistent with NIST marking SHA-1's non-signature uses as acceptable; but it only says the known collision attacks have not extended to HMAC, not that HMAC-SHA-1 is safe in every setting. On the governance side, the SHAttered paper says SHA-1 is a 1995 NIST standard and was officially deprecated by NIST in 2011 because of fundamental security weaknesses demonstrated by cryptanalysis; RFC 6194 records that NIST recommended against generating digital signatures with SHA-1 after 31 December 2010, and specified that U.S. federal agencies must not generate SHA-1 signatures for sensitive but unclassified information after 31 December 2013. Systems that still use SHA-1 today should restrict it to legacy settings that do not need collision resistance and replace it under a migration plan. - 1993 : SHA-0 is first published; RFC 6194 records that NIST withdrew SHA-0 in 1996. - 1995–1996 : the SHAttered paper calls SHA-1 a 1995 NIST standard; RFC 6194 records that SHA-1 was first published in 1996. SHA-0 is SHA-1's predecessor and the two differ only by a single rotation in the message-expansion function. - September 2001 : RFC 3174 is published, collecting the SHA-1 algorithm, C code and test vectors in an Informational document. - 2005 : Wang, Yin and Yu show collisions in the full 80 rounds in about 2^69 operations; about a month earlier, the first attack had targeted a version reduced to 53 rounds. - March 2011 : RFC 6194 is published, summarizing the security considerations for SHA-0 and SHA-1 and giving protocol-design guidance; around the same time NIST officially deprecated SHA-1 for digital signatures. - 2013 : Stevens gives an estimated full-SHA-1 collision cost of about 2^61 compression-function calls. - 2017 : the SHAttered result is published at CRYPTO 2017 (LNCS 10401, pp. 570-596), giving the first actual collision instance. - March 2019 : NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2 is published; its Table 8 gives the current status of SHA-1 for signature generation, signature verification and non-signature applications. - August 2020 : the Shambles result is published at the 29th USENIX Security Symposium, giving the first practical chosen-prefix collision and a PGP/GnuPG impersonation demonstration. - Wikipedia search entry for SHA-1 散列. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SHA-1%20%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 3174: US Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA1). https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3174 Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: SHA-2: the FIPS 180-4 256/512-bit hash family
items.text: Algorithm : SHA-2 (SHA-2 散列家族). SHA-2 is not one algorithm but six secure hash algorithms in FIPS 180-4: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256. Their digest lengths are 224, 256, 384, 512, 224 and 256 bits respectively. The family has two lines: SHA-224/256 use 32-bit words, 512-bit message blocks and 64 rounds; SHA-384/512 and the two SHA-512/t variants use 64-bit words, 1024-bit message blocks and 80 rounds. Algorithm Digest Block Word Rounds --- --- --- --- --- SHA-224 224 512 32 64 SHA-256 256 512 32 64 SHA-384 384 1024 64 80 SHA-512 512 1024 64 80 SHA-512/224 224 1024 64 80 SHA-512/256 256 1024 64 80 Padding has the same structure as SHA-1's but a longer length field: append a single 1 bit (an 0x80 byte in implementations), then enough 0 bits to make the length congruent to 448 modulo 512 (SHA-224/256) or 896 modulo 1024 (SHA-384/512 family), and finally the 64-bit or 128-bit big-endian message length. SHA-224/256 accept input shorter than 2^64 bits; the SHA-384/512 family accepts input shorter than 2^128 bits. The padded message is parsed into "512-bit or 1024-bit blocks"; each block is split into sixteen "32-bit or 64-bit words", written most significant byte first. For "abc", the SHA-224/256 padded block is 61 62 63 80 followed by 52 00 bytes and the 8-byte length 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 18 . The initial values of SHA-256/384/512 come from fractional parts of square roots of primes; SHA-224 and SHA-512/t use their own specified derived values: - SHA-256: the first 32 bits of the fractional square roots of the first eight primes, namely 6a09e667, bb67ae85, 3c6ef372, a54ff53a, 510e527f, 9b05688c, 1f83d9ab and 5be0cd19. - SHA-224: uses the same algorithm as SHA-256 but a different initial value, namely c1059ed8, 367cd507, 3070dd17, f70e5939, ffc00b31, 68581511, 64f98fa7 and befa4fa4; these are the low 32 bits of SHA-384's eight 64-bit initial values. - SHA-512: the first 64 bits of the fractional square roots of the first eight primes, namely 6a09e667f3bcc908, bb67ae8584caa73b, 3c6ef372fe94f82b, a54ff53a5f1d36f1, 510e527fade682d1, 9b05688c2b3e6c1f, 1f83d9abfb41bd6b and 5be0cd19137e2179. - SHA-384: the first 64 bits of the fractional "square roots of the ninth through sixteenth" primes, namely cbbb9d5dc1059ed8, 629a292a367cd507, 9159015a3070dd17, 152fecd8f70e5939, 67332667ffc00b31, 8eb44a8768581511, db0c2e0d64f98fa7 and 47b5481dbefa4fa4. SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 use the SHA-512/t IV generation function: XOR the eight SHA-512 initial words with a5a5a5a5a5a5a5a5, then compute SHA-512 over the string "SHA-512/224" or "SHA-512/256" (t replaced by 224 or 256) with that IV; the resulting eight words are the IV. FIPS 180-4 explicitly approves the t=224 and t=256 truncations. The round constants also come from primes: SHA-224/256 use 64 32-bit constants, the first 32 bits of the fractional cube roots of the first 64 primes, from 428a2f98 through c67178f2; the SHA-384/512 family uses 80 64-bit constants, the first 64 bits of the fractional cube roots of the first 80 primes, from 428a2f98d728ae22 through 6c44198c4a475817. The 32-bit variants use Ch(x,y,z) = (x and y) xor (not x and z) , Maj(x,y,z) = (x and y) xor (x and z) xor (y and z) , and four rotate/shift functions: Σ0 = ROTR2 xor ROTR13 xor ROTR22 , Σ1 = ROTR6 xor ROTR11 xor ROTR25 , σ0 = ROTR7 xor ROTR18 xor SHR3 , and σ1 = ROTR17 xor ROTR19 xor SHR10 . The 64-bit variants have the same structure with rotations 28/34/39, 14/18/41, 1/8/7 and 19/61/6. The message schedule starts with the sixteen block words and then computes W(t) = σ1(W(t−2)) + W(t−7) + σ0(W(t−15)) + W(t−16) ; SHA-256 expands to 64 words and SHA-512 to 80. Each round computes T1 = h + Σ1(e) + Ch(e,f,g) + K(t) + W(t) T2 = Σ0(a) + Maj(a,b,c) h←g g←f f←e e←d+T1 d←c c←b b←a a←T1+T2 All additions are modulo 2^32 in the 32-bit variants and modulo 2^64 in the 64-bit variants. After the 64 or 80 rounds of a block, the eight working variables are added back to the incoming eight hash words; after all blocks, the output is those eight words, or a 224/384/256-bit truncation for the relevant variant. SHA-2's lineage is larger digests alongside SHA-1. FIPS 180-2, published on 1 August 2002, supersedes FIPS 180-1 and adds SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, three algorithms "capable of producing larger message digests"; SHA-1 itself is unchanged as an algorithm, with notation adjustments. Change Notice 1 of 25 February 2004 adds SHA-224; FIPS 180-4 of August 2015 adds SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256. SHA-2 is not a simple truncation of SHA-1: it uses larger states, different word sizes and different round counts. The family deliberately has two lines: SHA-224/256 target 32-bit operations, while the SHA-384/512 family targets 64-bit operations. This lets one family cover different platforms and digest lengths: SHA-256 when a 256-bit digest is needed, the SHA-512 family when a longer digest or 64-bit arithmetic is advantageous, and the truncated variants when the SHA-256/512 compression function must be kept but a 224/384-bit output is required. The IVs and round constants come from fractional parts of square and cube roots of primes. This public, reproducible derivation reduces the room for hidden structure, but the standard does not treat it as a security proof. FIPS 180-2 calls the algorithms secure because it is computationally infeasible to find a preimage or a collision - the security assumption of its time, not a mathematical theorem. NIST SP 800-107 Table 1 gives the security strengths: SHA-224 has 112/224 bits of collision/preimage resistance, SHA-256 128/256, SHA-384 192/384, SHA-512 256/512, SHA-512/224 112/224 and SHA-512/256 128/256. SHA-2's typical uses include digital signatures, certificates, HMAC and hash-based key derivation. SP 800-107 lists digital signatures as a typical use of SHA-2 and notes that a digital signature's security strength is the hash function's collision resistance strength; it also devotes a section to HMAC, stating that HMAC security depends on the underlying hash, the key strength and the MacTag length, and uses SHA-2 in a two-step extract-then-expand key derivation structure. HMAC-SHA-2 has public conformance vectors. RFC 4231's Jefe case uses key "Jefe" and message "what do ya want for nothing?", with HMAC-SHA-256 5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843 and HMAC-SHA-512 164b7a7bfcf819e2e395fbe73b56e0a387bd64222e831fd610270cd7ea2505549758bf75c05a994a6d034f65f8f0e6fdcaeab1a34d4a6b4b636e070a38bce737 . RFC 6234 provides C reference code, test vectors and HMAC/HKDF implementations for SHA-224/256/384/512. NIST's current policy marks all six SHA-2 members acceptable for all hash function applications. Table 8 of SP 800-131A Rev. 2 states this explicitly. This is a standards-level statement, not a claim that every SHA-2 use is automatically secure; a protocol still has to choose the right property (collision, preimage, second preimage) and manage keys correctly. Truncated variants suit output-length-constrained settings, at the cost of collision resistance. SP 800-107 permits truncated message digests but requires collision resistance to be counted as half the truncated length; for example, a 96-bit truncated SHA-256 has only 48-bit collision resistance. SHA-256's 256-bit output must not be equated with 256-bit collision security. SHA-2 is currently a NIST-approved standard hash family; Table 8 of SP 800-131A Rev. 2 marks all six members acceptable for all hash function applications. But "acceptable" does not mean no attack surface; at least three boundaries matter. Length extension : SHA-2 uses Merkle-Damgård iteration, where the chaining value after each block is the input to the next and the final output is the chaining value. Given H(M) and the length of M, an attacker can compute H(M pad(M) X) without knowing M. This is not a collision, but it breaks the naive construction that uses the hash directly as a MAC. This batch demonstrates it with "abc": knowing SHA-256("abc") and the 64-byte padded length, it computes f4566a6bc1df12da948d3d1da5e67458ff0cb761d456bd7382438a8903b433b4 without rereading the original message, matching the direct hash of abc pad(abc) "extra" . Do not use H(K M) as a MAC : because of length extension, a MAC built by concatenating a key and a message with SHA-2 is insecure. Use HMAC; SP 800-107 gives guidance on HMAC use, and HMAC separates key processing from message hashing with its ipad/opad layers. The RFC 4231 vectors can be used to check an HMAC-SHA-2 implementation. Truncation lowers strength : a digest truncated to t bits provides at most about t/2 bits of collision resistance; SHA-224, SHA-384, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 provide about 112, 192, 112 and 128 bits of collision resistance respectively. When choosing a truncated variant, estimate by the target security strength, not by the nominal output length of the parent variant. NIST approval is a policy judgement, not a mathematical proof; better cryptanalysis of the SHA-2 compression function may appear in the future. Engineering practice should treat SHA-2 as a currently usable standard hash, not a guarantee of permanent security; when a different structural assumption is needed, SHA-3 is another NIST-approved family. - 1 August 2002 : FIPS 180-2 is published with SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512; it supersedes FIPS 180-1 and adds three algorithms capable of producing larger digests. - 25 February 2004 : Change Notice 1 to FIPS 180-2 adds SHA-224. - 17 October 2008 : FIPS 180-2 is superseded by a later edition; FIPS 180-4 Appendix C describes technical changes from FIPS 180-3. - May 2011 : RFC 6234 is published, obsoleting RFC 4634 and providing open-source implementations and test vectors for SHA-224/256/384/512, HMAC and HKDF. - August 2015 : FIPS 180-4 is published, adding SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 to FIPS 180-3. - March 2019 : NIST SP 800-131A Rev. 2 is published; Table 8 marks the SHA-2 family acceptable for all hash function applications. - Wikipedia search entry for SHA-2 散列家族. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SHA-2%20%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97%E5%AE%B6%E6%97%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: SHA-3: the FIPS 202 sponge hash and SHAKE extendable output
items.text: Algorithm : SHA-3 (SHA-3 与 Keccak). SHA-3 is the six-function family defined by FIPS 202: four fixed-length hash functions, SHA3-224, SHA3-256, SHA3-384 and SHA3-512, plus two extendable-output functions, SHAKE128 and SHAKE256. All six are built on the KECCAK-p[1600,24] permutation: the state is a 5×5 array of 64-bit lanes, 1600 bits in total, and the permutation iterates for 24 rounds. SHA-3 uses the sponge construction. With rate r and capacity c, r + c = 1600. The absorb phase splits the input into r-bit blocks: each block is XORed into the first r bits of the state, followed by one KECCAK-p[1600,24] call. The squeeze phase reads output from the first r bits of the state; if more output is needed, it permutes again and continues until the requested length is reached. The capacity is not directly exposed as input or output; it is the sponge's security parameter. The six rate/capacity pairs are: Function Rate (bits) Capacity (bits) Output --- --- --- --- SHA3-224 1152 448 224 bits SHA3-256 1088 512 256 bits SHA3-384 832 768 384 bits SHA3-512 576 1024 512 bits SHAKE128 1344 256 any d bits SHAKE256 1088 512 any d bits Padding uses pad10 1: append a 1, enough 0 bits and a final 1 so the total length is a multiple of the rate. SHA-3 also appends a two- or four-bit domain suffix: SHA3-224/256/384/512 append 01 , while SHAKE128/256 append 1111 ; the suffix puts hash-function and XOF inputs in different domains. Each KECCAK-p round applies five steps: θ does column parity mixing, ρ rotates within lanes, π permutes lanes, χ applies row-wise non-linear mixing and ι XORs a round constant. KECCAK-p[1600,24] uses 24 64-bit round constants, from 0000000000000001 through 8000000080008008; the ρ rotation amounts and π lane permutation are fixed tables. State lanes map to message/output bytes in little-endian order: the first byte of an eight-byte block enters the least significant byte of the lane. SHA3-224/256/384/512 output fixed 224/256/384/512-bit digests; SHAKE128/SHAKE256 can output any d bits. Shorter SHAKE outputs provide lower collision/preimage strength, as given by the FIPS 202 security-strength table. SHA-3 comes from NIST's public SHA-3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm Competition: FIPS 202 states that SHA-3 is based on KECCAK, the algorithm NIST selected as the winner of that competition. The Keccak reference defines Keccak as a family of sponge functions built on the Keccak-f permutation and pad10 1; the choice of rate and capacity determines the security strength. The sponge differs from SHA-2's Merkle-Damgård iteration: SHA-2 feeds the chaining value directly into the next block and finally uses it as the digest, while SHA-3 splits the state into rate and capacity, absorbs/squeezes only the rate part, and squeezes the final output from the state rather than exposing the chaining value directly. That structural difference is why SHA-3 is designed to resist length-extension and similar attacks that work against Merkle-Damgård constructions. Capacity is the security parameter: a larger capacity means a smaller rate and a higher generic-attack bound. SHA3-256 has c=512 bits and SHA3-512 has c=1024 bits. FIPS 202 Table 4 gives the security strengths: SHA3-224 112-bit collision/224-bit preimage, SHA3-256 128/256, SHA3-384 192/384, SHA3-512 256/512; SHAKE128/256 collision strength is min(d/2,128)/min(d/2,256) and preimage strength is min(d,128)/min(d,256). These numbers are the result of analysis and standards policy, not a mathematical proof of permanent security; the Keccak security claim is centered on capacity, and generic attacks are bounded by capacity, but that is not a proof against specific cryptanalysis. XOF is SHA-3's new capability relative to SHA-2: SHAKE can produce any requested length without first fixing a digest size and truncating. The cost is that the output length does not affect the prefix already produced: SHAKE128(M, d) is a prefix of SHAKE128(M, d+e), unlike a fixed-length hash. The domain suffix keeps SHA-3 hashes, SHAKE, RawSHAKE and other uses from being confused with one another. SHA3-224/256/384/512 are NIST-approved hash functions usable for all hash function applications. Table 8 of SP 800-131A Rev. 2 explicitly marks the SHA-3 family acceptable for all hash function applications; SHAKE128/256 are approved extendable-output functions whose specific uses are specified in NIST Special Publications. One direct use of SHAKE is as an XOF: when an arbitrary-length output is needed, call SHAKE128 or SHAKE256. SP 800-185 defines four types of SHA-3-derived functions on top of SHA-3 - cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash and ParallelHash - each with 128-bit and 256-bit security strengths. KMAC is the Keccak Message Authentication Code, providing keyed integrity and authentication; it is a SHA-3-derived function, not the SHA-3 hash itself. HMAC can also use SHA-3. FIPS 202 Table 3 gives the HMAC-SHA3 input block size B, which equals the rate in bytes for that SHA-3 hash: 144 bytes for SHA3-224, 136 for SHA3-256, 104 for SHA3-384 and 72 for SHA3-512. B is not the digest length; for example, SHA3-256 has B=136 bytes, corresponding to a rate of 1088 bits. SHA-3 is currently a NIST-approved standard hash family, but that does not mean there is no attack surface. At least three boundaries matter. Length extension : FIPS 202 says SHA-3 is designed to resist length-extension and similar attacks. Unlike Merkle-Damgård hashes, the classic H(M pad(M) X) length extension does not apply directly to SHA-3; the sponge absorbs and squeezes only the rate part, and the capacity is not directly exposed. Capacity limit : sponge security is bounded by capacity; making a SHAKE output longer does not raise security above the bound allowed by the capacity. SHAKE128's collision strength is capped at 128 bits and SHAKE256's at 256 bits; when the output length d is small, collision strength falls as min(d/2, …). XOF related outputs : SHAKE's output length does not affect the prefix it produces. An application must not treat SHAKE as a hash whose output length can be changed freely: if a protocol treats output length as a security parameter, a longer output contains all the bits of a shorter output, which can break domain separation or key-derivation assumptions. Domain/rate misuse : using the wrong domain suffix or rate produces a different output. items.title: Preimage Attack
items.text: Attack : Preimage Attack (原像攻击). A preimage attack, given a hash value y, looks for an input x such that h(x)=y. Preimage resistance requires that finding a preimage be infeasible for essentially all specified outputs. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Preimage attacks are used to assess the one-wayness of a hash function. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. A preimage attack is not the same as a collision attack; collisions are generally easier to find than preimages. Adv_A = Pr[Succ_A] − Pr[Succ_ideal]；Cost = D × T × M；Success = 1[advantage threshold]. Symbols are catalogue-level variables, not standard constants; parameters, test vectors and clauses remain with the registered source. The model states structural relations, not an implementation audit. HAC defines preimage resistance in §9.2.2. items.title: Algebraic Attack
items.text: Attack : Algebraic Attack (代数攻击). An algebraic attack represents cipher operations and S-boxes as polynomial equations over a finite field, then solves for key variables using linearization or elimination methods. Classical differential and linear analysis rely on probabilistic characteristics; algebraic attacks use deterministic equations that hold with probability 1, potentially bypassing the intuition that security grows exponentially with each round. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. The paper applies algebraic methods to Rijndael/AES and Serpent, discusses equation-system construction for XL and XSL, and analyzes their quadratic equation systems and equation counts. items.title: Biclique Attack
items.text: Attack : Biclique Attack (双团攻击). A biclique attack organizes internal cipher states as a complete bipartite graph (biclique) and connects the two sides through matching, amortizing key-recovery computation. items.title: Boomerang Attack
items.text: Attack : Boomerang Attack (回旋镖攻击). The boomerang attack splits the cipher into E0 and E1 and uses a high-probability differential for E0 and one for E1^{-1} to build a quartet P, P′, Q, Q′; when the first three differentials hold, Q and Q′ satisfy the E0^{-1} differential with high probability. The whole cipher may have no high-probability differential, while two short differentials can each have high probability, so the boomerang attack defeats the folk theorem that a low whole-cipher differential probability implies security. items.title: Cold Boot Attack
items.text: Attack : Cold Boot Attack (冷启动攻击). A cold boot attack exploits DRAM remanence: after cutting power, the attacker quickly reboots the machine (or transplants the memory chips into another computer), images memory and recovers keys from it. The paper defeated disk encryption systems including BitLocker, TrueCrypt and FileVault by recovering keys from memory images. DRAM contents do not vanish immediately after power loss but decay gradually: at normal temperatures they typically persist for several seconds before rapid decay, and at low temperatures they can persist for minutes or even hours. The paper also found that decay timing and ground states are often predictable, allowing key reconstruction with error correction. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. The paper recovered keys from disk encryption systems, as well as a Mac OS X login password and RSA private keys from an Apache server. The authors note that any sensitive data present in memory when an attacker gains physical access may be affected. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Cold boot attacks require physical access rather than remote execution; defenses include scrubbing or obscuring keys before losing physical control, restricting boot from network or removable media, protecting DRAM chips and making memory decay faster. The paper concludes that these measures only partially mitigate the risk and that no simple remedy eliminates it. items.title: Differential-Linear Cryptanalysis
items.text: Attack : Differential-Linear Cryptanalysis (差分线性). A differential-linear attack splits a block cipher into two parts: a high-probability differential covers the first part, a high-bias linear approximation covers the second, and chosen plaintexts connect the two to recover key bits. items.text: Attack : Differential Side-Channel (差分侧信道). items.title: Distinguishing Attack
items.text: Attack : Distinguishing Attack (区分攻击). A distinguishing attack uses a statistical test to decide whether cipher output looks random or like the output of a particular cipher; it need not recover the key, but it demonstrates a detectable non-random bias. Any measurable deviation from a uniform random distribution lets an attacker distinguish; the larger the bias and the less output required, the stronger the distinguishing attack. items.title: Fault Injection Attack
items.text: Attack : Fault Attack (故障注入攻击). A fault attack exploits errors produced by hardware during computation. For CRT-based RSA signatures, if the fault occurs in the computation for only one CRT prime, a correct and a faulty signature of the same message, or a single faulty signature on a known message, can reveal the factorization of N through a greatest common divisor; non-CRT implementations generally require many more faults. Hardware faults are rare but do occur, and an attacker with physical access can also induce them; faulty outputs let the attacker bypass the difficulty of directly factoring the modulus. items.title: Higher-Order Differential Attack
items.text: Attack : Higher-Order Differential Attack (高阶差分). A higher-order differential takes the k-th derivative of a function over a k-dimensional subspace; if the algebraic degree is less than k, the derivative is zero. items.title: Integral Attack
items.text: Attack : Integral Attack (积分攻击). items.title: Padding Oracle Attack
items.text: Attack : Padding Oracle Attack (填充预言攻击). A padding oracle attack targets CBC mode: after decryption the receiver checks whether the padding is valid. The attacker modifies the preceding ciphertext block, observes padding validity and gradually recovers intermediate values and plaintext. Receivers typically report padding errors with an acknowledgment or error message, which leaks one bit about padding validity. Vaudenay calls this a side channel and shows that one bit is enough to drive decryption. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. The paper lists standards using CBC and padding, including SSL/TLS, IPsec and WTLS, as application scenarios; the attacker needs chosen ciphertexts and an observable padding-validity signal. For 8-byte blocks and a 256-character alphabet, about 1024N oracle calls decrypt N blocks on average. items.title: Power Analysis
items.text: Attack : Power Analysis (功耗分析). Power analysis infers keys or intermediate values from the power consumption of a cryptographic device during computation. Simple power analysis (SPA) directly interprets power traces, while differential power analysis (DPA) statistically correlates guessed intermediate values with many traces. Semiconductor logic gates consume power and emit electromagnetic radiation as charge is applied or removed, so power consumption depends on the instructions executed and the data processed. Even constant-execution-path code can have serious power leakage on some microprocessors, and DPA can recover keys from noisy measurements using statistical methods. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. The paper focuses on tamper-resistant devices such as smart cards and notes that DPA can break implementations of almost any symmetric or asymmetric algorithm, and can even reverse-engineer unknown algorithms and protocols. The authors also stress that the attacks were not limited to smart cards in their lab: they extracted keys from almost 50 different products. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. items.title: Rainbow Table
items.text: Attack : Rainbow Table (彩虹表). Different columns use different reductions, so only collisions in the same column merge; lookup reduces the target column by column, and a matching endpoint allows the chain to be regenerated. Sequential rainbow took 13.6 seconds, ordinary rainbow 66.3 seconds, and the classic distinguished-points method 101 seconds. items.title: Rotational Attack
items.text: Attack : Rotational Attack (旋转攻击). A rotational attack exploits the rotational symmetry of ARX primitives. A rotational pair is an input pair of the form (X, X<<<r); XOR and rotation preserve the relation with probability 1, each modular addition preserves it with probability at most about 3/8, and round constants and key addition perturb it further. items.title: Timing Attack
items.text: Attack : Timing Attack (计时攻击). A timing attack infers secrets by carefully measuring the execution time of private-key operations. Kocher showed that, against a vulnerable implementation, an attacker can recover fixed Diffie-Hellman exponents, factor RSA keys and break other cryptosystems; the attack is computationally inexpensive and often needs only known ciphertext. Cryptosystems take slightly different amounts of time for different inputs because of performance optimizations, branches and conditional statements, cache hits and processor instructions with non-fixed timing, and the time typically depends on both the key and the input data. items.title: Credential Stuffing
items.text: Attack : Credential Stuffing (凭据填充). Credential stuffing uses username/password pairs obtained from breaches of unrelated accounts to log into target accounts, exploiting users’ tendency to reuse passwords across services. Large numbers of breached credential pairs become available online; if a target user reused a password, the attacker may log in without cracking anything. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Common targets include management services, single sign-on and federated authentication, cloud applications and externally facing email systems; attackers can automate large numbers of attempts. items.title: Manger’s Attack
items.text: Attack : Manger's Attack (Manger 攻击). Manger’s attack is an adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack against PKCS 1 v2.0 RSA-OAEP. It uses an oracle that indicates whether the decrypted value is below B=2^{8(k−1)}, recovering the plaintext rather than the private key. The OAEP specification requires integer-to-octet conversion errors and OAEP decoding errors to return the same information, but implementation differences in spelling, logs or timing can still distinguish the two stages; once distinguishable, the attack narrows the plaintext range step by step. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. The attack targets RSAES-OAEP implementations; for a 1024-bit RSA key it needs about 1100 oracle queries, on the order of log2 n queries. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Defenses require integer-conversion failures and OAEP integrity failures to be indistinguishable in error messages, logs and timing; using OAEP without removing this distinguishability remains vulnerable. items.title: Nonce Reuse
items.text: Attack : Nonce Reuse (nonce 复用). A nonce (initialization vector) is a value used for an encryption invocation; under one key, GCM requires IV uniqueness with a repetition probability no greater than 2^-32. Nonce reuse means the same key and IV are used for two distinct sets of input data. GCM confidentiality and authentication both depend on IV uniqueness. The standard requires the probability of repeating an IV under one key to be no greater than 2^-32, and notes that even one repetition can enable forgery attacks. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. GCM allows either a deterministic IV construction (fixed field plus invocation field) or an RBG-based construction; IVs shorter than 96 bits must use the deterministic construction. Deterministic construction commonly uses a counter, while the RBG construction requires a random field of at least 96 bits and imposes invocation limits for non-96-bit deterministic IVs and RBG-based IVs. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Nonce reuse essentially destroys GCM’s authentication assurance and may let an attacker construct forged ciphertexts for a desired plaintext of the same length. Defenses include unique counters, sufficiently random nonces, and respecting the 2^32 invocation limit for non-96-bit deterministic IVs or RBG-based IVs. items.title: Automatic Certificate Management Environment
items.text: Protocol : Automatic Certificate Management Environment (ACME 证书自动管理). ACME automates proof of domain control: §1 sets the premise "Certificates [RFC5280] in the Web PKI are most commonly used to authenticate domain names." the abstract describes the status quo it replaces — "As of this writing, this verification is done through a collection of ad hoc mechanisms." — and §4 gives the carrier: "ACME allows a client to request certificate management actions using a set of JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) messages [RFC8259] carried over HTTPS [RFC2818]." §6.2 sets request authentication: "All ACME requests with a non-empty body MUST encapsulate their payload in a JSON Web Signature (JWS) [RFC7515] object" and "The server MUST verify the JWS before processing the request." The document centres on domain validation for the Web PKI while leaving extension room on purpose: §1 states "while the focus of this document is on validating domain names for purposes of issuing certificates in the Web PKI, ACME supports extensions for uses with other identifiers in other PKI contexts." For DV certificates §1 also states "The only validation the CA is required to perform in the DV issuance process is to verify that the requester has effective control of the domain" and adds "The CA is not required to attempt to verify the requester's real-world identity." §2 explains why that can be fully automated: DV checks properties the issuer can observe online, so "all steps in the request, verification, and issuance process can be represented and performed by Internet protocols with no out-of-band human intervention." Authorization asserts two facts, listed in §7.5 as "That the client controls the private key of the account key pair" and "That the client controls the identifier in question." §7.1.4 enumerates the states: "Possible values are “pending”, “valid”, “invalid”, “deactivated”, “expired”, and “revoked”." §8.3's http-01 challenge works because "With HTTP validation, the client in an ACME transaction proves its control over a domain name by proving that it can provision HTTP resources on a server accessible under that domain name." and explains the cleartext port — "the challenge must be completed over HTTP, not HTTPS." §8.4's dns-01 instead lets a client "prove control of that domain by provisioning a TXT resource record containing a designated value for a specific validation domain name." §6.5 defines replay protection: "ACME POST requests have a mandatory anti-replay mechanism." Revocation travels the same channel: §7.6 states "To request that a certificate be revoked, the client sends a POST request to the ACME server's revokeCert URL." and notes its special status, "Revocation requests are different from other ACME requests in that they can be signed with either an account key pair or the key pair in the certificate." Nonces are single use: §6.5 requires "Once a nonce value has appeared in an ACME request, the server MUST consider it invalid, in the same way as a value it had never issued." Tokens need entropy — §8.3 states "This value MUST have at least 128 bits of entropy." and §11.3 explains the two purposes, one being to make an unconfigured “naive” validation server hard to build. §10.4 records the SSRF exposure: the validation GET "This request is made before the server has verified that the client controls the domain, so any client can cause a query to any domain." and a redirect widens it — "then they can send the server an HTTP redirect (e.g., a 302 response) which will cause the server to query an arbitrary URL." §10.3 acknowledges the cost of these outbound connections and §6.6 provides the backstop: "Creation of resources can be rate limited by ACME servers to ensure fair usage and prevent abuse." RFC 8555 is signed by R. Barnes (Cisco), J. Hoffman-Andrews (EFF), D. McCarney (Let's Encrypt) and J. Kasten (University of Michigan), published March 2019 with Category: Standards Track and no Obsoletes line. §1 describes the status quo it replaces: "Existing Web PKI certification authorities tend to use a set of ad hoc protocols for certificate issuance and identity verification." and §2 records the earlier deployment experience: "Prior to ACME, when deploying an HTTPS server, a server operator typically gets a prompt to generate a self-signed certificate." - Wikipedia search entry for ACME 证书自动管理. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ACME%20%E8%AF%81%E4%B9%A6%E8%87%AA%E5%8A%A8%E7%AE%A1%E7%90%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 8555: Automatic Certificate Management Environment. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555 - Published standard/RFC for ACME 证书自动管理. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8555 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Automatic Certificate Management Environment: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ACME Renewal Information
items.text: Protocol : ACME Renewal Information (ACME 续期信息). §1 defines the extension: "This document specifies the ACME Renewal Information (ARI) extension", where servers publish suggested renewal windows and clients signal that a certificate was replaced. §3 gives discovery: "An ACME server that wishes to provide renewal information MUST include a new field, “renewalInfo”, in its directory object." §4.1 fixes the query shape — "the client sends an unauthenticated GET request to a path under the server's renewalInfo URL." — with the path identifier built from the AKI keyIdentifier and the DER serial, and "All trailing “=” characters MUST be stripped from both parts of the unique identifier." The motivation is rigid client scheduling. §1 notes "Most ACME [RFC8555] clients today choose when to attempt to renew a certificate in one of three ways", criticises the first two — "The first two create significant barriers against the issuing Certification Authority (CA) changing certificate lifetimes." — and the shared consequence "All three ways may lead to load clustering for the issuing CA due to its inability to schedule renewal requests." The stated benefit is "Allowing issuing CAs to suggest a period in which clients should renew their certificates enables dynamic time-based load balancing." The abstract compresses the goal: "This allows servers to mitigate load spikes and ensures that clients do not make false assumptions about appropriate certificate renewal periods." The core field is suggestedWindow, defined in §4.2 by "which bound the window of time in which the CA recommends renewing the certificate." Client behaviour is required: "Clients MUST attempt renewal at a time of their choosing based on the suggested renewal window." The six-step RECOMMENDED algorithm in §4.2 begins with "Make a renewalInfo request to get a suggested renewal window." and only then "Select a uniform random time within the suggested window." Polling is governed by Retry-After, with §4.3 clarifying the meaning: "In this protocol, it indicates the desired (i.e., both requested minimum and maximum) amount of time to wait." §5 adds the replaces field to the Order object: "A string uniquely identifying a previously issued certificate that this order is intended to replace." Windows can be malformed, and §4.2 sets the rule: "A RenewalInfo object in which the end timestamp equals or precedes the start timestamp is invalid." — a client must treat such a response as if nothing arrived. §4.3 bounds when the resource is useful: "Clients MUST NOT check a certificate's RenewalInfo after the certificate has expired." §6 records two costs: moving to unauthenticated GETs is "a departure from the requirement in RFC 8555 that clients send POST-as-GET requests to fetch resources from the server." so "servers should take measures to ensure that unauthenticated requests for renewal information cannot result in denial-of-service attacks." and clock error matters: "this protocol could exhibit undesired behavior in the presence of significant clock skew between the ACME client and server." RFC 9773 is signed by A. Gable (Internet Security Research Group), published June 2025 with Category: Standards Track and no Obsoletes line; it extends RFC 8555. §2 fixes vocabulary — “renewal” covers any combination of Renewal, Re-Key and Modification as defined in RFC 3647. §4.2 also leaves an operational handle: explanationURL points at a page explaining the window, and the specification says "Clients SHOULD provide this URL to their operator, if present." - Wikipedia search entry for ACME 续期信息. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ACME%20%E7%BB%AD%E6%9C%9F%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] ACME Renewal Information: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Authentication Header
items.text: Protocol : Authentication Header (AH 认证头). Encryption appears nowhere in the §1 service list for AH: §1 states "The IP Authentication Header (AH) is used to provide connectionless integrity and data origin authentication for IP datagrams" and adds "and to provide protection against replays." §2 gives the protocol number — "The protocol header (IPv4, IPv6, or IPv6 Extension) immediately preceding the AH header SHALL contain the value 51 in its Protocol (IPv4) or Next Header (IPv6, Extension) fields [DH98]." §2.4 explains the index field: "The SPI is an arbitrary 32-bit value that is used by a receiver to identify the SA to which an incoming packet is bound." Coverage is both AH's reason for existing and its weakness: §1 says "AH provides authentication for as much of the IP header as possible, as well as for next level protocol data." But fields that change en route cannot be covered — "some IP header fields may change in transit and the value of these fields, when the packet arrives at the receiver, may not be predictable by the sender." The conclusion is "Thus, the protection provided to the IP header by AH is piecemeal." The same section places the AH/ESP difference in coverage: "ESP does not protect any IP header fields unless those fields are encapsulated by ESP". The sequence field is mandatory even when anti-replay is off: §2.5 requires "The field is mandatory and MUST always be present even if the receiver does not elect to enable the anti-replay service for a specific SA." and the increment duty is scoped — "For a unicast SA or a single-sender multicast SA, the sender MUST increment this field for every transmitted packet." §2.6 delegates the verification parameters to the algorithm specification: "The integrity algorithm specification MUST specify the length of the ICV and the comparison rules and processing steps for validation." §3.1 again offers two usages — "AH may be employed in two ways: transport mode or tunnel mode." — and §3.2 names the algorithm classes: "suitable integrity algorithms include keyed Message Authentication Codes (MACs) based on symmetric encryption algorithms". Multiple senders make anti-replay unavailable outright: §2.5 says "Thus, for a multi-sender SA, the anti-reply features of AH are not available". With anti-replay enabled — the default — the counter may not wrap: "If anti-replay is enabled (the default), the transmitted sequence number must never be allowed to cycle." §5 takes the engineering view on manually keyed SAs — if the ICV key is distributed by hand, anti-replay needs the sender to maintain counter state with no automatic recovery near overflow, so "a compliant implementation SHOULD NOT provide this service in conjunction with SAs that are manually keyed." The same section outsources the algorithm list: "The mandatory-to-implement algorithms for use with AH are described in a separate RFC [Eas04]". RFC 4302 is signed by S. Kent (BBN Technologies), published December 2005 as a Standards Track document with “Obsoletes: 2402” in the header; the abstract calls it "an updated version of the IP Authentication Header (AH)", "which is designed to provide authentication services in IPv4 and IPv6". §5 records that the mandatory algorithms moved to a separate RFC so the algorithm requirements can be updated independently. §7 lists the differences from RFC 2402, including the new counter option: "added a new option for a 64-bit sequence number for very high-speed communications." - Wikipedia search entry for AH 认证头. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=AH%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E5%A4%B4 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 4302: IP Authentication Header. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4302 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Authentication Header: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Grover's Algorithm
items.text: Attack : Grover's Algorithm (格罗弗算法). Grover's paper is titled "A fast quantum mechanical algorithm for database search" and uses a shuffled phone directory: "Imagine a phone directory containing N names arranged in completely random order. In order to find someone's phone number with a 50% probability, any classical algorithm (whether deterministic or probabilistic) will need to look at a minimum of N/2 names", whereas with the quantum scheme "the desired phone number can be obtained in only O(sqrt(N)) steps". The v3 comments record that the proof was simplified using a new interpretation termed "inversion about average", with the algorithm unchanged. The paper positions its advantage: "The algorithm is within a small constant factor of the fastest possible quantum mechanical algorithm". For cryptography this matters because exhaustive search over a symmetric key drops from a number proportional to the key space to a square-root order, so the security strength measured in bits halves. The paper frames its use as database and unstructured search, with the phone-directory lookup as its example, and gives the O(sqrt(N)) evaluation count. The comments field records that it "is an updated version of a paper that was originally presented at STOC 1996". Doubling symmetric key sizes to offset a square-root search is an applied consequence of this result; the paper itself sets no cryptographic parameter requirements. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The guarantee is probabilistic: the abstract states the success condition "with a 50% probability" and gives the classical floor as needing "a minimum of N/2 names". Its optimality claim is relative — within "a small constant factor of the fastest possible quantum mechanical algorithm" — rather than an unconditional statement of optimality. The words quadratic speedup , unstructured search and OPTIMAL do not appear in this text. The arXiv record is quant-ph/9605043 by Lov K. Grover (Bell Labs, Murray Hill NJ); v1 was submitted on 29 May 1996, v2 was withdrawn the next day, and the current v3 was revised on 19 November 1996. The journal reference is "Proceedings, 28th Annual ACM Symposium on the Theory of Computing (STOC), May 1996, pages 212-219". The abstract gives O(sqrt(N)) against the classical floor of N/2. - Wikipedia search entry for 格罗弗算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%A0%BC%E7%BD%97%E5%BC%97%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[Q=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{ \mathcal{K} }\right)=\Theta(2^{\kappa/2})\] Grover's Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
