items.title: Shor's Algorithm
items.text: Attack : Shor's Algorithm (肖尔算法). NIST IR 8547 is explicit about what Shor's algorithm threatens. After listing ECDSA, RSA (RFC 8017) and EdDSA (RFC 8032) and the curves specified in SP 800-186, §2.1.1 states: "These algorithms are vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer". Section 2.1.2 gives the same verdict for SP 800-56A — discrete-log key establishment over finite fields and elliptic curves, including Diffie-Hellman and MQV variants — and SP 800-56B's RSA-based schemes: "The key-establishment algorithms in both of these Special Publications are vulnerable to Shor's Algorithm on a cryptanalytically relevant quantum computer". FIPS 186-5 states the same position in §1: "Note that the algorithms in this standard are not expected to provide resistance to attacks from a large-scale quantum computer. Digital signature algorithms that will provide security from quantum computers will be specified in future NIST publications." That is the standards text explaining why RSA, ECDSA and EdDSA are classed as quantum-vulnerable and must be replaced. The reach of the algorithm follows from the standard's own taxonomy. The Appendix A introduction of FIPS 186-5 says "Discrete logarithm cryptography (DLC) is divided into finite field cryptography (FFC) and elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). … DSA is an example of FFC, and ECDSA is an example of ECC. Other examples of DLC are the Diffie-Hellman and MQV key agreement algorithms", and adds that "The most common example of integer factorization cryptography (IFC) is RSA". NIST IR 8547 says the same thing twice, in the algorithm list and again in its closing summary: both the discrete-logarithm and the integer-factorisation families fall to Shor's algorithm once a sufficiently capable quantum computer exists. IR 8547 gives conclusions, not complexity: “Shor” appears only twice, in §2.1.1 and §2.1.2, with no polynomial-time or qubit-count statement, and this entry goes no further. The mitigation path is in the same document: §4 states that "NIST will deprecate quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography after 2030 and disallow its use under NIST standards and guidelines after 2035", while the §1 introduction cites the "harvest now, decrypt later" threat — collecting ciphertext now and decrypting once such a machine exists — as the reason to act immediately. The standards timeline is: FIPS 186-5 (February 2023) concedes that its algorithms are not expected to resist a large-scale quantum computer and says quantum-safe signatures will come in future publications; NIST IR 8547 (October 2026) makes that concrete, naming both public-key families — signatures in §2.1.1 and key establishment in §2.1.2 — as vulnerable to Shor's algorithm and attaching migration dates in §4. - Wikipedia search entry for 肖尔算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%82%96%E5%B0%94%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[T=\mathrm{poly}(\log N)\] Shor's Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Concise Binary Object Representation
items.text: Protocol : Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR 二进制编码). The abstract states the aim: "The Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) is a data format whose design goals include the possibility of extremely small code size, fairly small message size, and extensibility without the need for version negotiation." §1 sets the model — "The underlying data model is an extended version of the JSON data model [RFC8259]." §3.1 enumerates the major types, e.g. "Major type 0: An unsigned integer in the range 0..2^(64)-1 inclusive.", "Major type 2: A byte string." and "Major type 5: A map of pairs of data items." §3.2.1 characterises the terminator: "It is not itself a data item: it is just a syntactic feature to close an indefinite-length item." §3.4 gives the extension mechanism: "In CBOR, a data item can be enclosed by a tag to give it some additional semantics". It targets goals earlier formats miss. §1 notes "In the IETF, probably the best-known formats in the latter category are ASN.1's BER and DER [ASN.1]." §1.1 lists the objectives in decreasing importance: "The representation must be able to unambiguously encode most common data formats used in Internet standards.", "The code for an encoder or decoder must be able to be compact in order to support systems with very limited memory, processor power, and instruction sets.", "Data must be able to be decoded without a schema description." and "The format must be extensible, and the extended data must be decodable by earlier decoders." One value admits several legal encodings, and §4.1 sets the trade-off: "it is desirable that an encoder always chooses a preferred serialization (preferred encoding); however, the present specification does not put the burden of enforcing this preference on either the encoder or decoder." Extension is managed by registry — §9.2 records "IANA has created the “Concise Binary Object Representation (CBOR) Tags” registry". The abstract also settles versioning: "It does not create a new version of the format." — it stays fully compatible with the RFC 7049 interchange format, so deployed CBOR needs no version negotiation. Encoding ambiguity is an exploitable surface, so the deterministic profile imposes three restrictions: §4.2.1 requires "Preferred serialization MUST be used.", "Indefinite-length items MUST NOT appear." and "The keys in every map MUST be sorted in the bytewise lexicographic order of their deterministic encodings." §5.3 puts malformed-but-valid items on the layer that understands them: "A well-formed but invalid CBOR data item (Section 1.2) presents a problem with interpreting the data encoded in it in the CBOR data model." §10 lands the risk in the parser: "Complex parsers are well known as a likely source of such vulnerabilities, such as the ability to remotely crash a node, or even remotely execute arbitrary code on it." and demands hostility by default — "A CBOR decoder needs to assume that all input may be hostile even if it has been checked by a firewall, has come over a secure channel such as TLS". RFC 8949 is signed by C. Bormann (Universität Bremen TZI) and P. Hoffman (ICANN), published December 2020 with “STD: 94” and “Obsoletes: 7049” in the header. The abstract characterises the replacement: "This document obsoletes RFC 7049, providing editorial improvements, new details, and errata fixes while keeping full compatibility with the interchange format of RFC 7049." - Wikipedia search entry for CBOR 二进制编码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CBOR%20%E4%BA%8C%E8%BF%9B%E5%88%B6%E7%BC%96%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 8949: Concise Binary Object Representation. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949 - Published standard/RFC for CBOR 二进制编码. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Concise Binary Object Representation: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption
items.text: Protocol : CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE 签名与加密格式). §1 fixes the scope: "This document defines the CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) standard, which does the same thing for the CBOR encoding format." The abstract covers signatures, MACs, encryption and key representation, adding "This specification additionally describes how to represent cryptographic keys using CBOR." §2 gives the shared array shape: "All of the message structures are built on the CBOR array type." with the first three elements being "The protected header parameters, encoded and wrapped in a bstr.", "The unprotected header parameters as a map." and the content — "The content is either the plaintext or the ciphertext, as appropriate." The driver is constrained devices: §1 notes "There has been an increased focus on small, constrained devices that make up the Internet of Things (IoT)." and "A need exists to provide message security services for IoT, and using CBOR as the message-encoding format makes sense." §1.3 lists the deliberate departures from JOSE: "A single overall message structure has been defined so that encrypted, signed, and MACed messages can easily be identified and still have a consistent view.", "Binary encodings are used, rather than base64url encodings, to encode binary data." and "The authentication tag for encryption algorithms has been combined with the ciphertext." §2 stresses shared parsing code, designing the structures so different security message types reuse the same processing. §2 enumerates four ways to identify a message type: "Identification of which type of message has been presented is done by the following methods:" — the first is contextual, "The specific message type is known from the context.", the second is the tag route, "The message type is identified by a CBOR tag.", and the fourth rides on the CoAP Content-Format option. §4.2 gives the single-signer tag — "A tagged COSE_Sign1 structure is identified by the CBOR tag 18." — and §5.2 the single-recipient encryption tag, "A tagged COSE_Encrypt0 structure is identified by the CBOR tag 16." §3.1 requires the algorithm field to be protected: "This header parameter MUST be authenticated where the ability to do so exists." §4.4 defines the bytes that get signed: "In order to create a signature, a well-defined byte string is needed. The Sig_structure is used to create the canonical form." with context strings including "“Signature1” for signatures using the COSE_Sign1 structure." §7 defines the key map: "The element “kty” is a required element in a COSE_Key map." Encoding ambiguity would break signature consistency, so §9 tightens CBOR — but states the scope first: "The restriction applies to the encoding of the Sig_structure, the Enc_structure, and the MAC_structure." — it is not a general requirement on whole COSE messages. Within that scope, "Encoding MUST be done using definite lengths, and the length of the (encoded) argument MUST be the minimum possible length." with the example "This means that the integer 1 is encoded as “0x01” and not “0x1801”." §12 gives two key warnings: "Use of the same key for two different algorithms can leak information about the key." and "Use of “direct” as a recipient algorithm combined with a second recipient algorithm exposes the direct key to the second recipient". §3.1 warns key hints are unreliable: "Applications MUST NOT assume that “kid” values are unique." §1 also records a removal made for security reasons — the countersignature properties described for COSE_Sign1 had been stated incorrectly. RFC 9052 is signed by J. Schaad (August Cellars), published August 2022 with “STD: 96” and “Obsoletes: 8152” in the header. §1.2 lists the changes from RFC 8152, starting with "Split the original document into this document and [RFC9053]." §1.4 explains why the structures are normative in prose rather than CDDL: "When COSE was originally written, the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL) [RFC8610] had not yet been published in an RFC". - Wikipedia search entry for COSE 签名与加密格式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=COSE%20%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E4%B8%8E%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A0%BC%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 9052: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9052 - Published standard/RFC for COSE 签名与加密格式. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9052 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] CBOR Object Signing and Encryption: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Certificate Revocation List
items.text: Protocol : Certificate Revocation List (证书吊销列表). The abstract of RFC 5280 says it "profiles the X.509 v3 certificate and X.509 v2 certificate revocation list (CRL) for use in the Internet." §3.3 describes the mechanism: "This method involves each CA periodically issuing a signed data structure called a certificate revocation list (CRL)." and its content — "A CRL is a time-stamped list identifying revoked certificates that is signed by a CA or CRL issuer and made freely available in a public repository." Identification is narrow: "Each revoked certificate is identified in a CRL by its certificate serial number." §5.1.2 lists the mandatory fields: "The required fields identify the CRL issuer, the algorithm used to sign the CRL, and the date and time the CRL was issued." Distribution cost is the reason CRLs exist: §3.3 notes "CRLs may be distributed by exactly the same means as certificates themselves, namely, via untrusted servers and untrusted communications." Relying parties check both signature and status — "that system not only checks the certificate signature and validity but also acquires a suitably recent CRL and checks that the certificate serial number is not on that CRL." To make caching and supersession decidable, §5.2 mandates two extensions: "Conforming CRL issuers are REQUIRED to include the authority key identifier (Section 5.2.1) and the CRL number (Section 5.2.3) extensions in all CRLs issued." §5.2.3 explains the purpose: "The CRL number is a non-critical CRL extension that conveys a monotonically increasing sequence number for a given CRL scope and CRL issuer." Triggers are enumerated, §3.3 including "Such circumstances include change of name, change of association between subject and CA" and "compromise or suspected compromise of the corresponding private key." The time fields carry hard rules: §5.1.2.5 states "Conforming CRL issuers MUST include the nextUpdate field in all CRLs." and §5.1.2.4 sets the encoding boundary — "CRL issuers conforming to this profile MUST encode thisUpdate as UTCTime for dates through the year 2049." Empty lists are specified too: §5.1.2.6 "When there are no revoked certificates, the revoked certificates list MUST be absent." §5.3 recommends detail: "CRL issuers SHOULD include reason codes (Section 5.3.1) and invalidity dates (Section 5.3.2) whenever this information is available." History cannot be dropped early: §3.3 requires "An entry MUST NOT be removed from the CRL until it appears on one regularly scheduled CRL issued beyond the revoked certificate's validity period." §6.3 assumes a refresh path: "if the next update time of a CRL has passed, the algorithm assumes a mechanism to fetch a current CRL and place it in the local CRL cache." Processability has limits, §5.2 saying "If a CRL contains a critical extension that the application cannot process, then the application MUST NOT use that CRL to determine the status of certificates." And CRLs are not the only route: §3 records "Revocation status information may be provided using the Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) [RFC2560], certificate revocation lists (CRLs), or some other mechanism." while §5 permits a CA to skip them: "Conforming CAs are not required to issue CRLs if other revocation or certificate status mechanisms are provided." RFC 5280 is signed by D. Cooper, S. Santesson, S. Farrell, S. Boeyen, R. Housley and W. Polk, published May 2008 with "Obsoletes: 3280, 4325, 4630" in the header. §1 places it in a standards family: "This specification is one part of a family of standards for the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) for the Internet." §5.1.1 records the key choice available to a CA: "MAY use one private key to digitally sign certificates and CRLs, or MAY use separate private keys". §8 clarifies that confidentiality is not assumed: "Since certificates and CRLs are digitally signed, no additional integrity service is necessary." - Wikipedia search entry for 证书吊销列表. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%AF%81%E4%B9%A6%E5%90%8A%E9%94%80%E5%88%97%E8%A1%A8 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Certificate Revocation List: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: NSEC3
items.text: Protocol : NSEC3 (NSEC3 哈希化否定证明). Section 3 defines the record: "The NSEC3 Resource Record (RR) provides authenticated denial of existence for DNS Resource Record Sets." It answers the claim that a name or type is absent, signed like the rest of DNSSEC. The motive is a side effect of the older record: §1.1 says "Though the NSEC RR meets the requirements for authenticated denial of existence, it introduces a side-effect in that the contents of a zone can be enumerated." Section 3 answers with hashed names: "To provide protection against zone enumeration, the owner names used in the NSEC3 RR are cryptographic hashes of the original owner name prepended as a single label to the name of the zone." Three parameters set the behaviour. Iterations "defines the number of additional times the hash function has been performed", buying resilience against dictionary attacks; the salt "is appended to the original owner name before hashing in order to defend against pre-calculated dictionary attacks"; and "If the Opt-Out flag is set, the NSEC3 record covers zero or more unsigned delegations." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Cost is raised, not risk removed: §12.1.1 concedes "The NSEC3 RRs are still susceptible to dictionary attacks", advising that "The salt SHOULD be at least 64 bits long and unpredictable" and be changed regularly; §12.1.2 notes that on a collision "it will be impossible to prove the non-existence of the colliding QNAME". SHA-1 is the only hash algorithm defined. RFC 5155 is a March 2008 Standards Track document (Laurie, Sisson, Arends and Blacka) with neither an Obsoletes nor an Updates line. items.title: Downgrade Attack
items.text: Attack : Downgrade Attack (降级攻击). A downgrade attack lets an on-path adversary force a connection onto an older protocol version. TLS 1.3 moved version negotiation into an extension: "the legacy_version field MUST be set to 0x0303, which is the version number for TLS 1.2. TLS 1.3 ClientHellos are identified as having a legacy_version of 0x0303 and a supported_versions extension present with 0x0304 as the highest version indicated therein". Section 4.1.3 adds that "TLS 1.3 has a downgrade protection mechanism embedded in the server's random value. TLS 1.3 servers which negotiate TLS 1.2 or below in response to a ClientHello MUST set the last 8 bytes of their Random value specially in their ServerHello", using the sentinel bytes 44 4F 57 4E 47 52 44 01 for TLS 1.2 and the same prefix ending 00 for TLS 1.1 or below. The Finished exchange already detects some tampering, but a version rollback needs an earlier and explicit signal: §1.3 states that "A version downgrade protection mechanism is described in Section 4.1.3", and §4.1.3 splits the duty: "TLS 1.3 clients receiving a ServerHello indicating TLS 1.2 or below MUST check that the last 8 bytes are not equal to either of these values", while "TLS 1.2 clients SHOULD also check that the last 8 bytes are not equal to the second value"; on a match "If a match is found, the client MUST abort the handshake" with an illegal_parameter alert. The same section admits that "This mechanism provides limited protection against downgrade attacks over and above what is provided by the Finished exchange" and that "It does not provide downgrade protection when static RSA is used". Forbidding fallback is a standards-level measure, not an implementation detail. RFC 7568 states that "The Secure Sockets Layer version 3.0 (SSLv3), as specified in RFC 6101, is not sufficiently secure. This document requires that SSLv3 not be used", and §3 says "SSLv3 MUST NOT be used. Negotiation of SSLv3 from any version of TLS MUST NOT be permitted", that clients "MUST NOT send a ClientHello with ClientHello.client_version set to {03,00}", and that although servers must still accept any {03,XX} record-layer version number "they MUST NOT negotiate SSLv3". The mechanism has stated limits: the sentinel is mandatory only for "TLS 1.3 servers … MUST", while the SHOULD applies only to the TLS 1.1-or-below sentinel, which TLS 1.3 servers MUST and TLS 1.2 servers SHOULD set, static RSA suites get no protection, and clients must actually perform the check. TLS 1.3 therefore also removes exploitable legacy capability: "The list of supported symmetric encryption algorithms has been pruned of all algorithms that are considered legacy", "Static RSA and Diffie-Hellman cipher suites have been removed; all public-key based key exchange mechanisms now provide forward secrecy", plus the removal of compression, DSA and custom DHE groups. Section 6.2 lists the inappropriate_fallback alert, sent by a server in response to an invalid connection retry attempt from a client (citing RFC 7507), and the Appendix C.3 deployment checklist asks whether "all support for SSL, RC4, EXPORT ciphers, and MD5 … is completely removed". RFC 7568, by Barnes, Thomson, Pironti and Langley, was published in June 2015 on the Standards Track and updates RFC 5246. Section 4.1 gives the reason: SSLv3's CBC padding "trivially permits the recovery of plaintext [POODLE]" and RC4 "exhibits serious biases and is also no longer fit for use [RFC7465]", so "This leaves SSLv3 with no suitable record protection mechanism", while §4.2 adds that the SSLv3 key exchange is vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks when renegotiation or session resumption is used. RFC 8446 (Rescorla, August 2018) then deprecated the TLS 1.2 version-negotiation mechanism in favour of a version list in an extension. - Wikipedia search entry for 降级攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%99%8D%E7%BA%A7%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Downgrade Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DSA (Digital Signature Algorithm)
items.text: Algorithm : Digital Signature Algorithm (DSA 数字签名算法). Digital signatures are used to detect unauthorised modification of data and to authenticate the signatory, which is the non-repudiation property. The DSA was approved for signature generation by earlier versions of the FIPS 186 series. FIPS 186-5 states: "This standard no longer approves the DSA for digital signature generation", while "the DSA may be used to verify signatures generated prior to the implementation date of this standard", and refers the full DSA specification back to FIPS 186-4. FIPS 186-5 approves three techniques: RSA (through IETF RFC 8017), ECDSA (including deterministic ECDSA from RFC 6979) and the EdDSA of RFC 8032 together with HashEdDSA. The standard describes ECDSA as "the elliptic curve analog of DSA" and concentrates signature generation on those schemes, while §4 retains the verification-only role for the DSA. Its current role is verifying DSA signatures generated before the implementation date of the standard, while new signing uses an approved scheme: ECDSA generation and verification are given in §6.4.1 and §6.4.2, and RSA signing is delegated to RFC 8017. Section 3 states that a key pair used for signature generation and verification "shall not be used for any other purpose", a restriction repeated for RSA in §5 and for ECDSA in §6. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. FIPS 186-5 states plainly that "the algorithms in this standard are not expected to provide resistance to attacks from a large-scale quantum computer", which is why signature generation moved on and the DSA left it. The finite-field parameters and discrete-logarithm setting of the DSA belong to FIPS 186-4, of which this standard keeps only the verification role in §4. Section 6 separately warns that implementations of the elliptic-curve schemes must be protected against "side-channel attacks or fault attacks". FIPS 186-5 was published and became effective on 3 February 2023, superseding FIPS 186-4. Appendix E records that the DSA is no longer approved for signature generation, and the announcement adds that FIPS 186-4 stays in effect for one year after publication and is then withdrawn. The DSA therefore keeps only the verification of older signatures. - Wikipedia search entry for DSA 数字签名算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DSA%20%E6%95%B0%E5%AD%97%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Digital Signature Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DTLS 1.0
items.text: Protocol : DTLS 1.0 (DTLS 1.0). The abstract fixes version and object: "This document specifies Version 1.0 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol. The DTLS protocol provides communications privacy for datagram protocols." — TLS-level protection over a transport that guarantees neither order nor delivery, preserving datagram semantics. The design aims at minimal change: §1 says "DTLS is deliberately designed to be as similar to TLS as possible, both to minimize new security invention and to maximize the amount of code and infrastructure reuse." Section 4 explains the presentation: "instead of presenting DTLS as a new protocol, we present it as a series of deltas from TLS 1.1 [TLS11]." Section 4.2 lists the three departures from TLS, first "A stateless cookie exchange has been added to prevent denial of service attacks.", then handshake-header changes for loss, reordering and fragmentation, plus retransmission timers. Section 4.1.1 adds a hard rule: "Each DTLS record MUST fit within a single datagram." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Replay detection is optional: §3.3 explains "The replay detection feature is optional, since packet duplication is not always malicious, but can also occur due to routing errors." Section 4.1.2.2 bans stream ciphers outright: "RC4 MUST NOT be used with DTLS." And the cookie answers only forged source addresses — §4.2.1 concedes "This mechanism does not provide any defense against DoS attacks mounted from valid IP addresses." The RFC 4347 header lists E. Rescorla (RTFM, Inc.) and N. Modadugu (Stanford University), Category: Standards Track, April 2006, with no Obsoletes or Updates line; the title line reads only "Datagram Transport Layer Security" and the version number appears in the abstract. - Wikipedia search entry for DTLS 1.0. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DTLS%201.0 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] DTLS 1.0: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DTLS 1.2
items.text: Protocol : DTLS 1.2 (DTLS 1.2). The abstract sets the scope: "This document specifies version 1.2 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol. The DTLS protocol provides communications privacy for datagram protocols." and adds "This document updates DTLS 1.0 to work with TLS version 1.2." Section 1 explains the numbering: "There is no DTLS 1.1; that version number was skipped in order to harmonize version numbers with TLS." The algorithm layer inherits TLS 1.2 outright — §4.1.2.4 says "The existing AEAD cipher suites, defined in [ECCGCM] and [RSAGCM], can be used with DTLS exactly as with TLS 1.2." The behavioural difference from TLS is fault tolerance: §4.1.2.7 says "In general, invalid records SHOULD be silently discarded, thus preserving the association; however, an error MAY be logged for diagnostic purposes." The record layer itself is near-identical, "The only change is the inclusion of an explicit sequence number in the record." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Choosing alerts is actively discouraged: such implementations "MUST generate fatal level alerts to avoid attacks where the attacker repeatedly probes the implementation to see how it responds to various types of error.", and over UDP "this practice is NOT RECOMMENDED for such transports." Section 4.1 adds that "implementations MUST NOT allow the same epoch value to be reused within two times the TCP maximum segment lifetime." The RFC 6347 header lists E. Rescorla (RTFM, Inc.) and N. Modadugu (Google, Inc.), Category: Standards Track, January 2012, with an ISSN line and “Obsoletes: 4347” and no Updates line; §8 "Changes since DTLS 1.0" enumerates the alignment with TLS 1.2, the new AEAD section and the rest. - Wikipedia search entry for DTLS 1.2. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DTLS%201.2 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] DTLS 1.2: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DTLS 1.3
items.text: Protocol : DTLS 1.3 (DTLS 1.3). The abstract gives scope and lineage: "This document specifies version 1.3 of the Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) protocol. DTLS 1.3 allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way that is designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery." The same abstract paragraph gives both the lineage and its exception: "The DTLS 1.3 protocol is based on the Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.3 protocol and provides equivalent security guarantees with the exception of order protection / non-replayability." Section 3 names the first reason the record layer must change: "TLS relies on an implicit sequence number on records." — a lost record breaks later decryption — so "DTLS solves this problem by adding sequence numbers to records." Section 5 states the reuse strategy: DTLS 1.3 keeps the TLS 1.3 handshake messages and flows and "reuses TLS 1.3's “cookie” extension to provide a return-routability check as part of connection establishment." The record layer is its own design: "The DTLS 1.3 record layer is different from the TLS 1.3 record layer and also different from the DTLS 1.2 record layer." Amplification risk and message deprecation form the boundary: §5.1 warns "Servers which process 0-RTT requests and send 0.5-RTT responses without a cookie exchange risk being used in an amplification attack if the size of outgoing messages greatly exceeds the size of those that are received." and sets "A server SHOULD limit the amount of data it sends toward a client address to three times the amount of data sent by the client before it verifies that the client is able to receive data at that address." Section 5.2 adds that "DTLS 1.3-compliant implementations MUST NOT use the HelloVerifyRequest to execute a return-routability check." The RFC 9147 header lists E. Rescorla (Mozilla), H. Tschofenig (Arm Limited) and N. Modadugu (Google, Inc.), Category: Standards Track, April 2022, marked “Obsoletes: 6347” with no Updates line; §1 describes the delta-on-TLS 1.3 presentation and states "It obsoletes DTLS 1.2." - Wikipedia search entry for DTLS 1.3. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DTLS%201.3 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] DTLS 1.3: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Extensible Authentication Protocol
items.text: Protocol : Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP 认证框架). EAP is a framework rather than a mechanism: §1 defines it as "This document defines the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), an authentication framework which supports multiple authentication methods." Extensibility comes from the authenticator not needing to know the methods: §1 explains "Rather than requiring the authenticator to be updated to support each new authentication method, EAP permits the use of a backend authentication server, which may implement some or all authentication methods, with the authenticator acting as a pass-through for some or all methods and peers." A pass-through authenticator checks little and forwards: §2.3 states "Compliant pass-through authenticator implementations MUST by default forward EAP packets of any Type." while §2.1 requires that "the peer and authenticator MUST utilize only one authentication method (Type 4 or greater) within an EAP conversation, after which the authenticator MUST send a Success or Failure packet." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The framework does not secure lower-layer negotiation or carry extra data: §7.11 warns "if the lower layer performs ciphersuite negotiation, it should be understood that EAP does not provide by itself integrity protection of that negotiation." and §2.2 forbids reuse of result packets: "the Success, Failure, Nak Response(s), and Notification Request/Response messages MUST NOT be used to carry data destined for delivery to other EAP methods." RFC 3748 is a June 2004 Standards Track document carrying “Obsoletes: 2284”. Section 6.2 describes the scarce identifier space: "The original EAP method Type space has a range from 1 to 255, and is the scarcest resource in EAP, and thus must be allocated with care. Method Types 1-45 have been allocated, with 20 available for re-use." - Wikipedia search entry for EAP 认证框架. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EAP%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 3748: Extensible Authentication Protocol. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3748 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Extensible Authentication Protocol: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: EAP-PWD
items.text: Protocol : EAP-PWD (EAP-PWD). The abstract defines the method: "This memo describes an Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP) method, EAP-pwd, which uses a shared password for authentication." and asserts strength — "The underlying key exchange is resistant to active attack, passive attack, and dictionary attack." §2.8.2 gives the shape: "EAP-pwd defines three message exchanges: an Identity exchange, a Commit exchange, and a Confirm exchange." §2.8.3 names the central value: the peers use each other's identities and the agreed ciphersuite to "fix an element in the negotiated group called the Password Element", and "From the point of view of an attacker who does not know the password, the Password Element will be a random element in the negotiated group." RFC 5931 is signed by D. Harkins (Aruba Networks) and G. Zorn (Network Zen), published August 2010 with Category: Informational in the header. The motivation is what passwords really look like: §1.1 notes "Typically these passwords are not stored on a user's computer for security reasons and must be entered each time the human desires network access." and admits the entropy problem — "They will likely not possess high-entropy, and it may be assumed that an adversary with access to a dictionary will have the ability to guess a user's password." The same section traces the lineage to "This problem was first described by Bellovin and Merritt in [BM92] and [BM93]." §1.3 sets the bar for the problem area: any protocol claiming to solve password-authenticated key exchange "must be resistant to active, passive, and dictionary attack and have the quality of forward secrecy." §2.8.2 says what the Commit exchange achieves: "the peer and server exchange information to generate a shared key and also to bind each other to a particular guess of the password." §2.10 sets the interoperability floor — "compliant EAP-pwd implementations SHALL support the following parameters" — including "Diffie-Hellman Group: group 19 defined in [RFC5114]" and "PRF: HMAC-SHA256 defined in [RFC4634]". §7 states the security claims RFC 3748 requires of new EAP methods: the mechanism is "mechanism: password." and the claims include "mutual authentication: the peer and server both authenticate each other by proving possession of a shared password." The same section makes dictionary-attack resistance a RFC 4017 mandate, since "The advantage gained by an attacker is through interaction not through computation." §6.1 lists what a passive attacker sees: "A passive attacker will see Scalar_P, Element_P, Scalar_S, and Element_S." §6.3 carries the key argument: "She is able to make one guess and one guess only per attack." and locates the advantage — "is solely through interaction with an honest protocol peer." §6.4 shows why forward secrecy holds: even if the password later leaks, the earlier runs' random values stay unknown, so "This is the definition of Forward Secrecy." §6.5 concedes that strength is bounded by the group: "The mandatory-to-implement group defined in this memo is group 19", chosen because "This group was chosen because the current best estimate of a symmetric key derived using this group is 128 bits". RFC 8146 is signed by D. Harkins (HP Enterprise), published April 2017 with Category: Informational and an “Updates: 5931” header line, i.e. it adds to the method defined in RFC 5931. The abstract states the gap: EAP-pwd had it "it does not include support for salted passwords." and gives the motive — "There are many existing databases of salted passwords, and it is desirable to allow their use with EAP-pwd." The same paragraph records what the original already covered: raw keys and "double hashing of a password in the style of Microsoft Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol version 2 (MSCHAPv2)". - Wikipedia search entry for EAP-PWD. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EAP-PWD - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] EAP-PWD: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: EAP-TLS
items.text: Protocol : EAP-TLS (EAP-TLS). The abstract and §1 give the same definition: "This document defines EAP-TLS, which includes support for certificate-based mutual authentication and key derivation." It is one concrete method inside the EAP framework, with TLS as its core. Mutual authentication rests on certificates: §2.2 says "As part of the TLS negotiation, the server presents a certificate to the peer, and if mutual authentication is requested, the peer presents a certificate to the server." The hard deployment requirement is revocation checking: §5.4 states that implementations "MUST support the use of Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs)" The §2.1.4 mandate is scoped to privacy support, where servers "MUST request a client certificate" — client certificates are not required unconditionally. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The protection has edges: §5.5 notes "The integrity protection of EAP-TLS packets does not extend to the EAP header fields (Code, Identifier, Length) or the Type or Flags fields." and the §5.1 claims table records channel binding as No. The baseline is TLS version 1.0 or later, and a footnote in §5.1 adds that "EAP-TLS inherits the secure ciphersuite negotiation features of TLS, including key derivation function negotiation when utilized with TLS v1.2 [RFC4346bis]"; TLS 1.3 is not addressed. RFC 5216 (March 2008, Standards Track, Simon, Aboba and Hurst) carries “Obsoletes: 2716” and says in §1 that "While this document obsoletes RFC 2716 [RFC2716], it remains backward compatible with it." Section 2.3 records the key origin: "In EAP-TLS, the MSK, EMSK, and Initialization Vector (IV) are derived from the TLS master secret via a one-way function." There is no Updates line and no update to RFC 3748. - Wikipedia search entry for EAP-TLS. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EAP-TLS - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] EAP-TLS: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: EAP-TTLS
items.text: Protocol : EAP-TTLS (EAP-TTLS). EAP-TTLS runs authentication on top of a TLS tunnel: §1 states "EAP-TTLS is an EAP method that provides functionality beyond what is available in EAP-TLS." §7 gives the two-phase shape — "A EAP-TTLS negotiation comprises two phases: the TLS handshake phase and the TLS tunnel phase." — and in phase 1 the server opens, per §7.1, "The TTLS server initiates the EAP-TTLS method with an EAP-TTLS/Start packet". The motive is that exposed challenge/response enables dictionary attacks: §2 notes "An issue with such an approach is that an eavesdropper that observes both challenge and response may be able to mount a dictionary attack" and "Because passwords typically have low entropy, such attacks can in practice easily discover many passwords." §2 also states the changed premise: "Wireless connections are considerably more susceptible to eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks." The strategy in §1 is to reuse existing password infrastructure — "EAP-TTLS extends this authentication negotiation by using the secure connection established by the TLS handshake to exchange additional information between client and server." §5.4 summarises the effect: identity and password information are transmitted securely. §7 ties phase 2 security to the phase 1 agreement: "Note that the type and degree of security in phase 2 depends on the cipher suite negotiated during phase 1; if the null cipher suite is negotiated, there will be no security!" §7.2 defines the tunnelled content: "In phase 2, the TLS record layer is used to securely tunnel information between client and TTLS server." §7.7 permits TLS 1.0, 1.1 or any later version and only recommends TLS 1.0 support with a SHOULD for maximum interoperability; §11.4 sets the floor: "To ensure interoperability, in the absence of an application profile standard specifying otherwise, an implementation compliant with this specification MUST implement EAP as a tunneled authentication method and MUST implement MD5-Challenge as an EAP type" — a MUST that holds only absent a conflicting application profile. §14.1 claims "Authentication mechanism: TLS plus arbitrary additional protected authentication(s)" and lists "Cryptographic binding: No". Four self-imposed limits are recorded in the document. §14.2 concedes anonymity can leak: implementers should know that "other factors -- both within EAP-TTLS and elsewhere -- may compromise a user's identity." §14.3 hands server trust to configuration: "The client should have a means of determining which server identities are authorized to act as a TTLS server and may be trusted, and should refuse to authenticate with servers it does not trust." §14.4 recommends validating the path to a trusted root and notes that a missing EKU means no constraint. §14.7 records that version negotiation happens outside the tunnel — "EAP-TTLS negotiates its own protocol version prior to, and therefore outside the security established by the TLS tunnel." — while noting version 0 is not exposed to that attack. RFC 5281 is signed by P. Funk (Unaffiliated) and S. Blake-Wilson (SafeNet), published August 2008 with Category: Informational and no Obsoletes line. §1 says plainly what kind of document it is: "EAP-TTLS has been widely deployed and this specification documents what existing implementations do." and admits "It has some limitations and vulnerabilities, however." pointing improvements at extensions and the later standardised tunneled methods. - Wikipedia search entry for EAP-TTLS. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EAP-TTLS - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] EAP-TTLS: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Encrypted Client Hello
items.text: Protocol : Encrypted Client Hello (加密客户端问候). RFC 9849 §1 defines the extension: "This document specifies a new TLS extension called Encrypted Client Hello (ECH) that allows clients to encrypt their ClientHello to the TLS server." The target is the plaintext SNI, described as "perhaps the most sensitive information left unencrypted in TLS 1.3." §3.2 gives the mechanics: the client builds a private ClientHelloInner and a public ClientHelloOuter which "contains innocuous values for sensitive extensions and an “encrypted_client_hello” extension". §5 fixes the code point: "enum { encrypted_client_hello(0xfe0d), (65535) } ExtensionType;". The aim is indistinguishability inside an anonymity set: §1 says "Usage of this mechanism reveals that a client is connecting to a particular service provider, but does not reveal which server from the anonymity set terminates the connection." §3.2 restates that as the primary goal and adds, in a lowercase should, that "it should achieve this goal without affecting any existing security properties of TLS 1.3". §10.1 lists the goals, including "3. Downgrade resistance. An attacker cannot downgrade a connection that attempts to use ECH to one that does not use ECH." while §1 concedes "ECH is not in itself sufficient to protect the identity of the server." Configuration rides on HPKE: §4 "ECH uses Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE) for public key encryption" and requires "Clients MUST ignore any ECHConfig structure with a version they do not support." §6.1 governs offering, with the inner hello forbidden to say "It MUST NOT offer to negotiate TLS 1.2 or below." to avoid version mismatch; §6.2 lets "a connection between an ECH-capable client and a non-ECH server to appear to use ECH". §9 mandates one HPKE cipher suite: DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256 and AES-128-GCM. §3.2 is blunt about rejection: "When ECH is rejected, the resulting connection is not usable by the client for application data." §8.1 concedes compatibility with existing servers and asks operators to "SHOULD ensure servers understand a given set of ECH keys before advertising them". §10.2 notes configuration delivery over DNS carries no authenticity — "any attacker which can inject DNS responses or poison DNS caches" can inject or strip it, while arguing that a DNS-controlling attacker could simply change the IP address anyway. §10.5 warns that outer fields leak inner properties: the client "SHOULD NOT send values in the ClientHelloOuter which would reveal a sensitive ClientHelloInner property, such as the true server name." RFC 9849 is signed by E. Rescorla (Independent), K. Oku (Fastly), N. Sullivan (Cryptography Consulting LLC) and C. A. Wood (Apple), published March 2026 with Category: Standards Track. §1 scopes it: "ECH is supported in TLS 1.3 [RFC8446], DTLS 1.3 [RFC9147], and newer versions of the TLS and DTLS protocols." the same paragraph notes that encrypted DNS and similar measures are needed alongside, since SNI encryption is not a standalone fix. - Wikipedia search entry for 加密客户端问候. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E5%AE%A2%E6%88%B7%E7%AB%AF%E9%97%AE%E5%80%99 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Encrypted Client Hello: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Enigma Cryptanalysis
items.text: Attack : Enigma Cryptanalysis (恩尼格玛破译). The Computer History Museum timeline describes the British Bombe: "Built as an electro-mechanical means of decrypting Nazi ENIGMA-based military communications during World War II, the British Bombe is conceived of by computer pioneer Alan Turing and Harold Keen of the British Tabulating Machine Company. Hundreds of allied bombes were built in order to determine the daily rotor start positions of Enigma cipher machines, which in turn allowed the Allies to decrypt German messages." The target of the operation was recovering the daily rotor start positions. The same timeline entry records the lineage of the method: “The basic idea for bombes came from Polish code-breaker Marian Rejewski's 1938 "Bomba."” — the British device extended earlier Polish work. The Bletchley Park Trust site's Enigma summary describes the machine itself: "The Enigma machine was invented by a German engineer Arthur Scherbius shortly after WW1. The machine (of which a number of varying types were produced) …", noting multiple variants that had to be handled. Both sources stress scale. The Bletchley Park page states that "Nearly 10,000 people worked in the wider Bletchley Park organisation", and its Bombe summary says "These Alan Turing-designed devices changed the course of the Second World War, saving millions of lives in the process". The CHM entry gives the machine count and the effect: "Hundreds of allied bombes were built … which in turn allowed the Allies to decrypt German messages". A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limits of this route are visible in the wording: the Bombe worked by searching "daily rotor start positions", that is, determining the rotor start positions day by day. The Bletchley Park page is also a public visitor summary — the saved content is the site's summary layout, with the full narrative absent — so this entry uses only its checkable sentences and does not treat it as a substitute for a technical account. items.title: Encapsulating Security Payload
items.text: Protocol : Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP 封装安全载荷). RFC 4303 pins the packet position and fields: §1 says "The ESP header is inserted after the IP header and before the next layer protocol header (transport mode) or before an encapsulated IP header (tunnel mode)." §2 fixes the protocol number — "The (outer) protocol header (IPv4, IPv6, or Extension) that immediately precedes the ESP header SHALL contain the value 50 in its Protocol (IPv4) or Next Header (IPv6, Extension) field" — and the layout "The packet begins with two 4-byte fields (Security Parameters Index (SPI) and Sequence Number)." §2.8 adds the optional trailer: "The Integrity Check Value is a variable-length field computed over the ESP header, Payload, and ESP trailer fields." and "The ICV field is optional." The services are a menu, but with a floor: §1 lists "ESP can be used to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, an anti-replay service (a form of partial sequence integrity), and (limited) traffic flow confidentiality." and stresses that the set depends on the options chosen when the SA is established and on where the implementation sits. §3.2 closes it as a hard rule: "although both confidentiality and integrity are optional, at least one of these services MUST be selected, hence both algorithms MUST NOT be simultaneously NULL." On encryption-only, §1 first notes "Using encryption-only for confidentiality is allowed by ESP." then warns "this will provide defense only against passive attackers." Encryption-only is not forbidden: §1 explains "ESP allows encryption-only SAs because this may offer considerably better performance and still provide adequate security" while adding "However, this standard does not require ESP implementations to offer an encryption-only service." Traffic-flow concealment is an explicitly designed option: §2.7 requires "An IPsec implementation SHOULD be capable of padding traffic by adding bytes after the end of the Payload Data, prior to the beginning of the Padding field." and "if TFC padding is added, the field containing the specification of the length of the IP datagram MUST NOT be modified to reflect this padding." The mode choice is one line in §3.1: "ESP may be employed in two ways: transport mode or tunnel mode." Anti-replay has an explicit failure condition: §2.2 states "for a multi-sender SA, the anti-replay features of ESP are not available". New features are gated on negotiation, and §2.7 requires "the SA management protocol MUST negotiate this service prior to a transmitter employing it, to ensure backward compatibility". §3.4 gives the security reason for the inbound order: when the two checks run in parallel, "integrity checking MUST be completed before the decrypted packet is passed on for further processing." The hardest boundary is in §8: "There is no version number in ESP and no mechanism enabling IPsec peers to discover or negotiate which version of ESP each is using or should use." — version shows up only indirectly through the negotiated algorithms. RFC 4303 is signed by S. Kent (BBN Technologies), published December 2005 as a Standards Track document with “Obsoletes: 2406” in the header; the abstract calls it "an updated version of the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol" and says "ESP is used to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, an anti-replay service". §8 sets out compatibility with the older line: "if none of the new features available in ESP v3 are employed, then the format of an ESP packet is identical in ESP v2 and v3." Combined-mode ciphers are defined only in the ESP v3 context. - Wikipedia search entry for ESP 封装安全载荷. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ESP%20%E5%B0%81%E8%A3%85%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E8%BD%BD%E8%8D%B7 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 4303: IP Encapsulating Security Payload. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4303 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Encapsulating Security Payload: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules (FIPS 140-3)
items.text: Standard : Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules (FIPS 140-3) (密码模块安全要求（FIPS 140-3）). FIPS 140-3 places itself in its explanation clause: "This standard specifies the security requirements that will be satisfied by a cryptographic module utilized within a security system protecting sensitive but unclassified information", and states the grading at once — "The standard provides four increasing, qualitative levels of security: Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, and Level 4." What is regulated is the module, not a single algorithm. Why a module standard at all: a correct algorithm does not imply a safe implementation, so the requirements span the whole design-and-operation chain. The abstract lists the scope: "These areas include cryptographic module specification; cryptographic module interfaces; roles, services, and authentication; software/firmware security; operating environment; physical security; non-invasive security; sensitive security parameter management; self-tests; life-cycle assurance; and mitigation of other attacks." Applicability sits in clause 6: "This standard shall be used in designing and implementing cryptographic modules that Federal departments and agencies operate or are operated for them under contract." That clause leaves two exits — "Cryptographic modules that have been approved for classified use may be used in lieu of modules that have been validated against this standard." and "The adoption and use of this standard is available to private and commercial organizations." Conforming modules must use approved pieces: §10 "Cryptographic modules that conform to this standard shall employ Approved security functions such as cryptographic algorithms, cryptographic key management techniques, and authentication techniques that have been approved for protecting Federal government sensitive information." Two limits are legible in the text. It is a federal procurement and validation instrument: the standard frames its use as "a security system protecting sensitive but unclassified information", and clause 6 offers two exits — "Cryptographic modules that have been approved for classified use may be used in lieu of modules that have been validated against this standard." and "The adoption and use of this standard is available to private and commercial organizations." Conformance is expressed through validation: "The Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP) validates cryptographic modules to Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 140-3 and other cryptography-based standards." and "Cryptographic modules that are validated under the CMVP will be considered as conforming to this standard." The version relationship is on the title page and in the explanation: the title page carries "(Supersedes FIPS PUB 140-2)" and the date line reads "Federal Information Processing Standards Publication 140-3 March 22, 2019"; the body states "This standard supersedes FIPS 140-2, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules, in its entirety." The keyword line also names the parallel international documents — "ISO/IEC 19790; ISO/IEC 24759". - Wikipedia search entry for 密码模块安全要求（FIPS 140-3）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E8%A6%81%E6%B1%82%EF%BC%88FIPS%20140-3%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 140-3: Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/140-3/final - Published standard/RFC for 密码模块安全要求（FIPS 140-3）. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/140-3/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules (FIPS 140-3): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Digital Signature Standard (FIPS 186-5)
items.text: Standard : Digital Signature Standard (FIPS 186-5) (数字签名标准（FIPS 186-5）). The job is stated in §1: "This standard defines methods for digital signature generation that can be used for the protection of binary data (commonly called a message) and for the verification and validation of those digital signatures." and the count is fixed: "Three techniques are approved." Only two of the three techniques lean on an outside specification — RSA on RFC 8017/PKCS 1 and EdDSA on RFC 8032: §1 records "The RSA digital signature algorithm is specified in the Internet Engineering Task Force Request for Comments (IETF RFC) 8017 [1] and was previously specified in Public Key Cryptography Standard (PKCS) 1 [2]", with FIPS 186-5 approving "the use of implementations of either or both of these standards" while specifying "key pair generation, as well as additional requirements", while ECDSA is stated as "The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is specified in this standard." and the third is "The Edwards Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) is specified in IETF RFC 8032 [6]." The explanation clause of the announcement block also anticipates growth — "In the future, additional digital signature schemes may be specified and approved in FIPS publications or in NIST Special Publications." The use is signing and verifying for federal systems, with one explicit advisory on keys: "Agencies are advised that digital signature key pairs shall not be used for other purposes." — the sentence names no specific alternative use, only "other purposes", and recurs verbatim in the notices of 186-5, 204 and 205. The limit is stated bluntly: conformance is not system security — "the use of a product containing an implementation that conforms to this standard does not guarantee the security of the overall system in which the product is used. The responsible authority in each agency or department shall ensure that an overall implementation provides an acceptable level of security." The judgement stays with the deploying authority, not the document. items.title: Advanced Encryption Standard (FIPS 197)
items.text: Standard : Advanced Encryption Standard (FIPS 197) (高级加密标准（FIPS 197）). The explanation clause of FIPS 197 defines it in one sentence: "The Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) … a FIPS-approved cryptographic algorithm that can be used to protect electronic data." It adds "The AES algorithm is a symmetric block cipher that can encrypt (encipher) and decrypt (decipher) digital information." and pins the parameters: "The AES algorithm is capable of using cryptographic keys of 128, 192, and 256 bits to encrypt and decrypt data in blocks of 128 bits." The origin is in the abstract: "In 2000, NIST announced the selection of the Rijndael block cipher family as the winner of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) competition." — the outcome of an open competition rather than an internal designation; the abstract also notes that block ciphers underpin many cryptographic services. The structural vocabulary is narrow: §3.5 defines words and blocks — "A word is a sequence of four bytes; a block consists of four words." The implementation duty is stated as "An implementation of the AES algorithm shall support at least one of the three key lengths … 128, 192, or 256 bits (i.e., Nk = 4, 6, or 8, respectively)." while the other sizes stay optional: "Implementations may optionally support two or three key lengths, which may promote the interoperability of algorithm implementations." FIPS 197 covers the algorithm only: clause 8 requires that "The algorithm shall be used in conjunction with a FIPS-approved or NIST-recommended mode of operation.", leaving modes and operation to other documents. §6.3 fixes this edition’s parameters — "the allowed values for the key length (Nk), block size (Nb), and number of rounds (Nr)" — but the very next sentence keeps the future open: "However, future revisions of this Standard could include changes or additions to the allowed values for those parameters." What is closed is this edition, not later ones. The identity and authority sit at the head of the file: the name line is "Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) (FIPS 197)", the category line reads "Computer Security Standard, Cryptography", approval is stated as "4. Approving Authority. Secretary of Commerce." with maintenance at NIST’s Information Technology Laboratory; the copy read here is the 2023 upd1 revision, whose abstract still dates the selection to 2000; the revision note at the end of the file records an editorial update: the original 197 was reviewed under NIST’s Crypto Publication Review Board, and public comments plus the AES security analyses in NIST IR 8319 were the basis for the decision to keep the technical specifications unchanged. - Wikipedia search entry for 高级加密标准（FIPS 197）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%AB%98%E7%BA%A7%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86%EF%BC%88FIPS%20197%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 197: Advanced Encryption Standard (AES). https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/197/final - Published standard/RFC for 高级加密标准（FIPS 197）. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/197/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Advanced Encryption Standard (FIPS 197): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC)
items.text: Standard : The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC) (键控散列消息认证码（FIPS 198-1）). The abstract defines the object: "This Standard describes a keyed-hash message authentication code (HMAC), a mechanism for message authentication using cryptographic hash functions." The abstract also gives the operating condition — "HMAC can be used with any iterative Approved cryptographic hash function, in combination with a shared secret key." Why a MAC construction: the standard states the goal as "The purpose of a MAC is to authenticate both the source of a message and its integrity without the use of any additional mechanisms." and notes that HMAC has two functionally separate inputs — "HMACs have two functionally distinct parameters, a message input and a secret key known only to the message originator and intended receiver(s)." The usage shape is sender-computed and sent with the message: "An HMAC function is used by the message sender to produce a value (the MAC) that is formed by condensing the secret key and the message input." The standard also names another application — "Additional applications of keyed-hash functions include their use in challenge-response identification protocols for computing responses, which are a function of both a secret key and a challenge message.". The boundary is set by sources, versions and implementation conditions: unregistered dates, quantities and roles are not filled in; parameters from different versions are not mixed; algorithm proofs do not replace side-channel and error-handling checks. Identity and dating are at the head: the name line reads "The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC) (FIPS PUB 198-1)", the date line is July 2008 and the category line "Computer Security Standard. Subcategory. Cryptography." Keywords listed are "computer security, cryptography, HMAC, MAC, message authentication, Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS)"; the -1 suffix marks this as the revision of FIPS 198, and clause 9 still points at "the list of Approved security functions for FIPS 140-2" — an anchoring in the FIPS 140-2 generation that FIPS 140-3 later supersedes in its entirety. - Wikipedia search entry for 键控散列消息认证码（FIPS 198-1）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%94%AE%E6%8E%A7%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97%E6%B6%88%E6%81%AF%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E7%A0%81%EF%BC%88FIPS%20198-1%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 198-1: The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/198-1/final - Published standard/RFC for 键控散列消息认证码（FIPS 198-1）. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/198-1/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] The Keyed-Hash Message Authentication Code (HMAC): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems
items.text: Standard : Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems (联邦信息与信息系统安全分类标准). The skeleton of FIPS 199 is objectives crossed with impact levels: §3 states "The security categories are based on the potential impact on an organization should certain events occur which jeopardize the information and information systems needed by the organization to accomplish its assigned mission, protect its assets, fulfill its legal responsibilities, maintain its day-to-day functions, and protect individuals." and takes the three objectives from FISMA — "The FISMA defines three security objectives for information and information systems" — confidentiality, integrity and availability, with confidentiality quoted from 44 U.S.C. as "Preserving authorized restrictions on information access and disclosure, including means for protecting personal privacy and proprietary information", the source appending the [44 U.S.C., Sec. 3542] attribution. A shared categorisation exists so risk judgements become comparable: the text stresses "Security categories are to be used in conjunction with vulnerability and threat information in assessing the risk to an organization." and defines the consequences outside the objectives themselves — "A loss of confidentiality is the unauthorized disclosure of information." — mapping disclosure, tampering and outage onto discussable impact values. Applicability and the aggregation rule are explicit: §2 "These standards shall apply to: (i) all information within the federal government other than that information that has been determined pursuant to Executive Order 12958, as amended by Executive Order 13292, or any predecessor order, or by the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended, to require protection against unauthorized disclosure and is marked to indicate its classified status" — the carve-out is classified information that is so marked — and "Agency officials shall use the security categorizations described in FIPS Publication 199 whenever there is a federal requirement to provide such a categorization". At system level the value is the maximum — "For an information system, the potential impact values assigned to the respective security objectives (confidentiality, integrity, availability) shall be the highest values (i.e., high water mark) from among those security categories that have been determined for each type of information resident on the information system". Two limits are in the sentence set: categorisation does not cover every system, because the same clause excludes "all federal information systems other than those information systems designated as national security systems as defined in 44 United States Code Section 3542(b)(2)"; and it binds only the federal government, others "may consider" it — "State, local, and tribal governments as well as private sector organizations comprising the critical infrastructure of the United States may consider the use of these standards as appropriate." The standard is named "Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems" and dated February 2004 in its own front matter; effectivity is stated as "These standards are effective upon approval by the Secretary of Commerce." and the division of labour with later guidance is set out in §1 — "Subsequent NIST standards and guidelines will address the second and third tasks cited." - Wikipedia search entry for 联邦信息与信息系统安全分类标准. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%81%94%E9%82%A6%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%E4%B8%8E%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%E7%B3%BB%E7%BB%9F%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E5%88%86%E7%B1%BB%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Standards for Security Categorization of Federal Information and Information Systems: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM)
items.text: Standard : Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM) (模块格基密钥封装机制标准（FIPS 203）). FIPS 203 states its mechanism class: "This standard specifies a set of algorithms for establishing a shared secret key. While there are many methods for establishing a shared secret key, the particular method described in this standard is a key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM)." — a KEM, not key management in general. Parameterisation exists for trade-offs: §1.1 states "This standard specifies three parameter sets for ML-KEM that offer different trade-offs in security strength versus performance." and fixes both the safety premise and the approval scope — "At present, ML-KEM is believed to be secure, even against adversaries who possess a quantum computer." and "All three parameter sets of ML-KEM are approved to protect sensitive, non-classified communication systems of the U.S. Federal Government." The applicability clause is the use statement: "This standard, or other FIPS or NIST Special Publications that specify alternative mechanisms, shall be used wherever the establishment of a shared secret key … is required for federal applications", under the name "Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (FIPS 203)" and the category line "Computer Security. Subcategory. Cryptography." Two limits: conformance is not system security — "the use of a product containing an implementation that conforms to this standard does not guarantee the security of the overall system in which the product is used." — the qualification clause adds that "the security guarantees of a KEM only hold under certain conditions" — and the waiver door is shut: "The Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) does not allow for waivers to Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) that are made mandatory by the Secretary of Commerce." Identity and legal basis appear together at the head: the announcement line is "Announcing the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard" and the authority sentence "Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) publications are developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) under 15 U.S.C. 278g-3 and issued by the Secretary of Commerce under 40 U.S.C. 11331." This is one of NIST’s post-quantum FIPS publications; the document itself only lists the CRYSTALS-Kyber submission in its references, so the candidate-to-standard lineage is carried by the algorithm and event entries reviewed in round R4 and is noted here as outside this document’s own wording. - Wikipedia search entry for 模块格基密钥封装机制标准（FIPS 203）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97%E6%A0%BC%E5%9F%BA%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%B0%81%E8%A3%85%E6%9C%BA%E5%88%B6%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86%EF%BC%88FIPS%20203%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 203: ML-KEM. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final - Published standard/RFC for 模块格基密钥封装机制标准（FIPS 203）. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/203/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard (ML-KEM): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
