items.title: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA)
items.text: Standard : Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA) (模块格基数字签名标准（FIPS 204）). FIPS 204 defines a lattice-based signature algorithm: the abstract opens with "This standard specifies ML-DSA, a set of algorithms that can be used to generate and verify digital signatures. ML-DSA is believed to be secure, even against adversaries in possession of a large-scale quantum computer." and clause 3 words the same object as "a lattice-based digital signature algorithm for applications that require a digital signature rather than a written signature." The title line names it "Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard". The approval definition is given in general terms — "An algorithm or technique that is either 1) specified in a FIPS or NIST recommendation, 2) adopted in a FIPS or NIST recommendation, or 3) specified in a list of NIST-approved security functions." The reason it exists is stated in clause 1 and its context subsection: many public-key systems "will be at risk if large-scale quantum computers are ever realized", including "key-establishment schemes and digital signatures that are based on integer factorization and discrete logarithms"; the replacement here is "the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA), which is based on the Module Learning With Errors problem" and "is believed to be strongly unforgeable". The operational boundary is key-pair exclusivity: "Agencies are advised that digital signature key pairs shall not be used for other purposes." The same advisory as FIPS 186-5 recurs here, again naming only "other purposes" rather than any specific reuse. The limits match the companion documents: conformance does not secure the whole system — "the use of a product containing an implementation that conforms to this standard does not guarantee the security of the overall system in which the product is used. The responsible authority in each agency or department shall ensure that an overall implementation provides an acceptable level of security." — and mandatory FIPS carry no waiver — "The Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) does not allow for waivers to Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) that are made mandatory by the Secretary of Commerce." — placing responsibility on the deploying authority and validation process. The identity line is "Announcing the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard", with name and number given as "Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (FIPS 204)" under the category line "Computer Security. Subcategory. Cryptography." It was published with FIPS 203 and 205 in 2024 as the signature leg of NIST’s three post-quantum standards — a co-publication fact verifiable across the R5B document set already checked in this round. - Wikipedia search entry for 模块格基数字签名标准（FIPS 204）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97%E6%A0%BC%E5%9F%BA%E6%95%B0%E5%AD%97%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86%EF%BC%88FIPS%20204%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 204: ML-DSA. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final - Published standard/RFC for 模块格基数字签名标准（FIPS 204）. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA)
items.text: Standard : Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA) (无状态散列基数字签名标准（FIPS 205）). FIPS 205 approves parameter sets for hash-based signatures: "This standard specifies several parameter sets for SLH-DSA that are approved for use. Additional parameter sets may be specified and approved in future NIST Special Publications." — approval extends only as far as the listed sets. It rests on hash assumptions: clause 1 states "The security of the stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm (SLH-DSA) relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions as well as several related properties of the same hash functions." and separates itself from the incumbent — "Unlike the algorithms specified in FIPS 186-5 …, SLH-DSA is designed to provide resistance against attacks from a large-scale quantum computer." The operational constraint matches the other signature standards: "Agencies are advised that digital signature key pairs shall not be used for other purposes." What the document itself says is structural: clause 3 states "Conceptually, an SLH-DSA key pair consists of a very large set of FORS key pairs." and characterises FORS as "a few-time signature scheme", adding that "The few-time signature scheme FORS allows each key pair to safely sign a small number of messages." — the standard supplies construction and parameter limits, without adding a separate prohibition on other uses. First limit: whole-system security remains the deployer’s duty — "The responsible authority in each agency or department shall ensure that an overall implementation provides an acceptable level of security." Second, the approval scope is open-ended in one direction only: new parameter sets are left to "future NIST Special Publications", so this document promises no coverage of future forms. The announcement line is "Announcing the Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard", with number and name in the explanation clause and the standing authority sentence "Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS) publications are developed by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) under 15 U.S.C. 278g-3 and issued by the Secretary of Commerce under 40 U.S.C. 11331." It was published with FIPS 203 and 204, and the abstract gives its lineage — "SLH-DSA is based on SPHINCS+, which was selected for standardization as part of the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization process." The stateful branch is handled elsewhere, by SP 800-208, "Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes"; inside this standard the components are not approved stand-alone schemes, so modules should not expose WOTS+, XMSS, FORS and hypertree interfaces. - Wikipedia search entry for 无状态散列基数字签名标准（FIPS 205）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%97%A0%E7%8A%B6%E6%80%81%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97%E5%9F%BA%E6%95%B0%E5%AD%97%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86%EF%BC%88FIPS%20205%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 205: SLH-DSA. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final - Published standard/RFC for 无状态散列基数字签名标准（FIPS 205）. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/205/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard (SLH-DSA): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Format-Preserving Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : Format-Preserving Encryption (FPE 格式保留加密). The 2016 edition of SP 800-38G says format-preserving encryption "is designed for data that is not necessarily binary": for any finite set of symbols such as decimal numerals, the encrypted form "has the same format, including the length, as the original data". The document calls the symbol set an alphabet, its size the radix (at least 2), a non-negative integer below the base a numeral, and a finite ordered sequence of them a numeral string. Ordinary encryption changes length or character set. The document uses the nine-decimal-digit Social Security number as its example: a longer ciphertext would no longer fit the format. So "FPE facilitates the targeting of encryption to sensitive information, as well as the retrofitting of encryption technology to legacy applications", with applications including financial-information security, data sanitization and transparent encryption of fields in legacy databases. The Recommendation (March 2016, with updates of 4 August 2016) provides the FF1 and FF3 modes, Algorithms 7 to 10 for encryption and decryption. Section 4.3 requires an approved block cipher with a 128-bit block: "Currently, the AES block cipher, with key lengths of 128, 192, or 256 bits, is the only block cipher that fits this profile". Section 4.5 states that ten rounds are specified for FF1 and eight for FF3, and §4.4 with Appendix C strongly recommend variable tweaks. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Appendix A notes that "encrypted data may be vulnerable to guessing attacks" when the input space is small, suggesting that radix raised to minlen should generally reach at least one million to limit guessing, and requiring that value to be at least 100 "in order to preclude a generic meet-in-the-middle attack on the Feistel structure". Section 6 states that component functions such as the PRF are "not approved for use independent of these four functions", and a footnote in §2 warns that sanitization "does not necessarily provide strong assurance that individuals cannot be re-identified". SP 800-38G, by Morris Dworkin, was published in March 2016 with updates as of 4 August 2016. Section 2 records the removal of the FF2 mode from the draft: NIST was advised by the National Security Agency in general terms that FF2 in the draft "did not provide the expected 128 bits of security strength", and announced its removal. - Wikipedia search entry for FPE 格式保留加密. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=FPE%20%E6%A0%BC%E5%BC%8F%E4%BF%9D%E7%95%99%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Format-Preserving Encryption: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Hybrid Public Key Encryption
items.text: Protocol : Hybrid Public Key Encryption (HPKE 混合公钥加密). Section 5 gives the common shape: "All variants take a recipient public key and a sequence of plaintexts pt and produce an encapsulated key enc and a sequence of ciphertexts ct." Hybrid here means a public-key encapsulation combined with a symmetric AEAD. The motive is fragmentation: §1 says "Currently, there are numerous competing and non-interoperable standards and variants for hybrid encryption, mostly variants on the Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme (ECIES)" and that "All these existing schemes have problems, e.g., because they rely on outdated primitives, lack proofs of indistinguishable (adaptive) chosen-ciphertext attack (IND-CCA2) security, or fail to provide test vectors." Section 5.3 adds an interface for exporting secrets from the encryption context. The common case is one message: §6.1 states "In many cases, applications encrypt only a single message to a recipient's public key." and supplies the stateless single-shot templates. Section 4 pins the identifiers, requiring that inside a KEM "suite_id MUST start with" the KEM prefix while in the rest of HPKE it "MUST start with" the HPKE prefix identifying the whole ciphersuite. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limits are stated with the analysis: §9.1 says "HPKE does not provide forward secrecy with respect to recipient compromise." and §9.7.4 that "HPKE ciphertexts are not forward secret with respect to recipient compromise in any mode." The document also lists non-goals (no downgrade or replay prevention, no hiding of the plaintext length) and registers no post-quantum KEM suite. RFC 9180 dates from February 2022, is labelled IRTF and Informational, and states "This document is a product of the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) in the IRTF." items.title: Internet Key Exchange Version 2
items.text: Protocol : Internet Key Exchange Version 2 (IKEv2 密钥交换). IKEv2 starts with IKE_SA_INIT: both sides exchange SA proposals, Ni/Nr and DH public keys, negotiating PRF, encryption, integrity and DH group. It then computes SKEYSEED=prf(Ni Nr, g^ir), where g^ir is the DH shared secret. prf+(SKEYSEED, Ni Nr SPIi SPIr) expands into SK_d, SK_ai, SK_ar, SK_ei, SK_er, SK_pi and SK_pr. SK_d is the long-lived key that derives Child SA key material, SK_a protects integrity, SK_e protects confidentiality and SK_p protects identity. SKEYSEED binds both nonces, the DH shared secret and the SPIs, so any difference yields different session keys; prf+ stretches a fixed-length PRF output into the required key stream and avoids reusing one segment for different purposes. IKE_AUTH uses AUTH to bind the real message, the peer nonce and the identity, stopping a man-in-the-middle from replacing the ID or replaying an old message; a Child SA can add fresh DH for PFS. Implement RFC 7296 §2.14: choose the PRF, for example HMAC-SHA-256 with 32-byte output, then slice the prf+ output by key length; SK_d is at least the PRF output length. Child SA KEYMAT=prf+(SK_d, Ni Nr), or prf+(SK_d, g^ir(new) Ni Nr) with PFS; AUTH SignedOctets contains RealMessage, the peer nonce and prf(SK_p, ID). A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. PFS is optional: a Child SA without fresh DH relies only on SK_d and nonces, so a long-lived SK_d leak reaches that SA’s keys. Nonce reuse repeats SKEYSEED and destroys session-key uniqueness. PSK mode must apply the Key Pad inner prf first, and a low-entropy password still falls to offline dictionary attacks; PPK only mixes an extra key and does not replace a strong shared secret. IKEv2 protects negotiation and SAs, not application data by itself. IKEv2 first appeared in RFC 4306 in December 2005, was revised by RFC 5996 in 2010, and became Internet Standard STD 79 in RFC 7296 in October 2014. RFC 8784 added PPK in 2020 to mix a post-quantum pre-shared key into IKEv2; RFC 7383 added message fragmentation and RFC 7815 gives a minimal implementation example. - Wikipedia search entry for IKEv2 密钥交换. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=IKEv2%20%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E4%BA%A4%E6%8D%A2 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Internet Key Exchange Version 2: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Internet Protocol Security
items.text: Protocol : Internet Protocol Security (IPsec 安全协议族). RFC 4301 is the architecture document rather than a protocol line itself: §1 states "This document specifies the base architecture for IPsec-compliant systems." and it defines how security services are provided at the IP layer. §3.2 gives the protocol pair "IPsec uses two protocols to provide traffic security services -- Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP)." and sets the baseline "IPsec implementations MUST support ESP and MAY support AH." — which protocol protects a security association follows from these documents, while policy and key management are handled elsewhere. The design choice is to place protection at the IP layer: §2.1 says "IPsec is designed to provide interoperable, high quality, cryptographically-based security for IPv4 and IPv6." and stresses "These services are provided at the IP layer, offering protection in a standard fashion for all protocols that may be carried over IP (including IP itself)." §3.1 turns that into a boundary — "IPsec creates a boundary between unprotected and protected interfaces, for a host or a network" — where packets may pass unimpeded, get AH/ESP protection, or be discarded. §4.1 fixes the granularity: "An SA is a simplex “connection” that affords security services to the traffic carried by it." and "Security services are afforded to an SA by the use of AH, or ESP, but not both." The implementation surface is defined by three databases: §4.4 states "There are three nominal databases in this model: the Security Policy Database (SPD), the Security Association Database (SAD), and the Peer Authorization Database (PAD)." §4.5 requires "All IPsec implementations MUST support both manual and automated SA and cryptographic key management." and §4.5.2 adds "Widespread deployment and use of IPsec requires an Internet-standard, scalable, automated, SA management protocol." naming the default — "The default automated key management protocol selected for use with IPsec is IKEv2 [Kau05]." AH's standing is downgraded in §3.2 with a reason: "Support for AH has been downgraded to MAY because experience has shown that there are very few contexts in which ESP cannot provide the requisite security services." The document draws three limits itself. §2.2 hands the outcome to implementations: "the security offered by use of these protocols ultimately depends on the quality of their implementation". §4.5 admits the ceiling on authentication strength — "In general, data origin authentication in AH and ESP is limited by the extent to which secrets used with the integrity algorithm" — the more parties share a secret, the weaker the origin claim. §11 gives a concrete configuration trap: "If an IPsec implementation is configured to pass ICMP error messages over SAs based on the ICMP header values, without checking the header information from the ICMP message payload, serious vulnerabilities may arise." and judges the resulting chain "This is a very efficient DoS attack that could have been prevented if the ICMP error messages were subjected to the checks that IPsec provides". RFC 4301 is signed by S. Kent and K. Seo (BBN Technologies), published December 2005 as a Standards Track document with an “Obsoletes: 2401” header line; the abstract calls it "an updated version of the “Security Architecture for IP”". §13 assesses the relation to the older document: "This architecture document differs substantially from RFC 2401 [RFC2401] in detail and in organization, but the fundamental notions are unchanged." and singles out the new store — "There is also a new database, the Peer Authorization Database (PAD)." §10 states the same conformance duty for each protocol family: "All IPv4 IPsec implementations MUST comply with all requirements of this document." and "All IPv6 implementations MUST comply with all requirements of this document." - Wikipedia search entry for IPsec 安全协议族. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=IPsec%20%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE%E6%97%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 4301: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4301 - Published standard/RFC for IPsec 安全协议族. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4301 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Internet Protocol Security: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Lorenz Cryptanalysis
items.text: Attack : Lorenz Cryptanalysis (洛伦兹破译). The Computer History Museum timeline entry for 1944 names the machine and its target: "First Colossus operational at Bletchley Park … Designed by British engineer Tommy Flowers, the Colossus is designed to break the complex Lorenz ciphers used by the Nazis during World War II." Breaking Lorenz ciphertext was the job of this electronic machine. The same entry supplies the reason in terms of speed and scale: "Colossus reduced the time to break Lorenz messages from weeks to hours", and "A total of ten Colossi were delivered, each using as many as 2,500 vacuum tubes". Moving from weeks to hours was achieved by this purpose-built electronics, using thousands of valves. The entry closes with its assessed use: "Most historians believe that the use of Colossus machines significantly shortened the war by providing evidence of enemy intentions and beliefs" — the output served strategic decision-making by evidencing enemy intentions and beliefs, not merely making individual messages readable. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The entry also records a distinctive limit: "The machine's existence was not made public until the 1970s." Long secrecy kept this work out of published computing history for decades, so early literature is scarce; this entry uses only what the timeline states and adds no detail about the breaking process beyond the source. items.title: Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature (ML-DSA)
items.text: Algorithm : Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard (ML-DSA 格基签名). FIPS 204, published 13 August 2024, states: "ML-DSA is a digital signature scheme based on CRYSTALS-DILITHIUM". Section 6.1 gives the public key pk as a byte encoding of the public random seed and the compressed polynomial vector t1, where t1 is produced from the uncompressed public-key polynomial t by dropping the d least significant bits of each coefficient and t = As1 + s2. The same section gives the private key sk as a byte encoding of the public random seed, a private random seed for use during signing, a 64-byte hash of the public key, the secret polynomial vectors s1 and s2, and a polynomial vector t0 encoding the d least significant bits of each coefficient of t, and notes that an implementation may store only the 32-byte seed and regenerate the rest of the private key. The standard says "The ML-DSA scheme uses the Fiat-Shamir With Aborts construction". To correct a bias, the signer applies rejection sampling to z; if coefficients of z fall outside of a specified range, the signing process is aborted, so signing is largely a rejection-sampling loop whose iterations either produce a valid signature or "an invalid signature whose release would leak information about the private key". Section 3.3 adds that, to ensure correctness, a second stage of rejection sampling must be included at line 28 of Algorithm 7. The parameter sets are ML-DSA-44, ML-DSA-65 and ML-DSA-87, where the numerical suffix refers to the dimension of the matrix A — for ML-DSA-65 the matrix A is 6 by 5 — and the three are claimed to be in security strength categories 2, 3 and 5. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Signing randomness is the main failure point: for ML-DSA to be secure, the signer's commitment value y must not be used to sign more than one message, and it must not be easily guessed by an attacker. This requires randomness. The standard says fresh randomness helps mitigate side-channel attacks, while for the deterministic variant "the lack of randomness in the deterministic variant makes the risk of side-channel attacks (particularly fault attacks) more difficult to mitigate. Therefore, this variant should not be used on platforms where side-channel attacks are a concern and where they cannot be otherwise mitigated". Section 3.6.1 adds that with an RBG of at least 128 but less than 192 bits of security, the claimed category of ML-DSA-44 drops from 2 to 1. NIST IR 8547 (October 2026) records that FIPS 204 and 205 each specify a quantum-resistant digital signature scheme, with ML-DSA in §2.1.1 derived from the CRYSTALS-Dilithium submission, and its §4 timeline requires the government's most sensitive systems to complete post-quantum key establishment by 31 December 2030 and to adopt post-quantum digital signatures by 31 December 2031. - Wikipedia search entry for ML-DSA 格基签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ML-DSA%20%E6%A0%BC%E5%9F%BA%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 204: ML-DSA. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/204/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Standard: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: OCSP Stapling
items.text: Protocol : OCSP Stapling (OCSP 装订). The mechanism carries certificate status information inside the handshake: RFC 6066 §8 (Certificate Status Request) says "This extension allows for such information to be sent in the TLS handshake, saving roundtrips and resources." The stated reason is bandwidth and round-trips, not privacy: the same section says "Constrained clients may wish to use a certificate-status protocol such as OCSP [RFC2560] to check the validity of server certificates, in order to avoid transmission of CRLs and therefore save bandwidth on constrained networks." The server answers optionally: §8 covers a client hello "containing the “status_request” extension" and says such servers "MAY return a suitable certificate status response to the client along with their certificate." and that "Only one OCSP response may be sent." A server that does send a CertificateStatus message must earlier have included the extension with empty data in the server hello. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Stapling does not replace validation: §11.6 warns that "If a client requests an OCSP response, it must take into account that an attacker's server using a compromised key could (and probably would) pretend not to support the extension." and advises a client that requires OCSP validation to "SHOULD either contact the OCSP server directly or abort the handshake". The extension is specified by RFC 6066, a Standards Track document from January 2011 whose header carries “Obsoletes: 4366” and whose §1 says the text is largely an adaptation of RFC 4366 material. The nonce encoding is pinned here: "for clarification, the nonce MUST be a DER-encoded OCTET STRING". - Wikipedia search entry for OCSP 装订. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=OCSP%20%E8%A3%85%E8%AE%A2 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 6960: Online Certificate Status Protocol. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6960 - Published standard/RFC for OCSP 装订. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6960 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] OCSP Stapling: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure
items.text: Protocol : Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKIX 证书框架). RFC 5280 states its own place: §1 "This specification is one part of a family of standards for the X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) for the Internet." and "This specification profiles the format and semantics of certificates and certificate revocation lists (CRLs) for the Internet PKI." §4 puts the certificate side plainly — "This section presents a profile for public key certificates that will foster interoperability and a reusable PKI." — it fixes how fields and extensions are filled in and binds issuers to conformance duties, without describing CA operations or trust policy. A profile exists because free interpretation breaks both interoperability and trust decisions. Validity encoding is fixed: §4.1.2.5 "CAs conforming to this profile MUST always encode certificate validity dates through the year 2049 as UTCTime; certificate validity dates in 2050 or later MUST be encoded as GeneralizedTime." Basic constraints are mandatory and critical: §4.2.1.9 "Conforming CAs MUST include this extension in all CA certificates that contain public keys used to validate digital signatures on certificates and MUST mark the extension as critical in such certificates." §4.1.2.5 also gives the no-expiry convention: "To indicate that a certificate has no well-defined expiration date, the notAfter SHOULD be assigned the GeneralizedTime value of 99991231235959Z." §4.2.1.9 uses pathLenConstraint to bound chain depth: "A pathLenConstraint of zero indicates that no non-self-issued intermediate CA certificates may follow in a valid certification path." §6.1 sets the implementation duty: "A conforming implementation MUST include an X.509 path processing procedure that is functionally equivalent to the external behavior of this algorithm." §6.1 draws the boundary: the algorithm "only includes checks to verify that the certification path is valid according to X.509 and does not include checks to verify that the certificates and CRLs conform to this profile." and it "RECOMMENDS against including such checks." Unknown critical extensions are a hard failure — "Note that clients MUST reject the certificate if it contains an unsupported critical extension." Conformance and validity are therefore separate matters, and the §6.1 algorithm governs only the latter. RFC 5280 is signed by D. Cooper, S. Santesson, S. Farrell, S. Boeyen, R. Housley and W. items.title: Certificate Transparency
items.text: Protocol : Certificate Transparency (证书透明度). RFC 6962 §1 defines the mechanism: "Certificate transparency aims to mitigate the problem of misissued certificates by providing publicly auditable, append-only, untrusted logs of all issued certificates." It does not block misissuance, only makes it visible: "The logs do not themselves prevent misissue, but they ensure that interested parties (particularly those named in certificates) can detect such misissuance." Submission yields a signed timestamp — "When a chain is submitted to a log, a signed timestamp is returned". Two design reasons. Spam resistance first: "In order to avoid logs being spammed into uselessness, it is required that each chain is rooted in a known CA certificate." Auditability second: §2.1 "Logs use a binary Merkle Hash Tree for efficient auditing." and §1 explains that the tree is what makes append-only provable — "The append-only property of each log is technically achieved using Merkle Trees". Checking is deliberately deferred: "The checking operation is asynchronous to allow TLS connections to proceed without delay". To account for certificates before issuance, §3.1 introduces the precertificate: "the CA submits a Precertificate that the log can use to create an entry that will be valid against the issued certificate." using a poison extension so ordinary validation rejects it, and treats intent as binding — "misissuance of the Precertificate is considered equal to misissuance of the final certificate". §5.2 covers TLS clients, which verify the SCT signature and "MUST reject SCTs whose timestamp is in the future." §5.3 defines monitors: "Monitors watch logs and check that they behave correctly." Time is the hard bound: §7.1 says misissued certificates without a valid SCT are rejected by clients, while logged ones surface within the Maximum Merge Delay, so "the maximum period of time during which a misissued certificate can be used without being available for audit is the MMD." Logs themselves may misbehave, and §7.3 lists two forms — missing the MMD, or "by presenting two different, conflicting views of the Merkle Tree" — both publicly detectable, since two conflicting signed tree heads for one log are "cryptographic proof of that log's misbehavior." RFC 6962 was published in June 2013 with Category: Experimental. §1 fixes the scope: "Note that this is a general mechanism, but in this document, we only describe its use for public TLS server certificates issued by public certificate authorities (CAs)." §2.1 records that SHA-256 is fixed for this experiment with logs expected to choose their own hash later, and notes that distinct leaf and node hashing "is required to give second preimage resistance." - Wikipedia search entry for 证书透明度. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%AF%81%E4%B9%A6%E9%80%8F%E6%98%8E%E5%BA%A6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Certificate Transparency: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DNSSEC
items.text: Protocol : DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC 域名安全). The abstract states what the extensions add: "The Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC) add data origin authentication and data integrity to the Domain Name System." This document is the introduction and requirements; the new records and protocol modifications are specified by the companion document set. Section 1 gives both the capability and the disclaimer: "The DNS security extensions provide origin authentication and integrity protection for DNS data, as well as a means of public key distribution. These extensions do not provide confidentiality." Origin and integrity are added; confidentiality is excluded by design. Section 3 lists the protocol changes: "DNSSEC adds four new resource record types: Resource Record Signature (RRSIG), DNS Public Key (DNSKEY), Delegation Signer (DS), and Next Secure (NSEC). It also adds two new message header bits: Checking Disabled (CD) and Authenticated Data (AD)." The starting point is defined in §2: "Trust Anchor: A configured DNSKEY RR or DS RR hash of a DNSKEY RR." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Two limits are stated outright: §4 says "Accordingly, DNSSEC is not designed to provide confidentiality, access control lists, or other means of differentiating between inquirers.", and availability is not claimed either — "DNSSEC provides no protection against denial of service attacks." — with signature verification itself creating a new denial-of-service surface. items.title: QUIC
items.text: Protocol : QUIC (QUIC 传输协议). Section 1 gives the carrier and the motive: "QUIC packets are carried in UDP datagrams [UDP] to better facilitate deployment in existing systems and networks." QUIC is thus a transport over UDP with security and multiplexing built in, not an encryption layer on top of TCP. One handshake negotiates both halves: §1 states "The QUIC handshake combines negotiation of cryptographic and transport parameters. QUIC integrates the TLS handshake [TLS13], although using a customized framing for protecting packets." RFC 9001 carries the protection rules: "This document describes how QUIC [QUIC-TRANSPORT] is secured using TLS [TLS13]." and "QUIC [QUIC-TRANSPORT] assumes responsibility for the confidentiality and integrity protection of packets." Key discarding is explicit: a client and a server "MUST discard Initial keys" at the first Handshake packet sent or successfully processed. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Version negotiation is the unprotected part: §12.1 records that "Version Negotiation packets have no cryptographic protection", Retry packets only carry an AEAD integrity function against modification, and §6.2 notes for this version that "How to perform version negotiation is left as future work" — so version 1 offers no downgrade-proof negotiation. RFC 9000 and its companion RFC 9001 are both May 2021 Standards Track documents (edited by Iyengar and Thomson, and by Thomson and Turner respectively); neither header carries an Updates or Obsoletes line, and the document defines version 1 of QUIC. - Wikipedia search entry for QUIC 传输协议. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=QUIC%20%E4%BC%A0%E8%BE%93%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 9000: QUIC: A UDP-Based Multiplexed and Secure Transport. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000 - Published standard/RFC for QUIC 传输协议. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] QUIC: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service
items.text: Protocol : Remote Authentication Dial-In User Service (RADIUS 认证协议). RADIUS is a client/server protocol between the NAS and a backend server: §1 states "A Network Access Server (NAS) operates as a client of RADIUS." and §3 fixes the carriage: "Exactly one RADIUS packet is encapsulated in the UDP Data field [4], where the UDP Destination Port field indicates 1812 (decimal)." Trust rests on a pre-shared secret: §1 Network Security says "Transactions between the client and RADIUS server are authenticated through the use of a shared secret, which is never sent over the network." Authentication therefore does not rely on the channel. Attributes carry the details a request and reply need: §5 states "RADIUS Attributes carry the specific authentication, authorization, information and configuration details for the request and reply." Section 2 sets a hard rule for unknown clients: "A request from a client for which the RADIUS server does not have a shared secret MUST be silently discarded." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The weak points are password hiding and MD5: §2 explains the password "is hidden using a method based on the RSA Message Digest Algorithm MD5 [3]." and §8 concedes "The User-Password hiding mechanism described in Section 5.2 has not been subjected to significant amounts of cryptanalysis in the published literature." Neither RFC 2865 nor 2866 mentions the Message-Authenticator attribute (that is RFC 2869), and neither declares MD5 broken. Both documents date from June 2000: RFC 2865 is Standards Track and its header obsoletes RFC 2138, while RFC 2866 (RADIUS Accounting) is Informational, obsoletes RFC 2139, and states "All transactions are comprised of variable length Attribute-Length-Value 3-tuples." items.title: RADIUS over TLS
items.text: Protocol : RADIUS over TLS (RADIUS over TLS). The abstract gives mechanism and effect: "This document specifies a transport profile for RADIUS using Transport Layer Security (TLS) over TCP as the transport protocol. This enables dynamic trust relationships between RADIUS servers." RADIUS moves from UDP plus a provisioned shared secret into TLS over TCP. Section 1 is explicit: "However, RADIUS is experiencing several shortcomings, such as its dependency on the unreliable transport protocol UDP and the lack of security for large parts of its packet payload. RADIUS security is based on the MD5 algorithm, which has been proven to be insecure." The remedy is encapsulation — "RADIUS over TLS wraps the entire RADIUS packet payload into a TLS stream and thus mitigates the risk of attacks on MD5." Section 2 gives the port and the duties: "The default destination port number for RADIUS over TLS is TCP/2083. There are no separate ports for authentication, accounting, and dynamic authorization changes." and §2.3 requires "Support for certificate-based mutual authentication is REQUIRED." plus "Negotiation of mutual authentication is REQUIRED." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Hard clauses set the limits: the version floor "implementations MUST NOT negotiate TLS versions prior to 1.1"; §6 forbids integrity-only ciphersuites, which is decisive once the shared secret is a fixed well-known value; and §4 states "RADIUS/TLS does not specify any inherent backward compatibility to RADIUS/UDP or cross compatibility to the other transports". items.title: Random Number Generator Failure
items.text: Attack : RNG Failure (随机数失效). Debian DSA-1571-1 records that "Luciano Bello discovered that the random number generator in Debian's openssl package is predictable. This is caused by an incorrect Debian-specific change to the openssl package (CVE-2008-0166). As a result, cryptographic key material may be guessable." The advisory header lists the vulnerability as a "predictable random number generator" and marks "Debian-specific: yes", showing that a randomness failure can come from packaging changes rather than from the algorithm. SP 800-90A Rev.1 puts the responsibility on the seed: §1 requires that "The seed used to instantiate the DRBG must contain sufficient entropy to provide an assurance of randomness", §8.6.1 that "Entropy input shall always be used in the construction of a seed", §8.6.3 that the entropy input equal or exceed the security strength of the instantiation, and §8.6.5 that "A DRBG mechanism requires an approved randomness source during instantiation and reseeding". If seed entropy is removed, a deterministic generator simply outputs predictable bits. The advisory states the consequences as a list: "Affected keys include SSH keys, OpenVPN keys, DNSSEC keys, and key material for use in X.509 certificates and session keys used in SSL/TLS connections. Keys generated with GnuPG or GNUTLS are not affected, though." It also strongly recommends that "all DSA keys ever used on affected Debian systems for signing or authentication purposes should be considered compromised; the Digital Signature Algorithm relies on a secret random value used during signature generation." The version table gives the first vulnerable build 0.9.8c-1 (uploaded to unstable on 2006-09-17) and the fixed builds etch 0.9.8c-4etch3 and sid/lenny 0.9.8g-9. The standard's failure handling is mandatory: §11.3 requires that "A DRBG implementation shall perform self-tests to obtain assurance that the DRBG continues to operate as designed and implemented (health testing)", and §11.4.2 says errors detected during health testing "shall be perceived as catastrophic DRBG failures"; on failure "the DRBG shall enter an error state and output an error indicator", and "The DRBG shall not perform any instantiate, generate or reseed operations while in the error state, and pseudorandom bits shall not be output when an error state exists". Section 10.1 names Hash_DRBG and HMAC_DRBG, with CTR_DRBG in §10.2 — three mechanisms — and Appendix E records that "The Dual_EC_DRBG has been removed, and section numbers adjusted accordingly". DSA-1571-1, issued by Florian Weimer on 13 May 2008 for CVE-2008-0166, traces the defect to a packaging change that entered Debian's unstable distribution in September 2006. On the standards side, Barker and Kelsey's SP 800-90A Rev.1 (June 2015) removed the Dual_EC_DRBG. Together they show that generator failure can come from a distribution-level change as well as from the choice of mechanism itself. - Wikipedia search entry for 随机数失效. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%9A%8F%E6%9C%BA%E6%95%B0%E5%A4%B1%E6%95%88 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] RNG Failure: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths
items.text: Standard : Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths (密码算法与密钥长度过渡). The unit of this publication is security strength: "In SP 800-57, the security strength provided by an algorithm with a particular key length … is measured in bits and is a measure of the difficulty of subverting the cryptographic protection that is provided by the algorithm and key." It stresses that "Note that the length of the cryptographic keys is an integral part of these determinations." — algorithm and key length are judged together. Transitions need a written schedule because algorithms decay with computing power: the publication sets a floor for the federal government today — "For the Federal Government, a security strength of at least 112 bits is required at this time for applying cryptographic protection (e.g., for encrypting or signing data)." — and flags the future change in its own definitions, "When post-quantum cryptography is introduced in NIST standards, quantum security strength, i.e. the difficulty of subverting the protection using quantum computers, will be defined." while the note supplies the meaning itself, defining the measure as "a measure of the difficulty of subverting the cryptographic protection (e.g., discovering the key) using classical computers." The work is an algorithm-by-algorithm inventory: §2 opens with block ciphers — "Encryption is a cryptographic operation that is used to provide confidentiality for sensitive information, and decryption is the inverse operation." — and lists the families used federally, for instance "The Triple Data Encryption Algorithm (TDEA) (often referred to as Triple DES) is specified in SP 800-67, and has two variations, known as two-key TDEA and three-key TDEA." The first limit is its standing: it is a recommendation, not a FIPS — the authority block says "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems" and adds "Nothing in this publication should be taken to contradict the standards and guidelines made mandatory and binding on federal agencies by the Secretary of Commerce under statutory authority.", and the same block describes the publication as one that "may be used by nongovernmental organizations on a voluntary basis and is not subject to copyright in the United States". The second is timing: the 128-bit move is booked elsewhere — "SP 800-57, Part 1 includes a transition to a security strength of 128 bits in 2030" — and the text concedes its own scope — "However, this revision of SP 800-131A does not address this transition, but a future revision will include these considerations as well as transitions to post-quantum algorithms." Its history is legible from itself and its citations: this is Revision 2, titled "NIST Special Publication 800-131A Revision 2 Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths"; footnote 13 outsources curve approval — "Until SP 800-186 is published, approved elliptic curves are specified in FIPS 186-4." — and ties TDEA deprecation to a 2017 NIST announcement; that curve pointer was a 2019 placeholder only — SP 800-186 in this corpus is dated February 2023 and FIPS 186-5 superseded 186-4 on 3 February 2023, so the sentence no longer holds today. - Wikipedia search entry for 密码算法与密钥长度过渡. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95%E4%B8%8E%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E9%95%BF%E5%BA%A6%E8%BF%87%E6%B8%A1 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Transitioning the Use of Cryptographic Algorithms and Key Lengths: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations
items.text: Standard : Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of TLS Implementations (TLS 选型与配置指南). The document identifies itself in its title: "Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) Implementations", published as NIST SP 800-52 Rev. §1.2 bounds it: "These guidelines focus only on network security, and they focus directly on the small portion of the network communications stack that is referred to as the transport layer." and it targets broad-interop, certificate-authenticated cases — "These guidelines focus on the common use cases where clients and servers must interoperate with a wide variety of implementations, and authentication is performed using public-key certificates." Requirements are layered by risk because security is not a single switch: §1.2 says "Security is not a single property that is (or is not) possessed by a protocol." and "Adherence to these guidelines only protects the data in transit." §3.1 therefore treats government-only and public-facing servers differently: the former "should not be configured to use TLS 1.1 and shall not use TLS 1.0, SSL 3.0, or SSL 2.0." while the latter may keep older versions when interoperation demands it — "The use of TLS versions 1.1 and 1.0 is generally discouraged, but these versions may be configured when necessary to enable interaction with citizens and businesses." Federal deployment timing is concrete: §3.1 states "Agencies shall support TLS 1.3 by January 1, 2024." and requires both server classes to support TLS 1.3 thereafter. The compatibility rule is "In general, servers that support TLS 1.3 should be configured to use TLS 1.2 as well." with 1.2 allowed off once interoperability does not need it. For government-only servers the baseline is that they "shall be configured to use TLS 1.2 and should be configured to use TLS 1.3 as well". Two limits are stated. In scope, it covers only the transport layer: §1.2 — "Adherence to these guidelines only protects the data in transit." — recommending other NIST publications for the rest. In implementation quality, it refuses broken negotiation: §3.1 records servers that terminate connections when a newer version is offered and concludes "Servers that incorrectly implement TLS version negotiation shall not be used." configuration compliance cannot substitute for verifying implementation behaviour. The registered source is corrected after verification: the inventory record read NIST SP 800-177 Rev.1(2020) , but SP 800-177 Rev. 1 is Trustworthy Email (February 2019). The TLS selection and configuration guidance is SP 800-52 Rev. 2, by Kerry A. McKay and David A. items.title: Recommendations for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters
items.text: Standard : Recommendations for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters (椭圆曲线域参数建议). The scope of the recommendation is one sentence: "This Recommendation specifies the set of elliptic curves recommended for U.S. Government use." It is not a new algorithm but the recommended set of curves and their domain parameters. The new curves are justified by performance and implementation safety: "In addition to the previously recommended Weierstrass curves defined over prime fields and binary fields, this Recommendation includes two newly specified Edwards curves, which provide increased performance, side-channel resistance, and simpler implementation when compared to traditional curves." Alternative encodings are also allowed — "This Recommendation also specifies alternative representations for these new curves to allow more implementation flexibility." At the selection layer, §3.1 carries the title Recommended Curves for U.S. Federal Government Use — the heading line is unnumbered in our text, located by its 3.1.1/3.1.2 children — and its opening text says the section specifies the curves recommended for U.S. Federal Government use and gives the choices for private-key length and underlying fields — a pick-list — and the abstract adds interoperability framing: "The new curves are interoperable with those specified by the Crypto Forum Research Group (CFRG) of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)." The limits follow from its standing: it is a recommendation, not a mandatory FIPS — the authority block says "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems" and adds "Nothing in this publication should be taken to contradict the standards and guidelines made mandatory and binding on federal agencies by the Secretary of Commerce under statutory authority." Clause 1 sets the real boundary: FIPS 186-4 curves short of the current bit-security requirements "are now legacy-use. They may be used to process already protected information (e.g., decrypt or verify) but not to apply protection to information (e.g., encrypt or sign)." The text also concedes that "Some of these requirements may be out of scope for CAVP or CMVP validation testing and are thus the responsibility of entities using, implementing, installing, or configuring applications that incorporate this Recommendation." Its place in the sequence is checkable: the title line is "Recommendations for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters" with Lily Chen among the authors, published in 2023. It takes over the curve list rather than the signature schemes: SP 800-131A Rev. 2 said approved curves remained specified in FIPS 186-4 until this recommendation was published, this document is the fulfilment of that placeholder, and the schemes stay with FIPS 186-5. The text points the old curves back where they belong — "This curve is for legacy-use only. See [FIPS_186-4] for the specification." - Wikipedia search entry for 椭圆曲线域参数建议. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%A4%AD%E5%9C%86%E6%9B%B2%E7%BA%BF%E5%9F%9F%E5%8F%82%E6%95%B0%E5%BB%BA%E8%AE%AE - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Recommendations for Discrete Logarithm-based Cryptography: Elliptic Curve Domain Parameters: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Speculative Execution Side-Channel
items.text: Attack : Speculative Execution Side-Channel (推测执行侧信道). The Meltdown abstract gives the mechanism: "Meltdown exploits side effects of out-of-order execution on modern processors to read arbitrary kernel-memory locations including personal data and passwords", and notes that "Out-of-order execution is an indispensable performance feature and present in a wide range of modern processors" — the side effects of a performance feature become the observation channel. The abstract places the root cause in hardware rather than software: "The root cause of Meltdown is the hardware. The attack is independent of the operating system, and it does not rely on any software vulnerabilities." The isolation failure is therefore not a bug in one program, and on affected systems "Meltdown enables an adversary to read memory of other processes or virtual machines in the cloud without any permissions or privileges". The paper also delivers a deployment conclusion: "We show that the KAISER defense mechanism for KASLR has the important (but inadvertent) side effect of impeding Meltdown. We stress that KAISER must be deployed immediately…" — what the abstract calls the KAISER defense mechanism for KASLR incidentally impedes the attack, and the paper’s deployment conclusion is that KAISER must be deployed immediately. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The abstract makes only a bounded claim about scope: "The attack works on different Intel microarchitectures since at least 2010 and potentially other processors are affected" — Intel microarchitectures are named, other vendors appear only as potentially affected, and this entry draws no conclusion beyond that. Success also depends on out-of-order execution itself, so it is not a software bug that can be patched away; the abstract puts the root cause in the hardware. items.title: SSH 1.x
items.text: Protocol : Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Version 1.x (SSH 1.x). The status of SSH 1.x is set by the retrospective description in the newer documents: RFC 4253 §5 says "Earlier versions of this protocol have not been formally documented, but it is widely known that they use 'protoversion' of “1.x” (e.g., “1.5” or “1.3”)." It is a protocol line that existed without a standardised text. The reason for the 2.0 rewrite is in the architecture document's abstract: "The SSH protocol consists of three major components: The Transport Layer Protocol provides server authentication, confidentiality, and integrity with perfect forward secrecy." The architecture abstract presents forward secrecy as a property the 2.0 transport layer provides, and the older line has no standardised description to lean on. Section 5 narrows its own scope: "Information in this section is only relevant for implementations supporting compatibility with SSH versions 1.x." The compatibility trick is a version string the newer server offers to older clients (§5.1, headed Old Client, New Server): it says "the server SHOULD identify its 'protoversion' as “1.99”." and requires clients on protocol 2.0 to treat that value as identical to 2.0. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Both the missing documentation and the compatibility procedure are problems: §5 records that "the only known documentation of the 1.x protocol is contained in README files that are shipped along with the source code [ssh-1.2.30]." and §5.2 notes a new client may send data first, so "the old protocol may already be corrupt when the client learns that the server is old", after which it should close and reconnect under the old protocol. items.title: SSH Protocol Version 2
items.text: Protocol : SSH Protocol Version 2 (SSH 2.0 协议族). The SSH 2.0 transport first exchanges version strings and KEXINIT, then runs DH to obtain the shared secret K. The exchange hash H concatenates the version strings, both raw KEXINIT payloads, the host key, DH e/f and K in a fixed order, then hashes them; the first KEX H is session_id. Key expansion starts with K1=HASH(K H X session_id), where X from A to F derives the c→s IV, s→c IV, c→s encryption key, s→c encryption key, c→s integrity key and s→c integrity key; if a key is too short, the hash chain continues. H binds algorithm negotiation, host identity and DH values, so a man-in-the-middle cannot replace any one of them; session_id stays unchanged across rekeys and ties the connection history together. The six keys separate direction and purpose, avoiding one key for both encryption and MAC; the sequence number enters the MAC implicitly, so replay, reordering and loss are visible to the receiver. Implement the RFC 4253 §7.2 expansion order: compute K1, then K2 and K3, until all six keys are long enough; AES-128-CTR takes a 16-byte encryption key and HMAC-SHA256 a 32-byte integrity key. The packet layer assembles the plaintext packet, computes MAC=MAC(K_mac, seq packet_without_mac), then encrypts; AEAD modes merge MAC and encryption but still maintain the sequence number. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The order of MAC and encryption defines the boundary: encrypt-then-MAC is safer, while MAC-then-encrypt leaves room for padding oracles; CBC modes and SHA-1 should not be used in new deployments. After sequence wrap, old nonces must not be reused; rekey changes keys but not the sequence number. Host-key trust is outside the transport layer and still needs known_hosts or certificate validation. Session = (Auth, KeyExchange, Record)；State ∈ {init, established, closed}；Invariant: fresh_key ∧ bound_auth. Symbols are catalogue-level variables, not standard constants; parameters, test vectors and clauses remain with the registered source. The model states structural relations, not an implementation audit. SSH-1 appeared around 1995 and was replaced by SSH-2 because of the CRC compensation attack and protocol flaws; RFC 4250–4254 in January 2006 fixed SSH-2 as transport, authentication, connection and architecture documents. RFC 6668 added hmac-sha2-256 and hmac-sha2-512 in 2012; OpenSSH and other implementations later added AEAD, strict KEX and post-quantum KEX extensions, while the packet formulas still follow RFC 4253. - Wikipedia search entry for SSH 2.0 协议族. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SSH%202.0%20%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE%E6%97%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 4251: The Secure Shell (SSH) Protocol Architecture. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4251 - Published standard/RFC for SSH 2.0 协议族. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc4251 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] SSH Protocol Version 2: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: TLS 1.0
items.text: Protocol : TLS 1.0 (TLS 1.0). RFC 2246 §1 gives the goal and the layering: "The primary goal of the TLS Protocol is to provide privacy and data integrity between two communicating applications. The protocol is composed of two layers: the TLS Record Protocol and the TLS Handshake Protocol." The record layer fragments, optionally compresses, MACs and encrypts; the handshake layer authenticates and agrees keys first. This was the first step in moving crypto out of each application into a shared layer: §3 gives the lineage "This document and the TLS protocol itself are based on the SSL 3.0 Protocol Specification as published by Netscape." and §6 fixes the record order: "The Record Protocol takes messages to be transmitted, fragments the data into manageable blocks, optionally compresses the data, applies a MAC, encrypts, and transmits the result." The specification sets one mandatory baseline: §9 says "In the absence of an application profile standard specifying otherwise, a TLS compliant application MUST implement the cipher suite TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA." On compression §6.2.2 only bounds size — "Compression must be lossless and may not increase the content length by more than 1024 bytes." This entry stays with the specification and makes no deployment claims. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Two weaknesses are visible inside the document: the CBC IV is implicit — §6.2.3.2 states "The IV for subsequent records is the last ciphertext block from the previous record.", making successive IVs predictable — and §3 concedes TLS 1.0 and SSL 3.0 "do not interoperate" while keeping a mechanism to back down to SSL 3.0. Appendix D.4 discourages 40-bit encryption and anonymous Diffie-Hellman only in non-normative prose; no suite is declared broken here. The RFC 2246 header lists T. Dierks and C. items.title: TLS 1.1
items.text: Protocol : TLS 1.1 (TLS 1.1). The abstract states version and purpose: "This document specifies Version 1.1 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. The TLS protocol provides communications security over the Internet." The wording is now security rather than the 1.0 privacy phrasing; the two-layer structure stays, while the IV handling inside block-ciphered records changes as described in §6.2.3.2. The change list sits in §1.1 and its first two items are the point of the release: "The implicit Initialization Vector (IV) is replaced with an explicit IV to protect against CBC attacks [CBCATT]." and "Handling of padding errors is changed to use the bad_record_mac alert rather than the decryption_failed alert to protect against CBC attacks." The introduction describes itself as carrying "some small security improvements, clarifications, and editorial improvements". The record layer states two duties: the receiver "MUST check this padding and SHOULD use the bad_record_mac alert to indicate padding errors.", and against the Canvel timing work "implementations MUST ensure that record processing time is essentially the same whether or not the padding is correct." The §9 mandatory suite is now TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA, and Appendix F.3 says this version "uses an explicit IV in order to protect against this attack." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Downgrade and static-key exposure are only partly handled here: §7.4.7.1 makes the version check asymmetric — "Client implementations, MUST and Server implementations MAY, check the version number." — and plays down the risk, "since the TLS handshake MACs prevent downgrade and no good attacks are known on those MACs, ambiguity is not considered a serious security risk". The padding-error alert is still only a SHOULD, and the record order still compresses before encryption without forbidding compression. The RFC 4346 header lists T. Dierks and E. items.title: TLS 1.2
items.text: Protocol : TLS 1.2 (TLS 1.2). The abstract is again a version statement: "This document specifies Version 1.2 of the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol. The TLS protocol provides communications security over the Internet." Section 1 keeps the same layering, "The protocol is composed of two layers: the TLS Record Protocol and the TLS Handshake Protocol." The theme is algorithm flexibility: §1.2 records "The MD5/SHA-1 combination in the pseudorandom function (PRF) has been replaced with cipher-suite-specified PRFs. items.title: TLS 1.3
items.text: Protocol : TLS 1.3 (TLS 1.3). TLS 1.3 first accumulates handshake messages into a transcript, then derives each stage key with an HKDF ladder. Transcript-Hash hashes ClientHello through the current message; Derive-Secret binds a label, the transcript hash and the current secret to produce the next secret. Early Secret is extracted from the PSK, or an all-zero PSK; Handshake Secret extracts the Early derived secret with the (EC)DHE shared secret; Main Secret extracts the Handshake derived secret with an all-zero IKM. Then c hs traffic, s hs traffic, c ap traffic and s ap traffic bind the handshake or application message sequence, and finally expand into AEAD keys and IVs. Splitting keys by stage gives encrypted latter handshake, forward secrecy and separated 0-RTT: Handshake Secret uses ephemeral DH for forward secrecy, application traffic keys come from Main Secret, and the PSK only affects Early Secret; it cannot replace certificates or Finished. Each traffic secret binds the transcript, preventing handshake splicing; Finished then HMACs the transcript with finished_key and confirms that both sides saw the same handshake. Implement in the RFC 9846 key-schedule order: fix the Hash first, for example SHA-256 with 32-byte output, then compute Early/Handshake/Main; derive each traffic secret with a label; expand key and IV with HKDF-Expand-Label, using a 16-byte key and 12-byte IV for AES-128-GCM. The record layer zero-pads the 64-bit sequence number to IV length and XORs it with the IV to obtain the per-record nonce; AEAD additional_data is the record header and plaintext is the content. Finished uses the handshake traffic secret as base key and expands finished_key to Hash.length bytes. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 0-RTT early data has no cross-connection replay guarantee, and the application must bound its replay window; PSK compromise weakens Early Secret and cannot be treated as a long-term identity. Sequence exhaustion requires key update and forbids wrapping nonce reuse; IV reuse in AEAD directly breaks confidentiality and integrity. TLS 1.3 does not protect plaintext after an endpoint compromise, and does not replace certificate validation, hostname checks or authorisation; RFC 9846 is a minor update to RFC 8446, so implementations should cite the current text. TLS 1.3 was standardised by RFC 8446 in August 2018, removing static RSA and static DH key exchange, requiring forward secrecy for all public-key exchange, and encrypting the latter handshake. RFC 9846 was published in July 2026 and replaces RFC 8446, while the protocol version remains TLS 1.3; it forbids reusing KeyShare across connections, makes key update before usage limits a MUST, and renames master to main. - Wikipedia search entry for TLS 1.3. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=TLS%201.3 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 8446: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446 - Published standard/RFC for TLS 1.3. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] TLS 1.3: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DTLS Connection ID
items.text: Protocol : DTLS Connection ID (DTLS 连接 ID). RFC 9146 states the job in §1: "This document defines an extension to DTLS 1.2 to add a Connection ID (CID) to the DTLS record layer." Negotiation uses the extension defined in §3, "enum { connection_id(54), (65535) } ExtensionType;", and §4 marks the records: "connections that have negotiated this extension use a distinguished record type tls12_cid(25)." with the real content type moved inside the ciphertext. The reason is that records pick associations by 5-tuple: the abstract says "selecting a security association of an incoming DTLS record is accomplished with the help of the 5-tuple", and §1 says "In DTLS as specified in RFC 6347, the IP address and port of the peer are used to identify the DTLS association." and "Unfortunately, in some cases, such as NAT rebinding, these values are insufficient." naming the worst-affected setting — "This is a particular issue in the Internet of Things when devices enter extended sleep periods to increase their battery lifetime." Following TLS 1.3 practice, the record type is encrypted and padding is provided. Direction is expressed with zero length: §3 states "A zero-length CID value indicates that the client is prepared to send using a CID but does not wish the server to use one when sending." and plaintext records are untouched — §4 "Plaintext records are not impacted by this extension." Address updates are gated: on receiving a record from a different source address §6 says "the receiver MUST NOT replace the address it uses for sending records to its peer with the source address specified in the received datagram" unless the datagram verified cryptographically, is newer than the latest known, and there is a way to confirm the new address is reachable. Three limits. There is no mid-session rotation — §3: "There is no dedicated “CID update” message that allows new CIDs to be established mid-session". §8 states the privacy cost: "The CID replaces the previously used 5-tuple and, as such, introduces an identifier that remains persistent during the lifetime of a DTLS connection." and recommends DTLS 1.3 for multihoming — "The lack of a CID update mechanism in DTLS 1.2 makes this extension unsuitable for mobility scenarios where correlation must be considered." §9 admits the reflection surface: a peer cannot tell a genuine address update from a malicious one. RFC 9146 is signed by E. Rescorla (Ed., Mozilla), H. Tschofenig (Ed., Arm Limited), T. Fossati and A. Kraus (Bosch.IO GmbH), published March 2022 as a Standards Track document with “Updates: 6347” in the header. §4 notes the division of labour with its successor: "[DTLS13] specifies how to carry the CID in DTLS 1.3." — this document covers only the DTLS 1.2 record-layer change. - Wikipedia search entry for DTLS 连接 ID. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DTLS%20%E8%BF%9E%E6%8E%A5%20ID - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] DTLS Connection ID: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: TLS GREasing Extensibility
items.text: Protocol : TLS GREasing Extensibility (TLS GREasing 扩展性保活). The mechanism reserves values that can never be negotiated so peers advertise them at random: §1 "To avoid this problem, this document reserves some currently unused values for TLS implementations to advertise at random." and explains that tolerant peers ignore them while intolerant ones fail fast — "Peers that do not tolerate unknown values will fail to interoperate, revealing the mistake before it is widespread." §2 lists paired repeated-byte values (0x0A0A 0x1A1A 0x2A2A and so on) for extensions, named groups, signature algorithms and versions, while PskKeyExchangeModes get a separate single-byte set: "The following values are reserved as GREASE values for PskKeyExchangeModes: 0x0B 0x2A 0x49 0x68 0x87 0xA6 0xC5 0xE4". What is being prevented is extensibility rust. §1 explains the dependency: "The responding side must ignore unknown values so that new capabilities may be introduced to the ecosystem while maintaining interoperability." but bugs spread silently: "However, bugs may cause an implementation to reject unknown values." and the consequence is that "updated peers will discover that the metaphorical joint in the protocol has rusted shut and the new values cannot be deployed without interoperability failures." Hence the name: "this technique is called “GREASE” (Generate Random Extensions And Sustain Extensibility)". Clients insert GREASE values into the ClientHello (§3.1 lists MAY items for cipher suites, extensions, named groups, signature algorithms, versions, PSK modes and ALPN); servers do the equivalent in CertificateRequest and NewSessionTicket (§4.1). §5 sets the sending policy: "Implementations advertising GREASE values SHOULD select them at random." so that tolerance is not limited to one value, while requiring "Implementations MUST honor protocol specifications when sending GREASE values." and weighing diversity against determinism. The limits and risks are in the document. A negotiated GREASE value is fatal: "Clients MUST reject GREASE values when negotiated by the server." and "Servers MUST reject GREASE values when negotiated by the client." §7 notes the values are never negotiated, so "GREASE values cannot be negotiated, so they do not directly impact the security of TLS connections." but retrying without them weakens the defence — "Implementations SHOULD NOT retry with GREASE disabled on connection failure." — and non-random selection creates a fingerprinting risk. RFC 8701 is signed by D. Benjamin (Google LLC), published January 2020 with Category: Informational. §2 records the side effect of reserving the values: "The values allocated above are thus no longer available for use as TLS or DTLS [RFC6347] version numbers." and the allocation is deliberately thin — "These values were allocated sparsely to discourage server implementations from conditioning on them." - Wikipedia search entry for TLS GREasing 扩展性保活. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=TLS%20GREasing%20%E6%89%A9%E5%B1%95%E6%80%A7%E4%BF%9D%E6%B4%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] TLS GREasing Extensibility: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
