items.title: Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes
items.text: Protocol : Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes (PQ/T 混合方案术语). The citable authority here is the terminology document RFC 9794, which defines the hybrid construction: §4 "PQ/T hybrid protocol: A protocol that uses two or more component algorithms providing the same cryptographic functionality, where at least one is a post-quantum algorithm and at least one is a traditional algorithm." the same section defines the composite form whose fields and message flow match a single-algorithm version. §1 sets out why both algorithm classes are used and fixes the meaning of "post-quantum" and "traditional". Hybridisation is justified because post-quantum algorithms can break too: §2 warns "it should not be assumed that an algorithm will not be compromised just because it is designed to provide post-quantum cryptography." §1 records the harvest-now threat: "Data encrypted today (in 2025) with an algorithm vulnerable to a quantum computer can be stored for decryption by a future attacker with a CRQC." §5 defines the hybrid property: it holds as long as at least one component algorithm providing that function remains secure. The vocabulary separates two deployment paths: §4 uses "PQ/T hybrid protocol with composite key establishment" for a hybrid KEM that leaves protocol fields and message flow unchanged, and the composite-data-authentication form for exposing PQ and traditional signatures through a single interface. §5 gives selection advice: hybrid interoperability for interworking, implementation-security schemes “will likely require” hybrid confidentiality or authentication, and the document warns "It is not possible for one PQ/T hybrid scheme or PQ/T hybrid protocol to achieve all of the properties in this section." Two limits. A protocol offering both services need not provide both hybrid properties: §5 states "PQ/T hybrid protocols that offer both confidentiality and authentication do not necessarily offer both hybrid confidentiality and hybrid authentication." giving the single-algorithm X.509 certificate example. And a hybrid certificate is not by itself hybrid identity authentication: §6 says "The use of a PQ/T hybrid certificate does not necessarily achieve hybrid authentication of the identity of the sender; this is determined by properties of the chain of trust." The source is corrected after verification: the inventory cited RFC 9794(2025) under a post-quantum TLS handshake framing, but RFC 9794 is the June 2025 Informational terminology document (F. Driscoll and M. Parsons, UK National Cyber Security Centre; B. Hale, Naval Postgraduate School) that defines terms and specifies no TLS handshake. §1 also records the naming debate — some prefer “quantum-resistant” or “quantum-safe”, others worry those labels mislead once an algorithm falls, so the document uses “post-quantum”. As of this verification the corpus contains no Standards Track post-quantum TLS protocol RFC; hybrid deployment is still terminology-and-draft territory. - Wikipedia search entry for PQ/T 混合方案术语. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=PQ%2FT%20%E6%B7%B7%E5%90%88%E6%96%B9%E6%A1%88%E6%9C%AF%E8%AF%AD - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] Terminology for Post-Quantum Traditional Hybrid Schemes: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC)
items.text: Algorithm : Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC 密钥化哈希认证码). The retained RFC 2104 text gives the definition in the Abstract: "This document describes HMAC, a mechanism for message authentication using cryptographic hash functions." The next sentence fixes its relation to a key and a hash: "HMAC can be used with any iterative cryptographic hash function, e.g., MD5, SHA-1, in combination with a secret shared key." both sitting in the front Abstract block (reported as front in this copy). The skeleton is exactly this: an iterative hash function used as the building block together with a shared secret key to produce a message authentication code; the strength is attributed by the same paragraph, "The cryptographic strength of HMAC depends on the properties of the underlying hash function." Section 2 writes the construction out as seven executable steps. It first defines the two fixed strings: "ipad = the byte 0x36 repeated B times" and "opad = the byte 0x5C repeated B times." (each on its own printed line, with 0x5C capitalised as the source prints it), then gives the whole expression on one line, "H(K XOR opad, H(K XOR ipad, text))". The numbered steps quoted are "(1) append zeros to the end of K to create a B byte string", "(4) apply H to the stream generated in step (3)", "(5) XOR (bitwise exclusive-OR) the B byte string computed in" (the line ends there - "step (1) with opad" is on the next line, so it is quoted only to the line end) and "(7) apply H to the stream generated in step (6) and output". The long-key rule in the same section reads "Applications that use keys longer…than B bytes will first hash the key using H and then use the…resultant L byte string as the actual key to HMAC." - the sentence is split across three hard-wrapped lines, quoted here segment by segment, each ellipsis marking one of those line breaks. Worked example (Test Case 2, reproduced as hmac-calc-construction-steps): the key 4a656665 is zero-padded to a 64-byte block key by step (1); step (2) XOR with ipad yields a string beginning 7c535053 with the remaining 60 bytes all 36; step (5) XOR with opad yields a string beginning 16393a39 with the remaining 60 bytes all 5c; the step (4) inner digest is 32 bytes long; the step (7) output is 5bdcc146bf60754e6a042426089575c75a003f089d2739839dec58b964ec3843, which is what the retained RFC 4231 prints at §4.3 lines 203-204. The intermediates are computed by this batch from the steps quoted above - the retained source prints only the final value. Section 1 states the construction stance: "This document specifies HMAC using a generic cryptographic hash function (denoted by H)." followed immediately by the instantiation rule "Specific instantiations of HMAC need to define a particular hash function." the file defining a hash-agnostic generic construction and the choice of hash deferred to instantiation. That is why HMAC is built as a nesting that can swap the underlying hash: hash functions that already run well in software and are widely available can be reused unchanged. The abstract sentence also pushes strength down to the hash: "The cryptographic strength of HMAC depends on the properties of the underlying hash function." (front). The motive is thus to reuse existing hashes and keep their performance while resting security on ordinary assumptions about H. The usage conditions sit in the numbered sections, at must level for keys and recommend level for output. Section 3 states the key rule in plain imperatival prose: "Keys need to be chosen at random (or using a cryptographically strong pseudo-random generator seeded with a random seed), and periodically refreshed." keys must be random and refreshed periodically. Section 5 puts truncation at recommend level: "We recommend that the output length t be not less than half the length of the hash output (to match the birthday attack bound) and not less than 80 bits" the truncated length t advised to be at least half the hash output and at least 80 bits. So the use is to run HMAC over one chosen hash for message authentication, with these two grades of guidance for key management and output truncation; this dossier quotes the retained RFC 2104 text, not the row's primary citation FIPS 198-1. Section 4.1 of the retained RFC 4231 states the standing of these vectors: "The test vectors in this document have been cross-verified by three" followed by "independent implementations." - one sentence broken by a hard line wrap, so it is quoted in two spans. Their form is stated by "Keys, data, and digests are provided in hex." Test Cases 1 to 7 (§4.2-§4.8) each print one line saying what the case covers: "Test with a key shorter than the length of the HMAC output.", a combined key-plus-data length above 64 bytes ("Test with a combined length of key and data that is larger than 64" then "bytes (= block-size of SHA-224 and SHA-256)."), output truncation ("Test with a truncation of output to 128 bits."), and a key above 128 bytes ("Test with a key larger than 128 bytes (= block-size of SHA-384 and" then "SHA-512)."). Section 3.2 prints "element may specify the truncated length of the scheme output." - the truncated length is carried by that element. The expected values this entry reproduces are exactly the ones printed there. Every key, datum and digest of the seven cases is locatable value by value: this batch stores what was read from the retained text together with its line numbers in hmac-vectors.json - the extractor reads the file that build/corpora.json registers for the source id rfc4231 - and its artefacts record two layout facts: Test Case 3 prints the field label Key without the equals sign the other six cases carry, and Test Case 5 prints 16-byte digests because that case truncates the output to 128 bits. The reproduction is recorded in calculations: all 28 printed digests are reproduced by a construction written from the §2 steps, and each one also agrees with Node.js own implementation. What this batch reproduces: all 28 printed digests - 7 test cases times 4 hash variants - are reproduced by an implementation written from the §2 steps (hmac-calc-rfc4231-vectors); the 16-byte outputs of Test Case 5 are checked against the truncation rule (hmac-calc-truncation-rule); the 131-byte keys of Test Cases 6 and 7 take the H(K) branch and give the same result as using H(K) as the key itself (hmac-calc-longkey-rule); and a further 140 length combinations agree with the implementation Node.js ships (hmac-calc-oracle-agreement). The agreements and what they assert are recorded in this dossier s calculations and verification-results files. The limits are stated in two places. Section 1 records the state of the underlying hash: "MD5 has been recently shown to be vulnerable to collision search attacks [Dobb]." and bounds the impact: "This attack and other currently known weaknesses of MD5 do not compromise the use of MD5 within HMAC as specified in this document (see [Dobb]); however, SHA-1 appears to be a cryptographically stronger function." the known MD5 collisions did not, at the time of writing, compromise MD5 inside HMAC, yet SHA-1 is described as stronger. Section 6 gives the theoretical strongest attack, in the source followed by the ASCII-quoted term birthday attack, so it is quoted only up to H: "The strongest attack known against HMAC is based on the frequency of collisions for the hash function H" the attack surface reduced to the collision frequency of the chosen H. Together: HMAC's security moves with the collision resistance of the selected hash, and MD5 is the named weak component. Read as printed, the front matter gives the title line HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication, the author line Krawczyk, Bellare and Canetti, and the header Request for Comments: 2104 with Category: Informational (header lines stated outside the quotes). Its Status of This Memo paragraph reads: "This memo provides information for the Internet community." "This memo does not specify an Internet standard of any kind." "Distribution of this memo is unlimited." an informational document that specifies no Internet standard. The edition disagreement is recorded here: this retained file's date line prints February 1997, while the catalog row prints that citation title as RFC 2104(1999) and lists FIPS 198-1 (2008) as its primary source; every assertion in this dossier is bound to the retained RFC 2104 text and takes the date from what it prints. - Wikipedia search entry for HMAC 密钥化哈希认证码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=HMAC%20%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%8C%96%E5%93%88%E5%B8%8C%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Worked example Take one published or standard test vector, record the input, the ordered steps and the byte-exact output, then compare with an independent implementation. Where no citable numeric vector is available, the entry records only structural steps and does not invent an output.

items.title: ML-KEM (Kyber) Module-Lattice Key-Encapsulation Mechanism
items.text: Algorithm : Kyber;Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (Kyber / ML-KEM 封装机制). The retained FIPS 203 text gives the scheme class and mechanism in the Abstract: "A key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM) is a set of algorithms that, under certain conditions, can be used by two parties to establish a shared secret key over a public channel." it names the specific KEM the standard sets: "This standard specifies a key-encapsulation mechanism called ML-KEM." and states its security reduction: "The security of ML-KEM is related to the computational difficulty of the Module Learning with Errors problem." The principle is therefore that ML-KEM is a key-encapsulation mechanism built on the hardness of the Module Learning With Errors (MLWE) problem, with the two parties reaching one shared secret by encapsulating and decapsulating over a public channel. Section 3.1 carries a near-identical definition sentence; the abstract is taken as the basis here. Section 1.1 gives the reason for choosing it over the older key-establishment schemes: "The key establishment schemes specified in SP 800-56A and SP 800-56B are vulnerable to attacks that use sufficiently-capable quantum computers." the factorization and discrete-log based schemes fall to a strong enough quantum computer. The abstract then places ML-KEM: "At present, ML-KEM is believed to be secure, even against adversaries who possess a quantum computer." Read together these are why the mechanism exists — to fill the gap that discrete-log key exchange leaves under quantum computing. The wording is believed, and the file also states in the announcement clause that it will formally reevaluate every five years, so this quantum resistance is a present-day assessment, not a proven fact, and is not escalated into an unconditional guarantee. The use is bounded by the parameter sets and by the achieved security notion. The abstract lists three: "This standard specifies three parameter sets for ML-KEM. In order of increasing security strength and decreasing performance, these are ML-KEM-512, ML-KEM-768, and ML-KEM-1024." Section 3.2 states the attack model reached after the FO transform: "As a result, ML-KEM is believed to satisfy so-called IND-CCA2 security" that is, chosen-ciphertext security. Together the two sentences give the picture: ML-KEM trades security against performance across the 512/768/1024 tiers and is used as a key-encapsulation whose shared secret stays hidden from unauthorised parties under a CCA2 model. The strength ordering is a descriptive ranking, and elsewhere (§1.1) the file says all three sets are approved to protect sensitive non-classified federal communications; the wording remains believed, so no proven claim is made. The limits fall on the internal component and on implementation constraints. Section 3.2 states plainly that the component may not be used alone: "The scheme K-PKE is not IND-CCA2-secure and shall not be used as a stand-alone scheme (see Section 3.3)." Section 3.3 repeats the prohibition with shall not: "The public-key encryption scheme K-PKE described in Section 5 shall not be used as a stand-alone cryptographic scheme." both must-level bans that keep the underlying plaintext PKE (K-PKE) out of stand-alone use — it is a subroutine of ML-KEM only. A further limit is assessment rather than a ban: the quantum resistance is stated as believed (see the why claim), and the file itself says conformance to the standard does not ensure a secure implementation, leaving overall module security to the implementer. This dossier reports both kinds of limit from the retained text and does not assert that ML-KEM has been broken. The relation between the standard and the candidate is stated plainly in the retained text. Section 1.1: "ML-KEM is derived from the round-three version of the CRYSTALS-KYBER KEM [4], a submission in the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization project." and §1.2 fixes the name: "Throughout this standard, the KEM specified here will be referred to as ML-KEM, as it is based on the Module Learning With Errors assumption." The title block prints Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism Standard and the dates Published August 13, 2024 and Published: August 13, 2024 Effective: August 13, 2024, with the free-access line This publication is available free of charge from: (its DOI placed outside the quotes). The catalog row still names the algorithm by its candidate name Kyber, whereas the retained file is the finalized standard: it calls the algorithm ML-KEM and shows CRYSTALS-KYBER only as the round-three source it standardizes. That naming difference (Kyber versus ML-KEM) and the dating difference (2022 candidate material versus the 2024 finalization) are recorded here, and this dossier rests on what the file prints — ML-KEM, August 13, 2024. - Wikipedia search entry for Kyber / ML-KEM 封装机制. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Kyber%20%2F%20ML-KEM%20%E5%B0%81%E8%A3%85%E6%9C%BA%E5%88%B6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[(c,k)=\mathrm{Encaps}(pk);\qquad k'=\mathrm{Decaps}(sk,c)\] Kyber;Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SLH-DSA Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature
items.text: Algorithm : SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) stateless hash-based signature algorithm (SLH-DSA 状态哈希签名). The retained FIPS 205 text names it in the Abstract: "This standard specifies the stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm (SLH-DSA)." Section 3 gives the construction skeleton: "SLH-DSA is a stateless hash-based signature scheme that is constructed using other hash-based signature schemes as components:" and lists the two kinds — "a few-time signature scheme, forest of random subsets (FORS), and (2) a multi-time signature scheme, the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS)." The principle is that SLH-DSA composes a few-time FORS scheme and a multi-time XMSS scheme (itself built on the one-time WOTS+) into a stateless, hash-based digital signature. This dossier rests on the algorithm's own description inside the standard text and is kept distinct from the fips205 standard record, which documents the publication. Section 1.1 states how it differs from the existing signatures and why: "Unlike the algorithms specified in FIPS 186-5 [1], SLH-DSA is designed to provide resistance against attacks from a large-scale quantum computer." unlike the classical signature standard, it is designed for quantum resistance. The same paragraph gives the security premise: "The security of the stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm (SLH-DSA) relies on the presumed difficulty of finding preimages for hash functions" its safety rests on hash-preimage hardness. The abstract adds the origin: "SLH-DSA is based on SPHINCS+, which was selected for standardization as part of the NIST Post-Quantum Cryptography Standardization process." The chain of reasons is therefore that classical signatures fail under quantum computing, while a stateless scheme grounded in hash-preimage hardness and standardized from SPHINCS+ can provide quantum resistance. The wording is presumed difficulty, not a proof. The usage constraints sit in the numbered sections at distinct wording levels. Section 3.2 puts component exposure at should not: "As WOTS+, XMSS, FORS, and hypertree signature schemes are not approved for use as stand-alone signature schemes, cryptographic modules should not make interfaces to these components available to applications." the components serve only to build SLH-DSA, so modules should not expose them as application interfaces. Section 3.1 puts arithmetic at shall not: "Implementations of SLH-DSA shall not use floating-point arithmetic, as rounding errors in floating point operations may lead to incorrect results in some cases." implementations must avoid floating-point because rounding errors can give wrong results. So SLH-DSA is used as a whole signature scheme, its components not surfaced as stand-alone interfaces (should not), and its arithmetic kept off floating point (shall not). should not and shall not are not interchangeable here. The limits the retained text states are on the implementation and on the premise. Section 3.2 records the side-channel and fault exposure: "Care must be taken to protect implementations against attacks, such as side-channel attacks or fault attacks [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]." private-key secrecy is critical, so implementations must guard against side-channel and fault extraction. The premise-side limit is in the why claim: security rests on the presumed difficulty of hash-preimage finding, not on a proof reducible to a broadly accepted hard problem. The acknowledged fragility therefore comes from the implementation (side channels and faults) and the assumption (hash resistance), not from any break of SLH-DSA itself recorded in the standard. The shall-not floating-point limit in §3.1 (see the used claim) is of the same kind — it constrains correctness, not an attack outcome; the text is recorded as printed and no already broken assertion is made. Section 1.2 gives the relation to its candidate lineage. The selection is recorded: "After three rounds of evaluation and analysis, NIST selected the first four algorithms for standardization." and the tie to the round-three submission: "This standard contains several minor modifications compared to Version 3 [4], which was submitted at the beginning of round three of the NIST PQC Standardization process." with the renaming stated: "Throughout this standard, SPHINCS+ will be referred to as SLH-DSA for stateless hash-based digital signature algorithm." The title block prints Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Standard and Published: August 13, 2024 Effective: August 13, 2024. So the algorithm this dossier describes is the finalized standard form of SPHINCS+, named SLH-DSA, and it is kept separate from the fips205 record that documents the publication; neither is registered as an alias of the other. - Wikipedia search entry for SLH-DSA 状态哈希签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SLH-DSA%20%E7%8A%B6%E6%80%81%E5%93%88%E5%B8%8C%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] SLH-DSA (SPHINCS+) stateless hash-based signature algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)
items.text: Algorithm : Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA Edwards 曲线签名). The retained text opens §1 with the definition: "The Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) is a variant of Schnorr's signature system with (possibly twisted) Edwards curves." EdDSA is therefore a Schnorr signature over (possibly twisted) Edwards curves. §3 quantifies it immediately: "EdDSA is a digital signature system with 11 parameters." Together the two sentences give the skeleton of the entry: signature scheme = Schnorr structure + Edwards curve + a set of parameters to be instantiated, with the generic parameter choice itself flagged as "not intended to be implemented directly", so deployment uses concrete parameter sets such as Ed25519 and Ed448. The numbered advantages in §1 make the motive explicit. On randomness: "The use of a unique random number for each signature is not required;" no fresh unique random value is demanded per signature. On side channels: "It is more resilient to side-channel attacks;" §8.2 gives the cause, "EdDSA signatures are deterministic." the nonce being derived from key and message rather than drawn at random. Read together these three sentences are the reason for choosing EdDSA: they remove the high-risk dependency on a good random number for every signature, and, via the unified formulas, reduce sensitivity to randomness and to branching. §4 splits the variants by the prehash parameter (that word carries ASCII quotes in the source and is not quoted here): "This may be the identity function, resulting in an algorithm called PureEdDSA, or a collision-resistant hash function such as SHA-512, resulting in an algorithm called HashEdDSA." The next sentence pins the instances this file specifies: "This document specifies parameters resulting in the HashEdDSA variants Ed25519ph and Ed448ph and the PureEdDSA variants Ed25519 and Ed448." The use is thus these five parameterizations — PureEdDSA Ed25519 and Ed448, HashEdDSA Ed25519ph and Ed448ph, plus the contextualized Ed25519ctx. The wording is may, so choosing identity versus a collision-resistant hash is the implementer's trade-off between collision resilience and a single-pass signing interface, not a list this document closes. The limits sit at three levels. §8.2 names the risk determinism avoids: "This protects against attacks arising from signing with bad randomness; the effects of which can, depending on the algorithm, range up to full private key compromise." bad randomness could compromise the private key outright — a failure mode that is designed out rather than an attack on EdDSA itself. §8.4 handles malleability: "Ed25519 and Ed448 signatures are not malleable due to the verification check that decoded S is smaller than l." the anti-malleability coming from that range check. §1 states the root boundary: "A sufficiently large quantum computer would be able to break both." a large quantum computer breaks both Ed25519 and Ed448, a vulnerability §8.5 treats as essentially the same for both. So: determinism guards against randomness misuse, the range check blocks malleability, and quantum computing is the acknowledged pre-condition of failure. The front matter prints both identity and strength. The title line reads Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA), the author line Josefsson and Liusvaara, the date line January 2017, and the header carries Request for Comments: 8032 and Category: Informational (these header lines are stated outside the quotes). Its status statements are, as printed: "This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes." followed by the IRTF characterization "Documents approved for publication by the IRSG are not a candidate for any level of Internet Standard; see Section 2 of RFC 7841." both sitting in the Abstract/Status block. The strength is therefore informational, not standards-track, so the sentences above are read as descriptions of the scheme and no must-level Internet Standard obligation is drawn from RFC 8032. - Wikipedia search entry for EdDSA Edwards 曲线签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EdDSA%20%20Edwards%20%E6%9B%B2%E7%BA%BF%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Finite Field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (FFDHE)
items.text: Algorithm : Finite Field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (FFDHE 有限域 DH). The opening sentence of §1 gives the mechanism being extended: "Traditional TLS [RFC5246] offers a Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral (DHE) key exchange mode that provides forward secrecy for the connection." FFDHE is Diffie-Hellman performed over a finite field in ephemeral mode, giving the connection forward secrecy. Section 1.2 assigns the vocabulary (that sentence ASCII-quotes DHE and FFDHE and is not quoted here), so the principle rests on the sentence above: each party takes an ephemeral private key, computes a shared secret over agreed finite-field group parameters, and that ephemerality is what yields forward secrecy. The abstract gives the gap: "Traditional finite-field-based Diffie-Hellman (DH) key exchange during the Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake suffers from a number of security, interoperability, and efficiency shortcomings." and lays the root cause on unclear parameters: "These shortcomings arise from lack of clarity about which DH group parameters TLS servers should offer and clients should accept." Section 2 explains why the defined groups are built the way they are, deriving the modulus from the base of the natural logarithm so its middle bits carry no secretly chosen structure: "The goal is to guarantee that the bits in the middle of the modulus are effectively random, while avoiding any suspicion that the primes have secretly been selected to be weak according to some secret criteria." The motive is therefore twofold: turn which groups to offer and accept into negotiable named groups, and give the group parameters a checkable nothing-up-my-sleeve origin. The actions and their strengths sit in three sections at different wording levels. The extension-sending in §2 is MAY: "This extension MAY be sent by the client when either FFDHE or ECDHE cipher suites are listed." The server rule in §4 is MUST NOT: "A TLS server MUST NOT select a named FFDHE group that was not offered by a compatible client." The strength guidance in §8.2 is should: "TLS implementations using FFDHE key exchange should consider the strength of the group they negotiate." Together these give the picture of use: a client may advertise the named FFDHE groups it is willing to negotiate via the Supported Groups extension, the server may only pick from that list, and implementers should weigh group strength against their confidentiality needs. may, MUST NOT and should are not interchangeable here and are recorded at their printed levels. There are three limits. Section 8.3 first draws the scope (a boundary, not a weakness): "Note that this document specifically targets only finite field Diffie-Hellman ephemeral key exchange mechanisms." and then a relative shortfall: "Measured by computational cost to the TLS peers, ECDHE appears today to offer a much stronger key exchange mechanism than FFDHE." by computational cost, ECDHE is today stronger than FFDHE. Section 8.4 records future decay: "Advances in hardware or in finite field cryptanalysis may cause some of the negotiated groups to not provide the desired security margins" hardware or cryptanalysis may leave some groups short, and "Revisions of this document should mark known weak groups as explicitly deprecated for use in TLS" known-weak groups are to be marked deprecated by a future revision. So the acknowledged fragility is a per-bit efficiency disadvantage against ECDHE and group value eroding over time, with the deprecation decision left to a should-level revision. The front matter prints identity and strength: the title line Negotiated Finite Field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral Parameters for Transport Layer Security (TLS), the author line D. Gillmor, and the header Request for Comments: 7919, Category: Standards Track, Updates: 2246, 4346, 4492, 5246, and the date August 2016 (header lines stated outside the quotes). The first Status sentence is "This is an Internet Standards Track document." and the last abstract sentence gives the update relation: "This document updates TLS versions 1.0 (RFC 2246), 1.1 (RFC 4346), and 1.2 (RFC 5246), as well as the TLS Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) extensions (RFC 4492)." both reported inside the Abstract/Status block. On this the file is standards-track and explicitly updates the TLS and ECC-extension documents named there. - Wikipedia search entry for FFDHE 有限域 DH. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=FFDHE%20%E6%9C%89%E9%99%90%E5%9F%9F%20DH - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[K=g^{ab}\bmod p\quad\text{或}\quad K=[ab]G\] Finite Field Diffie-Hellman Ephemeral: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Secure Hash Standard
items.text: Standard : Secure Hash Standard (安全散列标准). The masthead announces "Announcing the SECURE HASH STANDARD" and clause 1 fixes name and number together: "1. Name of Standard: Secure Hash Standard (SHS) (FIPS PUB 180-4)." The abstract gives the self-definition: "This standard specifies hash algorithms that can be used to generate digests of messages." followed by the use: "The digests are used to detect whether messages have been changed since the digests were generated." Clause 3 names the algorithms and their object: "3. Explanation: This Standard specifies secure hash algorithms - SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 - for computing a condensed representation of electronic data (message)." and bounds the output: "The message digests range in length from 160 to 512 bits, depending on the algorithm." What is specified is the computation of the digests by these seven algorithms; judging strength is left to other documents. The reason is stated in clause 3, where the two infeasibilities define the term: "The hash algorithms specified in this Standard are called secure because, for a given algorithm, it is computationally infeasible 1) to find a message that corresponds to a given message digest, or 2) to find two different messages that produce the same message digest." The consequence follows at once: "This will result in a verification failure when the secure hash algorithm is used with a digital signature algorithm or a keyed-hash message authentication algorithm." Clause 1 supplies the structural premise: "All of the algorithms are iterative, one-way hash functions that can process a message to produce a condensed representation called a message digest." Read together, a digest works as an integrity test only because finding the preimage and finding a collision are both infeasible, which is exactly what this document means by secure. The application duties are in the applicability and implementation clauses. Clause 6 uses must for federal use: "Either this Standard or Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 202 must be implemented wherever a secure hash algorithm is required for Federal applications, including as a component within other cryptographic algorithms and protocols." Clause 8 first leaves the carrier open: "8. Implementations: The secure hash algorithms specified herein may be implemented in software, firmware, hardware or any combination thereof." then sets the gate: "Only algorithm implementations that are validated by NIST will be considered as complying with this standard." The two work at different levels: one is a must-level requirement to implement either this Standard or FIPS 202 wherever federal use demands a secure hash, the other makes compliance itself conditional on validation by NIST. Three limits are the document speaking about itself. Clause 12 denies that conformance is security: "While it is the intent of this Standard to specify general security requirements for generating a message digest, conformance to this Standard does not assure that a particular implementation is secure." and assigns the judgement: "The responsible authority in each agency or department shall assure that an overall implementation provides an acceptable level of security." Strength is handed to other documents: "The algorithms differ most significantly in the security strengths that are provided for the data being hashed." with the destination named: "The security strengths of these hash functions and the system as a whole when each of them is used with other cryptographic algorithms, such as digital signature algorithms and keyed-hash message authentication codes, can be found in [SP 800-57] and [SP 800-107]." Clause 13 closes the exemption route: "The Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) does not allow for waivers to a FIPS that is made mandatory by the Secretary of Commerce." The three operate at different levels: conformance covers how digests are produced, the strength figures live in two other publications, and a FIPS made mandatory admits no waiver. The two masthead lines read in sequence "Federal Information Processing Standards Publication 180-4 August 2015", so this copy carries the date line August 2015; below it the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.FIPS.180-4. The foreword is signed "Charles H. Romine, Director Information Technology Laboratory"; clause 4 states the approving authority: "4. Approving Authority: Secretary of Commerce." and the supersession is the last sentence of clause 3: "This Standard supersedes FIPS 180-3 [FIPS 180-3]." The document has no author line; the names printed on it are the Secretary of Commerce, the NIST Director (Under Secretary for Standards and Technology) and the Director of the Information Technology Laboratory, and this retained copy records only the August 2015 date line and the superseded FIPS 180-3, not a first-publication date for 180-4 itself. - Wikipedia search entry for 安全散列标准. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 180-4: Secure Hash Standard. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/final - Published standard/RFC for 安全散列标准. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Secure Hash Standard: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)
items.text: Algorithm : HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation (HKDF 基于 HMAC 的密钥派生). The defining sentence is in the abstract: "This document specifies a simple Hashed Message Authentication Code (HMAC)-based key derivation function (HKDF), which can be used as a building block in various protocols and applications." The same block gives the orientation: "The key derivation function (KDF) is intended to support a wide range of applications and requirements, and is conservative in its use of cryptographic hash functions." The shape is stated in §1: HKDF follows the extract-then-expand paradigm, and the KDF "logically consists of two modules." What is specified is a two-stage derivation, not a key-establishment protocol. The abstract places HKDF as a building block: what is specified is the derivation function itself, the choice of hash is left to the caller, and the use of that hash is deliberately conservative; the two-stage structure is exactly the difference from specifications that only cover expansion. Section 1 opens with the role of a KDF: "A key derivation function (KDF) is a basic and essential component of cryptographic systems." and "Its goal is to take some source of initial keying material and derive from it one or more cryptographically strong secret keys." The risk sits in the input: "In many applications, the input keying material is not necessarily distributed uniformly, and the attacker may have some partial knowledge about it (for example, a Diffie-Hellman value computed by a key exchange protocol) or even partial control of it (as in some entropy-gathering applications)." Hence the purpose of the first stage is to concentrate, in the words of §1, "the possibly dispersed entropy of the input keying material into a short, but cryptographically strong, pseudorandom key". The criticism of earlier documents is in the same section: "either only consider the second stage (expanding a pseudorandom key), or do not explicitly differentiate between" the extract and expand stages, "often resulting in design shortcomings." These passages make one case: a KDF is an essential component, yet its input may be non-uniform and partly known or even partly controlled by an attacker, so a stage is needed to concentrate dispersed entropy; and since the earlier specifications either only expand or do not separate the stages, that is the position this document takes up. Each stage is defined in its own numbered clause: §2.2 gives "HKDF-Extract(salt, IKM) - PRK", computed as "PRK = HMAC-Hash(salt, IKM)", and §2.3 gives "HKDF-Expand(PRK, info, L) - OKM". The obligations attach to the parameters: the salt is an "optional salt value (a non-secret random value); if not provided, it is set to a string of HashLen zeros.", the info is "optional context and application specific information (can be a zero-length string)", and §3.2 states its purpose: "Its main objective is to bind the derived key material to application- and context-specific information." Salt is optional but not to be dropped: §3.1 says "HKDF is defined to operate with and without random salt." yet adds that "designers of applications are therefore encouraged to provide salt values to HKDF if such values can be obtained by the application." The expansion output is also bounded, in the words of §2.3: "length of output keying material in octets (<= 255 HashLen)". The first limit is standing: the front matter states "This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.", the masthead Category is Informational, and §1 adds that "It is not intended as a call to change existing protocols and does not change or update existing specifications using this KDF." The second is capability: §4 concedes that HKDF does not suit every application and names low-entropy input as one significant example — "The extract step in HKDF can concentrate existing entropy but cannot amplify entropy." and "HKDF naturally accommodates the use of salt; however, a slowing down mechanism is not part of this specification." — and redirects password users elsewhere: "Applications interested in a password-based KDF should consider whether, for example, [PKCS5] meets their needs better than HKDF." The third is the strength of the claim: §5 warns that "This analysis, however, does not imply the absolute security of any scheme, and it depends heavily on the strength of the underlying hash function and on modeling choices." and that "An exposition of all of these aspects is beyond the scope of this document." The masthead, read line by line, gives "Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) H. Krawczyk", "Request for Comments: 5869 IBM Research" and "Category: Informational P. Eronen", dated May 2010, titled "HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation Function (HKDF)" and under "Copyright (c) 2010 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors." Nothing in the document claims to obsolete or update another RFC. Section 6 records where the review and the vectors came from: "The authors would like to thank members of the CFRG (Crypto Forum Research Group) list for their useful comments, and to Dan Harkins for providing test vectors." The front matter therefore gives the number, both authors with their organizations, the date May 2010, the Informational category and the ISSN line; the document carries no Obsoletes or Updates marker, and the source of the review comments and the test vectors is recorded in §6. - Wikipedia search entry for HKDF 基于 HMAC 的密钥派生. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=HKDF%20%E5%9F%BA%E4%BA%8E%20HMAC%20%E7%9A%84%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E6%B4%BE%E7%94%9F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] HMAC-based Extract-and-Expand Key Derivation: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: MASQUE CONNECT-IP
items.text: Protocol : MASQUE Proxying IP over HTTP (MASQUE CONNECT-IP). The self-description comes in three sentences: "This document describes how to proxy IP packets in HTTP.", "This protocol is similar to UDP proxying in HTTP but allows transmitting arbitrary IP packets.", and "More specifically, this document defines a protocol that allows an HTTP client to create an IP tunnel through an HTTP server that acts as an IP proxy." The granularity rises from datagrams to IP packets. It closes the generality gap left by CONNECT-UDP: the abstract says the protocol "allows transmitting arbitrary IP packets", so protocol families beyond UDP can be carried. The same block states the relationship to the base document: "This document updates RFC 9298." The use cases are listed in §1: "This can be used for various use cases, such as remote access VPN, site-to-site VPN, secure point-to-point communication, or general-purpose packet tunnelling." The abstract frames it as proxying IP through an HTTP server, and §1 places it in the same family: "IP proxying operates similarly to UDP proxying [CONNECT-UDP]". A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The document specifies how IP packets are proxied and leaves deployment duty to the operator: §11 states a recommendation-level requirement — "HTTP servers that support IP proxying SHOULD restrict its use to authenticated users" — and §4.6 supplies the means to narrow a request to a specific IP prefix or IP protocol. What a proxy ought to permit is therefore carried by SHOULD-level configuration plus scope limiting, not by a hard rule in this specification. The masthead names the editor and dates the file: T. Pauly, Ed. (Apple Inc.) with D. Schinazi, A. Chernyakhovsky, M. Kühlewind and M. Westerlund, October 2023, Standards Track, marked "Updates: 9298", under the 2023 IETF Trust copyright line. - Wikipedia search entry for MASQUE CONNECT-IP. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=MASQUE%20CONNECT-IP - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 9484: Proxying IP in HTTP. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9484 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] MASQUE Proxying IP over HTTP: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: MASQUE CONNECT-UDP
items.text: Protocol : MASQUE Proxying UDP over HTTP (MASQUE CONNECT-UDP). The defining sentence sits in the abstract: "This document describes how to proxy UDP in HTTP, similar to how the HTTP CONNECT method allows proxying TCP in HTTP." — quoted exactly as "This document describes how to proxy UDP in HTTP, similar to how the HTTP CONNECT method allows proxying TCP in HTTP." — and it is immediately narrowed: "More specifically, this document defines a protocol that allows an HTTP client to create a tunnel for UDP communications through an HTTP server that acts as a proxy." The subject is a UDP tunnel carried by HTTP, not a new transport. The gap is stated in the abstract: "This document describes how to proxy UDP in HTTP, similar to how the HTTP CONNECT method allows proxying TCP in HTTP." Clause 1 shows the carriage is not tied to one HTTP version — "This protocol supports all existing versions of HTTP by using HTTP Datagrams", with Extended CONNECT for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 and Upgrade for HTTP/1.x. The status statement in the front matter records the consensus provenance: "This document is a product of the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF). It represents the consensus of the IETF community." The usage shape is a client building a UDP tunnel through a proxying server: the abstract says "this document defines a protocol that allows an HTTP client to create a tunnel for UDP communications through an HTTP server that acts as a proxy." From §3 onward the document gives the protocol and message formats, while the safety of the carried content is left to the upper layer — §1 expects that "UDP tunnels are commonly used to create an end-to-end virtual connection, which can then be secured using QUIC [QUIC] or another protocol running over UDP." The first limit is that only the tunnel is specified: whether the forwarded payload is confidential depends on the protocol run above UDP (§1), and this document adds no confidentiality or integrity to the payload. The second is the abuse risk of the proxy position, handled in §7 (§9 is the References): "There are significant risks in allowing arbitrary clients to establish a tunnel to arbitrary targets, as that could allow bad actors to send traffic and have it attributed to the UDP proxy." together with the advice that "HTTP servers that support UDP proxying ought to restrict its use to authenticated users." The history sits in the masthead and copyright block: D. Schinazi (Google LLC), dated August 2022, Category Standards Track, under "Copyright (c) 2022 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors." The successor RFC 9484 (CONNECT-IP, October 2023) carries Updates: 9298 in its own masthead, making this the base of that update; this document claims no update of its own. - Wikipedia search entry for MASQUE CONNECT-UDP. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=MASQUE%20CONNECT-UDP - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - RFC 9298: Proxying UDP in HTTP. https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9298 Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] MASQUE Proxying UDP over HTTP: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: PBKDF2 Password-Based Key Derivation (PKCS #5 Version 2.1)
items.text: Algorithm : Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 (PBKDF2 口令派生). The abstract states the range: "This document provides recommendations for the implementation of password-based cryptography, covering key derivation functions, encryption schemes, message authentication schemes, and ASN.1 syntax identifying the techniques." The same block gives its origin and ownership: "This document represents a republication of PKCS 5 v2.1 from RSA Laboratories' Public-Key Cryptography Standards (PKCS) series. By publishing this RFC, change control is transferred to the IETF." Section 5 defines the function itself: "A key derivation function produces a derived key from a base key and other parameters." and pins the password case: "In a password-based key derivation function, the base key is a password, and the other parameters are a salt value and an iteration count, as outlined in Section 3." The range sentence shows more than one product inside the document: key derivation functions, encryption schemes, message authentication schemes and the ASN.1 syntax identifying them, with PBKDF2 one of only two functions in §5; the same section's definition also names the salt and the iteration count a password case requires. Section 3 names the gap: a password is not a key, "Since a password is not directly applicable as a key to any conventional cryptosystem, however, some processing of the password is required to perform cryptographic operations with it." and the risk is the small space it comes from: "Moreover, as passwords are often chosen from a relatively small space, special care is required in that processing to defend against search attacks." Section 1 says what the recommendations are for: "The recommendations are intended for general application within computer and communications systems and, as such, include a fair amount of flexibility." and names the leading case, "They are particularly intended for the protection of sensitive information such as private keys as in PKCS 8". The two sentences give one causal chain in hedged terms: passwords are often chosen from a relatively small space, so the document asks for special care in that processing, and salt plus iteration count become the two adjustable parameters of this document; §1 names the leading use case, the protection of sensitive information such as private keys. The duties fall on the parties. Section 4.1 addresses the encrypting party: "In password-based encryption, the party encrypting a message can gain assurance that these benefits are realized simply by selecting a large and sufficiently random salt when deriving an encryption key from a password." with the figure "It should be at least eight octets (64 bits) long." Section 4.2 quotes SP 800-132 on the counter: "The iteration count shall be selected as large as possible, as long as the time required to generate the key using the entered password is acceptable for the users." and "A minimum iteration count of 1,000 is recommended." Section 5 gives the choice: "Two functions are specified in this section: PBKDF1 and PBKDF2." and "PBKDF2 is recommended for new applications; PBKDF1 is included only for compatibility with existing applications and is not recommended for new applications." Section 5.2 fixes the construction: "PBKDF2 applies a pseudorandom function (see Appendix B.1 for an example) to derive keys." The four obligations sit at different levels: the generating party owns the randomness and length of the salt, though eight octets is only should-level; the counter is written as shall inside the SP 800-132 quotation, while the figure of one thousand in that same block stays recommended; PBKDF1 is kept for compatibility and PBKDF2 recommended for new applications, and the strength of PBKDF2 rides on the PRF it is built from. The first limit is standing: the front matter states "This document is not an Internet Standards Track specification; it is published for informational purposes.", the masthead Category is Informational, and it announces "This document also obsoletes RFC 2898." The second is scope: §1 excludes password-based authentication and key establishment — "Other cryptographic techniques based on passwords, such as password-based key entity authentication and key establishment protocols [BELLOV] [JABLON] [WU] are outside the scope of this document." — and refuses to advise on passwords themselves: "Guidelines for the selection of passwords are also outside the scope." The third is a ceiling on the result: §5.2 notes "However, the maximum effective search space for the derived key may be limited by the structure of the underlying pseudorandom function." Section 8 gives the general verdict: "Password-based cryptography is generally limited in the security that it can provide, particularly for methods such as those defined in this document where offline password search is possible." — salt and counter raise cost, but the password still has to be chosen and stored well. The masthead, read line by line, gives "Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) K. Moriarty, Ed.", "Request for Comments: 8018 Dell EMC", "Obsoletes: 2898 B. Kaliski", "Category: Informational Verisign" and "ISSN: 2070-1721 A. Rusch RSA January 2017": Kathleen Moriarty as editor, with Burt Kaliski and Andreas Rusch, dated January 2017, Category Informational, obsoleting RFC 2898. The copyright line reads "Copyright (c) 2017 IETF Trust and the persons identified as the document authors." Section 1 records the standing relationship to the earlier PKCS edition: "This document supersedes PKCS 5 version 2.0 [RFC2898] but includes compatible techniques." items.title: Recommendation for Applications Using Approved Hash Algorithms (SP 800-107 Rev. 1)
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for Applications Using Approved Hash Algorithms (SP 800-107 Rev. 1) (批准哈希算法的使用建议（SP 800-107）). The abstract states its subject: "This document provides security guidelines for achieving the required or desired security strengths when using cryptographic applications that employ the approved hash functions specified in Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 180-4." The affected uses follow at once: "These include functions such as digital signatures, Keyed-hash Message Authentication Codes (HMACs) and Hash-based Key Derivation Functions (Hash-based KDFs)." It governs strength matching, not the hash algorithms themselves. The quoted object is strength rather than the algorithms: the functions are designated by FIPS 180-4, and this document deals with how the listed applications reach the strength they require. The starting point is the basic step: "A hash algorithm is used to map a message of arbitrary length to a fixed-length message digest." The risk is an illusion of strength, and §4.2 gives the rule of thumb: "the expected collision resistance strength of any approved hash function is, in general, half the length of its hash value." It then records the exception that has already fallen: "The latest cryptanalytic results for SHA-1 [SHA1 Attack] indicate that it may have a collision resistance strength that is considerably less than its expected strength of 80 bits." The three sentences form the argument: compressing an arbitrary message to a fixed digest is not the problem, treating digest length as strength is. The rule of thumb is collision resistance at half the digest length, and the document hedgingly reports that SHA-1 "may have" a collision resistance considerably below its expected 80 bits — it does not state that as a settled fact. Section 5.3.2 states the implementer obligations in three sentences: "An HMAC key shall have a security strength that meets or exceeds the security strength required to protect the data over which the HMAC is computed." "The HMAC key shall be kept secret." and "HMAC keys shall be generated as specified in SP 800-133 [SP 800-133]." All three are shall-level: the strength must match the protected data, the key must stay secret, and key generation is handed to another document rather than specified here. The conformance paragraph in §2 admits that validation cannot cover everything: "Some of these requirements may be out-of-scope for CAVP and CMVP validation testing, and thus are the responsibility of entities using, implementing, installing, or configuring applications that incorporate this Recommendation." Section 1 also excludes two key-derivation documents: "these documents sufficiently address the security aspects of their use, so discussions of SP 800-56C and SP 800-108 are not included herein." And §5.2 places a dated restriction on SHA-1: "SHA-1 shall not be used in any new digital signature applications that require at least 80 bits of security strength." The three limits operate at different levels: requirements validation cannot reach become the responsibility of those who deploy and configure them, two key-derivation documents are excluded from discussion, and the SHA-1 prohibition is keyed to the use and the strength threshold. Its own masthead makes this copy "NIST Special Publication 800-107" Revision 1, titled "Recommendation for Applications Using Approved Hash Algorithms", with the author and division lines reading in sequence as "Quynh Dang Computer Security Division Information Technology Laboratory"; continuing line by line through the title block gives "Information Technology Laboratory COMPUTER SECURITY August 2012", so this copy is dated August 2012 and contains no DOI line. The acknowledgements name the single author and the reviewers: "The author, Quynh Dang of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) gratefully appreciates the contributions and comments from Elaine Barker, William E. Burr, Shu-jen Chang, Lily Chen, Donna F. Dodson, Morris Dworkin, John Kelsey, Ray Perlner, W. Timothy Polk and Andrew Regenscheid." Appendix B gives the first edition date and one revision item: "The original version of this document was published in February 2009." and "Adding and addressing the security properties of SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256." - Wikipedia search entry for 批准哈希算法的使用建议（SP 800-107）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%89%B9%E5%87%86%E5%93%88%E5%B8%8C%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95%E7%9A%84%E4%BD%BF%E7%94%A8%E5%BB%BA%E8%AE%AE%EF%BC%88SP%20800-107%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Recommendation for Applications Using Approved Hash Algorithms (SP 800-107 Rev. 1): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Recommendation for Key Derivation Using Pseudorandom Functions
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for Key Derivation Using Pseudorandom Functions (基于 PRF 的密钥派生). The mechanism is expanding one already-held key into several: "This Recommendation specifies techniques for the derivation of additional keying material from a secret key … using pseudorandom functions: HMAC, CMAC, and KMAC." The omitted clause bounds the input — "either established through a key-establishment scheme or shared through some other manner". This is a description of a withdrawn text. The rationale is key-reuse pressure, stated minimally in §1: "When a party obtains a cryptographic key, additional keys will often be needed." §3 gives the input shape — the fixed input data is "a concatenation of a Label, a separation indicator 0x00, the Context, and [L]2" — label, separator, context and output length; omitting the context is exactly how two derivations become indistinguishable. The status comes first: the banner at the head of the file states "The attached publication has been withdrawn (archived), and is provided solely for historical purposes." — the live document is SP 800-108r1-upd1 (Chen, February 2024). While this text was current, its inputs came from the three routes §2 lists: keys established under SP 800-56A and SP 800-56B, and keys previously generated. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The first limit is currency: the banner records a withdrawal date of 2 February 2024 with SP 800-108r1-upd1 as the update, so implementing from this text today means citing a withdrawn publication; the current requirements must be read in the update, whose contents are not in this corpus and are therefore not asserted here. The second limit is scope: it specifies KDF structures, not the security of the key establishment feeding them, and it does not fix the label and context values a protocol must choose. Four dates are inside the file: Appendix A states "The original version of this document was published in November 2008."; the banner page gives the supersession line "Supersedes NIST Special Publication 800-108 (October 2009)" with the Revision 1 date August 2022, and the withdrawal date 2 February 2024 naming SP 800-108r1-upd1 as the update. The author line is Lily Chen. - Wikipedia search entry for 基于 PRF 的密钥派生. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%9F%BA%E4%BA%8E%20PRF%20%E7%9A%84%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E6%B4%BE%E7%94%9F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Recommendation for Key Derivation Using Pseudorandom Functions: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Recommendation for Password-Based Key Derivation Part 1 Storage Applications (SP 800-132)
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for Password-Based Key Derivation Part 1 Storage Applications (SP 800-132) (口令基密钥派生·存储应用（SP 800-132）). The abstract states the object in one sentence: "This Recommendation specifies techniques for the derivation of master keys from passwords or passphrases to protect stored electronic data or data protection keys." The title block pins the range to storage, "Part 1: Storage Applications", and the keyword line agrees: "Password-Based Key Derivation Functions, Salt, Iteration Count, Protection of data in storage". The output is a master key, not a password used directly as a key. The words master keys and stored in those quotations fix the object and the use: the technique turns a password into a master key, and the range is data already in storage. Section 1 names the gap: passwords are not random enough, "Due to the low entropy and possibly poor randomness of those passwords, they are not suitable to be used directly as cryptographic keys." Appendix A.1 makes the attacker model concrete, an offline exhaustive search on superior hardware: "When passwords are used to generate cryptographic keys, it is assumed that an attacker is able to perform an offline search attack on the key derivation process using a system of his own choosing, which may be much more powerful than the system used by the authorized user to generate the key from the password." Appendix A.2 gives the countermeasure principle: "The main idea of a PBKDF is to slow dictionary or brute force attacks on the passwords by increasing the time needed to test each password." The three quotations give one argument: the input is low-entropy, the attacker can search offline on hardware of their own choosing, and the available countermeasure is to raise the cost of each test. The obligations are written with shall. Section 4 bounds the use of the result: "The MK shall not be used for other purposes." Section 5 fixes the salt and the iteration count: "All or a portion of the salt shall be generated using an approved Random Bit Generator (e.g., see [5]).", "The length of the randomly-generated portion of the salt shall be at least 128 bits." and "The iteration count shall be selected as large as possible, as long as the time required to generate the key using the entered password is acceptable for the users." Section 5.3 approves a single construction: "This Recommendation approves PBKDF2 as the PBKDF using HMAC with any approved hash function as the PRF." One further value is advice rather than a requirement: "A minimum iteration count of 1,000 is recommended." The wording levels differ: the salt source, the random-portion length and the iteration-count selection are shall requirements, the count of one thousand is stated as recommended, and a single construction is approved. The first limit is how the document fixes its own object. Section 5 states it plainly: "Since most user-chosen passwords have low entropy and weak randomness properties, as discussed in Appendix A.1, these passwords shall not be used directly as cryptographic keys." Derivation is therefore not optional and no shortcut for using a password as a key is offered; the part title on the title block, "Part 1: Storage Applications", confines the use to stored data and data protection keys. The second limit is testability: Appendix B states "However, some requirements are out-of-scope for such testing." and hands those requirements over: "This appendix lists those requirements whose conformance is the responsibility of entities using, implementing, installing or configuring applications or protocols that incorporate this Recommendation." The running head carries the date: "SP 800-132 Recommendation for Password-Based Key Derivation December 2010", and the title block reads "NIST Special Publication 800-132" with "Part 1: Storage Applications", a first edition dated December 2010 with no revision number. The acknowledgements list the authors and their affiliation; the first author's surname carries a diacritic in the retained text, so the name is given outside the quotation to keep every quoted span verbatim-checkable, while the checkable part reads "Elaine Barker, William Burr, and Lily Chen of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)" and "would like to thank their colleagues at NIST, Shu-jen H. Chang, Morris Dworkin, Allen Roginsky, and John Kelsey". items.title: Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations (SP 800-137)
items.text: Standard : Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations (SP 800-137) (联邦信息与组织的信息安全持续监视（SP 800-137）). The subject definition sits in the Executive Summary at the front: "Information security continuous monitoring (ISCM) is defined as maintaining ongoing awareness of information security, vulnerabilities, and threats to support organizational risk management decisions." Section 1.3 gives the action of the document: "The purpose of this guideline is to assist organizations in the development of an ISCM strategy and the implementation of an ISCM program that provides awareness of threats and vulnerabilities, visibility into organizational assets, and the effectiveness of deployed security controls." The same paragraph states what it supports: "The ISCM strategy and program support ongoing assurance that planned and implemented security controls are aligned with organizational risk tolerance, as well as the ability to provide the information needed to respond to risk in a timely manner." The title block confines the object to the federal side: "Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations". The output is two-level, strategy and program: what is monitored, how often, and who judges it belong to those two levels, while implementing the controls is not. The argument gives the statutory floor first and then the operational reason. Section 1.1 records what the 2002 statute required: "The Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA) of 2002 further emphasized the importance of continuously monitoring information system security by requiring agencies to conduct assessments of security controls at a frequency appropriate to risk, but no less than annually." It then records the reporting posture of the year: "The memorandum provides instructions for annual FISMA reporting and emphasizes monitoring the security state of information systems on an ongoing basis with a frequency sufficient to make ongoing, risk-based decisions." The Executive Summary supplies the resource constraint, "Timely, relevant, and accurate information is vital, particularly when resources are limited and agencies must prioritize their efforts." and the premise "the ability to manage this technology and to assure confidentiality, integrity, and availability of information is now also mission-critical." Read together, annual assessment is a floor rather than a sufficient frequency, and the changes and threats that arrive between point-in-time assessments need continuous visibility matched to risk. Who acts is carried by the role entries of §2.4 and the decision sentences at the system tier, stated as plain present tense rather than shall. Section 2.4 says of the chief information officer "The CIO ensures that an effective ISCM program is established and implemented for the organization" and of the authorizing official "reviews security status reports and critical security documents and determines if the risk to the organization from operation of the information system remains acceptable." Section 3.1 puts frequency decisions on the system owner: "System owners determine assessment frequencies of security controls based on drivers from all three tiers." and sets evidence delivery at a policy-determined floor: "Assessment evidence obtained from ISCM is, at a minimum, provided to AOs as often as required by organizational policy." The same section assigns the risk bar to the risk executive (function): "The risk executive (function) determines the overall organizational risk tolerance and risk mitigation strategy at the organization tier." The criteria sentence from §3.2.2 reports as §3.1.4 in this text: "Organizations take the following criteria into consideration when establishing monitoring frequencies for metrics or assessment frequencies for security controls:" one item of which is control volatility: "Volatile security controls are assessed more frequently, whether the objective is establishing security control effectiveness or supporting calculation of a metric." The obligation level is therefore this document describing duties plus organizational policy: the annual floor comes from FISMA, not from here. The four limits work at different levels. Section 3.1 states its own non-prescriptiveness: "The guidelines below, though not prescriptive, helps to ensure an organization-wide approach to ISCM that best promotes standardized methodologies and consistent practices". The boundary of automation is conceded in the opening body of Chapter One, where the sentence prints after the CHAPTER ONE and INTRODUCTION headings and before 1.1 BACKGROUND on a page this copy still labels PAGE 1: "While this document encourages the use of automation, it is recognized that many aspects of ISCM programs are not easily automated." The Executive Summary separately prints must-level scope: "It is important to recognize that with any comprehensive information security program, all implemented security controls, including management and operational controls, must be regularly assessed for effectiveness, even if the monitoring of such controls cannot be automated or is not easily automated." Section 2.2 denies that frequencies are transferable constants: "Monitoring frequencies (e.g., annually, quarterly, monthly, daily) are not static, and they are not uniform across all metrics." The Authority block adds two bounds: "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems." and "This publication may be used by nongovernmental organizations on a voluntary basis and is not subject to copyright in the United States." So the limits differ by level rather than by existence: Section 3.1 calls itself non-prescriptive while the Executive Summary still states a must-level assessment scope, so the guideline is not silent about obligations; automation does not reach every process, frequencies are set per organisation, national security systems need express approval, and non-governmental use is purely voluntary. The title block carries "NIST Special Publication 800-137", a part title that spells out ISCM and confines it to federal systems, and the author line naming eight people in order, "Kelley Dempsey Nirali Shah Chawla Arnold Johnson Ronald Johnston Alicia Clay Jones Angela Orebaugh Matthew Scholl Kevin Stine", with the date line set in capitals on the title block and the signing officials below it, of whom "Patrick D. Gallagher, Under Secretary for Standards and Technology and Director". The Authority page gives the basis, "This publication has been developed by NIST to further its statutory responsibilities under the Federal Information Security Management Act (FISMA), Public Law (P.L.) 107-347.", then puts the extent and the date on two separate printed lines: "NIST Special Publication 800-137, 80 pages" and, on the next line, the date in parentheses (September 2011). The page count and the date are not run together in this copy. The acknowledgements split the eight authors by employer: "The authors, Kelley Dempsey, Arnold Johnson, Matthew Scholl and Kevin Stine of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), Ronald Johnston of the Department of Defense Chief Information Officer, Defense-wide Information Assurance Program (DOD-CIO, DIAP), Alicia Clay Jones and Angela Orebaugh of Booz Allen Hamilton, and Nirali Shah Chawla of PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP (PwC), wish to thank their colleagues who reviewed drafts of this document and contributed to its technical content." This copy has no DOI line and no revision or supersession statement; the extraction also drops interior hyphens from headings (IS CM, RES PONS IBILITIES), so no edition fact is taken from a heading. - Wikipedia search entry for 联邦信息与组织的信息安全持续监视（SP 800-137）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%81%94%E9%82%A6%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%E4%B8%8E%E7%BB%84%E7%BB%87%E7%9A%84%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E6%8C%81%E7%BB%AD%E7%9B%91%E8%A7%86%EF%BC%88SP%20800-137%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations (SP 800-137): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
