items.title: Developing Cyber Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach (SP 800-160 Vol. 2)
items.text: Standard : Developing Cyber Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach (SP 800-160 Vol. 2) (开发网络弹性系统：系统安全工程方法（SP 800-160 第二卷）). The abstract places the file beside existing ones: "This publication is used in conjunction with ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288:2015" and states its genre: "It can be viewed as a handbook for achieving the identified cyber resiliency outcomes based on a systems engineering perspective on system life cycle processes in conjunction with risk management processes, allowing the experience and expertise of the organization to help determine what is correct for its purpose." Section 1.1 gives its complementary role: "The purpose of this document is to supplement [SP 800-160 v1] and [SP 800-37]". The keyword line closes the subject with "risk management strategy; system life cycle; systems security engineering; trustworthiness."Together the four set the genre and the position: the file is not a standalone standard but a handbook used alongside the life cycle standard and the risk management framework, with the choice among the purpose-level constructs left to the organisation’s own experience. The premise sits in the front-matter overview: "All discussions of cyber resiliency focus on assuring the mission or business functions and are predicated on the assumption that the adversary will breach defenses and establish a long-term presence in organizational systems." The property sought is "the ability to anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to adverse conditions, stresses, attacks, or compromises on systems that use or are enabled by cyber resources", and the abstract draws the consequence for the reader: "Organizations can select, adapt, and use some or all of the cyber resiliency constructs".Premise and property stated side by side are the argument: if the adversary necessarily gets in and stays, defending a single breach does not assure the mission, and the resiliency constructs are listed for exactly that, to be selected and adapted by the organisation. Check the input, key or parameters and output format first, then locate the object in its protocol, standard or engineering workflow; do not treat one example parameter set as the only legal set. It declines to be a procedure manual: the front-matter usage note says "It is not intended to provide a specific recipe for execution." and offers itself as "it can be viewed as a catalog or handbook for achieving the identified cyber resiliency outcomes". Part of the subject is excluded outright: "Second-order effects are beyond the scope of this publication." The force is limited too — the authority paragraph states that "Such information security standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of the appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems.". Finally this very copy has been withdrawn, as the history claim records. The title block carries "NIST Special Publication 800-160" and "Developing Cyber Resilient Systems", with the author line "RON ROSS VICTORIA PILLITTERI RICHARD GRAUBART DEBORAH BODEAU ROSALIE MCQUAID"; the date line is November 2019, the citation reads "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-160, Volume 2, 229 pages (November 2019)" and the free-access line is followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2. The withdrawal banner at the head states "The attached publication has been withdrawn (archived), and is provided solely for historical purposes." and records "SP 800-160 Vol. 2 is superseded in its entirety by the publication of SP 800-160 Vol. 2 Revision 1.", the successor being Volume 2 Revision 1 of December 2021 with the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-160v2r1. The acknowledgements open with the reviewer list: "The authors gratefully acknowledge and appreciate the contributions from DJ Anand, Jon Boyens, Nicolas Chaillan, Ed Custeau, Holly Dunlap, Avi Gopstein, Suzanne Hassell, Bill Heinbockel, Daryl Hild, Scott Jackson, Lauren Knausenberger, Ellen Laderman".Title block, citation line, DOI and banner give this copy’s timeline and standing together: first published November 2019, withdrawn 9 December 2021, superseded in full by Volume 2 Revision 1, and retained here for historical reference only. - Wikipedia search entry for 开发网络弹性系统：系统安全工程方法（SP 800-160 第二卷）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%BC%80%E5%8F%91%E7%BD%91%E7%BB%9C%E5%BC%B9%E6%80%A7%E7%B3%BB%E7%BB%9F%EF%BC%9A%E7%B3%BB%E7%BB%9F%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E5%B7%A5%E7%A8%8B%E6%96%B9%E6%B3%95%EF%BC%88SP%20800-160%20%E7%AC%AC%E4%BA%8C%E5%8D%B7%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Developing Cyber Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach (SP 800-160 Vol. 2): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (SP 800-161 Rev. 1 upd. 1)
items.text: Standard : Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management Practices for Systems and Organizations (SP 800-161 Rev. 1) (网络安全供应链风险管理实践（SP 800-161）). The abstract gives its character: "This publication provides guidance to organizations on identifying, assessing, and mitigating cybersecurity risks throughout the supply chain at all levels of their organizations." The method is integration into existing risk management: "The publication integrates cybersecurity supply chain risk management (C-SCRM) into risk management activities by applying a multilevel, C-SCRM-specific approach". Section 1.1 defines the term: "Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management (C-SCRM) is a systematic process for managing exposure to cybersecurity risks throughout the supply chain and developing appropriate response strategies, policies, processes, and procedures." In order the three quotations give the character of the document, its method and its definition: guidance for organizations, delivered by embedding C-SCRM in existing risk management and working it through the levels, with the managed object stated as exposure together with response strategies, policies, processes and procedures. The starting point is the acquirer's lack of visibility. The abstract opens: "Organizations are concerned about the risks associated with products and services that may potentially contain malicious functionality, are counterfeit, or are vulnerable due to poor manufacturing and development practices within the supply chain." and attributes it to unseen processes: "These risks are associated with an enterprise's decreased visibility into and understanding of how the technology they acquire is developed, integrated, and deployed". Section 1 therefore defines the object first: "In this document, the term supply chain refers to the linked set of resources and processes between and among multiple levels of an enterprise, each of which is an acquirer that begins with the sourcing of products and services and extends through the product and service life cycle." The quotations separate two layers: products and services may carry malicious functionality, be counterfeit, or be weakly built, and the acquirer cannot see how the technology is developed, integrated and deployed. The §1 definition adds that every level of the chain is itself an acquirer. Section 2 gives the point of attachment: "C-SCRM should be integrated into the enterprise-wide risk management process described in [SP80039] and depicted in Fig. 3." The duty is shared organisationally: "Implementing C-SCRM requires enterprises to establish a coordinated team-based approach and a shared responsibility model to effectively manage cybersecurity risks throughout the supply chain." and cross-functional input is advised in should-aim-to terms: "Enterprises should aim to infuse perspectives from multiple disciplines and processes". Section 1.4 routes readers, telling enterprise risk owners: "The entire document is relevant to and recommended for readers fitting this profile." The subject of all three sentences is the enterprise itself: attach C-SCRM to the existing risk management process, build a coordinated team with a shared responsibility model, and infuse perspectives from several disciplines; the §1.4 reading routes are guidance. Two exclusions are its own. Section 1 separates C-SCRM from the wider discipline: "This publication does not address many of the non-cybersecurity aspects of SCRM." Section 1.1 declines to give a roadmap: "However, this publication does not offer a specific roadmap for enterprises to follow to reach various states of capability and maturity." and warns against copying it verbatim: "The C-SCRM guidance provided in this document is not one-size-fits-all." The first two mark a subject boundary and the third a method warning: the practices must be tailored to the size, resources and risk situation of each enterprise. A separate limit belongs to this retained copy: the masthead reads "May 2022 INCLUDES UPDATES AS OF 11-01-2024; SEE APPENDIX K", while the text held here stops at the responsibility table in section 2.3.1, so the key practices of Section 3 and the Appendix K named there are outside this file and their contents are not asserted. The first masthead line reads "NIST Special Publication 800 NIST SP 800-161r1-upd1", the date line reads "May 2022 INCLUDES UPDATES AS OF 11-01-2024; SEE APPENDIX K", and the DOI line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-161r1-upd1. items.title: Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations (SP 800-171 Rev. 3)
items.text: Standard : Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations (SP 800-171 Rev. 3) (保护非联邦系统中的受控非密信息（SP 800-171 Rev.3）). The first abstract sentence fixes audience, strength and object at once: "This publication provides federal agencies with recommended security requirements for protecting the confidentiality of CUI when the information is resident in nonfederal systems and organizations." The next narrows it to components: "The requirements apply to components of nonfederal systems that process, store, or transmit CUI or that provide protection for such components." The third states how it takes effect, through contracts rather than by itself: "The security requirements are intended for use by federal agencies in contractual vehicles or other agreements established between those agencies and nonfederal organizations." The last hands assessment over to the companion document: "This publication can be used in conjunction with its companion publication, NIST Special Publication 800-171A, which provides a comprehensive set of procedures to assess the security requirements." The keyword line lists the subject vocabulary in order, including "organization-defined parameter; security assessment; security control; security requirement." What this file supplies is a recommended-level requirement list: the control catalogue itself is SP 800-53 and the assessment procedures are SP 800-171A. The gap is laid out as a chain of consequence in Section 1. Responsibility does not move with the data: "The responsibility of federal agencies to protect CUI does not change when such information is shared with nonfederal organizations." Equivalent protection is therefore needed and has a hard precondition: "To maintain a consistent level of protection, the security requirements for safeguarding CUI in nonfederal systems and organizations must comply with Federal Information Processing Standards (FIPS 199) publication [6] and FIPS 200 [7]." The requirements are not invented but tailored: "The requirements are derived from the controls in NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-53 [8]." and "SP 800-171 security requirements represent a subset of the controls that are necessary to protect the confidentiality of CUI." The baseline comes from footnote 11, and that same footnote yields to higher authority in its next sentence: "In accordance with 32 CFR 2002 [5], CUI is categorized at no less than the FIPS 199 [6] moderate confidentiality impact value. However, when federal law, regulation, or government-wide policy establishing the control of CUI specifies controls that differ from those of the moderate control baseline, then the applicable law, regulation, or government-wide policy is followed." The moderate tier is therefore the floor this copy sets, not an unchangeable rule. Together these sentences give the reason: once CUI sits in nonfederal systems it may not be downgraded and no ready list exists, so the moderate baseline is tailored for confidentiality into a requirement set that can be put into a contract. The wording levels separate cleanly inside the numbered sections. Section 1.1 says who is bound: "The security requirements in this publication are only applicable to components of nonfederal systems that process, store, or transmit CUI or that provide protection for such components." and who invokes them: "The requirements are intended for use by federal agencies in contractual vehicles or other agreements that are established between those agencies and nonfederal organizations." Section 2.2 leaves more than one must for organization-defined parameters, both addressed to the nonfederal party: the body sentence "If a federal agency or a consortium of agencies do not specify a particular value or range of values for an ODP, nonfederal organizations must assign the value or values to complete the security requirement." and, in footnote 14, "NIST does not establish or assign values for ODPs. If ODP values for selected security requirements are not formally established or assigned by a federal agency or a consortium of federal agencies, nonfederal organizations must assign those values to complete the requirements." Section 3 only describes its own contents and naming: "This section describes 17 families of security requirements for protecting the confidentiality of CUI in nonfederal systems and organizations." and "Not all security requirements mention CUI explicitly." Inside §3.1 the requirements are lettered imperatives, for example the second item of account management: "Create, enable, modify, disable, and remove system accounts in accordance with policy, procedures, prerequisites, and criteria." So must-level wording is not confined to completing an ODP value and federal compliance: Section 2.2 itself prints two such sentences, a discussion section in Chapter 3 uses must for a system capability (under 03.03.01 Event Logging, organizations may determine that systems must have the capability to log every file access, activating it only under specific circumstances because of the burden on performance), and the Authority paragraph uses shall instead. That is an observation from reading the copy, not a closed list. What does hold is that the requirement statements themselves are lettered imperatives and gain their force through the contract. The limits sit at four levels. Section 2.2 states the standing of the discussion attached to each requirement: "The discussion section is informative, not normative." with the reason next: "It is not intended to extend the scope of a requirement or influence the solutions that organizations may use to satisfy a requirement." Section 1.1 excludes one class of holder: "The requirements do not apply to nonfederal organizations that are collecting or maintaining information on behalf of a federal agency or using or operating a system on behalf of an agency." Section 3 concedes that some systems cannot take everything: "Some systems, including specialized systems (e.g., industrial/process control systems, medical devices, computer numerical control machines), may have limitations on the application of certain security requirements." The Authority block makes application to national security systems conditional: "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems." And Appendix E bounds this very release: "The current release of this publication does not include any errata updates." Discussions create no duty, agencies on whose behalf information is held fall under FISMA instead, enduring exceptions go to the system security plan, and national security systems need express approval. Read line by line, this copy prints "NIST Special Publication 800 NIST SP 800-171r3" on the number line (the duplicated identifier is an artifact of the extraction), then the title line "Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations", the author line "Ron Ross Victoria Pillitteri", the division line "Computer Security Division Information Technology Laboratory", and the running head "NIST SP 800-171r3 May 2024", so the date is May 2024; the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-171r3. The publication history block gives review and supersession in one run: "Approved by the NIST Editorial Review Board on 2024-04-23 Supersedes NIST Special Publication 800-171r2 (February 2020; Includes updates as of 01-28-2021)", and the citation line gives both authors and the year: "Ross R, Pillitteri V (2024) Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations. (National Institute of Standards and Technology, Gaithersburg, MD), NIST Special Publication (SP) NIST SP 800-171r3." The acknowledgements name the editorial and production staff "Jim Foti, Jeff Brewer, Eduardo Takamura, Isabel Van Wyk, Cristina Ritfeld, Derek Sappington, and Carolyn Schmidt" and thank Kelley Dempsey for the initial research behind the prototype CUI overlay. Appendix E opens its revision list with "This publication incorporates the following changes from the original edition (February 2020; updated January 28, 2021):" and one entry reads "Eliminated the distinction between basic and derived security requirements". - Wikipedia search entry for 保护非联邦系统中的受控非密信息（SP 800-171 Rev.3）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E4%BF%9D%E6%8A%A4%E9%9D%9E%E8%81%94%E9%82%A6%E7%B3%BB%E7%BB%9F%E4%B8%AD%E7%9A%84%E5%8F%97%E6%8E%A7%E9%9D%9E%E5%AF%86%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%EF%BC%88SP%20800-171%20Rev.3%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information in Nonfederal Systems and Organizations (SP 800-171 Rev. 3): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SHA-3 Derived Functions: cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash and ParallelHash (SP 800-185)
items.text: Standard : SHA-3 Derived Functions: cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash and ParallelHash (SP 800-185) (SHA-3 派生函数：cSHAKE、KMAC、TupleHash 与 ParallelHash（SP 800-185）). The opening sentence of the abstract gives the character and the object: "This Recommendation specifies four types of SHA-3-derived functions: cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash, and ParallelHash, each defined for a 128- and 256-bit security strength." The four are then self-described one by one: "cSHAKE is a customizable variant of the SHAKE function, as defined in Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 202.", "KMAC (for KECCAK Message Authentication Code) is a variable-length message authentication code algorithm based on KECCAK; it can also be used as a pseudorandom function.", "TupleHash is a variable-length hash function designed to hash tuples of input strings without trivial collisions." and "ParallelHash is a variable-length hash function that can hash very long messages in parallel." What is specified is four function families in two strength tiers, all derived from FIPS 202. The abstract's range stops there: four families, two tiers, one self-description each, no value prescribed for any protocol, and no definition of KECCAK or SHAKE themselves, since FIPS 202 is the upstream standard and this file works at the layer of derived functions. Section 1 states the gap as domain separation: "Domain separation ensures that different named functions (such as SHA3-512 and SHAKE128) will be unrelated." It then explains what customization buys: "Customization is analogous to strong typing in a programming language; such customization makes it extremely unlikely that computing one function with two different customization strings will yield the same answer." The other three families answer to a second gap: "It then defines three additional SHA-3-derived functions, in Secs. 4 through 6, that provide new functionality not directly available from the more basic functions." The risk is therefore one thing seen twice: without domain separation outputs for different purposes may be related, and with the name N and the customization string S two computations can be treated as unrelated functions. The division of duties is stated in numbered sections. The function name is not the user's to invent: §3.4 says of N that "This is intended for use by NIST in defining SHA-3-derived functions, and should only be set to values defined by NIST", and addresses users directly: "Users of cSHAKE should not make up their own names--that kind of customization is the purpose of the customization string S, to be discussed in Sec. 3.5." Section 3.5 hands the choice of S to the caller: "The cSHAKE function also includes an input string (S) to allow users to customize their use of the function." Across that division the tiers are fixed: "cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash, and ParallelHash are all defined for two claimed security strengths: 128 bits and 256 bits." The two parameters therefore sit at different levels: N is NIST's to define and users are advised not to invent names, both in should-level wording, while S is the caller's to choose — §3.5 gives only examples and lets implementations restrict its length, and no customization string is prescribed here for any use. The limits are stated in four places. First, no parameter floor and no assigned use: "The customization string may be of any length less than 22040; however, implementations may restrict the length of S that they will accept." (the retained extraction drops the superscript: the bound prints as 22040 where the document gives 2 to the power 2040, and the same file renders right_encode’s validity condition ) — the values remain the caller's choice, and this Recommendation assigns none to a use. Second, the cost of overstepping: "Nonstandard values of N could cause interoperability problems with future NIST-defined functions." Third, a property cSHAKE lacks: "Note that cSHAKE does not share this property." and "For q1< q2, cSHAKE(X, q1, N, S) is a prefix of cSHAKE(X, q2, N, S)." — a short output is merely a prefix of a long one, unlike the other three families where changing the length changes the function. Fourth, the implementation boundary: "An implementation of cSHAKE may reasonably support only input strings and output lengths that are whole bytes; if so, a fractional-byte input string or a request for an output length that is not a multiple of 8 would result in an error." The functions are specified; how a protocol uses them is not, and one appendix marks itself non-normative: "Appendix B--Hashing into a Range (Informative)". The first title-block line reads "NIST Special Publication 800-185", the author and division lines read in sequence as "John Kelsey Shu-jen Chang Ray Perlner Computer Security Division Information Technology Laboratory", and the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-185. The citation inside the Authority block carries the date and length: "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-185, 32 pages (December 2016)", and the same block bounds application: "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems". The keyword line reads "authentication; cryptography; cSHAKE; customizable SHAKE function; hash function". The acknowledgements name the reviewers from the KECCAK team: "The authors thank the KECCAK team members: Guido Bertoni, Joan Daemen" — the next name carries a diacritic in the retained text, quoted here outside the name — plus "The authors also thank their colleagues for reviewing drafts of this document and contributing to its development." Together these are the front-matter facts of this file: the publication number, the three authors and their division, the free-access DOI line, the citation carrying its page count, and the outside reviewers named in the acknowledgements; the text claims no supersession of an earlier edition. - Wikipedia search entry for SHA-3 派生函数：cSHAKE、KMAC、TupleHash 与 ParallelHash（SP 800-185）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SHA-3%20%E6%B4%BE%E7%94%9F%E5%87%BD%E6%95%B0%EF%BC%9AcSHAKE%E3%80%81KMAC%E3%80%81TupleHash%20%E4%B8%8E%20ParallelHash%EF%BC%88SP%20800-185%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] SHA-3 Derived Functions: cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash and ParallelHash (SP 800-185): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines (SP 800-193)
items.text: Standard : Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines (SP 800-193) (平台固件韧性指南（SP 800-193）). The abstract states the object and the character of the document: "This document provides technical guidelines and recommendations supporting resiliency of platform firmware and data against potentially destructive attacks." and defines its subject: "The platform is a collection of fundamental hardware and firmware components needed to boot and operate a system." The three principles are given in one abstract sentence: "The technical guidelines in this document promote resiliency in the platform by describing security mechanisms for protecting the platform against unauthorized changes, detecting unauthorized changes that occur, and recovering from attacks rapidly and securely." The executive summary repeats it — "These guidelines are based on the following three principles:" — and opens the list with "Protection: Mechanisms for ensuring that Platform Firmware code and critical data remain in a state of integrity and are protected from corruption". The output is therefore mechanism-level guidance rather than an algorithm specification: resiliency is split into protection, detection and recovery, each carried by implementable guidelines, and the object is firmware and its configuration data across the platform rather than one machine's boot firmware. The risk is in the abstract: "A successful attack on platform firmware could render a system inoperable, perhaps permanently, or requiring reprogramming by the original manufacturer, resulting in significant disruptions to users." The executive summary says why repair is hard: "Much of this firmware is highly privileged in the system architectures, and because this firmware is necessary for the system to operate, repairing this firmware can be challenging." The gap in existing guidance is named next: "Earlier NIST publications have addressed the threat of attacks on one particular type of platform firmware: boot firmware, commonly known as the Basic Input/Output System (BIOS)." followed by "However, the platform consists of many other devices with firmware and configuration data." The four sentences give the shape of the gap: the loss need not be a disclosure but a long-lasting destruction of availability, repair depends on the original manufacturer, and earlier guidance covered only one class of firmware while the other devices carrying firmware and configuration data were left untreated. Readers and duties are set out in layers. The abstract splits them: "Implementers, including Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs) and component/device suppliers, can use these guidelines to build stronger security mechanisms into platforms." and "System administrators, security professionals, and users can use this document to guide procurement strategies and priorities for future systems." Section 1.1 restates the aim: "The purpose of this document is to provide security guidelines to support system resiliency at a platform level." Section 4 gives the selection rule and the modality register: "Devices may implement the requirements in one or more of these sections based on the firmware resiliency properties, as defined in Section 3.2, they aim to support." and "The use of shall, should, and may are used as defined in RFC 2119 [5]." The items in §4.1.1 are shall-level: "The security mechanisms shall be founded in Roots of Trust (RoT)." and "All RoTs and CoTs shall either be immutable or protected using mechanisms which ensure all RoTs and CoTs remain in a state of integrity." Reader and duty differ accordingly: implementers work through the numbered items of §4, while administrators and buyers use the three properties mainly as procurement criteria. The shall-level items are not limited to the two quoted above: the same section also states in shall terms that "All elements of the Chains of Trust for Update, Detection and Recovery in non-volatile storage shall be implemented in platform firmware.", while other items fall to should or may under RFC 2119. It is guidance, not a mandate. The Authority block says the guidelines change no existing authority: "Nor should these guidelines be interpreted as altering or superseding the existing authorities of the Secretary of Commerce, Director of the OMB, or any other federal official." and puts use outside federal systems on a voluntary footing: "This publication may be used by nongovernmental organizations on a voluntary basis and is not subject to copyright in the United States." Section 1.3 narrows the threat set: "The goal of this document is to provide principles and guidelines that can support platform resiliency primarily against remote attacks." Section 1.4 marks part of the text as background only: "Section 2 provides informative material describing platform components and architectures." The Audience section states the prerequisite: "The technical guidelines assume readers have expertise in the platform architectures and are targeted primarily at developers and engineers responsible for implementing firmware-level security technologies in systems and devices." The limits stack: the guidelines add no mandate of their own, the threat set is centered on remote attack, §2 declares itself background material, and the text presumes expertise in platform architectures on the reader's side. The first title-block line reads "NIST Special Publication 800-193", the author and division line reads as one sequence "Andrew Regenscheid Computer Security Division Information Technology Laboratory", and the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-193. The citation in the Authority block carries the date and length: "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-193, 45 pages (May 2018)", a May 2018 publication, and the front matter contains no statement of supersession. The acknowledgements bind author and reviewers together: "The author, Andrew Regenscheid of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), wishes to thank his colleagues who reviewed drafts of this document and contributed to its technical content." and list the outside experts, beginning "These experts included Chirag Schroff from Cisco; Mukund Khatri from Dell;". - Wikipedia search entry for 平台固件韧性指南（SP 800-193）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%B9%B3%E5%8F%B0%E5%9B%BA%E4%BB%B6%E9%9F%A7%E6%80%A7%E6%8C%87%E5%8D%97%EF%BC%88SP%20800-193%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Platform Firmware Resiliency Guidelines (SP 800-193): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Zero Trust Architecture (SP 800-207)
items.text: Standard : Zero Trust Architecture (SP 800-207) (零信任架构（SP 800-207）). The first abstract sentence places the term: "Zero trust (ZT) is the term for an evolving set of cybersecurity paradigms that move defenses from static, network-based perimeters to focus on users, assets, and resources." The second names the architecture: "A zero trust architecture (ZTA) uses zero trust principles to plan industrial and enterprise infrastructure and workflows." The working assumption follows: "Zero trust assumes there is no implicit trust granted to assets or user accounts based solely on their physical or network location (i.e., local area networks versus the internet) or based on asset ownership (enterprise or personally owned)." Section 1 adds: "A zero trust architecture (ZTA) is an enterprise cybersecurity architecture that is based on zero trust principles and designed to prevent data breaches and limit internal lateral movement." The two definitions work at different levels: the first moves the focus from the network perimeter onto users, assets and resources, the second places ZTA as an enterprise cybersecurity architecture and states its aim; the third abstract sentence fixes the condition on which trust is granted, for which location and ownership are no longer reasons. The motive is the network trend that dissolves the boundary: "Zero trust is a response to enterprise network trends that include remote users, bring your own device (BYOD), and cloud-based assets that are not located within an enterpriseowned network boundary." Section 1 says why perimeter defences fail: "Perimeter-based network security has also been shown to be insufficient since once attackers breach the perimeter, further lateral movement is unhindered." and states the adversary assumption: "Zero trust security models assume that an attacker is present in the environment and that an enterprise-owned environment is no different--or no more trustworthy--than any nonenterprise-owned environment." Section 2 records the shift of focus: "Zero trust focuses on protecting resources (assets, services, workflows, network accounts, etc.), not network segments, as the network location is no longer seen as the prime component to the security posture of the resource." The four sentences form one argument: the perimeter loses meaning first, because assets no longer sit inside enterprise networks; its failure costs unhindered lateral movement; so the model assumes an adversary already in the environment, and protection is decided per resource rather than per network segment. What the document sets out first are seven basic tenets, worded as design principles rather than mandates: "A zero trust architecture is designed and deployed with adherence to the following zero trust basic tenets:", the first being "All data sources and computing services are considered resources." Section 2 adds a general requirement: "Overall, enterprises need to develop and maintain dynamic risk-based policies for resource access and set up a system to ensure that these policies are enforced correctly and consistently for individual resource access requests." and advises against inferring later requests from one login, in should-not terms rather than a prohibition: "This means that an enterprise should not rely on implied trustworthiness wherein if the subject has met a base authentication level (e.g., logging into an asset), all subsequent resource requests are assumed to be equally valid." Section 3 places the duties on logical components — the policy engine, "This component is responsible for the ultimate decision to grant access to a resource for a given subject.", and the enforcement point, "This system is responsible for enabling, monitoring, and eventually terminating connections between a subject and an enterprise resource." — while declaring its own status: "Note that this is an ideal model showing logical components and their interactions." The document describes models and considerations, not a product or a plan. The abstract says: "This document contains an abstract definition of zero trust architecture (ZTA) and gives general deployment models and use cases where zero trust could improve an enterprise's overall information technology security posture." The Audience section adds: "It is not intended to be a single deployment plan for ZTA as an enterprise will have unique business use cases and data assets that require safeguards." Section 1 keeps the principles framing: "ZT is not a single architecture but a set of guiding principles for workflow, system design and operations" and "Transitioning to ZTA is a journey concerning how an organization evaluates risk in its mission and cannot simply be accomplished with a wholesale replacement of technology." Section 5 is explicit that risk is not removed: "No enterprise can eliminate cybersecurity risk." and names a new concentration of it: "Any enterprise administrator with configuration access to the PE's rules may be able to perform unapproved changes or make mistakes that can disrupt enterprise operations." The self-descriptions accumulate: the document supplies definitions and models, not a deployment plan, and claims no elimination of risk — it even lists the decision components themselves as an attack surface. The first title-block line reads "NIST Special Publication 800-207", the author and division lines read in sequence as "Scott Rose Oliver Borchert Advanced Network Technologies Division Information Technology Laboratory", with the other two authors and their affiliations given as "Stu Mitchell Stu2Labs" and "Sean Connelly Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency", and the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-207. The citation in the Authority block carries date and length: "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-207, 59 pages (August 2020)". The keyword line reads "architecture; cybersecurity; enterprise; network security; zero trust." The acknowledgements (spelled Acknowledgments here) record provenance: "This document is the product of a collaboration between multiple federal agencies and is overseen by the Federal CIO Council." and name participants, starting "These include Greg Holden, project manager of the Federal CIO Council ZTA project". Taken together these are the front-matter facts: the number and title, four authors with their affiliations, an August publication date with a page count, the free-access DOI line, and the statement of federal collaboration behind the signatures. - Wikipedia search entry for 零信任架构（SP 800-207）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%9B%B6%E4%BF%A1%E4%BB%BB%E6%9E%B6%E6%9E%84%EF%BC%88SP%20800-207%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Zero Trust Architecture (SP 800-207): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes (SP 800-208)
items.text: Standard : Stateful Hash-based Signature Schemes (状态散列基签名方案). The abstract names the object in its first clause: "This recommendation specifies two algorithms that can be used to generate a digital signature" and at once lists the schemes: "the Leighton-Micali Signature (LMS) system and the eXtended Merkle Signature Scheme (XMSS), along with their multi-tree variants, the Hierarchical Signature System (HSS) and multi-tree XMSS (XMSSMT)." The title block reads "Recommendation for Stateful Hash-Based Signature Schemes": both families hold only if the signing state is maintained.The abstract packs both base systems and their multi-tree forms into one sentence, so the word stateful in the title line is load-bearing: the scheme is secure only while the signer knows the index of the next available one-time key. The risk is stated in §1.2: a private key is a large set of one-time keys and "The signer needs to ensure that no individual OTS key is ever used to sign more than one message." Once one such key signs two messages, "then it would become computationally feasible for that attacker to forge signatures on arbitrary messages". Section 1 gives the trade being made: "The security of the stateful HBS schemes in this publication depends only on the security of the underlying hash functions", followed by "it is believed that the security of hash functions will not be broken by the development of large-scale quantum computers". Section 1.1 concedes the price: "Stateful HBS schemes are not suitable for general use because they require careful state management that is often difficult to assure".Read together the quotations give the trade: security rests only on the preimage and second-preimage difficulty of the hash functions, and the price is that the signer must hold the state, which is exactly what the not-suitable-for-general-use sentence in §1.1 states. The conventions block at the front defines the register — "indicate requirements to be followed strictly in order to conform to the publication and from which no deviation is permitted." Section 4 puts shall-level duties on whoever generates key pairs: "each LM-OTS key in the system shall use the same parameter set, and the hash function used for the LMS system shall be the same as the hash function used in the LM-OTS keys." and "When generating LMS or HSS key pairs using SHA-256, the LMS and LM-OTS parameter sets shall be selected from the following two tables". One sentence in §3.1 stays at advice level: "The size of x should generally correspond to the targeted security strength of the scheme."The registers separate cleanly: choosing the parameter sets is shall-level, while sizing the Winternitz secret seed x to the target strength is should-level, and the conventions block makes the first non-deviable and the second merely preferred. It does not replace the current digital signature standard: §1 places itself as "This publication supplements FIPS 186 [4] by specifying two additional digital signature schemes". Nor is it the post-quantum signature standard being awaited — §1.1 says "NIST is in the process of developing standards for post-quantum secure digital signature schemes", the text names no successor and grants no approval beyond its own statements. The range is bounded twice more in §1: only a subset is approved, "This publication approves the use of some but not all of the parameter sets defined in [1] and [2] and also defines some new parameter sets.", and the modules are fixed, "This recommendation requires that key and signature generation be performed in hardware cryptographic modules that do not allow secret keying material to be exported, even in encrypted form." The first title-block line is "NIST Special Publication 800-208"; the author lines carry "David A. Cooper Daniel C. Apon Quynh H. Dang" and "Morris J. Dworkin Carl A. Miller". The date line is October 2020, the citation reads "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-208, 59 pages (October 2020) CODEN: NSPUE2" and the free-access line is followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-208. The keyword line sets the subject: "cryptography; digital signatures; hash-based signatures; public-key cryptography." The retained copy carries no acknowledgements page and announces no later revision.These are the front-matter facts of the file itself: the number, the title line, the six authors, the page count, the publication month and the DOI; this text carries no acknowledgements page and announces no successor, so its edition history stops at the October 2020 printing. - Wikipedia search entry for 状态散列基签名方案. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%8A%B6%E6%80%81%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97%E5%9F%BA%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E6%96%B9%E6%A1%88 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Stateful Hash-based Signature Schemes: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1 (SP 800-218)
items.text: Standard : Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1 Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities (安全软件开发框架（SP 800-218）). The abstract names the object: "This document recommends the Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)" and gives its make-up: "a core set of high-level secure software development practices that can be integrated into each SDLC implementation". The title block reads "Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1" and "Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities", and §2 states the structure: "The practices are organized into four groups".Read together the three give the character: a high-level practice set to be folded into any life cycle model, introducing neither new practices nor new terminology, whose main output is the four-group structure. The gap is the abstract’s first sentence: "Few software development life cycle (SDLC) models explicitly address software security in detail, so secure software development practices usually need to be added to each SDLC model to ensure that the software being developed is well-secured." Section 1 carries the same judgement into practice: "secure software development practices should be integrated throughout it for three reasons: to reduce the number of vulnerabilities in released software". The abstract also gives the acquirer’s reason: "Because the framework provides a common vocabulary for secure software development, software acquirers can also use it to foster communications with suppliers in acquisition processes and other management activities."The quotations put the problem at both ends: on the producer’s side the gap is that security practice is not written into the models, on the acquirer’s side it is the missing common vocabulary, and the framework addresses both. The obligations are should-level and their subject is the organisation. The executive summary states the general duty: "Organizations should integrate the SSDF throughout their existing software development practices, express their secure software development requirements to third-party suppliers using SSDF conventions, and acquire software that meets the practices described in the SSDF." Each of the four groups in §2 is addressed to organisations, one of them being "2. Protect the Software (PS): Organizations should protect all components of their software from tampering and unauthorized access." Section 1 puts the cloud allocation on the tenant: "The tenant organization should establish an agreement with the providers that specifies which party is responsible for each practice and task and how each provider will attest to their conformance with the agreement."All three are addressed to organisations or tenants and all are should-level: the framework offers recommendations, not mandatory clauses, and the allocation of responsibility has to be written into an agreement stating who performs each practice and who attests to it. Section 1 states two things it does not do. It gives no implementation method: "This document identifies secure software development practices but does not prescribe how to implement them." and it invents neither practices nor terms: "This document does not introduce new practices or define new terminology." The same section bounds how the framework is used: "The intention of the SSDF is not to create a checklist to follow, but to provide a basis for planning and implementing a risk-based approach to adopting secure software development practices." Even the relation to the Cybersecurity Framework is limited — the note says "the SSDF practices do not map to them". The title block opens "NIST Special Publication 800-218"; the three authors are Souppaya, Scarfone and Dodson, the last marked "Former NIST employee; all work for this publication was done while at NIST." The date line is February 2022, the citation reads "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-218, 36 pages (February 2022) CODEN: NSPUE2" and the free-access line is followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-218. The audience block defines the readership: "There are two primary audiences for this document. The first is software producers". The acknowledgements list the colleagues: "The authors thank all of their NIST colleagues for their support throughout the SSDF update". The note to readers bounds the currency of the text: "The publication will be updated periodically to reflect your inputs and feedback." - Wikipedia search entry for 安全软件开发框架（SP 800-218）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E8%BD%AF%E4%BB%B6%E5%BC%80%E5%8F%91%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6%EF%BC%88SP%20800-218%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF) Version 1.1 Recommendations for Mitigating the Risk of Software Vulnerabilities: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation (分组密码工作模式建议). The abstract enumerates the five confidentiality modes: "This recommendation defines five confidentiality modes of operation for use with an underlying symmetric key block cipher algorithm: Electronic Codebook (ECB), Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), Cipher Feedback (CFB), Output Feedback (OFB), and Counter (CTR)." No new algorithm is defined — only ways to run one. The purpose is one sentence: §1 reads "This publication provides recommendations regarding modes of operation to be used with symmetric key block cipher algorithms." The abstract states what the five modes do — "The five modes--the Electronic Codebook (ECB), Cipher Block Chaining (CBC), Cipher Feedback (CFB), Output Feedback (OFB), and Counter (CTR) modes--can provide data confidentiality." The document adds no further rationale for needing several modes; it does this one job. Its use is as a validation basis — the conformance-testing paragraph inside §2 (Authority) reads: "Conformance testing for implementations of the modes of operation that are specified in this recommendation will be conducted within the framework of the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), a joint effort of the NIST and the Communications Security Establishment of the Government of Canada." Once a mode is chosen, implementations are checked against this recommendation. The first limit is scope: the abstract confines the offering to confidentiality, and no authenticated-encryption mode appears in this document. The second is authority: §2 states "Nor should this recommendation be interpreted as altering or superseding the existing authorities of the Secretary of Commerce, the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, or any other Federal official." It neither changes existing mandates nor reaches national security systems. The citation line reads "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-38A 2001 ED, 66 pages (December 2001)". §2 records the earlier arrangements: "FIPS Pub. 81 [4] specifies the ECB, CBC, CFB, and OFB modes of the Data Encryption Standard (DES)." plus FIPS 46-3 for the seven Triple DES modes. The document never claims to supersede FIPS 81; it positions itself under the existing authorities. - Wikipedia search entry for 分组密码工作模式建议. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E5%B7%A5%E4%BD%9C%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F%E5%BB%BA%E8%AE%AE - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: The CMAC Mode for Authentication
items.text: Standard : The CMAC Mode for Authentication (CMAC 认证模式). The abstract names the object in its first sentence: "This Recommendation specifies a message authentication code (MAC) algorithm based on a symmetric key block cipher." and the use in its second: "This block cipher-based MAC algorithm, called CMAC, may be used to provide assurance of the authenticity and, hence, the integrity of binary data." Clause 1 places it in the series: "This publication is the second Part in a series of Recommendations regarding modes of operation of symmetric key block ciphers." The keyword line carries authentication but no confidentiality: "KEY WORDS: authentication; block cipher; cryptography; information security; integrity; message authentication code; mode of operation." The document specifies MAC generation and verification, not encryption, and not how the key is established. The gap is an unusable existing construction: §3 states "The basic Cipher Block Chaining MAC algorithm (CBC-MAC) has security deficiencies [9]." and names the replacement: "The core of the CMAC algorithm is a variation of CBC-MAC that Black and Rogaway proposed and analyzed under the name XCBC in Ref. [2] and submitted to NIST in Ref. [1]." The improvement chain follows: "Iwata and Kurosawa proposed an improvement of XCBC and named the resulting algorithm One-Key CBC-MAC (OMAC) in Ref. [6] and in Ref. [5], their initial submission to NIST" and closes with "The OMAC1 variation efficiently reduces the key size of XCBC. CMAC is equivalent to OMAC1." The setting is stated separately: "CMAC may be appropriate for information systems in which an approved block cipher is more readily available than an approved hash function." The argument is a block-cipher-side authentication construction, not another hash-based MAC. The obligations sit in numbered sections at three wording levels. Section 5.2 constrains the cipher and the key with two shall requirements: "The underlying block cipher shall be approved, and the key shall be generated uniformly at random, or close to uniformly at random, i.e., so that each possible key is (nearly) equally likely to be generated." and "The key shall be secret and shall be used exclusively for the CMAC mode of the chosen block cipher." Establishing the key is advice only: "To fulfill the requirements on the key, the key should be established among the parties to the information within an approved key management structure". Appendix B puts a duty on the operating system: "For any system in which CMAC is implemented, the risk that an attacker can detect and exploit a collision shall be limited to a level that is appropriate to the value of the data." The levels separate cleanly: cipher and key carry shall duties, key establishment is should-level advice, and holding the collision risk to a level matched to the value of the data is left to the judgement of whoever deploys the system. The four limits work at different levels. Section 2 draws the applicability line: "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems." Section 5.2 hands the key work over: "the details of the establishment and management of keys are outside the scope of this Recommendation." Appendix A.1 concedes the ceiling on assurance: "however, this assurance, as for any MAC algorithm, is not absolute." and conditions short tags: "A value of Tlen that is less than 64 shall only be used in conjunction with a careful analysis of the risks of accepting an inauthentic message as authentic." Appendix C is the plainest statement of what the algorithm does not do: "In some protocols an attacker may even be able to present to a verifier a message-MAC pair that the verifier itself generated earlier in the protocol." A valid MAC therefore does not identify whoever presented it, and replay defence is left to sequence numbers, timestamps or nonces in the protocol. The file opens with the NIST archive banner: "The attached publication has been archived (withdrawn), and is provided solely for historical purposes." The banner records the successor relationship, "The attached publication has been superseded by the following publication(s)", and the superseding entry keeps the same 800-38B number and part title with the author and date lines reading "M. Dworkin Publication Date(s): October 6, 2016"; the update note reads "SP 800-38B is updated by the October 6, 2016 release of 800-38B, which includes editorial changes (as of October 6, 2016)." The publication masthead itself reads "NIST Special Publication 800-38B Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: The CMAC Mode for Authentication Morris Dworkin", dated May 2005, with the citation line "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-38B, 23 pages (May 2005) CODEN: NSPUE2". The body of this copy carries no free-of-charge DOI line; the identifier named on the banner is DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-38B. - Wikipedia search entry for CMAC 认证模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CMAC%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] The CMAC Mode for Authentication: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: The CCM Mode for Authentication and Confidentiality
items.text: Standard : The CCM Mode for Authentication and Confidentiality (CCM 认证与保密模式). The first abstract sentence is the mode definition: "This Recommendation defines a mode of operation, called CCM, for a symmetric key block cipher algorithm." The second gives the combination: "CCM may be used to provide assurance of the confidentiality and the authenticity of computer data by combining the techniques of the Counter (CTR) mode and the Cipher Block Chaining-Message Authentication Code (CBC-MAC) algorithm." The keyword line carries both services side by side: "KEY WORDS: authenticated encryption; authentication; block cipher; confidentiality; cryptography; encryption; information security; message authentication code; mode of operation." Clause 1 places the part in the series: "This publication is the third Part in a series of Recommendations regarding modes of operation of symmetric key block cipher algorithms." No new algorithm is proposed: two existing primitives are put into one process, authentication and confidentiality appear together, and neither the origin of the key nor the values a protocol chooses falls inside this specification. The problem is obtaining confidentiality and authentication in one pass: §3 states "CCM consists of two related processes: generation-encryption and decryption-verification, which combine two cryptographic primitives: counter mode encryption and cipher block chainingbased authentication." and bounds the primitives: "Only the forward cipher function of the block cipher algorithm is used within these primitives." The advantage of the authentication half is put in one sentence: "A MAC provides stronger assurance of authenticity than a checksum or an error detecting code." The burden is stated as a minimum condition: "The security properties of CCM depend, at a minimum, on the secrecy of the key." Together the four sentences give the document position: one key serves both primitives, only the forward cipher function is needed, and key secrecy is the floor. Section 5.1 is written mostly at shall level: "The underlying block cipher algorithm shall be approved, and a secret key for the block cipher algorithm shall be generated uniformly at random, or close to uniformly at random" and "The key shall be kept secret and shall only be used for the CCM mode." The same clause sets a hard ceiling on cipher calls: "The total number of invocations of the block cipher algorithm during the lifetime of the key shall be limited to 261." (the printed 261 is this extraction dropping the superscript of 2 to the power 61) Section 5.3 makes the nonce a non-repetition requirement: "The nonce shall be non-repeating in the sense that any two distinct data pairs to be protected by CCM during the lifetime of the key shall be assigned distinct nonces." and adds "The nonce is not required to be random." The wording level is uniform: the algorithm must be approved, the key stays secret and dedicated, the number of calls is capped, uniqueness is required of the nonce while randomness is not, and all five obligations bear on the implementation and its key values rather than on the strength of the primitives themselves. The limits are written layer by layer. Applicability: §2 states "such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems." Operating shape: §3 states "CCM is not designed to support partial processing or stream processing." The cipher choice follows from the block size: §3 gives "thus, CCM cannot be used with the Triple Data Encryption Algorithm". The borrowed primitive is not itself approved: §5.2 states "This Recommendation does not approve CBC-MAC as an authentication mode outside of the context of the CCM specification". Key work is handed elsewhere: §5.1 says "Key establishment and key management are outside the scope of this Recommendation." And the tag length carries a condition: Appendix B.2 states "a value of Tlen that is less than 64 shall not be used without a careful analysis of the risks of accepting inauthentic data as authentic." The six limits sit at different levels: national security systems are outside applicability, whole packets are required, the cipher choice is fixed by the block size, the borrowed CBC-MAC gains no approval of its own, key work belongs to other documents, and a short tag needs a separate risk analysis. The masthead reads "NIST Special Publication 800-38C Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: The CCM Mode for Authentication and Confidentiality Morris Dworkin", the part title using Confidentiality rather than Privacy; the date line reads "May 2004 (errata update 07-20-2007; corrected value of parameter B on p.19)", a May 2004 original with an errata update of 20 July 2007. The citation line gives extent and date: "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-38C 25 pages (May 2004) CODEN: NSPUE2", and this copy contains no DOI line. Appendix A records the pre-standardisation source: "With these functions, this specification of CCM is essentially equivalent to the specification of CCM in the draft amendment [4] to the IEEE Standard 802.11 for wireless local area networks [5]." - Wikipedia search entry for CCM 认证与保密模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CCM%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E4%B8%8E%E4%BF%9D%E5%AF%86%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] The CCM Mode for Authentication and Confidentiality: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC
items.text: Standard : Galois/Counter Mode and GMAC (GCM 与 GMAC 模式). The title is the definition: "NIST Special Publication 800-38D Recommendation for Block Cipher Modes of Operation: Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) and GMAC", by Morris Dworkin, dated "November 2007". It standardises GCM and GMAC together — the first an encrypting authenticated mode, the second the authentication-only use. The need it serves is encryption and authentication in one verifiable construction: the document gives GCM and GMAC and devotes a separate section to the uniqueness rule, §8 "Uniqueness Requirement on IVs and Keys". §2 places conformance in the Cryptographic Module Validation Program alone, naming no other validation programme. It is used as a validated block-cipher mode: §2 routes implementations through the CMVP, and §8 bounds the collision probability explicitly: "The probability that the authenticated encryption function ever will be invoked with the same IV and the same key on two (or more) distinct sets of input data shall be no greater than 2-32." How a calling protocol arranges its keys and IVs is outside this document. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The first limit is the caution itself, which is conditional: "a breach of the requirement in Sec. 8 for the uniqueness of the initialization strings may compromise the security assurance almost entirely", followed by the advice that "this mode of operation should not be deployed unless compliance with this uniqueness requirement is ensured". The second limit: the document does address both - section 8.1 is headed Key Establishment and points at the TLS, IKEv1/v2 and SSH key-derivation functions, section 8.2 is headed IV Constructions and gives deterministic and RBG-based ways to build them - what it does not do is define a key-agreement protocol or mandate how a given protocol draws its IV; that machinery stays outside its scope. Registered period: 标准化时代. Exact dates and institutions follow the source ledger. - Wikipedia search entry for GCM 与 GMAC 模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=GCM%20%E4%B8%8E%20GMAC%20%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Galois/Counter Mode and GMAC: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: The XTS-AES Mode for Confidentiality on Storage Devices
items.text: Standard : The XTS-AES Mode for Confidentiality on Storage Devices (XTS 存储加密模式). The abstract states the act of approval: "This publication approves the XTS-AES mode of the AES algorithm by reference to IEEE Std 1619-2007, subject to one additional requirement, as an option for protecting the confidentiality of data on storage devices." The next sentence subtracts a service: "The mode does not provide authentication of the data or its source." Clause 1 places the part in the series: "This publication is the fifth Part in a series of Recommendations regarding modes of operation of symmetric key block ciphers." The algorithm steps are not restated here; the subject is one additional requirement placed on top of an external standard, plus the scope in which the mode is approved. The object comes from another standard body: §3 records "The Security in Storage Working Group (SISWG) of the P1619 Task Group of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Inc (IEEE) developed and specified XTS-AES in IEEE Std. 1619-2007 [2]." What this Recommendation adds is incorporation into an approved list with the setting fixed: "The XTS-AES mode was designed for the cryptographic protection of data on storage devices that use of fixed length “data units,” as defined in Ref. [2]." The design is traced outward: "The XTS-AES mode is an instantiation of Rogaway’s XEX (XOR Encrypt XOR) tweakable block cipher". The document presents itself as approving an external standard and stating that the mode was built for stored data rather than for encryption in general. The single additional requirement is a shall addressed to the implementation: §4 states "The length of the data unit for any instance of an implementation of XTS-AES shall not exceed 220 AES blocks." (this 220 is likewise 2 to the power 20 with the superscript lost in extraction) and immediately marks the difference in obligation level: "Note that Subclause 5.1 of Ref.[2] recommends this limit but does not require it." Conformance is then defined conditionally: "An implementation of the XTS-AES encryption mode may claim conformance with this Recommendation if every supported instance satisfies this length requirement for a data unit, in addition to all of the requirements in Clauses 1-6 of Ref. [2]." The validation route is in the same section: "Conformance testing for implementations of XTS-AES is conducted within the framework of the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP), a joint effort of NIST and the Communications Security Establishment Canada." The four sentences mark the weight of this document: the algorithm steps stay inside the external standard, NIST adds one ceiling on the data-unit length, a conformance claim requires that ceiling together with Clauses 1-6 of the external standard, and testing runs through the CMVP. The first limit is the missing service: §3 states "Authentication is not provided, because the P1619 Task Group designed XTS-AES to provide encryption without data expansion, so alternative cryptographic methods that incorporate an authentication tag are precluded." The second is the setting: "The XTS-AES mode was not designed for other purposes, such as the encryption of data in transit." The third leaves placement to the implementation: "Subclause 5.1 of [2] indicates that an implementation of XTS-AES should include a mapping between the pairs of indices that define the blocks (and possibly a single partial block) of a data unit and their physical location in the storage device, but that the mapping itself is outside the scope of the standard." And §2 makes application to national security systems conditional: "but such standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems." Read together: no authentication, no use in transit, block placement left to the implementation and the external standard, and express approval required before the guidance reaches national security systems. The running head gives number and date, "NIST Special Publication 800-38E January, 2010"; the title block is dated January 2010 with Morris Dworkin as author, and the citation line reads "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-38E, 9 pages (January 2010) CODEN: NSPUE2"; this copy contains no DOI line. The acknowledgements name the external working group and the reviewers: "The author wishes to thank Matt Ball, the Chair of the Security in Storage Working Group of the IEEE P1619 Task Group, as well as the author’s colleagues who reviewed drafts of this publication and contributed to its development, especially Elaine Barker, Lily Chen, John Kelsey, Tim Polk, Bill Burr, and Sharon Keller." The bibliography in Appendix A dates the referenced standard itself: "IEEE Std 1619-2007, The XTS-AES Tweakable Block Cipher, Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers, Inc., Apr. 18, 2008." So the 2007-numbered standard appeared in April 2008, and this Recommendation approved the mode by reference to it in January 2010. - Wikipedia search entry for XTS 存储加密模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=XTS%20%E5%AD%98%E5%82%A8%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] The XTS-AES Mode for Confidentiality on Storage Devices: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Methods for Key Wrapping
items.text: Standard : Methods for Key Wrapping (密钥包装方法). The abstract opens with the subject and both services: "This publication describes cryptographic methods that are approved for “key wrapping,” i.e., the protection of the confidentiality and integrity of cryptographic keys." The second sentence names what is new: "this publication specifies two new, deterministic authenticated-encryption modes of operation of the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm: the AES Key Wrap (KW) mode and the AES Key Wrap With Padding (KWP) mode." The third keeps one for older systems: "An analogous mode with the Triple Data Encryption Algorithm (TDEA) as the underlying block cipher, called TKW, is also specified, to support legacy applications." Clause 1 compresses the purpose: "The purpose of this part is to provide approved methods for key wrapping, i.e., the protection of cryptographic keys." The three names are the output of this part, two AES modes plus one TDEA analogue, with the protected object stated as the keys themselves; how those keys are generated is not addressed here. Section 3.1 gives the design aim first: "KW, KWP, and TKW were designed to protect the confidentiality and the authenticity/integrity of cryptographic keys." Then the reasoning: "Each provides an option for protecting keys in a manner that is distinct from the methods that protect general data." and "Segregating keys from general data can provide an extra layer of protection." The same subsection immediately withdraws any necessity: "there is no requirement to protect cryptographic keys with a distinct cryptographic method." The robustness claim is stated as "each bit of output can be expected to depend in a nontrivial fashion on each bit of input", with the next sentence pricing it in throughput. What the document supplies is an approved way to keep keys in a separate protection regime, not an obligation to do so. Section 5.1 sets the cipher and the key at shall level: "For KW and KWP, the underlying block cipher shall be approved, and the block size shall be 128 bits." and "The KEK shall be secret, i.e., disclosed only to parties that are authorized to know the protected information." Section 5.3.1 sets the length ceiling: "the plaintext for KW-AE shall be limited to fewer than 254 semiblocks" (254 here is 2 to the power 54, superscript lost). Conformance is claimed per function, six in all: §8 lists "An implementation may claim conformance to one or more of the following six functions: KWAE, KW-AD, KWP-AE, KWP-AD, TKW-AE, and TKW-AD." The validation route is in §2: "Conformance testing for implementations of this Recommendation will be conducted within the framework of the Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program (CAVP) and the Cryptographic Module Validation Program (CMVP)." and the same clause fixes the wording level: "The requirements of this Recommendation are indicated by the word “shall.”" The levels run consistently: an approved cipher with a 128-bit block, a secret KEK, a capped plaintext length, conformance claimed function by function, and testing through the CAVP and the CMVP. The first limit is the standing of the legacy variant: §8 states "TKW-AE and TKW-AD are approved to support legacy systems but should not be used for new applications." and excludes the internals on their own: "The associated wrapping and unwrapping functions, W, W-1, TW, and TW-1, are not approved for use independently of these six functions." The second is scope: §5.1 says "The management of KEKs is outside the scope of this publication." and §2 concedes a validation gap: "Some of these requirements may be out-of-scope for CMVP or CAVP validation testing, and thus are the responsibility of entities using, implementing, installing, or configuring applications that incorporate this Recommendation." The third is what determinism leaks: Appendix A.1 states "Each key-wrap algorithm in this Recommendation is deterministic: for a given designated cipher function and KEK, any invocation of the authenticated-encryption function on a given plaintext produces the same ciphertext." with the consequence "any pair of ciphertexts reveals whether the corresponding plaintexts are equal". Appendix A.5 records an external criticism: "the authors emphasize the lack of a proof that the underlying structure of KW meets the goal of deterministic authenticated encryption". The running head reads "NIST Special Publication 800-38F December 2012", the title block carries the same December 2012 date with Morris Dworkin as author, and the citation line is "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-38F, 30 pages (December 2012) CODEN: NSPUE2"; this copy contains no DOI line, and the part title is Methods for Key Wrapping. The acknowledgements list the reviewers and an early contributor: "The author wishes to thank his colleagues who reviewed drafts of this publication and contributed to its development, especially Elaine Barker, Meltem Turan, Allen Roginsky, Lily Chen, Donghoon Chang, Sharon Keller, Tim Polk, John Kelsey, Ray Perlner, Tim Hall, and Souradyuti Paul." plus "Heather Pearce worked extensively on early drafts of this publication." Section 3.2 gives the pre-standardisation timeline: "In 2001, NIST posted a document entitled “AES Key Wrap Specification”", "In 2002, two industry groups published specifications of key-wrap algorithms" and "In 2009, a different padding scheme was specified in RFC 5649 [4], referencing elements of the specification in [11]." - Wikipedia search entry for 密钥包装方法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%8C%85%E8%A3%85%E6%96%B9%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Methods for Key Wrapping: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
