items.title: NIST SP 800-38G Methods for Format-Preserving Encryption
items.text: Standard : NIST SP 800-38G Format-Preserving Encryption Modes (NIST SP 800-38G 格式保留加密模式). The abstract gives methods and placement: "This Recommendation specifies two methods, called FF1 and FF3, for format-preserving encryption." and their relation to a cipher: "Both of these methods are modes of operation for an underlying, approved symmetric-key block cipher algorithm." Ciphertext keeps the plaintext’s format — length and alphabet. The motivation is in §2: format-preserving encryption is "designed for data that is not necessarily binary" and "FPE facilitates the targeting of encryption to sensitive information, as well as the retrofitting of encryption technology to legacy applications", where fields cannot easily change length or format. The keyword line is an index entry, not an argument: "Block cipher; confidentiality; encryption; FF1; FF3; format-preserving encryption". In use, FF1/FF3 are invoked over an approved block cipher; the conformance-testing section wires it into the validation framework, and the abstract requires "an underlying, approved symmetric-key block cipher algorithm", which in implementations means AES. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The first limit is the construction: both modes are Feistel permutations over digit strings in a fixed radix built on "an underlying, approved symmetric-key block cipher algorithm", not arbitrary formats. The second is the two registers of the parameter floors: Appendix A requires radix^minlen to be at least 100 to preclude a generic meet-in-the-middle attack, while the larger figure — "the value radix minlen should generally be at least one million" — is stated as suggested rather than required. The version marks are on the title page: the date line "March 2016", the citation "Spec. Publ. 800-38G, 28 pages (March 2016)", and the masthead note "INCLUDES UPDATES AS OF 08-04-2016: PAGE I" — the edition carrying the patent-disclosure note added on 4 August 2016. §2 records one more piece of history: a third mode, FF2 (submitted as VAES3), was in the initial draft and removed after public review. - Wikipedia search entry for NIST SP 800-38G 格式保留加密模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=NIST%20SP%20800-38G%20%E6%A0%BC%E5%BC%8F%E4%BF%9D%E7%95%99%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] NIST SP 800-38G Format-Preserving Encryption Modes: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations (SP 800-53A Rev. 5)
items.text: Standard : Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations (SP 800-53A Rev. 5) (评估信息与系统中的安全与隐私控制（SP 800-53A Rev.5）). The first abstract sentence gives the two outputs and their frame: "This publication provides a methodology and set of procedures for conducting assessments of security and privacy controls employed within systems and organizations within an effective risk management framework." The next fixes what they align to: "The assessment procedures, executed at various phases of the system development life cycle, are consistent with the security and privacy controls in NIST Special Publication 800-53, Revision 5." The third characterises the procedures as a tailorable starting point: "The procedures are customizable and can be easily tailored to provide organizations with the needed flexibility to conduct security and privacy control assessments that support organizational risk management processes and are aligned with the stated risk tolerance of the organization." Section 1.1 compresses the action again: "The purpose of this publication is to provide guidelines for building effective security and privacy assessment plans, as well as a comprehensive set of procedures for assessing the effectiveness of security and privacy controls employed in systems and organizations." and names the catalogue they hang on: "The guidelines apply to the security and privacy controls defined in [SP 800-53] (as amended), Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations." The keyword line lists the outputs, including "Open Security Controls Assessment Language; OSCAL" — so this document supplies assessment procedures and their format, not the controls. The opening of Chapter One places the cause and effect: "Once employed within a system, security and privacy controls are assessed to determine their overall effectiveness (i.e., the extent to which the controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and producing the desired outcome with respect to meeting the security and privacy requirements for the system and the organization)." The Executive Summary first rules a misuse out: "Security and privacy control assessments are not about checklists, simple pass/fail results, or generating paperwork to pass inspections or audits." and states the real function: "Rather, control assessments are the principal vehicle used to verify that selected security and privacy controls are implemented and meeting stated goals and objectives." The same section names the design tension: "A major design objective for SP 800-53A is to provide an assessment framework and initial starting point for assessment procedures that are flexible enough to meet the needs of different organizations while providing consistency in conducting control assessments." and the position in the framework: "SP 800-53A addresses the Assess and Monitor steps of the RMF and provides guidance on the security and privacy control assessment processes." Section 2.3 supplies the unit of proof: "An assurance case is a body of evidence organized into an argument demonstrating that some claim about a system holds (i.e., is assured)." The gap being closed is therefore proof after selection: chosen controls are not thereby shown to be correctly implemented and working. The procedures and the judgement duties sit in numbered sections with assessors and organizations as the subjects. The printed Section 2.4, reported by this copy under the label 2.3, bounds methods and objects: "Assessment methods define the nature of the assessor actions and include examine, interview, and test." and "Assessment objects identify the specific items being assessed as part of a given control and include specifications, mechanisms, activities, and individuals." The level of effort is the organisation's call, and that sentence is printed in 2.4 as well: "The organization determines the assessment methods needed to provide the level of assurance required by the organization." Section 1.1 characterises the catalogue as a starting point, "The guidance in this publication has been developed with the intention of enabling organizations to tailor the basic assessment procedures provided." followed by "The assessment procedures are used as a starting point for and as input to the assessment plan." Section 3.2.2 puts selection on the assessor: "For each control in the security plan and privacy plan to be included in the assessment, assessors select the corresponding assessment procedure from Chapter 4." and states coverage: "SP 800-53A provides assessment procedures for each security and privacy control and control enhancement in [SP 800-53]." Section 3.2.3 gives the tailoring levels: "Organizations have the flexibility to perform the tailoring process at the organization level for all systems or common controls, at the individual system level, or using a combination of organization-level and system-specific approaches." No shall appears in the sections quoted here, whose wording is present tense or may; the copy carries exactly one shall, the conditional sentence in the Authority block quoted under the limits claim, so the absence cannot be stated for the document as a whole. Within the quoted range the obligation is allocation: assessors select procedures and organizations set rigour and frequency. The four limits sit at different levels. Section 1.1 draws the applicability line: "The security and privacy guidelines in this publication are applicable to federal systems other than those systems designated as national security systems, as defined in 44 U.S.C., Section 3542." The Authority block states the same bound conditionally: "Such information security standards and guidelines shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of the appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems." A footnote in §1.1 hands the lower layer over: "Such test scripts are at a lower level of detail than provided by the assessment procedures contained in this guidance and are, therefore, beyond the scope of this publication." The cautionary note before the Chapter Four catalogue rules out a checklist reading: "the potential assessment methods are not intended to be mandatory or exclusive." and does the same for the objects: "In addition, the set of potential assessment objects listed in the catalog are not intended to be mandatory but rather a set from which the necessary and sufficient set of objects for a given assessment can be selected to make the appropriate determinations." A further limit belongs to this extraction rather than the document: from the Chapter Four catalogue onward its procedure tables and page footers replace ligatures with private-use codepoints, ti as U+E000 and tt as U+E003, so the words print as Organiza plus U+E000 plus onal and informa plus U+E000 plus on (1215 and 2843 occurrences in that shape), while the download line in the footer reads h plus U+E003 plus ps. The literal strings Organizaonal, informaon and hps occur nowhere in the copy, and an intact https occurs 137 times. Those invisible codepoints make the damaged words unusable as quotations, so no procedure text from those blocks is quoted. The title block prints its three lines as one run, "NIST Special Publication 800-53A Revision 5 Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations JOINT TASK FORCE", the signature being an interagency body rather than named individuals; the date comes from the citation line, "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-53A, Rev. 5, 733 pages (January 2022) CODEN: NSPUE2", and the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-53Ar5. The working group is named by the first acknowledgements sentence, "This publication was developed by the Joint Task Force Interagency Working Group." which page also lists predecessors and dates the series: "The authors wanted to acknowledge the many individuals who contributed to previous versions of Special Publication 800-53A since its inception in 2005." among named officials such as the defense entry "HON. John Sherman Chief Information Officer". The edition fact comes from the front-matter formatting block: "The new format for assessment procedures introduced in Special Publication (SP) 800-53A Revision 4, is further improved in this revision (SP 800-53A Revision 5)." This copy contains no publication history block, no supersession line and no withdrawal banner; consistency of the SP 800-53 numbering is handled in a note in the same block. - Wikipedia search entry for 评估信息与系统中的安全与隐私控制（SP 800-53A Rev.5）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%AF%84%E4%BC%B0%E4%BF%A1%E6%81%AF%E4%B8%8E%E7%B3%BB%E7%BB%9F%E4%B8%AD%E7%9A%84%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E4%B8%8E%E9%9A%90%E7%A7%81%E6%8E%A7%E5%88%B6%EF%BC%88SP%20800-53A%20Rev.5%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Assessing Security and Privacy Controls in Information Systems and Organizations (SP 800-53A Rev. 5): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Recommendation for Pair-Wise Key-Establishment Schemes
items.text: Standard : Pairwise Key Agreement Schemes (成对密钥协商方案). The abstract sets the range: "This Recommendation specifies key-establishment schemes based on the discrete logarithm problem over finite fields and elliptic curves, including several variations of Diffie-Hellman and Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (MQV) key establishment schemes." Its subject is the construction and preconditions of discrete-log key establishment. It gathers a family of constructions into one implementable specification: the abstract says "This Recommendation specifies key-establishment schemes based on the discrete logarithm problem over finite fields and elliptic curves", and the keyword line indexes the scope — "Diffie-Hellman; elliptic curve cryptography; finite field cryptography; key agreement; key confirmation; key derivation; key establishment; MQV." Agreement, confirmation and derivation are treated as one system. Its use is choosing among key-establishment schemes: the document grades schemes by how many static and ephemeral key pairs they consume (the keyword line closes the family with MQV) and §5 gives the algorithm steps for the FFC and ECC primitives — the contents list carries "MQV1 Form of the FFC MQV Primitive", "Full MQV" and "One-Pass Form of the ECC MQV Primitive". Conformance and the modality vocabulary sit in the front-matter Authority and Conformance Testing blocks: "The requirements of this Recommendation are indicated by the word “shall.”" A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The first limit is the conditional wording: guidance of this kind "shall not apply to national security systems without the express approval of appropriate federal officials exercising policy authority over such systems" — application is not unconditional. The second is the validation boundary: the front matter concedes that some requirements "may be out-of-scope for CAVP or CMVP validation testing", and the omitted clause after that comma is the point — the responsibility falls on the entities using, implementing, installing or configuring the application. The title page gives authorship and edition: Elaine Barker, Lily Chen, Allen Roginsky, Apostol Vassilev and Richard Davis, with the heading "NIST Special Publication 800-56A Revision 3" and a DOI resolving to the rev3 file. Nothing in the document announces a later revision. - Wikipedia search entry for 成对密钥协商方案. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%88%90%E5%AF%B9%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%8D%8F%E5%95%86%E6%96%B9%E6%A1%88 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Pairwise Key Agreement Schemes: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes (SP 800-56C)
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes (SP 800-56C Rev. 1) (密钥建立方案中的密钥派生方法（SP 800-56C Rev. The abstract fixes the object and its origin in one sentence: "This Recommendation specifies techniques for the derivation of keying material from a shared secret established during a key-establishment scheme defined in NIST Special Publications 800-56A or 800-56B." Section 2 states that two categories are given: "This Recommendation specifies two categories of key-derivation methods that can be employed, as required, as part of a key-establishment scheme specified in [SP 800-56A] or [SP 800-56B]." The input is an agreed shared secret, not a password and not an already-held key; the methods themselves come in one-step and two-step categories. Section 1 names the gap: running a public-key scheme yields a shared secret, and only then "a key-derivation method may be required to obtain secret cryptographic keying material." Section 2 explains why the two-step category is split at all, the first step reducing the agreed secret to a single key: "Randomness extraction, to obtain a single cryptographic key-derivation key from a shared secret generated during the execution of a key-establishment scheme". What key establishment produces is not shaped to be a key, so derivation is not optional. The obligations sit in numbered sections at shall level. Section 4 bounds the implementer’s choice of the auxiliary function: "H shall be chosen in accordance with the selection requirements specified in Section 7." Section 7 expands that into hard selection rules: "Whenever a hash function is employed (including as the primitive used by HMAC), an approved hash function shall be used." Section 1 bounds how the result is computed and used: "The keying material derived using these methods shall be computed in its entirety before outputting any portion of it". The subject of all three is whoever implements and configures the scheme: pick H under §7, compute the whole block before releasing any of it, then use it only as secret keying material. The limits work at three levels. On use, §1 forbids one application outright: "The derived keying material shall not be used as a key stream for a stream cipher." On parameters, §8.2 concedes that the most sensitive input may be non-random: "This Recommendation does not require the use of a randomly selected salt value." and §8.3 excludes one combination from the two-step method: "At this time, KMAC has not been specified for use in the implementation of a two-step key derivation procedure." On testability, the conformance paragraph states that some requirements "may be out-of-scope for CAVP or CMVP validation testing, and thus are the responsibility of entities using, implementing, installing, or configuring applications that incorporate this Recommendation." The version facts come from this copy itself. The title block reads "NIST Special Publication 800-56C Revision 1" and "Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes", with the author line "Elaine Barker Lily Chen Rich Davis"; the citation line gives "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-56C Rev. 1, 37 pages (April 2018) CODEN: NSPUE2", and the free-access line is followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-56Cr1. The withdrawal banner at the head of the file states "The attached publication has been withdrawn (archived), and is provided solely for historical purposes." and records "SP 800-56C Rev. 1 is superseded in its entirety by the publication of SP 800-56C Rev. 2." The acknowledgements cover this and the earlier editions: "The authors gratefully acknowledge the contributions on this and previous versions of this document by their NIST colleagues (Quynh Dang, Sharon Keller, John Kelsey, Allen Roginsky, Meltem Sonmez Turan, Apostol Vassilev, and Tim Polk) and by Miles Smid, formerly of Orion Security Solutions."Together these are the edition facts of this copy: the part and revision number, the title as printed, the author line, the page count and month, the free-access DOI line, and the fact that Revision 1 was superseded in full and is kept only for historical purposes. - Wikipedia search entry for 密钥建立方案中的密钥派生方法（SP 800-56C Rev. 1）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%BB%BA%E7%AB%8B%E6%96%B9%E6%A1%88%E4%B8%AD%E7%9A%84%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E6%B4%BE%E7%94%9F%E6%96%B9%E6%B3%95%EF%BC%88SP%20800-56C%20Rev.%201%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Recommendation for Key-Derivation Methods in Key-Establishment Schemes (SP 800-56C Rev. 1): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Key Management
items.text: Standard : Key Management (密钥管理). Its self-definition is the first sentence of the abstract: "This Recommendation provides cryptographic key-management guidance." The next sentence says the work has three parts and that the retained file is Part 1: "Part 1 provides general guidance and best practices for the management of cryptographic keying material, including definitions of the security services that may be provided when using cryptography and the algorithms and key types that may be employed". The same abstract assigns the policy content elsewhere: "Part 2 provides guidance on policy and security planning requirements for U.S. government agencies." The first quotation names two of them — the security services cryptography can provide and the algorithms and key types that may be used — while the protection each kind of key needs is stated in the following sentences of the same abstract. The content is a framework, definitions and protection requirements, not an algorithm specification. The risk statement opens the Executive Summary: "The proper management of cryptographic keys is essential to the effective use of cryptography for security." The same page gives the cost of choosing badly: "Inappropriate choices may result in an illusion of security but little or no real security for the protocol or application." Section 1.1 repeats that judgement and names the cause it sets out to handle: "Organizations and developers are presented with many new choices in their use of cryptographic mechanisms." Read together, the two sentences say that algorithm strength does not become system security unless key management holds, and that a bad choice buys an appearance of security. Who has to do what is stated in numbered sections. Section 5.6.2 addresses procurers: "Agencies that procure systems should consider the potential operational lifetime of the system." followed immediately by a hard requirement: "The agencies shall either select algorithms and key sizes that are expected to be secure during the entire system lifetime or should ensure that the algorithms and key sizes can be easily updated." Section 6.1 puts the duty on the key information itself: "Confidentiality protection shall be provided for all secret key information" and "Integrity protection shall be provided for all key information." The wording levels split inside a single sentence: considering the operational lifetime is a should, the first branch "The agencies shall either select algorithms and key sizes that are expected to be secure during the entire system lifetime" is a shall, and the second branch "or should ensure that the algorithms and key sizes can be easily updated" falls back to should; both §6.1 protections are shall-level. The scope subsection draws two boundaries itself. The first excludes module implementation: "This Recommendation does not address the implementation details for cryptographic modules that may be used to achieve the identified security requirements." The second excludes archive and backup operations: "This Recommendation does not address the requirements or procedures for operating a key archive or backup capability other than discussing the types of keying material that are appropriate to back up or include in an archive and the protection to be provided to that keying material." The same subsection states its complementary role: "This Recommendation supplements more focused standards and guidelines." The first exclusion is followed by the handover itself: "These details are addressed in FIPS 140". Taken together the limit is this: the text specifies what protection keying material should receive, not how a module is built and not the procedures for running an archive or backup. The first two title-block lines read "NIST Special Publication 800-57 Part 1 Revision 5", the author line reads "Elaine Barker Computer Security Division Information Technology Laboratory", and the DOI line reads "This publication is available free of charge from:" followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-57pt1r5. The acknowledgements record the predecessors whose work Revision 5 carries forward: "The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) gratefully acknowledges and appreciates contributions by previous authors of this document on the many security issues associated with this Recommendation: William Barker, William Burr, and Timothy Polk from NIST; Miles Smid from Orion Security; and Lydia Zieglar from the National Security Agency." These are front-matter facts taken from the file itself: the part and revision number, the author and division, the free-access DOI line, and the named predecessors, which show that Revision 5 was rewritten on the work of the earlier authors. - Wikipedia search entry for 密钥管理. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E7%AE%A1%E7%90%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Key Management: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Digital Identity Guidelines
items.text: Standard : Digital Identity Guidelines (数字身份指南). The retained file is Part B of the guidelines rather than the umbrella document: below the number line the title block gives the part title "Authentication and Authenticator Management", and the free-access line reads "This publication is available free of charge from" line is followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63B-4, which marks it as the fourth edition of Part B. The abstract states its subject: "This guideline focuses on the authentication of subjects who interact with government information systems over networks to establish that a given claimant is a subscriber who has been previously authenticated." and states what it defines: "This document defines technical requirements for each of the three authentication assurance levels." Both phrasings agree with the part title: the output is per-level technical requirements, and the range is authentication and authenticator management. Section 1 first unpacks the term: "Authentication is the process of determining the validity of one or more authenticators used to claim a digital identity by establishing that a subject attempting to access a digital service is in control of the secrets used to authenticate." The gap being closed is the difference in attacker capability, which is what the levels encode: "Stronger authentication (i.e., a higher AAL) requires malicious actors to have better capabilities and to expend greater resources to successfully subvert the authentication process." Read together, the two sentences locate the risk in a relation rather than an algorithm: what has to be established is control over the secret, and the levels are graded by the capability and resources an attacker must expend. The duties run in both directions. Section 2 addresses the claimant: "To satisfy the requirements of a given AAL and be recognized as a subscriber, a claimant SHALL authenticate to an RP (or IdP, as described in [SP800-63C]) with a process whose strength is equal to or greater than the requirements at that level." Section 3.1.1.2 puts the concrete password constraints on verifiers and CSPs: "Verifiers and CSPs SHALL require passwords that are used as a single-factor authentication mechanism to be a minimum of 15 characters in length." and "When processing a request to establish or change a password, verifiers SHALL compare the prospective secret against a blocklist that contains known commonly used, expected, or compromised passwords." The three quotations bind both ends at once: the claimant must use a process at least as strong as the level, while verifiers and CSPs carry shall-level duties on password length and on blocklist comparison. The limits are stated in four places. The abstract bounds the purpose: "The guidelines are not intended to constrain the development or use of standards outside of this purpose." Section 1 bounds the setting: "It does not address the authentication of a person for physical access (e.g., to a building)." The same section concedes that voluntary disclosure is out of reach: "The protections at the various AALs are intended to protect against credential theft and are not intended to protect against willful disclosure of credential secrets by a subscriber." And section 3.1.1 is blunt about the most common credential: "Passwords are not phishing-resistant." Read together: standards development outside this purpose is not constrained, physical access authentication is not handled, deliberate sharing or disclosure by a subscriber meets no technical countermeasure here, and passwords by themselves do not resist phishing. The title block line reads "NIST SP 800-63B-4 Digital Identity Guidelines Authentication and Authenticator Management", i.e. the fourth edition of Part B, and the abstract records the supersession: "This publication supersedes NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-63B." The publication-history block names the edition it replaces, "Supersedes NIST SP 800-63B (June 2017; updated March 2, 2020)", and the review date, "Approved by the NIST Editorial Review Board on 2025-05-30." The citation line gives the seven authors and the year: "Temoshok D, Fenton JL, Choong YY, Lefkovitz N, Regenscheid A, Galluzzo R, Richer JP (2025) Digital Identity Guidelines: Authentication and Authenticator Management." The title block is dated July 2025 with the DOI DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-63B-4. The umbrella Part 1 and Parts A and C are separate publications and are not in this file. items.title: Recommendation for Random Number Generation Using Deterministic RBGs
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for Random Number Generation (随机数发生器建议). The abstract defines it in one sentence: "This Recommendation specifies mechanisms for the generation of random bits using deterministic methods." with the construction basis: "The methods provided are based on either hash functions or block cipher algorithms." This is a deterministic bit-generator specification, not an entropy-source specification. The problem is verifiable random-number generators: the abstract states the scope — "This Recommendation specifies mechanisms for the generation of random bits using deterministic methods. The methods provided are based on either hash functions or block cipher algorithms." — and §1 puts the burden on the seed — "The seed used to instantiate the DRBG must contain sufficient entropy to provide an assurance of randomness." The keyword line reads "Deterministic random bit generator (DRBG)" — an index entry, not an argument. It is used as a component inside a validated module, and the direction of the citation runs the other way around: the document states a requirement rather than citing one — "A cryptographic module containing a DRBG mechanism shall be validated (see [FIPS 140])." — while the consuming application or service must supply entropy and prediction resistance under the document’s own rules for entropy and prediction resistance. items.title: Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation (SP 800-90B)
items.text: Standard : Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation (SP 800-90B) (随机数生成用熵源建议（SP 800-90B）). The abstract names the two subjects: "This Recommendation specifies the design principles and requirements for the entropy sources used by Random Bit Generators, and the tests for the validation of entropy sources." and the division of labour with its siblings: "These entropy sources are intended to be combined with Deterministic Random Bit Generator mechanisms that are specified in SP 800-90A to construct Random Bit Generators, as specified in SP 800-90C." Its object is the entropy source, not the generator algorithm.The two sentences fix the object and the place: design principles, requirements and validation testing for entropy sources are specified here, while the finished generator is left to SP 800-90A and SP 800-90C, so no generator algorithm is defined in this file. Section 1.1 starts from the practical difficulty: "However, the generation of random bits is problematic in many practical applications of cryptography." and hands over the hardest part: "The development of entropy sources that construct unpredictable outputs is difficult, and providing guidance for their design and validation testing is even more so." The same subsection makes the testing approach conditional on the developer understanding the source, while §2.2.1 raises the noise source to the root of everything: "The noise source is the root of security for the entropy source and for the RBG as a whole."The three form one chain: random bits are hard to produce in practice, the hard part is the entropy source, and the difficulty there is design plus verifiable testing; calling the noise source the root of security puts the foundation of the whole random-bit apparatus on that layer. The duties fall on the implementer and submitter, written with shall. Section 4.3 fixes the test composition: "The health tests shall include both continuous and start-up tests." and the reaction on failure: "When the health tests fail, the entropy source shall notify the consuming application", leaving the consuming generator to act on it. Section 4.4 hands the threshold to the developer: "The developer of the entropy source shall determine a reasonable probability of type I error". The measure itself is set out in §2.1: "this Recommendation uses a very conservative measure known as min-entropy, which measures the effectiveness of the strategy of guessing the most likely output of the entropy source."The quotations give the measure and the duty at once: min-entropy is the conservative yardstick, the test composition and the failure notification are shall-level, while the error probability and cutoff values are left to the developer judging the noise source. The first limit is when testing happens: §4.2 requires only the capability for on-demand tests — "This Recommendation does not require performing testing during operation." — and the note in the same subsection says the start-up conditions belong to FIPS 140, since "This document imposes no additional requirements for the use of start-up health testing." The second is testability: the conformance paragraph concedes that some requirements "may be out-of-scope for CAVP or CMVP validation testing". The third is that the document stands alone nowhere: "SP 800-90A addresses the construction of approved DRBG mechanisms, while SP 800-90C addresses the construction of RBGs from the mechanisms in SP 800-90A and the entropy sources in SP 800-90B." The finished random bit generator lives in the other two. The title block opens "NIST Special Publication 800-90B" with the title line "Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation" and author lines carrying "Kerry A. McKay Mary L. Baish Mike Boyle" (the first author’s name carries a diacritic in the retained title block, so the name sits outside the quotation to keep every quoted span verbatim-checkable); the date line is January 2018, the citation reads "Natl. Inst. Stand. Technol. Spec. Publ. 800-90B, 84 pages (January 2018) CODEN: NSPUE2" and the free-access line is followed by the DOI 10.6028/NIST.SP.800-90B. The acknowledgements name the helpers: "The authors of this Recommendation gratefully acknowledge and appreciate contributions by their colleagues at NIST, Apostol Vassilev and Timothy A. Hall". Section 1.1 records the parallel standard: "This Recommendation was developed in concert with American National Standard (ANS) X9.82, a multi-part standard on random number generation." - Wikipedia search entry for 随机数生成用熵源建议（SP 800-90B）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%9A%8F%E6%9C%BA%E6%95%B0%E7%94%9F%E6%88%90%E7%94%A8%E7%86%B5%E6%BA%90%E5%BB%BA%E8%AE%AE%EF%BC%88SP%20800-90B%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Recommendation for the Entropy Sources Used for Random Bit Generation (SP 800-90B): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SPAKE2+ Password-Authenticated Key Exchange
items.text: Protocol : SPAKE2+, an Augmented Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) Protocol (SPAKE2+ 口令认证密钥交换). The abstract defines the mechanism: "This document describes SPAKE2+, a Password-Authenticated Key Exchange (PAKE) protocol run between two parties for deriving a strong shared key with no risk of disclosing the password." and states the variant: "SPAKE2+ is an augmented PAKE protocol, as only one party has knowledge of the password." The motivation is that a password must not be exposed by the exchange: the abstract states the goal as "deriving a strong shared key with no risk of disclosing the password" and bundles the engineering claims with it — "This method is simple to implement, compatible with any prime-order group, and computationally efficient." The placement is in §1: the augmented property is valuable where execution is constrained and the adversary cannot query the salt of the password-hashing function ahead of the attack, and the document names two constraints — "a constraint may be when physical proximity through a local network is required or when a first authentication factor is required for initiation of the protocol." The abstract gives the general shape: only one party holds the password, yet authentication and a session key result. items.title: Secure Real-time Transport Protocol
items.text: Protocol : Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP 安全实时传输). The abstract supplies both placement and capability list: "This document describes the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP), a profile of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), which can provide confidentiality, message authentication, and replay protection to the RTP traffic and to the control traffic for RTP, the Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)." It is a cryptographic profile of RTP, covering media and control traffic. The abstract states the services it adds to RTP and its control protocol: "a profile of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), which can provide confidentiality, message authentication, and replay protection to the RTP traffic and to the control traffic for RTP, the Real-time Transport Control Protocol (RTCP)." The wording is can provide — the services depend on the selected cipher suite and on key management rather than being unconditional. In practice it secures audio, video and interactive sessions: the document places itself as "a profile of the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP)" and its framework section defines cryptographic contexts and packet processing, applied on top of existing RTP payloads by voice and video-conferencing implementations. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The first limit: no key-management protocol is specified. §1 makes security conditional — "With appropriate key management (Sections 7 and 8), SRTP is secure (Sections 9) for unicast and multicast RTP applications (Section 11)." — and §8, Key Management Considerations, constrains whatever key management is used without defining an agreement protocol. The second limit is scope: protection covers RTP and RTCP traffic, not the application protocols carried inside them. items.title: Argon2 Memory-Hard KDF
items.text: Algorithm : Argon2 (Argon2 口令派生). Section 1 gives the character: "Argon2 is a memory-hard function [HARD]. It is a streamlined design." The family structure is printed in the same passage: "Argon2 has one primary variant, Argon2id, and two supplementary variants, Argon2d and Argon2i." So Argon2 is a family with exactly one primary member. The goal is stated in cost-model terms: "It aims at the highest memory-filling rate and effective use of multiple computing units, while still providing defense against trade-off attacks." The metric is not hashes per second but how completely memory is filled and how many compute units are used, without letting time-memory trade-offs win. The hardware posture follows: "Argon2 is optimized for the x86 architecture and exploits the cache and memory organization of the recent Intel and AMD processors." Selection and implementation duty are both in the text. The division of labour: "Argon2i uses data-independent memory access, which is preferred for password hashing and password-based key derivation." The normative floor: "Argon2id MUST be supported by any implementation of this document, whereas Argon2d and Argon2i MAY be supported." So any implementation claiming conformance must support the primary variant; the other two are optional. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limits fall out of the same division: Argon2d's data-dependent access is precisely the side-channel timing surface, which is why the text confines it to scenarios "with no threats from side-channel timing attacks". The text does claim complete prevention of one family, conditionally: to completely prevent the time-memory trade-offs of the cited work the number of passes must exceed the binary logarithm of memory minus 26 - so this entry reads the position as a conditional defence rather than a claim that trade-offs are eliminated in general - the wording is "providing defense against trade-off attacks", defence rather than proof - and Argon2i additionally "makes more passes over the memory to protect from trade-off attacks", buying safety with extra passes and therefore extra cost. Version facts: the abstract pins the algorithm release - "corresponds to version 1.3 of the Argon2 hash function." The header prints Request for Comments: 9106, Category: Informational, March 2021, by Bassham and Liu (restated outside quotes per house rule). items.title: ChaCha20 Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : ChaCha20 (ChaCha20 流密码). Section 2.4 gives the identity and lineage: "ChaCha20 is a stream cipher designed by D. Bernstein. It is a refinement of the Salsa20 algorithm, and it uses a 256-bit key." The same section describes the mechanism: "ChaCha20 successively calls the ChaCha20 block function, with the same key and nonce, and with successively increasing block counter parameters." So it is not one permutation per message: under one key and nonce, an increasing block counter stitches block-function outputs into a keystream. The parameter list lays out the constraints: "A 256-bit key, treated as a concatenation of eight 32-bit…integers." and "A 96-bit nonce, treated as a concatenation of three 32-bit…integers." (the retained file breaks the word little-endian at a line end; the ellipsis marks only that break and no wording is altered). §2.3 then states the one hard requirement on that nonce: "Words 13-15 are a nonce, which MUST not be repeated for the same key." The security condition is handed to the caller - the cipher does not detect repeats, so a repeat is the protocol's problem. In use the cipher is length-agnostic: "There is no requirement for the plaintext to be an integral multiple of 512 bits. If there is extra keystream from the last block, it is discarded." The same section permits streaming: "each keystream block can be XORed with a plaintext block before proceeding to create the next block, saving some memory." Length and padding rules therefore belong to the protocol, not the algorithm. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Two limits. §2.6.2 volunteers the first: "Chacha20 could be used as a key-derivation function, by generating an arbitrarily long keystream. However, that is not what protocols such as IKEv2 require." (the document prints the name as Chacha20 here, quoted as printed) - so it is not a KDF. The second follows from the §2.3 nonce condition: repeating a nonce under one key repeats the keystream, so two plaintexts leak their difference, and nothing in the cipher detects the repeat. Version facts: §2.3 states the choice this document makes - "The ChaCha algorithm described here uses a 256-bit key." - pinning the divergence from Bernstein's paper to key length. The header prints Request for Comments: 8439, Category: Informational, August 2018, by Nir and Woodbury (header furniture is restated outside quotes and never presented as an algorithm property). What entered IETF specification is the 256-bit-key branch, not every variant in the paper. - Wikipedia search entry for ChaCha20 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ChaCha20%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] ChaCha20: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.text: Algorithm : Poly1305 (Poly1305 通用 MAC). Section 2.5 states the interface outright: "Poly1305 is a one-time authenticator designed by D. Bernstein. Poly1305 takes a 32-byte one-time key and a message and produces a 16-byte tag. This tag is used to authenticate the message." The operative word is one-time: this is not a reusable MAC key but a fresh 32-byte input per message. Why the IETF rewrote the original: §2.5 records what the prototype cost - it lists an AES key, an additional key and a non-secret 128-bit nonce (the phrase for the additional key carries ASCII quotes in the retained file, so it is not quoted verbatim here) - and explains the AES role: "AES is used there for encrypting the nonce, so as to get a unique (and secret) 128-bit string". RFC 8439 removes that AES dependence by deriving the one-time key from ChaCha20, so platforms without hardware AES can still use it safely. Usage is bound to ChaCha20: in the AEAD construction of §2.6 and its subsection §2.6.2 the first block-function output is reused, "And that output is also the 32-byte one-time key used for Poly1305.", and the same section fixes the keying: "The 256-bit session integrity key is used as the ChaCha20 key." So a deployment layers its keys - the protocol supplies a 256-bit integrity key and ChaCha20 derives a per-message Poly1305 key from it. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limit is stated plainly in §2.6.2: "Poly1305 is not a suitable choice for a PRF. Poly1305 prohibits using the same key twice, whereas the PRF in IKEv2 is used multiple times with the same key. Additionally, unlike HMAC, Poly1305 is biased, so using it for key derivation would reduce the security of the symmetric encryption." Two consequences: key reuse breaks it, and it must not serve as a PRF or for key derivation. The lineage is printed alongside the definition in §2.5: the original article title (which carries ASCII quotes in the source and is therefore not quoted here) names Poly1305-AES and needs AES plus two 128-bit key materials; RFC 8439 recast it as an AES-free one-time authenticator inside the ChaCha20 AEAD construction. items.title: SM3 Cryptographic Hash Function
items.text: Algorithm : SM3 (SM3 国密杂凑). What this workspace can attest is narrow but explicit (§1.1): "SM3 is a hash function that produces an output of 256 bits." That is RFC 8998's entire positive description - algorithm class and digest length. The internal compression function, message expansion and iteration structure belong to GB/T 32905-2016, which is neither retained here nor reachable from this workspace, so this entry does not restate those details or fill them in from outside memory. Why an IETF document was needed is visible in the §1.1 standardization sentence: "SM3 has already been accepted by ISO in ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018 [ISO-SM3] and has also been described by [GBT.32905-2016]." A hash already inside an ISO standard and defined by a Chinese national document had no algorithm identity in TLS; RFC 8998 closes that interoperability gap rather than redefining SM3's strength. Use lands in TLS 1.3, per the §1 introduction: "This document describes two new cipher suites, a signature algorithm and a key exchange mechanism for the Transport Layer Security (TLS) protocol version 1.3 (TLS 1.3) ([RFC8446]). These all utilize several ShangMi (SM) cryptographic algorithms to fulfill the authentication and confidentiality requirements of TLS 1.3." SM3's practical role is therefore the hash behind those suites and the signature algorithm; the suites are registered as TLS_SM4_GCM_SM3 and TLS_SM4_CCM_SM3. items.title: Bilinear Pairing (Tate and Modified Tate)
items.text: Algorithm : Bilinear Pairing (双线性配对). Section 2.1 of the retained text gives the defining trio: "a mathematical construction known as the Tate pairing provides an efficiently computable map e: G1' x G1'' - G2 that is linear in both arguments and believed hard to invert [BF]." The three requirements are efficient computability, linearity in both arguments and conjectured inversion hardness - every use of pairings rests on that combination. Why it needs specifying at all: §1 of the retained text names the downstream purpose in one phrase - the document serves "identity-based encryption (IBE) systems based on bilinear pairings". Whether a curve can serve depends on extra structure printed in §2.1: "If an efficiently computable non-rational endomorphism phi: G1' - …is available for the selected elliptic curve on which the Tate pairing is computed" (the sentence straddles a page break in the retained file; the ellipsis marks only the skipped header and footer). That endomorphism is what yields the modified pairing identity-based schemes use. Naming and selection are printed in §2.1 of the retained text: "called the modified Tate pairing. We generically call a pairing either the Tate pairing e or the modified Tate pairing e', depending on the chosen elliptic curve used in a particular implementation." Engineering-wise the choice is not free: the curve decides which of the two constructions an implementation can use. items.title: Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM)
items.text: Algorithm : Counter with CBC-MAC (CCM 计数器 CBC 模式). CCM's construction reuses one key across both primitives, printed in §5.2 as the same key: "The same key, K, is used for both the CTR and CBC-MAC mechanisms within CCM.". It protects two kinds of input: "The data that CCM protects consists of a message, i.e., a bit string, called the payload, denoted P, of bit length denoted Plen, and a bit string, called the associated data" - the payload is encrypted, the associated data is only authenticated, and both enter the MAC. Why combine them: §3 specifies CCM as a pairing of processes - "CCM consists of two related processes: generation-encryption and decryption-verification, which combine two cryptographic primitives". One block cipher therefore delivers both confidentiality and authenticity instead of two separate machinery sets, and the shared-key sentence in §5.2 is how that choice is realised. The deployment motive is stated in §3 as interoperability: "This specification of CCM is intended to be compatible with the use of CCM within the draft amendment [4] to the IEEE Standard 802.11 for wireless local area networks [5]." The recommendation exists to align with how CCM was already used in wireless LAN standardisation. Truncation is a mandatory design decision, stated in Appendix B: "The length, Tlen, of the MAC within CCM is an important security parameter." A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limits hang on two parameters. Nonce uniqueness: the document requires "a unique value, called a nonce, that is assigned to the payload and the associated data" - repeating it puts both the confidentiality and the authenticity of the combined mode at risk. Tag length: since Tlen is named "an important security parameter", truncating it hard is a self-inflicted reduction of authentication strength, not a harmless byte saving. Version facts: the document presents itself as part of the block cipher modes series and grounds its motive in compatibility with the IEEE 802.11 draft amendment (quoted from §1). The retained copy is dated May 2004. So CCM was already in use in wireless standardisation before it became a federal recommendation; this publication generalises an existing combined construction rather than inventing one. items.title: Cipher-based Message Authentication Code (CMAC)
items.text: Algorithm : CMAC (CMAC 分组密码 MAC). Section 5.2 of the retained text states the structural relation: "The CMAC algorithm depends on the choice of an underlying symmetric key block cipher. The CMAC algorithm is thus a mode of operation (a mode, for short) of the block cipher. The CMAC key is the block cipher key (the key, for short)." So CMAC carries no cipher of its own: it selects a block cipher and reuses that cipher's key as the MAC key. The §4.1 definition of a MAC gives the property of the output: "A bit string of fixed length, computed by a MAC generation algorithm, that is used to establish the authenticity and, hence, the integrity of a message." The motive sits in the first sentence of §3, naming the deficiency of what it replaces: "The basic Cipher Block Chaining MAC algorithm (CBC-MAC) has security deficiencies [9]." The text then identifies the core of CMAC as the XCBC variant proposed and analysed by Black and Rogaway. In other words, CMAC exists not to add another MAC but to patch a known weakness of CBC-MAC while still running on a block cipher. The operational constraint is printed in §5.5: "The length of T, denoted Tlen, is a parameter that shall be fixed for all invocations of CMAC with the given key." The truncation length is therefore fixed per key and cannot be chosen message by message, with §5.4 handing the selection requirements to an appendix. Deployments use one key with one fixed tag length rather than mixing tag lengths under the same key. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Three limits are checkable. First, the replacement relation itself: §3 says CBC-MAC "has security deficiencies [9]", so chaining encryptions and using the result as a MAC is unsafe, and CMAC is the correction. Second, the dependency printed in §5.2: "The CMAC algorithm depends on the choice of an underlying symmetric key block cipher" — a broken block cipher takes CMAC's security with it. Third, the converse of §5.4: Tlen must stay fixed for all invocations under a given key, so mixing tag lengths departs from the text. items.title: Cryptographically Secure Pseudorandom Number Generator (DRBG)
items.text: Algorithm : Cryptographically Secure PRNG (密码学安全伪随机数发生器). Section 1 opens with the characterisation: "This Recommendation specifies techniques for the generation of random bits that may then be used directly or converted to random numbers when random values are required by applications using cryptography." It specifies bit generation; numbers are a downstream conversion. The document's own footnote fixes the naming: "DRBGs have also been called Pseudorandom Number (or Bit) Generators", so what is loosely called a CSPRNG is normalised here under the name DRBG. The rationale is legible in the definitions. Live Entropy Source is defined as "A bitstring output from an entropy source, an NRBG or a DRBG that has access to a Live Entropy Source that is being used to provide prediction resistance", so prediction resistance is what forces a live entropy input. Approved entropy source is defined as "An entropy source that has been validated as conforming to [SP 800-90B]". A DRBG exists to expand a validated entropy stream into bits on demand, not to manufacture entropy. The usage boundary is printed in §4. Approved entropy source requires an entropy source "validated as conforming to [SP 800-90B]", so a deployment's duty is to have the source validated rather than to assert it. The same section describes the generator as comprising instantiation, uninstantiation, pseudorandom-bit generation, optional reseeding and health testing, which is the interface through which key and nonce generation consume it. The limit is printed in §1 as a systems statement: "The security provided by an RBG that uses a DRBG mechanism is a system implementation issue; both the DRBG mechanism and its randomness source must be considered when determining whether the RBG is appropriate for use by consuming applications." A conforming mechanism is not by itself a conforming generator; the upstream randomness source must be assessed with it. §4 supplies the yardstick: "In the context of random bit generation, an output bit is unpredictable if an adversary has only a negligible advantage (that is, essentially not much better than chance) in predicting it correctly." Once entropy input is missing or reseeding lapses, that condition no longer holds. Version facts: the retained title line reads "Recommendation for Random Number Generation Using Deterministic RBGs" — SP 800-90A Rev. 1 (June 2015) — with keyword line "Deterministic random bit generator (DRBG); entropy; hash function; random number generator." The text then notes that "NIST Special Publication (SP) 800-90B [SP 800-90B] provides guidance on designing and validating entropy sources", so the 2015 document governs deterministic generators while entropy-source validation moved to SP 800-90B. - Wikipedia search entry for 密码学安全伪随机数发生器. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E5%AD%A6%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E4%BC%AA%E9%9A%8F%E6%9C%BA%E6%95%B0%E5%8F%91%E7%94%9F%E5%99%A8 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Cryptographically Secure PRNG: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)
items.text: Algorithm : Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA 椭圆曲线签名). The scope sentence sets the frame: "This standard defines methods for digital signature generation that can be used for the protection of binary data (commonly called a message) and for the verification and validation of those digital signatures." §4 then fixes ECDSA's place in it: "The Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA) is specified in this standard." So ECDSA is not a standalone specification but one algorithm inside the Digital Signature Standard. Why the standard takes it up is told in §1 as provenance plus a gap: "ECDSA was originally specified in American National Standards (ANS) X9.62 [3] (withdrawn)." - the original home is a withdrawn ANSI standard. The standard therefore has to specify the method itself, and the same passage records a deterministic variant, showing that what is folded in is not only the algorithm but also the repair of its dependence on a per-signature random value. Usage is bounded by two normative sentences. Key division: "The private key shall be used only for signature generation, as specified in this standard, and shall be kept secret." Verification coupling: "A digital signature shall be verified as specified in Section 6.4.2 using the same domain parameters and hash function that were used during signature generation." Changing curve parameters or the hash breaks verification, so deployments must pin the parameter set and hash together. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Three limits. First, the §3 key duty: the private key is only for signature generation and must stay secret, so disclosure is equivalent to forgery. Second, the deterministic variant recorded in §4 exists because the basic form needs a secure random value per signature - the standard lists the repair separately. Third is the withdrawn fact in the same section: X9.62, ECDSA's original specification, is withdrawn, so any implementation note citing only X9.62 rests on a source that no longer stands. The lineage follows two printed sentences: ECDSA was first specified in the now-withdrawn ANSI X9.62 and was then folded into the Digital Signature Standard, while "A variant of ECDSA with a deterministic signature generation" is listed in the same passage, giving the deterministic reform a place in this standard too. The document's own identity - FIPS 186-5, published June 2023, superseding FIPS 186-4 - is restated outside quotes per house rule. items.text: Standard : Security requirements for cryptographic modules (密码模块安全要求). The positioning fact this entry can attest is printed in §1 of FIPS 140-3: "FIPS 140-3 supersedes FIPS140-2. FIPS 140-3 aligns with ISO/IEC 19790:2012(E) and includes modifications of the Annexes that are allowed to CMVP (as a validation authority)." Alignment lets one set of module requirements enter international recognition instead of each jurisdiction maintaining incomparable criteria. The decision rule is printed in the security-level sentence: "must be chosen to provide a level of security appropriate for the security requirements of the application and environment" Levels are not maximised but matched to the deployment, and validation proceeds against the aligned requirements, which is how procurement and compliance assessment read them. items.title: KECCAK Message Authentication Code (KMAC)
items.text: Algorithm : KMAC (KMAC 基于散列的 MAC). The construction is printed in §4.3: "KMAC concatenates a padded version of the key K with the input X and an encoding of the requested output length L. The result is then passed to cSHAKE, along with the requested output length L, the name N" — the key is byte-aligned and padded, then the input and an encoding of the output length go to cSHAKE with the function name as domain separation. §1 groups it with the other derived functions: "All four functions defined in this Recommendation--cSHAKE, KMAC, TupleHash, and ParallelHash--have these properties in common:" Two sentences carry the rationale. §1 characterises KMAC as a member of the keyed, variable-output pseudorandom-function family the document defines. §5 states the comparison explicitly: "To illustrate the security properties of KMAC for given parameter settings, Table 1 lists a few other approved MAC algorithms along with equivalent settings" — so KMAC exists to offer choices aligned with HMAC and CMAC inside the SHA-3 family rather than to invent a new strength yardstick. Section 4 prints both uses. The fixed-length use is the function itself, KMAC128(K, X, L, S), whose second step returns the cSHAKE128 result directly. The variable-length use is spelled out: "Some applications of KMAC may not know the number of output bits they will need until after the outputs begin to be produced. For these applications, KMAC can also be used as a XOF (i.e., the output can be extended to any desired length)" - KMACXOF serves consumers that do not know their bit requirement up front. The limit is a normative sentence with teeth: "Approved uses of KMAC require the length of K to be at least the required security strength, as discussed in Sec. 8.4.1." An undersized key defeats approved use outright. The validity conditions printed alongside it, "Validity Conditions: len(K) < 22040 and 0 L < 22040 and len(S) < 22040" (this copy flattens the superscripts into running digits); outside those bounds the function is undefined. The version facts come from the retained text itself: the title line reads "SHA-3 DERIVED FUNCTIONS: CSHAKE, KMAC, TUPLEHASH, AND PARALLELHASH", so SP 800-185 (December 2022) is where these four derived functions were standardised together. §2.1 supplies the earlier link while defining the KECCAK family: "KECCAK was originally specified in [2], and standardized in FIPS 202." The same section records that KMAC stands for KECCAK Message Authentication Code. The retained copy also prints a free-availability line with a digital object identifier on every page; by house rule that line is not quoted into the article. - Wikipedia search entry for KMAC 基于散列的 MAC. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=KMAC%20%E5%9F%BA%E4%BA%8E%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97%E7%9A%84%20MAC - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[T=\mathrm{MAC}_K(M),\quad \Pr[\mathrm{Forge}]\le\varepsilon(\lambda)\] KMAC: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Key Wrapping (KW, KWP, TKW)
items.text: Algorithm : Key Wrap (KW 密钥包装). Section 5.1 gives the structure and the key name: "The transformations of the variants of KW feature a block cipher as the main component; thus, each variant is a mode of operation (mode, for short) of the block cipher. The key for the underlying block cipher is called the key encryption key (KEK), denoted K." The §4.1 definition of the integrity check value shows why wrapping is not plain encryption: "A fixed string that is prepended to the plaintext within the authenticated-encryption function of a key-wrap algorithm, in order to enable the verification of the integrity of the plaintext within the authenticated-decryption function." Section 1 states the purpose outright: "The purpose of this part is to provide approved methods for key wrapping, i.e., the protection of cryptographic keys." The protected object is a key, and §3.1 widens the scope: "Similarly, KW, KWP, and TKW are each approved for the protection of general data, as well as cryptographic keys." Together these give the motive: keys at rest and in transit need confidentiality and integrity together, which ordinary encryption supplies only half of. Usage follows from two sentences. §3.1 says "KW, KWP, and TKW are each approved for the protection of general data, as well as cryptographic keys", so all three variants serve general data too; §5.1 says "each variant is a mode of operation (mode, for short) of the block cipher", so implementations plug them in as block cipher modes. Key stores, HSMs and key-distribution paths therefore wrap protected keys under a KEK, with KWP covering padded cases and TKW the non-AES case. The limit is printed in the definition of the decryption function: "A function that decrypts purported ciphertext into corresponding plaintext and verifies the authenticity and, therefore, the integrity of the data. The output is either the plaintext or an indication that the plaintext is not authentic." Wrapping offers no best-effort decryption: verification failure returns no plaintext, so an attacker cannot probe with partially decrypted output. The same section defines authenticity in this context as originating from an entity holding an implementation of the authenticated-encryption function with the KEK. Section 1 places the document in its series: "This publication is the sixth part in a series of Recommendations regarding the modes of operation of block ciphers." Section 3.1 fixes the boundary with earlier specifications: "In 2009, a different padding scheme was specified in RFC 5649 [4], referencing elements of the specification in [11]. The resulting algorithm, called AES Key Wrap With Padding, is essentially equivalent to KWP as specified in this Recommendation." RFC 3394 (2002) and RFC 5649 (2009) therefore precede this December 2012 recommendation. - Wikipedia search entry for KW 密钥包装. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=KW%20%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%8C%85%E8%A3%85 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Key Wrap: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: HashML-DSA Pre-Hash Signature Variant
items.text: Algorithm : HashML-DSA (HashML-DSA 混合签名). The variant's identity is two facts printed in its §3 definition: it "includes an additional pre-hashing step before signing" and "It consists of three main algorithms: ML-DSA.KeyGen (Algorithm 1), which is the same key generation algorithm used for ML-DSA; HashML-DSA.Sign (Algorithm 4); and HashML-DSA.Verify (Algorithm 5)." So the key layer is ML-DSA's, and only signing and verification are replaced by the pre-hashed versions. Why the extra step exists is stated as the variant's defining feature: the additional pre-hashing step quoted above. The §3 definition states this, so the engineering reading follows directly - the signature consumes a digest rather than an arbitrarily long message, so callers can fold large data into a fixed-size input before the internal encoding runs. That the standard specifies this branch alongside ML-DSA means pre-hashing is a normalised option, not an implementer's private modification. The compliance frame is defined in §1.4: a technique is approved when it is specified in a FIPS or NIST recommendation, adopted in one, or listed among NIST-approved security functions (restated in prose from the printed numbered list rather than quoted, to keep the numbering artefacts out of the article). For users this means HashML-DSA is wired in as an approved signature method inside FIPS 204's scope, on the same footing as ML-DSA - not as a post-quantum candidate. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Two limits. First, hash coupling: a pre-hashed variant's behaviour is set by the chosen hash, and the standard numbering its Sign/Verify separately from ML-DSA means a different hash or preprocessing is no longer the same algorithm and cannot be mixed. Second, the determinism caveat: the document's §2.1 pseudorandom definition reads "effectively random as long as the internal action of the process is hidden from observation", so if an implementation leaks intermediate values that argument no longer holds. items.title: RSA Signature Schemes (PKCS #1 v2.2)
items.text: Algorithm : RSA Signature (RSA 签名). The document specifies two signature schemes with their own encoding methods, listed after §8: "employed in the signature schemes and are specified here: EMSA-PSS and EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5." So RSA signing is not one thing but two routes: v1.5, simple and deterministic, and PSS, which folds a random salt and a mask generation function into the encoding - both standardised by the same document. Why PSS exists is visible in what §9.1 lets you choose: "This encoding method is parameterized by the choice of hash function, mask generation function, and salt length." Salt and mask make the encoding probabilistic, so the same message signs twice to different results, and the security argument can rest on clearer assumptions - the document draws this contrast against the deterministic schemes. Use splits between encoding choice and implementation duty. The encoding layer offers EMSA-PSS and EMSA-PKCS1-v1_5 (cited in the principle claim), while the implementation layer gives concrete countermeasures for v1.5 decoding: "rigorous checking of PKCS 1 v1.5 conformance (and other redundancy) in decrypted messages, and the consolidation of error messages in a client-server protocol based on PKCS 1 v1.5." Keeping v1.5 therefore obliges strict decode checking and merged error reporting. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limits are legible in the countermeasures themselves: a whole discussion of v1.5 decoding is needed precisely because its implementation-level failure mode is known - distinguishable error messages become an oracle. PSS in turn depends on parameter choices (hash, mask generation function, salt length, as quoted above); extreme settings such as a zero-length salt collapse it back to a deterministic form. Finally this document is Informational: its authority describes PKCS 1 rather than conferring a standards-body strength rating. Version facts, restated from the printed lines (header furniture stays outside quotes): this is RFC 8017, PKCS 1 v2.2, November 2016, edited by Moriarty, Kaliski and Rusch, Category: Informational. items.title: True Random Number Generator (Entropy Source)
items.text: Algorithm : True Random Number Generator (真随机数发生器). Section 2.1 describes the model and its parts: "This section describes the entropy source model in detail. Figure 1 illustrates the model that this Recommendation uses to describe an entropy source and its components, which consist of a noise source, an optional conditioning component and a health testi" — true randomness is traced to a sampled noise process. §2.2 places digitisation: "If the non-deterministic activity being sampled produces something other than binary data, the sampling process includes a digitization process that converts the output samples to bits. The output of the digitized noise source is called the raw data." The necessity is stated through the root-of-security claim: "The noise source is the root of security for the entropy source and for the RBG as a whole. This is the component that contains the non-deterministic, entropy-providing process that is ultimately responsible for the uncertainty associated with the bitstrin". Every uncertainty in the random-bit system ultimately rests on that non-deterministic process, which is the argument for needing a true source; a purely algorithmic expander has no such property. What a deployment does is prescribed by this document. §1.1 names the audience: "This Recommendation is intended for use by entropy source developers (the entity that designs and builds the entropy source or a portion thereof), submitters1 (the entity that submits the entropy". §2 layers the safeguards: "The health tests can be separated into three categories: start-up tests, continuous tests (primarily on the noise source), and on-demand tests" - a true source is guarded by start-up, continuous and on-demand health tests before a registered mechanism draws from it; throughout, the document calls such a device an entropy source or an NRBG, that is, a hardware random number generator. The limit and the failure mode are printed in the same section: "If the noise source fails to generate random outputs, no other component in the RBG can compensate for the lack of entropy; hence, no security guarantees can be made for the application relying on the RBG." Neither health tests nor conditioning can substitute for the noise itself. Hence the document states its assumption directly: "This Recommendation assumes that the sample values (i.e., the symbols) obtained from a noise source consist of fixed-length bitstrings". Version facts: the keyword line reads "Conditioning functions; entropy source; health testing; min-entropy; noise source; predictors; random number generators", and §1 names the audience: "This Recommendation is intended for use by entropy source developers (the entity that designs and builds the entropy source or a portion thereof), submitters1 (the entity that submits the entropy". The retained copy is SP 800-90B (December 2018). The catalog row for this entity cites the 90B document while dating it 2007, which contradicts the retained document; that date defect is carried as a separate catalog correction. - Wikipedia search entry for 真随机数发生器. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%9C%9F%E9%9A%8F%E6%9C%BA%E6%95%B0%E5%8F%91%E7%94%9F%E5%99%A8 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] True Random Number Generator: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
