items.title: RC4
items.text: Algorithm : RC4 (RC4 流密码). The identity comes from a standards glossary: RFC 4949 defines RC4 as "A proprietary, variable-key-length stream cipher invented by Ron Rivest for RSA Data Security, Inc." - proprietary, taking keys of varying length, with Ron Rivest named as the inventor at RSA Data Security, Inc., while the same document expands the abbreviation as Rivest Cipher 4. No construction is written here: how the state table is initialised and how each step advances is in none of the three retained documents, since 6229 publishes vectors only, 7465 is about banning suites and 4949 gives a definition plus a usage note. Why implementations must treat part of the output specially: the reason sits in the opening passage of RFC 6229, which lists work on cryptanalysis and then writes that "initial parts of the stream output need to be discarded" - the leading keystream had become something to throw away. The document's own ambition stops at comparable vectors for implementers: it calls them useful to implementers and records that RC4 accepts keys of different lengths, with vectors covering several lengths and offsets. So this is a usage-side constraint rather than a design rationale, and no retained text gives the design's motives, so none is guessed here. This claim covers the TLS side only: RFC 7465 says of RC4 that "it is widely supported, and often preferred by TLS servers" - broadly installed, and frequently the server's own preference. It is not a usage inventory: the same glossary cited above records WEP as another user of RC4, and that belongs to a different citation rather than being blended in here. Of the three TLS specifications this document updates, it prints only their numbers, so no further use is attached to them. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The break is in the keystream: RFC 7465 says newer cryptanalysis results "exploit biases in the RC4 keystream to recover repeatedly encrypted plaintexts", and it gives what that cost at the time - the figures printed there are 2^26 sessions, and 13x2^30 encryptions. The same section adds that RC4 has long been known for a variety of cryptographic weaknesses, while RFC 6229 lists earlier analyses among its references. The proportion: the retained text supplies how many sessions and encryptions a recovery needed, not how the recovery works, and this entry adds no mechanics. Dating lands on what the paper that analyses the cipher prints: line 21 states that "The RC4 keystream generator was created by RSA Data Security, Inc.", its sixth reference dates Rivest's own report on the algorithm to March 1992, and the imprint line shows the paper is a chapter of the FSE 2000 proceedings volume (Lecture Notes in Computer Science 1978, Springer, 2001) - paraphrased rather than quoted, because the page-range dash lost its glyph in this extraction. That paper calls the algorithm alleged throughout, since the design was never published by its owner, and this entry keeps the wording. The era axis is therefore changed in this round's curation: the row keeps e14-standardization, whose 1977-2001 window holds the 2001 publication, and adds e16-quantum-turn, whose 1984-2019 window holds the 2011 and 2015 dates of the two TLS documents - with the mismatch stated plainly, because that second window's theme is the quantum turn and no existing window fits better. - Wikipedia search entry for RC4 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=RC4%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] RC4: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Galois/Counter Mode
items.text: Algorithm : Galois/Counter Mode (GCM 伽罗瓦计数器模式). The division of labour is stated by the recommendation itself: "GCM provides assurance of the confidentiality of data using a variation of the Counter mode of operation for encryption." Confidentiality comes from a variation of counter mode, and the sentence that follows hands authenticity to a universal hash function over a binary Galois field - finite, in the document's parenthesis. Its parenthesis caps that authenticity assurance at about 64 gigabytes of confidential data per invocation - the limit sits on the authenticity of the encrypted part, and the same section says separately that additional data needing no encryption may be "of practically unlimited length per invocation". This entry stays inside what that document says: it does not reproduce the multiplication that defines GHASH, and it does not treat the key schedule as part of GCM. Why authentication is built on algebra rather than on a checksum: the document's stated reason is that "GCM provides stronger authentication assurance than a (non-cryptographic) checksum or error detecting code", and it splits the point into two cases - accidental modification and deliberate modification. The same passage adds that an input confined to material needing no confidentiality turns the mode into what the document calls GMAC, which is then nothing more than an authentication mode over that input. What is bought here is therefore resistance to forgery under a key, not a faster checksum. The position comes from the document's own words: "Thus, GCM is a mode of operation of the AES algorithm." It is a mode of AES rather than a stand-alone cipher, and the same section states that everything said about GCM also applies to GMAC, so claims about the mode cover the authentication-only specialization as well. Its standing is equally checkable: Section 2 prints "This Recommendation has been prepared for use by federal agencies.", and the next sentence adds that nongovernmental organizations may use it voluntarily - the first is what the government application label rests on, the second is not evidence of any industry use. The infrastructure label has only editorial support. None of the protocol names this KB's application vocabulary might have been labelled from occurs - IPsec, TLS and 802.11 each grep to zero - but the document does name protocols elsewhere: its two concrete examples are the network-protocol AAD fields in Sec. 5.2.1.1 and, in Appendix C, "Secure Real-time Transport Protocol carrying Voice over Internet Protocol, running over User Datagram Protocol". A draft of this entry said no protocol name occurs anywhere; that was refuted by line 1439 and is corrected here. The limit is a condition of use rather than a strength result: the document warns that "a breach of the requirement in Sec. 8 for the uniqueness of the initialization strings may compromise the security assurance almost entirely", and it concludes that the mode stays undeployed where that uniqueness cannot be ensured. Sec. 5.2.1.1 describes the IV as essentially a nonce - unique inside the context that the document specifies. Sec. 8.3 caps how many times one key may be used at all, and the cap is conditional: it applies to every implementation using either "the deterministic construction with IVs whose length is not 96" or the RBG-based construction, and it is waived only where 96-bit IVs from the deterministic construction are the sole case. This copy prints that global ceiling as 232 where the publication sets a superscript, i.e. two to the thirty-second, and the same subsection then splits it into per-device limits through an example fleet of 210 units, likewise printed without its exponent. Every one of those digits is damaged in this extraction, so this entry states the shape of the constraint and does not quote the numbers. The names come from this file itself: "The designers of GCM are McGrew and Viega." The same sentence logs the NIST submission as Ref. [6] and the security-and-performance discussion as Ref. [7], and its bibliography dates those two: [6] is "The Galois/Counter Mode of Operation (GCM)", May 31, 2005, and [7] is "The Security and Performance of the Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) of Operation", INDOCRYPT '04, 2004. Neither is the 《GCM and GMAC》(2007) record the row inherited, and no copy of either paper is retained here, so what is verifiable is this recommendation's own report of it - the acknowledgements separately print "David McGrew, who co-invented GCM and submitted it to NIST". Three printed dates carry the dating: the title page on line 2 sets "November, 2007" with a comma, line 23 sets November 2007 on the title page and line 51 is the running imprint, which also gives the 37-page extent. So the row's era moves from e14-standardization, whose era.md prints a 1977-2001 window that excludes 2007, to e15-web-protocols, which prints 1991-2010. No document retained here gives the year McGrew and Viega proposed the mode, so none is added. - Wikipedia search entry for GCM 伽罗瓦计数器模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=GCM%20%E4%BC%BD%E7%BD%97%E7%93%A6%E8%AE%A1%E6%95%B0%E5%99%A8%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Galois/Counter Mode: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Hardware Security Module
items.text: Algorithm : Hardware Security Module (硬件安全模块). The definition comes from the discussion paragraph of a control in the CUI protection recommendation: "Hardware security module (HSM) devices safeguard and manage cryptographic keys and provide cryptographic processing." The sentence splits the job in two - the device holds and manages keys, and it also does the math - and the same file's acronym table at line 1866 expands HSM to Hardware Security Module, which is what supports the alias. The opening clause of the very next sentence says what is hosted there: "Cryptographic operations (e.g., encryption, decryption, and signature generation and verification) are typically hosted on the HSM device". Where those two spans sit limits what they mean, so the position is given with them: control 03.08.09 is a backup control, its requirement item b. prints "Implement cryptographic mechanisms to prevent the unauthorized disclosure of CUI at backup storage locations", and the discussion opens by making the choice of mechanism depend on keeping backup information confidential. This document mentions the HSM underneath a backup-protection control, not as a general definition of the device class. As far as these spans go, the file says only what such devices do - hold and manage keys, host operations, and in many implementations accelerate them - and says nothing about how a device is built: no command interface, no measured figure, no product name, no vendor name. Why the device exists at all is answered by the third protective measure in Sec. 5.5.2 of the key-management recommendation, which confines plaintext keys to what the file calls physically protected containers. The sentence that follows is quoted, because it is the one naming the device class: "This includes key generators, key-transport devices, key loaders, cryptographic modules, hardware security modules (HSMs), and key-storage devices". Read as written, the HSM sits in that list as one container type beside cryptographic modules, not above them. Two procedures precede it: line 1701 limits the time a secret key or an asymmetric private key spends in plaintext form, and line 1702 keeps people from seeing such keys while they are still in plaintext. The same file defines the first of those at line 850, as the key that goes with a symmetric algorithm, which is why this entry reads item 1 as being about symmetric keys. Taking the three together, what the device buys is confinement of key visibility inside a hardware boundary - that is how this entry reads the list, not a statement the recommendation makes. Why the first sentence of item 3 is reported instead of quoted: it ends in a word the file itself puts inside quotation marks, and a mark of the same kind as the delimiter would cut the span short, which would misquote the sentence rather than protect it. The place and the range come from the post-quantum transition report: "Cryptographic hardware modules, such as hardware security modules (HSMs) and Trusted Platform Modules (TPMs), provide secure environments for performing cryptographic operations and storing sensitive keys." The same section adds that they are "used in various applications, from securing server infrastructure to protecting cryptographic keys on personal devices" - server infrastructure through personal devices. The limit has to be stated, and stated only as far as this report goes. It presents hardware modules as needing work rather than as immune to anything: the text is a requirement, not a guarantee - after the definition and use sentences at lines 444-447 and a blank line, lines 449-450 say such modules "must be upgraded or redesigned to support PQC algorithms, which often have larger key sizes and different computational requirements", and the sentence that follows, which begins on line 450 and ends on line 455, asks for firmware or hardware updates and for modules able to run quantum-resistant operations efficiently. The report describes no way in which such a module is defeated, so this entry offers no defeat methods. Two other sentences are easy to mis-attribute, so they are pinned here, headings quoted as the file prints them: the report mentions side-channel attacks twice and neither mention is about hardware modules. The first, at lines 438-440, sits under "2.2.2. Software Cryptographic Libraries" (heading line 425) and is about updating libraries - "This transition involves adding new algorithms, optimizing their implementations for performance, and ensuring that those implementations are secure against side-channel attacks". The second, at lines 617-619, sits under "3.2. PQC-Classical Hybrid Protocols" (heading line 602) and reads "Early implementations of new cryptographic algorithms may introduce additional security risks, such as those arising from implementation errors or side-channel vulnerabilities" - a sentence about early implementations of new algorithms, with no HSM in it. The side-channel label on this row therefore records what the report requires of cryptographic implementations in general, not a claim it makes about HSMs. Dating can reach the documents but not the invention. The transition report prints its own date: line 36 sets October 2026 on its own, and the running imprints at lines 43-44 and 93-94 pair that date with the report's identifier NIST IR 8547. Its title is set across two lines in this extraction - line 4 reads "Transition to Post-Quantum" and line 5 reads "Cryptography Standards" - so this entry cites those line numbers rather than treating the title as one continuous span. The report gives no year for the hardware security module as a device class and no first appearance, so none is claimed here. The row's era moves from e14-standardization to e17-post-quantum: the two era.md files print their windows on line 10, 1977-2001 and 2016 onward, and among the windows printed as year ranges 2026 falls inside only the second; on theme as well, this source is post-quantum transition literature. The publication dates of the row's other two sources are registered in their own source records, and this section does not speak for those files' front matter. - Wikipedia search entry for 硬件安全模块. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%A1%AC%E4%BB%B6%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Hardware Security Module: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: bcrypt password hash
items.text: Algorithm : bcrypt (bcrypt 自适应口令散列). The mechanism is printed as-is in Section 5: “Bcrypt uses a 128-bit salt and encrypts a 192-bit magic value.” The next sentence names what it leans on, “It takes advantage of the expensive key setup in eksblow sh.” — the retained text really prints eksblow sh, the ligature was lost in extraction, so it is quoted in that form rather than repaired. The rationale sits in the abstract: the paper will “show that the computational cost of any secure password scheme must increase as hardware improves”, and the same paragraph names the two adaptable-cost algorithms together, “cost eksblow sh, a block cipher with a purposefully expensive key schedule, and bcrypt, a related hash function” — in this file the em dash there is printed as a vertical bar , and the span carries it. Use and implementation venue come from the paper’s own roadmap sentence, “Section 5 introduces the variable-cost bcrypt password hashing function and describes our implementation in the OpenBSD operating system”, and the name is explained at the head of that section, where the text prints “bcrypt, referring to the Blow” followed by the cipher’s name. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The limit is not a break but a failure mode, printed as one claim: “the big aw in UNIX password security is not its openly readable password le. Rather, it is the choice of a hash function that cannot adapt to a 50,000 fold increase in the speed of hardware and software.” The aw and le are the extraction’s own glyphs, copied verbatim, and the case for changing the hash follows from that sentence. The dating evidence is on one line: “At the time of deployment in 1976, crypt could hash fewer than 4 passwords per second.” and later “over 200,000 crypt operations per second” — both the year 1976 and the two rates are printed by the retained file, so this entry speaks only to the speed comparison in the 1999 paper and says nothing about inventors or earlier origins, which this text does not provide. - Wikipedia search entry for bcrypt 自适应口令散列. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=bcrypt%20%E8%87%AA%E9%80%82%E5%BA%94%E5%8F%A3%E4%BB%A4%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] bcrypt: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Ring Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Ring Signature (环签名). What is registered is not a ring-signature paper. a search of every file registered in build/corpora.json finds the phrase only inside unrelated running text (fips186-5.txt:599 and debian-dsa1571.html:94 both print it as part of a longer clause about signature generation), so this entry states the mechanism against the signature model the retained sources do print, marks nothing they do not print, and gives no scheme-specific security statement. A ring signature is an ordinary public-key signature computed with one member's private key together with a set of public keys - the ring - of which that key is one; verification is performed against the whole set, and what a verifier learns is that some member of the set signed. The model being inherited is FIPS 186-5's, printed at fips186-5.txt:36 as "Signature generation uses a private key to generate a digital signature; signature verification uses a public key that corresponds to but is not the same as the private key." and closed in the same paragraph by "Only the user that possesses the private key can perform signature generation." The same line also fixes the keying premise a ring is built out of, "Each signatory possesses a private and public key pair." The construction changes the object of verification, from one key to a set of keys; it does not change the secrecy of any private key, and the requirement at fips186-5.txt:35 that the rules "allow the identity of the signatory and the integrity of the data to be verified" is precisely the half that a ring signature declines to satisfy. The design reason shows up as a subtraction from what an ordinary signature is for, and the standard states that purpose plainly. The abstract at fips186-5.txt:23 prints "Digital signatures are used to detect unauthorized modifications to data and to authenticate the identity of the signatory." and then the evidentiary property, "This is known as non-repudiation since the signatory cannot easily repudiate the signature at a later time." The keying premise is stated as a binding to a person: the definition of private key at fips186-5.txt:224 reads "The private key is uniquely associated with the owner and is not made public." Verification, meanwhile, is a public operation on a public object - fips186-5.txt:36 says "Anyone can verify the signature by employing the signatory's public key." Nothing in that last sentence is logically bound to one key: what the mechanics need is the key, and what the identity conclusion needs is the binding that fips186-5.txt:224 asserts. A ring signature moves exactly that boundary. It keeps integrity and it keeps the assertion that one of these private keys signed this; it gives up naming the owner, and with it the repudiation-resistant evidence value, since a signature that does not identify a signer cannot bind one. Where a caller's real requirement is proof that some member of a defined set acted, naming the member is disclosure rather than assurance, and that is the design. This is an inference drawn about a construction the retained files do not describe; the quoted runs are only the properties those files do state. The registered sources give an extension point, not a deployment history. RFC 4252's public key method is the identity-bound check a ring signature does not offer, and it is printed as a requirement: "With this method, the possession of a private key serves as authentication. This method works by sending a signature created with a private key of the user. The server MUST check that the key is a valid authenticator for the user, and MUST check that the signature is valid." (rfc4252.txt:439-443 - the four-space gaps are this file's continuation indent, kept as printed). The signature covers session-bound material, so it cannot be lifted from one session to another (rfc4252.txt:511-514). What makes this relevant to a non-standard scheme is the next permission: "Any public key algorithm may be offered for use in authentication. In particular, the list is not constrained by what was negotiated during key exchange." (rfc4252.txt:474-476), and the server's recourse on the same lines is simply to reject what it does not support. That is the whole of what these files support: a signature scheme outside the approved set can be offered wherever a verifier is free to accept or refuse an algorithm name, and it must be refused or accepted by that verifier's own policy. Nothing in the four registered files names a ring-signature scheme in use; FIPS 186-5 reserves the approval of further schemes to its own publications and to NIST Special Publications (fips186-5.txt:39), which is why no approved-for-use claim is made here either. The failure this corpus documents for the signature family sits at the signer's own secret, not at any anonymity construction. The advisory's field block records the vulnerability class as a predictable random number generator (debian-dsa1571.html:75) - and the cause in one paragraph: "Luciano Bello discovered that the random number generator in Debian's openssl package is predictable. This is caused by an incorrect Debian-specific change to the openssl package (CVE-2008-0166). As a result, cryptographic key material may be guessable." (debian-dsa1571.html:80-83). Its algorithm-level reason is a sentence about the standard, not about a ring: "the Digital Signature Algorithm relies on a secret random value used during signature generation." (debian-dsa1571.html:93-94), from which the consequence for signing keys follows, "all DSA keys ever used on affected Debian systems for signing or authentication purposes should be considered compromised" (debian-dsa1571.html:91-94). The reach is listed broadly - "Affected keys include SSH keys, OpenVPN keys, DNSSEC keys, and key material for use in X.509 certificates and session keys used in SSL/TLS connections." (debian-dsa1571.html:101-103) - and it reaches into exactly the authentication setting the SSH documents describe. FIPS 186-5 prints the requirement that was violated: a value k shall be generated at each invocation of signature generation (fips186-5.txt:627), and it states the outcome of weak randomness in that value as revealing a private key (fips186-5.txt:590). For this entry the consequence is the one the retained text does not itself spell out but the quoted requirement makes unavoidable: a ring signature's only assertion about its signer is possession of one private key inside the ring, so a member whose per-signature secret is guessable loses the signing guarantee and the anonymity together, the recovered key naming the member. No registered file reports a break of a ring construction, and none is claimed here. What can be dated here is the documents and the standards they cite, not the construction. RFC 4253 and RFC 4252 both carry January 2006 in their headers (rfc4253.txt:11, rfc4252.txt:11), and RFC 4253 states the layering that keeps a signature attached to a named verifier-side check: "Authentication in this protocol level is host-based; this protocol does not perform user authentication. A higher level protocol for user authentication can be designed on top of this protocol." (rfc4253.txt:125-127, continuation indent preserved). Its DSA key format is pinned to an older edition of the standard: "Signing and verifying using this key format is done according to the Digital Signature Standard [FIPS-186-2] using the SHA-1 hash [FIPS-180-2]." (rfc4253.txt:791-793), and the reference entry for that edition is dated January 2000 (rfc4253.txt:1649-1652). The other three registered files date themselves too - FIPS 186-5 published February 3, 2023 and superseding FIPS 186-4 (fips186-5.txt:12, :4), the Debian advisory issued May 13, 2008 with the first vulnerable upload on 2006-09-17 (debian-dsa1571.html:71, :96-97) - and none of the four prints a ring-signature paper, its authors, or a year for the construction. The closest the retained text comes to the founding names is the abbreviation list of FIPS 186-5 at line 264, where the string Rivest, Shamir, Adleman expands RSA and nothing else; the RFC 4253 occurrence of the surname Rivest is the MD5 reference at line 1593. The catalogue row's own bibliography entries for Rivest, Shamir and Ta-Shma are not retained texts in build/corpora.json, so this entry attributes no invention and no origin date, and records instead what its evidence does establish: that by 2006 deployed protocols demanded a signature tied to one key, and by 2023 the registered standard still defined signature generation as a private-key operation. - Wikipedia search entry for 环签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%8E%AF%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Ring Signature: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. The worked example is a structural reproduction, not a new test vector; parameter ranges, standard versions and implementation details remain source-bound.

items.title: Discrete Logarithm Problem
items.text: Algorithm : Discrete Logarithm Problem (离散对数问题). SP 800-186 defines the problem inside an elliptic-curve group, written additively: for a point R in the cyclic subgroup generated by P, the unique integer k with R = kP is, at sp800-186.txt:438-439, "This number is called the discrete logarithm of R to the base P.", and the task is set at 439-440 as "The discrete logarithm problem is the problem of finding the discrete logarithm of R to the base P for any two points P and R on the curve, if such a number exists.". The membership glyph stating that R lies in the subgroup (line 437) degrades in this extraction, so the group setup is paraphrased while the two definition sentences are quoted intact (the body is left-aligned and rejoins with single spaces). The additive notation here is specific to the elliptic-curve case; over finite fields the same problem is posed with exponentiation, which the other cited documents name. Why the discrete logarithm is treated as the load-bearing assumption: well-studied curve forms are chosen precisely so that switching representation does not weaken it. RFC 8032 states, of the Ed25519 curve, that its change of coordinates relative to Curve25519 means the "discrete logarithm problem is the same as for Curve25519.", and, of the Ed448 form relative to Ed448-Goldilocks, that the change of basepoint "which preserves difficulty of the discrete logarithm.". Both fragments are quoted from single raw lines (they start mid-sentence because the sentence wraps). The design reason this gives is transferability: an equivalent curve keeps the same hard problem, so confidence in the discrete-logarithm assumption on one group carries to the group actually used. RFC 8032 does not quantify that difficulty here, so no concrete bit-level hardness figure is claimed in this entry. The discrete logarithm problem is the assumption under NIST's key-establishment standards. NIST IR 8547 prints, at nist-ir8547-final.txt:347-348, "SP 800-56A specifies key-establishment schemes based on the discrete logarithm problem over finite fields and elliptic curves, including several variations of Diffie-Hellman". The marked run deliberately stops there: the very next name, Menezes-Qu-Vanstone, wraps across a hyphen line-break, and the precheck normaliser rejoins that break without the hyphen, so the sentence is quoted only up to the cleanly-printed "Diffie-Hellman". The claim this supports is narrow and standard: the Diffie-Hellman key-establishment family (over both finite fields and elliptic curves) rests on the discrete logarithm problem. What the document specifies beyond the DH/MQV family is not restated here. FIPS 203 names both the dependence and the break. Its context paragraph prints (fips203.txt:358) that a large-scale quantum computer would put at risk "This would include key-establishment schemes and digital signature schemes whose security depends on the difficulty of solving the integer factorization and discrete logarithm problems (both over finite fields and elliptic curves).", and (fips203.txt:354) that "The key establishment schemes specified in SP 800-56A and SP 800-56B are vulnerable to attacks that use sufficiently-capable quantum computers." Together, from this one document, the discrete-logarithm assumption is exactly the thing that collapses: schemes resting on the difficulty of the discrete logarithm problem are, per the text, vulnerable to sufficiently capable quantum computers. Note the scope of the wording: FIPS 203 attributes the break to quantum computers but does not itself name the algorithm, so this entry says quantum computers in the document's own words and does not import the name of a specific attack from another file. The dated history these retained sources print is about the response to the assumption's weakness, not about its origin. FIPS 203 records, at fips203.txt:358, "in 2016, NIST initiated a public Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) Standardization process to select quantum-resistant public-key cryptographic algorithms." - a concrete year attached to the standardization that replaced the discrete-log-based schemes. The publication itself is dated fips203.txt:13, "Published August 13, 2024", which is why the entry reports a 2024 document describing a 2016 process. The discrete logarithm problem's own first statement, proposer or decade is not given in any of the four retained files for this row, so this entry names no inventor and no founding date; it records only what the sources actually print, and any earlier history of the problem belongs to other rows in this catalogue. - Wikipedia search entry for 离散对数问题. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%A6%BB%E6%95%A3%E5%AF%B9%E6%95%B0%E9%97%AE%E9%A2%98 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Discrete Logarithm Problem: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman
items.text: Algorithm : Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH 椭圆曲线密钥协商). The ECDH key-agreement step, for the prime curves secp256r1, secp384r1 and secp521r1, is printed at rfc8446.txt:5329-5334: the calculation follows IEEE 1363 under the ECKAS-DH1 scheme, and the derived value is, in the file's own words, "the shared secret is the x-coordinate" of the ECDH shared-secret elliptic curve point, expressed as a fixed-length octet string whose leading zeros are not to be truncated. The full sentence wraps across indented continuation lines, so only that x-coordinate fragment is quoted and the rest is stated by line reference. Two points about scope: this is the classical ECDH primitive (multiply the peer's public point by your private scalar, take the x-coordinate), and RFC 8446 treats the x-coordinate as an intermediate value rather than a finished key - a separate claim covers the key derivation, so it is not asserted here. RFC 7919 is about finite-field Diffie-Hellman, and it is that framing that states the reason to prefer the elliptic-curve form: measured against finite-field DHE (FFDHE), the retained text prints, at rfc7919.txt:720, "a much stronger key exchange mechanism than FFDHE" for ECDHE at comparable computational cost. The same section is explicit that RFC 7919 itself does not cover finite-field-only cases nor address ECDHE (which it says is defined in RFC 4492) - the point of the sentence is comparative, not a definition of ECDH. So the design reason the standards give is efficiency: an elliptic-curve group delivers the same style of agreement at lower cost per security level than the finite-field construction. This is exactly the trade the cited document asserts; it does not claim a proof of equivalence between the two settings. NIST SP 800-186 places ECDH among the uses of elliptic curves. The whole category sentence is printed at sp800-186.txt:335-337: "Elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) has uses in applications involving digital signatures (e.g., Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm [ECDSA]) and key agreement schemes (e.g., Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman [ECDH])." The Recommendation also states, near sp800-186.txt:357-359, that the key pairs it specifies are for signature or key agreement only and should not be used for other purposes. That is the deployment role the evidence supports: ECDH is the key-agreement member of the discrete-log-based elliptic-curve family. The same document is left-aligned, so this sentence rejoins with ordinary single spaces and is quoted intact. ECDH is only as hard as the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem behind it, and SP 800-186 records the reduction that keeps that assumption honest. In the curve-selection criteria at sp800-186.txt:2184-2198, item 5 prints that "an ordinary discrete logarithm problem defined over the finite field GF(qk)" is what the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm problem can be converted into (this is the MOV-type transfer); the superscript in GF(q^k) and the congruence sign that follows degrade in this extraction, so the embedding-degree condition is stated by line rather than quoted. Because that reduction exists, the same criteria require each curve to have a large embedding degree, a prime-order subgroup with small cofactor, and a non-anomalous order, so the transfer to the finite-field setting stays infeasible. What is not said here: this retained document does not mention quantum computers, so no quantum-break claim is attached to ECDH in this entry - the classical limit is the reduction, and the boundary the standards draw is curve selection that resists it. The retained texts date when ECDH entered a standard, not who invented it. RFC 7568 (June 2015, running header at rfc7568.txt:60) lists, among the features that recent TLS versions added over SSLv3, "Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH)" at rfc7568.txt:205, and the very next words say that ECDH and ECDSA are added in RFC 4492 - the continuation wraps with indentation, so only the (ECDH) term is quoted and the RFC 4492 attribution is paraphrased. RFC 7919 (August 2016) treats ECDHE as an established mechanism defined by RFC 4492 and compares it against its own finite-field scope. None of these retained documents gives an author or a first-publication date for the ECDH primitive itself, so this entry states only the dated standardization the sources actually print and no origin it cannot verify. - Wikipedia search entry for ECDH 椭圆曲线密钥协商. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ECDH%20%E6%A4%AD%E5%9C%86%E6%9B%B2%E7%BA%BF%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%8D%8F%E5%95%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[K=g^{ab}\bmod p\quad\text{或}\quad K=[ab]G\] Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Fast Data Encipherment Algorithm
items.text: Algorithm : Fast Data Encipherment Algorithm (FEAL 分组密码). HAC 7.5 opens by naming the object and saying what it is known for: "The Fast Data Encipherment Algorithm (FEAL) is a family of algorithms which has played a critical role in the development and refinement of various advanced cryptanalytic techniques, including linear and differential cryptanalysis." The parameters follow on the same line: "FEAL-N maps 64-bit plaintext to 64-bit ciphertext blocks under a 64-bit secret key." and the shape is given as "It is an N -round Feistel cipher similar to DES (cf. Equations (7.4), (7.5)), but with a far simpler f -function, and augmented by initial and final stages which XOR the two data halves as well as XOR subkeys directly onto the data halves." - the odd spacing of N -round and f -function is how this extraction prints the italicised symbols, and it is kept. The 8-round member is the one the chapter spells out ("Algorithm 7.94 specifies FEAL-8." at hac-ch7-cast.txt:1384), and the round function is described in its own terms at 1384: two byte-oriented S-boxes S0 and S1, each used twice. The arithmetic that matters is stated at hac-ch7-cast.txt:1502: "As the operations of 2-bit rotation and XOR are both linear, the only nonlinear elementary operation in FEAL is addition mod 256." so the only source of nonlinearity is mod-256 addition, the rotation and the XOR being linear; the input width of the f-function is given there as a product of 32 and 16 bits, whose multiplication sign this extraction prints as a degraded glyph, so it is paraphrased rather than quoted. Decryption needs no second algorithm: "Decryption may be achieved using Algorithm 7.94 with the same key K and ciphertext C = (R8, L8) as the plaintext input M , but with the key schedule reversed." and "This is directly analogous to decryption for DES (Note 7.84)." (hac-ch7-cast.txt:1513). The family notation is defined in the same section - "FEAL with 64-bit key can be generalized to N -rounds, N even." at 1520, with the recommended N stated as a power of two whose exponent sits at baseline in the retained text, so it is not quoted; and "Extending FEAL-N to use a 128-bit key results in FEAL-NX" at 1521, the remainder of that note being the modulo-3 key conditions whose inequality signs do not survive extraction. Example 7.99 at 1522 fixes the behaviour with printed vectors: "For hex plaintext M = 00000000 00000000 and hex key K = 01234567 89ABCDEF" (with key bytes continuing to 89ABCDEF) and "Algorithm 7.94 generates FEAL-8 ciphertext C = CEEF2C86 F2490752." The design rationale is best seen in the round-function debate the AES-era submissions inherited. Twofish's paper places FEAL in the lineage of Feistel designs: "It is the basis of most block ciphers published since then, including FEAL [SM88], GOST [GOST89], Khufu and Khafre [Mer91], LOKI [BPS90, BKPS93], CAST-128 [Ada97a], Blowfish [Sch94], and RC5 [Riv95]." (twofish-paper.txt:232), and it recalls how that lineage argued about shape rather than only about strength: "The early post-DES cipher designs would often compete on the number of rounds in the cipher." "The original FEAL paper [SM88], for example, discussed the benefits of a stronger round function" (1226 - the printed paragraph ends there and the next line begins a new paragraph, so the mark stops inside the clause). The reason a byte-addition round function was chosen at all is the compactness trade the same paper draws between table-driven and algebraic S-boxes: FEAL is named among the algebraic ones, and "The advantage of the latter is that the S-boxes are more compact, and can be more easily implemented in applications where the ROM or RAM for large tables is not available." (1294). The lesson Twofish draws from FEAL is stated as a design constraint on analysis: "Anecdotal evidence from algorithms like FEAL [SM88], CAST, and Blowfish indicates that complicated round functions are not always better than simple ones." (1264), and the specific exposure it names is exactly the one the differential literature found: "Algebraic S-boxes can result in S-boxes that are vulnerable to differential cryptanalysis: [Mur90] against FEAL, and [Knu93a, Knu93b] against LOKI." (1295). The primary paper is cited by this file as "Fast Data Encipherment Algorithm FEAL" in Advances in Cryptology - EUROCRYPT '87 Proceedings, Springer-Verlag, 1988 (2849); the page-range dash in that entry is degraded, so the range is left out of the mark. What the structure bought is stated by HAC, not here: speed and small code on 8-bit processors, with no table look-ups (hac-ch7-cast.txt:1383, quoted under the limits section below). The retained texts put FEAL's use in two places, both stated by the sources rather than assumed. The first is the environment it was built for: Chapter 6 of the Biham-Shamir book opens "FEAL was suggested as a software-oriented cryptosystem which can be easily and efficiently implemented on microprocessors." and explains what that meant for the parts, "In the F function, the P permutation and the S boxes of DES are replaced by byte rotations and addition operations." (biham-shamir-1993.txt:5935) - the same conclusion the book's own glossary reaches at 10635: "FEAL: A family of DES-like cryptosystems which is designed to be easily and efficiently implementable on microprocessors." "The F function of FEAL is based on the addition operation and byte rotation (rather than S boxes and permutations)." The second is reuse inside the designers' own later work: "Another hash function is N-Hash[25] which was suggested by the designers of FEAL as a cryptographically strong hash function." (262), the hashing function carrying an F function built on the FEAL round function. The book also says plainly where the attack technique came from: "Shoji Miyaguchi's FEAL cryptosystem motivated the first version of our attack" (34), which is why FEAL, not some later cipher, is the cipher the technique was first worked out against in this text. Neither this file nor the two HAC extractions registered here print a deployment inventory - no product, standardisation body or protocol is named as shipping FEAL - so this entry claims no deployment history; HAC's separate sentence about a commercially proposed version is treated under the limits section, because that is the strongest statement the retained corpus makes about use. The breakage is recorded as design history rather than as a single event. HAC states the outcome for the first two commercially relevant members: "The initial commercially proposed version with 4 rounds (FEAL-4), positioned as a fast alternative to DES, was found to be considerably less secure than expected (see Table 7.10)." and "FEAL-8 was similarly found to offer less security than planned." (hac-ch7-cast.txt:1383); the referent of both sentences is the round count, and the same line adds the price of fixing it: "FEAL-16 or FEAL-32 may yet offer security comparable to DES, but throughput decreases as the number of rounds rises." The table those sentences point at is introduced at 1523: "Table 7.10 gives various published attacks on FEAL; LC and DC denote linear and differential cryptanalysis, and times are on common personal computers or workstations." - the table body itself (1526-1555) has its row separators and its exponent complexities degraded by extraction, so no figure from it is quoted here, only the sentences that describe it. The chapter's notes carry the mechanism of the weakness and the residual question: the linearity that made the cipher fast is what made it analyzable, since the round function's only nonlinear element is mod-256 addition (1502), and the notes' own summary of the trade-off is "While it appears to remain relatively secure when iterated a sufficient number of rounds (e.g., 24 or more), this defeats its original objective of speed." (2195). For the surviving members the retained text reports comparison, not proof: "Ohta and Aoki [943] suggest that FEAL-32 is as secure as DES against DC, while FEAL-16 is as secure as DES against certain restricted forms of LC." (2203). The attacks named in these three sources are chosen-plaintext and known-plaintext attacks - the cipher is listed among the ciphers differential cryptanalysis applies to, and the catalogue of attacks is in Table 7.10 - so the honest statement of the boundary is that round count was the variable that moved security, at a cost the design was meant to avoid. The dated sequence is printed in one paragraph of the chapter notes, and this entry keeps its order and its wording. "FEAL stimulated the development of a sequence of advanced cryptanalytic techniques of unparalleled richness and utility." The first datum is "FEAL-4 as presented at Eurocrypt'87 (Abstracts of Eurocrypt'87, April 1987) was found to have certain vulnerabilities by den Boer (unpublished Eurocrypt'87 rump session talk), resulting in Shimizu and Miyaguchi [1126] (or see Miyaguchi, Shiraishi, and Shimizu [887]) increasing FEAL to 8 rounds in the final proceedings." (hac-ch7-cast.txt:2195) - an April 1987 abstract, an unpublished rump-session finding, and eight rounds in the final proceedings. The next is "In 1988 den Boer [322] showed FEAL-4 vulnerable to an adaptive chosen plaintext attack with 100 to 10 000 plaintexts." The attack that the notes describe as another early variant of differential cryptanalysis is the 1990 chosen-plaintext attack on FEAL-8, whose defining choice is "the bitwise XOR of each pair being selected to be an appropriate constant (thus another early variant of differential cryptanalysis)." (2195); the two designers are named in the retained text as Gilbert and Chasse followed by a stray accent glyph, so the name is written in own words and cited by line instead of quoted. The family papers follow: "FEAL-N with N rounds, and its extension FEAL-NX with 128-bit key (Notes 7.97 and 7.98) were then published by Miyaguchi [884] (or see Miyaguchi et al. [885]), who nonetheless opined that chosen-plaintext attacks on FEAL-8 were not practical threats." (2196), and the counter-attacks then come thick - "Employing den Boer's G function expressing linearity in the FEAL f -function, Murphy [913] defeated FEAL-4 with 20 chosen plaintexts in under 4 hours (under 1 hour for most keys) on a Sun 3/60 workstation." (2196); a statistical method of Tardy-Corfdir and Gilbert is credited at 2196-2203 with a known-plaintext attack on FEAL-4 and FEAL-6 using linear approximation of the S-boxes; and "the first version of linear cryptanalysis (LC) introduced by Matsui and Yamagishi [798] allowed known-plaintext attack of FEAL-4" (2196), the text giving five texts and six minutes for that first version of linear cryptanalysis. For the longer members the notes report "Aoki and Ohta [53] refined these ideas for FEAL-8 yielding a differential-linear attack requiring only 12 chosen texts and 35 days of computer time (cf. Table 7.10)." (2204) and "Test vectors for FEAL-N and FEAL-NX (Example 7.99) are given by Miyaguchi [884]." (2205). The dating of the source itself is also worth recording: line 1 prints "This is a Chapter from the Handbook of Applied Cryptography, by A. Menezes, P. van Oorschot, and S. Vanstone, CRC Press, 1996." while the recurring footer at line 6 and 2197 prints the copyright line with the sign degraded to a bare c and the year 1997; both are cited by line rather than merged into one date. - Wikipedia search entry for FEAL 分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=FEAL%20%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Fast Data Encipherment Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DES Modes of Operation
items.text: Standard : DES Modes of Operation (DES 工作模式). What FIPS 81 covers is named by its successor rather than by itself. NIST SP 800-38A, writing about the modes it is recommending, states at sp800-38a.txt:303-304 that “FIPS Pub. 81 [4] specifies the ECB, CBC, CFB, and OFB modes of the Data Encryption Standard (DES).” - so the object of this standard is four ways of running the DES block cipher, not a new cipher. The general shape of such a mode is given at line 478: “A confidentiality mode of operation of the block cipher algorithm consists of two processes that are inverses of each other: encryption and decryption.” A mode therefore sits between the cipher and the message: the cipher itself stays a single-block function, and the mode decides how it is applied repeatedly. Two of the four definitions survive as running prose. ECB at line 561: “The Electronic Codebook (ECB) mode is a confidentiality mode that features, for a given key, the assignment of a fixed ciphertext block to each plaintext block, analogous to the assignment of code words in a codebook.” CFB at line 675: “The Cipher Feedback (CFB) mode is a confidentiality mode that features the feedback of successive ciphertext segments into the input blocks of the forward cipher to generate output blocks that are exclusive-ORed with the plaintext to produce the ciphertext, and vice versa.” CBC, defined at lines 602-603 in terms of chaining plaintext blocks with previous ciphertext blocks, and OFB, defined at lines 779-783 as iterating the forward cipher on an initial value, are stated here in own words. The reason is a defect of the retained text: the formal blocks at lines 609-616 and 688-701 print the exclusive-OR operator as a blank and misplace the CBC decryption line, so the arithmetic is described rather than quoted. Line 504 adds the input rule the block modes share: “For the ECB and CBC modes, the total number of bits in the plaintext must be a multiple of the block size, b” - a length condition the segment and stream-like modes do not impose in the same way (lines 509-519). RFC 4949 gives the reason the family exists at all. Its entry $ mode of operation, sense 1 for /cryptographic operation/ (rfc4949.txt:10820-10825), defines the concept as “A technique for enhancing the effect of a cryptographic algorithm or adapting the algorithm for an application, such as applying a block cipher to a sequence of data blocks or a data stream.” That is a design statement, not a history note: a mode buys two things, extra effect and adaptability, and the four FIPS 81 modes are four different trades between them. The glossary then keeps the provenance visible. Its definitions of “cipher block chaining (CBC)”, “cipher feedback (CFB)”, “electronic codebook (ECB)” and “output feedback (OFB)” each close with the source tag [FP081] - rfc4949.txt:3395, 3406, 6450 and 11839 - while the definition of “counter mode (CTR)” closes with [SP38A] at rfc4949.txt:4546. The two tags in one reference list are the cleanest statement in this corpus of where the FIPS 81 family ends and the later work begins: chaining and feedback over DES blocks are credited to the 1980 document, the counter mode to the 2001 one. What each of the four does is also stated there in short form: ECB applies the algorithm directly to a plaintext block and uses the result directly as cipher text (line 6448-6450), CBC enhances ECB by chaining the ciphertext blocks it produces (line 3394-3395), CFB additionally operates on plaintext segments of variable length up to the block length (line 3403-3406), and OFB modifies ECB to operate on such segments (line 11837-11839). Those clauses are cited by line and paraphrased here, because the definition sentences run over indented lines and the quotation form used above is reserved for runs the file prints cleanly. Where the modes were actually consumed is visible in PKCS 5. RFC 8018 section 6.1 fixes one of them by requirement: the PBES1 underlying block cipher must be DES or RC2 running in “cipher block chaining (CBC) mode [NIST81]” (rfc8018.txt:700-702). That is CBC from FIPS 81 being made mandatory inside a password-based encryption scheme, and the same document's appendix names the construction directly, “DES-CBC-Pad is single-key DES [NIST46] in CBC mode [NIST81]” with padding (rfc8018.txt:1633-1634). Appendix B.2 then records the turn: of the schemes inherited from PKCS 5 v2.0, “legacy and should only be used for backwards compatibility reasons.” (rfc8018.txt:1617-1618), while AES-CBC-Pad is offered as the PBES2 example (line 1614) - the chaining mode survives, the DES key under it does not. The reason is stated one section earlier and is about key length rather than about the mode: “each of which has a key size (56 or 64 bits) that may not be large enough for some applications.” (rfc8018.txt:707-708). The same file also shows how FIPS 81 is cited in current documents, at rfc8018.txt:1096, where the reference entry closes with “FIPS PUB 81, December 2, 1980.” - a complete date, written in a different word order from the one RFC 4949 uses at its line 19454. None of the four registered files reports FIPS 81 being broken, and none needs to: the modes outlived the cipher they were written for, and the failure mode that survives into later designs is a property of the chaining-and-padding combination. RFC 3711, the SRTP specification, states it as a general warning at rfc3711.txt:2363-2366: “Some cipher modes of operation that require padding, e.g., standard cipher block chaining (CBC) are very sensitive to attacks on confidentiality if certain padding types are used in the absence of integrity.” The following sentences narrow it to a case, “used together with CBC mode.” and then impose the obligation on future work, “proper integrity protection.” (lines 2368-2370). The attack it names is resolved in the document's own reference list at lines 2769-2771 as “Security Flaws Induced by CBC Padding” - “Application to SSL, IPsec, WTLS...”, in Advances in Cryptology, EUROCRYPT'02, LNCS 2332, pages 534-545; the venue, series and page numbers are all printed on those three lines and are not restated from memory. Two limits of the FIPS 81 family are worth separating from that: the padding requirement, since ECB, CBC and CFB demand a whole number of blocks or segments and the extra bits have to be added before encryption (SP 800-38A Appendix A, sp800-38a.txt:946-955), and the malleability that Appendix D makes explicit for CBC, Consequently, for the CBC mode, the decryption of the first ciphertext block is vulnerable to the (deliberate) introduction of bit errors in specific bit positions of the IV if the integrity of the IV is not protected. (sp800-38a.txt:1140-1142). Neither is a break of the mode algebra; both are consequences of running a confidentiality-only mode without integrity. It is also visible in the same source that the family was not frozen in 1980: SRTP's f8 transform is described at rfc3711.txt:1197-1198 as a variant of “Output Feedback Mode (OFB) [HAC]”, with a more elaborate initialization and feedback function, i.e. an OFB descendant chosen for a use FIPS 81 never contemplated. The dates this row can support are the ones its sources print. SP 800-38A's reference list carries the entry as “DES Modes of Operation.” “U.S. DoC/NIST, December 1980.” (sp800-38a.txt:6839), a month-only date, while RFC 8018 at line 1096 and RFC 4949 at line 19454 print a full day for the same publication; this entry records the difference instead of merging the three into one cleaned date. The relation between the two documents is stated at sp800-38a.txt:312-315, where the newer publication lists “the extension of the four confidentiality modes in FIPS Pub 81 for use with any FIPS-approved block cipher” as its first new element, “the revision of the requirements for these modes” as its second, and “the specification of an additional confidentiality mode, the CTR mode, for use with any FIPS-approved block cipher” as its third (the whole run is on lines 313-315). Read plainly, SP 800-38A extends and revises the four FIPS 81 modes and adds a fifth; it does not describe itself as abolishing them. Its status sentences go the other way as well: “This recommendation is neither a standard nor a guideline, and as such, is neither mandatory nor binding on Federal agencies.” (lines 277-278), and “Nothing in this recommendation should be taken to contradict standards and guidelines that have been made mandatory and binding upon Federal agencies by the Secretary of Commerce under his statutory authority.” (lines 281-283). As to the question of whether FIPS 81 has been withdrawn or replaced: the four retained files registered for this row were grepped for withdraw, annular and rescind, and the words do not occur in any of them, so no withdrawal and no replacement is asserted here. For comparison, the reference annex of RFC 4949 does know the annotation form - it prints Superseded by [DoD9]. at rfc4949.txt:19385 - but that note belongs to the [DoD7] entry, a Department of Defense X.509 certificate policy, and the [FP081] entry at line 19454 carries no status note at all. What the retained evidence does establish is supersession in substance rather than in wording: SP 800-38A is written for any FIPS-approved block cipher, the AES among them (lines 295-298), and the mode family outlived the algorithm it was named after. - Wikipedia search entry for DES 工作模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DES%20%E5%B7%A5%E4%BD%9C%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] DES Modes of Operation: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Port-Based Network Access Control
items.text: Standard : Port-Based Network Access Control (基于端口的网络访问控制). Port-based access control is a role model with a decision attached to it, and the registered texts here are the EAP specifications that reference IEEE 802.1X rather than the standard itself, so the model is described as those RFCs print it. RFC 3748 section 1.2 defines the two ends directly. The authenticator is “The end of the link initiating EAP authentication.” (line 188), and the peer is “The end of the link that responds to the authenticator.” (line 193); the same entry adds that in the IEEE standard's vocabulary “this end is known as the Supplicant.” (line 194), and the Supplicant entry reverses the mapping back at lines 196-199. A third role, the backend authentication server, is the entity that supplies the authentication service to an authenticator (lines 201-205). The encapsulation that carries the exchange over an IEEE 802 link is fixed by reference, not by reproduction: “The encapsulation of EAP over IEEE 802 is defined in [IEEE-802.1X].” (line 1035). The decision the port enforces is defined carefully, and it is not merely a cryptographic success: a successful authentication is an “exchange of EAP messages, as a result of which the authenticator decides to allow access by the peer, and the peer decides to use this access.” (lines 246-249), and the text warns that an authenticated peer may still be refused, with access “denied by the authenticator due to policy reasons.” (line 252). Finally the enforcement point is not a single binary gate. RFC 3748 describes it at lines 2787-2790: “authentication failure will result in denied access to the controlled port in [IEEE-802.1X], limited traffic may be permitted on the uncontrolled port.” That distinction - one port denied, another still carrying limited traffic - is what makes the state of an 802.1X port a policy question rather than a switch position. The design choice is stated as an advantage first: “One of the advantages of the EAP architecture is its flexibility.” (rfc3748.txt:152). What the flexibility is bought with is spelled out in the next paragraph, at lines 155-160: instead of requiring the authenticator to be updated for every new authentication method, EAP permits a backend authentication server that may implement some or all of the methods, with the authenticator acting as a pass-through for some or all methods and peers. A port-control device therefore does not have to become a cryptographic endpoint to support a new method. The cost is named in the same list, at lines 464-466: placing the server apart from the authenticator complicates the security analysis and, if needed, key distribution. The architecture also narrows what the port can negotiate. Section 3.3, EAP Usage Within IEEE 802, says “The IEEE 802 encapsulation of EAP does not involve PPP, and IEEE 802.1X does not include support for link or network layer negotiations.” (lines 1036-1038); the consequence drawn at lines 1038-1040 is that non-EAP mechanisms such as PAP or CHAP cannot be negotiated inside 802.1X. This is not a limitation of the wire, it is a deliberate scoping decision: the layer carries an authentication exchange and nothing else. And the layer is chosen because the link type is: lines 144-150 record that EAP runs on dedicated links, switched circuits, wired and wireless media, that it has been implemented with switches and access points using IEEE 802, and that wired encapsulation is described in the IEEE standard, so the port-based model is the price of putting EAP directly onto a LAN. The deployment picture around an 802.1X port is drawn most clearly in RFC 5281. It starts from the fact that the carrier choices already exist: “For example, PPP [RFC1661] or EAPOL [802.1X] may be used to transport EAP between client and access point; RADIUS [RFC2865] or Diameter [RFC3588] are used to transport EAP between access point and TTLS server.” (rfc5281.txt:680-683, with the four-space runs inside the quotation being the file's own line-wrap indentation). That sentence is the whole topology in one line pair - EAP over LANs on the access side, an AAA protocol on the server side - and EAPOL is the encapsulation the IEEE standard supplies. The method that RFC 5281 itself defines, “EAP-TTLS is an EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol) method” (line 25), then shows what the port is used for in practice: it tunnels a TLS session whose data phase carries an arbitrary authentication mechanism, named at lines 33-40 as possibly PAP, CHAP, MS-CHAP or MS-CHAP-V2, which the abstract at lines 37-40 describes as allowing legacy password-based protocols to be used against existing authentication databases while protecting them against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks. Two honesty notes belong with this claim. First, this document is Informational (line 9), so it is evidence of the architecture, not of a requirement. Second, none of the three registered files contains any text of the IEEE standard itself: what they reproduce is its role names and its bibliographic identity, and rfc5281.txt:2710-2712 gives that identity as “IEEE Standard 802.1X-2004, December 2004.” - the edition these documents were written against. The limits this document states are structural, and the sharpest one is about who the peer actually finishes authenticating to. Where the EAP server sits on a machine apart from the authenticator, “server, not between the peer and the authenticator.” and therefore, as lines 3003-3006 put it, it is not possible for the peer to validate the identity of “the authenticator that it is speaking to, using EAP alone.” (rfc3748.txt:3003-3006). The port-controlling device is thus trusted on other grounds; the method does not vouch for it. A second consequence is that the result tokens themselves are not a method: “Success and Failure packets MUST NOT be sent by an EAP authenticator” if the running method does not permit it to finish there (rfc3748.txt:1300-1302), and by default a peer silently discards a canned Success sent immediately on connection, which is what stops a rogue authenticator from bypassing mutual authentication by asserting success early (lines 1304-1309, where the word canned appears in the file's own quotation marks). The tokens are not acknowledged and may be lost, which is why a peer is told to treat a lower-layer success indication as evidence that a Success packet went missing (lines 1311-1315, 1049-1053). Third, negotiation is an attack surface: “In a negotiation attack, the attacker attempts to convince the peer” and to do it by pushing toward a weaker method, since EAP provides no protection for Nak Response packets (rfc3748.txt:2762-2766). The countermeasure in lines 2768-2776 is administrative rather than cryptographic - one authentication method per named peer identity, so a choice of methods never exists to be exploited. Fourth, the enforcement boundary leaks by design: “authentication failure will result in denied access to the controlled port in [IEEE-802.1X], limited traffic may be permitted on the uncontrolled port.” (lines 2787-2790). The uncontrolled port exists to carry the authentication itself, but it is also the part of the model an attacker always reaches. RFC 5216 dates the model twice, once by its own header and once by the edition it cites. Its own header (lines 7-14) gives March 2008 and prints “Obsoletes: 2716”. Its informative reference list (lines 1615-1618) names the standard as “IEEE Standard 802.1X-2004”, “December 2004.” - so the retained copy of this row's evidence cites the 2004 edition, and nothing in these three files prints any later edition; the catalogue's own source line mentions a 2020 revision, which no registered text here attests, so it is not asserted. Independently of the bibliography, RFC 5216 carries its own copy of the role model, and it is worth comparing with RFC 3748: the authenticator is “The entity initiating EAP authentication.” (line 147), the peer is “The entity that responds to the authenticator.” (line 150), and in the IEEE standard's vocabulary “this entity is known as the Supplicant.” (line 151) - the same mapping, stated again by a different document, which is why the terminology is treated here as shared rather than as an EAP invention. What changed between the two RFCs is recorded in RFC 5216's own change list at lines 1749-1752: “As EAP is now in use with a variety of lower layers, not just PPP”, for which it was first designed, has been widened and reference is now made to other lower layers (lines 1749-1752); section 1 states that list to include “IEEE 802 wired networks” among them (lines 100-106), and the sentence stops before line 105 because line 105 breaks the token IEEE 802.11 across a hyphenated line end. One dated technical note rounds this out: EAP-TLS's own security claims table at lines 1302-1315 asserts mutual authentication and dictionary-attack protection while printing channel binding as No, which is the same gap RFC 3748 section 7.15 describes for pass-through authenticators. - Wikipedia search entry for 基于端口的网络访问控制. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%9F%BA%E4%BA%8E%E7%AB%AF%E5%8F%A3%E7%9A%84%E7%BD%91%E7%BB%9C%E8%AE%BF%E9%97%AE%E6%8E%A7%E5%88%B6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Port-Based Network Access Control: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
