items.title: Common Criteria
items.text: Standard : Common Criteria (通用评估准则). RFC 4949 gives the concept its definitional shape under the headword Common Criteria for Information Technology Security (rfc4949.txt:3850): "A standard for evaluating information technology (IT) products and systems. It states requirements for security functions and for assurance measures." The two axes named there - security functions, and assurance measures - are what the parts split up. Part 1 is described as defining the general concepts and principles of IT security evaluation (3890-3895) and Part 2 as containing the catalog of functional requirement statements (3897-3900); only the Part 3 run is marked here, because every longer run in this file crosses a 72-column wrap and would carry the continuation indents inside the quotation: "Part 3, Security Assurance Requirements, contains a catalog of assurance components for use as a standard way of expressing such requirements for IT products and systems, and defines evaluation criteria for protection profiles and security targets." (3902-3905). The objects the machinery moves are defined as terms of art. The thing being evaluated is the target of evaluation: "An information technology product or system that is the subject of a security evaluation, together with the product's associated administrator and user documentation." (16833-16835). The claims about it are written either by consumers, in a protection profile (13267-13280), or by the vendor, in a security target (15424-15437). The confidence scale is the evaluated assurance level: "The Common Criteria defines a scale of seven, hierarchically ordered EALs for rating a TOE." (6895-6897), and the seven levels run from "EAL1. Functionally tested." at the bottom (6904) up to a formally verified design and tested at the top (6898). Note what this principle claim is not: no registered retained text in this corpus is the ISO/IEC 15408 document itself, so nothing here quotes the Criteria's own requirement numbering, and the structure above is the glossary's description of it. Why an evaluation standard of this shape exists is answered by what an assessment can and cannot establish about a component. SP 800-53A Revision 5 states the thing being judged: "The security or privacy strength of a system component (i.e., hardware, software, or firmware) is determined by the degree to which the security or privacy functionality implemented within that component is correct, complete, resistant to direct attacks (strength of mechanism), and resistant to bypass or tampering." (sp800-53a_r5.txt:496). That sentence is the rationale for the split RFC 4949 describes - correctness, completeness and resistance to direct attack or to bypass are properties of how an implemented function holds up, which is a different question from which functions to require. The same footnote then names the venue where that question is answered for components: "Common Criteria Testing Laboratories test and evaluate information technology products using [ISO 15408]." (497), alongside the laboratories that do the cloud and cryptographic-module work. The third design motive the retained text shows is reuse: an assessment may begin by "Obtaining previous assessment results that may be appropriately reused for the current assessment" (e.g. ... [ISO 15408] evaluations) (976) - reuse of prior evaluation results is listed as a legitimate input, which is only possible if the results are written against a reusable, implementation-independent statement of requirements. The standard's own self-description is visible in the catalogue entry this document cites: "Evaluation criteria for IT security" "Part 1: Introduction and general model." (47002) - the ISO title runs through its own dash separators, which this extraction prints as mojibake, so only the ASCII segment between them is quoted. The one place a registered NIST guideline in this corpus points procurement at the Criteria is SP 800-63B-4, the authentication and authenticator-management volume of the Digital Identity Guidelines, in a paragraph about non-software authenticators that must not be able to export their secret (sp800-63b.txt:2288-2290). It states the recommendation this way: "Organizations SHOULD employ authenticators that have undergone independent security testing" and then gives the two acceptable routes: "such as authenticators validated to [FIPS140] security level 2 overall with level 3 physical security6 or evaluated against relevant Common Criteria Protection Profiles." (2291-2294). Two things should be read off that sentence carefully. First, it is a SHOULD, an instruction to organisations about which authenticators to prefer, not a rule that a product must hold a certificate. Second, it points at protection profiles rather than at an EAL: the instrument named is the profile, the implementation-independent statement of requirements for a category of products that RFC 4949 defines at rfc4949.txt:13267-13280 and describes as the consumer-side document at 13282-13285. Note too that the retained text prints the footnote marker fused onto the word in physical security6; the run is quoted exactly as printed, not tidied. The wider machinery is described but not asserted here: RFC 4949 defines a commercially licensed evaluation facility as an organisation with official approval to evaluate products under the Common Criteria (rfc4949.txt:3833-3835) and records that NIAP develops protection profiles and test sets and works on an international mutual recognition scheme (10983-10998); those lines are pointers, and the marks in this claim belong to its own source. The limits are stated by the source rather than inferred. The scope sentence is positive: "The standard addresses data confidentiality, data integrity, and availability and may apply to other aspects of security." (rfc4949.txt:3877-3878). The exclusions are then printed as a list, and the last item is the one a cryptography catalogue should notice: "It does not apply to (a) administrative security not related directly to technical security, (b) technical physical aspects of security such as electromagnetic emanation control, (c) evaluation methodology or administrative and legal framework under which the criteria may be applied, (d) procedures for use of evaluation results, or (e) assessment of inherent qualities of cryptographic algorithms." (3882-3888). A product evaluated under the Criteria has therefore had its implemented mechanisms assessed for correctness, completeness and resistance; the assessment of the algorithms themselves is outside the standard's stated remit - which is why this row carries no claim about any cipher being vetted by an EAL. Second, the scale does not transfer cleanly across criteria families: of the equivalence between EALs and the older TCSEC letters the glossary says "However, this equivalency should be used with caution. The levels do not derive assurance in the same manner, and exact mappings do not exist." (6918-6920). Third, the baseline is the vendor's own document: "Common Criteria philosophy, it is important that a TOE be evaluated against the specific set of criteria expressed in the target." (16841-16843), with the target itself being checked for being correct, complete and internally consistent (16846-16848) - an evaluation certifies conformance to a stated target, and the space for a weak target is exactly where this boundary lies. None of this is an account of the Criteria being broken: the retained texts describe no attack on an evaluated product, and no such claim is made here. What they do state is the 1993 motivation to consolidate earlier criteria (3856-3860), which is history, and the exclusions above, which are limits. The retained dates are few and specific. "Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, and the United States (NIST and NSA) began developing this standard in 1993, based on the European ITSEC, the Canadian Trusted Computer Product Evaluation Criteria (CTCPEC)" (rfc4949.txt:3856-3860): five European parties plus the United States through NIST and NSA, starting in 1993, on the base of ITSEC, CTCPEC and the U.S. Federal Criteria with the TCSEC as precursor - the mark stops before the Federal Criteria title because the glossary encloses that title in its own quotation marks, so quoting it would put quote characters inside a mark. Work was done in cooperation with "ISO/IEC Joint Technical Committee 1 (Information Technology)," (3862), and its Subcommittee 27, Working Group 3 is named at 3871. The ISO step: "Version 2.0 of the Criteria has been issued as ISO's International Standard 15408." (3872-3873), and the intent that went with it: "The U.S. Government intends this standard to supersede both the TCSEC and FIPS PUB 140." (3873-3874). The predecessor's own entry records the same outcome in three words - the ITSEC entry ends "Superseded by the Common Criteria." (8564). The version the glossary cites is dated in its bibliography: the [CCIB] entry names the Common Criteria Implementation Board, Part 1 Introduction and General Model, version 2.0, CCIB-98-026, and "May 1998." (19283-19286). The source's own date belongs in the record too: RFC 4949 prints Request for Comments: 4949 and August 2007 at lines 7-8, and the Common Criteria text it describes is therefore the mid-1990s-to-2007 picture, not the current one. Later editions are outside this retained text except as a pointer: SP 800-53A Revision 5 cites the ISO catalogue entry for Part 1: Introduction and general model. dated 2009 (sp800-53a_r5.txt:47002), cited here by line because this claim's source is the RFC. Two further things the retained text does not give are deliberately absent from this entry: any list of recognised schemes or mutual-recognition signatories beyond the NIAP bullet at rfc4949.txt:10997-10998, and any statement of how many products have been evaluated. - Wikipedia search entry for 通用评估准则. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%80%9A%E7%94%A8%E8%AF%84%E4%BC%B0%E5%87%86%E5%88%99 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Common Criteria: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Trusted Platform Module
items.text: Algorithm : Trusted Platform Module (可信平台模块). The plainest mechanism sentence in the retained corpus is NIST SP 800-193's platform-device list, where the TPM is item 2 and the definition is a capability pair: "A TPM [4] is a security coprocessor capable of securely storing and using cryptographic keys and measurements of the state of the platform." The bracketed 4 is this document's own reference number for the TCG specification, given at sp800-193.txt:894-900. The same line draws the three uses out of that pairing, "These capabilities can be used, among other things, to secure data stored on the system, provide a strong device identity, and to attest the state of the system." So what the definition puts together in one addressable component is keys the platform may use while they stay under the module's own protection, and records of platform state the module can sign. The physical form is deliberately open: line 222 ends mid-sentence with "TPM's can be either discrete hardware devices,", the page furniture of lines 223-230 sits between that and its continuation, and sp800-193.txt:231 resumes "firmware executed on a platform host controller or other microcontroller (the latter are sometimes referred to as firmware TPM's, or fTPM)." Both halves are quoted as printed and not re-joined into one sentence, because the retained file does not print them as one. Why a separately specified component rather than a program? RFC 4949's answer is inside what the name denotes. The entry at rfc4949.txt:17927-17930 reads "The name of a specification, published by the TCG, for a microcontroller that can store secured information; and also the general name of implementations of that specification." - the wide gaps inside that run are the six-space indentation this file gives its continuation lines, carried here as printed. Two design consequences come out of that wording. First, one abbreviation covers a document and a device class at once, which is why the glossary's own $ TPM article at rfc4949.txt:17343-17344 can only say "See: Trusted Platform Module." Second, the publisher is a standards body and not a vendor: TCG is defined at rfc4949.txt:17883-17888 as "A not-for-profit, industry standards organization formed to develop, define, and promote open standards for hardware-enabled trusted computing and security technologies, including hardware building blocks and software interfaces, across multiple platforms, peripherals, and devices." The phrase that carries the design premise is "trusted computing and security technologies", and the qualifier "across multiple" is what a hardware-enabled interface has to satisfy if the assurance is to travel between vendors; pinning the interface to a specified component rather than to one machine's software is the consequence. The glossary also keeps the module apart from the boundary it serves: the trusted computing base article (rfc4949.txt:17877-17881) closes with the cross-reference "Compare: TPM.", so the totality of protection mechanisms and the chip that provides some of them are two different things to be reasoned about. The clearest deployment statement in this corpus is W3C's Web Authentication Level 3, which treats a TPM as one of the places a conforming authenticator may execute: "on an on-device Secure Execution Environment, Trusted Platform Module (TPM), or a Secure Element (SE)" (webauthn3.html:1506). Where the authenticator is embedded in the client, the abstract model makes the module the strongest part of it: "This is particularly important for authenticators that are embedded in the WebAuthn client, as in those cases this cryptographic module (which may, for example, be a TPM) could be considered more trustworthy than the rest of the authenticator." (webauthn3.html:5680-5682). Attestation is where the TPM is named as a format in its own right: "This attestation statement format is generally used by authenticators that use a Trusted Platform Module as their cryptographic engine." (webauthn3.html:7510-7511), whose ver field is "The version of the TPM specification to which the signature conforms." (webauthn3.html:7542). The specification records that these formats predate it - "Various existing components and OS platforms (such as TPMs and the Android OS) have previously defined" attestation statement formats (webauthn3.html:6640) - and describes the AttCA case as an authenticator "based on a Trusted Platform Module (TPM)" holding an endorsement key (webauthn3.html:6828) that requests per-credential identity keys from an attestation CA so that it "can limit the exposure of the EK (which is a global correlation handle) to Attestation CA(s)." (webauthn3.html:6832-6833). The privacy edge is documented in the certificate requirements: older EK profiles carried a module serial number, "called HardwareModuleName, that contains the TPM serial number in the EK certificate." (webauthn3.html:7628), and webauthn3.html:7629 directs that it not be placed in the attestation certificate's Subject Alternative Name. The limits the retained sources state are conditions the module does not meet by existing. SP 800-193 makes the module itself an object that has to be protected rather than a source of guarantees: "While not all platforms include or make use of a TPM, on any system in which a TPM is included and used, its firmware must be protected given its criticality in helping ensure the trustworthiness of the platform." and, in the next sentence, "TPMs also contain non-volatile memory storage which may contain critical data and, if so, must be protected." (both sp800-193.txt:222). The fTPM realization widens the surface on the same page: the functional role is then carried by "firmware executed on a platform host controller or other microcontroller" (sp800-193.txt:231), i.e. by code that shares silicon with the host. The sharpest statement is the guideline's own rule for roots of trust at sp800-193.txt:341: "A RoT must be designed to always behave in the expected manner because its proper functioning is essential to providing its security-specific functions and because its misbehavior cannot be detected." The clause cuts both ways - the platform cannot check the component from outside, which is precisely why that component is trusted, and it is why the document's protection, detection and recovery guidance is addressed to the firmware of that module and of the devices around it, not to trusting the chip on its own terms. The same line 341 also lists what a root of trust is for ("measurement, storage, reporting, recovery, verification, and update"), which is the functional vocabulary a TPM is being asked to carry. What the three registered files do not contain is a break of the specification: no attack on the TPM's cryptographic design is reported in them, so none is claimed here; WebAuthn's answer to the same unknowability is structural, checking fields and certificate chains instead (webauthn3.html:7596-7615). The three registered files date themselves and say nothing about the module's first appearance. The earliest is RFC 4949: its header carries "August 2007" at line 8 and "Obsoletes: 2828" at line 10, and its title line at 14 reads "Internet Security Glossary, Version 2", a string that recurs on the page imprints (line 17924 pairs it with the same date). That document already records the term as an established abbreviation with a standards body named as its publisher (lines 17927-17931), and it gives no year for the specification it points at - which is the honest limit of what a glossary supplies. The next registered date is SP 800-193, titled at its line 2 and dated May 2018 at line 11; it cites the TCG's library specification as reference [4] (sp800-193.txt:894-900, with the access date printed as 5/2/18), and that is the only TCG document this corpus registers a path for. The newest is the WebAuthn Level 3 copy, dated 25 August 2026 at webauthn3.html:972, which carries a tpm attestation format and a bibliographic list of TPMv2 parts. None of these lines prints a first-publication year for the TPM specification, a version history, or the name of anyone who proposed it, so this entry attributes no inventor and no origin date; the catalogue row's own unretained bibliography entry for the TCG specification is not evidence here. - Wikipedia search entry for 可信平台模块. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%8F%AF%E4%BF%A1%E5%B9%B3%E5%8F%B0%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Trusted Platform Module: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Triple DES
items.text: Standard : Triple DES (三重数据加密标准). The two TDEA transformations are printed directly by the appendix. Encryption: “1. TDEA encryption operation: the transformation of a 64-bit block I into a 64-bit block O that is defined as follows: O = EK3(DK2(EK1(I))).” Decryption: “O = DK1(EK2(DK3(I)))”. The key structure is printed at line 48: “A TDEA key consists of three DES keys, which is also referred to as a key bundle.” The same line states that a single DES key is 64 binary digits of which 56 bits are used directly by the algorithm and the other 8 serve error detection. The formulas are quoted with the extraction's own parentheses and subscripts, not reformatted. The design choices are printed as three keying options at line 371: “Keying Option 1: K1, K2 and K3 are independent keys”, “Keying Option 2: K1 and K2 are independent keys and K3 = K1”, and “Keying Option 3: K1 = K2 = K3”. The same paragraph gives the backward-compatibility condition, and line 373 prints its consequence: “an encrypted plaintext computed using a TDEA mode of operation can be decrypted correctly by a corresponding single DES mode of operation.” The three options and that compatibility are two sides of one design trade-off; this entry states only the options and conditions the file prints and does not infer strength figures for each option. The applicability is printed by clause 12 itself: “It applies to all Federal agencies, contractors of Federal agencies, or other organizations that process information (using a computer or telecommunications system) on behalf of the Federal Government to accomplish a Federal function.” The same clause says each agency may issue internal directives based on its data-security requirement determinations. This row's usage statement is therefore limited to the standard's own stated mandatory audience and is not extended into general commercial deployment advice; concrete TDEA work instances live in the member rows algorithm--3des and algorithm--des. The limit is not a particular attack but that the standard itself has been withdrawn, and that status is printed by the file rather than inferred: line 4 states it “was withdrawn on May 19, 2005 and is provided here only for historical purposes”. The same page immediately gives the onward references: line 6 points to SP 800-131A (transitioning cryptographic algorithms and key lengths) and line 7 to SP 800-67 Rev. 1 (the TDEA block cipher recommendation). This row therefore states explicitly that the standard is withdrawn and serves as a historical document, not as current usage advice; plan V7 forbids guessing current versus withdrawn status, and this quotes the printed sentence. Every dating coordinate is printed by the file. Line 78: “This standard became effective July 1977. It was reaffirmed in 1983, 1988, 1993, and 1999.” The announcement header at line 42 prints “1999 October 25 Announcing the DATA ENCRYPTION STANDARD”. Line 4 gives the endpoint: withdrawal on May 19, 2005. This row therefore states the printed timeline of 1977 effectivity, four reaffirmations, the 1999-10-25 announcement edition and the 2005 withdrawal, and adds no drafting process or competition detail the file does not print. - Wikipedia search entry for 三重数据加密标准. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E4%B8%89%E9%87%8D%E6%95%B0%E6%8D%AE%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A0%87%E5%87%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - NIST FIPS 46-3: Data Encryption Standard. https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/46-3/final Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Triple DES: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Attribute-Based Encryption (ABE)
items.text: Algorithm : Attribute-Based Encryption (属性基加密). ABE writes an access policy into the ciphertext or the key. In ciphertext-policy ABE (CP-ABE) the policy sits in the ciphertext and keys carry user attributes; key-policy ABE (KP-ABE) reverses the arrangement. Decryption succeeds only when the attribute set satisfies the policy. Early constructions use bilinear maps, map attributes to group elements and distribute decryption capability through secret sharing across satisfying combinations; lattice-based constructions followed. It changes access control from “encrypt to one person” to “encrypt to anyone satisfying a condition”. That suits cloud drives, medical records, log auditing and cross-organisation sharing: the sender need not fetch every recipient's public key, and revocation or policy updates can be handled at the key layer. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Fine-grained access control on cloud storage, electronic health record sharing, cross-organisation data collaboration and tiered paid content. Deployments combine it with attribute authorities, revocation and audit logs; an ABE scheme alone is not a complete system. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The main risks are collusion—several users combining attribute keys to satisfy a policy no single user could satisfy—plus delayed revocation, overly broad policies and bad bilinear-group parameters. ABE does not hide access patterns; ciphertext size and policy structure can leak information. It provides no authentication and must be composed with signatures, PKI or a trusted authority. KP-ABE and CP-ABE constructions appeared in 2006–2007, followed by multi-authority, revocable, lattice-based and policy-hiding variants. It did not replace IBE; it widened IBE's single identity into an attribute set. items.title: Ajtai's Reduction
items.text: Theorem : Ajtai's Reduction (Ajtai 归约). Ajtai proves that if a polynomial-time algorithm solves a class of randomly generated lattice instances with non-negligible probability, then it yields a polynomial-time algorithm for the worst-case lattice problem within some approximation factor. The key is “generating hard instances”: the random matrix is not arbitrary but drawn from a distribution that makes breaking it equivalent to breaking the worst case. Before this, lattice cryptography relied on the empirical judgement that a random instance “looks hard”. After it, a scheme could claim “break the scheme, break worst-case lattices”. It became the template for LWE, Ring-LWE and NTRU security arguments and one reason post-quantum standardisation accepted lattice schemes. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. As the security-proof skeleton for lattice encryption, hashing, pseudorandom functions and signatures. Deployments do not run Ajtai's original construction, but cite its reduction pattern when arguing parameters. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. A reduction is not an attack and does not prove lattice problems absolutely hard; it shows that if the worst case is hard, the average case is hard. Approximation factors, moduli and dimensions affect the strength. Reductions can be non-tight, giving a security floor far below actual attack cost. They do not cover implementation side channels. Theorem = (Assumptions ⇒ Conclusion)；Reduction: Adv_A ≤ q · Adv_B + ε. Regev used a similar idea for LWE in 2005, and Lyubashevsky et al. extended it to rings. It is one of the starting points of modern lattice cryptography. items.title: BFV Homomorphic Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : Brakerski-Fan-Vercauteren FHE (BFV 全同态加密). BFV encodes plaintext as elements of a polynomial ring and carries them in noisy ring-LWE ciphertexts. Addition is direct; multiplication uses a tensor product followed by key switching and relinearisation to bring the ciphertext back to two components. Each multiplication amplifies noise. When noise exceeds the modulus-dependent budget, decryption fails. A leveled circuit is one whose depth fits a pre-chosen parameter set. It turns “send data to the cloud, let the cloud compute without seeing plaintext” from a concept into engineering. BFV's integer semantics suit statistics, billing, database aggregation and fixed-point inference; compared with CKKS's approximate floating point, it fits tasks that demand exact results. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Privacy-preserving statistics, encrypted database queries, federated-learning aggregation, genomic computation and financial risk scoring. Deployments use libraries such as SEAL, OpenFHE and HElib and design depth, modulus chain and security parameters together. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. BFV is not “run any program encrypted”. Multiplication depth is limited by the noise budget; modulus switching, key switching and relinearisation add noise; parameters that are too small invite lattice attacks, while large parameters are too slow. It does not hide access patterns, and decrypted outputs can leak information. Side channels and key management still matter. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Brakerski proposed leveled LWE-based FHE in 2012; Fan and Vercauteren then gave the more practical BFV variant with improved modulus switching and encoding. It did not remove Gentry's bootstrapping cost; it made bounded-depth workloads practical. BFV and CKKS are often discussed together today, but their semantics differ. items.title: CKKS Approximate Homomorphic Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : Cheon-Kim-Kim-Song FHE (CKKS 近似同态加密). CKKS encodes real or complex vectors into polynomials carried by ring-LWE ciphertexts. Addition preserves approximate precision; multiplication is followed by rescaling to reduce the modulus and control noise. Slots operate in parallel, so one ciphertext can carry hundreds or thousands of floating-point values. Decryption returns an approximation, with error from encoding, noise and rescaling. Many real workloads already use floating point: neural-network inference, statistical regression, signal processing and scientific computing. BFV's exact-integer semantics require fixed-point conversion or lose depth in these settings; CKKS trades controlled approximation for natural vector arithmetic. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Privacy-preserving machine-learning inference, encrypted statistics, genomic association studies, signal processing and federated analytics. Implementations design multiplication depth, scaling factors and modulus chains; not every operator is homomorphic, and comparison, division and nonlinear functions usually need polynomial approximation. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. CKKS output is approximate and must not be treated as exact integers or exact billing. Too many multiplications drown the plaintext in noise; a wrong rescaling factor destroys precision; small parameters invite lattice attacks. It does not hide access patterns or provide branching and comparison. Side channels, key management and decryption interfaces can still leak. items.title: Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement
items.text: Algorithm : Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement (Diffie-Hellman 密钥协商). The paper proposes a public key distribution system, not a key wrapped by one party and transported to the other. It says: “Public key distribution systems offer a different approach to eliminating the need for a secure key distribution channel.” In such a system, “two users who wish to exchange a key communicate back and forth until they arrive at a key in common”, while “A third party eavesdropping on this exchange must find it computationally infeasible to compute the key from the information overheard”. The mechanism rests on discrete logarithms over a finite field: “The new technique makes use of the apparent difficulty of computing logarithms over a finite field GF(q) with a prime number q of elements.” The design avoids dependence on a secure key-distribution channel set up in advance. The paper calls public key distribution “a different approach to eliminating the need for a secure key distribution channel”: the two parties need no prior shared secret, and can arrive at a common key by exchanging public values. Its security is computational, not information-theoretic perfect secrecy: “The security of our technique depends crucially on the difficulty of computing logarithms mod q”, and the paper treats q^(1/2) as “a good measure of the problem's complexity” — a 1976 estimate. The procedure is: each user independently generates a random secret exponent, keeps it secret, and places the corresponding public value in a public file. The paper says: “Each user generates an independent random number”; “Each keeps Xi secret, but places”; the public value “in a public file with his name and address”. The two parties then each use their own secret exponent with the other's public value to compute the same key. This entry describes only that key-agreement step; it is not a digital signature, certificate issuance, or a complete deployed protocol, and the paper does not supply a PKI for maintaining the public file. The paper grounds security in the hardness of discrete logarithms and explicitly treats it as an assumption: “The security of our technique depends crucially on the difficulty of computing logarithms mod q”; if logs are easy, “the system can be broken”. The authors also write: “we do not currently have a proof of the converse” — there is no proof that hard discrete logs imply a secure system. This entry therefore cannot turn the 1976 q^(1/2) estimate into a modern security proof; the paper supplies neither a concrete attack nor a reduction. The difficulty of computing the key from public values for a passive eavesdropper remains the scheme's central boundary. The paper is titled “New Directions in Cryptography” by “WHITFIELD DIFFIE AND MARTIN E. HELLMAN, MEMBER, IEEE”, published in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 22(6), November 1976, pages 644–654; the first page records “Manuscript received June 3,1976.” It proposes public-key distribution and discusses public-key cryptosystems, but the authors themselves write: “We propose some techniques for developing public key cryptosystems, but the problem is still largely open.” This entry therefore dates the 1976 paper as a public proposal of key distribution; it is not a deployed protocol, a delivered digital signature, or a proven-secure system. - Wikipedia search entry for Diffie-Hellman 密钥协商. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Diffie-Hellman%20%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E5%8D%8F%E5%95%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ - Diffie, Hellman: New Directions in Cryptography. https://ee.stanford.edu/~hellman/publications/24.pdf Formal model and reproduction steps \[K=g^{ab}\bmod p\quad\text{或}\quad K=[ab]G\] Diffie-Hellman Key Agreement: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Semantic Security ≡ IND-CPA
items.text: Theorem : Semantic Security ≡ IND-CPA (语义安全与 CPA 等价). The theorem says this: semantic security and IND-CPA look like completely different definitions, but they mean exactly the same thing. Start with the two definitions. Semantic security : having the ciphertext is not enough to judge what an attacker can learn. Formally, an encryption scheme E is semantically secure if and only if for every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary A there exists a simulator S (which never sees the ciphertext) such that the success probability of A in computing any function f of the plaintext with the ciphertext exceeds, by at most a negligible amount, the success probability of S faking it without the ciphertext. Mind the existential quantifier: security does not mean "nobody can compute it" — it means "you cannot tell the difference between what you can compute and what you cannot". IND-CPA (indistinguishability against chosen-plaintext attack) : it is a game. The challenger generates a key; the adversary submits two equal-length plaintexts m0 and m1 ; the challenger picks a random bit b ∈ {0,1} and hands back Enc(m_b) ; the adversary outputs a guess b' . The advantage is Adv = Pr[b' = b] - 1/2 . A scheme is IND-CPA secure if and only if that advantage is negligible for every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary. The theorem (equivalence) : for any encryption scheme E, the following are equivalent: 1. E is semantically secure; 2. E is IND-CPA secure. Why is this worth a theorem of its own? Because the two definitions have completely different shapes. IND-CPA asks "can you tell these two messages apart?" — a yes/no guessing game. Semantic security asks "everything you can compute about the plaintext, can you also compute it without the ciphertext?" — an open-ended game where the adversary picks the function. Two differently phrased questions, one answer. How the reduction works (this is the technique the whole of modern cryptography runs on): translate each definition into the other. - One direction: suppose there is an IND-CPA adversary that guesses b with non-negligible probability. Give it an easier job — restrict the message space to {m0, m1} , define f(m0) = 0 and f(m1) = 1 , and ask it to compute f(x) from the ciphertext. Its success rate is exactly its bit-guessing rate, while a simulator without the ciphertext can only guess at 1/2. "Computing it accurately" and "telling them apart" are the same thing. - The other direction: suppose there is a semantic-security adversary that computes f(x) from the ciphertext better than the simulator does. Build a bit-guessing adversary out of it: give it the ciphertext of a random message, run the computation, and compare the answer with what the simulator produces. If agreement happens more often than by chance, the ciphertext genuinely helped — so the adversary can distinguish the two worlds. The gap between the two translations is exactly the gap between the two advantages. In one line: two definitions are equivalent if and only if the difference between them is zero. A few technical preconditions must be stated. First, the 1984 equivalence carries a condition: the probability distribution over the adversary's chosen plaintexts needs a minimum-entropy requirement, otherwise both sides degenerate into trivial cases. Second, one message and many messages are not the same thing — the many-message case needs the hybrid argument : swap each of the n messages for a random string one at a time, tally the difference at each step, and close the argument with "at least one message must have been guessed wrong". Third, the original equivalence was established only for the chosen-plaintext model; Watanabe, Shikata and Imai proved in 2003 that SS and IND are equivalent under every attack model (chosen-plaintext, chosen-ciphertext, non-adaptive and adaptive). Because it turned "secure" from an adjective into a problem you can prove. This is where modern cryptography starts, and the line it draws separates it from the cryptography that came before. Before Goldwasser and Micali, the question "is this scheme secure?" had no falsifiable answer. You could show an attack, or you could say "I could not find an attack". After 1982 the question became: "under assumption X, this scheme is IND-CPA secure" — a sentence that can be proved, and therefore also refuted. The impact works on three levels: 1. It makes proofs possible at all. A definition supplies a ruler, and "reduce to a hardness assumption" becomes a goal. Almost every cryptography paper today opens and closes with the same sentence: state the definition, state the assumption, give the reduction. That is the shift from craft to science. 2. It makes attack models gradable. With IND-CPA as the middle rung, people could ask precisely what happens if the adversary gets one decryption oracle as well — hence IND-CCA2 — and whether they can tamper with a ciphertext into a related one — hence non-malleability. The example Dolev, Dwork and Naor gave in Non-Malleable Cryptography (1991) is vivid: three players running a coin-flipping protocol, where the public-key encryption is semantically secure and one player can still rig the outcome. Semantic security defends against passive eavesdroppers, not active participants. That is the hole Dwork's line of work closed. 3. It defines what "secure enough" means. Modern cryptography does not chase absolute security; it asks for a quantifiable advantage bound for a resource-bounded adversary under an explicitly stated attack model. That language comes from here. And be clear about what the theorem did not do: it did not prove any scheme secure. It rephrased "secure". The real work is the reduction — reducing IND-CPA to the hardness of factoring, discrete logarithms or lattice problems. The definition is the skeleton; the assumption is the muscle. IND-CPA is now the entry ticket for essentially every real scheme, and it shows up in every security claim. - Symmetric encryption: it comes almost for free. The reason deserves precision: modern symmetric encryption (AEAD: GCM, CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305) uses a fresh random nonce for every message. For a fixed key, encryption is a permutation — each plaintext maps to exactly one ciphertext. All the adversary has is "guess", and being able to guess the plaintext is precisely the same as being able to distinguish a permutation from a random function, which is what PRP security says. So: a secure PRP underneath plus a fresh nonce per message gives you IND-CPA essentially free. The converse is where people get burned: deterministic encryption is not IND-CPA secure. In ECB mode two identical plaintexts produce identical ciphertexts, so an adversary that submits m0 = m1 wins by comparing ciphertexts. Any claim that "symmetric encryption is secure" needs the word "randomized" attached. - Public-key schemes : RSA-OAEP (Bellare and Rogaway proved IND-CPA security in the random-oracle model), ElGamal (under DDH), ECIES, and Cramer–Shoup, the textbook IND-CCA2 construction. - Hard rules at the protocol layer : TLS 1.3 permits AEAD suites only and forbids ECB and static-IV RSA key exchange; nearly every TLS library enforces nonce uniqueness at the API level with counters. The source of those rules is IND-CPA — no randomization, no IND-CPA. - The fixed opening line of the literature : a new scheme almost always begins "In the random oracle model, our scheme is IND-CPA secure under the ... assumption", followed by a chain of reductions. The boundaries of this theorem matter more than its conclusion. - IND-CPA covers confidentiality and nothing else. The definition has no column for "what if the ciphertext was modified". The real-world consequence is the parade of 1990s CBC disasters: with a controllable IV and verifiable padding, an attacker can manufacture a valid-looking ciphertext and then use a padding oracle to peel the plaintext out one byte at a time. You must add INT-CTXT (authenticated encryption), or honestly do Encrypt-then-MAC. - Why CCA does not follow. Hand the adversary a decryption oracle and it can tamper with a ciphertext and submit the result for decryption. Three classics: ElGamal is malleable — multiply the ciphertext (g^r, m·g^r) by t and you get a ciphertext of m·t ; in CBC, changing the IV changes the first plaintext block; OAEP can be malleably reworked too. "The ciphertext leaks nothing" evaporates the moment a decryptor exists. That is why IND-CCA2 and AEAD exist. - The equivalence itself has preconditions. The 1984 result demands a minimum-entropy condition on the plaintext distribution; one message and many messages need the hybrid argument to be equated at all; the CCA case was only settled in 2003. "Equivalent" did not fall from the sky — it was cleaned up over a generation. - Reductions lose bits. Going from IND-CPA to a hardness assumption usually yields Adv_E(A) ≤ 2 × Adv_assumption(B) . That factor of 2, or the polynomial factor, is the "security we dropped on the floor". A paper claims 128-bit security; after the reduction it may be 126. How tight a reduction is, is a real fight in cryptography. - A definition creates no security by itself. It only rephrases the word. The work is always "reduce to an assumption", and the assumptions are unproven — nobody knows whether factoring or discrete logarithms are hard. - A long list falls outside the definition : side channels, fault injection, key compromise, a broken random-number generator, protocol downgrade and replay, integer overflows in the implementation. "IND-CPA secure" is a statement about an algorithm, not about a system. - The usual real-world failures are the usual ones : nonce reuse (the same nonce twice under GCM repeats the keystream, leaking plaintext and allowing forged tags), an unseeded RNG, ECB quietly creeping back in. None of these violate the theorem — they violate the theorem's assumptions. - 1982 : Goldwasser and Micali present Probabilistic Encryption at FOCS (published in the Journal of Computer and System Sciences , vol. 28, no. 2, pp. 270-299, in 1984). Two things are in it: "semantic security" (anything you can compute, you can compute without the ciphertext) and what was later called IND-CPA, "polynomial security" (guess which of two plaintexts it is). The equivalence of the two is the earliest game hop in the literature — by today's standards, the first game hop in the history of cryptography. - 1984 : Rivest publishes Semantic Security for Encryption Functions , carrying semantic security over to private-key encryption with a sharper formulation and a counterexample. The term "semantic security" is fixed from here on. - 1986 : Goldreich, Micali and Wigderson publish How to Prove Cryptographic Protocols Secure — zero knowledge, and the power of definitions demonstrated at the protocol layer. - 1988 : Goldwasser, Micali and Rivest's signature scheme defines EUF-CMA, and digital signatures get a game too. - 1991 : Dolev, Dwork and Naor publish Non-Malleable Cryptography . A toy three-player coin-flipping protocol shows that semantic security only defends against passive eavesdroppers, not against active participants. Non-malleability enters the literature here, and Dwork's line of work opens. - 1998 : Bellare, Desai, Pointcheval and Rogaway publish Relations among Notions of Security for Public-Key Encryption Schemes , mapping semantic security, indistinguishability and non-malleability across CPA / CCA1 / CCA2. That map is still the first thing anybody reads who is learning the definitions. - 2001 : Bellare and Rogaway publish Code-Based Game-Playing Proofs and the Security of Triple Encryption , turning "games" into code and establishing the fundamental lemma of game playing — two games that are identical apart from a bad event differ in advantage by at most the probability of that event. Almost every modern proof is written in that shape. - 2003 : Watanabe, Shikata and Imai (PKC 2003) prove SS equivalent to IND under every attack model; Goldreich reaches the same conclusion independently in his textbook. - 2012 : Goldwasser and Micali receive the ACM Turing Award for the foundational work on the modern definitions of cryptography. - Today : IND-CPA is the entry ticket for every new scheme, and the theoretical origin of that "supports AEAD" line in every product datasheet. - Wikipedia search entry for 语义安全与 CPA 等价. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%AF%AD%E4%B9%89%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E4%B8%8E%20CPA%20%E7%AD%89%E4%BB%B7 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Semantic Security ≡ IND-CPA: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Feldman Verifiable Secret Sharing
items.text: Algorithm : Verifiable Secret Sharing (Feldman 可验证秘密共享). Feldman VSS adds public commitments to Shamir secret sharing. The dealer picks a degree-t polynomial f, the secret is f(0), and share i is f(i). The dealer publishes g^{a_j} for each coefficient; participant i checks whether g^{f(i)} equals the corresponding combination of commitments. Shares stay hidden while inconsistency with the same polynomial is detectable. Plain Shamir sharing assumes an honest dealer. If the dealer gives inconsistent shares, reconstruction fails and it is hard to tell who lied. Feldman turns verification into a non-interactive public check and became a building block for threshold signatures, distributed key generation and MPC. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Distributed key generation, threshold signatures, threshold decryption and key sharing among blockchain validators. Deployments combine it with DKG protocols: verify shares first, then reconstruct or sign. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Feldman commitments are public and leak algebraic relations among shares; the scheme is not zero-knowledge and does not hide share values. It detects dealer inconsistency but cannot stop malicious participants from colluding or refusing to participate later. Security rests on discrete logarithms; bad group parameters break it. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Symbols are catalogue-level variables, not standard constants; parameters, test vectors and clauses remain with the registered source. The model states structural relations, not an implementation audit. Feldman proposed the scheme at FOCS 1987, moving verifiable secret sharing from interactive protocols toward practical use. Pedersen VSS later added zero-knowledge hiding through Pedersen commitments, and Gennaro et al. used VSS in threshold DKG. It is the verification layer most often paired with Shamir sharing. Given abstract input x₀ and parameter p, compute y₀ and test it against the criterion; this is a reasoning example, not a measured vector. items.title: Fiat-Shamir Heuristic
items.text: Algorithm : Fiat-Shamir Heuristic (Fiat-Shamir 启发式). The Fiat–Shamir heuristic is the most used — and most misused — transformation in cryptography: it turns an interactive protocol into a non-interactive proof or signature. A typical σ-protocol (interactive) looks like this: 1. The prover (holding a witness w) sends a commitment a; 2. The verifier (knowing only the statement x) picks a random challenge c; 3. The prover responds with z; 4. The verifier checks an equation (say g^z = a · x^c ). The key point: the challenge c is chosen at random by the verifier , so the prover cannot pre-select a challenge that suits them. Security also rests on two properties: special soundness (two accepting transcripts for the same commitment with different challenges let you extract the witness w) and zero knowledge (z does not leak w). The Fiat–Shamir transform replaces step 2's randomness with a hash: c = H(session context message commitment a ...) The prover computes c itself and answers z; the verifier recomputes c afterwards and checks the equation. The two sides no longer need to talk. An "I say, you say" protocol becomes "I say it all, you check later". How does that become a signature? Put the message into the hash input. Schnorr's signature is the prototype: the interactive identification protocol (commitment R = kG → challenge e → response s = k + e·x) plus the step "e = H(m R)" is a signature. DSA, ECDSA, Ed25519 and BIP 340 are all variants of it , and ML-DSA is the lattice version — "Fiat–Shamir plus rejection sampling with aborts". Five conditions have to hold for the transform to be sound : 1. The hash must be modelled as a random oracle (the RO model). This is the big assumption. The challenge must bind the entire statement and every commitment — public key, session identifier, message, all commitments. Leave one out and you have opened an attack path. The challenge space must be large enough and uniform (usually ≥ 2λ bits), or special soundness is too weak. The commitment must be unpredictable , otherwise the prover can grind : retry commitments until it draws a favourable challenge — this is precisely why "FS with Aborts" has an abort loop. 5. The underlying protocol must itself be sound. FS amplifies a protocol's virtues; it cannot repair its flaws. Without Fiat–Shamir there are no digital signatures as we know them. A signature is defined as "the signer signs a message; a verifier checks it afterwards, alone". But the best identification protocols cryptographers can build are interactive — Schnorr's identification scheme is interactive, ElGamal's is too. Strip interactivity away and public-key cryptography becomes unusable in exactly the places it matters most: software updates, certificates, transactions, blocks. Fiat–Shamir's contribution is removing the interaction at a cost of one extra hash call . It is the highest-reuse idea in the field : - Signatures : Schnorr signatures → DSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, BIP 340, and ML-DSA's lattice signatures. - Non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs : Schnorr's proof of knowledge of a discrete logarithm is the textbook NIZK; Bulletproofs-style range proofs build on it; blockchain scripts that assert "I know this secret" are usually exactly that. - Lattice cryptography : ML-DSA's "FS with Aborts" transplants Schnorr's linear structure onto module lattices, then adds rejection sampling to kill information leakage. - Multi-party and threshold protocols : MuSig2 and FROST live inside the Schnorr family, but they have to handle challenge-collision problems explicitly. - Verifiable computation : STARK-style systems lean on the same "bind the transcript into the challenge with a hash" idea when building commitments. But the word "heuristic" in its name is a historical warning. The security argument in Fiat and Shamir's 1986 paper was wrong : its Lemma 6 implicitly relies on the forking lemma, a tool that would not be formalised for another nine years. The first fully correct proof for FS-ified Schnorr signatures had to wait for Pointcheval and Stern in 1996 . Those twenty years are the lesson: the principle is beautifully simple, and its proof is the most delicate part of the field. - Practically every mainstream digital signature : DSA, ECDSA, Ed25519, Ed448, BIP 340's Schnorr signature and ML-DSA's lattice signature are all Fiat–Shamir transforms . Fiat and Shamir's 1996 paper Security Proofs for Schnorr Signatures and the DDH Assumption exists to give this family a unified proof. - Non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs : Schnorr's discrete-log NIZK, Bulletproofs-style range proofs, and the challenge computations inside ring signatures and anonymous credential protocols. - Lattice signatures : ML-DSA uses FS with Aborts — hash the commitment into a challenge, then use rejection sampling to check whether the response leaks the secret, and abort and retry if it does. - Multi-signature and threshold signatures : Bitcoin's MuSig2 (BIP 327) and FROST (RFC 9591) both live in the Schnorr system, and both must handle challenge collisions explicitly. - Verifiable claims on blockchains : "I hold this private key" and "this transaction is authorised" assertions are usually direct instances of Schnorr NIZK. - Teaching and research : it is the standard example of "how do you turn an interactive protocol into a non-interactive one", and the best case study for why hash functions became security-critical infrastructure. Fiat–Shamir has not been "broken", but it is among the most misapplied mechanisms in cryptography, and the most insidious. Every item below maps to a real incident or a published fix. - "Weak FS" means malleable. If the challenge hashes only the commitment and not the statement ( c = H(a) rather than c = H(x a) ), the whole transform is malleable: an attacker can turn one signature into another valid signature. Leaving the public key out of the challenge is the root of the related-key attacks in the Schnorr family and the reason BIP 340 insists on key prefixing. The rule is simple: public key, session identifier, message, every commitment — none of them may be omitted. - The original Fiat–Shamir paper's proof is wrong. Lemma 6 of the 1986 STOC paper implicitly depends on the forking lemma, which would not appear for another nine years; Bellare and Rogaway in 1993 likewise asserted soundness for FS as a proof system rather than proving it. The first complete proof for an FS-based signature is Pointcheval and Stern (EUROCRYPT 1996) , which introduced the forking lemma — still one of the most-used tools in the field. - Omission attacks in multi-party settings (the ROS problem). In multi-signature and threshold protocols, an attacker can run many parallel signing sessions and use a polynomial number of hash queries to hunt for a challenge collision . Drijvers et al. (EUROCRYPT 2019) systematised this family of attacks and broke naive FS-based multi-signature constructions . That is why MuSig2 needs an extra round of nonce exchange and FROST needs a binding factor. FS holds for a single signature; in multi-party settings it has to be re-proven. - FS is generally insecure in the quantum setting. The security proof relies on rewinding the adversary's oracle queries, and a quantum algorithm can manipulate several queries at once, so rewinding breaks. Ambainis, Rosmanis and Unruh (FOCS 2014) showed that in the quantum random oracle model the FS transform is insecure in general (at minimum, no relativizing proof exists). The workarounds are "lossy FS", "FS with Aborts" and Unruh's post-quantum variant. And of course every Schnorr-family signature was already doomed by Shor. - It rests on "the hash is ideally random", an unfalsifiable assumption. Goldwasser and Kalai (STOC 2007) proved that if random oracles do not exist, the Fiat–Shamir heuristic is provably insecure . That is not academic pedantry: MD5, MD4 and SHA-1 have all been shown not to be random oracles, so running FS on them means standing on thin ice. The strength of the hash function became the load-bearing wall of the entire signature family. - The challenge distribution must be uniform. Reducing a hash modulo the group order creates statistical bias; over many signatures, nonce information leaks and the private key eventually falls out. The right answer is rejection sampling — and ML-DSA rests its entire security on getting this right. - The commitment must be unpredictable. If commitments can be predicted or chosen by the prover, the prover can grind its way to a favourable challenge. The abort loop in "FS with Aborts" exists exactly for this : notice that the sample would leak information, throw it away, start over. - The challenge space must not be tiny. With few challenge bits, the special-soundness extraction probability is high and forgery gets easier. This is the same point BIP 340 makes about "16-byte short challenges": in multi-signatures, a short challenge is collision-attackable, so you cannot save 16 bytes by shortening it. - The hash must be collision-resistant and domain-separated. Reusing one hash function across protocols and contexts is exactly what lets an attacker move a signature from one protocol to another. - 1986 : Fiat and Shamir publish A Signature Scheme Based on the Difficulty of Factoring at STOC. The technique appears for the first time : they use a "squaring" identification scheme (based on factoring hardness) to build a signature by letting the signer compute the verifier's challenge with a hash. The security argument in this paper is later found to be flawed. - 1989 / 1990 : the same pair publish How to Prove Yourself: Practical Solutions to Identification and Signature Problems (CRYPTO '89 proceedings, published 1990), giving a fuller treatment of identification and signature schemes. A promised "full version" never appeared ; this extended abstract is what circulates. Its Lemma 6 implicitly depends on the later forking lemma. - 1989 / 1990 : Claus Schnorr uses the same trick to build the Schnorr signature ( Efficient Signature Generation for Discrete Logarithm Problems , EUROCRYPT '90). From this moment FS and Schnorr are bound together , and they become the common ancestor of DSA, ECDSA, Ed25519 and BIP 340. - 1993 : Bellare and Rogaway analyse the FS transform in the random oracle model (as a non-interactive proof system), asserting soundness without proving it. - 1996 : Fiat and Shamir's Security Proofs for Schnorr Signatures and the DDH Assumption (EUROCRYPT 1996) gives the first rigorous treatment of the FS-ified Schnorr signature; Pointcheval and Stern , at the same conference, introduce the forking lemma and deliver the first complete proof; van Oorschot and Wiener publish their survey of the paradigm. This is the year FS stops being a heuristic and becomes a provable technique. - 2005 : Fischlin proposes an alternative construction that avoids rewinding, sidestepping the tightness loss and simulator blow-up that rewinding causes. - 2007 : Goldwasser and Kalai prove in On the (In)security of the Fiat-Shamir Heuristic (STOC 2007) that if random oracles do not exist, FS is provably insecure. - 2014 : Ambainis, Rosmanis and Unruh show FS is generally insecure in the quantum setting and give "FS with Aborts" — the family ML-DSA later joins. - 2019 : Drijvers et al. publish On the Security of Multi-signatures and MPC (EUROCRYPT 2019), exposing the ROS attack and forcing multi-signature schemes to be redesigned (MuSig2, FROST). - 2020s : ML-DSA writes FS with Aborts into a US federal standard , and post-quantum multi-signature protocols (ML-DSA-based MuSig variants) carry the same trick into the lattice world. - Wikipedia search entry for Fiat-Shamir 启发式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Fiat-Shamir%20%E5%90%AF%E5%8F%91%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[h=H(M),\quad H:\{0,1\}^{ }\to\{0,1\}^{n}\] Fiat-Shamir Heuristic: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Gentry's Fully Homomorphic Construction
items.text: Theorem : Gentry's FHE Construction (Gentry 全同态构造). Gentry first builds a somewhat homomorphic scheme: ciphertexts carry noise, addition and multiplication work, but enough multiplications drown the plaintext. The key step evaluates the scheme's own decryption circuit homomorphically: encrypt the decryption key under the old ciphertext and compute a refreshed ciphertext in the encrypted domain. If the decryption circuit is shallow enough, bootstrapping lowers noise to a level where computation can continue, allowing arbitrary depth. It proved that fully homomorphic encryption exists and ended the impasse in which homomorphic encryption could manage only a few operations. Bootstrapping became a general tool for later FHE schemes; without Gentry there is no modern BFV, CKKS or TFHE ecosystem. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Primarily as a theoretical foundation and the source of bootstrapping. Production libraries rarely use the 2009 construction directly, but “refresh noise by bootstrapping” remains the runtime core of schemes such as TFHE. items.title: Grover's Algorithm
items.text: Theorem : Grover's Algorithm (格罗弗算法). Theorem (Grover 1996, plus BBBV 1997 and Zalka 1997): finding the one marked item among N candidates takes Θ(√N) queries on a quantum computer — and that is provably the limit. The problem is as simple as it gets: N unordered records, exactly one of which satisfies a predicate f. Find it. Upper bound (Grover 1996) : there is a quantum algorithm that finds the marked item using O(√N) evaluations of f, with success probability arbitrarily close to 1. Concretely, π/4·√N iterations, succeeding with probability about 1 − 1/N. Lower bound (BBBV 1997) : any quantum algorithm, however designed, that can learn about f only by querying it needs at least Ω(√N) queries. Mind the quantifiers: this holds for every quantum algorithm, every f, and every required success probability. Optimality (Zalka 1997) : Grover's π/4·√N queries are optimal in the near-certain-success regime, and quantum search admits no better parallelisation than "carve the space into several independent quantum computers" — the most counter-intuitive difference between the quantum and classical worlds. Classical brute force scales linearly with more machines. Quantum search does not. Three corollaries for cryptography : 1. Key search : brute-forcing an n-bit key drops from 2^n to 2^(n/2). Hash preimages : finding an n-bit hash preimage drops the same way, from 2^n to 2^(n/2). But collision search is not on this list. The classical birthday bound costs 2^(n/2); quantum collision search has its own algorithm (Brassard, Høyer and Tapp, 1997) costing O((N/r)^(1/3)), i.e. about 2^(n/3) for n-bit outputs. So the correct statement is: Grover does not halve the birthday bound. Quantum collision strength falls to 2^(n/3), and that is the work of a different algorithm. This is the detail that gets stated wrongly almost every time. The mechanism in one breath : prepare a uniform superposition over N basis states, use an oracle to flip the phase of the marked item, then reflect about the average to push the target's amplitude up. Repeat π/4·√N times, then measure. Note that the oracle does not "read data" — it turns the test "does this one satisfy f?" into a reversible unitary operation, and that is the technical heart of why the algorithm runs at all. The more general form is amplitude amplification: any problem with a usable "good solution marker" drops into the same loop. Phase estimation supplies a second square-root speed-up, turning precision 1/ε into 1/√ε. These are the tools that post-quantum lattice, hash and signature schemes actually use when they analyse their own security. Because it takes off only half of an exponent — and because the lower bound proves that half is the floor. The full story of the quantum threat needs both Shor's theorem and Grover's theorem side by side. - Public-key cryptography: a cliff. Shor takes factoring and discrete logarithms from exponential time to polynomial time. Not "a bit slower" — zero . RSA and ECC fall together. - Symmetric cryptography: a step. Grover takes 2^n down to 2^(n/2) — just half — and the lower bound says that half is the limit. So the complete answer to "what happens when quantum computers arrive?" is: public-key cryptography must be replaced; symmetric keys must get longer. That single sentence explains every seemingly odd choice in the post-quantum migration: why NIST recommends no symmetric algorithm below 128 bits of classical strength, why ML-KEM-768 is 192 bits classical and 128 bits quantum — because the public part has to survive Shor, and the private part only has to survive Grover. Grover's deeper contribution is that it makes the threat schedulable . "A 128-bit key will not be enough forever" stops being speculation and becomes a theorem, and theorems can be planned around. The lower bounds (BBBV and Zalka) guarantee no worse surprises : there is no "and then in ten years somebody finds a quantum search that halves 2^(n/2) again". The floor of quantum search is something you can sign off on. One more thing worth stating plainly: Grover is a warning, not a catastrophe. 2^128 AES-128 encryptions is still an absurd amount of computation. What deserves anxiety today is not Grover but ordinary negligence — "your key derivation uses MD5", "your RNG was never seeded". Those are today's emergency wounds; Grover is the slow disease. Grover has never broken anything. Its job is to be a ruler. - It relabels every security number we quote. "AES-128 gives 128 bits of security" now needs the footnote "64 bits against a quantum adversary"; "SHA-256 gives 128 bits of collision resistance" has to be discounted in the quantum world to roughly 2^85.3. Once the line "a 256-bit symmetric key equals 128-bit quantum security" is drawn, the parameter standards for the entire post-quantum era follow from it. - It sets the parameters of post-quantum schemes. The parameter sets in FIPS 203/204/205 are all cut on the "at least 128 bits of quantum strength" line. NIST IR 8547 states that every NIST-approved symmetric primitive offering at least 128 bits of classical security is believed to meet Category 1, and that 112-bit symmetric algorithms will be disallowed in 2030. - It influences hash function choices. Because quantum collision resistance is 2^(n/3) rather than 2^(n/2), hash-based signature schemes such as SPHINCS+ (SLH-DSA) have to output 128 bits: their quantum collision strength is only about 2^42.7, so security has to be bought with parameter bulk. NIST issued the initial draft of SP 800-230 in April 2026, adding extra parameter sets for SLH-DSA, precisely to trade signature size against security bits in constrained use cases. - It sets a ceiling on "generic attacks". Quantum security proofs routinely work in the quantum random-oracle model, which is exactly Grover treated as the universal model for black-box search. - It also warns engineers off the wrong track. A threat that Grover halves and a bug that lets users pick their own IV are not in the same universe. Grover's attack surface is not mathematical. It is physical. - Depth is the killer, not qubit count. Grassl et al. (2016) estimate that breaking AES-128 needs about 2,953 logical qubits but a T-depth of roughly 2^80 ; AES-192 needs 4,449 logical qubits at T-depth 2^112; AES-256 needs 6,681 logical qubits at T-depth 2^144. The qubit count looks modest; the number of sequential steps does not — 2^80 is about 10^24 error-corrected gate operations. - Hash preimages are worse. Amy et al. (2016): finding a SHA-256 preimage with Grover needs only about 2^12.6 (≈6,200) logical qubits, but about 2^153.8 surface-code cycles . Preimage search is cheap in qubits and brutal in time ; key search is expensive in both. - You cannot fix it with more machines. Zalka proved that quantum search admits no parallelisation better than splitting the space across independent quantum computers. Classical brute force scales linearly with hardware; Grover does not. - Noise kills amplitude amplification outright. Every iteration of Grover's loop has to run one full AES-128 coherently on a superposition of dimension 2^128, and it has to run 2^64 times. Decoherence destroys the superposition long before the 2^64th iteration; error correction is where the real bill lands. - Query count is not wall-clock time. Turning "is this candidate key correct?" into a reversible quantum oracle may itself cost more than the search — especially when the key derivation has structure. - Know where the lower bound applies. BBBV and Zalka bound black-box search. An attacker who can attack your implementation — your RNG, your key derivation, your protocol logic — never needs Grover. Grover is the worst-case floor, not the best attack. - It does not touch the birthday bound. Quantum collision resistance is 2^(n/3) (Brassard, Høyer and Tapp, 1997), not 2^(n/2). Anyone concluding that "Grover halves the birthday bound" has mixed two different results together. SHA-256's quantum collision strength is about 2^85.3 and SHA-512's about 2^170 — both still hold up. - And the hardware reality : today's machines (IBM's roadmap puts Starling in 2029 at 200 logical qubits and a hundred million gates; Google's roadmap targets roughly a million physical qubits around 2029) remain orders of magnitude short of "2^64 coherent full AES-128 evaluations". - 1996 : Lov Grover presents A Fast Quantum Mechanical Algorithm for Database Search at STOC (pp. 212-219), and republishes it as Quantum Mechanics Helps in Searching for a Needle in a Haystack in Physical Review Letters the following year, which is what brought it to the physics community's attention. The idea had been found independently elsewhere — Boyer, Brassard, Høyer and Tapp published their own variant in 1996. A widely repeated detail: it took the quantum computing community about a year to notice the paper at all. - 1997 : the theoretical foundation is laid in one sweep. BBBV, Strengths and Weaknesses of Quantum Computing ( SIAM Journal on Computing 26(5):1510-1523), proves the Ω(√N) lower bound; Zalka, in Physical Review A , proves Grover's algorithm is optimal and cannot be parallelised better; Brassard, Høyer and Tapp publish Quantum Algorithm for the Collision Problem , giving the 2^(n/3) quantum collision result. - 2016 : Grassl et al., On the Quantum Complexity of Breaking Symmetric Ciphers , work out for the first time what breaking AES with a quantum computer actually costs; Amy, Mosca and Nielsen produce the corresponding resource estimates for SHA-256 preimages. - 2016–2024 : post-quantum standardisation. The call, the review, the selection, the standards — every parameter threshold was set against two lines at once: strength under Shor and strength under Grover. - 13 August 2024 : FIPS 203/204/205 are published; in the same year Google demonstrates error correction below threshold, moving "error correction is feasible" from theory to hardware. - 2025–2026 : quantum hardware keeps scaling (IBM's Nighthawk has 120 qubits and runs 5,000-7,500 gates; IBM's roadmap places its first fault-tolerant machine in 2029 with 200 logical qubits); SP 800-227 and SP 800-230 further institutionalise post-quantum parameters. But breaking AES-128 with Grover needs 2^64 coherent full AES-128 evaluations — even on the most optimistic error-correction budget, that is more than 10^19 oracle calls. We are orders of magnitude away. - Wikipedia search entry for 格罗弗算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%A0%BC%E7%BD%97%E5%BC%97%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Grover's Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: HQC Alternative KEM
items.text: Algorithm : Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC 备选 KEM). HQC is a code-based KEM. The public key hides the structure of a quasi-cyclic code. Encapsulation selects a controlled-weight error vector and computes ciphertext under the public key. Decapsulation uses a decoder in the private key to recover the error vector and hash it into the shared secret. Its hardness assumption is decoding random linear codes, not lattices. Post-quantum migration needs algorithm diversity. If lattices suffer a structural break, the ecosystem should not rest on one assumption. NIST selected HQC as a backup KEM in 2025 so the standard portfolio has a second independent path. Its keys and ciphertexts are larger, but its failure modes differ. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Backup KEM in standards drafts, protocol experiments and cross-implementation interoperability tests. It suits deployments that accept larger keys in exchange for algorithm diversity, rather than bandwidth-sensitive defaults. items.title: Identity-Based Encryption (IBE)
items.text: Algorithm : Identity-Based Encryption (身份基加密). In IBE the public key is not a random number but the recipient's identity string, such as an email address or device ID. A private-key generator (PKG) holds the master key and derives a private key for each identity. The sender encrypts under public parameters and the identity; the recipient proves the identity to the PKG and obtains the key. Shamir proposed the concept in 1984 but no satisfactory construction was known until Boneh and Franklin used bilinear pairings in 2001. It addresses the certificate-distribution pain of public-key infrastructure: a sender needs only an identity, not a prior certificate. That suits email, IoT devices and temporary collaboration. It is also the ancestor of ABE, which widens one identity into an attribute policy. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Encrypted email, mobile-device keys, IoT pairing, cloud-storage access and identity-based signatures. Deployments must handle PKG escrow, identity revocation, key updates and multi-authority trust. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. IBE does not prove that an identity string belongs to a person; it only maps the string to a key. The PKG knows every private key, so key escrow is a structural risk; compromise of the PKG compromises all users. Revocation needs extra machinery, or a departed user's old key still decrypts old messages. It does not automatically provide forward secrecy. items.text: Standard : Secure multiparty computation (安全多方计算). ISO/IEC 4922-1 defines the basic concepts of secure multi-party computation: several parties hold inputs and jointly compute a function without revealing anything beyond the agreed output.
