items.title: Linear Congruential Generator
items.text: Algorithm : Linear Congruential Generator (线性同余发生器). The Linear Congruential Generator (LCG) is the most important and most misused algorithm in the history of cryptography. It is one line of formula: X(n+1) = (a · X(n) + c) mod m Four things: modulus m , multiplier a , increment c , seed X(0) . The output is the state itself (or some bits of it). That is the whole thing. It became the default answer for half a century because of three virtues: it is fast (one multiply-add and one modulo), it is portable (three lines in any language), and its period can be made as long as the modulus . The Hull–Dobell theorem gives the necessary and sufficient conditions for the period to reach its maximum of m : 1. c is coprime to m ; 2. a − 1 is divisible by every prime factor of m ; 3. if 4 divides m , then a − 1 must also be divisible by 4. Satisfy those three and the sequence visits every value in 0 … m−1 exactly once before repeating. The classic ANSI C parameters a = 1103515245, c = 12345, m = 2^31 do; POSIX's rand48 family uses a = 0x5DEECE66D, c = 0xB, m = 2^48 , and Java's java.util.Random uses that same pair. But this has to be said immediately: an LCG is not cryptographically secure, and it is not "a little weak" — it is a different category of thing. Its output sequence is a deterministic linear trajectory . Given enough output, an attacker can recover the internal state with pure algebra, or even lattice reduction. RFC 1750's verdict in 1994 was blunt: "linear congruent generators have been broken," and there are techniques for breaking all polynomial congruent generators — "even if only one bit of the pseudo-random values is released, the seed can be determined from short sequences." There is one conclusion, with no exceptions: An LCG must never be used for key generation. Not for symmetric keys, IVs, nonces, salts, session tokens, password-reset tokens, or anything else where predictability is fatal. A key generated this way is equivalent to a published key. That is not a "it could be better" warning. It is a statement that the key is already public. The LCG is not a cryptographic algorithm, but it is a remarkable engineering artefact. Understanding why it succeeded — and why it cannot be used in cryptography — is the fastest route to understanding what "secure" actually means in modern crypto. - It is extremely fast. A modern CPU does one LCG step in a few nanoseconds, an order of magnitude faster than a hash. For Monte Carlo simulation, load-balancing jitter, or noise in a graphics shader, nothing is more economical. - The state is tiny. One 32-bit or 64-bit integer — it fits in a register, and in a cache line if you want lock-free access. - Its statistical behaviour is analysable. Period, correlation, lattice structure all have clean theoretical descriptions. In simulation this is a virtue; in cryptography it is the death sentence — because "analysable" means "predictable". - It is a straight line. No branches, no tables, no edge cases. It is one of the easiest algorithms in all of cryptography to audit — which is precisely why it is the textbook target. Why it fails in cryptography is the mirror image of why it succeeds in simulation. Mathematically, an LCG's output sequence is a lattice . That means adjacent outputs obey linear relations that can be written down. For an attacker: - Full-state output → one sample is enough. - Truncated high-bit output (Java's nextInt() gives 32 bits from a 48-bit state) → two outputs plus a 2^16 brute force restores the entire generator. - Low-bit output → the low bits have a tiny period (the lowest bit's period is 2) , so they are effectively a counter. In other words: an LCG is not "weak", it is "transparent". Why is it still alive? Because in statistical simulation , transparency is irrelevant. Researchers want speed, a long enough period and a flat enough distribution — not unpredictability . So the LCG rules the roost in numerical analysis and a forbidden zone in cryptography. Keeping those two worlds apart is a mark of a mature engineer. - C's rand() / srand() : the interface dates from C89; POSIX added random() / srandom() . glibc's random() defaults to a 128-byte-state trinomial additive-feedback generator (TYPE_3) producing 31-bit output, while rand_r() uses the plain LCG ( next = next 1103515245 + 12345 , returning next/65536 % 32768 ). - rand48 / drand48 / erand48 : the POSIX 48-bit LCG with m = 2^48 . The most entropy any standard library offers here — and still nowhere near enough for anything cryptographic. - Java's java.util.Random : a = 0x5DEECE66D, c = 0xB, m = 2^48 , returning the top 32 bits of the state each time. Java's SecureRandom is a completely different animal (by default it goes through the OS NativePRNG , reading /dev/urandom on Linux) — yet plenty of Java code wrongly uses java.util.Random to produce keys and nonces. - Microsoft Visual C++'s rand() : a 32-bit LCG whose return value is only 15 bits (0–32767) — a range that says everything about what it may be used for. - Hash table hashing : multiply-shift hashing is a direct descendant of the LCG — h = (a·k) (64−b) , taking the high bits of a multiply. Java's HashMap , Go's maps and most language runtimes use this trick. No unpredictability is needed here, only avalanche. - Simulation and Monte Carlo : physical modelling, queueing theory, financial risk models, molecular dynamics. - Games and graphics : dithering, particle effects, procedural generation, sampling. - Timing and scheduling jitter : pseudo-random jitter layered on fixed intervals to break up synchronised herds. - GPU shaders : the noise function in almost every graphics textbook is an LCG. - As the engine inside a better generator : PCG is an LCG plus an output permutation — the fast state advance of the LCG combined with the good statistics of a scrambler. That is the modern, correct way for the LCG family to be used. An LCG was never "broken". It has always been transparent. Every item on this list is common knowledge, and every year somebody re-learns it the hard way. - The low bits have absurdly short periods. For m = 2^n , the k-th low bit has period at most 2^(k+1) . The lowest bit's period is 2 — it just alternates. Any code still consuming the low bits is, in effect, outputting a counter. - Powers of two are the LCG's natural enemy : with m = 2^n the output sequence has a particularly ugly lattice structure , and hyperplanes are visible in higher dimensions. Knuth's spectral test exists precisely to measure this, and an LCG with badly chosen parameters shows up immediately under it. Prime moduli such as 2^31−1 , or a carefully chosen 64-bit multiplier, soften the visible structure but cannot remove the underlying linearity. - State recovery attacks : - Output equals state → one output suffices. - Truncated output → it becomes a Hidden Number Problem , solved with lattice reduction (LLL) . Frieze, Kannan and Kuperberg gave the systematic algorithm in 1994. - Java's java.util.Random : two nextInt() outputs plus a 2^16 brute force clone the whole generator , after which every future value is known. - The seed space is minuscule : srand() typically takes 32 bits. An attacker enumerates 2^32 seeds, replays each one and compares against the known output. No mathematics required — pure brute force. - Streams are correlated : two LCG sequences with the same a and c but different seeds are linearly related. Seeding with the current time and with the current time plus one gives you two sequences that are structurally almost the same. Seeding from the clock leaks a whole class of instances at once. - Modulo bias : rand() % n is not uniform. With RAND_MAX = 2^31−1 and n = 3 , the first few residues come up one extra time. This is an independent classic bug, but it tends to appear in the same line of code. - It fails statistical test suites : LCGs do not pass L'Ecuyer's TestU01. Note the direction of that statement — "fails" is evidence of a problem, not proof of unusability; for simulation it may still be fine. - Using it as a cryptographic generator : the one genuine catastrophe. An LCG-generated key is no encryption at all. The real-world failures are endless: the 2013 Android SecureRandom incident was fundamentally about PRNG predictability being used to recover an ECDSA private key ; and every tutorial that says "here is how to generate a key with a random number generator" is still running in production somewhere. RFC 1750 said it in 1994: "such sequences are clearly bad for use in security applications." - Quantum : no effect — but it does not matter. An LCG is just as transparent in front of a quantum computer. Its problem was never "hard to compute" but "too easy to compute". - 1951 : D. H. Lehmer publishes "On Pseudo-Random Sequences" ( Journal of the ACM , Vol. 3, No. 3, pp. 341–343), and describes the multiplicative congruential method in Mathematical Methods in Large-Scale Computing Units , in the Proceedings of the Second Symposium on Large-Scale Digital Calculating Machinery (Harvard University Press, same year) — the classic generator with the Mersenne prime modulus m = 2^31 − 1 , still the textbook example. - 1955 : T. E. Hull and A. R. Dobell publish "A Method for Simulating Non-Numerical Data" ( IBM Journal of Research and Development ), giving the full-period criteria — later expanded into the full theorem in their 1962 SIAM Review paper "Random Number Generators". Those three conditions remain the standard way to pick parameters. - 1960s–1970s : the LCG becomes the default choice for simulation. Knuth's The Art of Computer Programming , Volume 2 (1969) dissects its mathematical structure , and the spectral test and the lattice picture are fixed there. - 1980s : the ANSI C committee puts rand() into the language standard (C89) , explicitly requiring that "if the modulus is 2^31, the low-order bits should have at least 15 bits of randomness" — a requirement that itself concedes the short low-bit period. POSIX later adds the rand48 family. - 1980s–1990s : "LCGs are not secure" is common knowledge in cryptography and long ignored in engineering. RFC 1750 (1994) spends a chapter on the subject and is merciless about it. - 1998 : Matsumoto and Nishimura publish the Mersenne Twister , period 2^19937−1, which becomes the default in Python, MATLAB and R. It solved period length but not predictability — 624 consecutive 32-bit outputs restore the state. - 2003 : Marsaglia proposes the KISS family (Keep It Simple, Swapper, Xorshift), demonstrating that a good statistical PRNG should be a handful of lines of code rather than a giant state table. - 2014 : Melissa O'Neill publishes the PCG family — an LCG plus an output permutation , achieving "extremely fast, extremely small, statistically good" on 128 bits of state. She says so herself in the paper: "PCG has not had the level of scrutiny required to be seriously considered for use as a cryptographic stream cipher." - 2014 : Steele, Lea and Flood introduce SplitMix64 , which became the default tool for seeding fresh generators in language libraries. - 2018 / 2021 : Blackman and Vigna present the xoshiro / xoroshiro family ("Scrambled Linear Pseudorandom Number Generators", ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software , 2021), displacing the Mersenne Twister as the new standard for "fast and statistically good". Vigna later wrote the sentence that gets quoted constantly: "It is time to let go of the Mersenne Twister." - The 2010s onward : the cryptographic side changed tracks entirely — the Linux kernel switched to ChaCha20 in 4.8, Windows uses AES-CTR-DRBG, OpenSSL uses HMAC/ChaCha20, Rust uses ChaCha12. The LCG was pushed clean out of cryptography and stayed firmly put in simulation, games and hashing. - Wikipedia search entry for 线性同余发生器. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%BA%BF%E6%80%A7%E5%90%8C%E4%BD%99%E5%8F%91%E7%94%9F%E5%99%A8 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Linear Congruential Generator: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: The LPR Reduction
items.text: Theorem : Lyubashevsky-Peikert-Regev Reduction (LPR 归约). LPR moves LWE arithmetic into polynomial rings: secret, error and public polynomial are ring elements, and multiplication is polynomial multiplication modulo an irreducible polynomial. A key shrinks from n² coefficients to n, and NTT speeds up multiplication. The reduction shows that if a certain approximate ideal-lattice problem is hard, the decisional Ring-LWE problem is indistinguishable. It is the step that moved lattice cryptography from “theoretically feasible” to “engineering practical”. Without ring structure, Kyber/ML-KEM keys and multiplication would be far more expensive. LPR also exposed ideal-lattice risk: ring algebra may add attack surface, and Module-LWE later traded some efficiency for less structure. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Ring-LWE public-key encryption, key encapsulation, homomorphic encryption and pseudorandom functions. NewHope, Kyber's lineage and several NIST candidates were influenced by it; implementations use NTT and negacyclic convolution. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Ring-LWE is not “LWE but safer”. Ring algebra can be exploited: subfield attacks, special ideal-lattice structure and poor parameter choices reduce security. Approximation factors and moduli matter. It also does not cover side channels or implementation errors. Theorem = (Assumptions ⇒ Conclusion)；Reduction: Adv_A ≤ q · Adv_B + ε. Module-LWE later used smaller module rings to balance efficiency and structural risk, and Kyber won the NIST competition. LPR explains why post-quantum KEMs use polynomial rings. items.title: Learning With Errors (LWE)
items.text: Algorithm : Learning With Errors (带误差学习问题). LWE fixes a public matrix A and modulus q; a secret vector s and a short error vector e satisfy b = A·s + e mod q. Without the error, Gaussian elimination recovers s. With it, the problem becomes finding a close vector in a high-dimensional lattice, which is believed hard even for quantum algorithms. Regev's contribution is the reduction linking worst-case lattice hardness to the indistinguishability of random LWE samples. It turns lattice cryptography from a collection of constructions into a single analysable assumption. Kyber/ML-KEM, NewHope and FHE schemes trace back to LWE or its ring variant. For this site, LWE is the node that makes post-quantum KEMs, homomorphic encryption and the “quantum-resistant” story intelligible. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Public-key encryption and key encapsulation, fully homomorphic encryption, identity-based encryption and pseudorandom functions. Deployments rarely use bare LWE; they use Ring-LWE or Module-LWE to shrink keys and multiplication cost. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. LWE itself is not broken by Shor's algorithm. Risk comes from parameter choice, noise growth, decryption failure and implementation side channels. Too narrow an error distribution, too small a modulus or a biased sampler can turn the theoretical hardness into an attackable problem. It also provides no integrity or authentication and must be composed with AEAD and signatures. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Lyubashevsky, Peikert and Regev introduced Ring-LWE in 2010, moving arithmetic into polynomial rings. NIST's post-quantum process made Module-LWE the core of ML-KEM. It did not replace RSA overnight; parameters, reductions and implementations took more than a decade to mature. items.title: ML-KEM Hybrid Key Establishment
items.text: Algorithm : Hybrid ML-KEM Key Exchange (ML-KEM 混合密钥协商). A hybrid key exchange runs a classical path (usually X25519 or ECDH) and a post-quantum KEM path (ML-KEM) at the same time. Each party obtains two shared secrets, then a KDF such as HKDF derives the session key from both secrets plus protocol context and identities. The security requirement is that the final key remains unpredictable as long as at least one path is still secure. An adversary can record ciphertext today and decrypt it after a quantum computer arrives: harvest now, decrypt later. Hybrid schemes protect today's traffic under both classical and post-quantum assumptions. They are also the most practical migration path, because clients can gain quantum resistance incrementally instead of waiting for a pure post-quantum ecosystem. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. TLS 1.3 hybrid named groups, QUIC, experimental OpenSSH KEX, VPNs and cloud internal links. Implementations must handle group identifiers, negotiation priority, failure fallback and key confirmation; concatenating two byte strings is not enough. items.title: Oblivious Transfer (OT)
items.text: Algorithm : Oblivious Transfer (不经意传输). In 1-out-of-2 OT the sender holds m0 and m1, and the receiver holds a choice bit b. At the end the receiver learns m_b; the sender learns nothing about b, and the receiver learns nothing about m_{1-b}. Rabin's original version was a “coin-flip” OT in which the receiver obtains the secret with probability one half. Even–Goldreich–Lempel later gave the more common 1-out-of-2 form. Constructions use public-key encryption, trapdoor permutations or lattice assumptions. OT is the multiplication gate of secure multi-party computation: with OT, two parties can evaluate a circuit without revealing their inputs. It also underpins private set intersection, oblivious database access, key exchange and privacy-preserving machine learning. Without OT, many MPC protocols remain mere existence proofs. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. Private set intersection (PSI), private queries, federated learning, threshold signatures and general MPC. Implementations often extend a few base OTs into many, then add cut-and-choose or authentication against malicious parties. A receiver may try to obtain both messages, and a sender may substitute messages; unauthenticated OT does not prove identity. Choice bias, timing and replay can also break privacy. items.title: Regev's Reduction
items.text: Theorem : Regev's Reduction (Regev 归约). Regev proves a quantum reduction from worst-case GapSVP—deciding whether a lattice has a vector shorter than a bound—to average-case LWE samples; conversely, any LWE solver solves the corresponding GapSVP. The quantum step prepares lattice-related quantum states, while the protected encryption scheme remains classical. It gives LWE a worst-case anchor: breaking LWE means solving worst-case lattices, not merely one random instance. Post-quantum standardisation needs assumptions that can be formalised; otherwise parameters rest on experience alone. It is a core argument for why lattice cryptography is considered quantum-resistant. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. items.title: Salsa20
items.text: Algorithm : Salsa20 (Salsa20 流密码). Salsa20 is a stream cipher designed by Daniel J. Bernstein. Its state is sixteen 32-bit words (512 bits, or 64 bytes) and every operation it performs is one of three: addition, rotation, XOR. That is why it is called an ARX cipher. One invocation works like this: 1. Fill the state as a four-by-four grid: the first row holds the constants "expand 32-byte k" , the next two rows hold the 256-bit key, the next row the 64-bit nonce, and the last row the 64-bit block counter . Run 20 rounds (ten double rounds). Each round rotates, adds and XORs the words of each column, does the same to the rows, and then adds the sixteen words back in. Columns and rows use the same quarter-round function. Serialize the final state in little-endian order to produce a 64-byte keystream block, which is XORed with the plaintext. The properties that matter: - No S-boxes, no tables. Every operation is integer addition, a rotate, or an XOR. That makes it naturally constant time , with no data-dependent cache access to leak the key — the central selling point when it was designed. - No key schedule. The key simply sits in the state, so changing keys costs nothing. - Random access. Want the n -th keystream block? Set the block counter to n . - 64-byte blocks , four times AES's block size, which is kinder to serial CPUs. There are also reduced-round variants, Salsa20/8 and Salsa20/12 , proposed in the same design document: fewer rounds for speed, with a correspondingly thinner security margin. Salsa20 answered the question AES could not: how do you encrypt fast in software when your hardware has no AES instructions? The story is specific. Bernstein designed it in 2005 (originally "Snuffle 2005"), when most x86 servers still had no AES-NI and software AES was slow, while Salsa20 needs only additions, rotations and XORs — one or two instructions on any CPU. Bernstein later shipped both AES and Salsa20 inside NaCl and let people benchmark for themselves. Salsa20 also wins on engineering qualities: - Constant time. No tables means no cache-timing attack surface. A correct software implementation is simply not exposed to the class of attack Bernstein himself demonstrated against AES in 2005. - Key agility. The key goes straight into the state; rotating keys is free. - Small code. A few hundred lines of C get it right, unlike AES, which drags in multi-table optimizations and masking. - Open analysis. Bernstein published the full specification and security analysis in 2007 (eprint 2007/472), and in 2008 Salsa20 entered the final eSTREAM portfolio as the software stream cipher of choice. It also produced two descendants: XSalsa20 (2008, nonce extended to 192 bits) and ChaCha (2008, a redesigned round function with stronger diffusion). ChaCha is the one that conquered the Internet. - NaCl and libsodium : Bernstein's own networking and cryptography library (NaCl, 2008) and its community successor libsodium both make Salsa20 a primary primitive. libsodium ships Salsa20, Salsa20/12, Salsa20/8, XSalsa20 and ChaCha20. - Go's extended standard library : golang.org/x/crypto/salsa20 , whose documentation states it implements Bernstein's specification and also supports XSalsa20. - RustCrypto's salsa20 and salsa crates (20 rounds and 12 rounds respectively). - OpenSSL : the EVP interface exposes Salsa20 and ChaCha20 as ciphers. - The Linux kernel : its crypto API ships both a generic implementation, crypto/salsa20_generic.c , and an x86 assembly one, arch/x86/crypto/salsa20_glue.c — the latter was patched for the zero-length crash tracked as CVE-2017-17806. - Tor : its NaCl transport uses NaCl's secretbox, i.e. XSalsa20-Poly1305. - What actually conquered the Internet was the successor : ChaCha20 (RFC 8439, June 2018) ended up in TLS 1.3, WireGuard, OpenSSH ( chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com ), Signal's XChaCha20-Poly1305, the system crypto libraries of iOS and Android, and essentially every QUIC implementation. Put bluntly: Salsa20's own deployment footprint is modest, but it shaped nearly every place software encryption ended up. No practical attack on the full twenty rounds of Salsa20 is known. Its attack surface is entirely about usage. - Nonce reuse : repeating a nonce under one key repeats the keystream and directly exposes the XOR of two plaintexts. Salsa20's 64-bit nonce space looks roomy, but with random generation the birthday bound means the collision probability becomes non-negligible after roughly 2^32 messages. XSalsa20's 192-bit nonce exists precisely to remove that awkwardness. - No authentication whatsoever : Salsa20 is a keystream and nothing more. Flip a ciphertext bit and the plaintext bit flips with it, so content can be altered, truncated or spliced. Any real deployment needs a MAC — XSalsa20-Poly1305 is the standard answer. - Reduced-round variants have thinner margins : Crowley gave an attack on Salsa20/5 at about 2^165 operations, and Aumasson et al. (2008) gave a 2^151 attack on Salsa20/7 and estimated 2^251 for Salsa20/8. Twenty rounds remain secure, but Salsa20/8 is not "equally safe, just faster". - Segmentation must match : Salsa20 is message-oriented — keystream block boundaries depend on how the message was chopped up. If sender and receiver disagree on the segmentation, decryption goes wrong. The Go x/crypto/salsa20 documentation warns about this specifically. - No protection against related-key attacks : with no key schedule and the key sitting directly in the state, NaCl explicitly declines to promise related-key resistance. - Side channels : without tables, cache timing largely disappears; but an implementation that branches on secret data or compares in variable time still leaks. - Quantum : Grover cuts brute-force search on a 256-bit key from 2^256 to about 2^128 — still infeasible, and the shared fate of every 256-bit symmetric cipher. - One commonly misunderstood point : known "slid pair" collisions exist in the Salsa20 core function, and the built-in diagonal constants are exactly what block them. That is not a vulnerability; it is deliberate design. - 2005 : Bernstein designed Salsa20, originally Snuffle 2005, publishing the design document on April 27, 2005. - December 24, 2007 : Bernstein published "The Salsa20 Family of Stream Ciphers" as eprint 2007/472, with the full specification, test vectors and security analysis. Around the same time he wrote "Salsa20/8 and Salsa20/12", formally proposing the reduced-round variants. - April 2008 : the final eSTREAM portfolio was announced, with Salsa20 selected among the software stream ciphers. - 2008 : Bernstein submitted NaCl (the forerunner of libsodium), where Salsa20 became one of the main primitives. The same year he proposed XSalsa20 (192-bit nonce) and ChaCha , a Salsa20 variant with a redesigned round function and stronger diffusion. - Around 2010 : ChaCha landed in projects such as Tor and OpenSSH; the BLAKE team, finalists in NIST's SHA-3 competition, borrowed ChaCha's core. - 2013 : ChaCha20 was adopted at scale in Android 4.1 (KitKat) and iOS as the software encryption path for devices without AES hardware acceleration. - June 2016 : RFC 7905 brought ChaCha20-Poly1305 to TLS 1.2. - June 2018 : RFC 8439 standardized ChaCha20 and Poly1305 for IETF protocols, and TLS 1.3 listed the suite among those implementations should support. - Wikipedia search entry for Salsa20 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Salsa20%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Salsa20: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Schnorr Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Schnorr Signature (Schnorr 签名). The paper presents a public-key signature scheme and a corresponding authentication scheme, both based on discrete logarithms in a subgroup of Z_p . The parameters are not an arbitrary prime group: p must be sufficiently large, for example “p = 2^512”; the base α must have order a sufficiently large prime q, for example “q = 2^140”. The paper says: “We present a new public-key signature scheme and a corresponding authentication scheme that are based on discrete logarithms in a subgroup of units in Z_p where p is a sufficiently large prime, e.g., p = 2^512.” and “A key idea is to use for the base of the discrete logarithm an integer alpha in Z_p such that the order of alpha is a sufficiently large prime q, e.g., q = 2^140.” Relative to ElGamal, the paper claims improvements in both the speed of signature generation and verification and the bit length of signatures. It says: “In this way we improve the ElGamal signature scheme in the speed of the procedures for the generation and the verification of signatures and also in the bit length of signatures.” A second design point is preprocessing: the signer can precompute a message-independent random exponentiation. The paper says: “We present an efficient algorithm that preprocesses the exponentiation of a random residue modulo p.” These are the paper's design claims, not an independent benchmark; this entry does not turn “faster/shorter” into a concrete factor. The paper is titled “Efficient signature generation by smart cards”; its abstract gives a signature scheme, an authentication scheme, and an algorithm for preprocessing a random exponentiation. Together these point to a smart-card or constrained-signer setting. The paper reports no smart-card product, deployment count, side-channel test, or concrete implementation. This entry therefore treats “smart cards” only as the paper's target setting, not as a commercially deployed smart-card scheme. de Rooij's 1997 attack targets Schnorr's optional preprocessing, not the core signature without it. The paper says: “In this paper an attack on these preprocessing algorithms is presented.” The attack recovers the secret key: “For k=8, this amounts to about 2^31 steps and 700 signatures”, and applies to “Brickell-McCurley, ElGamal, and DSS signatures as well, if the same preprocessing algorithm is used”. The same abstract records the paper's conjectured 2^72 security for k=8 preprocessing. The boundary: this is not an unconditional break of Schnorr signatures; it shows that the preprocessing parameters and usage can lower security, and the attack needs signatures or identification transcripts. The article appears in Journal of Cryptology 4(3), January 1991, pages 161–174; the page records “Received: 17 August 1989” and “Revised: 15 March 1991”. The same page's additional information records “European patent application 89103290.6 from February 24, 1989.” and “U.S. patent number 4995082 of February 19, 1991.” This entry dates the text to the 1991 journal article; the 1989 patent application and the 1991 US patent are supplementary records on the same page, not the journal publication year, and do not automatically equal the paper's technical content. - Wikipedia search entry for Schnorr 签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Schnorr%20%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Schnorr Signature: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: scrypt
items.text: Algorithm : scrypt (scrypt 内存硬口令派生). scrypt does what PBKDF2 does — turn a passphrase into a key — but it makes you occupy a large block of memory first . Three steps (RFC 7914 §6): 1. B[0..p-1] = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(P, S, 1, p 128 r) 2. for i = 0..p-1: B[i] = scryptROMix(r, B[i], N) 3. DK = PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256(P, B[0] ... B[p-1], 1, dkLen) scryptROMix is the heart, and it runs two loops: - Fill : X = B; repeat N times, storing X into V[i] each round and setting X = scryptBlockMix(X). The result is N copies of the state sitting in memory. - Random walk : repeat N times, j = Integerify(X) mod N , then X = scryptBlockMix(X xor V[j]) . j is data-dependent — the attacker has to actually read that memory to continue. scryptBlockMix is the Salsa20/8 core (64-byte in, 64-byte out, eight rounds of Salsa20) plus a shuffle that interleaves even- and odd-indexed blocks, turning 2r 64-byte blocks into r 128-byte blocks. What the three parameters mean physically: - N (must be a power of two greater than 1): sets both time and memory. Memory use is exactly 128 × N × r bytes. - r (block size): mainly shapes the memory layout. - p (parallelism): splits the work into p independent pieces, without increasing memory use — it buys CPU time, not RAM. Take OWASP's recommended N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1 : memory = 128 × 131072 × 8 = 134,217,728 bytes, exactly 128 MiB . The central property is sequential memory-hardness : an adversary with less memory per core than the function needs pays a steep time penalty, and running b instances in parallel demands b times the memory. In other words, parallelism is dragged along by memory cost . RFC 7914 §14 puts it carefully: ROMix has been proven sequentially memory-hard under the random oracle model for H, and scrypt's security additionally rests on the assumption that the Salsa20/8 core offers no shortcuts. scrypt exists for one reason: GPUs and ASICs get cheaper much faster than memory does. Section 1 of RFC 7914 says this bluntly. Every classic password KDF — DES crypt, MD5 crypt, SHA-crypt, PBKDF2, bcrypt — is "iterate plus salt". You can raise the iteration count as hardware improves: keep the user's per-login time constant, and on paper nothing is lost. It is a paper-only peace. Brute-force password search is perfectly parallel by nature. Your server tests one password at a time; the attacker's GPU tests tens of thousands simultaneously. Multiplying the iteration count by ten slows the attacker's clock by ten, but the chip count in his hands has not changed. The metric that actually matters — compute per dollar — keeps sliding toward the attacker. Progress in semiconductors makes circuits not just faster but smaller, so the same money buys more parallelism. It gets worse every year. scrypt's answer is not "iterate more". It moves the battlefield from arithmetic to memory bandwidth , which is clever because: - Cores on a GPU do not share fast cache. Every extra parallel instance needs its own slab of memory. The cost structure of a GPU — vast compute, tiny cache — is completely dismantled. - Once an ASIC exists, the bottleneck shifts from compute to memory bandwidth. Memory bandwidth is the more expensive and harder-to-stack resource. RFC 7914 adds a pragmatic observation: the SMix instances are independent, so a large p raises computational cost without raising memory use — as CPU power and memory capacity diverge, scrypt can still be retuned. Its honesty : scrypt is not "the strongest", it is "the best value defensive position". Argon2, which came out of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition, has better memory-hardness and better side-channel behaviour, and OWASP now ranks Argon2id first and scrypt second. But Argon2 is more complex, has more parameters and is easier to get wrong; scrypt remains good enough almost everywhere. - Tarsnap : Colin Percival's own backup service uses it to protect the master key — scrypt's first real production deployment. - System passwords on Debian / Ubuntu : libxcrypt 's default password hash is yescrypt , a scrypt-based variant that displaced SHA-512crypt. A scrypt relative is running on most Linux machines shipped by distributions. - OpenSSL : since 1.1.1 the SCRYPT EVP_KDF implementation is available, usable for TLS PSK identity derivation and for encrypting PKCS 8 private keys. - Python : hashlib.scrypt() (over OpenSSL). Go : golang.org/x/crypto/scrypt . Rust : RustCrypto's scrypt crate. Java : Bouncy Castle. Every language has a ready-made implementation. - The ASN.1 definition in RFC 7914 : the id-scrypt OID is 1.3.6.1.4.1.11591.4.11 , usable directly inside PKCS 8 encrypted private keys; the RFC even includes a complete PKCS 8 example at N = 2^20, r = 8, p = 1 . - Embedded and compliance settings : memory-constrained devices use it for key derivation, and FIPS 140-3 validated libraries have room for it (unlike Argon2, which needs extra validation coverage). - OWASP's recommended parameters (2023 edition): N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1 (128 MiB) as the first choice, plus N = 2^16, p = 2 , N = 2^15, p = 3 , N = 2^14, p = 5 and N = 2^13, p = 10 as "roughly equivalent defence" alternatives that trade RAM for parallelism. scrypt has not been "broken", but it has failure modes you need to know. - Memory is both its defence and its denial-of-service surface. RFC 7914 §14 warns explicitly that parameters must not come from an untrusted party, or an attacker can specify an absurdly large N and make the server allocate gigabytes. Any system that lets the client influence password-hash parameters — tokens, config blobs, pasted hash strings — has a memory-exhaustion vulnerability. - There are published side-channel attacks. Forler, Lucks and Wenzel, in Memory-Demanding Password Scrambling (ASIACRYPT 2014), point out that scrypt's memory access pattern depends on the password (because j is derived from the state), so a cache-timing attack on the victim's own machine can recover the password; they also demonstrate a garbage-collector attack , and propose Catena as a remedy. This is scrypt's real regression versus PBKDF2: you buy memory cost and pay with access-pattern leakage. - Memory-hardness leans on the physical assumption that DRAM is slow. Choe et al. (MEMSYS 2019) note that as near-data processing and compute-capable memory push computation into the memory device, the latency and energy cost of a memory access drops sharply — and the entire argument that buys time with memory accesses weakens . - Mispick the parameters and the memory-hardness is gone. RFC 7914 warns plainly: tune the parameters so memory use shrinks and the properties of the algorithm change. The only way to save memory without losing memory-hardness is to raise p (parallelism), not to lower N. OWASP adds a caveat of its own: swapping N for p does not preserve exact equivalence under all attacker models. - The passphrase lives in memory the whole time. scrypt's final step runs PBKDF2 over the raw passphrase, so it must stay resident for the entire computation — swap, core dumps and memory images may all capture it. RFC 7914 §14 makes the same point: passwords and intermediate values may remain in memory, core dumps and swap areas long after the implementation is done, so sensitive data belongs in protected memory. - The attack surface has moved to the next generation. Argon2id (the 2015 competition winner) is more careful about memory-hardness, side channels and DoS resistance, and is OWASP's first choice today. scrypt has slid to "second choice, legacy systems, simple reliable parameters". - It cannot save a password that is in the dictionary. Memory-hardness buys time, not entropy. "Password123!" still falls to a 128 MiB scrypt in about a second. - Quantum computing neither helps nor hurts much : Grover halves the work factor, which is trivial for a function already costing 128 MiB of memory. But if a quantum computer ever arrives, anything scrypt protects still has to move to a post-quantum scheme. - May 2009 : Colin Percival presents Stronger Key Derivation via Sequential Memory-Hard Functions at BSDCan 2009 , and scrypt arrives. The thesis is in the title: a sequential memory-hard function is stronger than merely memory-hard, because it also pins down parallelism. - 2009–2010 : scrypt enters production at Tarsnap; implementations such as Perl's Crypt::Scrypt appear. The cryptography community starts paying attention. - 2014 : Forler, Lucks and Wenzel publish Memory-Demanding Password Scrambling , exposing the cache-timing and garbage-collector attacks against scrypt and proposing Catena. This is the first clear articulation of "memory-hard does not mean side-channel-free". - 2015 : the Password Hashing Competition crowns Argon2. From here on, scrypt is "the safe second choice" rather than "the only modern option". - 2015 : draft-josefsson-scrypt-kdf enters the IETF. - 2016 : RFC 7914 standardises scrypt, giving it ASN.1 syntax, the OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.11591.4.11 , PKCS 8 usage and the full test vectors — and writes "unreasonably large parameters cause a denial-of-service attack" into its security considerations. Later in 2016, Debian and Ubuntu's libxcrypt switched the default password hash to yescrypt, which is scrypt-based. - 2020s : OWASP lists Argon2id first and scrypt second, and the recommended parameter set has grown from the original N = 2^17, r = 8, p = 1 into a menu graded by memory budget. scrypt continues to serve embedded, compliance and legacy systems. - Wikipedia search entry for scrypt 内存硬口令派生. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=scrypt%20%E5%86%85%E5%AD%98%E7%A1%AC%E5%8F%A3%E4%BB%A4%E6%B4%BE%E7%94%9F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] scrypt: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Shamir Secret Sharing
items.text: Algorithm : Shamir Secret Sharing (Shamir 门限秘密共享). Shamir's Secret Sharing (SSS) answers a very plain question: how do you split one key into n pieces so that any t of them put it back together, and one short leaves you none the wiser? The mechanism is polynomial interpolation . Let the secret be s (it can be a large integer, or a byte string handled byte by byte): 1. Pick a large prime p and do all arithmetic in GF(p) . Draw a random degree-(t−1) polynomial f(x) = s + a₁x + a₂x² + … + a_{t−1}x^{t−1} . The constant term is the secret , and the coefficients a₁ … a_{t−1} must be uniformly random . Hand out n shares : holder i receives the value f(i) , i.e. the pair (x_i, y_i) with x_i = i . Recover the secret : take any t shares and evaluate the polynomial at zero using Lagrange interpolation : s = f(0) = Σ_{i∈S} y_i · Π_{j∈S, j≠i} (0 − x_j)/(x_i − x_j) (mod p) The underlying mathematics is elementary: t points determine a degree-(t−1) polynomial uniquely. Why "one short reveals nothing" is actually true — this is the most beautiful part of Shamir, and what separates it from every other key-protection scheme. Suppose an attacker holds t−1 shares. He knows the shape of f (degree t−1) but not the remaining degree of freedom. For every secret value s' he guesses, there is exactly one polynomial consistent with both those t−1 known points and the constant term s' . In other words, every guess he makes was equally likely a priori — his effort buys him literally nothing. This is perfect secret sharing , and its security is information-theoretic , not computational: - No hardness assumption is needed. Not that factoring is hard, not that discrete logs are hard, not any assumption at all. - Unlimited computing power does not help. The attacker learns precisely as much as if the secret were a uniformly random value uncorrelated with the shares. - This is one of the very few cryptographic constructions that survives quantum computing. Shor's algorithm has nothing to say about it, because there is no mathematical problem to solve. One clarification: SSS is not encryption . It does not hide the secret from someone who already holds t shares, and it provides no authentication whatsoever. All it does is turn "one key" into "a key you must assemble". Shamir sharing solves the most counterintuitive problem in key management: sometimes the safest way to keep a key is to break it up. A key sitting in a safe is a single point of failure: crack the safe and it's gone, lose the safe and it's gone. Split it into three and give one to each of three people, and: - Two colluding insiders still cannot get in (a 3-of-5 threshold). - One person quitting, vanishing or dying does not paralyse the system. - Auditing gains a handle. Every share becomes a traceable, attributable event, rather than "somebody has a master key". Shamir put the politics of it plainly in the closing lines of the 1979 paper: "we can give any sufficiently large majority the authority to take some action while giving any sufficiently large minority the power to block it." That is not a metaphor in a cryptography paper; it is separation of powers, stated literally. And there is a deeper point: this is one of the very few cryptographic constructs that depends on no hard problem. RSA rests on factoring, ECC on discrete logs, AES on computational irreversibility — all of those are beliefs . Shamir sharing's security is a theorem . In a world that grows ever more dependent on "assume some mathematical problem is hard", a construction whose security is information-theoretic has value precisely because that assumption does not have to be made. - Multi-party computation (MPC) — the native home of SSS. The BGW protocol of 1985 cuts each participant's secret input into shares, lets everyone compute on the shares, and no party ever sees another party's input . Today MPC shows up in sealed-bid auctions, privacy-preserving machine learning and cross-exchange balance proofs. - Threshold signatures : the private key is split into t shares, t signers each sign a piece, and the pieces combine into one ordinary-looking signature — while no individual ever holds the full key. FROST (RFC 9591, June 2024) , the standardised two-round Schnorr threshold protocol, uses Shamir shares; Shamir himself proposed threshold RSA in 1979; BLS threshold signatures, GG18/GG20 and CGGMP21 threshold ECDSA work the same way. - Distributed key generation (DKG) : Pedersen's 1991 construction means no trusted party ever generates the key at all — n participants jointly run a protocol that produces the shares, and the complete private key never exists in one place. Threshold wallets, DAO treasuries and multi-sig vaults increasingly use DKG. - Sharded seed phrases for hardware wallets : SLIP-39 (SatoshiLabs, 2020) replaces the single 24-word BIP-39 mnemonic with several 20-word Shamir mnemonics . Trezor supported it from firmware 2.4.0 in 2019; Electrum, Sparrow, Rabby and BlueWallet support it too. This is the first time SSS reached hundreds of millions of ordinary users. - CA offline root keys : the offline root keys of top-tier certificate authorities are distributed to a set of holders under a threshold arrangement — no single person can issue a root certificate alone, but a quorum can. - Boards of directors and the two-man rule : reactor start keys, military key release, corporate executive separation — the examples are in Shamir's own paper. - NIST's threshold cryptography programme : NIST is driving work on VSS and threshold signatures (the PiVer verifiable secret sharing framework), which is this road moving from academia into financial infrastructure. Shamir's mathematics has no weaknesses. The number of ways it fails in practice is long enough to be worth a list. - "Split" is not the same as "spread". The most common failure: a 3-of-5 split whose five shares all sit in the same cloud account, the same mailbox, the same folder on the same laptop. That is no split at all — one share is enough. Shamir protects a set's mathematical property; it will not spread files across five countries for you. - The shares themselves leak. Each share is a pair (x_i, y_i) . Putting five shares in one document hands over the private key — any one holder can reassemble it. In backup procedures the moment of "write it to a USB stick and then distribute it to five people" usually leaks before distribution even happens. - The dealer must be honest. The original scheme assumes the dealer does not hand different people values from different polynomials. A malicious dealer can distribute a biased sharing — the sharing is mathematically perfect, but the secret that comes back is wrong, and you only find out at recovery time. That is precisely why verifiable secret sharing exists. - A poisoned share at recovery time : one holder submits a forged share, the interpolation result is corrupted, and the result usually does not tell you who did it . VSS commitment mechanisms exist to catch exactly this. - Randomness that is not random voids the whole thing. The proof of perfectness assumes the coefficients a₁ … a_{t−1} are uniformly random . If the generator is biased — even slightly, even just low-entropy — "information-theoretic security" quietly becomes "information-theoretically approximately secure". This is the easiest mistake to make in all of cryptography and the hardest to audit. The randomness must come from a true entropy source or a validated CSPRNG. - Too small a field, or repeated x coordinates : when splitting byte-wise over GF(2⁸) (SLIP-39's approach) there are at most 255 usable x coordinates, so the threshold must stay well below the field size; repeated x coordinates mean repeated shares , and that must be checked. - Slow-drip theft : an attacker who can only take one share at a time still wins once they have collected t of them over months. The countermeasure is proactive refresh (proactive secret sharing, by Ostrovsky-Yung and by Herzberg et al., 1995): periodically re-share under a fresh random polynomial so the old shares expire. Static SSS cannot stop a patient adversary. - One typo during recovery : with 21 shares, 20 correct and one transcribed character wrong, the mathematics cannot tell you which one is wrong — threshold sharing provides no error correction. Real implementations therefore attach a checksum to each share (SLIP-39's word list is explicitly designed to make mistakes detectable and localisable). - After recovery : the reconstructed plaintext key is sitting in memory. "The shares are well protected" and "the process gets core-dumped" are two different problems. - Quantum? On the contrary — this is the part that is quantum-proof. It is a genuinely rare advantage today: ECC and RSA both have to be rewritten, and Shamir does not change by a single character. - November 1979 : Adi Shamir publishes "How to Share a Secret" ( Communications of the ACM , Vol. 22, No. 11, pp. 612–613) — two pages, and the starting point of all threshold cryptography. George Blakley independently publishes "Safeguarding Cryptographic Keys" the same year; two different insights converged. - 1979 : the same paper sketches threshold RSA and gives the "majority acts, minority blocks" framing. - 1982–1985 : GMW (1982) and BGW (1985) fold SSS into multi-party computation, making computation between mutually distrusting parties possible. - 1987 : Paul Feldman publishes "A Practical Scheme for Non-interactive Verifiable Secret Sharing" (FOCS 1987) — discrete-log commitments let a share carry its own proof , and a cheating dealer is caught on the spot. VSS gains a usable non-interactive form. - 1991 : Torben Pedersen publishes "Non-Interactive and Information-Theoretic Secure Verifiable Secret Sharing" (CRYPTO 1991). The Pedersen commitment g^s·h^r is perfectly hiding but computationally binding , so even a dealer with unlimited computing power learns nothing about the secret . The same year he introduces distributed key generation (EUROCRYPT 1991), which dissolves the question of "who generates the key" along with the key itself. - 1995 : Ostrovsky and Yung, and independently Herzberg et al., propose proactive secret sharing — periodic refresh against gradual compromise. - 2018–2020 : crypto wallets bring SSS to the mass market — Electrum 2.9 (2018) added sharded import; SLIP-39 (2020) defines composable Shamir mnemonics, with Trezor firmware 2.4.0 (2019) supporting them first. - June 2024 : RFC 9591 (FROST) standardises two-round Schnorr threshold signatures, with Shamir sharing as the default way to split the private key. - The 2020s : NIST launches threshold-cryptography and VSS standardisation work (the PiVer framework and related projects) — a line that began as a 1979 paper is becoming a standard component of financial infrastructure. - Wikipedia search entry for Shamir 门限秘密共享. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Shamir%20%E9%97%A8%E9%99%90%E7%A7%98%E5%AF%86%E5%85%B1%E4%BA%AB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[h=H(M),\quad H:\{0,1\}^{ }\to\{0,1\}^{n}\] Shamir Secret Sharing: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Shannon's Perfect Secrecy Theorem
items.text: Theorem : Shannon's Perfect Secrecy Theorem (香农完美保密定理). Perfect secrecy means one thing: the ciphertext tells you nothing about the plaintext. In 1949 Shannon gave that sentence a rigorous mathematical definition, and proved that only the one-time pad can reach it — at the price of a key as long as the message. Set the stage. A secrecy system has a plaintext space M , a key space K and a ciphertext space C . The key k is drawn independently of the plaintext m (that assumption is not optional), the encryption algorithm Enc_k maps plaintext to ciphertext, and Dec_k maps back. Definition (perfect secrecy) : for every plaintext distribution, every plaintext m and every ciphertext c , P(M = m C = c) = P(M = m) Seeing the ciphertext changes nothing about your beliefs. An equivalent formulation is Shannon's own: for any two plaintexts m1 and m2 , encrypting them under the same key must yield any given ciphertext with the same probability ( Pr_k[Enc_k(m1) = c] = Pr_k[Enc_k(m2) = c] ). Chinese textbooks often write this as C(K) = C(P) : the statistical distribution of ciphertexts does not depend on the plaintext, and the key may redistribute plaintexts onto ciphertexts any way it likes — any redistribution, as long as it carries no information about the message itself. In information-theoretic language it is mutual information I(M; C) = 0 , equivalently H(M C) = H(M) . Shannon proved in 1949 that these formulations are equivalent, which is why they get used interchangeably. Theorem 1 (the one-time pad achieves the bound) : take M = K = C = {0,1}^n , Enc_k(m) = m ⊕ k , with k uniform on K . Each ciphertext c corresponds to exactly one key ( k = c ⊕ m ), so Pr[C = c] = 2^{-n} regardless of m , and P(M = m C = c) = P(M = m) holds. Theorem 2 (the bound, Shannon's bound) : any perfectly secret system satisfies K ≥ M (in entropy form, H(K) ≥ H(M) ). The proof by contradiction is short: suppose there are fewer keys than plaintexts. Fix a ciphertext c that can occur. Decrypting it under every key yields at most K distinct plaintexts, so when K < M some plaintext m can never produce c . Then P(M = m C = c) = 0 while P(M = m ) 0 , and the definition breaks. In other words: the key must be at least as long as the message. That is not engineering advice, it is a mathematical necessity. Theorem 3 (uniqueness) : the structure of a perfectly secret system is completely pinned down. For every key k , Enc_k must be a bijection from M to C (otherwise one ciphertext decrypts to two plaintexts and the argument above applies), and each ciphertext c must correspond to exactly K plaintext-key pairs. When K = M , this says that every message gets its own random string, as long as the message itself — that is the one-time pad . Strictly speaking, every perfectly secret system is a one-time pad plus a fixed, key-independent relabelling, so "the OTP is the only solution" holds up to that equivalence, not literally. Finally, the quantifiers. The conclusion holds for all plaintext distributions, all key distributions independent of the message, and all adversaries — unbounded computing power, unlimited time, a quantum computer, an attacker who is also the cryptographer. That is information-theoretic security, also called unconditional security. Because it handed cryptography an absolute ruler. Before this theorem, the word "secure" had no mathematical content. Before it, people said a cipher was "strong enough" on the strength of testing, experience and the designer's own reputation. Shannon turned security from a feeling into a provable bound: he gave a definition, he gave the ceiling that definition allows, and he proved that everything beyond that ceiling is wasted effort. It directly determined two trajectories: 1. It explained why the one-time pad is mathematically unimpeachable and practically unusable. The key has to be as long as the message, and that single fact locks out almost every scenario — how do you distribute, store and destroy a key that size? 2. It forced the escape route of "computational security". If you allow the attacker's computing power to be finite, you can trade a much shorter key for "too expensive to break". Diffie and Hellman stated the trade-off bluntly in 1976: a system is secure either because breaking it costs too much (computationally secure) or because no amount of computing breaks it (unconditionally secure). Modern cryptography is almost entirely built on the first road. It is also the coordinate origin for everything that came later. What Goldwasser and Micali did in 1982 is, reduced to one sentence: swap "zero information" for "computationally zero information" . Shannon said the mutual information between ciphertext and plaintext must be zero; they said it may be non-zero as long as nobody can compute it out of it. Semantic security, IND-CPA, IND-CCA, non-malleability, UC security — all of them are later generations of the computational version of this theorem. And look one level deeper: every "provably secure" paper today ends up reducing to some hardness assumption (factoring, discrete logarithms, lattice problems). Those assumptions are defensible precisely because Shannon showed that if you cannot stay secret even with a key as long as the message, then any cheaper scheme must lean on some specific mathematical difficulty. That lower bound is the licence on which all assumption-based security operates. No mainstream system today claims perfect secrecy, but the theorem's ideas live on in several distinct forms. One: it really was deployed, and for a long time. In 1917 Gilbert Vernam at AT&T came up with the idea of adding two punched paper tapes modulo 2, and patented it in 1919 — the "one-time tape". The US military turned it into the SIGTOT system, used for high-level teletype traffic. The Soviets went further: random numbers printed in whole books, shipped to embassies in diplomatic pouches, one page torn off per message and destroyed after use. That is the only large-scale engineering success perfect secrecy ever had. Two: it taught modern cryptography its most expensive lesson — break the premise and everything collapses. The Venona project broke the Soviet one-time pad. Not because the mathematics fell. Because the German advance on Moscow in 1941 forced the Soviet key-material factory to rush production, and it printed roughly 35,000 pages of duplicate key material . In the duplicated pages, c1 ⊕ c2 = m1 ⊕ m2 , so the XOR of two plaintexts leaks out. Analyst Richard Hallock spotted the "depth" (the same key page used twice) in October 1943; Genevieve Feinstein found in November 1944 that the Soviets were even transmitting key groups in the clear; Meredith Gardner read the first message in February 1946. The project ran until 1 October 1980 and only ever recovered part of a few thousand telegrams. It is the best advertisement and the best warning perfect secrecy ever produced. Three: it survives inside quantum key distribution. The QKD protocols that followed BB84 attack exactly the distribution problem: both sides first share a random string over a quantum channel, then use it as a one-time pad, so the data layer achieves information-theoretic security. Bennett, Brassard and Breidbart proposed "quantum cryptography" and a quantum one-time pad back in 1984; the pattern today is called "QKD plus OTP". Four: it is the ruler behind almost every security definition. "Is this scheme semantically secure?", "is this the computational version of perfect secrecy?", "how long should a symmetric key be?" — all of these are measured against Shannon. So the theorem is alive: not as an algorithm that ships inside a device, but as a yardstick nailed to the ceiling. The theorem was never overturned — it was routed around. Its real attack surface is its three premises, and every one of them breaks easily. - It covers confidentiality and nothing else. A one-time pad is malleable: flip one bit of the ciphertext and the recipient decrypts a flipped plaintext, with no way to tell that anything was touched . So the OTP provides no authentication and no resistance to chosen-ciphertext attack. Shannon's definition has no column for integrity at all — that is a limit of the definition, not a bug in an implementation. - It leaks length. A perfectly secret system must leak the plaintext length (otherwise the ciphertext space would be infinite), unless a padding or fixed-block protocol is used to hide it. Real traffic analysis lives on length, timing and volume. - The premises are brittle in practice. The key must be truly random, at least as long as the message, never reused and never leaked. Venona fell over "reuse". And "truly random" still breaks in 2026: a broken pseudorandom generator, a seed drawn twice from a low-entropy pool, or a VM snapshot that rolls the RNG state backwards — any of these takes perfect secrecy apart. - Key distribution is a dead end. To be secret you must first get a secret as long as the message to the other party; if that channel can be eavesdropped, you have already handed over the secret in step one. Diffie–Hellman and QKD both exist to dodge this, and both pay in complexity. - The "unique solution" is strict and merciless. Shannon's theorem means any scheme that fails "key ≥ message" is information-theoretically broken: DES's 56-bit key is naked in theory, and so is AES's 128-bit key. Every real system is "breakable but expensive". Which means that in an engineering context, "my system provides perfect secrecy" is roughly synonymous with "my system has a bug". - The theorem has been "revised" twice. Once by Goldwasser–Micali, who relaxed "zero information" into "computationally zero information" at the price of a hardness assumption — from then on, security stopped being a theorem and became a theorem plus an assumption . Once more on the equivalence between semantic security and IND-CPA: the 1984 result carried a technical condition (a minimum-entropy requirement on the distribution of the adversary's chosen plaintexts), and it took Goldreich's textbook framework plus Watanabe–Shikata–Imai in 2003 to clean it up. Even the word "equivalent" needed later generations to tidy up. - One last boundary : perfect secrecy is a property of a single, static, stateless message. Several messages under one key, protocols with several rounds, an adversary who is an active participant in the system — Shannon addressed none of it. - 1945 : Shannon finished his wartime report A Mathematical Theory of Communication at Bell Labs. It was classified, and declassified in 1949. - 1948 : A Mathematical Theory of Communication appeared in the Bell System Technical Journal (vol. 27, no. 3, pp. 379-423). Information theory is born, and entropy arrives as the ruler. - October 1949 : Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems is published in the Bell System Technical Journal , vol. 28, no. 4, pp. 656-715. The definition of perfect secrecy, Shannon's bound (at least as many keys as plaintexts), the optimality of the one-time pad, and the "unicity distance" all come out of this one paper. - 1976 : Diffie and Hellman, in New Directions in Cryptography , draw the explicit line between computationally secure and unconditionally secure, and note that the one-time pad is the only unconditionally secure system in use — and is impractical because of the key length. The road of computational security opens here. - 1982 / 1984 : Goldwasser and Micali publish Probabilistic Encryption , translating Shannon's "zero information" into "computationally zero information". The modern definition paradigm starts, and Shannon's theorem stops being a target and becomes a starting point. - 1984 : Bennett, Brassard and Breidbart propose quantum cryptography and a quantum one-time pad, cracking the distribution dead end with physics. - Today : the one-time pad lives on in textbooks and in QKD textbooks; perfect secrecy lives on in the preamble of every security definition. It is the only theorem in cryptography that was never superseded, only bypassed. - Wikipedia search entry for 香农完美保密定理. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%A6%99%E5%86%9C%E5%AE%8C%E7%BE%8E%E4%BF%9D%E5%AF%86%E5%AE%9A%E7%90%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Shannon's Perfect Secrecy Theorem: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Shor's Algorithm
items.text: Theorem : Shor's Algorithm (肖尔算法). Theorem (Shor, 1994): integer factoring and the discrete logarithm problem can both be solved in polynomial time on a quantum computer. Start with the quantifiers, because that is the skeleton of the theorem: There exist a quantum algorithm A and a polynomial p such that, for every composite N (n = ⌈log₂N⌉ bits), A runs on a quantum computer capable of arbitrary unitary gates and of coherently executing O(p(n)) steps, and outputs the prime factorization of N in O(p(n)) time using O(p(n)) qubits. The same holds for the discrete logarithm problem in finite fields and in elliptic curve groups. Shor's 1994 result gives O(n³) time and O(n) space; the 1997 journal version spells it out further. Note that the theorem says "polynomial time", not "fast". n³ at n = 2048 is 8.6×10⁹ — unremarkable on its own, but it still has to be multiplied by the cost of error correction (see broken ). The reduction: the whole problem collapses into one subroutine, "find the period". Given a composite N and a random base a, consider f(x) = aˣ mod N . It has a period r ( aʳ ≡ 1 mod N ). Once you have r: if r is even and a^(r/2) ≠ -1 (mod N) , then at least one of gcd(a^(r/2) - 1, N) and gcd(a^(r/2) + 1, N) is a proper factor of N. So factoring is reduced to quantum period finding. The quantum part uses two weapons: superposition (one modular exponentiation yields all values of f(x) at once) and the quantum Fourier transform (which makes the period r visible in the amplitudes; a continued-fraction expansion then floats r out). The "semi-classical" version by Pedersen and Shor (1995) replaces the full QFT with phase estimation, dropping the cost from O(n²) gates to O(n) controlled rotations plus O(n log n) single-qubit gates. Zalka (1998) showed the QFT step needs only O(log n) qubits. Discrete logarithms use the same machine: find the order r of a in the group G, then solve a system of linear congruences. One algorithm, two death sentences: RSA and elliptic curves fall together. In complexity-class terms : factoring and discrete logarithms are in BQP. As a side note, Bernstein and Vazirani showed in 1997 that BQP ⊆ PSPACE, and that P = BQP would imply P = PSPACE — nobody believes the latter. But Shor's theorem does not need that assumption to be devastating: it turns "factoring is hard" from a belief into "factoring is incorrect on a quantum computer". Because it demolished the foundation under all of public-key cryptography in one stroke, and that foundation carries almost all of the digital trust on earth. The list is long: RSA encryption, RSA signatures, Diffie–Hellman, ElGamal, DSA, ECDSA, ECDH, SSL/TLS key exchange, PGP, SSH host keys, Bitcoin and Ethereum address signatures, root keys in code-signing certificates, root keys that have sat in HSMs for decades, kernel module signing, firmware update signing. They all share one mathematical assumption — that factoring and discrete logarithms are hard — and that assumption is no longer an assumption, it is a theorem with the wrong sign. The historical weight of it: in 1994, one paper, about a machine that did not yet exist, threatened every HTTPS connection on the planet, every code signature, every digital coin private key — and at that time the best quantum machine in the world could barely do anything with ten logical bits. Theory ran thirty years ahead of hardware, and it ran a long way. Three consequences follow directly: 1. Post-quantum cryptography happened because of it. NIST called for proposals in 2016 and published FIPS 203 (ML-KEM), FIPS 204 (ML-DSA) and FIPS 205 (SLH-DSA) on 13 August 2024. The entire migration roadmap traces back to that 1994 paper. 2. "Harvest now, decrypt later" became a real threat. Traffic captured today can be stored until the machine arrives. For anything that must stay secret for ten years, the exposure surface moves from "in transit" to "at rest". This is the one threat model that makes "we did not migrate" equivalent to "we already leaked". 3. Crypto agility became a hard requirement. If you are paying now for a machine that does not exist, then cryptography has to be replaceable, hybridisable and deployable in stages — hence hybrid KEMs, algorithm identifiers and the whole "crypto agility" practice. The boundary must be nailed down : Shor does not touch symmetric ciphers, hashes, one-time pads or the Kerckhoffs principle. The quantum threat to cryptography is never uniform — on the public-key side it is a cliff, on the symmetric side it is a step (halved), and that step is Grover's job. Nobody runs Shor's algorithm against live systems in production, because no machine can run it. Its real uses are these: - It is the yardstick for every post-quantum scheme. Every new algorithm has to answer the same question: "how much security do I still have against an adversary with Shor's algorithm?" ML-KEM-768's 192 bits of classical strength and roughly 128 bits of quantum strength — that 128 is anchored by Shor's algorithm. - It is the basis of the migration deadlines. NIST IR 8547 (initial public draft, November 2024) is blunt about it: 112-bit-strength RSA, DH, ECDSA and EdDSA are deprecated after 2030 and disallowed after 2035; NSM-10 sets 2035 as the target year for completing the federal migration. This is not caution, it is the logic of "we cannot afford to be late". - It is driving an entire industrial response. CISA refreshed its list of product categories that use PQC standards in January 2026, answering Executive Order 14306 of 6 June 2025; NIST published SP 800-227, Recommendations for Key-Encapsulation Mechanisms , in September 2025, and updated its crypto-agility guidance (CSWP 39) in June 2026. "Migration" has stopped being a research topic and become a line item in procurement. - It is the parent of half the quantum algorithm toolbox. Phase estimation, the QFT, amplitude estimation — the generic tools that quantum algorithms use today all grew out of Shor's algorithm. - It settles what "long-term confidentiality" means. Data that must still be unreadable in ten or twenty years has to be encrypted with a post-quantum scheme today. That is the most direct consequence of harvest-now-decrypt-later. What stands between the theorem and the weapon is physics, not mathematics. The theorem was never refuted — it has been blocked by hardware for thirty years, and it still is. - "Polynomial time" hides an enormous gap. Circuit-level estimates are the real invoice. Beauregard, Høyer and Mølmer (2011) give 0.3n³ Toffoli gates at depth O(n³). Gidney and Ekerå (2021) give, in the abstract circuit model, 3n + 0.002n·lg n logical qubits and 0.3n³ Toffoli gates for n-bit RSA, and about 830,000 physical qubits and 30 hours for a 256-bit elliptic curve discrete logarithm. Gidney (2025), using approximate residue arithmetic, concatenated surface codes and magic-state cultivation, pushed RSA-2048 down to under a million noisy physical qubits in under a week — while admitting he sees no way to gain another order of magnitude without changing physical assumptions. The word "polynomial" conceals three orders of magnitude. - Today's machines are several orders of magnitude short. IBM's roadmap: Nighthawk is a 120-qubit square lattice running 5,000–7,500 gates; the first large-scale fault-tolerant machine, Starling, is slated for 2029 with 200 logical qubits and a hundred million gates; Blue Jay comes after 2033 with 2,000 logical qubits and a billion gates. Google's roadmap targets roughly one million physical qubits around 2029 at its sixth milestone. Compare those numbers: Gidney's "a million physical qubits, under a week" for RSA-2048 sits almost exactly on Google's 2029 target, while IBM's 200 logical qubits for 2029 would not even cover a single shot (about 1,600 logical qubits are needed) by that estimate. - Error correction eats everything. A logical qubit needs a surface-code patch of distance d, costing 2(d+1)² physical qubits each — a factor of hundreds to thousands — and the physical gate error rate has to sit stably below threshold. "A million noisy qubits" sounds modest, but only if they can be corrected and can run for a week. - The theorem has preconditions. The modulus must be a product of two large primes: if the primes are close, small, or of Fermat-like shape, the general number field sieve breaks it in seconds and no quantum machine is needed. Factoring "a hard N" and factoring "an arbitrary N" are different problems , and the theorem is about the former. - What it does not touch, it does not touch at all. Symmetric ciphers, hash functions, one-time pads and quantum key distribution are unaffected by Shor; the halving of 2^n to 2^(n/2) belongs to Grover. And the symmetric half is far cheaper — which is why the priority today is obvious: replace the public-key part first. - There is a time asymmetry. Forward secrecy (ECDHE) means past session keys are already dead and will never be dug out by a future quantum computer. What stays exposed long-term are long-term signing keys, archived ciphertexts, and data that has to stay secret for thirty years . When to worry depends on how long you need to hide something, not on how strong today's machines are. - Do not mistake a theorem for a prophecy. The theorem says "if a large enough fault-tolerant quantum computer exists", not "one exists". From 1994 to today, thirty-two years on, cryptographers hold an algorithm already proven to win and not a single machine able to run it. Migration is not happening because the machine arrived; it is happening because we know it will. - 1994 : Shor presents Algorithms for Quantum Computation: Discrete Logarithms and Factoring at FOCS, giving the first polynomial-time algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms. The phrase "quantum cryptanalysis" comes from this paper's abstract. - 1995 : Pedersen and Shor introduce the efficient (semi-classical) quantum Fourier transform, cutting the QFT cost from O(n²) to O(n) gates; Shor publishes the gate-set analysis for universal quantum computation in Physical Review A . - 1997 : The journal version, Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer , appears in SIAM Journal on Computing 26(5):1484-1509, alongside Bernstein and Vazirani's Quantum Complexity Theory . - 2011 : Beauregard, Høyer and Mølmer give the circuit-level estimate — 2.8 billion qubits, eight hours to break 2048-bit RSA. That number gets compressed repeatedly over the next fourteen years. - 2016 : NIST calls for post-quantum candidates. The "death date" of public-key cryptography enters an official document for the first time. - 2021 : Gidney and Ekerå compress the estimate to twenty million noisy qubits and eight hours ( Quantum 5, 433). - 13 August 2024 : NIST publishes FIPS 203/204/205 and the post-quantum standards take effect. In November 2024 : the NIST IR 8547 initial draft sets the migration timeline (deprecate after 2030, disallow after 2035). - 2025 : Gidney brings RSA-2048 down to under a million noisy qubits and under a week; IBM and Google both publish fault-tolerance roadmaps targeting 2029; SP 800-227 is released. - To this day : there is still no cryptographically relevant quantum computer. The compute needed to factor a 2048-bit RSA remains science fiction in 2026. - Wikipedia search entry for 肖尔算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E8%82%96%E5%B0%94%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Shor's Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
