items.title: SIKE Supersingular Isogeny KEM
items.text: Algorithm : Supersingular Isogeny Key Encapsulation (SIKE 超椭圆同源 KEM). SIKE wrapped the SIDH key exchange into a KEM. Two parties walk secret isogeny paths on supersingular elliptic curves; the public key contains torsion points on the image curve. When the paths meet, both obtain the same j-invariant as the shared secret. Its selling point was very small public keys and ciphertexts for bandwidth-constrained settings. SIKE was an alternate candidate in NIST's post-quantum process and represented an isogeny assumption independent of lattices and codes. Its fall is instructive: the attack came from mathematics and auxiliary-point leakage, not from a quantum computer. “Post-quantum” does not mean “already secure”. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. It should not be used as a production KEM. Its value now lies in cryptanalysis history, isogeny research and teaching how a candidate is eliminated. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. In 2022 Castryck and Decru published an efficient key-recovery attack. Auxiliary torsion points exposed in the public key let an attacker turn reconstruction of the secret isogeny path into a computable isogeny problem. SIKE parameters fell quickly and NIST removed it from standardisation. The attack runs on classical computers. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Symbols are catalogue-level variables, not standard constants; parameters, test vectors and clauses remain with the registered source. The model states structural relations, not an implementation audit. Jao and De Feo proposed SIDH in 2011; SIKE entered NIST's second round in 2017. The attack appeared in July 2022 and was independently verified, eliminating SIKE. The lesson: post-quantum candidates need years of cryptanalysis, not early deployment because the keys look small and the paper looks elegant. items.title: Shortest Independent Vectors Problem (SIVP)
items.text: Algorithm : Shortest Independent Vector Problem (最短独立向量问题). SIVP asks, given an n-dimensional lattice, for n linearly independent lattice vectors whose longest vector is as short as possible; the approximation version only requires a factor γ from optimal. It is closely related to SVP (find one shortest nonzero vector): an SIVP solution gives a basis, and an SVP solution helps build short vectors. Basis-reduction algorithms such as LLL and BKZ solve approximations. Lattice cryptography usually reduces to approximate SVP, SIVP or GapSVP. Understanding SIVP explains why basis quality affects decryption and signing: a bad basis produces large coefficients, noise growth and decryption failure. It is also the entry point for estimating lattice-attack cost. Restate the chain as input → state → transform → output → criterion. Every step should identify who acts, what changes and what evidence remains. A step without evidence is marked unverified, not reproduced. As a hardness problem in security proofs, a target for basis reduction and a reference for parameter evaluation. It produces no ciphertext; implementations estimate attack complexity with BKZ and related algorithms. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. items.title: Acoustic side channel
items.text: Attack : Acoustic Side Channel (声学侧信道). Where the sound comes from When a computer runs, CPU power draw changes with instructions and data. The voltage-regulator circuit on the motherboard tries to hold a stable voltage; its capacitors and coils vibrate slightly as currents change, and that vibration reaches the air as sound. The relevant source is the regulator itself, not the fan or the speaker. Low bandwidth is not the same as no information A common microphone hears below 20 kHz; an ultrasound microphone can reach a few hundred kHz. That is orders of magnitude below the GHz clock. The noise of a single instruction is buried in the background, but when the same key-dependent operation is repeated thousands of times, the leakage accumulates into an envelope lasting hundreds of milliseconds and separable in the spectrum. An acoustic side channel does not attack the mathematical structure of RSA or AES; it attacks the implementation. Branches, table lookups and multiplication paths change with secret data, and power and sound change with them. If the attacker can get close, make the machine decrypt chosen ciphertexts and know the implementation, a mathematical security proof does not cover this physical path. GnuPG 1.4.14's RSA modular exponentiation used a window algorithm in which some all-zero intermediate words took a different branch. Genkin–Shamir–Tromer crafted ciphertexts that produced many all-zero words, amplifying a tiny branch into an audible difference lasting hundreds of milliseconds and recovering a 4096-bit RSA private key bit by bit. The 2014 demonstration used an ordinary mobile phone next to a laptop, or a sensitive microphone several metres away; full 4096-bit RSA key recovery took about an hour. It needs chosen ciphertexts and a decryption operation, usually a local or near-field setting, not a remote attack against an arbitrary HTTPS server. Engineering should use constant-time, branchless modular exponentiation, enable RSA blinding and keep secret data out of control flow. Physical defences include acoustic shielding, masking noise and chassis damping. For high-value machines, acoustic shielding belongs with power, electromagnetic and cache side-channel controls, not instead of them. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The chain requires a target running an affected GnuPG version, an attacker who can submit arbitrary ciphertexts and observe decryption, a microphone that can hear the machine, and knowledge of the implementation and key size. Remove any one and the one-hour demonstration no longer holds. The acoustic side channel recovers RSA key bits from the decryption process, not keystrokes, not fan noise. Its bandwidth is low and its signal weak, but it still matters for air-gapped machines: sound crosses air and some partitions where a network attack cannot reach. Shamir and Tromer first showed at the Eurocrypt 2004 rump session that different RSA keys have different acoustic fingerprints. IACR ePrint 2013/857 in December 2013 gave full key extraction; the 2014 CRYPTO paper and the 2017 Journal of Cryptology version refined the experiment and method. This work extended side channels from “electromagnetic, power and cache” to “sound and chassis potential”, and pushed GnuPG and similar implementations toward blinding, constant-time paths and stronger physical protection. It remains a research attack, not a mass-market tool. - Wikipedia search entry for 声学侧信道. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%A3%B0%E5%AD%A6%E4%BE%A7%E4%BF%A1%E9%81%93 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Acoustic Side Channel: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Blind Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Blind Signature (盲签名). Blind—sign—unblind A blind signature lets a signer sign without seeing the message; the user later unblinds the signature into a valid signature on the original message. In RSA: the user picks random r, computes m’ = r^e·H(m) mod n and sends m’ to the signer; the signer returns s’=(m’)^d mod n; the user computes s=s’·r^−1 mod n, obtaining H(m)^d, a valid RSA signature on m. Three properties Blindness: the signer cannot recover the message from the signing interaction. Unlinkability: the signer cannot match a signing session to a later signature/message. Unforgeability: the user cannot obtain more valid signatures than authorized, i.e. one-more-forgery security. Variants RSA-FDH/RSABSSA uses PSS encoding; RFC 9474 defines an interoperable RSA blind signature. Schnorr/BLS blind signatures are shorter, but concurrent sessions must resist ROS attacks. Blind signatures resolve the tension between “the signer must not know the content” and “verifiers must be able to verify the signature”. They underlie electronic cash, anonymous credentials, Privacy Pass, anonymous voting and blind tokens. The issuer signs only a blinded token, and later verification cannot link it to the issuance session. They separate authentication from anonymity: the signature proves authorization, while blinding cuts the link between signer and user. Typical uses include electronic cash/central-bank digital currency privacy, Privacy Pass-style anonymous tokens, anonymous credentials, electronic voting and license/timestamp tokens. RFC 9474 RSABSSA verifies with standard RSA-PSS, which fits existing PKIs. Requirements: high-entropy, one-time blinding factors; RSA blinding and constant-time private-key operations; limits on concurrent sessions and signature counts; domain separation and structural checks so a blind-signature oracle cannot be abused across protocols. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Blind signatures are not absolute anonymity: predictable blinding, a colluding signer and verifier, or a low-entropy message space enables linking attacks. RSA blind signatures also rely on the RSA assumption and FDH/PSS encoding; a signer willing to sign any blinded message becomes a signing oracle. Boundaries: a blind signature does not provide untraceable payments by itself and does not replace mixing or network anonymity; it only cuts the signer-to-message link. Concurrent Schnorr blind signatures must resist ROS attacks; RSA blind signatures need RSA blinding and constant-time private-key operations. David Chaum introduced blind signatures in the 1982 CRYPTO paper “Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments”, initially for untraceable electronic payments; the proceedings appeared in 1983, pp. 199–203. Chaum later used them in eCash. Bellare–Namprempre–Pointcheval–Semanko analyzed one-more RSA inversion in 2001, and RFC 9474 standardized RSABSSA in 2023. The primitive remains foundational for privacy protocols, though deployments moved from eCash to Privacy Pass, anonymous credentials and token services. - Wikipedia search entry for 盲签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%9B%B2%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Blind Signature: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ElGamal Public-Key Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : ElGamal (ElGamal 公钥密码). From Diffie–Hellman to encryption ElGamal encryption turns a Diffie–Hellman shared secret into a one-time mask. The public parameters are a cyclic group G of order q , a generator g , and a public key h=g^x ; the private key x stays secret. Encryption picks a random k and computes c1=g^k , c2=m·h^k ; decryption computes m=c2·(c1^x)^{-1} . Why it is correct c1^x=(g^k)^x=g^{kx}=h^k , so the mask h^k cancels. A message must first be encoded as a group element; arbitrary bytes cannot simply be multiplied as if they were group elements. How it is used Bare ElGamal is rarely used to encrypt long messages. Real systems use it as a KEM or inside hybrid encryption: ElGamal wraps a symmetric key, and an AEAD such as AES-GCM protects the body. The elliptic-curve variant is commonly called ECIES or DHIES. It turns “computing discrete logarithms is hard” into usable public-key encryption. Unlike RSA, which relies on integer factorization, ElGamal relies on the discrete-logarithm problem in a finite field or elliptic curve. The random value k makes every encryption of the same plaintext different. The price is a ciphertext roughly twice the size of the plaintext, two modular exponentiations for encryption and one for decryption. It is far slower than symmetric cryptography, so its practical role is key encapsulation and hybrid encryption, not bulk data. GnuPG and PGP ElGamal keys and the DSA signature scheme are tied to the same family of discrete-logarithm problems; elliptic-curve ElGamal variants appear in ECIES and similar hybrid schemes. TLS 1.3 does not use bare ElGamal: it uses ECDHE for key agreement and AEAD for record protection. Do not confuse ElGamal encryption with ElGamal signatures. They share a hardness assumption but solve different protocol problems. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Textbook ElGamal is malleable: multiplying c2 by t produces a valid ciphertext for t·m . It is therefore not chosen-ciphertext secure and must not be presented as authenticated encryption. Implementations must validate that group elements lie in the correct subgroup, avoid small-subgroup attacks, use audited group parameters or curves, and wrap the primitive in an authenticated KEM/DEM, DHIES or ECIES construction rather than exposing the raw transform to untrusted input. Taher ElGamal presented the scheme at CRYPTO 1984 and published it in IEEE Transactions on Information Theory 31(4):469–472 in 1985. It adapted Diffie–Hellman key agreement into public-key encryption and also introduced a signature scheme that became an important influence on DSA. ElGamal encryption and ElGamal signatures share the discrete-logarithm setting but have different goals. In a catalog they belong beside RSA, DSA and ECDSA, not merged into one “algorithm”. - Wikipedia search entry for ElGamal 公钥密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ElGamal%20%E5%85%AC%E9%92%A5%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] ElGamal: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Falcon / FN-DSA Lattice Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Falcon (Falcon 格签名). GPV hash-and-sign Falcon is a GPV-style NTRU lattice signature: it hashes the message to a target point, uses a trapdoor short basis to sample a short lattice vector near that target, and outputs the vector; verification checks that it is short and lies in the correct coset. NTRU lattice and fast Fourier sampling The private key is a solution (f,g,F,G) of the NTRU equation fG−gF=q, forming a short basis of an NTRU lattice. Signing recursively splits the problem in the FFT domain and samples at the leaves with the discrete Gaussian SamplerZ in O(n log n). Security reduces to SIS over NTRU lattices. Parameters Falcon-512 has an 897-byte public key and a signature averaging about 666 bytes; Falcon-1024 has a 1793-byte public key and a signature averaging about 1280 bytes. Signatures are variable-length, so verification must enforce the parameter set’s upper bound. Falcon targets the smallest public-key-plus-signature footprint: among the NIST lattice signatures it has the smallest combined size and the fastest verification, which suits bandwidth- and storage-constrained TLS certificates, JOSE/COSE tokens and embedded firmware signatures. It needs no AES or large matrices; verification is polynomial multiplication plus hashing. Fast Fourier sampling lets it reach thousands of signatures per second on a general CPU, with verification five to ten times faster. It is used in TLS 1.3 FN-DSA drafts, JOSE/COSE FN-DSA-512/1024, code signing and firmware signing; NIST is standardizing it as FIPS 206. Requirements: fresh random salt per signature; constant-time Gaussian sampling; guard floating-point FFT against NaN, exceptional values and side channels across platforms; never reuse internal randomness across signatures. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Falcon reduces to NTRU-SIS, but implementation risk dominates: signing uses double-precision floating point and discrete Gaussian sampling, so cache, timing and fault attacks can recover the private key; missing randomness enables differential fault attacks. Boundaries: signatures are variable-length, so protocols must budget the upper bound; Falcon is unsuitable when deterministic signatures are required; only 512/1024 parameter sets exist and cannot be rescaled; verification must check encoding length, ranges and subgroups. Falcon was designed by Fouque, Hoffstein, Kirchner, Lyubashevsky, Pornin, Prest, Ricosset, Seiler, Whyte and Zhang and submitted to NIST PQC on 30 November 2017. NIST selected it in 2022; the standardized name is FN-DSA and the standard is FIPS 206, expected in late 2026 or early 2027. items.title: Classic McEliece Code-Based KEM
items.text: Algorithm : Classic McEliece (Classic McEliece 编码型公钥). Classic McEliece implements a Niederreiter KEM with binary Goppa codes: the public key is a systematic generator matrix T and the private key is a Goppa polynomial plus support; a ciphertext is a codeword plus an error vector of weight t, and private decoding recovers the session key. Concretely, T is a randomized systematic generator matrix; the private key contains the Goppa polynomial g, support alpha and a column permutation; encapsulation samples random m and computes c=T·m+e. Decoding The private key uses Patterson decoding to find e in c and recover the codeword; a decapsulation failure yields an implicit rejection. Security rests on decoding random linear codes, not on lattices or number theory. Parameters mceliece348864 has a 261,120-byte public key, 6,492-byte private key and 96-byte ciphertext; mceliece6688128 has a 1,044,992-byte public key and 208-byte ciphertext; the session key is 32 bytes. McEliece is the most conservative post-quantum KEM: proposed in 1978, it has survived more than four decades of cryptanalysis without a practical full-parameter attack. Public keys are large but ciphertexts are small, which suits long-term identity keys and “one public key, many encapsulations”. It does not rely on structured lattices, so its security assumption is independent of ML-KEM and useful for algorithm diversity and backup. It serves long-term TLS/SSH/IPsec identity keys, code and firmware signing roots, and government/financial PQC migration; mceliece6688128 is often recommended as a long-term default. ISO standardized Classic McEliece in June 2026. Requirements: public-key caching and transport dominate cost; constant-time private-key decoding; implicit rejection on failure; pc variants add 32 bytes to ciphertext; never use it as a PKE for arbitrary messages—it is a KEM. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Public keys can reach megabytes, amplifying certificate chains and handshakes; key generation is slow and complex; decoding failure rates, timing/cache attacks and fault injection are the main implementation risks. Boundaries: McEliece encapsulates only a random key and does not encrypt user data; public-key reuse is by design, but the private key must be protected; parameter sets are tied to security levels and public keys/ciphertexts cannot be truncated; code-based and Goppa-structure cryptanalysis remain long-term concerns. Robert McEliece proposed the McEliece public-key cryptosystem in 1978. The Classic McEliece team converted it into a Niederreiter-form KEM, entered the NIST PQC process and was selected by NIST for standardization; ISO standardized it in June 2026. Parameters moved from the original 2^64 security to NIST levels 1/3/5, with public keys growing accordingly. - Wikipedia search entry for Classic McEliece 编码型公钥. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Classic%20McEliece%20%E7%BC%96%E7%A0%81%E5%9E%8B%E5%85%AC%E9%92%A5 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[(c,k)=\mathrm{Encaps}(pk);\qquad k'=\mathrm{Decaps}(sk,c)\] Classic McEliece: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Rabin Trapdoor Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Rabin Cryptosystem (Rabin 陷门公钥密码). Quadratic-residue trapdoor A Rabin signature hashes the message to a quadratic residue modulo n and returns a root of x²+bx≡H(m,u). The public key is n=pq and a constant b; the private factors p,q let the signer take square roots modulo each prime and combine them with CRT. Four roots and encoding Squaring has four roots for every value. The signer publishes only one; two distinct roots leak gcd and factor n. Standardized Rabin-Williams variants add redundancy, encode the message, and bind a random string u into the hash to prevent root ambiguity and chosen-message attacks. Security reduction In the random oracle model, forging reduces to computing a square root modulo n, which is equivalent to factoring n. Verification is one modular squaring plus an encoding check, hundreds of times faster than an RSA modular exponentiation. Rabin was the first practical signature family proven “forging is as hard as factoring”. RSA only gives “breaking signatures is no harder than factoring”; Rabin gives the converse reduction from forgery to factors. Verification is one squaring, and signing is one square-root extraction plus CRT, both cheaper than RSA at the same modulus size. That suits smart cards, sensors and low-power verifiers. The price is four-root handling and encoding, which made it harder to engineer than RSA; standardized variants moved to Rabin-Williams. Rabin-Williams variants appear in ISO/IEC 14888-2 (signatures with appendix) and ISO/IEC 9796-2 (message-recovery signatures), and IEEE P1363 includes Rabin. Uses are mainly standards education, embedded verification and settings that want a factoring-equivalence proof. Real deployment is far below RSA: signatures are probabilistic, root selection and encoding add cost, and patent/ecosystem effects favor RSA, ECDSA or Ed25519 in modern TLS, code signing and certificates. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. A raw square-root signature is vulnerable to a chosen-message attack: the attacker picks random x and asks for a signature on x² mod n. If the returned root is not ±x, gcd(x−s,n) directly reveals p or q. Redundant encoding and randomized hashing are required. The Rabin-Williams instance in ISO 9796-2 was hit by Coron–Naccache–Stern-style attacks and later improvements; short hashes or careless encoding enable forgery. Parameters, encoding and root selection must follow the standard. Rabin proposed the scheme in MIT/LCS/TR-212 in 1979; Williams gave the Rabin-Williams variant in 1980, making signatures closer to RSA form; Bellare and Rogaway gave exact security bounds in 1996; it later entered ISO/IEC 14888-2 and 9796-2. It influenced provably secure signatures and factorization-based cryptography, but engineering complexity kept it out of the mainstream. - Wikipedia search entry for Rabin 陷门公钥密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Rabin%20%E9%99%B7%E9%97%A8%E5%85%AC%E9%92%A5%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Rabin Cryptosystem: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SM4 Block Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : SM4 (SM4 中国商用分组密码). 128-bit block, 32 rounds SM4 has a 128-bit block and a 128-bit key, uses 32 rounds, and updates one word per round with an 8-bit S-box and a linear transform. The plaintext is split into four 32-bit words X0, X1, X2, X3; each round computes one new word: X_{i+4} = X_i ⊕ T(X_{i+1} ⊕ X_{i+2} ⊕ X_{i+3} ⊕ rk_i). T applies an 8-bit S-box to each byte and then a linear transform L(B) = B ⊕ (B<<<2) ⊕ (B<<<10) ⊕ (B<<<18) ⊕ (B<<<24). After 32 rounds, a reverse transformation produces the ciphertext. Key schedule and decryption The key schedule also runs 32 rounds, expanding the master key MK through system parameters FK and fixed constants CK into 32 round keys; it uses L’(B) = B ⊕ (B<<<13) ⊕ (B<<<23). Decryption uses the same structure with the round keys in reverse order. Engineering consequences Updating one word per round lets encryption and decryption share a datapath and keeps hardware small. The S-box supplies nonlinearity, while shifts and XOR supply diffusion. This is not AES’s SPN structure, so AES instructions and lookup-table optimizations do not transfer directly. SM4 is the symmetric base of China’s commercial cryptography system. WAPI wireless LAN, national VPNs, the TLCP record layer, cryptographic modules and financial terminals all need one common 128-bit block cipher; SM4 supplies that primitive and, with SM2 and SM3, completes the suite. Its engineering value is low implementation cost: an 8-bit S-box plus 32-bit addition and shifts is enough for smart cards, embedded devices and hardware security modules. It is not “a stronger AES”; it is the symmetric entry point of a different standards ecosystem. SM4 must be used with a mode. Common combinations are SM4-CBC with HMAC-SM3, SM4-GCM and SM4-CTR. TLCP uses ECDHE_SM4_CBC_SM3 and ECDHE_SM4_GCM_SM3 suites. Requirements: a 128-bit key, a unique IV or nonce, authenticated-then-decrypt or EtM for CBC, and no GCM nonce reuse. Do not use raw ECB on structured data, and do not reuse the same key material for SM4 and SM3. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. No practical key-recovery attack on full SM4 is publicly known, but reduced-round differential and linear cryptanalysis, side channels and related-key analysis remain real concerns. CBC padding oracles, GCM nonce reuse and non-constant-time MAC checks break deployments directly. Implementation boundaries: use certified modules and a real random source; protect S-box tables against cache timing; compare padding and tags in constant time; cap messages per GCM key; prefer forward-secret ECDHE suites in TLCP and disable downgrade fallbacks. SM4’s predecessor SMS4 was designed by Shu-Wang Lu and others, published in 2003 as part of the WAPI national standard GB 15629.11-2003, published independently by OSCCA in 2006, and renamed SM4 in GM/T 0002-2012 in 2012. GB/T 32907-2016 was published in August 2016 and took effect in March 2017; ISO/IEC 18033-3 Amendment 1 added SM4 in June 2021. Two confusions persist: SMS4 is the old name, and SM4 is both the algorithm and the standard. It was first designed for wireless LAN security and only later became a general commercial block cipher. - Wikipedia search entry for SM4 中国商用分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SM4%20%E4%B8%AD%E5%9B%BD%E5%95%86%E7%94%A8%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] SM4: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Threshold Signature / FROST
items.text: Algorithm : Threshold Signature (门限签名). Shamir sharing and Lagrange Threshold signing Shamir-shares the group secret s into n shares, and any t shares reconstruct it via Lagrange coefficients; FROST uses two rounds—publish nonce commitments, then aggregate z=Σz_i into an ordinary Schnorr signature. Two-round FROST In round one each signer generates a one-time nonce (d,e) and publishes commitments (D,E); in round two it computes z_i from the message, the commitment set and its share; the coordinator aggregates z=Σz_i. The result verifies like a single-signer Schnorr signature. DKG Key generation can use a trusted dealer or distributed key generation; DKG lets parties obtain shares without ever holding the full s, at the cost of a more complex protocol. Threshold signatures turn a single private key into t-of-n: fewer than t shares do not reveal s, and at least t honest parties must be online to sign. They suit exchange cold wallets, CA root keys, enterprise signing and blockchain validators. FROST needs only two rounds and does not restrict concurrent signing sessions; its signatures are indistinguishable from ordinary Schnorr, so the threshold structure is invisible on-chain or in protocols. It is used for blockchain custody and validators, CA and code signing, enterprise multisignature, DNSSEC and cross-institution approvals; RFC 9591 defines FROST and Ed25519/Ed448-compatible suites, with trusted-dealer or DKG key generation. Requirements: never reuse a nonce; bind every signing session to a unique message and commitment set; the coordinator must verify partial signatures; DKG must handle malicious shares and complaints; a threshold signature is not multisig—only one public key appears on-chain. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The most damaging implementation error is nonce reuse: two signatures sharing the same (d,e) directly solve for a share and then the group private key; RFC 9591 requires one-time nonces and recommends erasing them after signing. Boundaries: threshold signing protects the private key, not endpoints; a malicious coordinator can deny service or choose messages but cannot forge; t or more colluding parties can recover s; FROST is not post-quantum and relies on discrete logarithms. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Symbols are catalogue-level variables, not standard constants; parameters, test vectors and clauses remain with the registered source. The model states structural relations, not an implementation audit. FROST was proposed by Komlo and Goldberg in 2020 (ePrint 2020/852), entered CFRG in 2021 and became RFC 9591 in June 2024. It builds on Schnorr threshold signatures and Shamir sharing, improving earlier three-round and concurrency-limited schemes. RFC 9591 is Informational, not an IETF standard; production deployments must apply domain separation for their curve and protocol. - Wikipedia search entry for 门限签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%97%A8%E9%99%90%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Threshold Signature: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ZUC Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : ZUC (ZUC 祖冲之流密码). Three layers ZUC is a word-oriented stream cipher: a 128-bit key, a 128-bit IV and 32-bit keystream words. The top layer is a 16-stage LFSR of 31-bit cells restricted to 1…2^31−1; the middle Bit Reorganization extracts 128 bits into four 32-bit words; the bottom nonlinear function F uses two 32-bit memory cells R1/R2, S-boxes S0/S1 and linear transforms L1/L2. Initialization and working stages Key loading expands the 128-bit key/IV into sixteen 31-bit states. Initialization runs 32 clocks and feeds F back into the LFSR without producing keystream; the working stage outputs one 32-bit word per clock while updating the LFSR. Length and versions ZUC-128 powers LTE 128-EEA3/128-EIA3. ZUC-256 provides 256-bit keys for 5G, supports IVs up to 184 bits, and differs from ZUC-128 in initialization and MAC generation. ZUC is a stream cipher designed in China and adopted by 3GPP LTE, providing both 128-EEA3 confidentiality and 128-EIA3 integrity. It is one of the few Chinese-designed algorithms adopted by an international mobile standard. Stream ciphers need no block padding and fit frame- or bit-oriented wireless links; the LFSR plus nonlinear F structure has a small hardware footprint and high throughput, which suits baseband chips. It protects LTE/5G air-interface confidentiality and integrity: 3GPP 128-EEA3/128-EIA3 are built on ZUC, and 5G 256-NEA3/256-NIA3 use ZUC-256. It can also serve other streaming settings that need 128/256-bit keys. Requirements: one key/IV pair may generate only a bounded keystream; IVs must be unique; the MAC must be bound to the encryption context; do not use ZUC as a general hash or MAC—follow the 128-EIA3 MAC flow. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. ZUC 1.4’s initialization was not injective: differential analysis in 2010–2011 could make different IVs produce identical keystreams and recover keys, which led to ZUC 1.5/1.6. Final ZUC-128 has no publicly practical full-round attack, but side channels, IV reuse and over-long keystreams remain real risks. Boundaries: ZUC supplies only a keystream, not authentication; pair it with 128-EIA3 or an AEAD construction. ZUC-256 uses different parameters and IV lengths, so a 128-bit implementation cannot be reused unchanged. ZUC was designed by the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Data Assurance and Communication Security Research Center. ZUC 1.4 was published for evaluation in July 2010; 1.5 followed in January 2011 and 1.6 in June 2011; 3GPP adopted it for LTE 128-EEA3/128-EIA3 in September 2011. GM/T 0001 appeared in 2012, GB/T 33133.1-2016 was published in October 2016 and took effect in May 2017, and ISO/IEC 18033-4 Amendment 1 added ZUC in 2020. ZUC-256 was proposed in 2018 for 5G 256-bit suites. Its name honors the Northern and Southern Dynasties mathematician Zu Chongzhi; the standard splits the algorithm, confidentiality algorithm and integrity algorithm into three parts. - Wikipedia search entry for ZUC 祖冲之流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ZUC%20%E7%A5%96%E5%86%B2%E4%B9%8B%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] ZUC: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ASCON Lightweight AEAD and Hash
items.text: Algorithm : ASCON (ASCON 轻量级密码族). 320-bit state and SPN permutation All Ascon modes share a 320-bit state split into five 64-bit words. Each round has three steps: XOR a round constant into S2, apply 64 parallel 5-bit S-boxes, and diffuse within each word by XORing rotated copies. AEAD initialization/finalization use 12 rounds (p[12]); data blocks use 8 rounds (p[8]). Duplex AEAD Ascon-AEAD128 uses 128-bit keys, nonces and tags, with a 128-bit rate and 192-bit capacity. Initialization injects K N; AD and plaintext are injected in 128-bit blocks while ciphertext is extracted, with p[8] after each block; finalization injects K again and outputs a 128-bit tag. Hash and XOF Ascon-Hash256 absorbs 64-bit blocks and outputs 256 bits; Ascon-XOF128 produces arbitrary-length output. They share the same permutation as the AEAD mode. ASCON is NIST’s lightweight cryptography standard: on IoT, RFID, sensors and 8/16/32-bit MCUs, AES-GCM table or instruction overhead can be too high, while Ascon uses only AND/XOR/rotations and a 5-bit S-box, giving a small hardware footprint and bitsliced software. One permutation covers AEAD, hashing and XOF, reducing the number of cryptographic primitives in a chip or firmware image. It is used for Ascon-AEAD128, Ascon-Hash256, Ascon-XOF128 and Ascon-CXOF128; NIST SP 800-232 was published in August 2025. It suits short messages, low power and area-constrained devices. Requirements: unique nonces; truncation only down to 96/128 bits; p[12] for initialization/finalization and p[8] for data, never mixed; masked implementations for side channels; do not treat it as a high-throughput replacement for AES-GCM. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Ascon-AEAD128 is a nonce-based AEAD: encrypting different messages under the same key and nonce breaks confidentiality and authenticity; nonce reuse is the most direct attack surface. Boundaries: 128-bit security is not 256-bit; tag truncation lowers forgery cost; power/EM side channels on low-power devices need masking; Ascon software is slower than AES-NI on 64-bit servers, so choose by platform. ASCON was designed by Dobraunig, Eichlseder, Mendel and Schläffer, submitted to CAESAR in 2014 and selected for the CAESAR lightweight AEAD portfolio in 2019. NIST announced the Ascon family as its lightweight cryptography standard in February 2023, released the initial SP 800-232 draft in November 2024 and the final standard in August 2025. Its design targets low area, bitsliced friendliness and online authentication; the standard mainly uses the 12/8-round permutations. - Wikipedia search entry for ASCON 轻量级密码族. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ASCON%20%E8%BD%BB%E9%87%8F%E7%BA%A7%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E6%97%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S_{i+1}=f(S_i\oplus (M_i\,\ \,0^{ })),\quad h=\mathrm{Squeeze}(S)\] ASCON: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Canary Trap
items.text: Attack : Canary Trap (金丝雀陷阱). A canary trap is not about encryption; it is about distribution-side fingerprinting. The same sensitive text is prepared in several semantically equivalent versions with small differences in wording or details. Each possible recipient gets a different combination, and the version-to-holder map is kept secret. When a leaked text returns, a few quoted fragments can shrink the candidate set from “every holder” to a specific copy. Formally, let m positions be replaceable, with v_j variants at position j. The total variant space is N=∏v_j. Copy i has fingerprint F_i=(f_i1,…,f_im). A leaked excerpt covers position set Q, and the candidate set is C(Q)={i F_i[Q]=F_leak[Q]}. Attribution is complete when C(Q) =1. If variants are assigned uniformly, the birthday bound P_collision≤n(n-1)/(2N) estimates the chance of a collision among n copies. Real leakers edit, excerpt or retell. If each marked position survives with probability p, the number of visible positions is K~Binomial(m,p). Unique attribution needs at least q_min≈ceil(log n/log v) independent positions, with success P_unique=P(K≥q_min). This is the quantitative reason marks should be numerous but natural. Access control lowers the probability of a leak but cannot answer “who”. A canary trap turns an open set into a finite candidate set and does not depend on catching someone in the act. It supplies attribution evidence, not prevention. In leak investigations, board documents, M&A materials and reporter relationships, its value is turning “anyone could have” into “this copy went only to these people”. It is not a cryptographic proof. If a copy is photocopied, forwarded or read by several people, the fingerprint still points to the original copy holder, not necessarily the final publisher. It proves a copy path, not intent. Operational steps: 1) define the possible recipients and copy count n; 2) choose m slots that do not change meaning (dates, code names, last digits, harmless adjectives); 3) assign a unique fingerprint to each copy and record the map; 4) make every version look equally credible; 5) after a leak, collect the quoted fragments and compare them against C(Q); 6) if the candidate set is not unique, add slots or reduce distribution. Digital versions can use document watermarks, invisible characters, recipient-specific links, or honeytoken files. The key is that a mark can be carried verbatim by the leaker without changing the business meaning. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Failure conditions: rewriting or retelling erases marks; copies are photographed, OCRed or retypeset; several people share one copy; n exceeds N and collisions appear; marks are so obvious that they are detected and removed; legal or ethical limits forbid misleading content or inducement. A canary trap also cannot prove who published the material. Intelligence services used the technique long before the name; it is sometimes called a barium meal test. Tom Clancy's 1987 novel popularized “canary trap”, describing six versions of each summary paragraph, 96 copies and more than a thousand permutations. The digital age added document fingerprinting, watermarks and honeytokens. In the 2020s, a study combined biometrics and locality-sensitive hashing to link a document to its last handler, reporting an average 89.31% success rate even after modifications such as deleting 100 words. The idea of “the document itself as evidence” keeps evolving. - Wikipedia search entry for 金丝雀陷阱. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%87%91%E4%B8%9D%E9%9B%80%E9%99%B7%E9%98%B1 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Canary Trap: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Contact Analysis
items.text: Attack : Contact Analysis (接触分析). Contact analysis, or contact chaining, turns communication metadata into a graph. Nodes are phone numbers, accounts, devices or identifiers; edges are calls, texts, emails or other contact events; edge weights can be counts, duration or a time window. Starting from a target s, the one-hop neighbors Γ(s) are direct contacts, and the k-hop set C_k(s)={v d_G(s,v)≤k} is the extended contact chain. Candidate associations can be ranked with common neighbors and similarity scores: CN(a,b)= Γ(a)∩Γ(b) ; Jaccard J(a,b)= Γ(a)∩Γ(b) / Γ(a)∪Γ(b) ; Adamic-Adar AA(a,b)=Σ_{z∈Γ(a)∩Γ(b)}1/log deg(z). These scores are not proof of guilt; they turn “who may know whom” into rankable hypotheses. Evaluation uses a threshold τ: score≥τ marks a positive candidate, then precision=TP/(TP+FP) and recall=TP/(TP+FN) trade off. Larger k broadens coverage, but C_k and false positives grow. Investigation design is therefore constrained by hop count, time window, node type and review capacity. Contact chains turn scattered records into network structure and help find direct contacts, shared contacts, bridge nodes and isolated subnetworks. They matter for counterterrorism, fraud, law enforcement and incident response, but they are also a privacy fault line: metadata has no content, yet it can reveal relationships, location, routines and social circles. The key distinction: contact chaining produces “suspicion by association”, not guilt by association. Discovery, review, deletion and audit must remain separate so that graph edges are not treated as facts. Steps: 1) define nodes, edges and a time window; 2) expand 1..k hops from the seed; 3) compute common neighbors, Jaccard and Adamic-Adar; 4) rank candidates by τ; 5) review shared numbers, NAT, support lines, switchboards and two-factor numbers; 6) record precision/recall and a deletion policy. In adversarial settings, limit query scope, retention and use of results. Treat high-degree hubs such as support lines, VoIP gateways and SMS gateways separately; otherwise two hops will connect many unrelated users through a hub. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Failure modes: metadata errors, number reuse, shared phones, NAT/carrier proxies, disposable numbers; encryption hides content, not metadata; k-hop expansion multiplies false positives; missing ground truth makes precision/recall unreliable; legal authorization and retention limits may make results unusable. SIGINT contact chaining matured in the mid-to-late 20th century. After the 2013 Snowden disclosures of the NSA domestic telephone metadata program, three hops versus two hops and five years versus eighteen months became public disputes. A 2015 National Academies report treated contact chaining as one technical option; a 2016 open paper proposed auditable contact-chaining protocols; telephone-metadata research showed that high-degree hubs make “two hops” reach far beyond intuition. - Wikipedia search entry for 接触分析. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%8E%A5%E8%A7%A6%E5%88%86%E6%9E%90 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Contact Analysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Crib Dragging
items.text: Attack : Crib Dragging (拖crib法). The algebraic fact of keystream reuse Let two messages P1 and P2 use the same keystream K: C1 = P1 ⊕ K, C2 = P2 ⊕ K. XOR the two ciphertexts: C1 ⊕ C2 = (P1 ⊕ K) ⊕ (P2 ⊕ K) = P1 ⊕ P2. The keystream K cancels completely, leaving the XOR of the two plaintexts. It is still not plaintext, but it turns “two independently encrypted messages” into one tightly coupled problem. The basic crib-dragging operation If the attacker guesses that P1 contains a known word w of length ℓ at offset i, XOR w with (C1⊕C2)[i…i+ℓ-1] to obtain the candidate fragment of P2 at the corresponding position: P2[i…i+ℓ-1] = (C1⊕C2)[i…i+ℓ-1] ⊕ w. If the candidate is readable, w is likely present in P1 and the corresponding segment of P2 has also been recovered. Slide w across every offset, collect readable candidates, and cross-check them with a language model, a word list and more ciphertexts. From manual guessing to a language model Manual crib dragging depends on the attacker’s guess about the plaintext. An automated method scores candidate text with a language model: for a candidate character sequence it computes Σ log Pr(c_j context), keeps high-scoring paths, and extends them with dynamic programming or beam search. Mason et al. systematised this process and reported high character accuracy on realistic data. The one-time pad relies on the key being used once. Once two messages share K, K is no longer an unknown; it is a common term cancelled by XOR. The attacker does not need to recover K, only to exploit the language structure of the two plaintexts. A greeting, an HTML tag, a protocol header or a fixed field is enough as an anchor. Readability of the candidate turns “is the guess right?” into a testable signal; after anchoring, a language model can extend the plaintext on both sides. Nonce/IV uniqueness is the lifeline of a stream cipher. SIV, GCM nonce management, random-number generation and key rotation must ensure that the same key never uses the same nonce twice; otherwise confidentiality and authenticity can fail together. 1. Confirm that two or more ciphertexts use the same keystream: inspect the nonce, IV, counter or protocol implementation. 2. XOR any two ciphertexts to obtain P1⊕P2. 3. Choose plausible cribs: language words, HTML tags, protocol headers, known file names or fixed error messages. 4. Slide the crib across all offsets, collect readable candidates on the other side, and rank them with a word list, n-grams or a language model. 5. Extend the recovered fragments into adjacent plaintext and cross-check with a third ciphertext; finally re-encrypt to test the hypothesis. 6. The report may state “candidate plaintext under the same-keystream hypothesis”, not “verified original text”. One-time-pad nonce reuse, WEP IV reuse, stream-cipher implementation errors, many-time pads in CTFs, and any protocol that mistakenly uses a fixed value as a counter or randomiser. 1. The keystream is never reused: each message uses an independent random key or a unique nonce, so XOR does not yield P1⊕P2. 2. Authenticated encryption with correct nonce management: tampering is rejected and reuse can be detected by the protocol. 3. The plaintext language is unknown or highly random: no crib anchors, and language-model scoring fails. 4. The messages are too short or the crib is in neither message: the sliding window produces no readable candidate. 5. The plaintext is compressed, encrypted or encoded: candidates do not show natural-language structure. 6. Recovering a fragment is not recovering the full text: more ciphertexts, language models and external constraints are needed. Crib dragging is a known-plaintext or guessed-plaintext attack, not a universal decryptor; it exploits keystream reuse, not an algebraic weakness of the cipher. A report must state the reuse evidence, crib source and candidate verification. The danger of keystream reuse was clear in the theory of the one-time pad: encrypt two messages under one key and XOR cancels the key. Traditional cryptanalysis relied on the analyst guessing common words or protocol fields and sliding them by hand. In 2006 Mason, Watkins, Eisner and Stubblefield published an automated method at CCS: treating the XOR of two ciphertexts as a constraint, they used a statistical language model and dynamic programming to recover the most probable plaintext pair, reporting high accuracy on realistic data. This moved crib dragging from a manual trick to a repeatable language-model attack. WEP IV reuse, stream-cipher nonce mismanagement and many-time pads in CTFs repeatedly show that keystream uniqueness is part of the security definition, not an implementation detail. - Wikipedia search entry for 拖crib法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%8B%96crib%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Crib Dragging: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Depth
items.text: Attack : Depth (深度). Cancelling the keystream Let two messages use the same keystream K: C_i=P_i⊕ K, C_j=P_j⊕ K. XORing the ciphertexts gives C_i⊕ C_j=P_i⊕ P_j: the keystream cancels and only the difference of the plaintexts remains. For a digit-wise mod 10 additive cipher, the same relation is C_i⊖ C_j=(P_i⊖ P_j)mod 10. Alignment and statistics If the messages have different lengths, first find the alignment offset. The Friedman index of coincidence IC=Σ_x f_x(f_x-1)/N(N-1) measures how concentrated the letter distribution is: English is about 0.065, random 26-letter text about 0.038. Two natural-language texts over N aligned positions have an expected NΣ_x p_x^2 equal letters; this peak identifies the offset, after which cribs or a language model recover the plaintext. Depth shows that key reuse is a vulnerability by itself, without a statistical defect in the cipher. It turns the one-time-pad condition—use the key once—into a testable attack model, and explains why the same additive page or keystream creates many message pairs. This is the generic depth mechanism; VENONA and JN-25 are historical cases. Depth is not differential cryptanalysis: differential analysis uses round-function probabilities, while depth uses keystream reuse. Both XOR or subtract, but their objects and assumptions differ. 1. Confirm that several messages use the same keystream or additive page. 2. Find the alignment offset, using a known crib or an IC peak. 3. XOR or subtract two ciphertexts to obtain the plaintext difference. 4. Recover both sides with language statistics, a crib dictionary or segmented candidates. 5. Cross-check with another pair so an accidental match is not reported as plaintext. Do not treat depth as a known key; do not use it against a true one-time key that is never reused; do not ignore misalignment from different pages, encodings or compression. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. One-time use: C_i⊕ C_j is still the product of two independent random streams and leaks no plaintext difference. 2. Different pages or keys: the difference still contains an unknown key difference. 3. Wrong alignment: a one-character offset destroys the statistical peak. 4. Encoding changes: compression, transcoding or padding alter the letter distribution and break IC and cribs. 5. Short messages: too few overlapping positions make the statistic insignificant. Friedman systematised the index of coincidence in 1922 for estimating the key length and language of polyalphabetic text. In World War II, reuse of the same additive page created depth in JN-25 and VENONA: the JN-25 additive book had 300 pages × 100 groups, and VENONA had about 35,000 duplicate-key pages. - Wikipedia search entry for 深度. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%B7%B1%E5%BA%A6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Depth: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Forward–Inverse Meet-in-the-Middle Attack
items.text: Attack : Forward–Inverse Meet-in-the-Middle Attack (正反向中间相遇攻击). Composition and the middle state Let a block cipher E have key space {0,1}^k. Two-key double encryption is C=E_{K2}(E_{K1}(P)). The forward–inverse attack does not enumerate 2^{2k} key pairs: it enumerates 2^k single keys from each side and treats the middle state as the meeting point. Forward table and backward scan Fix one known plaintext–ciphertext pair (P,C). Compute X=E_{K1}(P) forward and store (X,K1) in table T; compute Y=D_{K2}(C) backward and look up Y in T. If X=Y, then (K1,K2) is a candidate pair; a second pair verifies it and filters false alarms. Complexity The table has M=2^k entries, and each side performs about 2^k block operations, so total time is T≈2^{k+1}. For double DES (k=56), this is about 2^57 operations and 2^56 intermediate states. For block size n, false alarms are about 2^{2k−n}; a second pair makes them negligible. Double encryption alone expands the key space from 2^k to 2^{2k}, but meet-in-the-middle splits the search into two 2^k tables. It shows that adding key lengths is not the same as adding security, and it is a key counterexample for multiple encryption, key separation and block-size choices. This is a generic time–memory trade-off, not a break of one block cipher. Unlike differential or linear cryptanalysis, it uses composition structure rather than round-function bias; it therefore applies to any composable cipher, at a high memory cost. 1. Check the conditions: one known plaintext–ciphertext pair; encryption decomposes into two independent-key stages; the middle space is small enough to store. 2. Build the table: enumerate K1 forward and store X with K1. 3. Scan: enumerate K2 backward and look up Y. 4. Filter: verify candidates with a second pair. 5. Report: time 2^{k+1}, memory 2^k, false-alarm rate 2^{2k−n}. Do not quote time 2^{k+1} without the 2^k storage and access cost; do not apply the double-DES result directly to triple DES, AES, or compositions with key binding. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Memory: 2^56 states remain enormous on real equipment; time–memory trade-offs (distinguished points, rainbow tables) change the parameters. 2. False alarms and uniqueness: one pair produces many candidates; a second pair or redundancy filters them. 3. Key independence: if K1 and K2 are derived from one master key or have algebraic relations, complexity can drop further; three independent keys are not directly covered. 4. Block size: the false-alarm rate 2^{2k−n} varies with n, and short blocks are worse. Diffie and Hellman proposed the time–memory trade-off in their 1977 assessment of DES key search. Merkle and Hellman made the meet-in-the-middle attack explicit for double encryption in 1981, showing that a 112-bit two-key double encryption can be broken with about 2^56 operations and 2^56 words. This result drove the deployment of triple DES and the later migration to AES. This entry covers the classic two-key meet-in-the-middle only; multidimensional meet-in-the-middle, partial matching and quantum search have different costs and must not be conflated. - Wikipedia search entry for 正反向中间相遇攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%AD%A3%E5%8F%8D%E5%90%91%E4%B8%AD%E9%97%B4%E7%9B%B8%E9%81%87%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Forward–Inverse Meet-in-the-Middle Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Invariant Subspace Attack
items.text: Attack : Invariant Subspace Attack (不变量子空间攻击). Affine subspaces and the round function Let the block size be n and the round function be F_K(x)=F(x⊕K). Take an affine subspace u⊕A, where A is a linear subspace. If F maps u⊕A as a whole to v⊕A: When the round key K lies in u⊕v⊕A, F_K(v⊕A)=F((v⊕A)⊕K)=F(u⊕A)=v⊕A, so the subspace is preserved in that round. Multi-round preservation and weak keys If every round key lies in the corresponding coset, the full encryption satisfies E_K(v⊕A)=v⊕A. The number of weak keys is A . PRINTcipher-48 has 2^52 weak keys out of 2^80, and PRINTcipher-96 has 2^102 out of 2^160; for those keys, very few chosen plaintexts distinguish E_K from a random permutation. An invariant-subspace attack uses a structural invariant, not a probabilistic approximation, and does not require recovering each round key. It shows that block-cipher security depends not only on S-box nonlinearity but also on whether round constants, key schedule and linear layer leave a subspace closed for weak keys. The old catalog translation “invariant subtract” refers to this line of work; the standard name is invariant subspace attack. This entry does not treat a nonexistent “invariant subtract” paper as a source. Differential and linear attacks track probabilistic bias; invariant subspaces track probability-one orbits. 1. Choose a candidate affine subspace u⊕A and check that the linear layer preserves A. 2. Compute the image of u⊕A under one round F; obtain v⊕A. 3. Solve the weak-key coset u⊕v⊕A. 4. Check whether the key schedule places every round key in the required coset. 5. Verify E_K(v⊕A)=v⊕A with chosen plaintexts and estimate the weak-key fraction. Do not call a weak-key distinguisher a break of all keys; do not ignore round constants and key schedule; do not transplant the PRINTcipher parameters to other lightweight ciphers. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Weak-key restriction: the property holds only for keys in the coset, and the fraction A /2^k may be tiny. 2. Round constants and key schedule: one constant or round key outside the subspace breaks the multi-round invariant. 3. A distinguisher is not key recovery: it proves that weak keys exist but does not automatically yield the master key. 4. Design fixes: add nonlinear round constants, move round keys across cosets, or add diffusion in the linear layer; after a fix, the invariant search must be rerun. In 2011 Leander, Abdelraheem, AlKhzaimi and Zenner analyzed PRINTcipher with the invariant-subspace attack at CRYPTO 2011, giving weak-key sets of 2^52/2^80 and 2^102/2^160. In 2015 Leander, Minaud and Rønjom turned invariant-subspace detection into a generic algorithm and applied it to Robin, iSCREAM and Zorro, with weak-key density up to 2^-32. This entry follows the 2011 PRINTcipher paper; the 2015 paper is used only for the generalization. - Wikipedia search entry for 不变量子空间攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E4%B8%8D%E5%8F%98%E9%87%8F%E5%AD%90%E7%A9%BA%E9%97%B4%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Invariant Subspace Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Universally Composable Security (UC)
items.text: Theorem : Universally Composable Security (UC) (可组合安全框架（UC）). Real and ideal executions Let EXEC_{π,A,Z}(k,a) be the execution of protocol π with environment Z and adversary A, and EXEC_{F,S,Z}(k,a) the execution of ideal functionality F with simulator S. UC security (UC-emulation) requires: ∀A ∃S ∀Z: EXEC_{π,A,Z}(k,a)≈EXEC_{F,S,Z}(k,a), equivalently, the environment's distinguishing advantage satisfies Pr[Z=1 real]−Pr[Z=1 ideal] ≤negl(k). Composition theorem If π UC-realizes F, then for every protocol context ρ, ρ^π UC-realizes ρ^F. A proved component can be replaced inside any system while preserving the ideal specification; composition allows concurrent, nested and arbitrary protocol instances. Non-black-box boundary Barak 2001 gives the adversary's code to the simulator as auxiliary input and constructs a non-black-box simulator; under collision-resistant hashing this yields a constant-round NP argument that remains zero-knowledge under n concurrent sessions. This shows that simulation need not treat A as a black box, but the technique is not automatically an efficient construction for every UC task. UC writes security as indistinguishability from an ideal functionality in every environment. This is stronger than “no adversary wins a particular game”: the protocol must not leak extra information when called concurrently, nested, or composed with other protocols. The ideal functionality F is the specification, and simulator S accounts for everything the real protocol may leak. This is a framework and composition theorem, not a concrete cipher. It unifies MPC, key exchange and commitments under the real/ideal paradigm; Barak's non-black-box simulation is one boundary of simulator technique, not the UC definition itself. 1. Write the specification: define F's inputs, outputs, leakage and error behaviour before discussing a protocol. 2. Prove simulation: for every A construct S so that no Z distinguishes real from ideal; do not prove only an isolated game. 3. Use composition: prove π realizes F, then replace it inside context ρ; check setup, joint state and concurrency assumptions. 4. State boundaries: identify the corruption model, whether the environment is non-uniform, and whether CRS/PKI/trusted parties are required. Do not treat the UC label as an unconditional security proof; do not claim every task is realizable in plain UC without setup; do not present Barak's non-black-box simulation as a general efficiency recipe; do not ignore implementation side channels. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Setup assumptions: many tasks need a CRS, PKI, trusted party or global setup in plain UC; omitting setup invalidates the composition theorem's premises. 2. Simulator limits: black-box simulation is not universal; Barak's non-black-box simulation depends on the adversary's code and CRH, and may be inefficient or hard to audit. 3. Corruption and environment: adaptive corruption, environment auxiliary input, non-uniform adversaries, joint state and global subroutines all change the definition and proof. 4. Implementation: a UC proof does not cover side channels, fault injection, code bugs or deployment configuration; this entry is not implementation certification. Canetti introduced the UC framework and universal composition in ePrint 2000/067 (FOCS 2001), writing protocol security as real/ideal indistinguishability in every environment and proving a composition theorem. Barak 2001 at FOCS introduced non-black-box simulation, breaking the black-box simulation barrier and constructing a constant-round concurrent zero-knowledge argument. The 2020 revision of ePrint 2000/067 explicitly states that definitional and result details changed from earlier versions; this entry follows that revision's framework and does not treat early-version lemmas as the current definition. - Wikipedia search entry for 可组合安全框架（UC）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%8F%AF%E7%BB%84%E5%90%88%E5%AE%89%E5%85%A8%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6%EF%BC%88UC%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Universally Composable Security (UC): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Bellare–Rogaway Authenticated Key Exchange
items.text: Theorem : Bellare–Rogaway Authenticated Key Exchange (Bellare–Rogaway 认证密钥交换). Parties, oracles and sessions The model writes the s-th session of party i with peer j as oracle Π^s_{i,j}. Adversary E may issue send, reveal and test queries. A conversation is a time-ordered message sequence; two oracles have a matching conversation when their message prefixes correspond one-for-one in time order. Authentication and key indistinguishability Protocol Π is a secure AKE when both conditions hold: under a benign adversary, matching oracles both accept and α^s_{i,j}=α^t_{j,i} is sampled from S_k; and for every PPT adversary E the advantage Adv^E(k)=max{0, Pr[GoodGuess^E(k)]−1/2} The adversary selects a fresh oracle: accepted, not revealed, and with no revealed matching partner. The challenger flips b: b=0 returns the real α and b=1 a random sample from S_k; E outputs Guess. GoodGuess is the event Guess=b. The AKEP1 construction A shared 2k-bit long-term key is split into a1 and a2; a1 drives PRF f for message authentication and a2 drives f′ to encrypt the session key: {α}_{a2}=(r, f′_{a2}(r)⊕α). B samples α from S_k and places this ciphertext in Text2; the MAP2 flow authenticates with f_{a1}. Theorem 5.2 states that AKEP1 is a secure AKE when f and f′ are PRFs; in the random MAP1 experiment, acceptance without matching is at most T_E(k)^2·2^−k. Bellare–Rogaway separate “both parties accept” from “the adversary cannot distinguish the session key”. Message authentication alone is insufficient because both parties may accept while the adversary still distinguishes the key; key indistinguishability alone is insufficient because without a matching conversation the key cannot be attributed to the right peer. 1. Define sessions: give every party, peer and session a unique oracle so sessions cannot be confused. 2. Prove authentication: first prove correctness under a benign adversary, then bound acceptance without a matching conversation. 3. Prove key security: reduce the test query to a PRF or ideal-cipher assumption and state freshness precisely. 4. Separate keys: use distinct PRF domains for authentication and encryption, such as a1 and a2. Do not treat “both parties accept” as AKE security; do not reveal the target session after the test query; do not present this model as a proof of forward secrecy or UC security. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Model boundary: long-term key compromise, temporary-key compromise, forward secrecy and key escrow are outside this definition; a stronger model is needed. 2. Session binding: matching depends on unique session identifiers and message order; if a protocol permits reordering, reflection or session confusion, the definition cannot add identity binding by itself. 3. Implementation: replacing the PRF with a hash lacking domain separation, reusing randomness or mismanaging state bypasses the reduction assumptions. 4. Overclaiming: the two-party AKEP1 of this paper is not every AKE protocol; this entry is not implementation certification and does not claim to cover every unknown-key-share variant. The paper appeared at CRYPTO '93, proceedings pages 232–249. It placed entity authentication and session-key distribution in one security game, defined matching conversations, freshness and test advantage, and constructed AKEP1 from PRFs. - Wikipedia search entry for Bellare–Rogaway 认证密钥交换. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Bellare%E2%80%93Rogaway%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E4%BA%A4%E6%8D%A2 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Bellare–Rogaway Authenticated Key Exchange: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: BIKE Code-Based KEM
items.text: Algorithm : BIKE (BIKE 备选 KEM). Key, encapsulation and decapsulation BIKE works in the polynomial ring modulo x^r−1 with h=h1·h0^{-1}, and encapsulation forms c=(e0+e1h,m⊕L(e0,e1)). QC-MDPC structure The private key is a pair of sparse polynomials (h0,h1), each of weight w/2; the code length is n=2r, the error vector (e0,e1) has total weight t, and decapsulation uses decoder(c0h0,h0,h1) to recover e′ and check e′=H(m′). Parameters and sizes NIST Round-4 parameters: Level 1 r=12323, w=142, t=134; Level 3 r=24659, w=206, t=199; Level 5 r=40973, w=274, t=264. LibOQS 5.1 reports BIKE-L1 public key 1541 B, secret key 5223 B, ciphertext 1573 B and shared secret 32 B. BIKE is a code-based KEM whose security rests on quasi-cyclic syndrome decoding and code distinguishing; its public key is far smaller than McEliece, and encapsulation/decapsulation are fast, suiting ephemeral TLS keys. It needs one symmetric primitive (Keccak/SHAKE) and polynomial arithmetic, giving a small hardware footprint. As a NIST alternate it offers assumption diversity from lattice cryptography. BIKE entered NIST PQC Round 4 as an alternate candidate, and liboqs provides a C implementation; typical uses are ephemeral TLS/QUIC KEMs, hybrid key exchange and research comparison. Because NIST did not standardize it, production should use a hybrid KEM and wait for standards and side-channel audits; it is not an approved algorithm. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The decoding failure rate must be provably low (targets 2^-128/192/256); otherwise reaction attacks can recover the private key. The decoder must be constant-time against timing and faults. Key reuse, multi-target attacks, weak private polynomials and a wrong FO transform break IND-CCA. BIKE’s proof relies on an ideal decoder and random-oracle assumptions, not unconditional security. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Symbols are catalogue-level variables, not standard constants; parameters, test vectors and clauses remain with the registered source. The model states structural relations, not an implementation audit. BIKE grew from QC-MDPC codes and the Niederreiter framework and was submitted to NIST PQC in 2017; after Rounds 2/3/4 and several parameter and decoder revisions, the 2022/2023 v5.x specification fixed a single variant and the BGF decoder.
