items.title: Bit-Plane Analysis
items.text: Attack : Bit-Plane Analysis (位平面分析). Bit-plane decomposition Write an 8-bit grey image as a pixel matrix I(x,y). The k-th bit plane is b_k(x,y) = ⌊I(x,y) / 2^k⌋ mod 2. k=0 is the least significant bit plane (LSB); k=7 is the most significant. High planes retain contours while low planes look closer to noise. LSB replacement changes only k=0, so it leaves large-scale brightness almost intact but alters the local correlation of the LSB plane. The LSB flipping function For a pixel value x, let F(x) flip the least significant bit: even x becomes x+1 and odd x becomes x-1; F₋₁ maps even x to x-1 and odd x to x+1. RS analysis partitions pixels into groups G under a mask M and evaluates a discrimination function f on F(G) and G. A group is regular (R) if f(F(G)) f(G) and singular (S) if it is smaller. Natural images have a stable bias between R and S counts. Reading the embedding rate LSB replacement pushes the group LSBs toward independent random bits, so R and S counts converge. Counting R_M, S_M, R_{-M} and S_{-M} for masks M and -M gives four curves from which an embedding rate p can be estimated; p near 0 means little replacement and p near 1 means the LSB plane has been heavily overwritten. The exact estimator depends on group size, discrimination function and image content, so one threshold is not a universal answer. LSB bits in natural images are not perfectly random: sensor noise, quantisation, demosaicing and compression leave correlations among neighbouring low bits. LSB replacement overwrites this layer with message bits, replacing local structure with nearly independent bits; both the bit-plane texture and the RS counts change. Chi-square analysis looks at histograms of adjacent value bins; bit-plane and RS analysis look at spatial groups and a discrimination function after flipping. The former is sensitive to the global histogram, the latter to local texture and group structure. They complement each other but both mainly target naive LSB replacement. To resist bit-plane and RS detection, an embedder should not simply replace bits one by one. It should use matrix embedding, wet-paper coding, F5, adaptive embedding or spread spectrum so that the locations and directions of changes resemble the cover distribution. Encrypting the message before writing it into the LSB is not the same as making it undetectable. 1. Record the image format, bit depth, colour space, compression history and possible resampling. 2. Extract bit planes k=0…7 and inspect them visually; an unnatural uniform noise or block structure in the LSB plane makes the image a candidate. 3. Choose a group size and mask M, then compute R_M, S_M, R_{-M} and S_{-M}. 4. Calibrate against known covers and known embedding rates to estimate an interval for p; do not decide from one threshold on one image. 5. Report “a statistical trace of LSB replacement with an estimated embedding rate”, not “the message was extracted”. 1. Not LSB replacement: LSB matching, matrix embedding, F5 and wet-paper coding do not guarantee the same RS-count behaviour. 2. Low embedding rate: a few changes drown in cover noise and compression traces. 3. Strong compression, cropping, scaling, filtering or resampling destroys the bit-plane correlation and the calibration. 4. Covers with uniform texture or synthetic images shift the R/S baseline and produce false positives. 5. Adaptive embedding concentrates changes in textured regions and dilutes the global RS statistic. 6. Palette or indexed images: changing an LSB can map to a very different colour, altering both the visual and statistical assumptions. Bit-plane texture is a visual clue and RS is a statistical test; neither proves the message content or proves its absence. They report the strength of “this looks like LSB replacement”, and must be read together with the carrier type, embedder and calibration samples. In 2001 Fridrich, Goljan and Du moved LSB detection from visual observation to a repeatable regular/singular group statistic, reporting detection of messages as short as about 0.03 bpp under randomly scattered embedding. The paper stressed that the target is a statistical trace of LSB replacement, not message semantics. Dumitrescu, Wu and Wang proposed sample-pair analysis in 2003, using relations between adjacent samples as the statistical object. Later calibration, feature fusion and machine-learning methods addressed low rates, adaptive embedding and compressed images, but “bit planes plus group statistics” remains a core forensic reading. - Wikipedia search entry for 位平面分析. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E4%BD%8D%E5%B9%B3%E9%9D%A2%E5%88%86%E6%9E%90 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Bit-Plane Analysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: BLS Pairing-Based Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Boneh-Lynn-Shacham Short Signatures (BLS 短签名). Pairing and short signatures BLS works on a pairing-friendly curve: private key sk, public key PK=sk·P2, signature σ=sk·H(m), where H hashes the message to G1. Verification checks e(σ,P2)=e(H(m),PK). On BLS12-381, a signature is 48 bytes and a public key is 96 bytes. Aggregation n signatures add pointwise into one 48-byte aggregate signature; verification uses the multi-pairing e(σ,P2)=∏e(H(m_i),PK_i). Public keys can also be aggregated. Three rogue-key defenses Basic requires all aggregated messages to be distinct; message augmentation prepends PK to the message; proof of possession requires a PoP with each public key. A protocol must choose one and not mix them. BLS’s value is signature aggregation: n validators, transactions or votes occupy one signature, so bandwidth and storage grow sublinearly in n. It is deterministic, non-malleable and batch-verifiable with multi-pairings, fitting consensus votes, certificate transparency and light clients. In Ethereum consensus, hundreds or thousands of attestations aggregate into one BLS signature, a key enabler of Ethereum scalability. It is used for Ethereum consensus attestation aggregation, Dfinity threshold signatures, Cloudflare certificate transparency and some bridges; the standards text is the CFRG BLS draft (07). Requirements: BLS12-381 and hash-to-curve; aggregate verification must reject the identity public key and check signatures lie in the correct subgroup; choose distinct messages, augmentation or PoP per scheme; do not invent domain separation. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. BLS aggregation is “signatures add”, but protocol mistakes dominate: a rogue-key attack can cancel honest signatures with a crafted public key; checking only the aggregate equation without the message set can accept forgeries. Boundaries: BLS is not post-quantum; pairing parameters and subgroup checks must be correct; identity/zero-signature attacks require rejecting identity PK and σ; aggregate security depends on the scheme, and Basic is safe only with distinct messages. BLS was introduced by Boneh, Lynn and Shacham in the 2001 ASIACRYPT paper “Short Signatures from the Weil Pairing”; pairings compress a signature to one group element. IETF CFRG has standardized BLS since 2018; the current draft defines Basic, message augmentation, PoP and the BLS12-381 suite. BLS saw large-scale deployment after 2020 through Ethereum 2.0 consensus. - Wikipedia search entry for BLS 短签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=BLS%20%E7%9F%AD%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Boneh-Lynn-Shacham Short Signatures: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: NP-Completeness of PARTITION
items.text: Theorem : NP-Completeness of PARTITION (平分问题（PARTITION）NP 完全性). Decision problem Input a multiset S={a_1,…,a_r} with total ΣS=2B; decide whether a subset T⊆S has ΣT=B. The certificate is T: add its elements and compare with B in O(r) time, so PARTITION ∈ NP. Karp reduction Karp 1972 reduces from KNAPSACK. Given (a_1,…,a_r,b), construct c_i=a_i (i=1,…,r), c_{r+1}=b+1, c_{r+2}=Σa_i+1−b. The new total is Σc=2(Σa_i+1), so set B′=Σa_i+1. If the original KNAPSACK has a subset summing to b, take the corresponding elements plus c_{r+1} to reach B′; conversely, any subset summing to B′ either contains c_{r+1} and leaves b, or contains c_{r+2} and leaves b. Conclusion Thus KNAPSACK ≤_p PARTITION. Karp's Main Theorem lists PARTITION among the NP-complete problems, so PARTITION is NP-complete. PARTITION is the shortest decision form of “split numbers into two equal-sum groups”. It places NP-completeness, certificate verification, reduction direction and pseudo-polynomial DP on one chain, showing that “the problem is hard” is not “every instance is hard”. It is a combinatorial decision problem, not a cryptographic algorithm; it is adjacent to subset sum, knapsack and exact cover, but the objective and reduction chain differ. Cryptographic hardness also needs average-case distributions and a concrete reduction, which NP-completeness alone does not supply. 1. Establish difficulty: reduce a new problem to PARTITION, or PARTITION to the new problem; never reverse the direction. 2. Verify a certificate: a subset T summing to B is a polynomial-time NP certificate. 3. Exact small cases: use O(rB) dynamic programming when B is small; for large B use branch-and-bound or heuristics and state the lack of a worst-case bound. 4. State the encoding: numbers are binary encoded; the pseudo-polynomial bound is in the numeric value B, not its bit length. Do not claim every instance is hard because PARTITION is NP-complete; do not present the pseudo-polynomial DP as polynomial; do not turn worst-case NP-completeness into a cryptographic assumption. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Special cases: equal numbers, small B or many duplicates are easy; NP-completeness only asserts the existence of hard instance families. 2. Pseudo-polynomial: the O(rB) DP can be 2^n in the binary length n of B; it is not polynomial time. 3. Reduction direction: reducing PARTITION to KNAPSACK only places PARTITION within KNAPSACK's difficulty; it does not prove KNAPSACK hard. 4. Cryptographic boundary: NP-completeness gives no average-case hardness, random self-reduction or concrete security parameter; this entry is not a cryptographic protocol proof. items.title: Bulletproofs
items.text: Algorithm : Bulletproofs (Bulletproofs 简洁证明系统). Inner-product argument and range proofs At the core of Bulletproofs is a logarithmic-size inner-product argument: the prover shows that two Pedersen commitment vectors a, b satisfy c=⟨a,b⟩ with 2log₂(n) group elements of communication. A range proof encodes “the committed value lies in an interval” as an inner-product relation and feeds it to this argument. A range proof uses 2log₂(n)+9 group/field elements; proving and verification are linear in n . It needs no trusted setup, relies only on the discrete-logarithm assumption, and becomes non-interactive via Fiat–Shamir. Bulletproofs occupy the middle ground between “no trusted setup” and “short proof”. Groth16 proofs are shorter but need a ceremony; Bulletproofs need no toxic waste and grow logarithmically with the witness, making them suitable for on-chain range proofs. They reduced confidential-transaction proofs from over 10KB to under 1KB and support aggregating many range proofs into one. Bulletproofs are used for Monero’s RingCT range proofs, Mimblewimble/Grin confidential transactions, and proposed Bitcoin confidential transactions. They also serve verifiable shuffles, proofs of solvency and general arithmetic circuits. They are not a drop-in replacement for general SNARKs: verification is linear, so they suit small-to-medium statements rather than huge circuits with constant-time verification. Bulletproof verification is linear in witness size, not fully succinct; for million-gate circuits verification remains expensive. Security relies on discrete logarithms and is not post-quantum. A range proof establishes only an interval, not arbitrary business constraints. Upper-layer protocols must still handle commitment binding, blinding factors, aggregation MPC and Fiat–Shamir domain separation. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. items.title: CA/Browser Forum TLS Baseline Requirements
items.text: Standard : CA/Browser Forum TLS Baseline Requirements (CA/Browser Forum TLS 基线要求). A baseline CP, not browser code The CA/Browser Forum is a voluntary organization of CAs and browser/software suppliers. The TLS Baseline Requirements use the RFC 3647 framework to state minimum requirements for publicly trusted TLS server certificates: identity proofing, domain/IP control validation, certificate profiles, validity, audits, revocation and incident response. They are not automatically mandatory; they bind only after a root program adopts and enforces them. Hard constraints in the certificate profile BR Section 7 defines certificate content: serial numbers must be greater than zero and contain at least 64 bits of CSPRNG output; RSA keys must be at least 2048 bits, or use P-256/P-384/P-521; SHA-1 is prohibited; end-entity certificates must carry a CA/B reserved policy OID (DV 2.23.140.1.2.1, OV 2.23.140.1.2.2, IV 2.23.140.1.2.3). These fields let relying parties identify the certificate type and policy. Before 2011, CAs differed in validation, validity, fields and audit scope, producing misissuance and inconsistent browser trust. A common baseline lets root programs evaluate every CA against the same audit evidence and gives relying parties a predictable minimum security line. A baseline is a minimum, not a complete security proof; CA compromise, validation bugs and domain hijacking still happen. Root programs add their own requirements such as CT, CAA, multi-perspective validation and revocation SLAs. v1.0 was adopted on 2011-11-22 and became effective on 2012-07-01; v2.0.0 (the SC62 certificate-profile rewrite) was adopted on 2023-04-22 and effective on 2023-09-15. The current 2.3.1 (2026-10-04) schedules compliance dates through 2029: from 2026-03-15 subscriber certificates may live at most 200 days, from 2027-03-15 at most 100 days, and from 2029-03-15 at most 47 days; domain/IP validation data reuse shrinks from 200 days to 100 and then 10 days. Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs require CAs to meet the TLS BR and pass WebTrust/ETSI audits; serious violations can lead to distrust or removal. Microsoft's root program also requires DV/OV/EV/IV policy OIDs, annual audits and CCADB disclosure. The BR governs certificate issuance and profiles, not a CA's internal network, HSMs and staff; those are covered by the Network and Certificate System Security Requirements and root-program rules. A leaked CA private key or misissuance can still enable interception. Domain control validation proves control at application time, not against later hijacking; reuse periods and CAA reduce but do not eliminate the risk. Revocation depends on relying parties checking OCSP/CRL, and soft-fail and delay remain practical problems. Shorter validity, key scopes and CT mandates raise operational cost for CAs and customers; small CAs or private PKIs can be marginalized. The BR is a multi-party voted product, not a cryptographically optimal design. The CA/Browser Forum formed in the mid-2000s from CAs and browser vendors. v1.0 was adopted on 2011-11-22 and took effect on 2012-07-01; SC62 rewrote the certificate profiles as v2.0.0 in 2023, effective 2023-09-15. The 2026 version 2.3.1 continues to shorten validity and validation reuse. “Baseline” does not mean “low standard”; it is the floor every publicly trusted TLS certificate must meet. The EV Guidelines add a higher identity-proofing layer on top. - Wikipedia search entry for CA/Browser Forum TLS 基线要求. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CA%2FBrowser%20Forum%20TLS%20%E5%9F%BA%E7%BA%BF%E8%A6%81%E6%B1%82 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] CA/Browser Forum TLS Baseline Requirements: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Cache timing attack
items.text: Attack : Cache Timing Attack (缓存计时攻击). Table lookups carry the key into the cache AES software often uses four T-tables, each 256 entries of 4 bytes, about 1 KB total. The CPU fetches a 64-byte cache line; a hit or miss changes the encryption time by hundreds of cycles. In the first round the lookup index is p_i ⊕ k_i, so changing plaintext p lets the attacker observe which index is cached. From time to key The attacker first profiles “plaintext byte versus time” on a similar machine with a known key, then samples the unknown key and correlates the two profiles under each key hypothesis. The correct hypothesis aligns the cache patterns; wrong ones do not. After filtering byte candidates, a known plaintext-ciphertext pair brute-forces the remaining bits. Fast AES software depends on S-box/T-table lookups, and the lookup address is determined by key and plaintext. To be both fast and safe, memory access time must be independent of the address; on a general-purpose CPU that is difficult, and constant-time code is often much slower. Leakage exists whenever the target shares a cache with the attacker or the attacker can time encryption precisely. Bernstein's 2005 experiment sent requests over a network to an OpenSSL server from another machine and recovered the full AES key from response time alone. Network jitter dilutes the signal, but enough samples still expose the statistical difference; this is the origin of the term “remote timing attack”. Cache attacks apply across processes, virtual machines, cloud co-tenancy, browser timing and embedded devices. They do not require reading the victim's memory, only a shared cache level and a fine-grained timing source; variants such as Flush+Reload reduce noise further. Prefer constant-time hardware instructions such as AES-NI; software can use bitslicing, Boolean S-boxes or implementations that avoid secret indices. Systems can add cache colouring, core isolation, timing-source randomisation and noise. Defenders must consider performance, not merely replace table lookups with slow bit-by-bit operations. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Bernstein's original attack needed about 2^27.5 plaintext/timing samples and required the reference and target machines to match closely in software, CPU and background load. Bonneau–Mironov moved the attack to the final round and recovered the full key with about 2^15 samples, or about 2^13 for the expanded final round; fewer samples, but still precise timing and a matched environment. AES-NI, constant-time bitsliced implementations and hardware coprocessors with no secret-indexed tables do not emit this cache signal. The attack mainly hits fast T-table software AES, especially old OpenSSL, cross-process shared caches and multi-tenant cloud hosts. Daniel J. Bernstein published “Cache-timing attacks on AES” in 2005, recovering a full 128-bit AES key from a network server running OpenSSL 0.9.7a on a Pentium III, with reproducible code. This is the landmark cache-timing attack. Osvik–Shamir–Tromer introduced Prime+Probe and cache collisions in 2006; Bonneau–Mironov used final-round collisions to cut samples to 2^15/2^13; Yarom–Falkner's 2014 Flush+Reload pushed resolution to the cache-line level. Meltdown/Spectre later made cache side channels a central general-purpose CPU security issue. - Wikipedia search entry for 缓存计时攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%BC%93%E5%AD%98%E8%AE%A1%E6%97%B6%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Cache Timing Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Canetti–Halevi–Katz (CHK) Transform
items.text: Theorem : Canetti–Halevi–Katz (CHK) Transform (Canetti–Halevi–Katz（CHK）变换). Building blocks Take an IBE Π′=(Setup,Der,E′,D′) that is only selective-identity CPA secure, and a strongly unforgeable one-time signature Sig=(G,Sign,Vrfy). Construct PKE Π=(Gen,E,D): Gen(1^k) runs Setup(1^k,ℓ_s(k)) to obtain (PK,msk), with public key PK and secret key msk. Encrypt m: run G(1^k)→(vk,sk), then C←E′_PK(vk,m), σ←Sign_sk(C), and output (vk,C,σ). Decrypt: check Vrfy_vk(C,σ)=1 first, otherwise reject; then SK_vk←Der_msk(vk) and m←D′_{SK_vk}(vk,C). Theorem If Π′ is selective-identity CPA secure and Sig is strongly one-time unforgeable, then Π is a CCA-secure PKE. In the reduction, let Forge be the event that the adversary submits a new (C,σ) for vk that verifies; then Pr_{A′,Π′}[Succ]≥Pr_{A,Π}[Succ]−½Pr_A[Forge]. Since Forge is negligible, A's CCA advantage is also negligibly close to 1/2. The CHK transform replaces the identity by a one-time verification key vk. The challenge ciphertext is bound to vk ; a decryption query with vk≠vk lands at a different identity and can be answered under IBE CPA security; if vk=vk , any new valid (C,σ) directly yields a forgery against the strong one-time signature. This is a reduction/construction, not an IBE algorithm. It shows that CCA security can come from IBE plus a one-time signature without attaching a non-interactive zero-knowledge proof to every ciphertext; it is not the same layer as a concrete scheme such as RSA-OAEP. 1. Choose IBE: confirm selective-identity CPA security and that the identity space accommodates a ℓ_s(k)-bit vk. 2. Choose signature: use a strong one-time signature and sign exactly one C; never reuse vk/sk. 3. Encrypt: encrypt then sign, with the signature covering the full C; do not put σ inside the IBE plaintext. 4. Decrypt: verify fully before deriving the identity key and decrypting; a failed verification must not leak decryption information. Do not treat a weak one-time signature as strong; do not reuse one vk across two ciphertexts; do not call IBE decryption before verification; do not present selective-identity security as adaptive-identity security. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Security model: the underlying IBE is only selective-identity CPA secure; adaptive identity needs a stronger IBE or additional techniques. 2. Signature strength: if the signature is only weakly one-time unforgeable, an adversary can change σ on the same C and the Forge event is no longer excluded. 3. Identity space: a short ℓ_s(k), non-unique vk encoding or replaceable verification key breaks the vk-to-identity binding. 4. Reduction boundary: the proof gives an existence construction; it does not guarantee concrete IBE efficiency, key escrow, side-channel or implementation security, and does not claim a black-box CCA construction from any CPA PKE. The paper was published as ePrint 2003/182 by Ran Canetti, Shai Halevi and Jonathan Katz; this catalogue keeps the Canetti–Halevi shorthand while the entry follows the three-author CHK transform. items.title: Chi-Square Steganalysis
items.text: Attack : Chi-Square Steganalysis (卡方隐写分析). The paired-value histogram LSB replacement overwrites the least significant bit of each sample with a message bit. If the message bits are close to random, samples originally in the adjacent values 2i and 2i+1 are mixed; the higher the embedding rate, the closer the two bins become. Write the observed counts of pair i as h_{2i} and h_{2i+1}. Under the null hypothesis the expected count is y_i^ = (h_{2i} + h_{2i+1}) / 2. The chi-square statistic Using y_i = h_{2i} as the observation, compute χ² = Σ_i (y_i - y_i^ )^2 / y_i^ . Keep only pairs with y_i^ 4. If a pair has too few counts, pool adjacent categories first and reduce the degrees of freedom accordingly. The degrees of freedom ν equal the number of pooled pairs minus one. The statistic measures the deviation between the observed even-bin counts and the paired-average expectation. Reading the embedding probability In the original test, p = 1 - F_{χ²,ν}(χ²), where F is the chi-square cumulative distribution. Smaller χ² and p closer to 1 support the explanation that the paired values have been flattened; a large χ² gives p near 0. This p is not the probability that a secret message exists; it is a goodness-of-fit reading under the LSB-replacement hypothesis. A sliding-window scan can estimate where a sequential embedding ends. Natural images do not have independent least significant bits; adjacent grey levels or DCT coefficient pairs are usually unequal. LSB replacement turns a pair into interchangeable bins, so “paired equality” becomes a detectable trace. It requires no key and no message content, only a histogram. A bit-plane visual attack relies on a human looking at the structure of the LSB plane; the chi-square attack turns the same phenomenon into a repeatable statistic. Both target simple LSB replacement and neither is valid for every steganographic scheme. Matrix embedding, F5, wet-paper coding, spread spectrum and adaptive embedding disturb the paired-value relation; randomly scattered embedding dilutes the statistic in a fixed window. A designer must make the statistical distribution of modifications resemble the cover, not merely write message bits into the LSB. 1. Obtain the suspect carrier and record its format, quantisation tables, colour space and resampling history. 2. Build histograms by value pairs; for DCT coefficients pair adjacent quantised values, and for indexed images follow the palette order. 3. Pool bins whose expected counts are too small, then compute χ² and ν. 4. Read p = 1 - F(χ²,ν) as the strength of the “pairs flattened” explanation, and scan with a sliding window to locate a possible embedding interval. 5. Calibrate against known covers, known embedders and several embedding rates. The report may say “a statistical trace of LSB replacement”, not “the message was extracted”. Stegdetect combines chi-square, RS analysis and other tests into a candidate filter. Chi-square provides a fast screen for paired-value anomalies; a human or a specialised extractor must still verify the result. 1. Not LSB replacement: LSB matching, matrix embedding, F5 and wet-paper coding do not guarantee equal paired bins. 2. Randomly scattered embedding dilutes a fixed-window statistic, so the original sequential scan may find no clear interval. 3. A low embedding rate is buried in the cover’s natural noise. 4. Covers whose paired bins are already nearly equal (synthetic images, palette images, strongly quantised images) can produce false positives with high p. 5. Message bits are not random, or the embedder applies statistical compensation. 6. Lossy recompression, cropping, scaling or filtering destroys the trace. The chi-square test examines a histogram fit, not a cipher. A high p does not prove a secret message, and a low p does not prove its absence. Conclusions depend on the cover, embedder and window parameters, and must be reported with calibration samples. In 1999 Westfeld and Pfitzmann systematised attacks on EzStego, Jsteg, Steganos and S-Tools, combining visual anomalies in the LSB plane with a paired-value chi-square test. They stressed that LSBs are not naturally random and that naive replacement leaves a statistical structure. In 2002 Provos and Honeyman put chi-square and other detectors into an Internet-scale image scanning framework, and noted that statistical detection only yields candidates; it does not replace key recovery or message extraction. Extended chi-square tests, RS analysis, calibration and machine-learning methods later addressed scattered embedding and low embedding rates. - Wikipedia search entry for 卡方隐写分析. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%8D%A1%E6%96%B9%E9%9A%90%E5%86%99%E5%88%86%E6%9E%90 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Chi-Square Steganalysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Chosen-Target Attack
items.text: Attack : Chosen-Target Attack (选择目标攻击). Define “chosen-target attack” precisely In Chaum’s RSA blind signature, the signer’s public key is (N,e) and the private exponent is d. A user wants a signature on a message m without revealing m to the signer: 1. Pick a random blinding factor r and compute m′ = r^e · H(m) mod N. Send m′ to the signer and receive s′ = (m′)^d mod N. Remove the blinding: s = r^{-1} · s′ mod N. s^e = (s′)^e · r^{-e} = m′ · r^{-e} = H(m) mod N. The signer sees only m′ and not m; the user obtains a valid signature on m. The one-more reduction If an adversary can turn q signing queries into q+1 valid message-signature pairs, those pairs can be embedded into the chosen-target inversion game, producing more RSA inversions than the number of oracle queries. Conversely, if chosen-target inversion is hard, Chaum’s scheme has one-more unforgeability in the random-oracle model. The “attack” here is a capability in a reduction, not a directly runnable factoring algorithm. A blind signature has a different privacy goal from an ordinary signature: the signer does not know the message, so it cannot impose message-based access control. If security only required “cannot forge a signature on a new message”, an adversary might obtain several usable signatures from one signing query and break the “withdraw once, spend once” accounting of electronic cash. One-more unforgeability compares the number of queries with the number of valid signatures, which is exactly the excess forgery this setting must exclude. Known-target inversion requires the adversary to invert all given targets; chosen-target lets it choose a subset, as long as the number of inverted targets exceeds the number of queries. One of Bellare et al.’s main results is that the two problems are polynomially equivalent, so proving either hard suffices to support Chaum’s scheme. The equivalence is a reduction result; it does not mean the two games are identical in implementation. Blind signatures also depend on the blinding function, signer state management, randomness quality and double-spend prevention. One-more unforgeability does not solve those engineering problems; it covers only the “number of signatures” dimension. 1. State the model: RSA blind signature, blind Schnorr, blind BLS or an OPRF variant; the hardness assumption differs. 2. Write down the query count: how many valid signatures may be output after q signing queries; q+1 is a failure under one-more unforgeability. 3. Check the blind/unblind algebra: whether m′ and s preserve the relation, and whether the verification equation holds. 4. Check the reduction: is the scheme reduced to chosen-target/known-target inversion, or only to ordinary RSA one-wayness? 5. Check the random-oracle assumption and the hash domain; Chaum’s proof is in the ROM. 6. Check the engineering layer: predictability of blinding factors, signer records of used blinded values, and double-spend prevention. Electronic cash, privacy tokens, anonymous credentials and Privacy Pass-style protocols use blind signatures or OPRFs. Do not treat “blind” as a synonym for “secure”; prove privacy (blindness) and unforgeability (one-more) separately. 1. Not a generic RSA attack. Chosen-target inversion assumes RSA inversion is hard; it does not provide a way to factor N. 2. Not true for every blind signature. Different blind-signature schemes have different blinding relations and hardness problems; Chaum’s reduction cannot be copied directly onto blind Schnorr or blind BLS. 3. Blindness does not imply unforgeability. A scheme can hide the message perfectly and still allow one query to produce several signatures; privacy and unforgeability are independent goals. 4. Random-oracle model. Chaum’s proof is in the ROM; instantiation in the standard model needs additional argument. 5. Signer state and double spending. If the signer does not record used blinded values, or a user can reuse one signature, engineering attacks outside the one-more model remain possible. 6. Blinding-factor quality. Predictable or repeated r links messages, leaks privacy, and may even break the algebraic relation. Chaum introduced blind signatures in his 1983 CRYPTO paper and used them for untraceable electronic payments: a bank signs without seeing the message, and the user can later prove that a payment is valid while the bank cannot link the signature to the user. This is the starting point of blinding as a privacy primitive. Bellare, Namprempre, Pointcheval and Semanko formalised the one-more-RSA-inversion problem in their 2003 Journal of Cryptology paper, defined the chosen-target and known-target variants, proved them polynomially equivalent, and proved the security of Chaum’s blind signature scheme in the random-oracle model. One-more unforgeability then became standard language for blind-signature security. - Wikipedia search entry for 选择目标攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%80%89%E6%8B%A9%E7%9B%AE%E6%A0%87%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Chosen-Target Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: CMC wide-block enciphering mode (CBC–Mask–CBC)
items.text: Algorithm : CMC wide-block enciphering mode (CBC–Mask–CBC) (CMC 宽块加密模式（CBC–Mask–CBC）). CBC–Mask–CBC CMC turns an n-bit block cipher into a tweakable enciphering scheme on mn-bit strings (m≥2). Encryption makes one CBC-encryption pass, derives a mask from the chaining values, XORs the mask into every intermediate block, then makes one CBC-decryption pass. Decryption mirrors it: CBC-encrypt, XOR the same mask, CBC-decrypt. The name is literally CBC–Mask–CBC. Two passes, 2m+1 calls, two keys CMC is a sequential two-pass construction: neither CBC pass is parallel, and an m-block sector costs 2m+1 block-cipher calls. It uses two keys K1 and K2, one per pass; the tweak (usually a sector number) feeds the first-block IV and the mask derivation, so the same plaintext in different sectors yields different ciphertext. Its target is a tweakable strong PRP: under a strong-PRP assumption the ciphertext is indistinguishable and non-malleable. Disks read and write sectors, commonly 512 bytes. With per-block ECB, an attacker can reorder, replace or replay blocks. CMC treats the whole sector as one wide block; any block change diffuses across the sector, and only the same sector number plus the same plaintext reproduces the same ciphertext. It needs no universal hash and adds no extra primitive, which suits in-place encryption. CMC gets diffusion from the CBC chains and a global mask without EME's mixing layer. The price is two sequential passes, so blocks inside a sector cannot be parallelized. It uses two keys, adding key-schedule material compared with single-key modes; in return the proof targets a tweakable strong PRP rather than a weak PRP. CMC was introduced in a 2003 CRYPTO paper. Halevi–Rogaway then built EME, which parallelizes the two passes while keeping 2m+1 block-cipher calls. Disk encryption standardization ultimately chose XTS (IEEE 1619); CMC and EME survive more as design lineage and teaching comparisons. None of them is AEAD. CMC fits storage-encryption prototypes where a whole segment must diffuse together and two-pass latency is acceptable; it does not fit protocols needing random access, parallel throughput or authentication. Before putting it in a real system, verify sector size, tweak uniqueness and key management rather than comparing round counts alone. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. CMC provides confidentiality only; it produces no authentication tag. An attacker who flips a ciphertext block turns the decryption into another seemingly random plaintext, and the receiver cannot tell. The tweak must be unique: encrypting the same plaintext under the same tweak reproduces the same ciphertext and leaks equality. The sequential two-pass structure adds latency, and m=1 is outside the domain. CMC requires m≥2 and cannot encrypt a single block directly. The decryptor must validate the block count, or an incomplete sector enters the wrong path. The tweak is n bits; when the sector number exceeds that range, change the key or the encoding. It resists neither traffic analysis nor access-pattern leakage. Halevi and Rogaway published “A Tweakable Enciphering Mode” at CRYPTO 2003, defining CMC and proving it a tweakable strong PRP. The 2004 EME paper used CMC as the sequential baseline and proposed a parallel alternative. Disk-encryption standardization then moved to XTS; CMC never became a mainstream deployed mode, but its “wide block + tweak” idea influenced later designs. CMC is not “ciphertext MAC” and provides no MAC; it stands for CBC–Mask–CBC. Confusing it with CCM (CBC-MAC + CTR) turns “encryption only” into “authenticated encryption”, one of the most dangerous mistakes in mode selection. - Wikipedia search entry for CMC 宽块加密模式（CBC–Mask–CBC）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CMC%20%E5%AE%BD%E5%9D%97%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F%EF%BC%88CBC%E2%80%93Mask%E2%80%93CBC%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] CMC wide-block enciphering mode (CBC–Mask–CBC): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Crypto AG Backdoor
items.text: Attack : Crypto AG Backdoor (Crypto AG 后门). The Crypto AG backdoor was not “a secret formula inside one machine”. It was supply-chain control: secretly own the vendor, sell both “strong” and “weak” devices, make the weak devices breakable with realistic effort, and turn decryption into intelligence through communications interception. The public record supports a conditional model: P_read=P_own·P_use·P_collect. P_own is the chance the target's device came from the controlled vendor; P_use is the chance the target actually used it; P_collect is the chance the relevant traffic could be collected. Missing any one condition yields no readable intelligence. On the work-factor side, if the original key space is K =2^k and the device is weakened by b bits, then K_eff =2^(k-b) and the relative work factor is ρ=2^-b. With T trial decryptions, one-attempt success is P_trial(T)=min(1,T/2^(k-b)). This is an analytical conversion of “weaker” into computable effort, not a reconstruction of Crypto AG's actual algorithms. The public investigation shows that the value came from scale: one device sold to many governments, militaries and diplomatic services lets the same class of weakness be reused. Customers saw a “normal product” and had no reason to suspect the vendor. A supply-chain backdoor is therefore stealthier and more durable than a one-off cyberattack. It also exposes a security boundary: weak devices do not serve only one intelligence service; third parties may reverse or exploit them; export controls, alliances and vendor reputation can backfire. For buyers, the trust chain must extend to vendor ownership, code/hardware provenance and independent testing. Historical steps: Boris Hagelin founded Crypto AG in Switzerland in 1952; the CIA and West German BND secretly bought it together in 1970 under Thesaurus/Rubicon; encryption devices were sold to many countries; some devices had weakened algorithms; the BND exited in 1993 and the CIA retained control; the company was liquidated in 2018; a joint investigation published the story in 2020. Defense: do not rely on one vendor's closed algorithm for high-value traffic; require published algorithms, independent audit, transparent key management and supply-chain provenance; treat “unusually cheap or unusually available” devices with suspicion. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Failure and boundaries: the public record does not contain per-device algorithms, key lengths or customer lists, so no specific device can be asserted broken; P_read is an analytical model, not a historical statistic; weak devices also harm allies and domestic firms; export controls and political blowback can erode the long-term gain. Ethics and law: this is intelligence history, not a replicable attack tutorial; it must not be used to infer implementation details of modern devices. The useful lesson is supply-chain governance, procurement audit and cryptographic transparency. Crypto AG was founded by Boris Hagelin in Steinhausen, Switzerland, in 1952. The CIA and West German BND secretly bought it in 1970; the BND exited around 1993 and the CIA remained sole owner until about 2018, after which the company was liquidated. In February 2020, the Washington Post, ZDF and SRF published a joint investigation. The Swiss Parliament's GPDel issued its report in November 2020 and the Federal Council responded in May 2021. The case became a classic study in supply-chain trust and export control. - Wikipedia search entry for Crypto AG 后门. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Crypto%20AG%20%E5%90%8E%E9%97%A8 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Crypto AG Backdoor: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: CWC authenticated encryption mode
items.text: Algorithm : CWC authenticated encryption mode (CWC 认证加密模式). CTR encryption + Carter–Wegman hash CWC is authenticated encryption (AEAD): CTR mode turns plaintext into ciphertext, and a Carter–Wegman polynomial universal hash compresses ciphertext, associated data and nonce into a tag. The block cipher is 128-bit, the nonce is 88-bit, the counter is 40-bit, and messages are capped at 2^32−1 blocks; the tag can be truncated to tl bits, up to 128. The polynomial over GF(2^127−1) CWC-HASH splits input into 96-bit blocks, treats them as polynomial coefficients over GF(2^127−1), and evaluates at secret point Z with Horner's rule; Z is the block cipher applied to a constant with the top bit cleared. The hash output is encrypted once more by the block cipher to form the final tag. Multiplication modulo 2^127−1 can be reduced in parallel, which is the key to CWC's hardware throughput. CWC's signature choice is to share one block-cipher key between encryption and authentication: the CTR keystream and the polynomial hash key material both derive from it, avoiding extra key memory in high-speed hardware. CTR blocks are independent and the polynomial hash can reduce in parallel, so the pipeline can sustain 10 Gbps. Around 2003, IPsec routers needed a line-rate AEAD with no patent burden. CWC simultaneously offered provable security, parallelism, 10 Gbps hardware, fast software and no intellectual-property claims. It brought Carter–Wegman's short-tag advantage to high-throughput links, which is why the designers brought it to IETF CFRG. CWC entered IETF CFRG as draft-irtf-cfrg-cwc-01, targeting high-speed IPsec authenticated encryption. GCM's designers cite CWC as the prior Carter–Wegman counter-mode scheme. NIST ultimately chose GCM; CWC never became a widely deployed standard, but its “CTR + polynomial hash” route was inherited by GCM. CWC fits link-encryption prototypes with high throughput, parallelism and a reliable unique-nonce discipline; it does not fit stateless devices with poor nonce management or protocols that rotate keys frequently. The tag can be shortened, but shorter tags raise forgery probability. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. CTR requires a unique nonce: reusing one under the same key repeats the keystream, so XORing two ciphertexts recovers the XOR of the plaintexts. The polynomial hash key also depends on the nonce, and reuse raises tag-forgery risk. Truncating the tag to tl bits raises forgery probability to roughly 2^-tl; the message cap is 2^32−1 blocks, after which the key must change. CWC has no built-in key derivation or nonce management, so the deployment must enforce both. CWC stopped at an IETF draft and an FSE paper: no NIST standard, no broad AES-NI optimization, no default protocol suite. It was not broken; it was not carried by the standards ecosystem, which leaves it structurally disadvantaged in engineering selection. Kohno, Viega and Whiting submitted CWC to IETF CFRG in 2003 and published the full paper at FSE 2004. It met IPsec's need for a high-speed AEAD but lost to GCM, standardized by NIST in 2007; GCM also combines CTR with a GF(2^128) polynomial hash, but its implementation and standards ecosystem were smoother. CWC is now an important waypoint for understanding GCM's design lineage. CWC is not “carried working-group cipher”; it stands for Carter–Wegman + Counter. Reading it as an organization or product name misses its AEAD structure entirely, which is why this entry was upgraded from a catalog identity card to a mechanism article. - Wikipedia search entry for CWC 认证加密模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=CWC%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] CWC authenticated encryption mode: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: DEAL block cipher
items.text: Algorithm : DEAL block cipher (DEAL 分组密码). 128-bit block, 64-bit halves DEAL splits a 128-bit plaintext into two 64-bit halves and runs a balanced Feistel network. The round function is not a new S-box; it calls DES on one 64-bit half: y_j = y_{j-1} ⊕ E_{R_j}(x_{j-1}), then swaps halves for the next round. Each round key is nominally a 64-bit DES key but only 56 bits are used; the parity bits are ignored. Rounds and key schedule DEAL-128 and DEAL-192 run 6 rounds; DEAL-256 runs 8. The key schedule uses a fixed DES key 0123456789abcdef and chains the 64-bit master-key blocks K0, K1, ... into R0 = E(K0), R_i = E(K_i ⊕ R_{i-1} ⊕ constant). Decryption uses the same round keys in reverse order. DES still had a large installed hardware base and years of analysis in the 1990s. DEAL aimed to keep that base while doubling the 64-bit block to 128 bits, avoiding matching-ciphertext attacks; a 128-bit block gives a 2^64 birthday bound. Its round function calls DES directly, which the designer treated as more conservative than building a new S-box. DEAL's speed was close to Triple DES, far slower than candidates optimized for the AES competition. NIST wanted high throughput, low latency and broad-platform implementations; DEAL's “reuse old hardware” became a performance burden. The later Kelsey–Schneier and Lucks analyses also exposed weaknesses in the key schedule and round margin. Richard Outerbridge submitted DEAL to the AES competition in 1998; it did not reach the five finalists. Today it is better used as a teaching example of “build a larger block from an existing block cipher” than as a production algorithm. No mainstream standard adopted DEAL; modern storage and protocols use AES-XTS or AES-GCM. DEAL's kinship with Ladder-DES keeps it relevant in Feistel-construction and security-proof literature, but engineering selections do not treat it as an AES replacement. Lucks presented a certificational attack on DEAL-192 at FSE 1999: using the separability of the six-round Feistel round keys, a large number of chosen ciphertexts significantly narrows the key search space. The paper also notes meet-in-the-middle bounds of about 2^168 for six rounds and 2^224 for eight, showing the effective key length is below the nominal value. The attack needs an enormous number of chosen ciphertexts, so it is a “design is not sound enough” result rather than a practical break. Kelsey–Schneier found structural problems in the key schedule at SAC 1999: DEAL-128 has equivalent-key pairs, finding one costs about 2^64 DES operations; DEAL-192/256 need only 6 or 8 DES operations to construct 256 equivalent keys. They also gave a related-key attack with about 2^33 related keys and 3 plaintexts per key. The root cause is that round keys are generated by a DES chain under a fixed key while parity bits are ignored. DEAL provides only a 128-bit block permutation; CBC, CTR, IV/nonce rules and authentication are separate choices. Six or eight rounds leave a thin margin against modern analysis, so it is not an AES replacement. Lars Knudsen proposed DEAL at SAC 1997; Richard Outerbridge submitted it to the AES competition in 1998. DEAL stands for “Data Encryption Algorithm with Larger blocks”, literally “a larger-block version of DES”. DEAL did not reach the AES final and never became an ISO or NIST standard. Its life is mainly in AES analysis papers, Feistel teaching designs and reflections on the “reuse DES” route; after AES was chosen in 2000, DEAL left the engineering scene. - Wikipedia search entry for DEAL 分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=DEAL%20%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] DEAL block cipher: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: EAX Authenticated Encryption Mode
items.text: Algorithm : EAX (EAX 认证加密). A two-pass AEAD mode EAX encrypts with CTR mode, then authenticates the nonce, header and ciphertext with OMAC; the tag is the XOR of the three values, truncated. It is a two-pass AEAD: first M becomes C, then three values over N, H and C are XORed and truncated into the tag. Tag construction Let N = OMAC_K(0 N), H = OMAC_K(1 H) and C = OMAC_K(2 C). Then T = N ⊕ H ⊕ C , truncated to τ bits. Decryption recomputes the tag and only decrypts with CTR after verification. The 0/1/2 prefixes are domain separation, so the three input classes cannot be substituted for one another. Properties EAX accepts arbitrary-length nonces, headers and messages, supports configurable tag lengths, needs only the encryption direction of the block cipher, and can pre-process a fixed header. It is a two-pass scheme: it cannot finish the tag while still reading the message the way OCB can. EAX’s niche is simple, provable, patent-free two-pass AEAD: it avoids CCM’s elaborate length encoding and supports arbitrary-length nonces, headers and messages, with truncatable tags. For developers the API is just encrypt/decrypt, which reduces the chance of miscombining encryption and a MAC. It trades two passes for simplicity and a security proof. That made it an attractive conventional AEAD when one-pass designs were still encumbered by patent concerns. EAX can be used for disk/file encryption, message authentication, VPNs and embedded protocols; ISO/IEC 19772:2020 lists EAX as authenticated-encryption mechanism 4. It is not a mandatory TLS 1.3 suite—TLS 1.3 uses AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305—so EAX appears more often where arbitrary nonces/headers or patent-free operation matter. Engineering rules: never repeat a nonce under one key; nonce reuse breaks both confidentiality and authenticity. Do not truncate tags too aggressively; 128 bits, or at least 64 bits, is common. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. EAX security depends on nonce uniqueness and on the block cipher being a PRP. Nonce reuse is the direct attack surface: CTR keystreams repeat and tags can become forgeable. EAX does not hide the nonce; the nonce is authenticated but not secret. It is two-pass, so encryption must finish the message before the tag is known, which rules out very low-latency streaming. Implementations must also compare tags in constant time, account for truncated-tag forgery probabilities and parse headers unambiguously. EAX was proposed by Mihir Bellare, Phillip Rogaway and David Wagner in 2003 and published at FSE 2004, LNCS 3017, pp. 389–407. The paper presents EAX as a one-key version of EAX2: CTR for encryption, OMAC for authentication, then the two keys collapsed into one. It later entered ISO/IEC 19772:2020 as mechanism 4 and appeared in protocols and libraries, but it did not become a mainstream TLS suite; TLS 1.3 chose GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305. - Wikipedia search entry for EAX 认证加密. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EAX%20%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] EAX: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ECMQV Authenticated Key Agreement
items.text: Algorithm : Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone (ECMQV 椭圆曲线 Menezes-Qu-Vanstone). Shared secret A computes s_A=x+X̄·a from its static a and ephemeral x, and B computes s_B=y+Ȳ·b; both share K=h·s_A·(Y+Ȳ·B)=h·s_B·(X+X̄·A)=h·s_A·s_B·P. Static and ephemeral keys A has a static key (a,A=aP) and an ephemeral key (x,X=xP); B has (b,B) and (y,Y); they exchange X,Y. X̄=2^ℓ+(X mod 2^ℓ) with ℓ= q /2, and Ȳ likewise; h is the cofactor and a KDF derives the session key from K. Implicit authentication The static private key binds identity into the shared secret: only a party holding a and knowing x can compute K. The protocol has no key confirmation; a MAC or confirmation message must be added. ECMQV completes authenticated DH in one round and two messages, with only about half an extra scalar multiplication over plain DH; it needs no signatures and no per-member certificate-chain verification, suiting constrained devices. It provides implicit key authentication and forward secrecy once ephemeral keys are erased; it is the elliptic-curve version of MQV and a classic design for efficient authenticated key exchange. It appears in SEC 1, IEEE 1363, ANSI X9.63, NIST SP 800-56A and ISO/IEC 11770-3; it is used in wireless, VPN, payment terminals and embedded secure channels. Deployment is limited by patents and implementation complexity; TLS favors ECDHE plus signatures rather than ECMQV, and protocols needing explicit confirmation add a MAC over the shared key. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Kaliski’s 2001 unknown key-share attack applies if an attacker can bind its own public key to the victim’s identity, so the victim may share a key with an unintended party. Public-key validation and identity binding are mandatory. Original MQV lacked a complete formal proof for years; HMQV hashes identities and the transcript, fixes the issues and proves security. Static-key compromise, ephemeral reuse or leakage must be handled within the boundary. Menezes, Qu and Vanstone proposed MQV in 1995; Law and Solinas refined it in 1998; Law–Menezes–Qu–Solinas–Vanstone published the journal version in 2003; Krawczyk proposed HMQV in 2005; it later entered NIST SP 800-56A and ISO/IEC 11770-3. It influenced HMQV, FHMQV and later efficient AKE designs. - Wikipedia search entry for ECMQV 椭圆曲线 Menezes-Qu-Vanstone. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ECMQV%20%E6%A4%AD%E5%9C%86%E6%9B%B2%E7%BA%BF%20Menezes-Qu-Vanstone - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[K=g^{ab}\bmod p\quad\text{或}\quad K=[ab]G\] Elliptic Curve Menezes-Qu-Vanstone: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Electromagnetic Analysis
items.text: Attack : Electromagnetic Analysis (电磁分析). The physical entry point of EM leakage A CMOS gate draws a transient current when it switches, and the interconnect and package radiate an electromagnetic field that varies with the operation. Place a probe near a decoder, register or bus and sample it with an oscilloscope; the result is an EM trace aligned to time. A simplified leakage model is L(t) = a·HW(v(t)) + b + n(t), where a is the gain, HW is the Hamming weight of the intermediate value, b is a static offset and n is noise. This is not a full physical simulation of the chip; it is the approximation an attacker uses to rank key hypotheses. From traces to key hypotheses For each key guess k, compute the model H_k(t) of the target intermediate value v_k(t), then compare it with the observed trace L(t). DPA compares the mean difference between the groups whose guessed bit is 0 and 1: Δ(t) = E[L(t) b=0] - E[L(t) b=1]. CPA computes the Pearson correlation: ρ(t,k) = Cov(L(t), H_k(t)) / √(Var L(t) · Var H_k(t)). The correct key produces a stable extremum at some time; peaks from wrong hypotheses fade as more traces are added. Why it is “analysis”, not “reading” An EM probe picks up a near field that superposes several modules, so time alignment, triggering, denoising and averaging are needed to isolate the target operation. It does not directly reveal key bits; it turns physical leakage into a testable statistical hypothesis. Trace count, SNR and probe position determine whether recovery works. EM and power analysis share the same statistical core: choose an intermediate value, build a leakage model, partition traces by hypothesis, and compare means or correlations. The difference is the sensor and spatial selectivity: an EM probe can sit near a local module, reduce unrelated circuit contributions, and sometimes bypass shielding inside a package. Algorithm-level masking, hiding and constant-time code can reduce data-dependent leakage, but the probe, package, supply and clock can still carry residual leakage. An evaluation must consider the algorithm implementation, the physical package and the acquisition conditions together. Smart cards, HSMs, TEEs, MCUs and hardware wallets all need side-channel threats in their models. Designers should run leakage evaluations, not just functional tests; “the algorithm is AES-256” does not imply “the device resists EM analysis”. 1. Choose the target operation and intermediate value, such as the first-round AES S-box output, an RSA modexp word, or an ECC scalar-multiplication branch. 2. Fix the probe position and use an external trigger to align each operation; record many traces with their inputs. 3. Denoise, align and reject outlier traces; estimate SNR and the required trace count. 4. Compute DPA differences or CPA correlations for key guesses, rank the peaks, and re-test the top candidates. 5. Calibrate on a test chip with a known key, then acquire from the target; the report must separate laboratory conditions from remote or non-contact conditions. AES/DES S-boxes, RSA modexp, ECC scalar multiplication, KEM decoding and hardware-wallet mnemonic derivation are common EM leakage targets. 1. Masking: the secret is split into random shares, weakening the correlation between a single trace point and the intermediate value; higher-order analysis needs more traces and a more complex model. 2. Hiding: random delays, clock jitter, dual-rail logic, noise injection and constant-current logic reduce alignment and SNR. 3. Physical protection: shielding, in-package filtering, difficult probe access and increased distance. 4. Implementation differences: asynchronous circuits, low-power processes and strong noise can invalidate a simple Hamming model. 5. Acquisition conditions: unstable triggering, unaligned traces or a shifted probe directly destroy the statistics. 6. Authorisation and evidence: without laboratory equipment and lawful authorisation, “theoretically possible” must not be written as “reproduced on a real device”. EM analysis can recover keys, but it does not guarantee success on every device or implementation; one success is not a universal attack tool. A report must state the device, probe, trace count, SNR and verification key. In 2001 Quisquater and Samyde systematised electromagnetic analysis (EMA) and its countermeasures; in the same year Gandolfi, Mourtel and Olivier experimented on three CMOS chips running DES, COMP128 and RSA, and reported recovery of complete key material. DEMA, CPA, template attacks and higher-order analysis later became standard tools of side-channel evaluation. Modern secure chips combine shielding, masking, random delays and sensors; evaluation has moved from “can one key be recovered” to “how much advantage remains under a given trace budget and leakage model”. This is why a side-channel evaluation must be reported together with the device’s physical package. - Wikipedia search entry for 电磁分析. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%94%B5%E7%A3%81%E5%88%86%E6%9E%90 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Electromagnetic Analysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: EUF-CMA signature unforgeability
items.text: Theorem : EUF-CMA signature unforgeability (EUF-CMA 签名不可伪造). The game EUF-CMA is “existential unforgeability under adaptive chosen-message attack”. The challenger generates (pk, sk), gives pk to the adversary and opens a signing oracle: the adversary adaptively submits any messages m_i and receives σ_i. At the end the adversary outputs (m , σ ); it wins if m was never queried and Verify(pk, m , σ ) = 1. Why “existential” The adversary need not forge a designated message; any valid new message/signature pair it did not query is a win. This is weaker than “universal forgery” (forge any message) and “selective forgery” (forge a message chosen in advance), but it is still the minimum acceptable bar for a signature scheme: EUF-CMA security means no efficient adversary wins this game with non-negligible probability. Diffie–Hellman proposed signatures in 1976 and RSA gave the first usable construction in 1978, but early definitions only asked whether an adversary with the public key could forge; they did not model an adversary who first obtains many signatures. Goldwasser–Micali–Rivest in 1988 separated attack capabilities from attack outcomes and gave the GMR scheme with a proof of EUF-CMA. GMR uses a claw-free pair of permutations (realizable from factoring) for randomized signing, then tree authentication extends a one-time signature into a multi-message one. The paper proves that even an adaptive signing-oracle adversary's forgery is equivalent to factoring; this was the first rigorous EUF-CMA scheme of practical type. EUF-CMA is the security target for RSA-PSS, DSA, ECDSA and EdDSA, and the analysis baseline for TLS certificates, code signing, software updates and blockchain signatures. When a protocol says “signatures cannot be forged”, it usually means EUF-CMA unless SUF-CMA is stated. SUF-CMA (strong unforgeability) also forbids a new signature on the same message: given (m, σ), the adversary cannot output σ′ ≠ σ with Verify(m, σ′) = 1. Deterministic signatures such as FDH-RSA are usually SUF by construction; ECDSA is not SUF because (r, s) is malleable, while DSA has been proved SUF. If replay or transaction-ID mutation matters, specify SUF-CMA. It does not cover key-substitution/rogue-key attacks, the signer's implementation (nonce reuse, side channels), model differences in aggregate signatures, or quantum security. EUF-CMA is asymptotic; concrete parameters still need exact security bounds. Treating ECDSA's (r, s) malleability as a “forgery”; treating EUF-CMA as SUF-CMA; verifying individual signatures in an aggregate without key binding; reusing a nonce in EdDSA. These are selection or implementation errors, not flaws in the EUF-CMA definition. Goldwasser, Micali and Rivest published “A Digital Signature Scheme Secure Against Adaptive Chosen-Message Attacks” in SIAM Journal on Computing in 1988, systematically defining key-only/known-message/adaptive-chosen-message attacks and total/universal/selective/existential forgeries. Bellare–Micali, Naor–Yung and Rompel weakened the assumption toward one-way functions; Bellare–Rogaway gave exact bounds and RSA-PSS in 1993/1996; Fersch–Kiltz–Poettering proved DSA's SUF-CMA, and Brendel et al. proved IETF EdDSA's SUF-CMA in 2021. - Wikipedia search entry for EUF-CMA 签名不可伪造. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=EUF-CMA%20%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E4%B8%8D%E5%8F%AF%E4%BC%AA%E9%80%A0 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] EUF-CMA signature unforgeability: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Fiat–Shamir Heuristic
items.text: Theorem : Fiat-Shamir Heuristic (Fiat-Shamir 启发式). Three moves compressed into one hash A sigma protocol has a commitment a, a challenge c and a response z. The Fiat–Shamir transform replaces the verifier’s random challenge with c=H(x,a), so the prover sends only (a,z); the verifier recomputes c and checks whether the original protocol accepts (x,a,c,z). Schnorr instantiation In Schnorr the prover samples r and sets R=g^r; then c=H(x R), s=r+c·x, and the proof is (R,s). The verifier checks g^s=R·y^c. Hashing turns an interactive challenge into a verifiable pseudorandom one and binds the statement or message into it. Strong transform and knowledge soundness The weak transform hashes only the commitment a, so it does not bind the statement x or public parameters; an attacker can grind for a challenge that favors a false statement. The strong transform hashes x, a and all public inputs. In the random oracle model FS preserves special soundness and knowledge extraction; lattice signatures additionally need rejection sampling (Fiat–Shamir with aborts). FS turns an interactive proof into a one-message NIZK or signature, removing the online verifier and suiting blockchains, credentials, TLS and embedded devices. It lets Schnorr/EdDSA signatures use one hash and one group operation; in zkSNARKs FS compresses a polynomial identity check into one proof verifiable on chain. The saving comes from hashing, not from extra trusted setup. Schnorr, EdDSA, Bulletproofs, PLONK, Groth16, Spartan and STARK verifiers derive challenges with FS; Dilithium uses a rejection-sampling FS variant. FROST threshold signatures also bind nonce commitments and the message through FS. It is also used for authentication and verifiable random functions: the verifier only recomputes the challenge and keeps no interactive session. The IRTF CFRG Fiat–Shamir draft is unifying input encoding, domain separation and serialization. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Weak FS has caused real incidents: Bulletproofs, Plonk and Girault proofs were forgeable when the challenge omitted public values (Frozen Heart, CVE-2022-29566). A small challenge space can be brute-forced; omitting the “last challenge” also breaks knowledge soundness of KZG SNARKs. Fiat and Shamir introduced the identification-to-signature transform in 1986; Pointcheval and Stern gave random-oracle security arguments for signatures and blind signatures in 2000; “How not to Prove Yourself” distinguished weak and strong transforms in 2016 and exposed Helios; Frozen Heart disclosed several production proof systems in 2022; CFRG began standardizing the transform in 2026. It started in smart-card identification and became a foundational compiler for zkSNARKs and modern signatures. - Wikipedia search entry for Fiat-Shamir 启发式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Fiat-Shamir%20%E5%90%AF%E5%8F%91%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Fiat-Shamir Heuristic: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Franklin-Reiter Related-Message Attack
items.text: Attack : Franklin-Reiter Related-Message Attack (Franklin-Reiter 相关消息攻击). One modulus, low exponent, known relation Suppose two messages m1 and m2 are encrypted under the same RSA public key (N,e), and the attacker knows the affine relation m2 = α m1 + β. Let c1 = m1^e mod N and c2 = m2^e mod N. Construct two univariate polynomials f2(z) = (α z + β)^e - c2. Both have z = m1 as a root modulo N. The goal is not to factor N, but to separate this common root from the two high-degree polynomials. Polynomial gcd removes the high-degree terms Compute g(z) = gcd(f1, f2) over the ring Z/NZ[z]. If the leading coefficients are invertible and the case is not one of the exceptions listed in the paper, g is the linear polynomial z - m1. Its root recovers m1, and the affine relation gives m2. Intuitively, the gcd isolates the common root of two degree-e polynomials without knowledge of the factors of N. Complexity and the usable exponent range Plain Euclid costs about O(e^2) ring operations; fast polynomial gcd algorithms reach O(e log^2 e). The attack is therefore almost immediate for e=3 and still far cheaper than a 2^16 brute force for e=65537. The paper notes that, with a good implementation, exponents up to roughly 32 bits may remain practical. The cost grows with e, not with the size of the factors of N. e=3 or e=65537 is often chosen to reduce encryption and verification cost. The low exponent itself is not the problem; it turns a relation between messages into a solvable low-degree equation. If a protocol preserves a known affine relation, for example a counter, timestamp, sequence number or shared padding, the attacker can cancel the unknown high-degree terms using the ciphertexts. Franklin-Reiter requires one modulus N; Hastad's broadcast attack uses distinct moduli and CRT. Both exploit a low exponent, but the mathematical entry points differ: a polynomial gcd over one ring versus CRT plus an integer e-th root across moduli. Calling both simply “low-exponent attacks” hides the difference in defences. Deterministic padding is not automatically safe when the message relation is predictable. Randomised padding, hashing the message into a randomised encoding, or a scheme that destroys the algebraic relation makes the “known polynomial relation” premise false. The audit questions are: does the attacker know the exact algebraic relation between the m_i, is the modulus the same, and is e small enough for a polynomial gcd? 1. Collect several ciphertexts under one public key and confirm that they share both modulus and exponent. 2. Identify a known relation between the messages: affine, same-degree polynomial, or a linear constraint imposed by the protocol. 3. Build f_i(z) = (p_i(z))^e - c_i and compute the polynomial gcd; a linear factor recovers the message. 4. If the gcd has higher degree, use resultants, algebraic elimination or a Coppersmith-style lattice method. 5. Record e, the relation degree δ and the number of messages k; these parameters decide whether the attack is polynomial time. When auditing RSA protocols, look for the combination “same key + low exponent + predictable relation”; check whether padding is randomised; check whether the message is used directly as a polynomial variable instead of being passed through a randomised encoding. Raising e is not always feasible, but it is one repair explicitly discussed in the paper when the relation cannot be removed. 1. Different moduli. The Franklin-Reiter gcd runs over one Z/NZ; distinct moduli move the problem into the Hastad/CRT route. 2. Unknown or uncertain relation. If the relation contains an unknown random quantity, the attacker cannot write f2. 3. Non-invertible leading coefficient or an exceptional case. The paper lists rare cases where the gcd may not be linear; an implementation must check them. 4. e too large. The polynomials have degree e and the gcd cost grows with e; for very large e the attack is no longer practical. 5. Effective randomised padding. If padding makes the relation between m1 and m2 non-fixed, the algebraic premise is broken. The paper also warns that not every padding is sufficient; it must be randomised and analysed. 6. Homogeneous relations. The paper notes that in the homogeneous case one may recover only homogeneous polynomials, not the individual message. Franklin and Reiter first gave the k=2, e=3, δ=1 affine case. In 1996, Coppersmith, Franklin, Patarin and Reiter generalised it at EUROCRYPT: e can be arbitrary, the relation degree δ can exceed 1, and the number of messages k can grow. The paper explicitly separates this route from the attacks of Moore, Hastad and Simons: those target different public keys, while this one targets one public key. The paper turned “known algebraic relation” into an independent entry point in RSA cryptanalysis. Later Coppersmith small-root methods and lattice reductions extended the same idea to more general modular equations; in modern RSA attack literature, Franklin-Reiter is the standard starting point for “same modulus, low exponent, related messages”. - Wikipedia search entry for Franklin-Reiter 相关消息攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Franklin-Reiter%20%E7%9B%B8%E5%85%B3%E6%B6%88%E6%81%AF%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Franklin-Reiter Related-Message Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Garbled Circuits
items.text: Algorithm : Garbled Circuit (混淆电路). Labels, gate tables and evaluation A garbled circuit gives every wire two labels L_i^0 and L_i^1; gate tables encrypt output labels under input labels, and the evaluator obtains its input labels by OT and decrypts gate by gate. FREE-XOR makes XOR gates free, while half-gates reduce an AND gate to two ciphertexts. Point-and-permute and correctness Point-and-permute attaches a select bit to each label so the evaluator indexes one row directly; XOR gates use a global offset R with L_i^1=L_i^0⊕R, and AND gates split into two gates with one known input each. Gate tables are encrypted with H(L_a L_b tweak), and a failed decryption is rejected. Security boundary Half-gate security relies on circular-correlation-robust (CCR) hashing. The default protocol is only semi-honest; a malicious garbler can build wrong tables, requiring cut-and-choose, authenticated garbling or zero-knowledge proofs. The evaluator may leak intermediate labels, and output privacy needs separate handling. Yao’s protocol needs only symmetric encryption and OT to evaluate any Boolean circuit between two parties; it is orders of magnitude faster than fully homomorphic encryption for medium-size circuits. It turns computation into encrypted table lookup, letting both parties learn the same output without revealing their inputs. That makes it an engineering foundation for private set intersection, private inference and MPC. PSI, privacy-preserving machine-learning inference, private auctions, genomic comparison, blockchain sealed-bid auctions and key management use GC; EMP-toolkit, MP-SPDZ and Fresco provide implementations. Half-gates are the mainstream choice: two AES calls and two ciphertext segments per AND gate, with XOR free. Fixed-key AES speeds this further but needs concrete-security parameters.
