The evaluator may leak intermediate labels, and output privacy needs separate handling. Side channels, circuit size, OT bandwidth and the joint security bound of fixed-key AES are boundaries; encrypted gate tables are not fully homomorphic encryption. items.title: Message Authentication Codes—Part 1: Mechanisms Using a Block Cipher
items.text: Standard : Message Authentication Codes—Part 1: Mechanisms Using a Block Cipher (GB/T 15852.1-2020 消息鉴别码 第1部分：采用分组密码的机制). GB/T 15852.1-2020 turns a block-cipher MAC into an eight-step pipeline: optional key induction, message padding, data splitting, initial transform, repeated block-cipher application, final iteration, output transform and truncation. The base CBC-MAC sets H0=0^n, computes Hi=E_K(Pi⊕Hi-1) block by block, and outputs Hm. The other seven algorithms change the start, the end or the truncation rule of this chain to handle arbitrary lengths or reduce key and storage overhead. CBC-MAC is reliable only for fixed-length messages. If arbitrary-length messages are fed in directly, an attacker can extend the chain and forge a valid new message. EMAC adds an independent final encryption, ANSI retail MAC uses an encrypt-decrypt transform with two keys, and CMAC uses K1/K2 for complete and incomplete blocks; each cuts the concatenation attack without adding many block-cipher calls. The standard places all eight algorithms under one model so implementers can choose by message length, key length, storage and call count, while checking padding, initial transform, final iteration and truncation against one test-vector set. Start with the message space: fixed-length messages can use CBC-MAC; arbitrary lengths favour CMAC, EMAC or TrCBC; MacDES suits a key twice the block-cipher key length; storage-limited settings can use TrCBC/CBCR. Implement against Annex B step by step: SM4 has a 128-bit block and a 128-bit key; CMAC subkeys are K1=dbl(E_K(0^n)) and K2=dbl(K1); truncation takes only the specified bits and must not be replaced by XOR or a hash. A MAC gives integrity and origin authentication, not confidentiality; reusing a key across protocols or directions weakens the boundary. With an m-bit tag the ideal forgery probability is about 2^-m, but a short m is hit faster by birthday bounds and online queries. Verification must compare in constant time, not short-circuit by byte; CBC-MAC is not for variable-length messages; TrCBC tags are limited to below n/2 and cannot be treated as a general long-tag MAC. GB/T 15852.1-2020 was published on 2020-12-14 and took effect on 2021-07-01, fully replacing GB/T 15852.1-2008. It is a modified adoption of ISO/IEC 9797-1:2011, adds TrCBC and CBCR to the six base algorithms, and changes the test vectors from DEA to SM4. This edition consolidates block-cipher MACs into eight selectable mechanisms while retaining the 2008 user requirements and general model, so domestic cryptographic modules and protocol implementations can cite it directly. - Wikipedia search entry for GB/T 15852.1-2020 消息鉴别码 第1部分：采用分组密码的机制. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=GB%2FT%2015852.1-2020%20%E6%B6%88%E6%81%AF%E9%89%B4%E5%88%AB%E7%A0%81%20%E7%AC%AC1%E9%83%A8%E5%88%86%EF%BC%9A%E9%87%87%E7%94%A8%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E7%9A%84%E6%9C%BA%E5%88%B6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Message Authentication Codes—Part 1: Mechanisms Using a Block Cipher: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: GB/T 29829-2022 Trusted Cryptography Module Platform
items.text: Standard : Trusted Cryptography Module (可信密码模块). GB/T 29829-2022 defines the functions and interfaces of a trusted-computing cryptographic platform, centred on the TCM: a hardware/firmware security chip, with a TSM outside it providing measurement, reporting and storage services. The platform has three roots RTM/RTS/RTR, and the TCM carries RTS/RTR; the EPS/PPS/SPS primary seeds belong to the endorsement/platform/storage hierarchies and are controlled by endorsementAuth/platformAuth/ownerAuth. PCR extension compresses an arbitrary measurement into a fixed register: PCR_new=Hash(PCR_old digest), while the event log keeps the original measurement; Quote signs PCRs and a nonce with an AK to stop replay. A policy session accumulates authorization conditions into policyDigest, and PolicyPCR binds selected PCR values and updateCounter into the policy; commands and responses use the TCM2_ interface. Design first draws the TCM/TSM boundary, then fixes the three seeds and authorization domains; a measurement chain stores both PCRs and the event log, and remote attestation uses Quote+AK+nonce. The key-object tree derives from the SRK; migration and backup are controlled by the migrate attribute and parent keys, while the EK is unique and non-migratable. items.title: SM3 Cryptographic Hash Function
items.text: Standard : SM3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm (SM3 杂凑算法). 512-bit blocks, 256-bit digest SM3 uses 512-bit blocks, a 132-word message expansion and 64 compression rounds to map a message to a 256-bit digest. It accepts messages shorter than 2^64 bits; padding appends a 1 bit, the minimum number of 0 bits so the length is 448 modulo 512, and a 64-bit length field. Message expansion and 64 rounds Each block is split into sixteen 32-bit words W0…W15 and expanded into W16…W67 plus W’0…W’63: 132 words in total. The compression function keeps eight registers A…H and runs 64 rounds. Each round mixes message and state with Boolean functions FF/GG, permutations P0/P1, addition modulo 2^32 and rotations; the result is XORed with the input chaining value. Design trade-offs SM3 shares the Merkle–Damgård structure, 256-bit output and 64 rounds with SHA-256, but its Boolean functions, constants, message schedule and register updates differ. It is not a truncated SHA-256, and SHA-256 test vectors or hardware instructions cannot be reused directly. SM3 is the hash base of China’s commercial cryptography system. SM2 signatures first compress the user identity and curve parameters into ZA, then compute e = SM3(ZA M); certificate fingerprints, TLCP PRF/HMAC, code integrity and audit records also depend on SM3. It maps arbitrary-length input to a 256-bit digest and gives signatures, authentication and integrity checking one common entry point. Without SM3, SM2 signatures and TLCP key derivation would not close the loop. SM3 is used for digital signatures, message authentication codes, KDFs, random-number generation and integrity checks. Typical combinations are SM2+SM3 signatures, HMAC-SM3, the TLCP SM3 PRF, and digest/address derivation in blockchains and electronic invoices. Rules: do not use SM3(secret message) as a MAC; use HMAC-SM3 or a standard KDF. Use HMAC when length extension matters, and specify input encoding, byte order and domain-separation tags across systems. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. SM3 targets a 256-bit hash, with a generic birthday bound near 2^128; reduced-round analysis is not a full-round break. Real risks come from construction errors: length extension, MAC concatenation, truncated output, side channels, and mixing SM3 with SHA-256 in one protocol. Boundaries: SM3 is not encryption and is not a password hash. Passwords need Argon2, scrypt or PBKDF2. SM3 security also depends on correct HMAC, KDF and domain-separation implementation by the caller. OSCCA published SM3 in December 2010. GB/T 32905-2016 was published in August 2016 and took effect in March 2017; ISO/IEC 10118-3:2018 added SM3 in October 2018. Drafting units included Tsinghua University, the OSCCA Commercial Cryptography Research Center and the PLA Information Engineering University; Xiaoyun Wang was one of the principal drafters. It filled the 256-bit hash slot in China’s commercial cryptography system and, with SM2 and SM4, formed the SM family. Internationally, SM3 became an ISO/IEC dedicated hash function. - Wikipedia search entry for SM3 杂凑算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SM3%20%E6%9D%82%E5%87%91%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] SM3 Cryptographic Hash Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SM4 Block Cipher Algorithm
items.text: Standard : SM4 Block Cipher Algorithm (SM4 分组密码算法). Block and round function SM4 uses a 128-bit block and 128-bit key over 32 rounds. Let the round state be X_i…X_{i+3}; then X_{i+4}=X_i⊕T(X_{i+1}⊕X_{i+2}⊕X_{i+3}⊕rk_i), where T(B)=L(τ(B)): τ applies the S-box to four bytes in parallel, and L(B)=B⊕(B≪2)⊕(B≪10)⊕(B≪18)⊕(B≪24). Key schedule The initial K0…K3 is formed from FK constants and the key; round keys follow rk_i=K_{i+4}=K_i⊕T′(K_{i+1}⊕K_{i+2}⊕K_{i+3}⊕CK_i), with L′(B)=B⊕(B≪13)⊕(B≪23). Decryption uses the same structure with rk0…rk31 reversed. Modes and authentication SM4 is only a block permutation; ECB hides no pattern, CBC needs a separate MAC, and CTR requires a non-repeating counter/IV. TLS 1.3 AEAD_SM4_GCM and AEAD_SM4_CCM use SM4 as the underlying block cipher under GCM/CCM rules. SM4 obtains diffusion and confusion through 32 nonlinear rounds; its 128-bit block fits TLS, IPsec and cryptographic-module suites together with SM3 and SM2. Public standards and test vectors make it an interoperable baseline. SM4 is a block cipher; SM3 is a hash and SM2 is an elliptic-curve public-key scheme. They are combined in protocols but have different security goals and are not substitutes. 1. Choose a mode: use CBC+MAC or CTR+MAC for confidentiality without built-in authentication; use GCM/CCM for authenticated encryption. 2. Manage IVs: GCM IVs must be unique; CBC IVs may be public but should be unpredictable; CTR counters must not wrap. 3. Manage keys: round keys are expanded from the master key, which stays inside the module boundary. 4. Verify vectors: run standard test vectors and check reverse-key decryption. Do not use ECB for multi-block messages; do not treat SM4 itself as a MAC; do not reuse a GCM key with a fixed IV. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Mode misuse: ECB leaks block structure, CBC without a MAC permits padding/replay attacks, and CTR/GCM IV reuse breaks confidentiality or authentication. 2. Implementation leakage: table-based S-boxes and cache access are side-channel targets; fault injection can skip rounds or corrupt the last round. 3. Key management: plaintext master keys, unisolated round keys and open debug interfaces bypass algorithmic strength. 4. Overclaiming: SM4 has no known practical full-round classical attack, but that does not make every implementation secure; this entry is not implementation certification. SM4 entered the domestic standard sequence as SMS4, moved into GM/T in 2012 and was published as GB/T 32907—2016 in 2016; it later entered ISO/IEC 18033-3 and became the block cipher behind the TLS 1.3 SM4 suites in RFC 8998 (2021). items.title: SM2 Public-Key Cryptography
items.text: Standard : SM2 Public Key Cryptography Algorithm (SM2 公钥密码算法). Curve and keys SM2 implements signatures, encryption and key exchange over a 256-bit prime-field elliptic curve; signing binds SM3, the user ID and the curve parameters. The base point G has order n, the private key is d in [1, n−1] and the public key is P = [d]G. The standard has five parts: general, digital signature, key exchange, public-key encryption and parameters. Signature Signing first computes ZA = SM3(ENTL ID a b xG yG xA yA), then e = SM3(ZA M). Pick a random k, compute (x1, y1) = [k]G and r = (e + x1) mod n; if r = 0 or r + k = n, restart. Then s = ((1 + d)^−1)(k − r d) mod n. Verification computes t = (r + s) mod n and [s]G + [t]P, recovers x1 and checks R = r. Encryption and key exchange Encryption uses the recipient’s public key: C1 = [k]G, shared point [k]P = (x2, y2), t = KDF(x2 y2, klen), C2 = M ⊕ t, C3 = SM3(x2 M y2), and ciphertext C1 C3 C2. Key exchange computes a shared point from both private keys and the peer’s public key, then feeds xA yA ZA ZB and related values into the KDF to derive a session key. SM2 is the public-key base of China’s commercial cryptography system. One 256-bit curve carries signatures, encryption and key exchange, and SM3 binds the user identity, curve parameters and message into the signature, creating an interoperable national public-key infrastructure. Compared with RSA, SM2 keys and signatures are shorter and signing is faster; the price is more complex management of curve parameters, the user ID in ZA and the random k. Its value is not “replacing one algorithm” but bringing certificates, electronic seals, TLCP and financial terminals onto one public-key standard. SM2 signatures are used in certificates, electronic seals, code signing, identity authentication and blockchains; SM2 encryption wraps session keys and protects sensitive data; SM2 key exchange serves TLCP, VPNs and government networks. TLCP uses dual certificates: a signing certificate proves identity and an encryption certificate participates in key exchange. Engineering rules: signing and verification must use the same user ID and curve parameters; do not treat SM2 signatures as ECDSA DER signatures without a defined profile; keep private keys in modules or smart cards; and generate a fresh k for every signature. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. SM2 security rests on the elliptic-curve discrete logarithm, SM3 and the random k. Reused, biased or fault-injected k can leak the private key; curve-parameter substitution, invalid-point attacks, side channels and error handling are also real risks. Boundaries: SM2 is not symmetric encryption and cannot protect bulk data alone; it does not replace certificate chains, revocation, timestamps or auditing. Deployments must validate curve parameters and public points, enforce r, s in [1, n−1], and use side-channel-resistant implementations. OSCCA published SM2 in December 2010, issued the GM/T 0003 series in 2012, and published the GB/T 32918 series in August 2016, effective March 2017; the parameter-definition part followed in May 2017. In November 2018, the SM2 signature mechanism entered ISO/IEC 14888-3:2018. Its historical significance is not merely “a Chinese ECC”. It put signatures, encryption, key exchange and curve parameters into one standard family, creating an interoperable commercial public-key system. - Wikipedia search entry for SM2 公钥密码算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SM2%20%E5%85%AC%E9%92%A5%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] SM2 Public Key Cryptography Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SM2 Digital Signature
items.text: Standard : SM2 Digital Signature (SM2 数字签名). Curve and keys SM2 signatures use the 256-bit prime-field curve curveSM2 with base point G of order n. The private key is d∈[1,n−2] and the public key is P=dG. Signing Compute e=SM3(Z_A‖M), where Z_A binds the user identity, curve parameters and public key. Choose random k∈[1,n−1], compute (x1,y1)=kG and if r=0 or r+k=n, choose a new k. Then compute s=((1+d)^{-1}(k−r d)) mod n; if s=0, retry. The signature is (r,s). Verification Check r,s∈[1,n−1]; set t=(r+s) mod n and reject if t=0; compute (x1,y1)=sG+tP and R=(e+x1) mod n; accept only if R=r. SM2 binds the SM3 digest, curve arithmetic and user identity into one signing flow, fitting certificates, TLS authentication and electronic seals. Unlike ECDSA’s truncated x-coordinate, it closes the loop over e, r and s. SM2 also defines public-key encryption and key exchange; this entry covers signatures only. SM3 is a hash and SM4 a block cipher, with different security goals. 1. Generate keys: create d inside a cryptographic module and authenticate P by certificate or out-of-band channel. 2. Compute Z_A: use the standard ENTL, ID, curve parameters and public key; do not omit the identity. 3. Nonce: k must be unique and unpredictable, preferably from a DRBG or hardware source. 4. Verify: check the curve, point, order and r/s range before computing t and R. Do not reuse k; do not skip Z_A; do not verify r without s; do not present SM2 as quantum-resistant. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Nonce reuse: the same d and k over two messages exposes the private key; this is the most direct fatal error. 2. Missing curve/point checks: failing to verify that P lies on curveSM2 with the right order enables invalid-curve or small-subgroup attacks. 3. Side channels and faults: timing, cache access and fault injection in scalar multiplication can recover d; use constant-time code and redundancy. 4. Protocol layer: missing identity binding, domain separation or certificate chain lets a valid signature serve the wrong context. SM2 was released in 2010, entered GM/T 0003 in 2012 and was published as the GB/T 32918 series in 2016; RFC 8998 (2021) uses SM2 signatures and curveSM2 in TLS 1.3. Signature format, Z_A computation and curve parameters follow the claimed standard edition; this entry is not a clause substitute. - Wikipedia search entry for SM2 数字签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SM2%20%E6%95%B0%E5%AD%97%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] SM2 Digital Signature: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ZUC Algorithm
items.text: Standard : ZUC Algorithm (ZUC 算法). LFSR and state ZUC’s LFSR has 16 31-bit cells s0…s15, each in 1…2^31−1 and operating modulo 2^31−1. In working mode the feedback is s16=2^15 s15+2^17 s13+2^21 s10+2^20 s4+(1+2^8)s0 mod (2^31−1), with 0 replaced by 2^31−1. Bit reorganisation and keystream Each clock takes high/low 16-bit halves of s15/s14, s11/s9, s7/s5 and s2/s0 into X0…X3: X0=s15H‖s14L; X1=s11L‖s9H; X2=s7L‖s5H; X3=s2L‖s0H. The keystream word is Z=X3⊕F(X0,X1,X2); F uses two 8-bit S-boxes S0/S1, linear transforms L1/L2 and 32-bit registers R1/R2. Initialization and authentication A 128-bit key and 128-bit IV enter 32 initialization rounds before keystream generation. 128-EEA3 encrypts with the keystream; 128-EIA3 accumulates ZUC words with the message into a 32-bit MAC. ZUC combines a 31-bit LFSR with a nonlinear F for low latency and small area in hardware, fitting LTE confidentiality and integrity. Its 128-bit key and IV map directly to 3GPP bearer context. ZUC is a stream cipher; SM4 is a block cipher and SM3 a hash. ZUC alone does not authenticate; 128-EIA3 or the upper protocol does. 1. Initialization: bind key and IV to the 3GPP bearer, counter and direction; never reuse across contexts. 2. Encryption: 128-EEA3 encrypts the bit/word stream, and counters must not wrap. 3. Authentication: compute the 128-EIA3 MAC and follow the protocol’s encrypt-then-MAC order. 4. Verify vectors: run the ZUC and EEA3/EIA3 standard test vectors. Do not reuse a fixed IV and keystream; do not encrypt with ZUC alone without integrity; do not truncate the 32-bit MAC further. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. IV/counter reuse: the same keystream XORs into multiple messages and leaks plaintext relations. 2. Initialization and state: wrong round count, LFSR modulus or bit reorganisation breaks interoperability and security. 3. Side channels and faults: state updates and S-box access are timing/cache/fault targets. 4. Weak authentication: a raw stream has no integrity and a 32-bit MAC has a limited forgery bound; the protocol must specify replay and direction. ZUC was designed by the 3GPP SAGE task force and became the core of 128-EEA3 and 128-EIA3, specified in SAGE ZUC Specification v1.6; 3GPP TS 35.222 and ETSI TS 135 222 reference it. Initialization and documentation differ between ZUC v1.5 and v1.6; implementations follow the claimed version and test vectors. - Wikipedia search entry for ZUC 算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ZUC%20%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] ZUC Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: GB/T 33560 Cryptographic Application Identifier Specification
items.text: Standard : Coding Rules for Cryptography Application Identifiers (密码应用标识规范). GB/T 33560-2017 defines cryptographic application identifiers as 32-bit unsigned integers, transmitted in network byte order (big-endian). Algorithm, data, protocol, role, key, system and device identifiers all share one number space. Bit fields are not arbitrary strings: block ciphers use the low and high 8-bit fields for mode and bits 8-31 for the algorithm; hash uses the low 8 bits; signature is asymmetric OR hash; data encoding sits in the high 8 bits; management identifiers set bit 8 to 1. A common numbering scheme lets devices, interfaces and protocols interoperate; bit-field composition lets suites combine, e.g. SM3_SM2=0x00020201. But an identifier says what a thing is, not how secure it is. The 32-bit space, reserved ranges and custom ranges must follow the standard, and wire serialization must fix byte order. When integrating a cryptographic device, first confirm the edition (2017 current / 2026 upcoming), then decode algorithm, data, protocol and management identifiers by bit field; use big-endian on the wire instead of writing host integers directly. Typical values: SM4-ECB 0x00000401, SM3 0x00000001, SM2 0x00020100, SM3_SM2 0x00020201, DER 0x01000000; management bit 8 is 1, SGD_MAIN_KEY is 0x00000101. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Common errors: little-endian transmission, treating an OID as a 32-bit identifier, treating an algorithm ID as strength, mixing 2017/2026 tables, occupying reserved ranges, or treating custom encoding as standard encoding. The 2026 edition takes effect on 2026-12-01; until then the 2017 edition applies, and both must be kept side by side. The standard defines representation only, not algorithm implementation or key management. items.title: GB/T 37092-2018 Cryptographic Module Security Requirements
items.text: Standard : Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules (密码模块安全要求). GB/T 37092-2018 breaks module security into 11 domains: specification, interfaces, roles/services/authentication, software/firmware, operating environment, physical, non-invasive, sensitive parameter management, self-tests, lifecycle assurance and mitigation of other attacks. Each domain is rated separately, and the overall level is the minimum of the 11 ratings, not an average. The levels rise cumulatively: L1 is the baseline; L2 adds tamper evidence and role-based authentication; L3 adds identity authentication, trusted channels, EFP/EFT and non-invasive mitigation evidence; L4 adds a full envelope, tamper-responsive zeroization, fault-injection protection and 2-of-3 multi-factor authentication. A pure software module caps at L2. The minimum-domain formula prevents one strong area from masking a weak one. Module type, cryptographic boundary and operating environment decide which domains apply; the same product can change level when its boundary or mode changes. The rating is a security-requirement matrix, not algorithm strength, a side-channel proof or product certification. It says which level a module reaches in which domains, not whether its algorithm remains secure. Design starts by fixing the module type and boundary, then lists requirements and evidence per domain; assessment rates each domain and takes the minimum. Software modules must decide the L2 ceiling at architecture time, before discovering that the physical domains cannot reach L3/L4. L3/L4 evidence focuses on trusted channels, identity authentication, EFP/EFT, full envelopes and tamper response, sensitive-parameter zeroization, and audit records that never contain sensitive parameters. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Common errors include treating module L4 as system L4, averaging the 11 domains, treating self-tests as certification, ignoring the software ceiling, or treating a revision plan “in approval” as a published edition. The standard does not fix algorithm suites and does not guarantee the absence of side channels; a module pass is not system security, and certification still needs an independent laboratory using the applicable scheme. items.title: SM9 Identity-Based Cryptographic Algorithm
items.text: Standard : SM9 Identity-Based Cryptography Algorithm (SM9 标识密码算法). Pairing and system parameters SM9 uses a bilinear pairing e:G1×G2→GT. The key-generation centre holds master secret ks and publishes Ppub=ksP2. The identity ID and hid are mapped by H1 to a scalar, and the user private key is d_{ID}=ks·(H1(ID‖hid,N)+ks)^{-1} mod N·P1. Signing The signer picks random r, computes w=e(P1,Ppub)^r, h=H2(M‖w,N) and l=(r−h) mod N, retrying if l=0; the signature is S=l·d_ID and output (h,S). Verification and encryption Verification computes u=e(S,H1(ID‖hid,N)P2+Ppub), w=u·g^h and checks H2(M‖w,N)=h. Encryption/KEM maps the identity to Q=H1(ID‖hid,N)P1+Ppub, picks random r, sets C1=rQ, derives from g=e(Ppub,Q)^r through a KDF. SM9 binds the public key directly to an identity and removes certificate chains; the KGC derives user private keys. It suits email, private networks and settings that want simpler certificate management. SM9 is identity-based; SM2 is certificate-based elliptic-curve public-key cryptography and SM4 is a block cipher. SM9’s trust root is the KGC, unlike SM2’s certificate model. 1. System parameters: use the standard curve, pairing and hash, and fix hid and identity encoding. 2. Key derivation: the KGC authenticates the identity, derives d_ID and delivers it securely, with update support. 3. Signing/encryption: use fresh random r; encrypt by KEM then symmetric encryption. 4. Verification: check pairings, h/S ranges and identity binding. Do not treat the KGC as a zero-trust party; do not mix keys across hid/parameters; do not present SM9 as quantum-resistant. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Key escrow: the KGC can derive any user key and must be audited as a trust root; master-key compromise breaks the system. 2. Pairing implementation: timing, cache and faults in pairing can leak keys or enable forgeries. 3. Identity and parameters: inconsistent hid, curve, hash or encoding causes interoperability failure or cross-domain attacks. 4. Protocol layer: missing identity binding, C1 checks or KDF output validation enables substitution or decryption errors. SM9 entered GM/T 0044 in 2016 and was published as GB/T 38635.1/2—2020 in 2020; ISO/IEC 18033-5 also covers identity-based ciphers. RFC 8998 does not cover SM9. SM9 signatures, key exchange, KEM and encryption are separate parts; implementations follow the claimed part and edition. - Wikipedia search entry for SM9 标识密码算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SM9%20%E6%A0%87%E8%AF%86%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] SM9 Identity-Based Cryptography Algorithm: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: TLCP Transport Layer Cryptography Protocol
items.text: Standard : TLCP (传输层密码协议). TLCP key calculation is TLS 1.2-style. First \(P\_hash(secret,seed)=HMAC(secret,A_1\ seed)\ HMAC(secret,A_2\ seed)\ \cdots\), with \(A_0=seed\) and \(A_i=HMAC(secret,A_{i-1})\); then \(PRF(secret,label,seed)=P\_hash(secret,label\ seed)\). The master secret is \(PRF(pre\_master,\text{“master secret”},client\_random\ server\_random)[0..47]\), exactly 48 bytes. The key block is \(PRF(master,\text{“key expansion”},server\_random\ client\_random)\), carved in client MAC, server MAC, client key, server key, client IV, server IV order. Finished takes \(verify\_data=PRF(master,label,SM3(handshake\_messages))[0..11]\), exactly 12 bytes. The record MAC covers \(seq\ type\ version\ length\ fragment\); AEAD additional data covers \(seq\ type\ version\ length\). TLCP is often mistaken for a “Chinese TLS 1.3”. Its version field is 0x0101 and its key schedule is TLS 1.2 PRF/P_hash, not HKDF; it uses SM2 for authentication and key exchange, SM3 for hashing and SM4 for record encryption. Dual certificates are another key difference: the signature certificate is only for authentication and the encryption certificate only for key exchange; they cannot be merged. Writing PRF, key_block, Finished and record MAC as formulas is how “Chinese TLS” is separated from TLS 1.3. When reading a handshake, check version 0x0101 and the suite ID, verify the signature certificate, then use the encryption certificate to recover the pre-master. Both sides compute the 48-byte master from \(client\_random\), \(server\_random\) and the pre-master, then the key_block; the carving order must not be reversed. For CBC records, the MAC covers sequence through fragment; for GCM, additional data covers only sequence, type, version and length, while the ciphertext is authenticated by AEAD. Finished hashes the handshake transcript with SM3 and verifies 12 bytes of \(verify\_data\). There are four boundaries. First, TLCP is TLS 1.2-style and does not support TLS 1.3 0-RTT, PSK or KeyUpdate; do not apply HKDF \(Extract/Expand\). Second, CBC suites must handle padding and MAC-then-Encrypt order correctly or fall into padding-oracle classes; GCM suites need unique nonces. Third, dual certificates require separate signature and encryption private keys; merging them or letting one key serve both uses breaks the standard separation. Fourth, the standard specifies protocol and key calculation, not implementation side channels, certificate lifecycle or deployment audits. GB/T 38636—2020 was published on 2020-04-28 and took effect on 2020-11-01, specifying the record layer, handshake family and key calculation; it positions TLCP as a transport-layer cryptographic protocol for SSL VPN gateways, browsers and similar products. Its suites use SM2/SM3/SM4 and retain RSA/IBC key-exchange branches; this account restates the standard text, not vendor implementations or TLS 1.3 features. - Wikipedia search entry for 传输层密码协议. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E4%BC%A0%E8%BE%93%E5%B1%82%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] TLCP: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: GB/T 39786-2021 Cryptography Application Baseline
items.text: Standard : Basic Requirements for Cryptography Application in Information Systems (信息系统密码应用基本要求). GB/T 39786-2021 writes information-system cryptography requirements as a four-level matrix. Levels 1 to 4 give both technical and management requirements; level 5 says only “omitted” and gives no technical/management clauses. The four technical layers are physical/environment, network/communication, device/computing, and application/data; the four management dimensions are policy, personnel, construction/operation and emergency response. The row count: technical 30 = physical 5 + network 7 + device 8 + application/data 10; management 19 = policy 6 + personnel 5 + construction/operation 5 + emergency 3; 49 rows total. Each row takes —/可/宜/应 across the four levels, in increasing strength; “可” is optional, “宜” recommended and “应” mandatory. The cryptographic-module level follows the system level: from L2 the module must be GB/T 37092 level 1+, L3 level 2+, L4 level 3+; the L1 product row is “—”. System level, technical/management rows and module level are therefore three different tables and cannot replace one another. The decision formula is Conform(S,k)=∀i R(i,k) satisfied ∧ P_k satisfied. It says whether the system at level k satisfies all applicable rows and the module level simultaneously; it is not a score. This is a baseline, not an assessment method. It states what levels 1-4 should do, not how an assessor samples, scores or records nonconformity; assessment also depends on the companion assessment standard and cryptographic-product certification. Why 49 rows rather than 30: the 30 technical rows are specific control points in four layers, while the 19 management rows are organisational controls for policy, personnel, construction/operation and emergency response; looking only at technology misses key management, job roles and response. Why level 5 is separate: the standard gives only general requirements and says the technical/management clauses are “omitted”; treating level 5 as “level 4 plus a few rows” misreads it. Why module level is separate: a level-3 system requires a level-2+ module, not “system level 3 = module level 3”; module level is the assurance level of a certified product, system level is the business/data protection level. Deployment order: 1) determine the system level from business/data; 2) take the applicable technical and management rows of that level from the 49; 3) map each row to a cryptographic service, product or process; 4) choose the module level for the system level; 5) manage the ten key-life-cycle stages per Annex B; 6) keep evidence of policy, records, assessment and emergency response. A typical mapping: L1 has minimum technical measures plus basic policy/key rules; L2 adds operating procedures, job responsibility, training and response plans; L3 adds authenticity/confidentiality, policy revision/release/records, assessment and drills; L4 adds integrity/non-repudiation. The ten key stages are generation, distribution, storage, use, update, archive, revocation, backup, recovery and destruction; an archived key only decrypts/verifies historical data, and destruction must be irreversible. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. “可” does not mean “recommended”: in this baseline it is optional; but once the system level is set, assessment judges the value at that level and does not pass a row merely because it says “可”. The standard does not replace an assessment verdict, GB/T 37092 product certification or a key-life-cycle audit, and it does not guarantee a particular algorithm or product. Level 5 has no technical/management clauses; do not infer it from L4. Common errors: reading only the 30 technical rows and missing the 19 management rows; equating module level with system level; writing “应” as “宜”; treating Annex B’s informative advice as mandatory; treating the 49 rows as a score sheet. items.title: GB/T 43206-2023 Cryptography Application Assessment Requirements
items.text: Standard : Requirements for Cryptography Application Assessment (信息系统密码应用测评要求). GB/T 43206-2023 targets information systems built to GB/T 39786: it judges assessment units, performs an overall assessment and risk analysis, and then gives one of three conclusions: conform, basically conform or nonconform. A unit is judged by objects and checks: a single object conforms only if every check is yes; a no on key item 6.x.3c is direct nonconform; otherwise partial. Multiple objects conform only if all conform and are nonconform only if all fail; a mix is partial. Unit results cannot simply be averaged; the overall assessment may adjust for object count or importance, while high risk can veto. This prevents a high-scoring area from hiding a critical gap. The standard provides decision logic, not a percentage. Quantitative scoring comes from separate rules; both may be used, but the percentage must not be written as a GB/T 43206 conclusion formula. Evidence covers algorithm/product compliance, key management, physical/network/device/application data, and policy/people/construction/emergency management. For multi-object systems, sampling, object count and importance must be stated; high-risk items need their trigger conditions and impact recorded separately, not merely deducted from a total score. items.title: Glitch Attack
items.text: Attack : Glitch Attack (毛刺攻击). CRT-RSA first computes \(S_p=m^d\bmod p\) and \(S_q=m^d\bmod q\), then combines them by the Chinese remainder theorem: \(S=S_q+q\,(i_q(S_p-S_q)\bmod p)\). If a glitch corrupts only one half exponentiation, say \(\hat S_p\neq S_p\), the combined signature \(\hat S\) is still output-shaped, but its difference from the correct \(S\) is a multiple of \(q\). Thus \(\gcd(N,S-\hat S)=q\) (or \(p\)) and one fault factors \(N\). Even without the correct signature, \(\gcd(N,\hat S^e-m)=q\) works, where \(e\) is the public exponent. A glitch turns an implementation error into a factor leak: RSA assumes \(N\) is hard to factor, but a CRT implementation with one bad half exponentiation leaks \(p\) or \(q\). This is far cheaper than trial factoring and needs no private key; it exploits an observable computation error, not a mathematical flaw in the algorithm. Smart cards, TPMs and secure elements therefore treat “verify before output” and redundant computation as mandatory. A typical run fixes a known message \(m\), asks the device for a CRT-RSA signature, injects a clock/voltage glitch during one half exponentiation to corrupt a register or skip an instruction, and collects the faulty \(\hat S\). Then it computes \(\gcd(N,S-\hat S)\) or \(\gcd(N,\hat S^e-m)\). A nontrivial factor recovers \(p,q\) and the private key. The experiment must localize the glitch window, corrupt only one half exponentiation and avoid a reset or an output check that blocks the faulty signature. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Dates, counts and device parameters without a source are left blank; primary material outranks secondary summaries. Boneh, DeMillo and Lipton systematized this attack in 1997; Lenstra then gave a variant needing only one faulty signature and the message. Later literature calls the CRT-RSA fault model BellCoRe and develops verification, redundancy and infective countermeasures. Rauzy and Guilley in 2014 classified existing countermeasures and discussed instruction-skip faults. Glitch attacks are therefore a declared attack surface in secure-element certification, not a laboratory curiosity. - Wikipedia search entry for 毛刺攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%AF%9B%E5%88%BA%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Glitch Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: GM/T 0002-2012 SM4 Block Cipher
items.text: Standard : GM/T 0002-2012 SM4 Block Cipher Algorithm (GM/T 0002-2012 SM4 分组密码算法). GM/T 0002-2012 specifies SM4 as a 128-bit block, 128-bit key, 32-round iterated cipher. The key MK is split into MK0..MK3 and XORed with FK to form K0..K3; each schedule step mixes K_i..K_{i+3} and CK_i through T′ to produce rk_i=K_{i+4}. Encryption loads X0..X3 from the plaintext and computes X_{i+4}=X_i⊕T(X_{i+1}⊕X_{i+2}⊕X_{i+3}⊕rk_i). T applies an 8×8 S-box and a linear layer with 2/10/18/24-bit rotations; after 32 rounds X35..X32 are written out in reverse word order. Decryption keeps the same structure and only reverses rk_0..rk_31. SM4 is a foundational block cipher in the Chinese commercial cryptography stack: TLCP, IPsec, cryptographic modules and many sector standards reference it. Writing the round function, key schedule and test vectors makes an implementation checkable instead of merely labelled “SM4-capable”. Implement the four 32-bit state words and 32 round keys first, then generate rk through T′. A practical check order is: FK/CK constants, rk_0=f12186f9, the first plaintext block to 681edf34d206965e86b3e94f536e4246, and finally the million-iteration example. A block cipher only permutes one 128-bit block. Multi-block data needs CBC, CTR, GCM or another mode; authentication needs a MAC or AEAD. Do not treat “SM4 encryption” as a complete protocol, and do not use a passphrase directly as the key. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. S-box lookups, rotations and round-key loads can leak cache, power, electromagnetic or fault information; smart cards, embedded devices and shared CPUs need masking, randomization and constant-time code. The block cipher alone gives no integrity, replay protection or identity authentication. CBC padding errors, CTR nonce reuse and careless GCM failure handling can bypass the algorithm’s security boundary. The key is fixed at 128 bits; a longer passphrase does not repair a weak key. SM4’s predecessor SMS4 was declassified in January 2006 and first used in WAPI. On 2012-03-21 the NCA published GM/T 0002-2012, renaming it SM4 and specifying the structure, key schedule and two worked examples. The national standard GB/T 32907-2016 followed in 2016, and SM4 entered ISO/IEC 18033-3/Amd 1 in 2021. items.title: GM/T 0003-2012 SM2 Public Key Algorithms
items.text: Standard : GM/T 0003-2012 SM2 Public Key Cryptographic Algorithms (GM/T 0003-2012 SM2 椭圆曲线公钥密码算法). GM/T 0003-2012 divides SM2 into general, digital signature, key exchange, public-key encryption and parameter definition. Signing starts from a 256-bit prime-field curve E: y²=x³+ax+b mod p, base point G of prime order n, cofactor h=1; private key d_A∈[1,n-2] and public key P_A=[d_A]G. Before signing, ENTL_A, ID_A, a, b, x_G, y_G, x_A and y_A are bound into Z_A, and Z_A‖M is hashed into e. Choose k∈[1,n-1], compute (x1,y1)=[k]G and r=(e+x1) mod n; retry if r=0 or r+k=n. Then s=((1+d_A)^-1(k-r d_A)) mod n; retry if s=0 and output (r,s). Verification computes t=(r+s) mod n, rebuilds (x1,y1)=[s]G+[t]P_A, sets R=(e+x1) mod n and accepts only if R=r. SM2 is not “ECDSA with another curve”. Z_A binds the user identity, curve parameters and public key into the signed input, so the same message yields different e under different identities or parameters; the (1+d_A)^-1 factor in s also differs from ECDSA’s k^-1 form. Writing these formulas makes the separation between SM2 signing, encryption and key exchange explicit, and explains why range checks alone are insufficient: verification must rebuild R and reject t=0. For signing, record the intermediate values in Z_A→e→k→r→s order and retry on any zero. Verification first checks r,s∈[1,n-1], then computes t and rejects t=0. For encryption, take the recipient public key P_B, choose k, compute C1=[k]G, S=[k]P_B, K=KDF(x2‖y2,klen), C2=M⊕K and C3=H(x2‖M‖y2); decryption checks C3 before recovering M. Use the Part 5 p, a, b, n and G values; a homemade curve or altered base point breaks interoperability. Signing and encryption are domain-separated flows: a signature is not a ciphertext, and C1 is not a signature. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Reusing, predicting or sharing k across devices exposes the private key through repeated r; checking only r,s ranges without t≠0 can accept degenerate inputs. A wrong Z_A concatenation order, ENTL byte order or ID encoding breaks interoperability. SM2 is a public-key system: certificates, name constraints and revocation still bind the key. Signing gives no confidentiality; encryption gives no signer authentication. Scalar multiplication, modular inversion and KDF must be constant-time against side channels. SM2 was published in 2010 and issued on 2012-03-21 as the five-part GM/T 0003-2012, covering general, signature, key exchange, encryption and parameters; it became the GB/T 32918 series in 2016. items.title: SM3 Hash Standard
items.text: Standard : SM3 Industry Standard (SM3 杂凑行标). Padding and blocks SM3 outputs 256 bits. The message is padded with a 1 bit, zeros and a 64-bit length so that its length is ≡ 448 mod 512; each 512-bit block enters the compression function. Message expansion The first 16 words W0…W15 come from the block; the rest follow W_j=P1(W_{j−16}⊕W_{j−9}⊕ROL15(W_{j−3}))⊕ROL7(W_{j−13})⊕W_{j−6}, with W′_j=W_j⊕W_{j+4} for 64 rounds. Compression State A…H is updated over 64 rounds; each round computes SS1, SS2, TT1 and TT2 using FF/GG and P0/P1, with SS1=ROL7(ROL12(A)+E+ROL_j(T_j)). Finally V_{i+1}=CF(V_i,M_i), and the 256-bit chaining value is output. SM3 provides a 256-bit output, 64-round compression and fixed IV, giving a birthday bound near 2^128 for signatures, certificates, TLS handshakes and HMAC. It joins SM2 and SM4 in the national protocol suite. SM3 is a hash, not encryption; it gives integrity but not authentication by itself, which needs HMAC or a signature. 1. Integrity: hash the message with SM3, then sign with SM2 when a signature is needed. 2. Authentication: use HMAC-SM3 with the standard key and output sizes. 3. Domain separation: prefix different purposes or contexts to avoid cross-protocol reuse. 4. Verify vectors: run standard test vectors and check padding and length fields. items.title: GM/T 0028 Cryptographic Module Security
items.text: Standard : GM/T 0028 Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules (GM/T 0028 密码模块安全要求). GM/T 0028 describes cryptographic modules with four increasing security levels: Level 1 gives basic security functions and CSP establishment; Level 2 adds tamper evidence and role-based authentication; Level 3 adds stronger physical protection and a trusted channel; Level 4 adds a full envelope, environmental zeroization, multi-factor authentication and design consistency verification. The 2024 edition organizes requirements into 11 domains: specification, interfaces, roles/services/authentication, software/firmware, environment, physical security, non-invasive security, CSP management, self-test, lifecycle and other-attack mitigation. Each domain is rated independently, and the overall level is the minimum of the 11; a high rating in one domain cannot hide a weak domain elsewhere. A cryptographic module is the physical or logical carrier of keys, algorithms and randomness. Saying “supports SM4/SM2” does not answer whether it resists tampering, zeroizes safely or self-tests. Writing the 11 domains and the minimum rule as a decision formula lets procurement, testing and development use the same table. The 2014/2024 difference must also be kept: the older edition used 12 clauses including general requirements, while the 2024 edition states 11 domains and an overall minimum. Mixing the two produces inconsistent level conclusions. List the 11 domains for the product form and attach evidence to each: specification and interface documents, role/service matrix, software/firmware update and integrity, environment assumptions, physical envelope and tamper response, non-invasive testing, CSP generation/input/storage/zeroization, self-test cases, lifecycle configuration and delivery, and other-attack mitigation. The overall level is the lowest domain; if one domain misses the target, the module drops. Level 4 additionally checks that multi-factor authentication covers at least two of know/have/be, and that tamper or environmental anomalies zeroize unprotected CSPs. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. A module level does not replace a system assessment: key lifecycle, access control, backup/recovery, operator privileges and supply chain can still break overall security. Software modules have limited physical assurance; a software claim is not a hardware envelope. A high-level module can still fail through bad deployment, a weak RNG or key leakage. Self-test failure must enter an error state and stop cryptographic services, not “log and continue”; tamper response must cover unprotected CSPs, not just a warning lamp. Mixing 2014 and 2024 clauses, or treating the 11-domain minimum as an average, produces the wrong level. GM/T 0028-2014 Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules was published and effective on 2014-02-13, 64 pages, non-equivalent to ISO/IEC 19790:2012, with four levels, 12 clauses and 11 security domains. GM/T 0028-2024 Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules was published on 2024-12-27, effective 2025-07-01, 60 pages, fully replacing the 2014 edition; NCA Announcement No. 50 abolished the old edition. items.title: GM/T 0044 SM9 Identity-based Algorithms
items.text: Standard : GM/T 0044 SM9 Identity-based Cryptographic Algorithms (GM/T 0044 SM9 标识密码算法). SM9 uses a bilinear pairing e:G1×G2→GT on a BN curve. The KGC keeps the signing master secret ks and publishes P_pub-s=[ks]P2; user A’s signing key is identity-derived: ds_A=[ks/(H1(ID_A)+ks)]P1. Signing computes g=e(P1,P_pub-s), chooses r, sets w=g^r and h=H2(M‖w,N), then l=(r-h) mod N and S=[l]ds_A, outputting (h,S). Verification computes t=g^h, P=[H1(ID_A)]P2+P_pub-s and u=e(S,P), sets w′=u·t and checks H2(M‖w′,N)=h. KEM uses the encryption public key P_pub-e to form Q_B=[H1(ID_B‖hid,N)]P1+P_pub-e, chooses r, and computes C=[r]Q_B, g=e(P_pub-e,P2), w=g^r and K=KDF(C‖w‖ID_B,klen). SM9 removes certificates from public keys: a user public key is derived from the identity, and the KGC issues private keys with its master secret. The cost is a single point of trust: master-key compromise affects the whole identity domain, and signing and encryption master keys must be separated so one domain does not drag down the other. Writing the pairing, ds_A, g/w/h and rehash makes clear why (h,S) cannot be split, and why verification must check S∈G1, pair and rehash rather than compare h alone. Deployment fixes the system parameters, BN curve, P1/P2 and hash functions H1/H2; the KGC generates separate signing and encryption master keys and protects them. User registration derives signing/encryption keys from the ID, and private keys must be delivered over a trusted channel. Signing records g→r→w→h→l→S; verification checks S∈G1, then computes t, P, u, w′ and h′. KEM/encryption forms Q_B from the recipient ID, computes C=[r]Q_B, w and KDF, then wraps data with SM4 or another symmetric cipher. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The KGC is a single point of trust: master-key compromise, a forged private key or identity-registration takeover breaks the ownership of signatures and ciphertexts. Identity privacy also needs assessment: the ID directly enters public-key derivation and is not anonymous by default. A signature (h,S) cannot be published as h alone or treated as a key; verification must check S∈G1 and reject infinity or wrong subgroups. Pairing, all-zero KDF output and r reuse must be handled; KEM only encapsulates a key and does not provide message confidentiality by itself. Identity-based cryptography was proposed by Shamir in 1984. SM9 was published on 2016-03-28 as the five-part GM/T 0044-2016, covering general, signature, key exchange, KEM/encryption and parameters. The GB/T 38635 series raised it to a national standard in 2020. The 2025 revision GM/T 0044.1—0044.5-2025 took effect on 2026-07-01 and abolished the 2016 parts on the same date; current use should check parameters, signatures and KEM against the current edition. - Wikipedia search entry for GM/T 0044 SM9 标识密码算法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=GM%2FT%200044%20SM9%20%E6%A0%87%E8%AF%86%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E7%AE%97%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] GM/T 0044 SM9 Identity-based Cryptographic Algorithms: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: GM/T 0054-2018 Cryptography Baseline
items.text: Standard : GM/T 0054-2018 General Requirements for Information System Cryptography Application (GM/T 0054-2018 信息系统密码应用基本要求). GM/T 0054-2018 splits information-system cryptography into four technical layers: physical/environment, network/communication, device/compute and application/data. Each layer states requirements by protection level 1 to 4 and marks them shall/should/may for mandatory, recommended and permitted. Besides the technical layers, the standard separates key management and requires security policy, people, implementation and response. Formally, given system S, level L, layer d and item p, R(L,d,p) is shall/should/may; Pass(S,L) requires every shall item to hold, and Overall(S) is the highest level that passes. This 2018 industry standard was the early baseline for cryptography assessment pilots: it answers “how should systems at different levels use cryptography”, while GM/T 0115 answers “how to assess it”. Merging the two turns requirements into a score and erases the difference between the 2018 edition and the 2021 national GB/T 39786. The shall/should/may semantics also decide conformity: a system cannot offset a missing shall item with strong should items; key management and security management are baseline parts, not appendices. For a gap analysis, fix the system level L, then fill R(L,d,p) and current S(d,p) for the four technical layers plus key management, policy, people, implementation and response. Only shall items are mandatory remediation; should items are improvements; may items are context-dependent. Assessment uses the GM/T 0115 units, objects and quantitative rules; the Pass predicate here is not a scoring formula. When citing the national baseline, use GB/T 39786-2021 and keep the 2018 industry edition as a version coordinate. items.title: GM/T 0115-2021 Testing Requirements for Information System Cryptography Application
items.text: Standard : Testing and Evaluation Requirements for Information System Cryptography Application (信息系统密码应用测评要求). GM/T 0115-2021 sets testing requirements for information-system cryptography application. The companion quantitative rule turns results into a reproducible score chain. At object level each tested object is scored 0, 0.25, 0.5 or 1; at unit level the object scores are averaged; at layer level applicable units are weight-averaged; at overall level the eight layers are weight-averaged and multiplied by 100. An object score is not a single pass/fail: it combines deployment effectiveness, algorithm/technique compliance and key-management security. All three give 1; effectiveness alone with gaps in the other two gives 0.5 or 0.25; no cryptography or ineffective use gives 0. The design separates “cryptography is used” from “it is used correctly, compliantly and with protected keys”, preventing a feature checklist from masking weak deployment. Practitioners list applicable units under GB/T 39786 and GM/T 0115, collect evidence per object, average the unit, weight the layer, compute the 100-point total and then perform risk judgement. Not-applicable indicators must be justified and leave the numerator and denominator; if an entire layer is NA, the remaining weights are renormalised, e.g. physical NA leaves a denominator of 90. items.title: GM/T 0125 Chinese JOSE
items.text: Standard : Chinese JSON Object Signing and Encryption (国密 JSON Web 语法). GM/T 0125.2—2022 JWS has a JOSE header, payload and signature. The protected header is UTF-8 then base64url: \(protected\_b64=base64url(UTF8(header))\); the payload is \(payload\_b64=base64url(payload)\). The signing input is \(M=ASCII(protected\_b64\ \text{“.”}\ payload\_b64)\). \(SGD\_SM3\_SM2\) signs \(M\) with an SM2 private key, hashes with SM3 and encodes the signature in DER; \(SGD\_SM3\_HMAC\) computes \(HMAC\text{-}SM3(K,M)\) with 256-bit output. Compact serialization is \(protected\_b64\ \text{“.”}\ payload\_b64\ \text{“.”}\ base64url(sig)\); JSON serialization supports multiple signatures, but the union of protected and unprotected headers must have a required \(alg\) and unique names. Chinese JOSE is not just “JWT with a different signature algorithm”. It treats \(alg\) as the algorithm identifier, \(kid/jwk/x5c/x5t sm3\) as key identifiers, and separates protected from unprotected headers; a verifier that reads only the \(alg\) string without checking the key type repeats JWS algorithm confusion. The formula-level split is threefold: signing input is protected_b64 dot payload_b64; SM2 output is DER; HMAC output is 256 bits; verification requires \(alg\in Allow(key)\) and \(key=KeyStore[Id]\). To generate, choose the algorithm first: \(SGD\_SM3\_SM2\) for SM2 signatures or \(SGD\_SM3\_HMAC\) for a shared-key MAC; build and encode the protected header, form \(M\), compute the signature and base64url it. To verify, parse compact or JSON serialization, check that \(alg\) exists and is allowed for the key, locate the key by \(kid/jwk/x5c/x5t sm3\), rebuild \(M\) and verify. In multi-signature cases verify each signature; unprotected headers may carry presentation data but must not be the sole basis for a security decision. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. There are four boundaries. First, unprotected headers are outside the signature and can be changed; any header that affects a security decision belongs in the protected header. Second, \(alg\) and key type must bind: treating an SM2 public key as an HMAC key or accepting \(none\) breaks verification. Third, base64url must omit padding and decode by the standard, and duplicate header parameters in JSON serialization must be rejected. Fourth, SM2 signatures are DER-encoded and not a fixed 64 bytes; implementations must not slice DER as a fixed-length value. The standard does not define JWT claim semantics, key lifecycle or side-channel protection. GM/T 0125 “JSON Web cryptographic application syntax specification” was published on 2022-11-20 and took effect on 2023-06-01, in four parts: algorithm identifiers, signatures, data encryption and keys. Part 2 specifies JWS, with \(SGD\_SM3\_SM2\) and \(SGD\_SM3\_HMAC\) generation/verification and compact/JSON examples. items.title: GM/T 0128-2023 Datagram Transport Layer Cryptography Protocol
items.text: Standard : Specification of Datagram Transport Layer Cryptography Protocol (数据报传输层密码协议规范). GM/T 0128-2023 defines DTLCP: it adapts the TLCP record layer, handshake family and key calculation to UDP loss, reordering, duplication and amplification attacks. The record header adds epoch and a 48-bit seq_num; handshake messages add message_seq, fragment_offset and fragment_length. Large messages are fragmented to path MTU and reassembled by the receiver. UDP has no TCP connection state or byte-stream semantics, so TLS record rules cannot be copied directly. Cookies let the server validate the source before spending state; explicit sequence numbers let the receiver make replay decisions without a connection. Epoch increments on key change, separating “sequence under the old key” from “sequence under the new key” and preventing cross-key replay. The handshake starts with ClientHello; the server returns HelloVerifyRequest with a cookie, and the client resends with the cookie. Parameters, certificates, ClientKeyExchange and Finished follow. Key material derives in three levels: pre-master → master → working keys. Working keys split into client/server encryption, integrity and IV keys, selected by direction at the record layer. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. A common error is treating DTLCP as “TLCP over UDP”: DTLCP records carry explicit sequence numbers, fragmentation and reassembly, unlike TLS implicit sequence numbers and byte streams. Cookies stop spoofed sources and amplification, not identity; replay-window size is not a fixed standard value. Certificates, trust chains, revocation and Finished still follow PKI and protocol rules. items.title: Goldreich–Levin theorem
items.text: Theorem : Goldreich-Levin Theorem (Goldreich-Levin 定理). The inner product is a hard-core bit for any OWF Let f:{0,1}^n→{0,1}^{m(n)} be a one-way function. Write the input as (p,x) with p = x =n and define g(p,x) = (p, f(x)), b(p,x) = p·x mod 2 = Σ_i p_i x_i mod 2. The Goldreich–Levin theorem says b is a hard-core predicate for g. Even given p and f(x), every polynomial-time algorithm has negligible advantage in predicting b unless it can invert f. The prediction advantage If A satisfies Pr[A(p,f(x)) = b(p,x)] ≥ 1/2 + ε(n) with non-negligible ε, then a probabilistic polynomial-time inverter B exists, running in time poly(n,1/ε), that recovers x from f(x) with probability poly(ε). The least significant bit of RSA and particular bits of discrete log have their own concrete hard-core proofs; GL gives a generic result: every one-way function has a hard-core bit. It lifts “hide one bit” from a specific assumption to a general theorem. GL supplies one bit of computational entropy; HILL combines these bits, OWF iteration and universal hashing into a pseudorandom generator. Without GL, the OWF→PRG chain lacks its first block. - Hard-core bit: after f(x) is public, a linear function of x remains hidden; it can build PRGs, commitments and hidden challenges in zero knowledge. - PRG: iterate the OWF and extract hard-core bits, then use a hybrid argument to show unpredictability; this generalizes the Blum–Micali generator. - Reduction: turn a predictor of the inner product into an algorithm that inverts f; this is a standard step in OWF-to-PRG proofs. Reading: fix f and the input length, check that p and x have equal length; if f is not length-preserving, pad first. items.title: Goldwasser–Micali Probabilistic Encryption
items.text: Theorem : Goldwasser-Micali Probabilistic Encryption (Goldwasser-Micali 概率加密). One bit at a time Goldwasser–Micali (GM) encrypts a single bit per operation. The public key is (N,x) , where N=pq and x is a quadratic non-residue modulo N ; the private key is p,q . To encrypt bit m_i , pick a random y and compute c_i=y²·x^{m_i} mod N : bit 0 yields a quadratic residue, bit 1 a non-residue. Decryption and homomorphism The holder of p,q decides whether c_i is a quadratic residue modulo N and recovers the bit. Multiplying two ciphertexts XORs the bits: E(b1)·E(b2)=E(b1⊕b2) . GM is XOR-homomorphic, not additively homomorphic. Security definition GM’s importance is not efficiency but the first provable definition of probabilistic public-key encryption and semantic security: under the quadratic residuosity assumption, the ciphertext leaks no polynomially computable information about the plaintext. GM answered the question “how secure should public-key encryption be?” Before it, “the attacker cannot recover the plaintext” was often the standard. GM introduced semantic security: given a ciphertext, the adversary cannot guess any function of the plaintext better than guessing without the ciphertext. Its second contribution is probabilistic encryption: every encryption of the same bit differs, so an attacker cannot re-encrypt candidate plaintexts and compare. The modern IND-CPA definition grew out of this line. Because of its expansion, GM is rarely used for bulk data. Its value is in theoretical constructions and protocol subroutines: zero-knowledge proofs, secure multiparty computation, private information retrieval and small XOR-homomorphic circuits. Read this entry as a milestone of semantic security, not as a recommended production cipher. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. GM encrypts one bit into roughly N bits; a message expands by hundreds of times and encryption is slow. It supports XOR homomorphism only, not ordinary addition or multiplication. The original scheme is not IND-CCA2 secure. Implementations must also ensure x is a quadratic non-residue, N is a product of two large primes, and the random y is coprime to N . Real systems do not use GM in place of AES or RSA-OAEP. Goldwasser and Micali presented “Probabilistic Encryption & How to Play Mental Poker, Keeping Secret All Partial Information” at STOC 1982 and published the journal version “Probabilistic Encryption” in Journal of Computer and System Sciences 28(2):270–299 in 1984. The paper established the language of semantic security, probabilistic encryption and polynomial-time indistinguishability. Later IND-CPA and IND-CCA definitions extended this tradition. - Wikipedia search entry for Goldwasser-Micali 概率加密. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Goldwasser-Micali%20%E6%A6%82%E7%8E%87%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Goldwasser-Micali Probabilistic Encryption: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Goldwasser–Sipser Ladder
items.text: Theorem : Goldwasser-Sipser Ladder (Goldwasser-Sipser 层次化方法). The promise problem of a set lower bound Let S ⊆ {0,1}^m be a set whose membership can be efficiently certified. The verifier knows a parameter K and must distinguish two cases: S ≥ K (YES) and S ≤ K/16 (NO). The protocol does not count S ; it uses a random hash to make the prover demonstrate that the set is large enough. The catalog labels this entry “ladder”; here we unfold its executable mechanism, the Goldwasser–Sipser set lower bound protocol. A one-round public-coin protocol The verifier selects h: {0,1}^m → {1,…,K/4} from a pairwise-independent hash family H_{m,k}, samples y uniformly from the same range, and sends (h,y) to the prover. The prover finds x∈S with h(x)=y and attaches a certificate that x∈S; the verifier checks the certificate and the hash hit. Completeness and soundness If S ≥ K, the probability that a random y is hit by S is 1 - (1 - 4/K)^K ≥ 2/3. If S ≤ K/16, then h(S) covers at most (K/16)/(K/4) = 1/4 of the hash range, so no prover can make a random y hit with probability above 1/4. The protocol is therefore a public-coin approximate lower bound: it does not give the exact S , only a 2/3 versus 1/4 gap between “large enough” and “much smaller”. Computing S exactly can be P-hard, but many protocols only need to distinguish “large enough” from “half as large”. A hash hit turns a cardinality comparison into one membership proof, and the verifier need not enumerate S. Arora and Barak’s textbook simplifies the original lemma to one hash, one random y and a K/16 promise gap: the hash range is K/4, a large set is hit with probability at least 2/3, and a small set lets no prover succeed with probability above 1/4. The original paper instead used l random linear hashes and l² target strings to amplify the hit probability and prove IP[k] ⊆ AM[k+2]. The set lower bound protocol is not an encryption scheme, but it demonstrates the pattern of compressing cardinality information with random hashing; membership proofs, approximate counting and private set intersection use related hash/commitment structures. 1. Both parties agree on K and the hash range R = K/4; the verifier selects a pairwise-independent h and a random y. 2. The prover finds x∈S with h(x)=y and supplies a membership certificate. 3. The verifier checks the certificate and the hit; acceptance means S is very likely ≥ K. 4. For higher confidence, repeat independently; the error decreases exponentially with the number of rounds. 5. Record the hash family, range, repetition count and the membership-certificate check. The AM protocol for GNI, simulations of IP=AM, approximate counting, set-size lower bounds, and the teaching and design of interactive proofs. 1. No K/16 promise gap: if S lies between K/16 and K, the protocol does not guarantee a correct decision. 2. Membership is not efficiently certifiable: the prover cannot supply a certificate for x∈S. 3. The hash family is not pairwise-independent, or its randomness is predictable: the completeness/soundness proof fails. 4. The verifier reuses the same y or h: the prover can precompute a hit. 5. The prover is unbounded but the verifier implementation is flawed: the protocol proves an interactive proof, not implementation security. 6. Reading “the set is large” as “the set contents are known”: the protocol does not reveal the elements of S. The GS protocol is an interactive proof, not encryption or a signature; it provides no zero knowledge and does not prove the exact value of S . The constants 2/3 and 1/4 are common parameters, not the only choice. In their STOC 1986 paper, Goldwasser and Sipser proved that private-coin interactive proofs and public-coin Arthur–Merlin proofs recognise the same languages. The key tool was the approximate lower bound lemma: Carter–Wegman universal hashing turns a lower bound on set size into a hit probability. The original paper used l random linear hashes and l² target strings to amplify the hit probability, obtaining IP[k] ⊆ AM[k+2]. Later textbooks simplified it to one hash, one random y and a K/16 gap, producing today’s common set lower bound protocol. The set lower bound protocol remains a basic component of interactive proofs and counting complexity; in cryptography it is more a methodology for compressing cardinality information with random hashing than a directly deployed protocol. - Wikipedia search entry for Goldwasser-Sipser 层次化方法. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Goldwasser-Sipser%20%E5%B1%82%E6%AC%A1%E5%8C%96%E6%96%B9%E6%B3%95 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Goldwasser-Sipser Ladder: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: GRAIN Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : GRAIN (GRAIN 流密码). A hardware stream cipher with an 80-bit key and 64-bit IV GRAIN loads an 80-bit key K into an 80-bit nonlinear feedback shift register (NFSR) B, and a 64-bit IV plus a 16-bit all-ones constant into an 80-bit linear feedback shift register (LFSR) S. The LFSR recurrence guarantees a long period; the quadratic and cubic terms of the NFSR supply nonlinearity; an output filter mixes taps from both registers into one keystream bit. 160 initialization clocks After loading, the cipher runs 160 blank clocks. Each clock still updates B and S, but the output bit is XORed back into both feedback inputs, so every key and IV bit diffuses through the 160-bit state. Only then does output begin: z_t = ⊕_{i∈A} b_{t+i} ⊕ h(s_{t+3}, s_{t+25}, s_{t+46}, s_{t+64}, b_{t+63}), A={1,2,4,10,31,43,56}. Family and standards Grain-128 extends the key/IV to 128/96 bits and uses 256 initialization clocks; Grain-128a adds optional authentication and enters the ISO/IEC 29167-13 RFID crypto suite; Grain-128AEAD v2 reached the final of the NIST lightweight cryptography competition as the only stream cipher in that round. GRAIN targets gate count, power and memory, not software throughput. One 80-bit LFSR, one 80-bit NFSR and a combinational filter produce the keystream without AES S-boxes or large lookup tables. The simplest implementation emits one bit per clock; unrolling to 16 bits per clock trades area for speed. That makes it suitable for RFID tags, wireless sensors and extremely tight embedded secure boot. Grain v1 is in the eSTREAM hardware portfolio and Grain-128a is standardized in ISO/IEC 29167-13, so its role is a dedicated stream cipher for constrained environments, not general server encryption. Grain-128A provides authentication and encryption between RFID tags and interrogators over ISO/IEC 18000 air interfaces, with authentication as an optional service. Grain-128AEAD targets lightweight IoT links that need confidentiality and integrity together. Grain v1 appears mostly in hardware crypto cores, sensor nodes and cryptographic teaching and analysis. It can also serve as a pseudorandom bit generator, but encryption use requires XOR with plaintext and strict IV discipline. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. GRAIN is a synchronous stream cipher: reusing the same key and IV reproduces the same keystream, and the XOR of two ciphertexts reveals the XOR of the plaintexts. Grain v1 has no built-in authentication. Grain-128a authentication is an optional protocol capability; a deployment must actually enable and verify the tag, or an attacker can alter ciphertext undetected. Initialization depth is part of the security boundary. Grain v1 uses 160 clocks and Grain-128 uses 256 to achieve diffusion; cutting initialization to a few dozen clocks exposes cube attacks, guess-and-determine attacks and near-collision analysis. Published results mostly target reduced rounds or weakened initialization, but that is not permission to reduce the round count. Bit-serial hardware also leaks power and electromagnetic information. A physical adversary requires masking, dual-rail logic or constant-power design. Algorithmic security and implementation security are separate acceptance criteria. Hell, Johansson and Meier submitted Grain to eSTREAM in 2005, and Grain v1 entered the hardware portfolio. Grain-128 moved to a 128-bit key in 2006; Grain-128a added optional authentication in 2011 and later became the ISO/IEC 29167-13 RFID crypto suite. Grain-128AEAD v2 reached the final of the NIST lightweight cryptography process as the only stream cipher in the last round. The line shows the evolution of minimal hardware design: first gate count, then key size, then authentication and AEAD. - Wikipedia search entry for GRAIN 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=GRAIN%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] GRAIN: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
