items.title: Groth16 zk-SNARK
items.text: Algorithm : Groth16 zk-SNARK (Groth16 证明系统). From R1CS to three group elements Groth16 is a preprocessing zk-SNARK for arithmetic circuits. The circuit is encoded as R1CS (one multiplication constraint per row), then converted through a Quadratic Arithmetic Program (QAP) into polynomial equations. Using a common reference string (CRS), the prover commits to the witness polynomials and outputs three bilinear-group elements A, B, C . The verifier checks one pairing-product equation plus a linear combination of public inputs. The proof reveals nothing about the witness, and verification is essentially independent of circuit size — the efficiency breakthrough of 2016. Groth16 compresses “this computation is correct” into a few hundred bytes and a handful of pairings. Compared with earlier Pinocchio-style systems, it reduced the proof to three group elements and verification to a single equation, making it attractive for recursive proofs and on-chain verification. The price is a circuit-specific CRS. Change the circuit and the parameters must be regenerated, so Groth16 suits fixed circuits rather than frequently changing universal virtual machines. Groth16 became one of the most common backends for privacy transactions and early zk-Rollups; Zcash Sapling uses a Groth16-based proving system. It is also used as an inner proof in recursive constructions because proofs are small and verification is cheap. In practice it appears with Circom, snarkjs, bellman and similar toolchains. Proving remains expensive; verification is light. If the “toxic waste” in the CRS is not destroyed, its holder can forge proofs; every circuit change needs a new ceremony. It also relies on R1CS encoding, pairing-friendly curves and random-oracle/generic-group assumptions; it is not post-quantum. Prover work grows with circuit size and needs parallelism for very large circuits. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. The paper does not prove that three elements are the absolute minimum; it explicitly leaves open whether two-element proofs can be ruled out. items.title: Group Signature
items.text: Algorithm : Group Signature (组签名). Group public key and member credentials A manager generates a group public key gpk and member credentials; in BBS04 the credential is A=(g1·h0^{sk}·h1^{m})^{1/(x+e)}, the signature hides A in a proof of knowledge, and the opener recovers A with x. BBS instantiation BBS04 uses pairing groups: gpk contains g1,g2,h0,h1; the manager’s secret is x; a member credential is A=(g1·h0^{sk}·h1^{m})^{1/(x+e)}. A signature is (A,e) plus a Fiat–Shamir-transformed zero-knowledge proof; the opener uses x to recover A and trace the member. Opening, linking and revocation Opening authority is held by the manager; linking is optional and lets a verifier tell whether two signatures come from the same member; revocation can use a revocation list or verifier-local revocation. Signature size is independent of group size, but verification/revocation has a cost. Group signatures separate “membership” from “identity”: anonymous inside, verifiable outside, traceable by the manager. They suit vehicle networks, anonymous credentials, e-voting, whistleblowing and Direct Anonymous Attestation. One group public key means verifiers need not hold every member certificate; BBS04 pushes signatures under 200 bytes, far shorter than earlier schemes, making privacy authentication usable on bandwidth-limited links. ISO/IEC 20008-2 standardizes group-public-key anonymous signatures, including opening, linking and revocation; BBS04 is one of the shortest pairing-based instantiations. It is used in Intel SGX/TPM Direct Anonymous Attestation, Hyperledger anonymous credentials, V2X and privacy-preserving voting; BBS+ is used by the W3C verifiable-credential community, but BBS+ itself is a composable signature, not a full group signature. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Anonymity is computational: the opener can deanonymize with the master key, and if the manager is compromised every signature is traceable. Member collusion/credential forgery, stale revocation lists and signing side channels all break security. BBS relies on pairing assumptions such as q-SDH and DLIN and is not post-quantum; group size and revocation strategy affect verification cost; strong exculpability (the manager cannot forge a member’s signature) needs an extra construction and must not be assumed by default. Chaum and van Heijst introduced group signatures in 1991; BBS04 used SDH and pairings to shrink signatures under 200 bytes; ISO/IEC 20008-2:2013 standardized them and was amended in 2023; DAA brought group signatures to hardware anonymous attestation. BBS+, LRSW and Groth-type schemes later advanced anonymous credentials and privacy authentication. - Wikipedia search entry for 组签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%BB%84%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[s=k^{-1}\big(H(m)+r d\big)\bmod n\] Group Signature: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Halo2 zero-knowledge proof system
items.text: Algorithm : Halo2 (Halo2 证明系统). The PLONKish matrix Halo2 writes a circuit as a matrix: columns are advice, fixed or instance, and rows are gates. Each gate is a polynomial constraint linking neighboring rows and multiple columns; a custom gate can read several columns at once, and a lookup argument constrains a column's values to a table. The row count is a power of two, column polynomials are interpolated over a roots-of-unity domain, and constraints vanish on the whole domain. Permutation, lookup and IPA Copy constraints use a permutation argument to force two cells to be equal; range checks use a lookup table. The prover commits to column polynomials with Pedersen commitments and opens them with an inner-product argument (IPA) over Pallas/Vesta. There is no pairing and no trusted setup. Fiat–Shamir turns the interaction non-interactive; the verifier checks commitments, challenge points and quotient polynomials. Halo2 needs no trusted setup: public parameters come from fixed curves, so there is no “toxic waste”. PLONKish columns and gates are customized to the circuit, lookups make 8-bit/16-bit range checks cheaper than long constraint chains, and IPA relies only on discrete logarithms, not pairing curves. Recursive composition lets a proof verify another proof, which suits rollups and privacy pools with multiple circuit layers. Transparent setup is not free: IPA proofs and verification are heavier than Groth16, and the recursive verifier itself consumes rows. Halo2 trades “one-time risk at setup” for “ongoing compute at proving time”, which fits teams with many circuits, fast iteration and no way to run a trusted ceremony. Zcash's Orchard shielded pool uses Halo2 to prove “I know the note witness and the funds satisfy the rules”. PSE's halo2-lib moves EVM-compatible circuits into Halo2 for zkEVM proving layers; recursive aggregation compresses several application proofs into one outer proof. Halo2's Rust implementation provides halo2_proofs and halo2_gadgets; the latter includes chips for Sinsemilla, ECC and lookups. It is used as a proving backend by several privacy applications and rollups. A deployment should check the circuit version and parameters, not just the phrase “built with Halo2”. No trusted setup does not mean no trust: the constraint system, lookup tables and public inputs are defined by the application. A missing or wrong gate can let a proof “prove” a false statement. IPA verification is not constant-size, and a recursive verifier consumes many rows; proving time scales with circuit size, column count and lookup count. Halo2 also does not automatically provide input privacy; public inputs stay public. Halo2 circuits require manual column, row and gate layout. Too few columns bloat the circuit; oversized lookup tables slow proving. Wrong parameters (k, column count, lookup width) can cause a performance cliff, and a library upgrade may change the transcript or parameters, requiring a fresh trust assessment. Halo proposed replacing trusted setup with IPA in 2019 (ePrint 2019/1021). Halo2 in 2020 combined PLONK's arithmetization with Halo's recursion into the PLONKish matrix, then entered Zcash Orchard. The 2022 NU5 upgrade brought Orchard to mainnet, and Halo2 grew from an internal chain tool into a general proving library. Halo and Halo2 are not merely “protocol version two”: Halo2's core change is PLONKish column arithmetization and lookups, while IPA still comes from Halo. items.title: HC-128 Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : HC-128 (HC-128 流密码). Two secret tables of 512 words HC-128 takes a 128-bit key and a 128-bit IV and keeps two tables P and Q, each of 512 32-bit words: 32,768 bits, or 4 KiB. Each step updates one element of one table and reads from the other table through a nonlinear filter, emitting one 32-bit keystream word. Key expansion and a 1024-step warm-up The key and IV first expand into W[0..1279] in the style of the SHA-256 message schedule: W_i = f2(W_{i−2}) + W_{i−7} + f1(W_{i−15}) + W_{i−16} + i. P is loaded from W[256..767] and Q from W[768..1279]; the cipher then runs 1024 steps, feeding outputs back into P and Q to finish initialization. Update and output The P step updates P[i] ← (P[i] + g1(P[i−3], P[i−10], P[i−511])) ⊕ h1(P[i−12]); the Q step is symmetric. The g functions use rotations, XOR and 32-bit addition, while h uses the other table as an S-box. Each step emits 32 bits, and the keystream is capped at 2^64 bits. HC-128 is built for bulk software encryption: it runs on scalar 32-bit operations without AES instructions. The designer reports about 3.05 cycles per byte on a Pentium M, well ahead of table-driven software ciphers of its time. It is an eSTREAM software-portfolio member and is unpatented. The price is a 4 KiB state and a 1024-step initialization. It suits long connections, disk or network bulk data and pseudorandom generation, not large numbers of short messages where initialization dominates. HC-128 appears in software stream-cipher implementations, pseudorandom generators such as Rust rand_hc, and cryptanalysis baselines. It provides confidentiality only, so protocols must add a MAC or use an AEAD construction. It has no broad standard suite comparable to AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305. Its value is high-throughput software encryption without hardware acceleration, plus its role as an eSTREAM design sample. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Key/IV reuse is fatal: the same K and IV produce the same keystream, and two ciphertexts XOR to the XOR of the plaintexts. HC-128 has no built-in authentication, so the protocol must add integrity protection. The h1/h2 functions index P/Q with secret data, so software implementations expose key-dependent cache access patterns. SPACE 2012 showed that cache analysis can recover about half of the HC-128 state, and that this can be cascaded with differential fault analysis toward full state and key recovery. Shared CPUs, cloud tenancy and observable caches must account for this. The 2^64-bit keystream limit and the 1024-step initialization are hard boundaries; exceeding the limit or reusing an IV breaks the security target rather than degrading performance. Hongjun Wu proposed HC-256 in 2004 and the 128-bit-security simplification HC-128 in 2008. HC-128 entered the eSTREAM software portfolio, and the paper appeared in LNCS 4986. It then became a standard sample for software stream ciphers, PRNGs and side-channel research, with cache analysis, differential fault analysis and structural analysis built around it. - Wikipedia search entry for HC-128 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=HC-128%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] HC-128: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Håstad's Broadcast Attack
items.text: Theorem : Håstad's Broadcast Attack (Håstad 广播攻击). Broadcasting one message to several moduli Suppose a message m is encrypted for k recipients with the same small exponent e and pairwise coprime moduli N1,…,Nk: c_i = m^e mod N_i. If k ≥ e and m^e < ∏ N_i, the Chinese Remainder Theorem combines the congruences into C ≡ m^e (mod ∏ N_i), with 0 ≤ C < ∏ N_i. Since m^e is also below the product, C equals the integer m^e, not merely a power modulo the product. Taking the integer e-th root of C recovers m. The general theorem for linearly related messages Hastad’s 1988 theorem handles a more general setting: under the i-th modulus, a polynomial equation P_i(x) ≡ 0 (mod n_i) of degree at most d holds. If the number of equations satisfies k d(d+1)/2 and the smallest modulus is large enough (the paper requires min n_i 2^{d^2}), x can be recovered in time polynomial in k and log n_i. For RSA, d=e, so “affine related messages” need more than e(e+1)/2 recipients; this is a different threshold from the e recipients needed for the same message. The thresholds are not decoration The basic broadcast condition k≥e comes from CRT: at least e congruences are needed to place m^e inside a full product. The general k d(d+1)/2 condition comes from the dimension of the lattice/resultant elimination. Mixing the two thresholds produces false security conclusions. With randomised padding, the m_i no longer satisfy one low-degree polynomial, and both CRT and integer-root premises disappear. RSA with e=3 is fast and attractive for constrained devices; but broadcasting the same message to three or more recipients without randomised padding places m^3 inside an integer ring larger than m^3, so CRT reconstructs it exactly. Hastad’s generalisation shows that even when the messages differ, enough recipients still leak the message if the messages follow a known affine relation. OAEP-style randomised padding gives every recipient an independent random encoding, so the encodings no longer satisfy one low-degree polynomial. CRT then combines ciphertexts of different random polynomials, and the integer root no longer corresponds to the plaintext. “Some padding” is not enough: deterministic padding, fixed timestamps or predictable counters may preserve the relation. When evaluating a broadcast protocol, ask: is the message the same, is e equal to 3 or 65537, are there at least e recipients, is every encoding independently randomised, and are the moduli pairwise coprime? These questions matter more than the nominal RSA modulus size. 1. Confirm a common e and distinct N_i, with the N_i pairwise coprime; if two moduli share a factor, gcd(N_i,N_j) factors them and the attack is even simpler. 2. Collect at least e ciphertexts of the same message; check that m is below min N_i so that m^e < ∏ N_i. 3. Combine the ciphertexts by CRT to obtain C; take the integer e-th root; verify the result against every c_i. 4. If the messages are affinely related rather than equal, apply Hastad’s general theorem with k e(e+1)/2 and the modulus lower bound. 5. Record the failure reason: randomised padding, too few recipients, message too large, or non-coprime moduli. Treat broadcast as a special case of related messages in protocol review; require randomised padding for low-exponent encryption; require independent encoding for every recipient in group messaging. Test vectors should cover e=3 and e=65537, and the boundaries k=e and k=e+1. 1. Too few recipients. The basic attack needs k≥e; the general affine theorem needs k e(e+1)/2. One recipient short can be enough to fail. 2. m^e not below the product. CRT then yields only m^e modulo the product, and the integer root is not m; lattice methods or extra information are needed. 3. Non-coprime moduli. The CRT condition fails; however, gcd may then factor a modulus, which is a different attack. 4. Randomised padding. Every encoding differs, so the low-degree relation does not hold. 5. e too large. Thresholds and polynomial degrees grow with e; for e=65537 the general affine attack needs an unrealistic number of recipients. 6. Messages not affinely related. Hastad’s theorem requires a known low-degree polynomial; an arbitrary relation is not guaranteed to be solvable. Hastad’s 1988 SIAM Journal on Computing paper proved the “solving simultaneous modular equations of low degree” theorem and applied it to low-exponent RSA broadcast. Its conditions k d(d+1)/2 and min n_i 2^{d^2} became standard parameter language for later related-message attacks. The 1996 Franklin-Reiter attack handles related messages under one modulus; Hastad handles broadcast and affine relations under distinct moduli. Around 1997, Coppersmith’s small-root method systematised “known partial message or small root” problems. The three are often listed together, but their assumptions and mathematical tools differ. - Wikipedia search entry for Håstad 广播攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=H%C3%A5stad%20%E5%B9%BF%E6%92%AD%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Håstad's Broadcast Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: HILL theorem
items.text: Theorem : Håstad-Impagliazzo-Levin-Luby Theorem (HILL 定理). OWF and PRG are equivalent The Håstad–Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby theorem: a pseudorandom generator exists if and only if a one-way function exists. PRG→OWF is direct: a generator that stretches a pseudorandom string is itself hard to invert. The hard direction is OWF→PRG. Three construction stages 1. GL hard-core bit: extract one bit from any OWF so that, given f(x), it remains unpredictable. Iteration and pseudoentropy: apply f repeatedly and collect many bits; statistically they may be dependent or even predictable, but they carry “computational entropy”. Universal hashing: a pairwise-independent hash family compresses computational entropy into a nearly uniform short string; the leftover hash lemma makes the output indistinguishable from true randomness. Parameters If f is a one-way function, then for every polynomial ℓ(n) there is a polynomial-time G:{0,1}^n→{0,1}^{n+ℓ(n)} such that G(Un) and U_{n+ℓ(n)} are computationally indistinguishable. The proof runs in poly(n) with polynomial advantage loss, but the constants are enormous. It lifts the minimal assumption of cryptography (OWF) to its most-used resource (pseudorandomness). Stream ciphers, key derivation, salts, commitments and zero-knowledge randomness all trace back to a PRG; HILL says this needs no extra number-theoretic assumption. HILL’s “pseudoentropy” lets the proof bypass intermediate distributions that are statistically uneven: an intermediate string may be visibly biased, yet carry computational entropy if no efficient algorithm can exploit the bias. Universal hashing only turns that entropy into a uniform-looking string. - Theory: OWF→PRG→encryption, commitments, zero knowledge, derandomization; a pillar of complexity-based cryptography. - Engineering: real stream ciphers (AES-CTR, ChaCha20) are not HILL constructions; they assume a block/stream cipher is a PRG. - Teaching: HILL explains “why one may assume only an OWF”, not “how to build a running generator”. Reading: check whether the assumption is an OWF or a concrete OWF; whether the stretch is polynomial; whether the hash family is pairwise independent. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Asymptotic construction. HILL’s constants and polynomial degrees are enormous; it cannot be deployed directly. 2. It needs an OWF. If no OWF exists, the theorem gives nothing; it does not prove that OWFs exist. 3. Stretch is limited by computational entropy. The output cannot exceed the intermediate distribution’s computational entropy; hashing does not create entropy. 4. It needs a universal hash family. The family must be pairwise independent or close enough; a fixed hash function does not guarantee the leftover hash lemma. 5. It is not public-key encryption. OWF can build a PRG, but public-key encryption needs a stronger trapdoor structure. “OWF is equivalent to PRG” is an existence equivalence, not the same object. Given an OWF, HILL yields a (possibly very slow) PRG; given a PRG, one can build an OWF. They live in the same asymptotic world. The paper by Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby appeared as an extended abstract at STOC 1989 and as “A pseudorandom generator from any one-way function” in SIAM Journal on Computing 28(4) in 1999. It builds on Goldreich–Levin 1989 and the Impagliazzo–Levin–Luby pseudoentropy work. HILL became the standard lemma for “OWF is the minimal assumption”; tighter constructions, efficiency improvements and quantum-security variants use it as a reference. It is a paradigm of existence proofs, not a patent on one algorithm. - Wikipedia search entry for HILL 定理. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=HILL%20%E5%AE%9A%E7%90%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Håstad-Impagliazzo-Levin-Luby Theorem: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Hybrid argument
items.text: Theorem : Hybrid Argument (混合论证). A chain, not a single step To show that two distributions X and Y are computationally indistinguishable, the hybrid argument does not compare them directly. It constructs t+1 distributions H0=X, H1, …, Ht=Y so that each adjacent pair differs in one component. If every adjacent pair is indistinguishable under the same kind of assumption, the endpoints are indistinguishable too. The triangle inequality gives the bound For any distinguisher D, define its advantage Adv(H0,Ht;D) = Pr[D(H0)=1] − Pr[D(Ht)=1] . Insert H1…Ht−1; the intermediate terms cancel: Adv(H0,Ht;D) ≤ Σ_{i=1}^{t} Adv(Hi−1,Hi;D). This is not probability amplification but error addition: if each of t adjacent advantages is ε/t, the total is ε. Standard use: replace one component at a time For multi-message IND-CPA, define H_i as “the first i ciphertexts are real, the rest are random”. Single-message IND-CPA makes every adjacent pair indistinguishable; t=q(n) is polynomial, so q ciphertexts remain indistinguishable. The hybrid argument turns “the whole system is indistinguishable” into “replace one component at a time”. Multi-bit PRG stretch, KEM/DEM hybrid encryption, ideal/real games and compositional security all use this chain to split a large jump into small ones. It buys: if the adjacent assumptions hold, the endpoints hold. It does not buy: any conclusion beyond those adjacent assumptions. If a component is broken, the chain does not repair it. It also gives no concrete bit-security, only an asymptotic or lossy bound. - Multi-message IND-CPA: in H_i the first i ciphertexts are real and the rest random; q queries reduce to one query. - PRG iteration: in H_i the first i outputs come from the PRG and the rest from true randomness; each extra bit crosses one adjacent hybrid. - KEM/DEM: first replace the session key by a random key (KEM security), then replace the DEM ciphertext by a random string (DEM security); add the two advantages. - Code-level game hopping: each code change defines a hybrid; reduce each adjacent gap in turn. Reading: count the hybrids t, then check that t is polynomial, every hybrid is efficiently samplable, and every adjacent gap is reducible. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. The number of hybrids is not polynomial. If t=2^n, splitting ε into 2^n shares makes each share negligible, and the reduction yields no contradiction. 2. Some hybrid cannot be sampled efficiently. A probability ensemble is useful in a reduction only when a polynomial-time algorithm can sample it. 3. The adjacent gap does not follow from an assumption. The hybrid argument itself creates no computational assumption. 4. Adaptive state. If component i can read the secret state of component i+1, “replace one component” may fail; a stronger hybrid or simulation is needed. A standard hybrid proof usually loses a factor t. A scheme with q queries gets a “q times advantage” bound; a 128-bit security claim cannot look only at the single-query advantage. Tight reductions need direct arguments, public coins or other techniques; the hybrid argument does not provide them automatically. Goldwasser and Micali introduced computational indistinguishability as a security definition in “Probabilistic Encryption” (1984) and used a hybrid argument to show that multiple samples do not increase distinguishing advantage. Goldreich later wrote it as a standard lemma in Foundations of Cryptography. It is a basic proof tool, not a technique owned by one algorithm. The name comes from “hybrid distributions”: insert middle distributions between real and ideal, and move through them layer by layer. - Wikipedia search entry for 混合论证. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%B7%B7%E5%90%88%E8%AE%BA%E8%AF%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Hybrid Argument: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: IEEE 1619 XTS-AES storage encryption
items.text: Standard : IEEE 1619 XTS-AES storage encryption (IEEE 1619 XTS-AES 存储加密). XEX: XOR tweak, AES, XOR again XTS-AES is an instance of XEX (XOR–Encrypt–XOR). For block P_j inside data unit i, let T_j = E_{K2}(i) ⊗ α^j, with multiplication in GF(2^128) and α a primitive element; encryption is C_j = E_{K1}(P_j ⊕ T_j) ⊕ T_j, and decryption reverses it. The same plaintext in a different sector or block position gives a different ciphertext; rewriting the same position gives the same ciphertext. Two keys The XTS key is K1 K2: K1 encrypts data, K2 only generates tweaks. AES-128 corresponds to a 256-bit XTS key and AES-256 to 512 bits. The two subkeys must differ; if K1 = K2, a chosen-ciphertext attack defeats XTS's main confidentiality assurance. Ciphertext stealing A data unit need not be a multiple of 128 bits. The last two blocks use ciphertext stealing: encrypt the penultimate block to CC, take its first b bits as the final ciphertext block, concatenate the remaining 128−b bits with the last plaintext block into PP and encrypt it, then swap the last two ciphertext pieces on output. The ciphertext length equals the plaintext length, with no padding, which suits fixed-size sectors. Storage devices read and write sectors randomly and cannot depend on a whole-file CBC chain. XTS decrypts each block independently; the tweak is derived implicitly from the sector/LBA and block index, so no IV or nonce is stored on disk. The ciphertext does not expand, which suits in-place encryption. Under ECB, equal plaintext blocks produce equal ciphertext and leak sector structure; XTS uses an address-dependent tweak to break up equal blocks. It is not authenticated encryption and does not prevent tampering, but it fits the random-access model of disks better than plain ECB or CBC. IEEE Std 1619-2007 defines XTS-AES; NIST SP 800-38E (2010) approves it for storage devices and requires each data unit to contain at most 2^20 AES blocks (16 MiB). IEEE 1619-2018 wrote that limit into the standard and capped the total number of blocks at 2^64; IEEE 1619-2025 added a key scope limiting blocks per key pair to 2^36 through 2^44. dm-crypt/LUKS, BitLocker, FileVault 2, OpenSSL and NetBSD cgd use XTS-derived implementations. A typical sector is 512 B or 4 KiB, far below the 16 MiB data-unit limit; but the total data volume written under one key approaches the key-scope boundary. XTS has no authentication tag; an attacker can replay, reorder or modify ciphertext blocks. If the attacker can observe plaintext–ciphertext pairs and overwrite data, decryption can be manipulated. Integrity must be added at the file-system or application layer (AEAD, HMAC, a Merkle tree), or XTS must be treated as “protection against offline theft”, not “protection against active tampering”. K1 and K2 must be independent, and blocks under one key scope must be capped. The 2025 standard limits a key scope to 2^36–2^44 blocks; under the 2^128 birthday bound the collision probability is roughly 2^-56 to 2^-40. Sector numbers must be unique and never reused: cloning, snapshots and disk remapping must preserve tweak uniqueness. XTS targets block storage, not TLS or network transport; transport should use AEAD. IEEE 1619-2007 was published in 2007 and defined XTS-AES; NIST SP 800-38E followed in January 2010, approving it as a storage confidentiality mode. IEEE 1619-2018 revised the data-unit and total-block limits; IEEE 1619-2025 appeared in June 2025 with key-scope requirements. XTS derives from Rogaway's XEX; the earlier LRW was also a tweakable disk-encryption mode but was replaced by XTS because of security and implementation issues. XTS stands for “XEX Tweakable Block Cipher with Ciphertext Stealing”, naming its three components. - Wikipedia search entry for IEEE 1619 XTS-AES 存储加密. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=IEEE%201619%20XTS-AES%20%E5%AD%98%E5%82%A8%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] IEEE 1619 XTS-AES storage encryption: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: IEEE 2883-2022 Storage Sanitization
items.text: Standard : Storage Sanitization (存储净化). IEEE 2883-2022 divides storage sanitization into three methods: Clear uses logical overwrite/block erase through the interface against simple non-invasive recovery; Purge uses overwrite, block erase or cryptographic erase against laboratory recovery; Destruct shreds, incinerates or melts media so it cannot be reused. The standard covers logical and physical storage and gives media-specific requirements for HDD, SSD, optical and removable media, plus SATA/SAS/NVMe interfaces. The three methods map to different threat models and verification strengths. Clear needs representative sampling; Purge needs a full read; Destruct needs physical inspection. Mixing method and verification strength produces overclaims such as “Clear performed, Purge claimed”. Cryptographic erase (CE) takes another path: data remains as ciphertext, but the media encryption key is destroyed; without the key, residual ciphertext cannot be decrypted. The data lifecycle first chooses a method: reuse/resale may use Purge to retain media value; disposal may use Destruct; low-sensitivity temporary cleanup may use Clear but accepts the detection probability of sampling. Clear samples at least 5% of addressable space, or two points per 10,000 equal subsections plus first/last; Purge reads the whole addressable space; CE keeps key-destruction, key-hierarchy and access-control evidence; Destruct keeps physical-inspection records. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Common errors include: treating Clear as Purge; treating one overwrite as effective on all media; ignoring SSD wear levelling, over-provisioning and bad blocks outside the addressable range; treating a 5% sample pass as proof of unrecoverability. CE is not automatically safe: whether the key is truly destroyed, whether backup keys exist and whether key management is auditable decide whether CE holds. items.title: MACsec link encryption (IEEE 802.1AE)
items.text: Standard : MACsec link encryption (IEEE 802.1AE) (MACsec 链路加密（IEEE 802.1AE）). A security header inside the Ethernet frame MACsec inserts a SecTAG after the source MAC address and an ICV at the frame end, optionally encrypting the frame body. SecTAG is 8 or 16 bytes: 2-byte EtherType 0x88E5, 1-byte TCI/AN, 1-byte SL, 4-byte PN and an optional 8-byte SCI. The SCI combines a 48-bit MAC with a 16-bit port number and identifies a unidirectional secure channel. Cipher suites The current standard centres on AES-GCM: GCM-AES-128 is mandatory; GCM-AES-256 and GCM-AES-XPN-128/256 are optional. GCM provides confidentiality and integrity together; the IV is built from the SCI (or SSCI under XPN) and the PN. The default PN is 32 bits; extended packet numbering uses 64 bits so a single SAK does not hit the 2^32-frame limit too early. MACsec protects link-layer frames, so ARP, LLDP, IP and MPLS all ride under the same protection regardless of whether higher layers enable TLS or IPsec. It suits switch-to-switch, router-to-router, data-centre leaf-spine links and carrier Ethernet that needs line-rate encryption. MACsec defines frame protection only; key agreement lives in MACsec Key Agreement (MKA) in IEEE 802.1X-2010. Devices authenticate with a long-term CAK, elect a key server, and the server generates and distributes short-term SAKs; SAK rotation does not break the link, and the two-bit AN lets one secure channel hold four simultaneous security associations. MACsec can protect a point-to-point link or an end-to-end path with intermediate devices; it is common in campus cores, data-centre interconnect, carrier Ethernet and automotive Ethernet. Hardware MACsec engines encrypt and decrypt at line rate, suitable for 10G/25G/100G ports. MACsec does not replace TLS, IPsec or application encryption. It protects one hop or one segment, and the switches at both ends see plaintext; true end-to-end confidentiality still comes from an upper-layer protocol. Deployment must also cover key management, device authentication, replay windows and failover. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The receiver verifies the ICV and drops a frame on failure; the PN increases, and the replay window tolerates some reordering while rejecting too-old frames. The SL field handles short frames, and the confidentiality offset can encrypt only part of the frame body (offset 0/30/50 bytes) when some protocol headers must remain visible. MACsec stops at the link layer; it cannot stop leakage inside the devices at either end, nor replace end-point encryption. It depends on correct MKA configuration, CAK protection and SAK rotation; wrong keys, disabled validation or an oversized replay window all weaken security. The ICV can be 8 or 16 bytes, with 16 bytes (128 bits) common in deployment. IEEE 802.1AE-2006 first standardized MACsec; 802.1AE-2018 is the main current edition. 802.1AEbw-2013 added 64-bit extended packet numbering (XPN), and 802.1X-2010 defined MKA. Later revisions brought in GCM-AES-256 and related suites. MACsec moved from carrier equipment into data-centre switches and automotive Ethernet; it layers with IPsec and TLS: MACsec protects a hop, IPsec protects the IP layer, TLS protects an application session. They are complementary, not mutually exclusive, and are stacked according to the trust boundary. - Wikipedia search entry for MACsec 链路加密（IEEE 802.1AE）. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=MACsec%20%E9%93%BE%E8%B7%AF%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86%EF%BC%88IEEE%20802.1AE%EF%BC%89 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] MACsec link encryption (IEEE 802.1AE): the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: IEEE 802.1AR-2018 Secure Device Identity
items.text: Standard : Secure Device Identity (安全设备标识). IEEE 802.1AR-2018 defines a Secure Device Identifier (DevID) for network devices: an X.509 certificate bound to a device private key. IDevID is manufacturer-provided at production, globally unique and protected from modification; LDevID is issued by a local administrator or domain CA when the device joins a domain. The goal is to let a device prove “which device I am” without a human login, using EAP-TLS, BRSKI/EST and similar protocols. Device identity is not a certificate filename but proof of private-key possession. The IDevID private key normally sits in a secure element and cannot be exported; LDevID must bind to the same device IDevID, otherwise copying an LDevID to another device would impersonate it. The binding is maintained by the IDevID certificate fingerprint/public key and the enrollment proof; the verifier also checks the LDevID path to the domain trust anchor and revocation status. Typical flow: the manufacturer burns in IDevID and private key; at domain join the device presents the IDevID certificate and signs a nonce/domain ID with the IDevID key; the domain CA verifies and issues LDevID; later EAP-TLS uses LDevID for device authentication. Certificate fields follow RFC 5280; serial, vendor and model can sit in subject or SAN otherName; the 2018 revision adds the ECDSA P-384/SHA-384 suite for Suite B alignment. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Common errors include treating a certificate as an authorization token, validating LDevID without the IDevID binding, ignoring revocation and time, copying the IDevID private key like a normal file, or treating 802.1AR as EAP itself. 802.1AR defines identity and binding only; business roles, access policy and the EAP method are supplied by 802.1X, RADIUS/AAA, BRSKI and local policy. items.title: IND-CCA2 equivalence with non-malleability
items.text: Theorem : IND-CCA2 equivalence with non-malleability (IND-CCA2 与非延展性等价). Two games IND-CCA2: the challenger generates pk/sk and gives adversary A a decryption oracle; A picks two equal-length messages m0 and m1, receives y = E(mb), may keep querying the decryption oracle except on y, and guesses b. Security means the advantage is negligible. NM-CCA2: after receiving y, A outputs a vector of ciphertexts y' different from y and a relation R; it wins if the plaintexts decrypted from y' are “meaningfully related” to the challenge plaintext (for example x' = x + 1) with probability significantly above random. Six notions Combining goals {IND, NM} with attacks {CPA, CCA1, CCA2} gives six definitions. NM-ATK ⇒ IND-ATK for every attack model; IND-CCA2 ⇒ NM-CCA2; together they are equivalent under CCA2. Weaker models lack this equivalence: IND-CCA1 does not imply NM-CPA, NM-CPA does not imply IND-CCA1, and NM-CCA1 does not imply NM-CCA2. The proof is a reduction: from an NM-CCA2 adversary B, build an IND-CCA2 adversary A. After B outputs y', A decrypts it with the CCA2 oracle, obtains x', and checks R(x_b, x'). If B can relate x_b to a related plaintext with non-negligible advantage, A can guess b with about half that advantage. The key is that CCA2 still allows decrypting y' after the challenge; CCA1 does not. IND-CCA2 is the strongest practical confidentiality notion for public-key encryption and also rules out malleability attacks that turn a ciphertext into a related one. Cramer–Shoup and RSA-OAEP (in the random-oracle model with the Fujisaki–Okamoto transform) are proven under this definition; proving IND-CCA2 automatically gives NM-CCA2, with no separate non-malleability proof. Modern public-key encryption and KEM/DEM constructions often target IND-CCA2; a protocol proof that establishes IND-CCA2 automatically yields NM-CCA2. It is also the central node in the textbook graph relating confidentiality and integrity. This is a public-key encryption definition; symmetric AEAD has its own CCA model, nonce handling and authentication tags. Do not treat IND-CCA2 as an AEAD security proof, and do not mistake “non-malleable” for “tamper-proof”. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The asymptotic definition ignores concrete parameters, key-generation defects, side channels and implementation bugs; Bleichenbacher's attack on PKCS 1 v1.5 shows that “it encrypts” does not mean CCA2 security. Proofs also rely on computational assumptions such as DDH, CDH or RSA. NM has simulation-based and comparison-based definitions; Bellare et al.'s equivalence uses their comparison-based definition, which is equivalent to Dolev–Dwork–Naor's simulation definition. Equivalence under CCA2 does not imply the same relation under CPA or CCA1. OAEP's CCA2 proof is in the random-oracle model; efficient standard-model schemes are rarer. The definition itself does not guarantee an efficient construction, nor does it automatically hold in a quantum model. Non-malleability was introduced by Dolev–Dwork–Naor in 1991; Bellare, Desai, Pointcheval and Rogaway compared the six notions at CRYPTO 1998, proved IND-CCA2 ⇔ NM-CCA2 and gave the separations; the journal version expanded in 2001. The graph became a standard figure in public-key cryptography textbooks. - Wikipedia search entry for IND-CCA2 与非延展性等价. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=IND-CCA2%20%E4%B8%8E%E9%9D%9E%E5%BB%B6%E5%B1%95%E6%80%A7%E7%AD%89%E4%BB%B7 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] IND-CCA2 equivalence with non-malleability: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ISO/IEC 10116 modes of operation
items.text: Standard : ISO/IEC 10116 modes of operation for an n-bit block cipher (ISO/IEC 10116 分组密码工作模式). Five modes ISO/IEC 10116:2017 defines five modes for an n-bit block cipher: ECB, CBC, CFB, OFB and CTR. ECB encrypts each block independently; CBC XORs the previous ciphertext into the next plaintext; CFB feeds ciphertext back to produce a key stream; OFB feeds output back; CTR encrypts a counter and XORs it with plaintext. Key formulas CBC encryption is C_i = E_K(P_i ⊕ C_{i-1}) with C_0 = IV; CFB is C_i = P_i ⊕ E_K(C_{i-1}) (implemented in s-bit segments); OFB is O_i = E_K(O_{i-1}), C_i = P_i ⊕ O_i; CTR is C_i = P_i ⊕ E_K(T_i) with the counter incremented per block. ECB has no IV; CBC/CFB/OFB need an initial vector; CTR needs a unique counter. ECB is deterministic and parallel but equal plaintext blocks produce equal ciphertext blocks, leaking structure; CBC hides structure but is serial and sensitive to IV predictability; CFB handles segments and can self-synchronize; OFB produces a plaintext-independent key stream for noisy channels; CTR is parallel and randomly accessible, but counter reuse is catastrophic. The fourth edition brought padding into the normative scope and added methods for avoiding ciphertext expansion for CBC/CFB/OFB/CTR; CBC also gained three ciphertext-stealing variants. The standard no longer assumes plaintext length is always a multiple of the block size, which is closer to storage and network implementations. ISO/IEC 10116 is a foundational mode standard: Annex A gives object identifiers, Annex B security guidance, Annex C figures and Annex D numerical examples. It is often used with ISO/IEC 9797-1 (MACs) and ISO/IEC 18033-3 (block ciphers). Disk/file encryption often uses CBC + ESSIV or XTS (XTS is IEEE 1619, not 10116); network protocols often use CTR plus authentication; databases may use CBC or CTR but must add a MAC/AEAD. Choose the mode by length handling, parallelism, random access and error propagation before choosing the cipher. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The standard states that these modes provide confidentiality only; integrity is out of scope, and most modes do not hide message length. ECB structure leakage, CBC padding oracles and CTR counter reuse can break security directly. Do not treat a 10116 mode as authenticated encryption. The CBC IV must be unpredictable (usually random) and never reused; the CTR counter must not repeat under one key, or XORing two key streams reveals plaintext; OFB/CFB IVs must also be unique. Implementations must also handle short blocks, final blocks, length expansion and key rotation, or correct clauses can still be misused. ISO/IEC 10116 first appeared in 1991, was revised in 1997 and 2006, and its 2017 fourth edition brought padding and expansion-avoidance methods into the norm. Amendment 1 in 2021 added CTR-ACPKM for regular key updates. NIST SP 800-38A defines ECB/CBC/CFB/OFB/CTR, SP 800-38B defines CMAC, SP 800-38D defines GCM and SP 800-38E defines XTS. items.title: ISO/IEC 11770-1 Key Management Framework
items.text: Standard : Key management — Part 1: Framework (密钥管理框架). ISO/IEC 11770-1:2010 is valuable not for a particular algorithm but for treating a key as a stateful object. The standard reduces the key life cycle to three principal states: PendingActive (generated but not enabled), Active (encryption, decryption, signing or verification) and PostActive (only decryption or verification of data processed earlier). Five transitions connect them: generation, activation, deactivation, reactivation and destruction. A key known to be compromised becomes PostActive immediately and shall not be reactivated. The framework lists 11 services: Generate-Key, Register-Key, Create-Key-Certificate, Distribute-Key, Install-Key, Store-Key, Derive-Key, Archive-Key, Revoke-Key, Deregister-Key and Destroy-Key. They cover administrative and technical actions from generation to destruction; the security policy decides which are mandatory and which optional. Keying material is more than the key: it also includes associated data such as identifiers, validity, purpose and algorithm parameters. Protection is cryptographic, non-cryptographic, physical or organisational. Key establishment has only two broad routes: key agreement, where both parties exchange data and neither can predetermine the result, and key transport, where one party chooses the key and protects it with asymmetric techniques for the other. A compact audit notation is K=(state, purpose, protection, custodian). Ask these four fields first; if one is missing, the key-management chain is broken. Part 1 is the upper framework for Parts 2 and 3: the KDC/KTC mechanisms of Part 2 and the agreement/transport mechanisms of Part 3 all refer to its states and services. Misreading Part 1 as an algorithm standard causes two errors: assuming it specifies ciphers, and reducing the life cycle to “generate, use, delete”, which omits the read-only constraint of PostActive. It also does not specify how a KDC or KTC is implemented. A KDC normally generates or acquires a key and distributes it; a KTC only translates or repackages keying material supplied by one party. Their trust models differ: a KDC knows the key, and a KTC may also see or rewrite it. The framework gives roles and services, not protocol messages. “Reproducible at formula level” here means being able to draw the state machine, list the 11 services, explain four protection means and two establishment routes, not recite an algorithm. An engineering audit follows five steps: 1) label every key with state and purpose; 2) check which services that state permits; 3) check that protection covers storage, transport and use; 4) check that derived keys pass through a KDF with context; 5) check that revocation, deregistration and destruction leave evidence. A typical mapping: a long-term master key stays Active or PostActive; a session key is Active for a short period; a historical key is PostActive and only decrypts or verifies old data; a compromised key becomes PostActive at once and may still decrypt old data but must not enter new business. An archived key is for recovery of old data only and must not be reactivated for new encryption. Destruction must cover all copies, backups, HSM slots and caches; deregistration must remove the key from directories or registries; revocation must publish status and block new use. The framework does not define algorithms, parameters, message formats or protocol proofs, and it does not guarantee implementation security. The three principal states may be subdivided, but the standard does not require sub-states; the “decrypt or verify only” rule of PostActive is a constraint, not advice. Common errors: reactivating a compromised key; treating an archived key as current; deleting only the primary copy; conflating KDC and KTC; treating “registered” as “activated”; treating a purpose/algorithm binding as a security policy. It also does not cover cross-domain key management, the custody details of key recovery or hardware-module certification; those belong to Parts 2/3, Part 6 and ISO/IEC 19790. The first edition established the framework in 1996; the second edition in 2010 was a technical revision, runs to 30 pages, was confirmed in 2021 and remains current. After Part 1, Part 2 covers symmetric mechanisms, Part 3 asymmetric mechanisms, Part 4 weak secrets, Part 5 group keys, Part 6 key derivation and Part 7 cross-domain passwords. - Wikipedia search entry for 密钥管理框架. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E7%AE%A1%E7%90%86%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Key management — Part 1: Framework: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ISO/IEC 11770-2 Symmetric Key Establishment
items.text: Standard : Key management — Part 2: Mechanisms using symmetric techniques (对称技术密钥管理). ISO/IEC 11770-2:2018 divides symmetric key establishment into three environments: six Point-to-Point mechanisms, four KDC mechanisms and three KTC mechanisms, 13 in total. It specifies only the keying material and conditions that messages must carry; message formats, error messages, initial key establishment, inter-domain management and implementation compatibility are outside its scope. The general form is K=f(F,I_A,I_B,TVP_A,TVP_B,SID): F is keying material, I are entity identifiers, TVP is a random number, timestamp or sequence number, SID is a session identifier, and f is a KDF. Mechanism 1 derives from TVP only; mechanism 2 has A choose F and encrypt it under an existing K_AB; neither provides entity authentication. Mechanism 6 derives K from F_A and F_B plus TVPs, optionally with I_A, I_B, Text and SID, and uses random numbers for key confirmation. Mechanism 7 has a KDC generate or acquire F and encrypt two messages under A's and B's long-term keys with the KDC; A forwards the second part to B. Mechanism 12 is a KTC: A chooses K_AB and the server only translates it into a package B can open; the server does not generate the key. Key confirmation is not a synonym for entity authentication: it proves possession of the same K, while entity authentication also proves that the peer is the claimed entity, usually through a signature or an additional protocol. The formula-level value of Part 2 is separating “who chooses the key, who sees it, and who confirms it”. Point-to-Point suits parties that already share a long-term key; a KDC suits central distribution but the centre knows the key; a KTC suits a case where one party controls the key and the centre only translates it. Their trust assumptions differ and cannot be hidden under one “key distribution” label. The 13 mechanisms are not 13 algorithms; they are message choreographies. KDF choice, TVP freshness, direction of key confirmation and SID binding determine whether the protocol resists replay, reflection and unknown-key sharing. That is why the formula includes I_A, I_B and SID: without identity and session binding, keys can repeat across sessions; without TVP binding, replay can pass. Selection order: first ask whether the parties already share a long-term key. If yes, use Point-to-Point; if a centre is required, use KDC; if one party must keep control of the key, use KTC. Then choose a KDF: ISO/IEC 11770-6 or a mature HKDF/KDF, with identities, random numbers, SID and purpose labels as input. Messages should bind at least protocol version or mechanism identifier, initiator and responder identities, TVP and key purpose. Key confirmation should use a binding such as MAC_{K_AB}(TVP_B I_A I_B), not a bare “OK”. Engineering checks: is the long-term key pre-shared and non-reused; is each TVP unique; are KDC/KTC inside the trust boundary; is confirmation mutual; do error messages leak key state; are MAC and encryption keys separated. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The standard does not establish an initial long-term key; without initial trust every mechanism stalls. Mechanisms 1 and 2 have no entity authentication and are exposed to man-in-the-middle and replay; a compromised KDC exposes all derived keys; a KTC may see or replace keying material. TVP reuse, insufficient KDF input, missing key confirmation, unbound SID, or using one key for both encryption and MAC all break security. Product compliance is not product interoperability; message formats are out of scope. It also does not handle cross-domain key management, key life cycle or implementation side channels; see Part 1, Part 7 and implementation standards. The first edition appeared in 1996; the second edition in 2008 was a technical revision that changed mechanism 12 to address a security shortcoming; the third edition in 2018 updated Clause 5 requirements, added an optional message/mechanism identifier to encrypted strings, expanded the key-calculation inputs of mechanism 5, made minor changes to the fourth message of mechanism 8 and the second message of mechanism 10, and was confirmed in 2024. - Wikipedia search entry for 对称技术密钥管理. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%AF%B9%E7%A7%B0%E6%8A%80%E6%9C%AF%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E7%AE%A1%E7%90%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Key management — Part 2: Mechanisms using symmetric techniques: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ISO/IEC 11770-3 Asymmetric Key Establishment
items.text: Standard : Key management — Part 3: Mechanisms using asymmetric techniques (非对称技术密钥管理). ISO/IEC 11770-3:2021 divides asymmetric key management into three classes: 15 key-agreement (KA), 6 secret-key-transport (SKT) and 3 public-key-transport (PKT) mechanisms, 24 in total. Key agreement has both parties exchange data and jointly compute a shared value F that neither can predetermine; secret-key transport has A choose K_AB and encapsulate it under B’s public key; public-key transport authenticates a public key without requiring secrecy. The mathematics covers finite fields, elliptic curves and bilinear pairings. A finite field uses F=g^{r_A r_B} mod p; an elliptic curve uses F=[r_A r_B]G, multiplied by cofactor h when the curve has one; pairing mechanisms use e([r_A]P,[r_B]Q). F is not the session key: it must pass through a KDF bound to identities, random numbers, TVPs and SID to produce K. The standard also discusses key confirmation (a MAC proving possession of the same K) and key commitment (H(K nonce) to resist unknown-key sharing). The 2025 amendment adds TFNS identity-based key agreement, while the 24 mechanisms of the 2021 body remain unchanged. A compact notation is K=KDF(F, context), with context=(I_A,I_B,R_A,R_B,SID,purpose). If one context field is missing, the protocol may reuse a key across sessions or accept unknown-key sharing. The three mechanisms are not synonyms. Key agreement depends on both private keys and the exchanged messages, and neither party can predetermine K; secret-key transport depends on B’s public key and decryption capability, so A can choose K but B must trust the encapsulation; public-key transport only answers “who owns this public key” and does not provide confidentiality. A KDF is not decoration: raw F may be biased or not uniformly random, and using it directly as a key leaves distribution problems; binding identities and TVPs into the KDF blocks unknown-key sharing and cross-session replay. EC cofactor multiplication maps the point into the correct subgroup; omitting it opens small-subgroup attacks. The formula-level value is stating which mechanism class, which group operation and which binding layer are used, not collapsing 24 mechanisms into “asymmetric key exchange”. Selection: use KA when both parties must contribute and neither may predetermine K; use SKT when A must control the key value; use PKT when only public-key ownership needs authentication. Then choose the group: finite field, elliptic curve or pairing; pairing mechanisms also require checking the PKG/trusted centre and key escrow. Implementation order: validate domain parameters and public keys; generate the private key and compute the public key; exchange or encapsulate; compute F; multiply by the EC cofactor; run the KDF with I_A/I_B/TVP/SID/purpose; perform key confirmation; add key commitment when needed. Engineering checks: is the RNG fit for purpose; is the private key in a protected environment; is the certificate chain verified; is the KDF a standard one; is F used directly as a key; is the cofactor missing; is confirmation one-way only; are SID and purpose recorded. items.title: ISO/IEC 14888-3 Discrete-Log Signatures
items.text: Standard : Digital signatures with appendix — Part 3: Discrete logarithm based mechanisms (基于离散对数的数字签名). ISO/IEC 14888-3:2018 specifies digital signatures with appendix based on the discrete logarithm problem. The 2018 body has 14 mechanisms; the November 2026 amendment adds EdDSA, making 15: 12 certificate-based and 3 identity-based. All are randomized; the signature is appended to the message and the message is not recovered from the signature. The general model is not “hash and sign”: it has five stages: produce randomizer K; compute pre-signature Π; prepare M1/M2; compute witness R (first signature part); compute assignment (T1,T2) and second part S. The general signature equation is A·K+B·X+C≡0 (mod q), where X is the private key and A/B/C come from a permutation of (S,T1,T2). DSA works in Z_p : R=(g^K mod p) mod q and S=K^{-1}(h(M)+XR) mod q; verification recomputes R. ECDSA works on curve points: R=x([K]G) mod q and S=K^{-1}(e+Rd) mod q. SM2 prepares M1=Z M, where Z binds the identity ID, curve parameters and public key; it signs r=(e+x1) mod n and s=(1+d)^{-1}(k-rd) mod n. EdDSA works on a twisted Edwards curve: R=[k]G and S=(k+H(R A M)x) mod L. A compact notation is Sig=(R,S) and Verify(pk,M,(R,S))∈{0,1}; the standard gives mechanisms, not side-channel protection. Putting 14/15 mechanisms together reveals “one equation, different groups and witness functions”. DSA/ECDSA/SM2/EdDSA are not four unrelated algorithms: each starts from a random K and private X and uses a verifiable equation to bind R and S to the message. The 2018 fourth edition added SM2 and Chinese IBS; the 2026 amendment added EdDSA and reworded the key-substitution note as “can be vulnerable”, making clear that the standard does not supply that protection. EdDSA binds the public key A into the hash by design and therefore carries a layer of key-substitution protection. Identity-based mechanisms (IBS-1, IBS-2, Chinese IBS) have a different trust model: the KGC generates private keys and therefore escrows them; certificate-based mechanisms have a CA authenticate public keys. Formula-level writing must keep these trust models separate. Implementation order: 1) choose mechanism and group; 2) validate domain parameters and public keys; 3) generate private X and public Y; 4) use a fresh random K for every signature; 5) compute R/S; 6) encode in DER or the standard appendix format; 7) the verifier recomputes the equation and checks R/S ranges. SM2 first computes Z=Hash(ENTL ID a b x_G y_G x_A y_A), then M1=Z M; EdDSA follows the standard/RFC 8032 Edwards encoding and cofactor handling. Identity-based schemes must validate KGC parameters and private-key derivation. Engineering checks: is K truly random and unique; are R/S in [1,q-1]; is the hash collision-resistant; is the public key bound into the signed message; is key-substitution protection present; are certificate chain/KGC identities verified; is the implementation constant-time. Nonce reuse is fatal: two messages signed with the same K let an attacker solve the two S equations for the private key. K bias, low-entropy RNG and fault injection can also leak the key. EC-DSA, EC-GDSA, EC-RDSA and EC-FSDSA can be vulnerable to key substitution: an attacker finds two distinct public keys and one signature valid for both; the standard suggests adding the public key to the signed message. Identity-based mechanisms have KGC escrow, so the KGC can create any user’s private key. The standard does not cover side channels, fault injection, API misuse or signature-encoding ambiguity, and does not prove “signature equals security”. The EdDSA amendment is a 2026 addition and does not change the count of the other 2018 mechanisms. The 1998 first edition was certificate-based and contained DSA and Pointcheval/Vaudenay; the 2006 second edition reorganized the part around discrete-log mechanisms and added KCDSA, IBS-1 and IBS-2; Amd 1:2010 added SRA, EC-RDSA, EC-SDSA and EC-FSDSA; the third edition appeared in 2016; the 2018 fourth edition added SM2 and Chinese IBS for 14 mechanisms; Amd 1:2026, published in November 2026, added EdDSA for 15. - Wikipedia search entry for 基于离散对数的数字签名. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%9F%BA%E4%BA%8E%E7%A6%BB%E6%95%A3%E5%AF%B9%E6%95%B0%E7%9A%84%E6%95%B0%E5%AD%97%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] Digital signatures with appendix — Part 3: Discrete logarithm based mechanisms: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: ISO/IEC 18033-3 Block Ciphers
items.text: Standard : Encryption algorithms — Part 3: Block ciphers (分组密码算法标准). ISO/IEC 18033-3:2010 specifies block-cipher primitives, not modes. The generic interface is \(C=E_K(P)\), \(P=D_K(C)\) with \( P = C =b\). Seven algorithms form two families: 64-bit blocks TDEA, MISTY1, CAST-128 and HIGHT; 128-bit blocks AES, Camellia and SEED. TDEA is \(C=E_{K_3}(D_{K_2}(E_{K_1}(P)))\), the EDE composition of three DES calls. One AES round applies SubBytes, ShiftRows and MixColumns, then AddRoundKey; the number of rounds is 10 for a 128-bit key, 12 for 192 and 14 for 256. In the d08-block-ciphers reading path, Encryption algorithms — Part 3: Block ciphers connects to government contexts; the main risks are protocol, implementation. In engineering, choose the block size from data lifetime first: new systems should prefer 128-bit blocks and keep 64-bit blocks for legacy interoperability. Then choose the key size from the security target. TDEA with a 128-bit key is 2-key (about 112-bit strength); 192-bit is 3-key (about 168-bit), so key bits are not the same as security strength. After choosing the primitive, enter the ISO/IEC 10116 mode layer: CBC needs an unpredictable IV, CTR/GCM needs a unique nonce, and GCM also needs additional authenticated data. This standard supplies none of those by itself. First, the standard defines primitives only; it does not define modes, padding, IV generation or authentication, so treating it as a complete encryption scheme loses integrity. Second, a 64-bit block reaches a birthday collision bound near \(2^{32}\) blocks; TDEA, MISTY1, CAST-128 and HIGHT should not carry new long-lived or high-volume data. Third, 2-key TDEA is about 112-bit strength and 3-key about 168-bit; do not advertise 128/192-bit strength. Fourth, the standard does not assess implementation side channels, key storage or protocol composition; those need separate audits. The 2005 edition specified TDEA, MISTY1, CAST-128, AES, Camellia and SEED; the 2010 second edition added HIGHT, giving four 64-bit and three 128-bit algorithms. AES comes from FIPS 197; Camellia and SEED are widely used 128-bit block ciphers from Asian standardization; MISTY1, CAST-128 and HIGHT remain in the 64-bit family. items.title: ISO/IEC 18033-4 Stream Ciphers
items.text: Standard : Encryption algorithms — Part 4: Stream ciphers (流密码算法标准). The generic stream-cipher interface is \(KS=G(K,IV,state)\), with state advanced by \(state_{t+1}=Next(state_t)\); binary-additive output is \(C_t=P_t\oplus KS_t\) and decryption is \(P_t=C_t\oplus KS_t\). ISO/IEC 18033-4:2011 separates output functions from generators: two output functions, binary-additive and MULTI-S01; five generators, MUGI, SNOW 2.0, Rabbit, Decimv2 and KCipher-2. Amendment 1:2020 adds ZUC, making six generators; ZUC uses a 128-bit key \(K\) and a 128-bit \(IV\). A synchronous stream cipher derives the keystream only from \(K,IV\); a self-synchronizing one also uses past ciphertext. In the 一次性密码本与流密码 reading path, Encryption algorithms — Part 4: Stream ciphers connects to government contexts; the main risks are protocol, implementation. Choose a generator and output function, then check \(K\), \(IV\) lengths and uniqueness. Binary-additive output is a bitwise XOR and suits streaming; MULTI-S01 needs the standard multi-block combiner and must not be treated as plain XOR. If the keystream repeats, XOR leaks plaintext directly, so every session needs a fresh IV and the same key must not reuse an IV. For integrity, add a MAC or use an AEAD outside the stream cipher; do not rely on the stream cipher alone. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. There are four boundaries. First, binary-additive output is malleable: flipping a ciphertext bit flips the corresponding plaintext bit, and the standard supplies no authentication. Second, IV reuse repeats the keystream and is catastrophic; the standard defines the IV interface but does not manage IVs for the application. Third, the standard lists algorithms and interfaces, not security proofs; claims for MUGI, SNOW 2.0, Rabbit, Decimv2, KCipher-2 and ZUC must go back to their design analyses and later cryptanalysis. Fourth, ZUC is the 2020 amendment, so the 2011 “five” must not be silently rewritten as “six” without a version note. ISO/IEC 18033-4:2005 first listed MUGI and SNOW 2.0 and gave OFB, CTR and CFB keystream constructions from block ciphers; the 2011 second edition expanded to five dedicated generators and kept the binary-additive and MULTI-S01 output functions. items.title: ISO/IEC 18033-5 Identity-Based Ciphers
items.text: Standard : Encryption algorithms — Part 5: Identity-based ciphers (标识密码标准). ISO/IEC 18033-5:2015 specifies identity-based ciphers. In BF, the parameters are \(e:G_1\times G_1\to G_2\), \(P\in G_1\), master secret \(s\in\mathbb{Z}_p^ \), public key \(P_{pub}=sP\) and \(g=e(P,P)\). An identity \(ID\) maps to \(Q_{ID}=H_1(ID)\), and the private key is \(d_{ID}=sQ_{ID}\). Encryption picks random \(r\) and outputs \(U=rP\), \(V=M\oplus H_2(g^r)\), \(W=rQ_{ID}\); decryption computes \(M=V\oplus H_2(e(U,d_{ID}))\), since \(e(U,d_{ID})=e(P,Q_{ID})^{rs}=g^{rs}\). SK and BB1 are KEM+DEM hybrids; the 2021 amendment adds SM9. In the 非对称公钥 reading path, Encryption algorithms — Part 5: Identity-based ciphers connects to government contexts; the main risks are protocol. An encryptor needs only the recipient ID and the public key: compute \(Q_{ID}=H_1(ID)\), pick random \(r\) and output \((U,V,W)\). A decryptor obtains \(d_{ID}\) from the PKG and recovers \(g^{rs}\) through \(e(U,d_{ID})\). In hybrid mode, \(Encaps(MPK,ID)\) yields a session key \(K\) and encapsulation \(C\), then \(DEM.Enc(K,M)\) encrypts the data; decryption reverses the order. The SM9 amendment must be checked against SM9 parameters and encapsulation, not by forcing BF’s \((U,V,W)\) onto it. First, the PKG holds the master secret and can decrypt every user’s data; key escrow is structural, not an optional setting. Second, BF’s \(V=M\oplus H_2(g^r)\) is an ElGamal-style mask, and CCA security needs additional ciphertext checks or a consistency argument; “listed in a standard” does not mean “any implementation is secure”. Third, pairing implementation, group parameters and hash-to-point must be correct, or \(e(U,d_{ID})=g^{rs}\) fails. Fourth, the standard does not prescribe certificates, proof of possession or implementation audits; SM9 is an amendment and must not be folded into the 2015 body formulas. items.title: ISO/IEC 29192 Lightweight Cryptography
items.text: Standard : Lightweight cryptography (轻量级密码). ISO/IEC 29192 is the constrained-environment family of lightweight cryptography: chip area, energy, code/RAM, bandwidth and latency decide whether a mechanism fits; security goals cover confidentiality, integrity, entity authentication, data-origin authentication, non-repudiation and key exchange. Part 1 gives the general framework and security-strength scale; Part 2 block, Part 3 stream, Part 4 asymmetric, Part 5 hash, Part 6 MAC, Part 7 broadcast authentication and Part 8 AE. Lightweight does not mean low security: security strength n costs about 2^n work; an n-bit block used beyond about 2^{n/2} blocks under one key loses birthday-bound security. Mechanism selection must weigh security strength, implementation cost and protocol constraints; PRESENT/CLEFIA/LEA, Enocoro/Trivium, PHOTON/SPONGENT and LightMAC/Chaskey-12 differ in area, latency and mode. For IoT, RFID and sensors, list the constraint vector first, then select components: confidentiality from Parts 2/3, integrity from Parts 5/6, authentication from Parts 4/7, AE from Part 8; finally check strength against Part 1. Fix parameters such as MAC length, counter bits and nonce rules; changing parameters under one key breaks the security assumptions. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. items.title: ISO/IEC 9797-1 block-cipher MAC
items.text: Standard : ISO/IEC 9797-1 block-cipher MAC (ISO/IEC 9797-1 分组密码 MAC). One model, six algorithms ISO/IEC 9797-1 does not define a single MAC; it defines a model for MACs based on an n-bit block cipher: key derivation, padding, splitting, initial transformation, iteration, final/output transformation and truncation. The MAC length m is at most the block length n; strength depends on key length and secrecy, block-cipher strength, m and the specific mechanism. Padding and the CBC chain The standard defines three padding methods: method 1 appends zero bits; method 2 appends a single 1 then zeros; method 3 prefixes an n-bit length block, then pads with zeros. Algorithm 1 is CBC-MAC: H1 = E_K(D1), H_i = E_K(H_{i-1} ⊕ D_i), output H_q, optionally truncated to m bits. Algorithms 2/3 add one or two final transforms, with Algorithm 3 also called Retail MAC; Algorithm 4 adds transforms at both ends; Algorithms 5/6 are single-chain optimized variants. What changed in 2011 The first edition appeared in 1999. The 2011 second edition replaced the 1999 Algorithms 5/6 (two parallel CBC-MAC computations) with more efficient single-CBC-chain algorithms, added OID Annex A, updated security analysis Annex C and added Annex D on relations to older standards. Amendment 1 followed in 2023. A block-cipher MAC reuses existing AES/DES hardware and introduces no new hash; the CBC chain is simple and streamable, which suits financial messages, smart cards and protocol authentication. It bases message integrity and origin authentication on the same block-cipher assumption. Plain CBC-MAC is provably secure only for fixed-length messages. With Padding 1, an attacker can append blocks and preserve the MAC, a trivial forgery; a final transform (Algorithms 2/3/4) or CMAC is needed for variable-length messages. Truncating to m bits lowers forgery probability to about 2^-m but also weakens the tag. The MACs in ISO 8731-1, ANSI X9.9, X9.19 and ISO 9807 are special cases of ISO/IEC 9797-1; banking messages, EMV and ISO 8583 deployments commonly use CBC-MAC or Retail MAC. NIST SP 800-38B's CMAC is a separate standardized path, often compared with these mechanisms. Saying “use ISO/IEC 9797-1” is not enough. Both sides must agree on the block cipher, padding method, algorithm number, MAC length and key-derivation method; any mismatch breaks interoperability or lowers security. Annex B explicitly notes that Padding 1 can suffer trivial forgery; the CBC-MAC security proof assumes fixed-length messages. For variable-length messages, use a final-transform algorithm or CMAC, and never share the MAC key with encryption. An m-bit tag has forgery probability about 2^-m; a 32-bit tag is too short for high-speed networks. Key derivation needs domain separation, and verification must compare in constant time. Implementations must also assess timing, fault injection and side channels, because MAC verification failures are often used as padding oracles. ISO/IEC 9797-1:1999 first consolidated CBC-MAC and its variants; the March 2011 second edition made a technical revision, replaced Algorithms 5/6, added OIDs and updated the security analysis; it was confirmed current in 2022, and Amendment 1 appeared in 2023. It grew out of banking MAC practice in ISO 8731-1 and ANSI X9.9 and later expanded to general IT security. - Wikipedia search entry for ISO/IEC 9797-1 分组密码 MAC. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=ISO%2FIEC%209797-1%20%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%20MAC - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[S=\min_i S_i,\quad S_i\in\{\text{密钥强度},\text{分组安全},\text{实现安全}\}\] ISO/IEC 9797-1 block-cipher MAC: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
