items.title: JN-25 Cryptanalysis
items.text: Attack : JN-25 Cryptanalysis (JN-25 破译). Codebook and additive JN-25 first looked up Japanese text in a five-digit codebook, producing code groups x_i; it then took five-digit groups k_i from an additive book and added them digitwise modulo 10: c_i=(x_i+k_i) mod 10. This is not binary XOR but non-carrying decimal addition; the receiver subtracts digitwise with the same additive book. The book is organized by page and line, and an indicator group at the start of the message names the page and line used. Depth and codebook recovery When several messages reuse the same additive page, subtract two ciphertexts digitwise: c_i⊖c_i′=(x_i⊖x_i′) mod 10. The additive cancels, leaving differences of codebook groups. Enough depth, known code groups, guessed cribs and frequency analysis recover codebook meanings; new groups are then looked up and the plaintext grows. JN-25 is a canonical codebook-plus-additive system. Its weakness is not the addition itself but additive-page reuse and a finite codebook; once depth is sufficient, statistical attack turns a one-time-looking mask into analyzable codebook differences. VENONA also exploits repeated one-time-pad pages, but its failure is reuse of an OTP page; the JN-25 additive book was never an OTP, and reuse was normal, so depth accumulated more easily. The two are not the same key-reuse error. 1. Read the indicator to identify the additive page and line. 2. Subtract the additive digitwise to obtain code groups. 3. Align messages using the same page to build depth. 4. Recover the codebook with known groups, cribs, frequency and traffic analysis. 5. Iterate: add newly read groups to the codebook and extend the next decryption pass. Do not write JN-25’s digitwise mod-10 addition as XOR; do not ignore indicators and the garble check; do not call a partial codebook recovery a fully readable message. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Additive-book change: a new page or book destroys existing depth and forces a new accumulation. 2. Codebook growth: new groups have no known meaning and must be guessed from context. 3. Indicator or copying errors: digitwise subtraction produces garbage and needs a garble check. 4. Not a modern cipher: the codebook-plus-additive structure is not equivalent to a modern stream or block cipher, and the historical break must not be extrapolated to OTP or AES. JN-25 entered service in 1939; from 1940 the British Far East Combined Bureau and the U.S. OP-20-G worked on it. By the additive-book change in August 1941, the Americans had recovered about 2,000 code groups, roughly 4% of 27,500, mostly numerals and stereotypes; another book change on 4 December 1941 forced the work to restart. Breaking JN-25 was incremental; no single battle result should be attributed to one decrypt. This entry covers the cryptographic mechanism, scale and progress, not tactical outcomes as algorithmic conclusions. - Wikipedia search entry for JN-25 破译. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=JN-25%20%E7%A0%B4%E8%AF%91 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] JN-25 Cryptanalysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: KISS Pseudorandom Number Generator
items.text: Algorithm : KISS Pseudorandom Number Generator (KISS 伪随机数生成器). KISS combines four 32-bit sub-generators into one 32-bit output over a 128-bit state. MWC updates two 16-bit halves: \(z'=36969\,(z\bmod 2^{16})+\lfloor z/2^{16}\rfloor\), \(w'=18000\,(w\bmod 2^{16})+\lfloor w/2^{16}\rfloor\), then shifts \(z'\) left by 16 and adds \(w'\). SHR3 applies three shift-xor steps: left 17, right 13, left 5. CONG is \(x'=69069x+1234567\bmod 2^{32}\). The output is \((MWC\oplus x')+SHR3\bmod 2^{32}\). The sub-generator periods constrain one another; a single LCG period \(2^{32}\) is not the whole period. KISS means “Keep It Simple, Stupid” and targets a very fast, very short PRNG for simulation and statistical tests, not a block cipher. It has no key, authentication or side-channel goal; using KISS as a stream cipher or CSPRNG mistakes “statistically random” for “unpredictable”. This card also corrects the old catalog label “lightweight block cipher”: KISS updates a PRNG state, and its output is not \(E_K(x)\). An implementation fixes four 32-bit initial states, never all zero, then updates MWC, SHR3 and CONG in the same order and combines the outputs. To verify, reproduce the first few 32-bit outputs from a known seed, then check the \(x'\) wrap at \(2^{32}\), the 16-bit split in MWC and the SHR3 shift directions. It suits Monte Carlo, game drafts and test data; it does not suit keys, nonces, session tokens or anything requiring unpredictability. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Rose gives two key boundaries: the 32-bit KISS maximum period is about \(2^{119.5}\), not the earlier \(2^{123}\); about 70 output words recover the state with complexity near \(2^{29.1}\). A long period is therefore not cryptographic security. The 64-bit/256-bit variants (KISS64/KISS11) have a larger state and period near \(2^{247}\), but remain statistical PRNGs; their parameters must not be mixed into the 32-bit formulas. Marsaglia and Zaman proposed the KISS-style combination in 1993; the 1998 C version combined LCG, SHR3 and two MWC components into a four-word state; Rose’s 2018 analysis established the period bound and state-recovery attack. The 2009 64-bit KISS expanded the state to 256 bits and a period near \(2^{247}\). R128 also changes the catalog title from “lightweight block cipher” to “pseudorandom number generator”, because the old classification contradicts the algorithm. - Wikipedia search entry for KISS 伪随机数生成器. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=KISS%20%E4%BC%AA%E9%9A%8F%E6%9C%BA%E6%95%B0%E7%94%9F%E6%88%90%E5%99%A8 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] KISS Pseudorandom Number Generator: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: LEA lightweight block cipher
items.text: Algorithm : LEA (LEA 轻量级分组密码). 128-bit block and 32-bit ARX LEA has a fixed 128-bit block split into four 32-bit words X0..X3. Its round function uses only three operations: addition modulo 2^32, bitwise rotation and XOR. Three sub-transforms use rotate-left 9, rotate-right 5 and rotate-right 3, mix two words with round keys and write back, while the fourth word moves directly to the next round; there is no S-box and no lookup table. Rounds and key schedule LEA-128/192/256 runs 24/28/32 rounds, with six 32-bit round keys per round. The key schedule expands the master key into 6×(rounds) 32-bit words, with round constants derived from a golden-ratio constant; decryption runs the same round keys in reverse. A 128-bit block gives a 2^64 birthday bound, so multi-block data under one key must be capped. LEA targets “software lightweightness”: 32-bit ARX instructions are one or a few native instructions on Intel, AMD, ARM and ColdFire, with small code, low register pressure and no table-lookup cache leakage. The paper's experiments show it faster than AES on those platforms, which suits phones, embedded gateways and bulk cloud encryption. ARX has no S-box and a small hardware footprint, but differential and linear analysis apply directly to addition and rotation; implementations usually add masking or hiding for side-channel resistance. LEA's lightweight claim is “small code, high speed”, not “built-in side-channel protection”. LEA is a Korean KS X 3246 standard and an approved algorithm in Korea's KCMVP cryptographic-module validation; it entered ISO/IEC 29192-2 in 2019 alongside PRESENT and CLEFIA as lightweight block ciphers. It appears in mobile devices, IoT firmware and crypto libraries that need a small code footprint. LEA has implementations in Crypto++, Bouncy Castle and hardware IP, but its protocol adoption is far below AES; cross-organization interoperability still defaults to AES. Choosing LEA is usually about Korean compliance, code size or throughput on a specific CPU, not global ecosystem. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. The public literature has no practical key recovery against all 24/28/32 rounds; reduced-round differential, linear and impossible-differential analysis continues, so the security margin must be assessed by round count. LEA is a block cipher only, not authentication; CBC, CTR, GCM and their nonce/IV rules are separate choices. A 128-bit block hits the 2^64-block birthday bound on large data, and CTR mode also caps blocks per key. ARX timing can depend on data, so software needs constant-time checks; hardware needs fault-injection and power-analysis assessment. LEA was proposed at WISA 2013 by Hong, Lee, Kim, Kwon, Ryu and Lee of ETRI Korea, in “LEA: A 128-Bit Block Cipher for Fast Encryption on Common Processors”. It entered ISO/IEC 29192-2:2019, becoming part of the international lightweight-cipher standard. LEA stands for “Lightweight Encryption Algorithm”, not a product model. Its difference from AES is not block length but the round function: AES uses S-boxes and column mixing, while LEA uses 32-bit ARX. - Wikipedia search entry for LEA 轻量级分组密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=LEA%20%E8%BD%BB%E9%87%8F%E7%BA%A7%E5%88%86%E7%BB%84%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] LEA: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Length-Extension Attack
items.text: Attack : Length Extension Attack (长度扩展攻击). Merkle–Damgård state A Merkle–Damgård hash splits the message into blocks and iterates a compression function f over a chaining value: h_i=f(h_{i−1},m_i). The final digest is the last chaining value; padding pad=0x80 0… len encodes the message length in the final block. Length-extension forgery Given H(K m) and the length of K, an attacker treats the digest as a chaining value and continues compressing m′, obtaining H(K m pad m′) without knowing K. If a protocol uses MAC=H(K m) and compares digests, the attacker can append any message and forge a valid MAC. HMAC and sponge constructions HMAC uses H((K⊕opad) H((K⊕ipad) m)); the outer hash hides the inner chaining value and blocks extension. A SHA-3 sponge output is not a reusable chaining value, so it is also unaffected. This is the classic “hash as MAC” mistake: H(K m) looks like a keyed hash but exposes the internal state to the attacker. It explains why HMAC is not redundant and why protocols must distinguish hash, MAC, KDF and signature primitives. Given MAC=H(K m) and its digest, an attacker guesses the length of K, computes the padding, treats the digest as an IV and continues compressing m′ to obtain H(K m pad m′); sending the new message with the new digest passes verification. The old Flickr API, custom tokens and “key-prefix” file-integrity schemes exhibited the flaw. Modern practice uses HMAC, KMAC, BLAKE3 keyed mode or AEAD; if a hash-based MAC is unavoidable, use HMAC or length-encode and domain-separate first. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Affected: MD5, SHA-1 and Merkle–Damgård SHA-256/512; unaffected: SHA-3/SHAKE, BLAKE2/3, HMAC and KMAC. Truncated SHA-384/512-256 outputs also cannot be extended directly. Merkle and Damgård independently introduced the MD construction in 1989; RFC 2104 standardized HMAC in 1997 to fix key-prefix MACs; NIST SP 800-107r1 regulates HMAC usage; SHA-3’s sponge changed the state-output model. It became a required counterexample in protocol-design courses and pushed MAC primitives toward standardization. - Wikipedia search entry for 长度扩展攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%95%BF%E5%BA%A6%E6%89%A9%E5%B1%95%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Length Extension Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Maurer’s Bound
items.text: Theorem : Maurer's Bound (Maurer 界). The unconditional authentication model Sender and receiver share one key K and must authenticate n messages M1,…,Mn under that same key. The adversary has unlimited computation and knows the system design and the distribution of ciphertexts/tags, but not K. Attacks are impersonation (forge a message that the receiver accepts) and substitution (modify a legitimate message into another). If the receiver never rejects a valid message, Maurer’s bound states max(PI,1,…,PI,n,PS,n) ≥ 2^{-H(K)/(n+1)} ≥ K ^{-1/(n+1)}. For n=1 this becomes max(PI,PS) ≥ 2^{-H(K)/2} ≥ 1/√ K . Why n+1 parts Intuitively, the key must supply uncertainty for n decisions of “is this message authentic”, and one more part for the final substitution. Each authenticated message consumes a slice of the key budget. Split K into n+1 parts; if the adversary guesses the effective information in one part, it succeeds in one of the attacks. The formal proof treats authentication as hypothesis testing: between the null hypothesis (legitimate sender) and the alternative (forgery), key entropy limits how well the two distributions can be distinguished. Entropy bound and uniform keys H(K) is the Shannon entropy of the key. Since H(K) ≤ log K , 2^{-H(K)/(n+1)} ≥ K ^{-1/(n+1)}. This ties key length, number of authenticated messages and achievable deception probability together: to keep success at most 2^{-b}, the key needs about (n+1)b bits of entropy. It explains why an information-theoretic MAC cannot use a short key to authenticate many messages. Unconditional security does not rely on computational assumptions, so even an unbounded adversary is constrained by this lower bound. It also explains the price of “key used once”: larger n leaves less key entropy per message. HMAC, CMAC and similar computational MACs authenticate many messages with a fixed-length key because their security rests on PRF/block-cipher assumptions and the adversary is polynomial-time. Maurer’s bound belongs to unconditional authentication theory; it does not refute computational MACs. It says that without computational assumptions there is a hard lower bound. Mixing the two frameworks produces the false conclusion that “all MACs must be as long as the message”. An information-theoretic MAC must report key length, number n of authenticated messages and target deception probability together. “128-bit key” without n does not establish a 2^-64 deception bound. 1. Fix n: how many messages will use the same key. 2. Fix the target ε: the adversary’s success probability. 3. From ε ≥ 2^{-H(K)/(n+1)}, derive H(K) ≥ (n+1) log2(1/ε). 4. Check that the key actually has that entropy; short, biased or predictable keys do not qualify. 5. If n is large, use key derivation, per-message keys or a computational MAC instead of forcing an unconditional bound. - Unconditional MAC / authentication codes: Carter–Wegman universal hashing with one-time keys must account for key consumption across n messages. - Authentication after quantum key distribution: a one-time MAC must match key length to message volume and target failure probability. - Teaching and audit: the n=1 case, 1/√ K , shows that a 128-bit key does not give 128-bit authentication security. 1. The model assumes the receiver never rejects a valid message. If rejection, retransmission or arbitration is allowed, the bound changes and cannot be applied directly. 2. It covers impersonation and substitution only; not key leakage, implementation side channels, replay or denial of service. 3. It is a lower bound, not a construction. It says every scheme has at least this deception probability; it does not guarantee a scheme meeting equality. Achieving the bound needs specific key partitioning and encoding. 4. n must be fixed in advance. If the scheme adds messages dynamically, recompute the key budget; treating n as infinite yields a meaningless bound. 5. Entropy is not length. H(K) can be far below the bit length; all-zero keys and low-entropy passwords do not satisfy the model. 6. It provides no confidentiality. Authentication and secrecy are different goals; Maurer’s bound does not replace Shannon’s key-entropy bound. Simmons opened the study of authentication lower bounds in 1984; Gilbert, MacWilliams and Sloane and others gave combinatorial bounds. Maurer’s 1996 STACS paper unified these results in a hypothesis-testing framework and gave a general bound for n messages; his 2000 IEEE Transactions on Information Theory paper gave a fuller hypothesis-testing treatment. The bound remains foundational for information-theoretic authentication, authentication after quantum key distribution and unconditional MAC parameter analysis. It reminds engineering that the “short key” of a computational MAC is not free: security has been moved into a computational assumption. - Wikipedia search entry for Maurer 界. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Maurer%20%E7%95%8C - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Maurer's Bound: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Miller–Bleichenbacher Low-Exponent RSA Signature Forgery
items.text: Theorem : Miller–Bleichenbacher Low-Exponent RSA Signature Forgery (Miller–Bleichenbacher 低指数 RSA 签名伪造). Expected encoding RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 encodes a signature as EM=00‖01‖FF…FF‖00‖ASN.1(H)‖H(M), where H(M) must be right-justified. Verification computes s^e mod n, parses ASN.1 and H(M), and compares the digest with a fresh hash of the message. Lenient parsing If the verifier finds the end of padding and ASN.1, extracts a fixed-length H(M), but never checks whether bytes follow H(M), the trailing garbage G is ignored: EM′=00‖01‖FF…FF‖00‖ASN.1(H)‖H(M)‖G. For e=3, the attacker searches s near the cube root of the target prefix so that s^3=EM′ and EM′<n; submitting s as the signature makes the verifier extract the correct H(M) and accept. Why it works Small e makes the integer cube-root search feasible; a longer modulus leaves more room for G after the prefix and H(M). For larger e, extracting an e-th root is hard and the attack condition fails. This is not a break of RSA itself but of the parsing boundary in signature verification: the same s^e mod n must match the whole EM under a strict verifier, while a lenient verifier matches only a prefix and digest. Separating encoding, parsing and comparison shows that the flaw is in the implementation, not the mathematics. This is a signature-verification attack, not Bleichenbacher's 1998 padding-oracle attack on RSA encryption; both carry the name but differ in target, padding structure and conditions. It also differs from Håstad's broadcast attack, which targets unpadded low-exponent encryption. 1. Strict verification: rebuild the full EM from the message and compare it byte-for-byte with s^e mod n; do not extract only a digest. 2. Reject trailing data: reject any bytes after H(M); consume the entire ASN.1 structure and match OID and parameters exactly. 3. Choose an exponent: do not use e=3 for signatures; prefer RSA-PSS or a standard-approved scheme. 4. Negative tests: add vectors with trailing garbage, wrong ASN.1 and wrong OID, and confirm that every one is rejected. Do not check only the leading 00 01 and the digest; do not ignore ASN.1 lengths; do not assume a library default is safe without testing; do not treat this entry as an exploit tool. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Attack premises: a lenient verifier, small e and the ability to make a target verify the forged signature are all required. 2. Variants: beyond trailing garbage, weak checks of algorithm parameters, OID prefixes, padding byte values or ASN.1 lengths form the same family of flaws. 3. Strict implementation: full EM reconstruction, trailing-byte rejection, exact DER/OID checks and a larger e remove this route; RSA-PSS does not depend on this encoding parser. 4. Boundary: this entry covers signature-forgery verification flaws only, not private-key recovery, side channels or RSA factorisation; it provides no exploit steps or code. Daniel Bleichenbacher demonstrated the attack at the CRYPTO 2006 rump session; NIST then published a note describing the lenient parsing of PKCS 1 v1.5 and ANS X9.31 and giving fixes. A 2019 Black Hat white paper re-audited implementations and found variants involving trailing bytes, algorithm parameters, OID prefixes and padding checks. The catalogue keeps the Miller–Bleichenbacher juxtaposition; this entry expands only the Bleichenbacher 2006 route with public primary sources, because Miller's earlier observation is not in a verifiable source here. Repair status differs by PKCS 1 edition and verifier implementation, so the claimed edition governs. - Wikipedia search entry for Miller–Bleichenbacher 低指数 RSA 签名伪造. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Miller%E2%80%93Bleichenbacher%20%E4%BD%8E%E6%8C%87%E6%95%B0%20RSA%20%E7%AD%BE%E5%90%8D%E4%BC%AA%E9%80%A0 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Miller–Bleichenbacher Low-Exponent RSA Signature Forgery: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Multicollision
items.text: Attack : Multicollision (多重碰撞). The chaining structure of an iterated hash A Merkle-Damgard hash splits the message into blocks B_1,…,B_t and iterates h_i = f(h_{i-1}, B_i), with h_0 = IV, outputting h_t. If, at some chaining value h_{i-1}, one finds a pair of blocks (B_i, B_i′) such that f(h_{i-1}, B_i) = f(h_{i-1}, B_i′), then one block can be replaced without changing any later chaining value. Joux’s multicollision construction Starting from h_0 = IV, for i=1,…,t: 1. Call the collision finder to obtain B_i and B_i′ with f(h_{i-1}, B_i) = f(h_{i-1}, B_i′). Set h_i to this common chaining value. Continue to the next stage. At the end, choosing either B_i or B_i′ at every position yields 2^t distinct messages that pass through exactly the same intermediate chaining values and therefore hash to the same output. The cost is about t collision searches; for an n-bit output, each search costs about 2^{n/2}, so the total is about t·2^{n/2}. Why cascading hashes do not double security Concatenate two iterated hashes as F(M) = H_1(M) H_2(M), which looks like a 2n-bit output. Joux’s point is: first build a 2^t multicollision for H_1, then look for a collision in H_2 among those 2^t messages. For large enough t, the probability that both chains collide rises sharply. For two n-bit chains, finding a collision in the concatenation costs about O(n·2^{n/2}), not the 2^n expected from a birthday attack on a 2n-bit output. The cascade is about as secure as the easier chain, not the sum of the two. Many designers assumed that H_1 H_2 provides 2n-bit collision security, so two shorter hashes could resist a birthday attack. Joux showed that for iterated hashes this intuition is false: a multicollision turns “find one pair” into “find a collision on the second chain inside an exponentially large message set”, and the set size amplifies the second-chain collision probability. Hash-based signatures, Merkle trees and commitment schemes often rely on collision hardness. With an iterated hash, multicollisions let an attacker produce many messages with the same hash far below 2^n cost; in a commitment this may mean one commitment opens to several values, and in a signature it may mean message substitution. The exact impact depends on whether the protocol relies only on collision resistance or also on second-preimage and preimage resistance. Sponge constructions such as SHA-3, wide-pipe designs, randomised hashing and HAIFA do not automatically fit Joux’s “fixed chaining value + interchangeable blocks” argument. Judge the compression function, chaining-value width, message-block processing and final output, not just the number of output bits. 1. Confirm whether it is a Merkle-Damgard iteration and whether the chaining value equals the output length. 2. Check whether the compression function yields same-chaining-value collisions easily; if so, estimate the cost of a t-stage multicollision. 3. For a cascade, check whether the two chains are independent and equally sized; estimate the t needed to find a second-chain collision in a 2^t message set. 4. Check whether the protocol needs only collision resistance, or also second-preimage/preimage resistance; multicollisions mainly attack collision resistance. 5. For SHA-3/sponge designs, do not apply the formula mechanically; re-analyse the concrete structure. 6. Record the output length n, chain length t and collision-search cost; never treat “2n-bit output” as an automatic “n-bit security”. - Legacy MD5/SHA-1 cascades: do not use “double hashing” as a collision repair. - Merkle trees and hash signatures: assess multicollision effects on leaves and internal nodes. - Commitments and randomness generation: check whether H(x) is treated as a unique binding. 1. Non-iterated structure. Joux’s construction depends on fixed chaining values and replaceable message blocks; sponge/wide-pipe designs do not fit directly. 2. Hard-to-find compression collisions. If the compression function itself resists collisions, the t searches still carry their real cost. 3. Preimage/second-preimage only. Multicollisions mainly break collision resistance; they do not automatically give a preimage attack. 4. Output length differs from chaining-value length. A wide-pipe design may prevent an internal collision from becoming an output collision. 5. Randomised or salted hashing. If the input is randomised, the attacker cannot freely choose interchangeable blocks. 6. Cascades with unequal or strongly independent chains. The cost estimate changes; O(n·2^{n/2}) cannot be applied mechanically. “2^t messages with one hash” does not mean “a preimage was found”; “a cascade is always secure” is also false. Judge by the concrete construction and the security goal. In his CRYPTO 2004 paper, Joux proved that for an iterated hash, building a 2^t multicollision costs about t times an ordinary collision search, not 2^t times; he used this to settle the long-standing question of whether cascading several iterated hashes strengthens security. The result applies directly to Merkle-Damgard designs such as MD5 and SHA-1. After the SHA-1 collision attacks became public, the “double insurance” intuition for cascaded hashes was abandoned; the SHA-3 standardisation chose a sponge construction, and the structural weakness of iterated hashes became part of the design discussion. Joux’s multicollision is now a basic review item for hash design, hash signatures and commitment protocols. - Wikipedia search entry for 多重碰撞. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%A4%9A%E9%87%8D%E7%A2%B0%E6%92%9E - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[P\approx 1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{q(q-1)}{2\,2^n}\right)\] Multicollision: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: NTRU Lattice Public-Key Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : NTRU (NTRU 公钥加密). Ring and keys NTRU uses short private polynomials f,g in the polynomial ring modulo x^N−1 and public key h=p·g/f mod q; encryption is c=r·h+m, and decryption computes f·c, center-lifts and reduces modulo p to recover m. Here q is a power of two and p=3. Encryption and decryption Encode the message as a short polynomial m and pick a short random r; the ciphertext is c=r·h+m mod q. Decryption computes a=f·c mod q, center-lifts to [−q/2,q/2), then computes m=f_p^{-1}·a mod p. Correctness requires the noise f·r·g to stay in range. KEM and parameters The NIST submission turns NTRU into an IND-CCA2 KEM: encapsulation derives m and r from a random seed and hashes the ciphertext; decapsulation failure outputs an implicit rejection. ntruhps2048509 uses N=509 and q=2048, with a 699-byte public key/ciphertext, a 935-byte private key and a 32-byte shared secret. NTRU encryption is polynomial multiplication plus one inversion, and its keys are hundreds of times smaller than McEliece’s; on a CPU it is faster than RSA/ECC at comparable security and resists quantum attacks. It has more than two decades of public analysis, a simple structure and adjustable parameters, making it a conservative but usable lattice KEM: a roughly 0.7 KB public key suits TLS handshakes and embedded long-term keys. It has no worst-case reduction; security rests on the NTRU lattice assumption. NTRU was a NIST PQC finalist (July 2020), but NIST selected ML-KEM in 2022 and NTRU did not enter a FIPS standard; ISO/IEC 29192-4 Amd 2 is standardizing the NTRU KEM and reached FDIS in October 2026. It is used in Open Quantum Safe/liboqs, hybrid TLS, embedded firmware and long-term identity keys; ANSI X9.98 and IEEE P1363 had NTRUEncrypt profiles, and NTRU Prime is a separate branch. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Published parameters are not broken by lattice reduction (BKZ), but the decryption-failure rate must be provably negligible; failing ciphertexts can enable distinguishing or key recovery, so implementations must be constant-time and validate ciphertexts. Center lifting, modular inversion and key generation carry side-channel/fault risk; weak or non-invertible f causes decryption failure; NTRU lacks a worst-case reduction, and while Shor does not apply directly, lattice algorithms need continued evaluation. Boundaries: public keys/ciphertexts are larger than ML-KEM’s; encapsulation failure must be implicitly rejected; parameter sets cannot be mixed; NTRU and NTRU Prime use different rings and parameters. Hoffstein, Pipher and Silverman introduced NTRU at ANTS III in 1998; NTRU Cryptosystems commercialized it; it was submitted to NIST PQC in 2018, became a finalist in 2020 and was not selected for a NIST standard in 2022; in 2025–2026 it moved to ISO/IEC 29192-4 Amd 2. It is one of the earliest practical lattice public-key schemes and influenced NTRU Prime, NTRU+ and later designs. - Wikipedia search entry for NTRU 公钥加密. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=NTRU%20%E5%85%AC%E9%92%A5%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[(c,k)=\mathrm{Encaps}(pk);\qquad k'=\mathrm{Decaps}(sk,c)\] NTRU: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: OCB Authenticated Encryption Mode
items.text: Algorithm : Offset Codebook (OCB 偏移密码块模式). Offsets and one pass OCB3 derives a sequence of offsets Δ[i] from nonce N. Each plaintext block is XORed with an offset, encrypted by the block cipher and becomes a ciphertext block; the plaintext block is also accumulated into a checksum. The final block uses a special offset and length handling, and the tag is the encrypted checksum XORed with an offset. Associated data AD is authenticated but not encrypted: an offset-based MAC compresses it into a value that is folded into the tag. OCB needs only the encryption direction of the block cipher, all blocks can be parallelized, and one key with one pass adds only the tag length to the ciphertext. Parameters RFC 7253 requires a 128-bit block, allows nonces up to 120 bits (96 bits recommended), and supports configurable tag lengths; AES-OCB commonly uses a 128-bit tag, while TLS drafts use 96 bits. A nonce must be unique under one key. OCB’s selling point is one pass, one key and parallelism: authentication is woven into encryption, avoiding the two passes and two keys of Encrypt-then-MAC. On CPUs with AES instructions, OCB throughput approaches CTR, which suits low-latency networks and embedded devices. It is also a key name in AEAD history: OCB1 in 2001, OCB3 in 2011, RFC 7253 in 2014. OCB2 was completely broken in 2019, which shows why the version must be stated explicitly and OCB2 must never be used as OCB3. OCB is used in low-latency networking, disk/file encryption, embedded protocols and some TLS 1.2 drafts; OCB1 was an optional WRAP in IEEE 802.11i, OCB2 entered ISO/IEC 19772:2009, and OCB3 is RFC 7253. Requirements: unique nonces; at most 2^48 blocks under one key; tags of at least 96/128 bits; never treat OCB2 as OCB3; verify the tag before releasing plaintext. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. OCB is a nonce-respecting AEAD: encrypting two different messages with the same key and nonce breaks both confidentiality and authenticity, and an attacker can recover authentication secrets and forge later messages. RFC 7253 explicitly points such settings to SIV. Implementation boundaries: partition nonce counters; bind tag length; cap key usage at 2^48 blocks; verify before decrypting; the 2019 OCB2 attack shows why the version and implementation must be locked to OCB3. OCB1 was proposed by Rogaway, Bellare, Black and Krovetz in 2001; OCB2 followed in 2004; OCB3 was proposed by Krovetz and Rogaway in 2011; RFC 7253 appeared in 2014. OCB2 entered ISO/IEC 19772:2009 but was shown forgeable and decryptable by Inoue–Iwata–Minematsu–Poettering in 2019. Patents: Rogaway held four US patents, then intentionally let them lapse and placed his OCB-related IP in the public domain. Whether other AE patents apply is still hard to determine, so commercial deployments should perform an IP review. - Wikipedia search entry for OCB 偏移密码块模式. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=OCB%20%E5%81%8F%E7%A7%BB%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81%E5%9D%97%E6%A8%A1%E5%BC%8F - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Offset Codebook: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: One-Way Functions Imply P≠NP
items.text: Theorem : One-Way Functions Imply P≠NP (单向函数蕴含 P≠NP). One-way functions A one-way function f: {0,1} → {0,1} requires a polynomial-time algorithm for f(x), but for every probabilistic polynomial-time adversary A, given y=f(x) for x sampled from a distribution, the probability that A outputs a preimage x′ with f(x′)=y is negligible. The hardness is average-case, not a single worst-case instance. Writing inversion as an NP language L_y = { x : f(x) = y }. x is a membership witness: given x, verifying f(x)=y takes one polynomial-time evaluation. Hence L_y is in NP. If P=NP, a polynomial-time decider for L_y exists; for each y it can find a preimage in polynomial time (or decide that none exists). That directly contradicts the definition of a one-way function. The contrapositive Therefore P=NP ⇒ no one-way function exists; equivalently, a one-way function exists ⇒ P≠NP. The proof uses only “P=NP solves NP search” and says nothing about the converse from P≠NP to a one-way function. It connects cryptography’s minimal assumption to complexity theory’s biggest open problem: if P=NP one day, it is not just a particular structure in RSA or AES that breaks; every one-way function whose security relies on average-case inversion hardness becomes insecure. P≠NP says that some NP problem is hard in the worst case; it does not say that an average-case hard function exists. Cryptography needs random instances to be hard, not the existence of one hard instance. P≠NP is necessary, not sufficient. A cryptographic construction cannot cite “P≠NP, therefore secure”. Security must be reduced to a concrete one-way function, pseudorandom generator or lattice assumption with an explicit adversary-advantage bound. 1. Textbooks use this implication to explain why one-way functions are cryptography’s minimal hardness assumption. 2. In a security proof, a construction from one-way functions indirectly depends on P≠NP, but the proof still has to supply the concrete reduction. 3. In complexity teaching, it turns inversion into NP search and is the standard example of an NP witness and search complexity. 4. As a negative result, it says that any P=NP algorithm breaks all OWFs, not just one scheme. It cannot justify a concrete key length, and it cannot prove that a particular function is one-way. The existence of one-way functions remains an unproven assumption. P≠NP does not imply that a one-way function exists. An NP problem can be worst-case hard while almost all instances are easy; cryptography needs average-case hardness. Impagliazzo’s “five worlds” makes the gap explicit: in Pessiland, P≠NP but no one-way functions exist. 1. Quantum adversaries: quantum algorithms can break the specific OWFs behind RSA/ECC, but “OWF ⇒ P≠NP” remains a classical complexity statement. 2. Non-uniform adversaries: circuit complexity and non-uniform security need a different set of assumptions. 3. Distribution dependence: an OWF’s hardness depends on the input distribution; a function that is easy on some distribution is not an OWF. 4. Worst-case to average-case bridges: constructing an OWF from a worst-case hard problem usually needs an additional reduction. 5. Proof technique: P≠NP itself is unproven, so the implication is conditional, not an established existence theorem. The implication is a logical relation, not a security proof. It says “P=NP would destroy OWFs”; it does not say “P≠NP is enough to build OWFs”. Diffie and Hellman made one-way functions a conceptual foundation of public-key cryptography in 1976. Goldreich’s Foundations of Cryptography formalised the definition and the distinction between average-case hardness and worst-case complexity. Katz and Lindell’s Introduction to Modern Cryptography starts from OWFs and uses “if P=NP, no OWF exists” to connect cryptographic assumptions with complexity theory. The statement appears as an exercise or lemma, not as a full solution to P versus NP. - Wikipedia search entry for 单向函数蕴含 P≠NP. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%8D%95%E5%90%91%E5%87%BD%E6%95%B0%E8%95%B4%E5%90%AB%20P%E2%89%A0NP - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] One-Way Functions Imply P≠NP: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: P vs NP
items.text: Theorem : P vs NP (P vs NP). P and NP P is the class of languages decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time; NP is the class of languages with a polynomial-length witness that can be verified in polynomial time. A decision problem asks “does a solution exist”; a search problem asks “give me one”. For an NP language, a witness can be built bit by bit, but each step still calls the NP decider. NP-completeness and reductions Cook and Levin proved that Boolean satisfiability (SAT) is NP-complete: every NP language L reduces in polynomial time to SAT, with x∈L iff the reduced formula is satisfiable. Karp then listed 21 NP-complete problems. A reduction propagates “a polynomial algorithm for one problem” into “a polynomial algorithm for the whole class”. Why it is open Neither P=NP nor P≠NP has been proved. Known techniques face barriers: relativising proofs cannot distinguish worlds with and without an oracle; natural proofs, if sufficiently constructive and large, would break pseudorandom functions; algebrisation extends relativisation but still does not settle P versus NP. P versus NP asks whether easy verification implies easy solving. If P=NP, SAT, travelling salesman and many optimisation and search problems would have a unified polynomial algorithm, and many worst-case problems behind cryptography would collapse. Cryptography needs random instances to be hard, not merely one hard instance. P≠NP only rules out worst-case easiness; it does not guarantee average-case hardness. One-way functions, pseudorandom generators and lattice assumptions are stronger and more specific than P≠NP. A security proof cannot say “because P≠NP”. It must reduce to a concrete assumption and state success probability, query counts and parameter relations; it must also avoid mistaking worst-case hardness for average-case security. 1. Complexity classification: P, NP, NP-complete, coNP and PSPACE form a hierarchy; P versus NP is the nearest separation. 2. Reduction toolbox: reduce a new problem to SAT/3-SAT/clique/TSP to bound its difficulty. 3. Cryptographic parameter assessment: reduce attacks to known hard problems and estimate key length and adversary advantage. 4. Proof barriers: before designing a new proof, check whether relativisation, natural proofs or algebrisation applies. 5. Teaching: SAT is the standard example of witnesses, reductions and nondeterminism. The open status of P versus NP cannot endorse a concrete protocol; nor does NP-completeness imply that all instances are hard. 1. “NP-hard” is not “average-case hard”: an NP-complete problem can have many easy instances. 2. “P≠NP” is not “one-way functions exist”: average-case assumptions and reductions are needed. 3. “SAT is satisfiable” is not “a solution can be found quickly”: decision differs from search. 4. “A reduction” is not “a practical algorithm”: a polynomial reduction may have enormous constants. 5. “A quantum algorithm” does not automatically settle P versus NP: Shor solves specific algebraic problems, not SAT. Relativisation (Baker–Gill–Solovay) says any proof using only oracle-relativising techniques cannot separate P and NP; natural proofs (Razborov–Rudich) say a broad class of combinatorial lower-bound proofs conflicts with pseudorandom-function assumptions; algebrisation (Aaronson–Wigderson) covers more algebraic techniques but still falls short. A barrier is not “impossible”, only “current techniques are insufficient”. Cook proved SAT NP-complete in 1971, Levin independently obtained a similar result in 1973, and Karp listed 21 NP-complete problems in 1972. P versus NP then became a central open problem in complexity theory and a Clay Millennium Problem. Baker, Gill and Solovay described the relativisation barrier in 1975; Razborov and Rudich proposed natural proofs in 1994/1997; Aaronson and Wigderson proposed algebrisation in 2008. These results changed expectations about how a proof of P≠NP could work. - Wikipedia search entry for P vs NP. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=P%20vs%20NP - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] P vs NP: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Paillier Cryptosystem
items.text: Algorithm : Paillier (Paillier 陷门公钥密码). Addition modulo n² Paillier’s public key is (n,g) ; the private key is derived from p,q and usually written (λ,μ) . Encryption picks a random r and computes c=g^m·r^n mod n² . Decryption uses L(x)=(x-1)/n and computes m=L(c^λ mod n²)/L(g^λ mod n²) mod n . A common choice is g=n+1 . Why it is homomorphic Multiplying two ciphertexts gives E(m1)·E(m2)=g^{m1+m2}(r1r2)^n , which decrypts to m1+m2 mod n . Raising a ciphertext to k gives an encryption of k·m . It supports addition and scalar multiplication, not arbitrary multiplication, so it is not fully homomorphic. Security assumption The scheme rests on the Decisional Composite Residuosity Assumption (DCRA): distinguishing n -th residues modulo n² is hard. The original scheme is IND-CPA secure, but its homomorphism makes it malleable, so it is not IND-CCA2 secure as written. Paillier fills the slot for “private addition without the weight of full FHE”. Private statistics, electronic voting, secure aggregation in federated learning, threshold cryptography and MPC often need only ciphertext addition or scalar multiplication; Paillier provides exactly that layer. It is slower than RSA and its ciphertext is about n² bits, but for addition-only workloads its parameters and implementation are far simpler than a full homomorphic system. In electronic voting, ciphertexts are multiplied and the decrypted result is the tally; in private aggregation, counts or gradients are encrypted and added; threshold Paillier splits decryption among parties so no single server sees the plaintext. It also serves as a subprotocol in zero-knowledge proofs and MPC. These uses assume only a bounded number of homomorphic operations. Deep circuits call for BFV, CKKS, TFHE or another fully homomorphic scheme. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Paillier ciphertexts are about n² bits, larger than RSA, and modular exponentiation is slower. It supports addition but not general multiplication or comparison. The original scheme is malleable and not chosen-ciphertext secure. Deployments should use a hash-bound variant such as Paillier–Pointcheval, or wrap Paillier in a KEM/DEM. Use at least 2048-bit moduli under current guidance, check gcd(L(g^λ mod n²),n)=1 , and require fresh r coprime to n . Pascal Paillier published “Public-Key Cryptosystems Based on Composite Degree Residuosity Classes” at EUROCRYPT 1999, LNCS 1592, pp. 223–238. The paper introduced the composite residuosity problem and gave a trapdoor permutation plus two homomorphic probabilistic encryption schemes. Paillier and Paillier–Pointcheval later became standard building blocks for privacy-preserving computation and voting. items.title: PLONK
items.text: Algorithm : PLONK (PLONK 通用证明系统). Circuit proofs over a universal SRS PLONK encodes an arithmetic circuit as gate constraints plus copy constraints: each gate is addition or multiplication, and a permutation argument enforces that the same wire carries the same value at different positions. The prover commits to wire values, permutation polynomials and quotient polynomials using a polynomial commitment (usually KZG); the verifier checks several openings. It uses a universal, updatable structured reference string (SRS) : one parameter set can prove any circuit up to a size bound, instead of a fresh ceremony per circuit. PLONK removes Groth16’s “one setup per circuit” problem. A universal SRS can be updated by a multi-party ceremony; security holds if at least one participant is honest, so developers can reuse parameters and iterate on circuits quickly. Proofs remain constant-size and verification sublinear. Compared with Sonic, the prover performs far fewer group exponentiations, making PLONK practical to deploy. PLONK and its variants (TurboPLONK, UltraPLONK, PlonKup) are used by Aztec, zkSync and other privacy/scaling projects; custom gates and lookup tables make hashes and range checks cheaper. It is also the main entry point for engineering universal zk-SNARKs: Circom, Halo2 and snarkjs offer PLONK-style backends. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. PLONK’s universal SRS is still a trusted setup: KZG relies on pairing groups and q-SDH-style assumptions, so it is not post-quantum. Proofs are constant-size but usually larger than Groth16, and verification is heavier. The zero-knowledge argument of the original PLONK specification was later found incomplete; subsequent versions patched the simulator. Implementations must use the patched specification and enforce domain separation, challenge derivation and polynomial-commitment checks. TurboPLONK, UltraPLONK and PlonKup later added custom gates, lookups and faster proving; PLONK became the name of a broad family of universal SNARKs. items.title: Pretexting
items.text: Attack : Pretexting (借口欺诈). Pretexting is social engineering that uses a false identity, invented situation or fabricated reason to obtain information or access. It is not simply lying; it builds a script that makes the target willing to lower the verification threshold: “I am IT support”, “I am bank risk”, “I am a new colleague”, “I am handling an urgent transfer”. Success decomposes into three factors: P_success=P(pretext accepted)·P(target holds the information accepted)·P(verification bypassed accepted and informed). If the target has n independent checks, each with block probability v_i, then P_bypass=∏(1-v_i). Adding one reliable out-of-band callback sharply lowers the product. A logistic approximation can describe the behavioral side: P(accept)=σ(β0+β1·credibility+β2·authority+β3·urgency-β4·verification salience). This is this card's behavioral model, not a formula published by the FTC or any standard; it explains why “urgent + authoritative + seemingly internal” works so often. When technical boundaries are bypassed, people are the weakest link. Pretexting can obtain phone records, bank information, cloud accounts and customer data, or prepare a later intrusion. It turns identity verification from a single check into an attack chain: obtain a small fact to build credibility, then ask for more access. The defensive value is shifting verification from “what the caller says” to “what I confirmed through an independent channel”. Every sensitive action should have callback, ticket, dual review and least privilege. Steps: reconnaissance (public information, org chart, scripts) → pretext (identity/reason/emotion) → contact (phone/email/SMS/in person) → extraction (split requests, escalate gradually) → monetize or persist. Controls: distrust caller ID, call back on a public number, require a ticket number, use dual review for transfers, password changes and record lookups; run scenario drills, not only security emails. FTC cases show phone-record pretexting once supported a whole market; CISA classifies vishing as social engineering and warns that VoIP makes caller-ID spoofing easy. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Failure: the target insists on out-of-band verification, calls the official number, does not reveal internal structure; the organization has tickets or dual review; pretexting may violate GLBA, FCRA, computer-fraud law or other rules; security culture recognizes the script. The FTC acted against Touch Tone in 1999; the complaint describes impersonating account holders to induce financial institutions to disclose private information. FTC testimony in 2007 defined pretexting as obtaining personal information under false pretenses, noted that GLBA did not cover phone records, and used Section 5. In the 2020s, vishing, deepfake voice and outsourced call centers make scripts more convincing, but independent callback remains the strongest break point. - Wikipedia search entry for 借口欺诈. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%80%9F%E5%8F%A3%E6%AC%BA%E8%AF%88 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Pretexting: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SM9 Identity-Based Cryptography
items.text: Protocol : SM9 Identity-Based Cryptography (SM9 标识密码). Identity is the public key SM9 is identity-based cryptography: a user’s public key is determined by an identity string (email, ID number, domain name), and the private key is derived by a key generation center (KGC) from the master secret and the identity. Separate signature and encryption master key pairs exist; the master public keys are public and the master secrets are held by the KGC. Bilinear pairing and signatures SM9 uses a bilinear pairing e: G1×G2→GT on a 256-bit BN curve of prime order N. The signing key is dsA = [ks/(H1(IDA hid,N)+ks)]P1. A signature (h,S) uses g=e(P1,Ppub-s), w=g^r, h=H2(M w,N), l=(r−h) mod n and S=[l]dsA; verification recovers w from e(S, [H1(IDA hid,N)]P2+Ppub-s). Encryption and key exchange Encryption uses the recipient identity IDB and encryption master public key Ppub-e to compute a shared pairing value, KDF-derives a key, and outputs C1=[r]Q, C2 and C3. Key exchange computes a shared value from both identities and private keys, then derives a session key. SM9’s value is removing certificate chains: the public key is the identity and the KGC derives private keys, which suits IoT, government, email and enterprise intranets where identities already exist. One identity-based standard family covers signatures, encryption, key exchange and KEM, reducing certificate issuance, distribution and revocation overhead. The price is key escrow: the KGC knows or can generate every user’s private key, and master-key leakage compromises the whole system. It fits closed domains with centrally managed identities, not fully decentralized settings. It is used for identity authentication, encrypted mail, electronic seals, IoT device identity and government/enterprise networks; outside TLCP, SM9 has separate signature, encryption and key-exchange flows. The standards are the GM/T 0044 series, raised to GB/T 38635 in 2020; identity-based encryption entered ISO/IEC 18033-5 in 2021. Requirements: fix hid and curve parameters; protect or threshold-share the KGC master secret; distribute user private keys securely; check the h range and that S lies in G1; validate C1 lies in G1 during decryption. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. SM9 security rests on bilinear Diffie–Hellman-type problems, SM3, the KGC master secret and user private keys. Single-point master-key leakage, a malicious KGC, key escrow, pairing side channels, identity-string ambiguity and private-key revocation are real risks. Boundaries: SM9 is not a certificateless decentralized scheme; it concentrates trust in the KGC. Identity canonicalization (case, encoding, hid) must be consistent across systems, and one master key should not serve signature and encryption without domain separation. Identity-based cryptography was proposed by Shamir in 1984. SM9 was organized by OSCCA: the GM/T 0044 series (five parts) appeared on 28 March 2016, and GB/T 38635.1/.2-2020 was published on 28 April 2020 and took effect in November 2020. SM9 signatures entered ISO/IEC 14888-3 in 2018; identity-based encryption entered ISO/IEC 18033-5 Amendment 1 in February 2021. SM9’s significance is turning identity-based cryptography from a paper concept into an interoperable Chinese commercial standard with an international standards footprint. - Wikipedia search entry for SM9 标识密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SM9%20%E6%A0%87%E8%AF%86%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] SM9 Identity-Based Cryptography: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Physical Unclonable Functions
items.text: Algorithm : Physically Unclonable Function (物理不可克隆函数). Challenge–response and delay mechanism A PUF maps fabrication randomness to a challenge–response pair R=PUF(C): the same chip is repeatable and another chip cannot be cloned. An arbiter PUF races two paths through k switching stages and a latch compares arrival order; responses are noisy, so error correction and a fuzzy extractor recover a stable key. Delay-based and memory-based designs The arbiter delay difference is Δ=w^TΦ(C); RO PUFs compare oscillator frequencies, SRAM PUFs use power-up values, and butterfly PUFs use cross-coupled latches. Strong PUFs have an exponential CRP space; weak PUFs have only a few CRPs. Key derivation Enrollment collects several CRPs, produces helper data and a stable key; reconstruction uses the helper data to correct noise. Helper data must not leak the key, so designs pair it with a fuzzy extractor and a strong extractor. A PUF keeps no long-term key in NVM: the secret disappears when power is removed, resisting cloning and readout at low cost for RFID, FPGA, IoT and chip roots of trust. It turns “physically unclonable” into a measurable value for device identity, license binding and anti-counterfeiting. Unlike a secure element, a PUF is a key source rather than a complete protocol. PUFs are used for FPGA IP protection, device authentication, anti-counterfeiting labels, secure-boot key release and TPM/root-of-trust functions; SRAM PUFs are commercial, while arbiter and RO PUFs serve lightweight authentication. Strong PUFs offer an exponential CRP space for stateless authentication; weak PUFs have few CRPs and suit key generation. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Delay PUFs are learnable with logistic regression and machine learning: a plain arbiter PUF falls at about 640 CRPs, while XOR and feed-forward variants need more but are not unbreakable. Reliability varies with temperature, voltage and aging. Helper data can leak information, and fault injection or invasive readout can break the assumptions. A PUF is not an encryption algorithm; it must be bound to a challenge–response protocol with rate limiting and replay protection. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. Optical and silicon PUFs appeared in 2002; Suh and Devadas gave a ring-oscillator PUF and key generation in 2007; Rührmair et al. systematically demonstrated modeling attacks in 2010; XOR PUFs, lightweight PUFs and standardization discussions followed. items.title: Purple Cryptanalysis
items.text: Attack : Purple Cryptanalysis (紫密破译). The 6-20 structure Purple, the Japanese Type 97 alphabetical typewriter, maps 26 letters through an input plugboard into an internal alphabet fixed as six “sixes” and twenty “twenties”. Encryption is E=P_{out}(T_{20}(T_6(P_{in}(p)))): the sixes pass through one 25-position stepping switch and the twenties through three 25-position switches, after which the output plugboard maps back to letters. The break The naive key space is 26!×6×25^4≈9.45×10^{32}. The 6-20 split restricts the alphabet permutation to 6!·20!; once the six letters are identified, settings drop from 6×25^4=2,343,750 to 6×25^3=93,750, and the switch period is at most 25^3=15,625. In September 1940 Genevieve Grotjan found repeated patterns linking the sixes and twenties, moving the US team from an 18-month deadlock to rebuilding a Purple analog. The Purple break shows that a large key space is not the same as security: a fixed 6-20 partition splits 26! into 6!·20! and makes statistical identification possible. It relies on finding a structural invariant before rebuilding the stepping, not on raw machine speed. This is the break mechanism; the machine--purple entry covers the machine structure. The machine entry answers what Purple is made of; this entry answers how the 6-20 split, stepping and known plaintext recover the settings. 1. Collect diplomatic traffic from one key period and find a predictable opening or crib. 2. Separate sixes from twenties by frequency and repeated patterns. 3. Fix the 25-position sixes and recover the 20-letter permutation. 4. Expand the three twenties switches by the stepping rule and match known plaintext. 5. Verify the settings on a second passage before reconstructing the full text. Do not generalise the 6-20 structure to all rotor ciphers; do not declare a unique key from one crib; do not ignore plugboard and stepping differences between versions. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Structural change: if the partition is no longer 6-20, the statistical separation and the 6!·20! reduction fail. 2. Insufficient known plaintext: without a crib, the stepping phase is hard to fix. 3. Message variation: transcoding, abbreviations or padding destroy the pattern. 4. Non-unique settings: short messages can leave several candidates and need a second passage. 5. Rebuild error: wrong switch wiring or stepping order makes decryption fail completely. Japan upgraded to Purple in 1939, and the US Signal Intelligence Service failed to break it for 18 months. In September 1940 Genevieve Grotjan found the repeated relation between sixes and twenties; on 27 September the team read the first messages. Leo Rosen rebuilt an analog with uniselectors—six telephone stepping switches with 25 contacts. - Wikipedia search entry for 紫密破译. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%B4%AB%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%B4%E8%AF%91 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Purple Cryptanalysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Quantum Collision Bound
items.text: Attack : Quantum Collision Search (量子碰撞搜索). Classical collision search For an n-bit hash, sampling about 2^{n/2} inputs finds a collision with high probability by the birthday paradox. This is optimal up to constants in the classical black-box model: Ω(2^{n/2}) evaluations. Preimage search needs about 2^n evaluations. BHT’s quantum algorithm Brassard–Høyer–Tapp 1998 gave a quantum collision algorithm: for an r-to-one function f:{0,1}^N→{0,1}^M, it finds a collision in expected O((N/r)^{1/3}) evaluations. For an n-bit hash this is O(2^{n/3}). The algorithm first builds and sorts a list of about 2^{n/3} inputs and their images; it then uses Grover search to find a collision between the list and a fresh input. Quantum search square-roots the remaining search, yielding total cost 2^{n/3}. Why not 2^{n/2} The classical birthday attack stores and compares up to 2^{n/2} samples; BHT reduces the sample count to 2^{n/3} and uses Grover over the remaining space. Grover gives only a square-root speedup for unstructured search, so the classical 2^{n/2} becomes 2^{n/3}, not 2^{n/4}. For preimages, Grover only turns 2^n into 2^{n/2}; collision and preimage are different complexity curves. If the target is 128-bit security against classical collision attacks, a 256-bit hash suffices (2^{128}). To resist quantum collision attacks, 2^{n/3}=2^{128} needs n≈384. NIST post-quantum signatures such as SPHINCS+ therefore use longer hash outputs or adjusted parameter sets. Treating a 256-bit hash as “still 128-bit collision security under quantum” is a common error. Grover on AES-256 preimage/key search costs 2^{128}, not 2^{256/3}; BHT targets collisions. The main public-key threat is Shor, not BHT. Parameter evaluation must be done per primitive and per target, not with one “quantum speedup factor”. BHT needs quantum random-access memory, coherent queries and many logical qubits; current hardware is nowhere near 2^{85} coherent evaluations. It is a lower-bound analysis for parameter selection, not an executable attack schedule. 1. State the target: classical collision, quantum collision, preimage or second preimage. 2. Classical collision: an n-bit output gives n/2 bits of security. 3. Quantum collision: estimate by 2^{n/3}; a target of b bits needs n≥3b. 4. Preimage: classical 2^n; quantum Grover 2^{n/2}. 5. Check whether the protocol relies on properties beyond collision resistance (PRF, commitments, Merkle trees). 6. Include memory, coherence time and error correction in practical feasibility; do not look only at the asymptotic exponent. - Hash-based signatures such as SPHINCS+/XMSS: choose hash output and tree height against both classical and quantum collisions. - Post-quantum security categories: interpret NIST category 1/3/5 parameters. - Blockchains and code signing: long-lived data needs a “store-now, decrypt-later” quantum assessment. 1. Black-box model. BHT assumes a black-box function; algorithms that exploit the hash internals may do better. 2. Quantum memory model. The algorithm needs quantum RAM or substantial coherent storage; different cost models change constants and feasibility. 3. Collisions only. It does not lower preimage search to 2^{n/3}; Grover preimage remains 2^{n/2}. 4. Asymptotic notation hides constants. The constant in 2^{n/3}, parallelization and memory access all affect real cost. 5. Current hardware. Logical qubits, error correction and coherence time are practical bottlenecks; an exponent is not a near-term timeline. 6. Not every hash use rests on collisions alone. MACs, PRFs, commitments and zero knowledge may rely on different properties and need separate analysis. Grover gave the square-root speedup for unstructured search in 1996; Brassard, Høyer and Tapp applied it to collision and claw search in 1997/1998, obtaining O((N/r)^{1/3}). The paper became the standard citation for post-quantum hash-security assessment. NIST launched its post-quantum cryptography process in 2016 and published NISTIR 8105 in 2017 on the quantum impact. Hash-based signatures and symmetric primitives began reporting classical and quantum collision bounds together; BHT moved from a theoretical algorithm into the language of standard parameters. - Wikipedia search entry for 量子碰撞搜索. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%87%8F%E5%AD%90%E7%A2%B0%E6%92%9E%E6%90%9C%E7%B4%A2 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[P\approx 1-\exp\!\left(-\frac{q(q-1)}{2\,2^n}\right)\] Quantum Collision Search: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Quantum Resource Estimation
items.text: Attack : Quantum Resource Estimation (量子资源估算). From algorithm to resources Shor’s algorithm reduces integer factoring to order finding: choose a, find the least r 0 with a^r ≡ 1 (mod N), then use gcd(a^{r/2}±1,N) to obtain a factor. Elliptic-curve discrete logarithm reduces to period finding: given Q=[k]P, find k. The quantum circuit contains controlled modular exponentiation or point addition, a quantum Fourier transform and its inverse. The resource ledger A resource estimate is not just “how many qubits”. It must separate logical qubits, Toffoli (or T) counts, circuit depth, ancilla qubits, measurement and initialisation counts, and the physical qubits and runtime needed for fault-tolerant error correction. For ECC over an n-bit prime field, Roetteler et al. give the upper bounds 9n + 2⌈log₂n⌉ + 10 logical qubits, 448 n³ log₂n + 4090 n³ Toffoli gates. Physical overhead A surface code encodes each logical qubit in a d×d physical patch, where the distance d is chosen for the target error rate; physical qubit count grows roughly as d², and runtime is constrained by the code cycle, measurement feedback and magic-state distillation. Gidney and Ekerå’s RSA-2048 estimate uses 20 million noisy qubits and 8 hours, explicitly assuming a 10⁻³ gate error rate, a 1 μs code cycle and a 10 μs reaction time. Change the assumptions and the numbers change. “A quantum computer can break RSA” is an algorithm-level statement; “2048-bit RSA can be broken before a given year” needs a physical-layer ledger. Resource estimation separates the two and lets migration plans discuss parameters, time windows and uncertainty instead of a slogan. NIST post-quantum migration does not start when a quantum computer appears. Key sizes, certificate chains, protocol handshakes and hardware accelerators must be changed in advance. Resource estimates help identify which parameters are most exposed (for example, ECC often needs fewer qubits than RSA at a comparable security level) and which “quantum-safe” proposal merely changes the mathematical assumption. A resource estimate is an upper or lower bound under stated hardware assumptions, not a calendar prediction. It does not show that a machine exists, and it does not extrapolate a laboratory demonstration into an Internet-scale attack. 1. Identify the algorithm, key length, certificate lifetime and data-confidentiality horizon to protect. 2. Read the logical-resource tables in the original paper: qubits, Toffoli counts, depth and ancillas. 3. Convert to physical resources using the target hardware’s error rate, code distance, code cycle and magic-state distillation cost. 4. Combine several independent estimates into an interval; do not turn one point estimate into a fixed date. 5. Feed the result into a crypto-agility plan: hybrid key exchange, certificate rotation, performance budget and rollback. NIST post-quantum standardisation, national migration roadmaps and industry assessments use resource estimates as inputs. They focus on “within what time window and at what cost” migration must happen, not on proving that a particular machine does not exist. 1. Treating logical qubits as physical qubits underestimates error-correction overhead by orders of magnitude. 2. Treating asymptotic complexity as a constant ignores coefficients, ancillas and data movement. 3. Ignoring fault-tolerance assumptions: gate error, code distance, measurement speed, magic-state distillation and connectivity all change the ledger. 4. Treating an algorithmic upper bound as a lower bound: “at most” does not mean “at least”. 5. Extrapolating a small laboratory demonstration into a large-scale attack: a small circuit is not a scalable fault-tolerant machine. 6. Ignoring the classical side: data collection, linear algebra, post-processing and the time window also consume resources. A resource estimate is neither a security proof nor a threat prophecy. It is a reviewable cost model; every number must be cited with its algorithm, parameters, error-correction scheme and hardware assumptions. “How many qubits” without those assumptions is meaningless. Shor’s 1994 polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms turned the quantum threat from speculation into an algorithmic fact. Early estimates focused on logical qubits and gate counts; later work brought fault tolerance, surface codes, magic-state distillation and parallelism into the ledger. Roetteler, Naehrig, Svore and Lauter gave gate-level upper bounds for ECC discrete logarithms in 2017 and noted that, at comparable security levels, ECC usually needs fewer qubits than RSA. Gidney and Ekerå advanced the RSA-2048 estimate in 2021 to an engineering scenario of “8 hours, 20 million noisy qubits”, with an explicit list of hardware assumptions. - Wikipedia search entry for 量子资源估算. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%87%8F%E5%AD%90%E8%B5%84%E6%BA%90%E4%BC%B0%E7%AE%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[Q=\Theta\!\left(\sqrt{ \mathcal{K} }\right)=\Theta(2^{\kappa/2})\] Quantum Resource Estimation: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Rabbit Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : Rabbit (Rabbit 流密码). A 513-bit state with eight counters Rabbit has a 513-bit internal state: eight 32-bit state variables X0..X7, eight 32-bit counters C0..C7, and one carry bit b. Each clock adds fixed constants a0..a7 (0x4D34D34D, 0xD34D34D3, 0x34D34D34 in rotation) to the counters; a 32-bit overflow produces the carry used by the next word. Key setup and IV mixing The 128-bit key is split into eight 16-bit subkeys and interleaved into X and C by parity; the system iterates four times, then sets C_j ^= X_{j+4} and b = 1. The 64-bit IV is XORed into the counter words and the system iterates four more times. In each output clock, g_j = (x_j + c_j)^2 is formed, its high and low halves are XORed to update the eight state words, and the eight words are combined into a 128-bit output block. No S-boxes Rabbit uses only 32-bit addition, XOR, rotation and squaring. There are no lookup tables; each clock emits 128 bits, so software pipelines stay busy. Nonlinearity comes from the coupled squaring function and counter carries, not from an S-box. Rabbit was designed for high software throughput. The FSE 2003 paper reports 3.7 cycles per byte on a Pentium III. The absence of table lookups also makes cache behavior predictable, unlike AES T-table implementations with secret-dependent indices. It entered the eSTREAM software portfolio, and RFC 4503 gives an interoperable description. The goal was to run fast on ordinary 32-bit instructions, not to minimize gate count; Rabbit and Grain/Trivium therefore sit on opposite ends of the software-hardware trade-off. RFC 4503 specifies Rabbit key setup, IV setup, next-state function, output extraction and test vectors, making it suitable for software libraries and embedded protocols. It can encrypt data streams, generate pseudorandom bits and serve as a high-speed software stream-cipher benchmark. Rabbit is not a TLS cipher suite and lacks the deployment breadth of AES-GCM. Using it means the protocol must define key/IV management and integrity protection itself. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Rabbit has only a 64-bit IV. Under one key, random IVs will collide at high message volumes; RFC 4503 requires a fresh IV per encryption, but the birthday bound in a 64-bit space is already material around 2^32 messages. It has no built-in authentication, so a MAC is required. Key/IV reuse directly reveals plaintext XOR. A physical adversary can also inject faults: the SAC 2009 differential fault analysis recovers the full internal state from about 128 to 256 random bit faults in roughly 2^38 work, so device-level protection is not optional. The design limit is on the order of 2^64 bytes per key; beyond that the counter period and the security argument no longer hold. No practical chosen-plaintext attack is publicly known on the full cipher, but absence of a published attack does not excuse skipping IV and implementation defenses. Boesgaard, Vesterager, Pedersen, Christiansen and Scavenius presented Rabbit at FSE 2003, then submitted it to eSTREAM, where it entered the software portfolio. RFC 4503 standardized the description in 2006, and the algorithm became public domain in 2008. Its discretized chaotic map plus counter design made it a reference point for high-throughput software stream ciphers. - Wikipedia search entry for Rabbit 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Rabbit%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Rabbit: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
