items.title: Random self-reduction
items.text: Theorem : Random Self-Reducibility (随机自归约). Randomize a worst-case instance Let f be a one-way function. If a polynomial-time algorithm R exists such that for every x it samples r and outputs y=R(x;r), where y’s distribution is independent of x (usually close to uniform), and given f(y) and r one can recover f(x) in polynomial time, then f is random self-reducible. Hence: if f is hard on average random instances, it is hard on every instance. Discrete logarithm In a cyclic group G of order q with generator g, let y=g^x. Choose r←Z_q and compute y' = y·g^r = g^{x+r}. If an oracle A returns the discrete log x' of y', then x = x'−r mod q. y' is uniform in G and independent of y; one random-instance answer recovers the original. RSA blinding For an RSA public key (N,e) and ciphertext c=m^e mod N, choose r←Z_N^ and compute c' = c·r^e = (m·r)^e mod N. If an oracle decrypts c' to m', then m = m'·r^{-1} mod N. r is invertible, so the blinding factor cancels modulo N; this is the algebra behind RSA blinding. A cryptographic assumption usually says “no polynomial algorithm inverts on worst-case instances”; a real attacker only needs success on random instances. Random self-reduction connects the two worlds: success on average instances moves to any instance, and worst-case hardness spreads to random instances. Blinding hides the message and makes decryption time independent of the ciphertext: multiply by random r^e, decrypt, then remove r at the end. A side-channel attacker sees intermediate values unrelated to the real m; this is the engineering use of random self-reduction. - Average-to-worst case: DL, RSA and CDH often use random self-reduction to turn worst-case assumptions into average-case ones. - Blinding: RSA decryption and signing blind before use to resist timing and chosen-ciphertext side channels. - Hardness amplification: repeat independent random instances to raise success δ to 1−(1−δ)^k, then choose parameters with error correction. Reading: check that the randomization is a group homomorphism, the inverse map is computable, and the random-instance distribution is close to uniform. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. It needs algebraic structure. Randomization must preserve the instance’s homomorphic relation; an arbitrary OWF or hash has no such structure. 2. It needs an invertible blinding factor. RSA’s r must lie in Z_N^ ; if r shares a factor with N, the inverse does not exist and blinding fails. 3. The oracle’s success is on average. If it succeeds only on some random instances, repetition can amplify success, but independence or a good distribution is needed. 4. It does not automatically give a concrete security bound. Blinding hides intermediate values but does not prove RSA secure; it moves the attack surface from “any instance” to “random instances”. 5. Group order and representation matter. Randomization for discrete log in composite-order or elliptic-curve groups takes a different form; rewrite the formula in the group operation. Random self-reduction is a reduction tool, not a defence by itself. If the underlying problem is easy on random instances, blinding adds only constant overhead and does not change breakability. Blum and Micali used the random self-reduction of discrete log in 1984 to build a pseudorandom bit generator: predicting the next bit on random instances would solve discrete log on any instance. Goldwasser and Micali described random self-reduction as the royal road from worst-case to average-case reductions. RSA blinding entered implementations in the 1980s against timing attacks; chosen-ciphertext security and side-channel defences later made it a standard component. Random self-reduction remains the first step in proofs for DL/RSA-type assumptions. - Wikipedia search entry for 随机自归约. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%9A%8F%E6%9C%BA%E8%87%AA%E5%BD%92%E7%BA%A6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Random Self-Reducibility: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Rogue Key Attack
items.text: Attack : Rogue Key Attack (流氓密钥攻击). Simple addition of aggregate public keys Many multisignature or aggregate-signature schemes combine signer public keys by simple arithmetic: PK = PK_1 + PK_2 + … + PK_n in an additive group, or PK = PK_1 · PK_2 · … · PK_n in the multiplicative group used by BLS. The verifier only checks whether the aggregate signature σ is valid under the aggregate public key PK. If key registration does not require proof of possession of the private key, a last-joining attacker can choose its public key so that the aggregate key equals a key it controls. The simplest two-party construction Let the victim’s public key be PK_1 = x_1 G in an additive group, or g^{x_1} in a multiplicative group, and let the attacker control x_A. In the multiplicative group it registers PK_2 = PK_1^{-1} · g^{x_A}, so PK_1 · PK_2 = g^{x_A}. The attacker knows x_A and can produce an aggregate signature σ = H(m)^{x_A} on any message by itself. The verifier checks it under the aggregate key and sees “both signed”, although the victim never participated. In an additive group the same cancellation is written as PK_2 = x_A G - PK_1, so PK_1 + PK_2 = x_A G. The attack lives in key registration, not inside the signature scheme This is not a forgery of a single BLS or Schnorr signature. It is a key-setup flaw of a multisignature protocol in the “plain public-key model”. The attacker must be able to register its key after seeing the victim’s key; if the key set is fixed before the attack, or registration requires proof of possession, the conditions change. The selling point of a multisignature is that the aggregate behaves like one ordinary public key and signature; that makes key registration a security boundary. As long as the aggregation function treats every public key equally, an attacker can cancel or replace another signer’s contribution with a key of its choice. Several early multisignature schemes fell to such attacks, which is why Bellare-Neven 2006 formalised the “plain public-key model”: a signer only needs a public key, without proving knowledge of the private key at registration; but the scheme itself must be provably secure in that model. 1. Proof of possession (PoP): registration requires a signature on a challenge under the key being registered, proving knowledge of the private key. This changes “choose any key” into “must know the matching secret key”, but not every implementation is sufficient; Bellare-Neven note that the “proof” required by some KOSK models is stronger than a PKCS 10 self-signature. 2. Key-aggregation coefficients: MuSig sets a_i = H(PK_i, L) and aggregates as Σ a_i PK_i. The coefficients depend on the whole key list, so the attacker can no longer cancel PK_1 with a simple PK_2; but the coefficient design itself needs a security proof. Adding an arbitrary hash is not a proof. Bellare-Neven’s MS-BN is provably secure in the plain public-key model, so “PoP is mandatory” is not a general theorem. The correct statement is narrower: simple coefficient-free aggregation combined with PoP-free key registration is exposed; a specific scheme must be judged by its security proof. 1. List every signer public key and determine whether aggregation is simple addition/multiplication or coefficient-based. 2. Check whether key registration requires proof of possession, and whether the proof binds identity, public key and protocol context. 3. Try to register an adversarial key computed from the victim’s key and check whether the aggregate key becomes a key the attacker controls. 4. Check whether verification uses only the aggregate key, or also requires every partial signature. 5. For BLS aggregation, confirm whether proof of possession or coefficient-based aggregation is used; for Schnorr multisignatures, confirm whether MuSig-style coefficients are used. Exchange multisigs, cross-chain bridges, validator aggregate signatures and wallet multisigs all aggregate keys. Treating a multisignature as “several ordinary signatures stapled together” is the quickest way to miss key registration; audit it as a separate attack surface. 1. The attacker cannot register its key after the victim’s key; the key set is fixed in advance or registration order is controlled. 2. Registration requires a real proof of possession, and the proof cannot be replayed or transferred. 3. Aggregation uses coefficients bound to the whole key list, so simple cancellation fails. 4. The scheme has a security proof in the plain public-key model; “it uses BLS” is not enough. 5. Verification requires every partial signature and the aggregate key cannot be replaced by one key. 6. The attacker does not know x_A, or cannot make the aggregate key equal a known key; the construction fails. “A rogue-key attack means BLS is broken” is false; it breaks the key aggregation or registration method. “Adding PoP solves everything” is also false; the PoP implementation, binding and model must all be correct. Key-setup attacks recurred in the early multisignature literature. Bellare and Neven formalised the plain public-key model at CCS 2006 and gave the MS-BN scheme, provably secure in that model. The paper is explicit that rogue-key attacks are a real threat, not a theoretical curiosity. In 2018, Maxwell, Poelstra, Seurin and Wuille introduced MuSig, using key-aggregation coefficients to build a provably secure Schnorr multisignature in the plain public-key model, with applications to Bitcoin. Since then, “simple aggregation without PoP” has been treated as a high-risk configuration, and key registration plus coefficient design have become standard review items. - Wikipedia search entry for 流氓密钥攻击. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E6%B5%81%E6%B0%93%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E6%94%BB%E5%87%BB - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] Rogue Key Attack: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Rompel theorem
items.text: Theorem : OWF Implies Digital Signatures (Rompel 定理). One-way functions suffice for signatures Rompel’s theorem: secure digital signatures exist if and only if one-way functions exist. Necessity is direct: a signature scheme itself yields a one-way function (for example, mapping a public key or message to a hard-to-invert string). The hard direction is sufficiency: given only an arbitrary OWF, construct a signature secure against adaptive chosen-message forgery. Three construction layers 1. OWF → UOWHF. A universal one-way hash function (UOWHF) compresses long messages and makes it hard, given one preimage, to find a different preimage of the same value. Rompel proved that any OWF constructs a UOWHF. UOWHF → one-time signature. The Lamport one-time signature maps each message bit to two secret strings; the public key consists of their hashes. A signature reveals one secret string per bit, and verification re-hashes. One-time signature → many signatures. A Merkle tree puts N one-time public keys at the leaves and the root as the overall public key; each signature carries the leaf key, the one-time signature and the path to the root. Lamport’s algebra Private key s_{i,b}←{0,1}^n, public key pk_{i,b}=H(s_{i,b}). A signature on m is (s_{1,m_1},…,s_{n,m_n}). Verification hashes each revealed string and compares it with pk_{i,m_i}. Signing two different messages under one key leaks both preimages at some differing bit, letting an attacker forge a third message. Public-key encryption needs a trapdoor; signatures do not: Rompel showed signatures can rest on OWF alone. He combined Lamport’s one-time signature, Merkle’s tree and the Naor–Yung UOWHF into a complete EUF-CMA scheme. Hash-based signatures (XMSS, LMS, SPHINCS+) all follow the “one-time signature + tree” path. Rompel’s theorem gives a theoretical guarantee: even without RSA/ECC, an OWF suffices for signatures; in the post-quantum era this matters even more. - Theory: proves OWF is necessary and sufficient for signatures; supplies the reduction skeleton for hash-based signatures. - Engineering: Lamport/Merkle one-time signatures and trees are used in code signing, blockchains and post-quantum signature candidates; practical schemes optimize key/signature size and state management. - Reading: check that a one-time signature is used once, the tree covers all leaves, and the UOWHF resists target collisions. Rompel’s original construction is asymptotic; it is not a replacement for ECDSA, but an existence proof that signatures need no number-theoretic assumption. 1. Very inefficient. A Lamport public key contains 2n hashes and a signature contains n secret strings; a Merkle tree adds log N nodes. Deployment needs optimization or a more compact hash signature. 2. Stateful. A Merkle-tree signer must record used leaves; reusing a leaf breaks one-time security. Stateless schemes (such as SPHINCS+) use different trees/randomization to avoid state. 3. The UOWHF construction is complex. Rompel’s proof was long, and several arguments in the original conference paper were later found flawed; Katz–Koo 2005 gave a complete rewrite. “OWF→UOWHF” is not one line of code. 4. Reduction loss. Tree height, message length and hash-family parameters enter the bound; concrete parameters must be computed for the scheme’s security target. 5. It is not public-key encryption. OWF suffices for signatures but not for public-key encryption; the latter still needs a trapdoor. “Hash signatures are therefore absolutely secure” is false. They rely on OWF/hash collision or second-preimage assumptions and on one-time keys never being reused; implementation errors can still break security. Lamport proposed one-time signatures in 1979; Merkle proposed extending them to many messages with a tree in 1979; Naor–Yung 1989 built signatures from UOWHFs. Rompel 1990 at STOC proved that any OWF constructs a UOWHF, completing the OWF→signature chain. Rompel’s conference paper was influential, but several proof details were never fully published; Katz and Koo gave a complete rewrite in 2005 and noted errors in the original. Hash-based signatures later entered the NIST post-quantum process (SPHINCS+ and others); the route is more realistic today than in 1990. - Wikipedia search entry for Rompel 定理. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Rompel%20%E5%AE%9A%E7%90%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] OWF Implies Digital Signatures: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: OTP & Stream Ciphers: subtopic scope
items.text: Domain : OTP & Stream Ciphers. Stream ciphers encrypt bit by bit or byte by byte with a keystream; the core requirements are unpredictability and never reusing the stream. The one-time pad is the theoretical limit. This page settles the 1 subtopics in this domain that do not yet have their own article: - otp (OTP 与复用灾难): A one-time pad is perfectly secure only when the key is truly random, as long as the message and never reused; one reuse degrades it to an analysable stream cipher. items.title: Cryptanalysis: subtopic scope
items.text: Domain : Cryptanalysis. Cryptanalysis is not guessing a key; it exploits structure, statistical bias, implementation leakage or mathematical weakness to reduce the search space to a computable range. This page settles the 12 subtopics in this domain that do not yet have their own article: - cold-boot (Cold Boot): A cold-boot attack exploits key material that survives briefly in memory after power-off; it shows that keys in RAM are part of the attack surface. - Algebraic Cryptanalysis (代数密码分析): Algebraic cryptanalysis writes a cipher system as low-degree polynomial equations and uses linearisation, XL or SAT solvers to recover the key. - Generic Composition and Search Attacks (通用组合与搜索): Generic composition studies how encryption and a MAC combine into an authenticated-encryption scheme, and which combinations are provably secure in which model. - Integral and Higher-Order Differential Attacks (积分与高阶差分): Integral attacks track bit balance through multi-round integral distinguishers, often combined with higher-order differential and zero-correlation linear distinguishers. - Linear Cryptanalysis (线性密码分析): Linear cryptanalysis finds linear approximations among plaintext, ciphertext and key bits, turning key recovery into a statistical decision by accumulating bias. - Quantum Attacks (量子攻击): Quantum attacks split into Shor-type algorithms that break public-key hard problems and Grover-type algorithms that give a square-root speed-up for symmetric search; their protocol impact differs. - Side-Channel Attacks (侧信道): Side channels exploit timing, power, electromagnetic, cache or fault leakage to bypass mathematical proofs; evaluation must include the implementation environment. - Steganalysis (隐写分析): Steganalysis decides whether a carrier hides a secret, using statistical tests, feature classifiers and carrier-model comparison; detection and robustness trade off. - grover-s-algorithm (Grover's Algorithm): Grover's algorithm gives a square-root speed-up for unstructured search; against a 128-bit symmetric key it reduces brute force from 2^128 to about 2^64. - known-plaintext (Known Plaintext): A known-plaintext attack assumes the adversary holds some plaintext and its ciphertext to recover key structure or build a codebook; it is especially common in classical and codebook eras. - meet-in-the-middle-attack (Meet-in-the-Middle Attack): A meet-in-the-middle attack uses a time-memory trade-off to reduce key search from 2^n to about 2^(n/2), often against double encryption and intermediate block states. - speculative-execution-side-channel (Speculative Execution Side-Channel): Speculative-execution side channels use cache traces left by out-of-order or predicted execution to read data that should not be accessible; Spectre and Meltdown are canonical examples. items.text: Domain : Asymmetric Public-key. Public-key cryptography separates encryption and decryption with a key pair whose halves cannot be derived from each other; security rests on factoring, discrete logarithms or lattice problems. items.title: Digital Signatures: subtopic scope
items.text: Domain : Digital Signatures. Digital signatures bind a private-key-controlled signature to public verification, providing integrity, authentication and non-repudiation; the security model must state which signatures the adversary can obtain. This page settles the 2 subtopics in this domain that do not yet have their own article: - digital-signature-algorithm (Digital Signature Algorithm): DSA is a discrete-log signature scheme; reusing the per-signature random k leaks the private key directly. items.title: Protocols & PKI: subtopic scope
items.text: Domain : Protocols & PKI. Security protocols arrange primitives into message flows among parties, using certificates, identities and freshness to resist replay and man-in-the-middle attacks. Protocol errors are often more damaging than primitive weaknesses. This page settles the 7 subtopics in this domain that do not yet have their own article: - cbor-cose (CBOR 与 COSE 编码): CBOR is a compact binary data model; COSE defines signature, encryption and MAC objects on top of it, common in IoT and FIDO. - dilithium (Dilithium): Dilithium (ML-DSA) is a lattice-based signature standard with larger signatures and public keys but simple verification; it is part of the NIST post-quantum standards. - dtls (DTLS 数据报传输安全): DTLS moves the TLS handshake and record layer onto UDP for datagram security in real-time media and IoT, and must handle loss and replay. - HTTP CONNECT tunnelling (HTTP CONNECT 隧道): HTTP CONNECT lets a client establish an end-to-end tunnel through a proxy that forwards bytes; authentication and a target allow-list are its security boundary. - media session security (媒体会话安全): Media session security concerns SRTP, DTLS-SRTP and key agreement, focusing on confidentiality, integrity and synchronisation of media streams. - network-access-authentication (Network Access Authentication): Network access authentication (EAP/802.1X) checks identity and policy before a device joins the network; credential protection and tunnel method determine its real strength. - tls (TLS 握手): The TLS handshake negotiates algorithms and keys, validates certificates and establishes record-layer keys; configuration, certificate validation and downgrade are main failure points. items.title: Applied Security Engineering: subtopic scope
items.text: Domain : Applied Security Engineering. Applied security concerns deployment in real systems: configuration, keys, protocol implementation, supply chain and user experience; one bad default can cancel a strong algorithm. This page settles the 7 subtopics in this domain that do not yet have their own article: - Information Security Continuous Monitoring (信息安全持续监视): Continuous monitoring turns one-off compliance checks into ongoing observation of assets, vulnerabilities and configuration, with emphasis on measurement and traceability. - Security and Privacy Control Assessment (安全与隐私控制评估): Control assessment checks whether security and privacy controls are deployed as designed and effective, recording evidence and remediation in a closed loop. - Controlled Unclassified Information Protection (受控非密信息保护): Controlled unclassified information protection concerns how sensitive but unclassified data is classified, marked, transmitted and destroyed, often in defence supply-chain compliance. - Digital Identity and Authenticator Assurance (数字身份与认证器保证): Digital identity assurance evaluates identity proofing, authenticator strength and federation assertions separately, answering “why should this identity be trusted”. - format-preserving-encryption (Format-Preserving Encryption): Format-preserving encryption keeps the original format and length after encryption, common for database fields and payment card numbers; its security goals differ from ordinary block-cipher modes. - Systems Security Engineering and Cyber Resiliency (系统安全工程与网络弹性): Systems security engineering builds security and cyber resiliency into requirements, architecture, verification and operations rather than post-launch patching. - security-categorization (信息与系统安全分类): Security categorisation rates information and systems by impact of compromise and selects a control baseline; a wrong categorisation misaligns every later control. items.title: Searchable Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : Searchable Encryption (可搜索加密). Symmetric searchable encryption The owner encrypts documents and builds an encrypted index. A trapdoor T_w for keyword w is derived with a PRF and keys; the server uses T_w to locate ciphertext documents containing w and returns them to the owner, who decrypts. The server neither decrypts documents nor learns w. Public-key PEKS PEKS lets anyone holding the public key create keyword ciphertexts; the receiver gives a gateway a trapdoor, and the gateway tests the keyword with a pairing equation without decrypting the body. It suits multi-sender email and logs. Leakage profile SSE security is described by a leakage function: access pattern (which documents match), search pattern (whether two queries are the same word), result volume and update pattern. Adaptive security lets the adversary choose queries from prior results; forward privacy prevents new inserts from being linked to old queries. Searching in the cloud cannot mean downloading every ciphertext and decrypting it locally; SSE reduces search cost to roughly the number of hits while keeping plaintext keywords from the cloud. PEKS lets a gateway route encrypted mail by keyword without receiving the decryption key; it is one of the earliest searchable-encryption applications and a canonical example of giving a server limited capability. SSE is used in encrypted cloud drives, mail archives, medical-record retrieval, DLP and backups; PEKS is used in encrypted mail gateways and multi-sender logs. Dynamic SSE supports insert/delete; Boolean, range and ordered queries need structures such as OXT; high-privacy settings add ORAM to hide access patterns. Leakage-abuse attacks recover keywords from access patterns, search patterns and result volumes: frequency matching, query recovery and file injection. Encrypting keywords alone is insufficient; the leakage must be defined and accepted. Deletes/inserts in dynamic schemes can break forward privacy; a malicious server can omit or alter results, so verifiable results or integrity are needed; hiding access patterns requires ORAM at a high cost. items.title: Shannon’s Key-Entropy Bound
items.text: Theorem : Key Entropy Bound (香农密钥熵下界). The definition of perfect secrecy For every message m, m' and every ciphertext c with P(M=m) 0 and P(M=m') 0, P(C=c M=m) = P(C=c M=m'). After seeing the ciphertext, the adversary’s posterior distribution over messages is exactly the prior; equivalently, H(M C)=H(M). This is information-theoretic secrecy and imposes no bound on the adversary’s computation. The key-entropy bound Shannon proved: if a system achieves perfect secrecy over a finite message space, then H(K) ≥ H(M). Since H(K) ≤ log K and H(M) can approach log M , the key space must be at least as large as the message space. The one-time pad meets equality: K is as long as M, uniform and independent, C=K⊕M, and K is used once. Proof intuition Fix a ciphertext c. For each possible message m there must be at least one key k mapping m to c. If there are fewer keys than messages, or key entropy is insufficient, some messages become more likely given c and perfect secrecy fails. The formal proof uses key equivocation: with deterministic encryption and independent keys, H(M C)=H(M)+H(K)−H(C); combined with H(C)≤log C , this yields H(K)≥H(M). It gives a hard answer to “can the key be shorter than the message?”: under perfect secrecy, no. It explains the length cost of the one-time pad and why reusing a stream-cipher nonce/key is catastrophic: XORing two ciphertexts cancels the keystream and leaves the XOR of the two messages. Modern block ciphers and public-key encryption protect long messages with short keys because security rests on computational assumptions and the adversary is polynomial-time. Shannon’s bound does not apply to computational security; it constrains unconditional, perfect-secrecy systems. Comparing “AES-256 has a 256-bit key” with “the message is 1 GB” confuses two security models. Perfect secrecy is not integrity. A one-time key can hide a message but cannot stop an adversary from flipping ciphertext bits; active security needs a MAC or authenticated encryption. Shannon’s bound covers confidentiality only. 1. State the goal: perfect secrecy or computational security? 2. For perfect secrecy, compute H(M); key entropy must be at least that value. 3. Check that the key is independent, uniform and one-time; reuse breaks the equality condition. 4. If the message is long, a one-time key does not scale; switch to a computational scheme with explicit assumptions. 5. If integrity is needed, add a MAC; do not claim that OTP provides authentication. - One-time pad: key length, randomness, distribution and destruction are the entire security boundary. - Information-theoretic key agreement: the agreed key entropy must cover the message entropy to be encrypted. - Teaching: use C1⊕C2=M1⊕M2 to demonstrate the disaster of two-time pads. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. It applies only to perfect secrecy. Computational schemes can violate H(K)≥H(M) because they do not require an unbounded adversary. 2. The key must be one-time. Reusing the same keystream gives C1⊕C2=M1⊕M2 and perfect secrecy fails immediately. 3. The key must be independent of the message and correctly distributed. Low-entropy, biased or predictable keys do not satisfy the theorem’s premises. 4. It provides no integrity. OTP can be bit-flipped; an adversary can modify it without recovering the plaintext. 5. Finite message space. Infinite message spaces need a finer rate/capacity analysis; the finite equality cannot be applied directly. 6. Key distribution is the practical bottleneck. The theorem assumes shared keys; it does not solve authentication, storage or destruction. Vernam proposed one-time keystream encryption in 1917; Shannon gave the definition of perfect secrecy and the key-entropy bound in his 1945 confidential report and the 1949 paper “Communication Theory of Secrecy Systems”, proving the necessity of a one-time key. Information-theoretic secrecy remains the language of quantum key distribution, physical-layer security and unconditional-security research. After computational security became dominant, Shannon’s bound serves as a boundary condition: when someone claims “a key shorter than the message, unconditionally secure”, test it against H(K)≥H(M). - Wikipedia search entry for 香农密钥熵下界. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E9%A6%99%E5%86%9C%E5%AF%86%E9%92%A5%E7%86%B5%E4%B8%8B%E7%95%8C - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Key Entropy Bound: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Shoulder Surfing
items.text: Attack : Shoulder Surfing (肩窥). Shoulder surfing is an observation attack: an attacker directly watches, photographs or records a PIN, password, pattern or one-time code as it is entered. It does not break the password algorithm; it lowers the secret's effective entropy. Let the character set have size C and the secret length L. The original entropy is H0=L log2 C. If the attacker sees k exact character positions, the remaining entropy is H_eff=(L-k)log2 C. If the attacker sees the set of k characters but not their positions, the number of remaining strings is C^(L-k)·P(L,k), with entropy (L-k)log2 C+log2 P(L,k). Repeated observations do not simply add independent success. If one observation succeeds with probability p, n independent views approximate P_n=1-(1-p)^n, but real attacks involve learning and angle differences and must be calibrated against experimental baselines. Mobile devices are exposed on transit, in meeting rooms and in cafés. A 6-digit PIN is attacked 10.8% of the time from one observation and 26.5% from multiple observations; a 6-dot pattern is 64.2% and 79.9%; removing feedback lines lowers it to 35.3%/52.1%. “Patterns are more intuitive than PINs” does not mean “more secure”. Shoulder surfing also leaks one-time codes, payment passwords and chat content. For a high-value account, one observation can be enough to reduce the cost of later guessing or brute force. Defense: privacy screens or films, body shielding, entry in trusted settings, biometrics or hardware keys, limited viewing angles, randomized keyboards, hidden feedback lines and short-lived codes. Attack: direct observation, phone video, telephoto lenses, screen reflections and AI video analysis. Defense evaluation should test different angles, distances, phone sizes and hand occlusion, not a single screenshot. Failure: laboratory videos differ from real scenes; angle, light and occlusion; fast user entry; limited observer memory; multi-factor authentication makes a single password leak insufficient; but cameras and slow motion amplify it. items.title: Shoup’s Generic Group Bound
items.text: Theorem : Shoup's Generic Group Bound (Shoup 通用界). The generic group model In the generic group model (GGM), group elements are not readable integers or rational points; they are random encodings σ(g). An algorithm may do only three things: apply group operations to known elements, test whether two encodings are equal, and receive challenge encodings. It cannot exploit special properties of a concrete group, such as the algebraic structure of finite-field elements or the coordinate equations of an elliptic curve. Shoup’s bound Let the group have prime order p and let the algorithm make m group operations, with challenges σ(g) and σ(g^x). Shoup proved Pr[A(p, σ(g), σ(g^x)) = x] ≤ (m+2)^2/(2p) + 1/p. The proof idea: a simulator maintains an encoding table and a list of linear polynomials aX+b; each group operation corresponds to polynomial addition. If two distinct polynomials receive the same random encoding, the algorithm may “accidentally” distinguish them; the collision probability is controlled by (m+2)^2/(2p). Without a collision, every encoding the algorithm sees is independent of x, so it cannot guess x with probability above 1/p. From probability to operation lower bound For non-negligible success, (m+2)^2/(2p) must reach a constant, so m=Ω(√p). Every generic algorithm for discrete logarithm therefore needs Ω(√p) group operations. This matches baby-step giant-step and Pollard rho up to constants; generic attacks are asymptotically optimal in such groups. In elliptic-curve groups there is no known non-generic discrete-log algorithm; the best attacks are Pollard rho, about √p group operations. Shoup’s bound says that as long as an algorithm does not exploit the special algebraic structure of curve coordinates, √p is a hard lower bound. This is why a 256-bit curve gives about 128-bit security: p≈2^256 and √p≈2^128. The GGM is a model, not a theorem about every algorithm. Index calculus over F_p^ exploits field algebra and runs in subexponential time, bypassing the GGM. Shoup’s bound also does not rule out special attacks on a particular curve, pairing attacks or quantum attacks. Treating a GGM lower bound as “DLP is hard in every group” is a common misreading. A GGM bound measures the cost of generic attacks, not the cost of the best attack. Curve selection must also check that the curve is in a security standard, resists pairing/twist security issues, has a suitable CM discriminant and was generated with trustworthy parameters. 1. State the model: does the algorithm use only group operations and equality tests? 2. Give the group order p and query count m; substitute into (m+2)^2/(2p)+1/p. 3. Convert the probability bound into an operation lower bound: m=Ω(√p). 4. Compare with known upper bounds: do BSGS/Pollard match up to constants? 5. State which algorithm classes are excluded: index calculus, special-curve attacks, quantum algorithms. - Elliptic-curve parameter selection: estimate generic attack cost by √p. - Proving protocol security in the GGM: restrict the adversary to generic algorithms. - Teaching: show why “group operations only” limits an attacker, and when the model assumption fails. 1. Model restriction. Real algorithms can read encodings and exploit field operations, pairings or coordinate equations; none are in the GGM. 2. Counterexamples in concrete groups. Index calculus over F_p^ is subexponential; some special curves have faster attacks. The GGM bound does not apply to them. 3. Preprocessing and multi-party computation. Shoup’s original bound targets online queries; offline preprocessing or precomputed tables change the statement. 4. Meaning of m. The bound counts group operations, not bit operations or memory accesses; different cost models change constants. 5. Quantum algorithms. The GGM is classical; a quantum adversary with superposition queries obtains different bounds, so the classical bound cannot be transplanted. 6. A probability bound is not a security proof. It says generic algorithms have low success; other protocol components can still leak x. Nechaev gave a lower bound for deterministic generic algorithms in 1994; Shoup gave the probabilistic bound at EUROCRYPT 1997, covering discrete logarithm and related problems, and added a method for correcting a faulty Diffie–Hellman oracle. The result became a standard tool for GGM proofs. Elliptic-curve standards (SECG, NIST, Brainpool, GM/T) use √p to estimate generic attack cost. Shoup’s bound therefore entered not only theory but also the practical language of curve-parameter selection. - Wikipedia search entry for Shoup 通用界. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Shoup%20%E9%80%9A%E7%94%A8%E7%95%8C - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Shoup's Generic Group Bound: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Sigma Protocol
items.text: Algorithm : Sigma Protocol (Sigma 协议). A three-move public-coin protocol A Σ-protocol is a three-move interaction between a prover and a verifier: the prover sends a commitment a , the verifier sends a random challenge e , and the prover returns a response z . The verifier checks whether (a,e,z) satisfies the relation. It is normally used to prove “I know a witness w such that (x,w) belongs to an NP relation”. Three properties Completeness: an honest verifier accepts an honest prover. Special soundness: two valid responses z,z' to the same commitment a under different challenges e,e' let one extract a witness. Special honest-verifier zero knowledge (SHVZK): given a challenge e , a simulator can produce (a,z) indistinguishable from a real interaction. Canonical examples The Schnorr protocol proves knowledge of a discrete logarithm; Guillou–Quisquater proves knowledge of a modular square root. After Fiat–Shamir, these protocols become signatures. A Σ-protocol compresses “prove that you know a secret” into three messages with light computation and communication. It is a basic building block of efficient zero-knowledge proofs and is simpler than generic circuit ZK for discrete-logarithm, RSA and lattice relations. Its three properties answer separate questions: can the honest party pass, can a cheater forge, and does the verifier learn anything. Understanding them is necessary to know what a “zero-knowledge proof” actually proves. Schnorr identification and signatures, Bulletproof range proofs, anonymous credentials, ring signatures and knowledge proofs inside MPC are built on Σ-protocols or their composition. Several Σ-protocols can share challenges to build OR, AND and threshold proofs. Deployments usually apply Fiat–Shamir to remove interaction and bind the challenge to the message, session and domain tag. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. SHVZK holds only against an honest verifier; a malicious verifier may choose challenges to extract information and needs a stronger zero-knowledge property or a commitment scheme. A Σ-protocol is not transferable by itself: an interaction transcript cannot simply be shown to a third party. Parallel repetition can raise soundness, but careless composition can break zero knowledge; domain separation and sufficient challenge entropy are also required. It later became the language behind Bulletproofs, PLONK and other modern proof systems, which combine Σ-protocols with polynomial commitments and Fiat–Shamir. - Wikipedia search entry for Sigma 协议. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Sigma%20%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Sigma Protocol: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: SIV Deterministic Authenticated Encryption
items.text: Algorithm : Synthetic IV (SIV 确定性认证加密). Synthetic IV and two keys SIV splits the key K into two halves: K1 drives a PRF/CMAC and K2 drives CTR. It first computes S2V over associated data AD1…ADn and plaintext P to obtain a synthetic IV V, then encrypts P with CTR using V as the initial counter. The output is V C; V is both the counter start and the authentication tag. S2V is not plain CMAC S2V compresses multiple variable-length inputs into one block: it iterates dbl and XOR over the first n−1 inputs; the last input is xorend if at least 128 bits, otherwise doubled, padded and XORed; a final CMAC produces V. This handles multiple AD components without a separate length encoding. Deterministic vs nonce-based Without a nonce, SIV is deterministic: the same key, plaintext and AD produce the same ciphertext, which suits key wrapping. Putting a random nonce into AD yields a nonce-based, misuse-resistant AEAD that retains DAE security under nonce reuse. SIV solves the problem of encrypting safely when no reliable nonce exists. Key wrapping, disk blocks and database fields often lack a unique nonce; ordinary GCM/CBC fails catastrophically on nonce reuse. SIV derives the IV from plaintext and AD, so nonce reuse at most reveals that identical plaintext/AD produced identical ciphertext; it does not leak the CTR keystream. It is also the standard construction for deterministic authenticated encryption (DAE): same input, same output; decryption verifies the tag before releasing plaintext, which makes it natural for key wrapping. SIV is used for key wrapping (AES-SIV commonly uses 256/384/512-bit keys), DNS records and JOSE A128SIV; with a nonce it serves as a misuse-resistant AEAD. Requirements: derive K1 and K2 independently; fix S2V input order and AD domain separation; do not encrypt low-entropy guessable plaintext deterministically without randomization; SIV itself outputs a 128-bit synthetic IV and a fixed tag length. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. SIV security rests on CMAC being a PRF, CTR being IV-based encryption and correct key separation. Nonce reuse does not leak the keystream as in GCM, but deterministic mode reveals that two inputs are identical; low-entropy plaintext can be enumerated and verified. Implementation boundaries: implement doubling and padding correctly; verify V before decrypting or releasing plaintext; do not treat V as an ordinary public IV and skip verification; key wrapping must resist downgrade and key-separation errors. SIV was proposed by Rogaway and Shrimpton at EUROCRYPT 2006 as a provably secure treatment of key wrapping; Harkins specified AES-SIV in RFC 5297 in 2008. It is not AES-GCM-SIV: RFC 8452 defines a different nonce-based construction. SIV later appeared in JOSE A128SIV/A256SIV algorithms, but never became a mainstream TLS suite. - Wikipedia search entry for SIV 确定性认证加密. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=SIV%20%E7%A1%AE%E5%AE%9A%E6%80%A7%E8%AE%A4%E8%AF%81%E5%8A%A0%E5%AF%86 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Synthetic IV: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Spartan
items.text: Algorithm : Spartan (Spartan 证明系统). Transparent R1CS proofs Spartan targets R1CS: it encodes the circuit as a low-degree polynomial and runs a sum-check protocol. The prover first makes a one-time “computation commitment” to the circuit description, turning the R1CS matrices into multilinear polynomials that can be opened efficiently; the verifier then checks in sublinear time. It needs no trusted setup: all public parameters are publicly verifiable and there is no toxic waste. Proof size ranges from about O(log² n) to O(√n) , verification is O(n^{1-1/c}) , and the prover runs in O(n) . Spartan was the first transparent zk-SNARK with sublinear verification for arbitrary R1CS and a time-optimal prover. It combines “no ceremony” with “the verifier need not recompute the whole circuit”, filling the gap between Bulletproofs (linear verification) and Groth16 (trusted setup). For settings that cannot run a trusted setup but need moderately large circuits, Spartan is an attractive compromise. Spartan’s Rust library is used for R1CS proofs, verifiable state transitions and recursive-proof research; its sum-check plus polynomial-commitment framework influenced later transparent proof systems. It suits transparent-parameter settings that can tolerate larger proofs than Groth16, not applications that minimize on-chain footprint. Spartan’s proof and verification are not constant: the verifier still does sublinear work and proofs are larger than Groth16. It relies on discrete logarithms, polynomial commitments and the random-oracle model, and is not post-quantum. The computation commitment needs a one-time O(n) preprocessing; frequent circuit changes repeat that cost. items.title: Strong Unforgeability (SUF-CMA)
items.text: Theorem : SUF-CMA Security (强不可伪造). The game definition A signature scheme consists of Gen, Sign and Verify. The challenger generates (pk,sk), gives pk to an adversary A, and lets A query Sign(sk,·). Let Q be the set of (m_i,σ_i) pairs returned by the oracle. A outputs (m ,σ ). EUF-CMA: A wins if m was never queried and Verify(pk,m ,σ )=1. SUF-CMA: A wins if (m ,σ ) ∉ Q and Verify(pk,m ,σ )=1. Even if m was queried, a different valid signature still counts as a forgery. The advantage is Adv^{SUF-CMA}_{SIG}(A)=Pr[A wins]; the scheme is SUF-CMA secure if it is negligible for every PPT A. Why Q must record complete signatures If Q recorded only messages, an adversary who receives a signature σ on m could output a different valid signature σ′ on m and be misclassified as “m was never queried”. SUF-CMA distinguishes σ from σ′: the elements of Q are (m,σ) pairs, not a set of messages. Relation to EUF-CMA SUF-CMA ⇒ EUF-CMA: a forgery on a new message also violates SUF-CMA. The converse fails: there are EUF-CMA secure schemes that are re-randomisable or malleable. EUF-CMA only forbids a forgery on a new message; it allows an adversary who receives a signature on m to output another valid signature on m. SUF-CMA treats such a signature transformation as a break. For signcryption, authenticated encryption, group signatures and some CCA constructions, uniqueness/non-malleability of signatures is needed in the security proof. If Sign is deterministic and Verify accepts only one encoding, no second valid signature on the same message exists, so SUF-CMA and EUF-CMA coincide. Randomised signatures need not: both (r,s) and (r,n-s) verify in ECDSA, so without canonicalisation it is not SUF-CMA. A protocol must check not only “the signature is valid” but also canonicalisation, replay protection and unique encoding. Treating the high-s variant of ECDSA as “another signature” can break deduplication, tickets and signature aggregation. 1. Write down the probabilistic algorithms and verification equation. 2. Define Q as the complete set of (m,σ) pairs returned by the oracle, not just the queried messages. 3. Let the adversary output (m ,σ ); check Verify=1 and (m ,σ )∉Q. 4. For randomised signatures, check for re-randomisation or malleability; for deterministic signatures, check whether verification accepts multiple encodings. 5. When SUF-CMA is required, use a strongly unforgeable construction, canonical encoding, or an explicit signature-uniqueness check. Signcryption, CCA-secure hybrid encryption, group signatures, licence/ticket deduplication, and blockchain transaction signatures. 1. SUF-CMA does not prevent key leakage, side channels or implementation errors; it is only a signature-forgery game. 2. If verification accepts multiple encodings, a mathematically unique signature can become several valid strings at the protocol layer. 3. Uncanonicalised ECDSA has the (r,n-s) transformation; some deployments enforce a low-s rule, but this is not every implementation’s default. 4. A randomised scheme may be EUF-CMA secure and still re-randomisable; SUF-CMA must be proved separately. 5. Strong unforgeability does not provide anonymity, unlinkability or non-repudiation; those are separate goals. 6. A proof in the ROM or standard model does not automatically transfer to a concrete implementation. SUF-CMA is a definition, not a property label for an algorithm; calling a scheme SUF-CMA requires the concrete scheme, verification rules and a proof or assumption. Goldwasser, Micali and Rivest gave the definition of existential unforgeability under adaptive chosen-message attacks in 1988 and established a hierarchy of signature security. That definition only requires that the adversary cannot forge a signature on a “new message”. Later work on signcryption and strong signatures added “a new signature on the same message” to the attack target, yielding SUF-CMA/sEUF-CMA. In 2006 Boneh, Shen and Waters gave a strongly unforgeable construction based on CDH, showing that strong security need not rely on stronger assumptions such as Strong-RSA or Strong-DH. Deterministic signatures such as EdDSA are naturally close to strong unforgeability; ECDSA needs low-s canonicalisation; randomised schemes such as RSA-PSS require a separate analysis. Protocol designers should write signature-encoding uniqueness into the specification instead of relying on the mathematical definition alone. - Wikipedia search entry for 强不可伪造. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E5%BC%BA%E4%B8%8D%E5%8F%AF%E4%BC%AA%E9%80%A0 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] SUF-CMA Security: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: TFHE
items.text: Algorithm : Fully Homomorphic Encryption over the Torus (TFHE 全同态加密). Fully homomorphic encryption over the torus TFHE is a fully homomorphic encryption scheme defined over the torus, built on LWE/RLWE and the external product with GSW. Its most basic mode is gate bootstrapping: every binary gate performs a bootstrap that refreshes noise, enabling arbitrary-depth Boolean circuits. TFHE also offers a leveled mode that packs data and evaluates lookup tables and arithmetic functions efficiently; circuit bootstrapping converts LWE ciphertexts into low-noise RingGSW ciphertexts, making the leveled mode composable. TFHE reduced bootstrapping from tens of seconds per level to about 13 ms per gate with a 16 MB bootstrapping key, making FHE over arbitrary Boolean circuits practical on general CPUs for the first time. Its strengths are low latency, gate-level programmability, lookup tables and automata; it is attractive for private set intersection, encrypted database queries and private ML inference on small circuits. TFHE is used for encrypted database queries, privacy-preserving machine-learning inference, confidential smart contracts on blockchains, and MPC/outsourced computation that needs arbitrary Boolean circuits. It suits Boolean and small arithmetic circuits; for huge matrix multiplications or deep neural networks, parameters, key size and noise management remain bottlenecks. TFHE ciphertexts and bootstrapping keys are still large; every gate needs a bootstrap, so throughput is far below plaintext computation. Parameter selection must trade security, noise and performance, and wrong parameters can leak the key. Security relies on LWE, not information-theoretic guarantees; implementations need constant-time sampling, correct distributions and side-channel protection. An open-source library being usable is not the same as being audited. T_K: M → C；T_K^{-1}: C → M；Correctness: D_K(E_K(M)) = M； K = k. The paper reduced FHEW bootstrapping from 690 ms to 13 ms and the bootstrapping key from 1 GB to 16 MB. It became one of the main FHE families, complementing BFV/BGV for exact arithmetic and CKKS for approximate floating-point computation. items.title: Tight Reduction
items.text: Theorem : Tight Reduction (紧致归约). A reduction turns “break the scheme” into “solve the assumption” A tight reduction does not prove a scheme secure directly. It proves: if a polynomial-time adversary A breaks the scheme with advantage ε, then a polynomial-time algorithm B solves the underlying assumption with advantage about ε/ℓ(k). With simulation error ε_sim, Adv_scheme(A) ≤ ℓ(k) · Adv_assump(B) + ε_sim. The factor ℓ(k) is the security loss. The reduction is tight when ℓ=1 or a constant; it is loose when ℓ=q_s (signing queries), the number of users, or the number of hash queries. A game chain splits one large jump Insert G1,…,Gt−1 between the real game G0 and the assumption game Gt. The triangle inequality gives Pr[G0]−Pr[Gt] ≤ Σ_{i=1}^{t} Pr[Gi−1]−Pr[Gi] . Each step replaces one component, and a reduction turns “distinguish an adjacent pair” back into “solve one assumption”. The hybrid argument is the special case; tightness requires that the total loss not grow with the number of queries. Where the loss comes from Four common sources are random-oracle programming (each query may fail), rewinding, abort (the reduction guesses which query will be forged), and multi-user or multi-instance reductions. Each converts one adversary success into a smaller assumption advantage. A tightness analysis identifies these losses and proves either that they cancel or that they cannot. Suppose the target is 128-bit security. If the reduction loses q_s=2^40, the underlying assumption must provide about 168-bit security for the scheme to reach 128 bits; this changes group sizes, modulus lengths and performance. Multi-user settings are worse: if ℓ equals the number of users, deploying 2^20 users loses 20 bits. An asymptotic proof only says “polynomial reduction”; it does not give parameters. Concrete security substitutes adversary time, query counts, success probability and reduction time. A tight reduction makes the concrete bound close to the assumption itself; it cannot turn a weak assumption into a strong one, nor replace implementation review. Coron 2000 and Bader–Jäger–Li–Schäge 2015 used meta-reductions to show that some schemes cannot have fully tight reductions from single-user to multi-user settings, or from very general non-interactive assumptions. “All losses can be removed” is therefore the wrong expectation; the right practice is to prove which losses cancel and state which lower bounds remain. 1. State the assumption: RSA inversion, CDH, DDH, OWF or PRF. 2. Describe the reduction B: how it simulates A’s view, when it aborts, and how it extracts the assumption solution from A’s output. 3. Compute the loss: programming failures, abort probability, rewinding count and number of users. 4. Plug in concrete parameters: use ε_scheme ≤ ℓ·ε_assump to derive the required assumption strength. 5. Check time: B must run in A’s time plus polynomial overhead; an exponential B makes the bound useless. When a text says “secure”, ask: single-user or multi-user? What is the loss factor? Does the reduction actually reach the assumption? “Reduces to CDH” without a loss statement is usually insufficient for concrete parameter selection. 1. The reduction is not polynomial-time. If B enumerates 2^n candidates, an advantage bound exists but is unusable. 2. The simulated view is distinguishable. If B cannot simulate the challenge, random oracle or signatures seen by A, A’s advantage does not transfer. 3. The loss factor is ignored. Treating 128 bits as 128 bits when ℓ=q_s is a parameter-selection error. 4. The assumption is weakened. A tight reduction to DDH still assumes DDH; ℓ=1 does not make DDH true. 5. Multi-user lower bounds. Results of Bader et al. show that some single-user-to-multi-user losses cannot be fully removed; one cannot claim “fully tight”. “A tight reduction proves the scheme is absolutely secure” is false. It only says the ratio between scheme and assumption advantages is constant; a broken assumption, implementation leak or bad randomness still breaks the scheme. Bellare–Rogaway brought “concrete security” into provable security in the 1990s: not only polynomial time, but explicit relations among query counts and success probabilities. Coron’s 2000 tighter proof for Full Domain Hash showed that a better simulation can reduce the loss for the same scheme. Bader, Jäger, Li and Schäge used a new meta-reduction in 2015/2016 to prove that some multi-user losses cannot be removed, and to give lower tightness bounds for non-interactive assumptions. Tightness became not only a proof technique but also a “when it is impossible” theorem. - Wikipedia search entry for 紧致归约. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=%E7%B4%A7%E8%87%B4%E5%BD%92%E7%BA%A6 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\Pr[\mathrm{Bad}_A(\lambda)]\le \varepsilon(\lambda)\] Tight Reduction: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: TLCP Transport Layer Cryptography Protocol
items.text: Protocol : TLCP (TLCP 国密 TLS). Record layer and handshake TLCP defines a record layer, a handshake protocol family and key calculation. The record layer fragments, MACs and encrypts upper-layer data; the handshake negotiates the version, cipher suite, certificates and keys. It follows TLS’s layered design, but its cipher suites and certificate system are national. National cipher suites The standard lists ECDHE_SM4_CBC_SM3, ECDHE_SM4_GCM_SM3, ECC_SM4_CBC_SM3 and ECC_SM4_GCM_SM3, plus IBSDH, IBC and RSA variants. Key exchange uses SM2 in ECC/ECDHE modes (or RSA/IBC); the record layer uses SM4-CBC or SM4-GCM; integrity and the PRF use SM3. Dual certificates TLCP separates a signing certificate from an encryption certificate: the signing certificate proves identity, while the encryption certificate participates in key exchange and encryption. This dual-certificate system is the most visible difference from ordinary single-certificate TLS deployments. TLCP solves the problem of bringing national algorithms into the TLS ecosystem. It combines SM2, SM3 and SM4 into an interoperable transport protocol, so browsers, VPN gateways, government systems and financial terminals can negotiate national cipher suites inside one framework. Without TLCP, SM2, SM3 and SM4 would remain separate algorithms. With it, certificates, handshakes, key derivation, record protection and alerts form a complete chain. It is used in SSL VPN gateways, national-cipher browsers, government clouds, financial networks and trusted-computing systems. Deployments usually need a dual-certificate CA, SM2 certificate chains, SM3 signatures and SM4-GCM/CBC cryptographic modules. Read this entry carefully: TLCP is not “TLS 1.3 with SM algorithms swapped in”. Its handshake and cipher-suite definitions are its own, and ordinary TLS endpoints usually cannot interoperate without both sides supporting TLCP or a protocol gateway. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. TLCP’s security boundary is not the algorithm alone but protocol configuration and implementation: CBC suites need constant-time MAC and padding checks, GCM suites need nonce uniqueness, dual-certificate chains must bind signing and encryption certificates correctly, and downgrade, version rollback, certificate substitution and side channels must be handled. It is not “secure by default”: changing algorithms while keeping weak randomness, broken certificate validation or old-version fallback still leaves the link vulnerable. TLCP’s predecessor was GM/T 0024-2014, the SSL VPN specification published in February 2014. It built on a TLS 1.1 framework, added ECC/IBC authentication and key exchange, and redefined national cipher suites. In April 2020, GB/T 38636-2020, Transport Layer Cryptography Protocol (TLCP), was published and took effect in November 2020, turning the industry standard into a national standard. The 2023 revision of GM/T 0024 added Hello extensions; TLCP and TLS 1.3 remain different protocols. - Wikipedia search entry for TLCP 国密 TLS. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=TLCP%20%E5%9B%BD%E5%AF%86%20TLS - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\Pi}_A(\lambda)\le n\cdot\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{prf}}_F(\lambda)+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{aead}}(\lambda)\] TLCP: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Trivium Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : Trivium (Trivium 流密码). A 288-bit state in three NLFSRs Trivium has a 288-bit state split into three nonlinear feedback shift registers A, B and C of lengths 93, 84 and 111. The 80-bit key is loaded into the first 80 bits of A, the 80-bit IV into the first 80 bits of B, the last three bits of C are set to 1, and the remaining bits are zero. Three bits updated per clock Each clock computes t1 = s66 ⊕ s93 ⊕ s91·s92 ⊕ s171 t2 = s162 ⊕ s177 ⊕ s175·s176 ⊕ s264 t3 = s243 ⊕ s288 ⊕ s286·s287 ⊕ s69 The three new bits shift into the heads of A, B and C while the other bits shift right; the output bit is z = t1 ⊕ t2 ⊕ t3. The registers are connected end to end, so each register feeds another. 1152 initialization clocks After loading, the cipher runs 4×288 = 1152 blank clocks and discards the output, diffusing the key and IV through all 288 bits. Only then does it produce keystream, up to 2^64 bits for one key/IV pair. Trivium targets minimal hardware area: 288 flip-flops, a few AND and XOR gates, no S-box, lookup table or large memory. It is an eSTREAM hardware-portfolio member and an ISO/IEC 29192-3 lightweight stream-cipher standard, suitable for RFID, sensors and gate-count-limited embedded chips. Software can use bitslicing or 64-way parallelism for respectable throughput, but hardware is its main home. Compared with AES-CTR, Trivium is far smaller and lower-power, at the cost of one output bit per clock and a long initialization. Trivium serves lightweight IoT links, RFID and sensor hardware crypto cores, and data-stream encryption on constrained devices; ISO/IEC 29192-3 standardizes its keystream generator. It provides confidentiality only, so a MAC or AEAD layer is required for integrity. On the software side it is a standard cryptanalysis benchmark: cube attacks, guess-and-determine attacks and algebraic side-channel analysis all use Trivium because its structure is simple, its rounds are adjustable and its state can be fully modeled. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. Trivium security depends on the full 1152-clock initialization. Published attacks mostly target reduced rounds, such as cube attacks on 784 or 799 rounds and guess-and-determine attacks on reduced initialization; no practical key recovery is public for the full 1152 rounds, but reduced-round analysis is not permission to cut initialization. A synchronous stream cipher requires a unique IV; reusing the same key/IV directly exposes plaintext XOR. Trivium has no built-in authentication, and the 2^64-bit keystream limit is a hard boundary. Physical implementations also need side-channel defense: IET 2024 algebraic side-channel analysis recovers the full 288-bit state from a single power trace on 8/16/32-bit microcontrollers in a short time; ASIC implementations were not broken in that leakage model, but hardware is not automatically safe. Masking, dual-rail logic and power balancing remain necessary. De Cannière and Preneel designed Trivium in 2005, submitted it to eSTREAM and reached the hardware portfolio; it became a member of the final eSTREAM portfolio in 2008. ISO/IEC 29192-3 standardized it alongside Enocoro in 2012. It has since become a standard object of study for lightweight stream ciphers and cube attacks. - Wikipedia search entry for Trivium 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Trivium%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] Trivium: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: VENONA Cryptanalysis
items.text: Attack : VENONA Cryptanalysis (VENONA 破译). Codebook plus one-time pad Soviet trade, diplomatic and intelligence messages were looked up in a codebook to obtain x_i, then superenciphered with a one-time-pad stream k_i by digitwise addition modulo 10: c_i=(x_i+k_i) mod 10. If k_i is truly random, used once and as long as x_i, the ciphertext is perfectly secret about the message; VENONA’s opening was not the algorithm but reuse of pad pages. Reuse and depth When two messages reuse the same page: c_i⊖c_i′=(x_i⊖x_i′) mod 10. The mask cancels, leaving differences between two codebook groups. More duplicate pages and longer messages give more depth; codebook frequency, known fragments and English/Russian cribs then recover group meanings and translations. VENONA shows that the security condition of a one-time pad is non-reuse. It turns “key reuse” from an abstract prohibition into an operational case: once reused, the OTP degenerates into a statistically analyzable running-key problem. JN-25’s additive book was reused by design; VENONA’s OTP should have been used once but about 35,000 duplicate pages created depth. Their institutional settings and failure modes differ, and both should not be described as “additive-book reuse”. 1. Find duplicate pages by matching ciphertext sequences at the same positions. 2. Align messages and subtract digitwise to obtain codebook differences. 3. Recover groups with depth, frequency and cribs. 4. Look up the codebook to obtain plaintext; use language guesses for unresolved fragments. 5. Record coverage and translation confidence. Do not present a partial decrypt as the full text; do not ignore codebook changes and copying errors; do not claim the OTP algorithm itself was broken. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. 1. Correct OTP use is unbreakable: truly random, non-reused, message-length keys defeat VENONA methods. 2. Duplicate pages are rare: about 35,000 duplicated pages are still a minority of huge traffic, and only part of the messages can be read. 3. Codebook changes or compilation errors produce systematic misreads. 4. Translation bottleneck: even recovered groups can be misread in names, abbreviations and Russian grammar; a partial decrypt is not the full text. In February 1943 the U.S. Army Signal Intelligence Service began the secret program later codenamed VENONA; depth clues appeared in 1945, and Meredith Gardner read the first message in February 1946; the project ran until October 1980. From July 1995, six releases made about 3,000 translations public. Public records confirm about 35,000 duplicate key pages, but not every duplicate page was exploitable. This entry covers the mechanism, scale and public timeline; it does not turn intelligence-history conclusions into cryptographic theorems. - Wikipedia search entry for VENONA 破译. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=VENONA%20%E7%A0%B4%E8%AF%91 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[\mathrm{Adv}^{\mathrm{attack}}_A(\lambda)=\Pr[\mathrm{Game}_A(\lambda)=1]-\frac12\] VENONA Cryptanalysis: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: Whirlpool 512-bit hash
items.text: Algorithm : Whirlpool (Whirlpool 散列). 512-bit block, 512-bit key, 8×8 state Whirlpool's compression function is a dedicated 512-bit block cipher W: 512-bit block, 512-bit key, 10 rounds. The state is an 8×8 matrix of GF(2^8) bytes; each round applies byte substitution SB, column shift SC, row mixing MR and round-key addition AK. The key schedule reuses the same round functions with key-schedule constants. Miyaguchi–Preneel and Merkle–Damgård Messages are processed in 512-bit blocks with the Miyaguchi–Preneel construction: H_i = W_{H_{i-1}}(M_i) ⊕ M_i ⊕ H_{i-1} The previous chaining value is both the block-cipher key and a feed-forward term; the message block is both the plaintext and a feed-forward term. The outer iteration is Merkle–Damgård, with a message-length bound of 2^256 bits and a 512-bit digest. Whirlpool uses an AES-like wide-trail design: SB, SC and MR provide byte-level nonlinearity and row/column diffusion over the 8×8 state, and 10 rounds spread a one-byte difference across the whole state. A 512-bit digest pushes the birthday bound to 2^256, a comfortable margin over 256-bit hashes. It avoids 64-bit multiplication, so both 8-bit microcontrollers and 64-bit CPUs can implement it; that portability is what NESSIE valued. The round function is table lookups and XORs. An 8-bit implementation can keep the 8×8 state in registers; a 64-bit implementation packs eight columns into eight 64-bit words and processes a column at a time. It has neither SHA-2's 32/64-bit addition chain nor SHA-3's Keccak permutation, so its performance curve resembles AES. Whirlpool is one of the hashes selected by NESSIE 2003 and Dedicated Hash-Function 7 in ISO/IEC 10118-3; the 2018 fourth edition still includes it. It appears in “512-bit hash beyond SHA-2” lists, for legacy systems that need a long digest without moving to SHA-3's new construction. It can appear in digital signatures, file-integrity manifests and password-derivation chains for disk encryption; those uses value the 512-bit output and mature implementations, not novelty. A new protocol without a compatibility constraint normally chooses SHA-512 or SHA3-512 instead. Whirlpool's outer Merkle–Damgård iteration permits length extension: anyone who knows H(M) can compute H(M pad X) without a key. It therefore cannot serve as a MAC by itself; wrap it in HMAC or use a keyed construction. As a 512-bit hash its birthday bound is 2^256. That is not “post-quantum security”: Grover-style search reduces an ideal 512-bit hash to roughly the square root of its security level. No practical collision is known on all 10 rounds, but reduced-round distinguishers show the round function is not invulnerable. Whirlpool provides neither authenticated encryption nor input hiding; it only makes the compressed digest hard to collide. Truncating the digest directly lowers collision cost, so a 512-bit output should not be cut below 256 bits for collision-resistant use. Paulo Barreto and Vincent Rijmen designed Whirlpool and submitted it to NESSIE in 2000. Whirlpool-T in 2001 adjusted the diffusion matrix; the 2003 final revision changed the S-box and circulant matrix to the current 10-round form. It entered the NESSIE 2003 portfolio, then ISO/IEC 10118-3, and remained in the 2018 fourth edition. Whirlpool-0 used a randomly generated S-box, Whirlpool-T switched to a structured S-box and adjusted MR, and the final version changed both the S-box and circulant matrix. The three versions produce incompatible digests; an upgrade must recompute every historical digest. - Wikipedia search entry for Whirlpool 散列. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=Whirlpool%20%E6%95%A3%E5%88%97 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[h=H(M),\quad H:\{0,1\}^{ }\to\{0,1\}^{n}\] Whirlpool: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion. items.title: XSalsa20 Stream Cipher
items.text: Algorithm : XSalsa20 (XSalsa20 流密码). Salsa20’s 512-bit state Salsa20 arranges a 256-bit key, a 64-bit nonce, a 64-bit block counter and 128 bits of constants into sixteen 32-bit words in a 4×4 matrix. Twenty ARX rounds (32-bit addition, rotation and XOR) are followed by adding the input back, producing a 64-byte keystream block. There are no S-boxes or secret-index table lookups. XSalsa20 derives a subkey first XSalsa20 extends the nonce to 192 bits. It first runs HSalsa20 with the key and the first 128 nonce bits. HSalsa20 shares the 20-round core but omits the final input addition and selects eight words to form a 256-bit subkey; standard Salsa20/20 then uses that subkey, the remaining 64 nonce bits and a 64-bit block counter to generate the stream. Why the longer nonce matters With a 64-bit nonce, random nonces under one key collide around 2^32 messages; a 192-bit nonce pushes that risk to about 2^96 messages. For protocols that choose a fresh random nonce per message, this is simpler than maintaining a global counter. XSalsa20 is about nonce management, not a new round function. NaCl crypto_box uses X25519 for key agreement, XSalsa20 for encryption and Poly1305 for authentication; each message can carry an independent random 192-bit nonce without a cross-session counter. It keeps Salsa20’s speed and ARX side-channel behavior, adding only one HSalsa20 subkey derivation whose cost is below one Salsa20 output block. The SKEW 2011 paper proves that a fast attack on XSalsa20 converts into an attack on Salsa20, so its security reduces to Salsa20. libsodium exposes XSalsa20/20 as crypto_stream and crypto_stream_xor; NaCl crypto_box combines XSalsa20 with Poly1305; many language bindings and message-encryption libraries follow that combination. It fits protocols that want long random nonces and high software speed. It is not a TLS cipher suite; TLS 1.3 uses ChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM, while XSalsa20 lives mainly in the NaCl ecosystem and custom protocols. A shared name may belong to an algorithm, standard, event, person or term; this entry is responsible only for its catalogue binding and does not absorb adjacent records. If versions, regions or institutions define the name differently, the differences stay side by side. XSalsa20 provides confidentiality only, not integrity; it must be paired with Poly1305 or a higher-level AEAD. The nonce must still be unique: reusing the same key/nonce reproduces the same keystream, and ciphertext XOR reveals plaintext XOR. A 192-bit nonce lowers the collision probability to an acceptable level; it does not permit reuse. The 64-bit block counter bounds one key/nonce pair to about 2^64 blocks of 64 bytes; after that the counter wraps and the key or nonce must change. ARX software resists timing attacks, but hardware power and electromagnetic analysis can still recover state; HSalsa20 is not a general KDF, and the same key should not be reused across unrelated purposes. Bernstein designed Salsa20 in 2005, and Salsa20/12 entered the eSTREAM software portfolio. In 2008 he proposed XSalsa20, extending the nonce to 192 bits with a security reduction; NaCl then combined XSalsa20 with Poly1305 in crypto_box, and libsodium continued the construction. It is a key node in ARX stream ciphers and in random-nonce design. - Wikipedia search entry for XSalsa20 流密码. https://zh.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?search=XSalsa20%20%E6%B5%81%E5%AF%86%E7%A0%81 - Handbook of Applied Cryptography (Menezes, van Oorschot, Vanstone). https://www.cacr.math.uwaterloo.ca/hac/ Formal model and reproduction steps \[C=E_K(P;r),\qquad P=D_K(C)\] XSalsa20: the registered public parameters, key material or randomness, and message are mapped through the stated transformation to an output checked against the registered criterion.
